All the orthodox Fathers press this hard against the Pelagians. Ambrose on Luke 7:9: God calls whom he deigns, and makes devout whom he wills. Augustine, Epistle 107: We know grace is not given to all people, nor according to the merits of the will of those who receive it. In the same letter he adds that those denied this grace often differ by no merit and no will, but share a like condition with those who receive it. Fulgentius, On the Incarnation and Grace, chapter 19: As in fleshly birth the formation of the divine work precedes every will of the one being born, so in spiritual birth, by which we begin to put off the old self, no one can have a good will by his own motion. And chapter 21: If God has not given to a person through his grace, that person can never will to believe in God, because grace does not find this will already there—it works it in the person. So God does not hand out these inward means promiscuously to everyone who might apply Christ’s death to himself. Nor may our opponents claim that God’s giving or withholding of faith springs from human wills resisting or not resisting, since Scripture expressly refers this to God’s good pleasure to pity or not to pity, and the Fathers in plain words shut out any disparity of human wills before grace is received.

source_text: Hactenus de mediis immediatis disputatum est: Ad media horum mediorum descendamus. Christi mors ac meritum habuit in acceptatione Dei ab origine mundi suam efficaciam: Deus tamen sub Vetere Testamento externa applicationis media non omnibus hominibus universim concessit, sed, ut loquitur Psalmista, Verbum suum denunciat Jacobo: non fecit taliter omni nationi, Psal. cxlvii. 19, 20. Et in eandem sententiam Paulus, Act. xiv. 16. Deus praeteritis aetatibus sivit omnes gentes ambulare in viis suis. Prosper hoc idem annotavit, Non est, inquit, remotum ab inspectione communi, quot secula, quam innumera hominum millia erroribus suis impietatibusque dimissa, sine ulla veri Dei cognitione defecerint, De lib. arbitr. pag. 225. Et De vocat. Gent. 2, 17, Novi Testamenti tempora respiciens, dicit, Sunt etiam nunc in extremis mundi partibus aliquae nationes, quibus gratia Salvatoris nondum illuxit. Ex quibus sequitur, etiam posita Christi morte, Deum nihilominus haud teneri ratione bonitatis aut justitiae suae media omnibus & singulis providere & offerre, quibus possunt Christum sibi applicare. In Deo enim a facto ad jus optime sequitur argumentum tam affirmando quam negando; Deus hoc facit, ergo juste facit; Deus hoc non facit, ergo nullo jure tenetur ut faciat.
english: So far we have argued about the immediate means. Now we come down to the means of those means. Christ’s death and merit have had their force in God’s acceptance from the world’s beginning. Yet under the Old Testament God did not grant the external means of application to every human being alike. As the Psalmist says, “He declares his word to Jacob; he has not done thus to every nation” (Psalm 147:19–20). Paul speaks the same way: “In past ages God allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways” (Acts 14:16).

Prosper marked the same point: it is not far from ordinary observation, he says, through how many ages countless thousands of people, left to their errors and impieties, have perished without any knowledge of the true God (On Free Choice, page 225). Looking to New Testament times (On the Calling of the Gentiles 2.17), he adds: even now in the farthest parts of the world there are nations on whom the Savior’s grace has not yet shone. From this it follows that even with Christ’s death granted, God is still not bound by his goodness or justice to provide and offer to every person the means by which they can apply Christ to themselves. In God the move from fact to right works both ways: God does this, therefore he does it justly; God does not do this, therefore no right binds him to do it.

source_text: Sed huic argumento occurrunt nonnulli respondendo, Quod Evangelium ubique non praedicetur, causa non tam haec est, quod a Deo non mittantur qui praedicent, quam quod qui mittuntur ire recusent. Sic Corvinus, contra Tilenum, pag. 105. Verum si Deus ratione bonitatis suae & justitiae, quasi ex congruitate quadam, Christi morte supposita, teneretur media applicationis sufficientia omnibus communicare, non sineret quenquam ob incuriam alterius debito beneficio fraudari, praesertim tali, absque quo nulla salus est sperabilis. Imo contradictionem implicat, Deum ex lege ordinaria providere & administrare omnibus haec media ad Christi applicationem spectantia, & quibusdam eadem non administrare, obstante scilicet praedicatorum incuria: Cum ipsa cura praedicatorum non esset annumeranda hisce mediis, sine quibus cognitio & applicatio Christi praedicati haberi nequit. Porro, Si Dei bonitas aut justitia hoc requireret, ut haec media Christi applicandi omnibus administrarentur, proculdubio in aliquibus saltem praedicatoribus hunc animum & hanc curam praedicandi & proferendi Evangelii ad singulas nationes accendisset. Ipse enim est qui operarios pro beneplacito suo novit in messem protrudere. Denique quae incuria praedicatorum in causa fuit, quod ducentis ab hinc annis Evangelium Americanis a nemine fuit praedicatum, quando de hisce nationibus nemo per somnium cogitaverat? Redeundum itaque est ad causam altiorem, nempe liberum Dei beneplacitum in hisce mediis gratificandis, aut negandis, qui per specialem quandam providentiam ea procurat administranda populis, vel non administranda per ministros suos, ut videre licet Actor. xvi. 6 &c. Vetiti sunt loqui verbum Dei in Asia, & tendebant ire in Bithyniam, & non permisit Spiritus, &c. Secundo respondent, eos qui longo tempore gratia Evangelica caruerunt, eam a majoribus suis repudiavisse: & sic posteros merito privari praeconio Evangelii, quod majores illorum contempserunt: Non itaque ad absolutam Dei voluntatem referendum esse, quod quidam salutari luce Evangelii non illustrentur. Sed neque haec bene cohaerent cum istorum placitis. Nam si Deus, ad mortem Christi habito respectu, omnibus hominibus tenetur media salutis sufficienter administrare, parum aequum videtur ut, propter praedicationem verbi temporibus Noachi a majoribus contemptam, Evangelium post multa annorum millia eorundem posteris denegatur. Si enim, non obstante Adami peccato, Christi morte impetratum sit (ex istorum sententia) ut media salutis sufficientia omnibus administrentur, a ratione & aequitate alienum est, hanc legem quasi ordinariam infringere, praetextu peccatorum ab aliis quibuscunque majoribus nostris commissorum. Sicut igitur propter ipsum Adami peccatum Deus juste possit posteris ejus quodvis beneficium spirituale denegare, ita fatemur, ex peccatis aliorum majorum posse quoque Deum occasionem sumere negandi nobis quodvis beneficium gratuitum. Verum si Christi morte, Dei bonitate concurrente, lex stabilita sit de administrandis gratiae mediis; jam sicut propter Adami peccatum, qui gessit in se personam omnium suorum posterorum, Deus non vult hoc suum quasi statutum abrogare, ita propter peccata aliorum, qui minime sustinent hanc communem humani generis personam, multo minus consentaneum est ut posteri hoc beneficio priventur. Frustra igitur ad peccata majorum confugiunt, ut ejus rei negatae rationem reddant, quam virtute mortis Christi ac bonitatis Divinae omnibus & singulis, ex decreto Divino praeparatam atque statuta lege quasi debitam, praefitentur.
english: Some meet this argument by saying the gospel is not preached everywhere less because God fails to send preachers than because those who are sent refuse to go. So Corvinus against Tilenus, page 105. But if God, by his goodness and justice, as if by a kind of congruence, and with Christ’s death supposed, were bound to communicate sufficient means of application to everyone, he would not let anyone be cheated of an owed benefit by another’s carelessness—least of all a benefit without which no salvation can be hoped for. It is even a contradiction to say that by ordinary law God provides and administers to all these means that look to applying Christ, and yet withholds them from some because of the preachers’ neglect—when the very care of the preachers would have to be counted among those means, without which knowledge and application of the Christ who is preached cannot be had.

Further, if God’s goodness or justice required that these means of applying Christ be administered to all, he would without doubt have kindled in at least some preachers the will and care to preach and carry the gospel to every nation. He himself knows how to thrust laborers into the harvest according to his good pleasure. Finally, what preacher-neglect explains that two hundred years ago the gospel was preached by no one among the Americans, when no one had even dreamed those nations existed? We must therefore rise to a higher cause: God’s free good pleasure in granting or denying these means. By a special providence he sees to it that they are administered to peoples, or not administered, through his ministers—as Acts 16:6 and following shows: “They were forbidden to speak the word of God in Asia, and they were intending to go into Bithynia, and the Spirit did not permit them,” and so on.

Second, they answer that those long without evangelical grace had already repudiated it in their ancestors, and so the descendants are rightly stripped of the gospel proclamation their ancestors despised; therefore the fact that some are not lit by the gospel’s saving light should not be referred to God’s absolute will. But this does not hang with their own views. If God, with an eye to Christ’s death, is bound to administer sufficient means of salvation to all people, it is hardly fair that, because ancestors despised the preached word in Noah’s day, the gospel should be denied to their posterity after many thousands of years. If—Adam’s sin notwithstanding—Christ’s death has (on their showing) secured that sufficient means of salvation be administered to all, it is alien to reason and equity to break that quasi-ordinary law on the pretext of sins committed by any other ancestors of ours.

Just as God could justly deny any spiritual benefit to Adam’s posterity because of Adam’s own sin, so we grant that from other ancestors’ sins God may also take occasion to deny us any free benefit. But if by Christ’s death, with God’s goodness concurring, a law has been set about administering the means of grace, then just as God will not abrogate that quasi-statute because of Adam’s sin—who bore in himself the person of all his posterity—so it is far less fitting that posterity be robbed of this benefit because of the sins of others who do not sustain that common person of the human race. They flee in vain to ancestral sins to explain the denial of a thing which, by the virtue of Christ’s death and of divine goodness, they themselves claim was prepared for all and each by divine decree and as if owed by fixed law.

source_text: Tertio respondent, Evangelicam gratiam quibusdam denegari, quia continuis contra legem praevaricationibus indignos sese praestiterunt quibus gratia Divina offeratur. Sed haec responsio sententiae nostrae veritatem magis illustrabit. Nam illud imprimis sumo (quod nemo sanus negabit) quemlibet hominem in statu corruptae naturae Evangelica gratia indignum (si ejus peccata attendantur) sese praestitisse: tum & illud addo, Dignitatem & indignitatem hominum, sive majorem & minorem indignitatem, non esse illam regulam secundum quam Deus procedit in dispensando vel denegando Evangelio sive singularibus personis sive nationibus. Quibus positis, sequetur indignitatem semper reperiri in iis quibus Evangelium negatum, sed in iis etiam quibus conceditur. Habebit ergo haec indignitas naturam circumstantiae, quae semper concomitatur personas quibus datur & quibus non datur Evangelium; sed non habebit rationem causae discriminantis, cur hisce detur, illis non detur Evangelium. Hac igitur in re ad solum placitum Divinae voluntatis est deveniendum, qui facientibus & non-facientibus quod in se est, quando sibi placet auxilia confert, ut loquitur Alvarez, De Auxil. disp. 58. Sed quia haec responsio, quae indignitate hominum gratiam Evangelicam arceri docet, videtur tacite innuere, quosdam dignitate eorundem eandem procurari potuisse, audiamus quid orthodoxi Patres contra Pelagianos in hoc ipso negotio docuerint. Augustinus Epist. 107. pag. 500. ostendit salvificam Christi gratiam non concedi aut negari hominibus secundum hanc regulam majoris aut minoris indignitatis. Brevitatis causa verba non appono. Prosper saepissime hoc inculcat: De vocat. Gent. l. 1. c. 15. Liberatur pars hominum, parte pereunte: & si hoc voluntatum meritis voluerimus adscribere, ut malos neglexisse gratia, bonos autem elegisse videatur, resistet nobis innumerabilium causa populorum, quibus per tot secula nulla caelestis doctrinae annunciatio coruscavit. Nec meliores fuisse illorum posteros possumus dicere, quibus lux orta est, &c. Idem Prosper in Carmine De Ingratis, cap. 12, ostendit hanc fuisse Pelagianorum ipsissimam sententiam, nempe, Quod Deus pro bonitate sua omnes ad gratiam vocare velit, sed quod voluntas nonnullorum, Lumine primo Per vitia oppressa, sit facta indigna secundo, At ille e contra, cap. 14. exempla proferri posse contendit Quae doceant virtute Dei conversa malorum Corda, quibus rei nihil unquam insiderat, & quae Nullum justitiae signum sensumve gerebant. Summa hujus argumenti huc redit, Gratiam Evangelicam non dari hominibus quia digni eadem judicantur, cum nemo dignus tanto munere reperitur; neque negari hominibus quia indigniores caeteris exstiterunt, cum pessimis hoc lumen concessum fuerit, & aliis interim minus depravatis denegatum. Acquiescendum igitur in arcano voluntatis Divinae beneplacito, qui, ut magis splendeat sua misericordia, non regulariter lumen Evangelii concedit bene aut minus male utentibus lumine naturae; sed e contra infideles & negligentes vocat ad seipsum, atque peccatores indignos & ingratos. Atque hinc patet, semper liberum Deo manere, & a bonitate ejus nullo modo alienum esse, dare vel non dare quibusvis hominibus Evangelium aliaque media ad applicationem meritorum Christi necessaria, pro beneplacito voluntatis suae, nulla habita ratione dignitatis aut indignitatis, vel majoris & minoris indignitatis humanae.
english: Third, they answer that evangelical grace is denied to some because by continual law-breaking they have made themselves unworthy of those to whom divine grace should be offered. This reply will only make our position clearer. First I take what no sober mind will deny: every person in corrupted nature has made himself unworthy of evangelical grace, if you attend to his sins. Then I add that human dignity and unworthiness—or greater and lesser unworthiness—is not the rule by which God proceeds in dispensing or denying the gospel to particular persons or to nations. That being so, unworthiness is always found in those denied the gospel, and also in those who receive it. So this unworthiness has the nature of a circumstance that always accompanies both those who get the gospel and those who do not; it does not have the force of a discriminating cause why it is given to these and not to those. In this matter we must come down to the sole pleasure of the divine will, who, when it pleases him, confers helps both on those who do and on those who do not do what is in them—as Alvarez says in On Helps, disputation 58.

But because this reply, which teaches that human unworthiness fences off evangelical grace, seems quietly to hint that some could have procured the same by their dignity, hear what the orthodox Fathers taught the Pelagians on this very point. Augustine, Epistle 107, page 500, shows that Christ’s saving grace is not granted or denied by the rule of greater or lesser unworthiness. For brevity I omit the words. Prosper presses this again and again (On the Calling of the Gentiles, book 1, chapter 15): a part of humankind is set free while a part perishes; and if we ascribe that to the merits of wills, so that grace seems to have neglected the bad and chosen the good, the case of innumerable peoples will rise against us, to whom through so many ages no announcement of heavenly teaching has flashed. Nor can we say that those later ones on whom the light has risen were better, and so on. In the Poem On the Ungrateful, chapter 12, the same Prosper shows that the Pelagians’ own opinion was this: God by his goodness wills to call all to grace, but the will of some, oppressed by vices under the first light, has been made unworthy of the second. Against them, in chapter 14, he contends that examples can be brought of wicked hearts converted by God’s power, hearts in which nothing of the matter had ever settled, and which bore no sign or sense of justice.

The sum of the argument comes to this: evangelical grace is not given because people are judged worthy of it—no one worthy of so great a gift is found—nor is it denied because some have stood more unworthy than the rest, since this light has been granted to the worst and meanwhile denied to others less depraved. We must therefore rest in the secret good pleasure of the divine will, who, that his mercy may shine the more, does not regularly grant the gospel’s light to those who use nature’s light well or less badly, but on the contrary calls the faithless and negligent to himself, and unworthy, ungrateful sinners. From this it is plain that it always remains free for God, and in no way alien to his goodness, to give or not to give to any people whatever the gospel and the other means needed for applying Christ’s merits, according to the good pleasure of his will, with no account taken of dignity or unworthiness, or of greater and lesser human unworthiness.

source_text: Hoc idem probari potest ex incommodis manifestis quibus urgetur sententia contraria. Nam si hoc morte Christi sit universaliter impetratum, ut Deus ex ipso decreto, sive lege quadam congruitatis teneatur, quantum in se est, omnibus & singulis hominibus gratiam Evangelicae praedicationis atque internae sanctificationis concedere, tum sequetur, rationem primariam cur hic de facto fiat particeps utriusque gratiae, ille non fiat, in eo sitam, quod hic obice opposito hanc gratiam repulerit, aut ne offeretur omnino impedierit, ille nec repulerit nec impedierit. Hanc consequentiam non refugiunt adversarii. Nam vocationis Evangelicae & gratiae salutiferae negatae aut concessae discrimen non in meram Dei voluntatem reducunt, sed in conditiones sive dispositiones diversas ex parte hominum consideratas. Sic Corvinus, Contra Tilen. pag. 489. Deus licet ubique verbum crucis non praedicet, omnibus tamen iis illud praedicare paratus est, qui ministerio legis sese debite subjiciunt, hoc est, qui sequuntur lucem legis naturalis etiam in Ethnicorum cordibus vigentis. De donis naturalibus differens, pag. 118. dicit, Deum haec dona gentilibus reliquisse, ut siquidem secundum Dei intentionem istis donis uterentur, ad Deum pro mensura suae cognitionis glorificandum, ad Christum ipsiusque cognitionem ducerentur: contra vero, in sua ignorantia relinquerentur, si veritatem quam habebant in injustitia detinerent. Hic aperte suspendit vocationem Evangelicam ex usu aut abusu donorum naturalium.
english: The same point can be proved from the plain inconveniences that press the contrary view. If by Christ's death it has been universally obtained that God is bound—by the decree itself, or by some law of congruity—to grant, as far as in him lies, to every human being the grace of gospel preaching and of inward sanctification, then the chief reason why one person in fact shares both graces and another does not will lie here: that one has thrust up an obstacle and pushed the grace away, or has blocked it from being offered at all, while the other has neither pushed it away nor blocked it. Our opponents do not shrink from that consequence. They do not reduce the difference between evangelical calling and saving grace denied or granted to God's bare will, but to different conditions or dispositions on the human side. So Corvinus against Tilenus, page 489: though God does not preach the word of the cross everywhere, he is still ready to preach it to all who duly submit themselves to the ministry of the law—that is, who follow the light of the natural law alive even in Gentile hearts. Writing on natural gifts, page 118, he says God left those gifts to the nations so that if they used them according to God's intention, they would be led to glorify God in the measure of their knowledge, and on to Christ and the knowledge of him; but if they held down in injustice the truth they had, they would be left in their ignorance. Here he openly hangs the gospel call on the use or abuse of natural gifts.

source_text: Idem Corvinus internam gratiam vivificantem ita ex ordinaria lege omnibus expositam tuetur, ut ipsum discrimen cur hic de facto particeps talis gratiae evadat, ille non evadat, ad discrimen humanarum voluntatum reducat, non ad beneplacitum Divinum. Imo Certum esse, ait, nullius conversionem praecise a Deo intendi. Verum utcunque haec adblandiantur rationi humanae, tamen contrariantur Scripturae Divinae, & incommodis manifestis obrui possunt. Nam si admittamus vel exteriorem vocationem Evangelicam, vel interiorem & efficacem infusionem gratiae regenerantis, dari & negari pro diversis hominum dispositionibus aut operationibus; Primo sequeretur, liberum arbitrium in statu corrupto, Evangelica luce nondum collustratum, posse adeo bene uti donis suis naturalibus, ut Deus inde secundum legem ordinariam, a bonitate sua sibi dictam, teneatur homini animali spiritualem gratiam impertire. At hoc est contra Apostolum dicentem, Si ex operibus, gratia non est gratia, Rom. xi. 6. Non enim miseratione tribuentis, sed aequitate retribuentis eam acciperemus, ut loquitur Fulgentius De Incarn. & grat. Christi, cap. 18.
english: The same Corvinus so defends inward life-giving grace as laid open to all by an ordinary law that he reduces the very difference why one person in fact shares that grace and another does not to a difference of human wills, not to the divine good pleasure. Indeed he says it is certain that no one's conversion is precisely intended by God. But however much this flatters human reason, it still runs against divine Scripture and can be crushed by plain inconveniences. If we grant that either the outward gospel call, or the inward and effectual infusion of regenerating grace, is given and denied according to different human dispositions or operations, then first it would follow that free choice in the corrupted state, not yet lit by gospel light, can so well use its natural gifts that God is bound—by the ordinary law his own goodness dictates to him—to give spiritual grace to the natural man. That is against the Apostle: if it is from works, grace is no longer grace (Romans 11:6). We would receive it not by the pity of the giver, but by the equity of a repayor, as Fulgentius says in On the Incarnation and Grace of Christ, chapter 18.

source_text: Secundo (quod omnes orthodoxi aversantur) sequeretur etiam praedestinationis & praeteritionis rationem ex hominum diversis qualitatibus, aut actibus esse assignandam. Ratio siquidem praedestinationis, quae est gratiae praeparatio, non potest diversa esse a ratione gratiae, quae est ipsa collatio. Qui igitur gratiae datae aut non datae rationem ab humanis dispositionibus aut operationibus petendam docet, idem praedestinationis & praeteritionis rationem inde petat est necesse. Tertio, sequeretur Deum legi a se positae contravenire, quando ponentibus obicem gratiae hanc gratiam quasi ingerit; quod Paulo factum ipse Apostolus humillime confitetur: quem in flagranti peccato deprehensum, & contra Christum ruentem, ad cognitionem & gratiam Christi Deus misericorditer vocavit. De quo praeclare Fulgentius, De Incarn. & Grat. cap. 18. In quo Dei misericordia nos praeveniat, vel praeveniens quales inveniat, non in quolibet alio, sed in se ipso nobis gentium Magister ostendit, dicens, Qui prius fui blasphemus, &c. Innuit scilicet Pater, omnes mortales esse refractarios, donec gratia praeveniens eos subjugaverit.
english: Second—and every orthodox writer shrinks from this—it would also follow that the reason of predestination and of preterition must be assigned from people's different qualities or acts. For the reason of predestination, which is the preparation of grace, cannot differ from the reason of grace, which is the gift itself. So anyone who teaches that the reason grace is given or withheld must be sought in human dispositions or operations must of necessity seek the reason of predestination and preterition there too. Third, it would follow that God breaks the law he himself set when he as good as forces this grace on those who have put an obstacle in its way—which the Apostle himself most humbly confesses happened to Paul: caught in open sin and rushing against Christ, God mercifully called him to the knowledge and grace of Christ. Fulgentius puts it finely in On the Incarnation and Grace, chapter 18: how God's mercy goes before us, and what sort it finds when it does, the Teacher of the nations shows not in someone else but in himself, saying, I who was formerly a blasphemer, and so on (1 Timothy 1:13). The Father hints that every mortal is refractory until preventing grace has brought him under.

source_text: Quarto, admitte hanc gratiae donationem aut negationem, prout humanae voluntates obicem posuerint aut non posuerint, everteris fere omnia in Conciliis contra Pelagianos definita; quale est illud inprimis in Diospolitano Concilio sancitum contra Pelagium, Fateatur gratiam non dari ex merito, ut vera sit gratia, id est gratis data, per ejus misericordiam qui dixit, MISEREBOR CUIUS MISERTUS FUERO. Dari enim aut non dari gratiam prout quis recte naturalibus donis usus fuerit aut non fuerit, vel (ut alii loquuntur) prout quis fecerit aut non fecerit quod in se est, apud Patres idem est quod dari ex meritis, & negari ex demeritis. Porro, nec stabit illud Patrum Africanorum in Epistola sua synodica. Ipsa gratia nullatenus agnoscitur, nisi detur: quae quamdiu non est in homine, tamdiu necesse est ut ei sermone repugnet aut opere. Quomodo intelligi potest, Ethnicis in statu corruptae naturae constitutis, ea quasi lege gratiam Evangelicam donandam, si gratiae obicem non posuerint, cum tamdiu necesse sit (necessitate nimirum pravae & habitualis dispositionis) ut gratiae resistant, quamdiu eadem careant? Denique, corruent illa Arausicani Concilii decreta, canone 4. Si quis, ut a peccato purgemur, voluntatem nostram Deum expectare contendit, non autem, ut etiam purgari velimus, per sancti Spiritus operationem & infusionem in nobis fieri confitetur, resistit Apostolo. Et Can. 6. Si quis humilitati & obedientiae humanae subjungit gratiae adjutorium, &c. resistit Apostolo. Mitto caetera.
english: Fourth, grant that grace is given or denied according as human wills have or have not set an obstacle, and you overturn nearly everything the Councils defined against the Pelagians. First among them is what the Council of Diospolis sanctioned against Pelagius: let him confess that grace is not given from merit, so that it may be true grace—that is, freely given—through the mercy of him who said, I will have mercy on whom I have mercy (Exodus 33:19; Romans 9:15). For to give or withhold grace according as someone has used natural gifts rightly or not, or (as others put it) according as someone has or has not done what lies in him, is for the Fathers the same as giving from merits and denying from demerits. Nor will that word of the African Fathers in their synodical letter stand: grace itself is not recognized at all unless it is given; and as long as it is not in a person, he must of necessity resist it in word or deed. How can it make sense that Gentiles in corrupted nature are to receive evangelical grace by that quasi-law if they have not set an obstacle to grace, when by the necessity of a depraved and habitual disposition they must resist grace the whole time they lack it? Finally those decrees of the Council of Orange fall—canon 4: if anyone contends that God waits for our will so that we may be purged from sin, but will not confess that even our willing to be purged is wrought in us by the Holy Spirit's operation and infusion, he resists the Apostle; and canon 6: if anyone subjoins the help of grace to human humility and obedience, and so on, he resists the Apostle. I leave the rest.

source_text: Exponant nobis quomodo Deus non dicatur expectare voluntatem humanam, & obedientiae naturalis legis in cordibus hominum scriptae subjungere gratiae supernaturalis adjutorium, si posita Christi morte secundum hunc agendi modum Deus gratiam indat omnibus, si donis naturalibus recte utantur, non indat, si non utantur. Cum ergo haec omnia sint a veritate alienissima, restat ut dicamus Deum, non obstante merito mortis Christi, gratiam applicandi hoc meritum dare, vel negare posse, & solere singularibus hominibus, pro beneplacito & libertate voluntatis suae, non pro meritis aut operationibus diversis voluntatum humanarum.
english: Let them explain how God is not said to wait for the human will, and to hang the help of supernatural grace on obedience to the natural law written in human hearts, if—Christ's death once granted—God on this way of acting gives grace to all who use natural gifts rightly, and withholds it from those who do not. Since all of that is utterly foreign to the truth, it remains to say that God, the merit of Christ's death notwithstanding, can give or deny the grace of applying that merit, and ordinarily does so to particular persons by the good pleasure and freedom of his will—not by merits, or by the different operations of human wills.

source_text: Confirmatur sententia nostra a finibus utilissimis quibus illustrandis inservit, quique per contrariam sententiam plane abrogantur. Verbi causa: Si Deus, Christi morte posita, sumatur tamen distribuere gratiam qua applicetur, vel non distribuere hominibus secundum beneplacitum suum, & non secundum disparitatem aliquam voluntatum aut actionum humanarum.
english: Our view is confirmed by the most useful ends it serves to bring out—ends the contrary view plainly abolishes. Take this case: grant Christ's death, and still take God as distributing or withholding the grace by which that death is applied to human beings according to his good pleasure, and not according to some difference among human wills or actions.

source_text: Primo, inde elucebit absoluta libertas Dei in primae gratiae collatione: quod Divinum attributum hac in re est omnibus agnoscendum. Volo huic dare sicut & tibi, etiam in disparibus hominum meritis, Dei vox est libertatem suam sibi asserentis, Matth. xx. 14. Sed & illud, Volo huic dare, & non tibi, ubi omnia ex parte hominum paria agnoscuntur, aeque Deo digna vox est, & pariter spectat ad illustrandam Dei supremam libertatem, ut Paulus probat Rom. ix. Nam quamvis Deus virtute & efficacia mortis Christi ad dandam remissionem credentibus, ac ad dandam gloriam regeneratis & in Christum insertis sese obstrictum esse voluit, tamen ad dandum Evangelium hisce nationibus aut hisce singularibus hominibus, aut ad dandam fidem & gratiam efficacem hisce determinatis personis, nulla eorundem actione, nulla eorundem dispositione in statu naturae corruptae extra Christum considerata, voluit sese obligatum. Imminuunt igitur eam libertatem Divinam, quam Deus sibi reservavit, qui docent gratiam communicari & negari hominibus pro bono & malo usu naturae: quod idem est ac si dicerent, Gratiam a natura praeveniri.
english: First, absolute liberty of God in giving first grace then shines out—an attribute everyone must acknowledge here. "I choose to give to this one as to you," even when human merits are unequal, is God asserting his own liberty (Matthew 20:14). And "I choose to give to this one, and not to you," where on the human side everything is equal, is a voice just as worthy of God, and likewise serves to display his supreme liberty, as Paul proves (Romans 9). For although by the power and efficacy of Christ's death God willed himself bound to give remission to believers, and glory to the regenerate grafted into Christ, yet he did not will himself bound—by any act of theirs, or any disposition of theirs considered in corrupt nature outside Christ—to give the Gospel to these nations or these particular persons, or to give faith and efficacious grace to these definite individuals. So those who teach that grace is given or denied according to the good or bad use of nature diminish the divine liberty God reserved for himself: which is as much as to say that nature anticipates grace.

source_text: Secundo, ex nostra sententia conspicua fit illa, quam Scripturae adeo urgent, gratuita & specialis Dei misericordia in quibusdam hominibus donandis tam luce Evangelii quam gratia salutifera. De qua apposite Prosper, Est quaedam pars generis humani, quae specialibus beneficiis ad aeternam salutem provehitur, De vocat. Gent. lib. 2. cap. 31. Hanc specialem misericordiam plane tollunt, qui Christi morte hoc actum arbitrantur, ut Deus media gratiae salutiferae omnibus offerat, proprio autem arbitrio singulorum relinquat parere an resistere velint gratiae oblatae, ita ut, si obicem non ponant, gratia donentur, si ponant, gratia priventur. Nam ex horum sententia Deus non exseruit specialem aliquam misericordiam erga Jacobum aut Petrum, quam non exseruit erga Esauum & Judam; sed Jacobus & Petrus speciali quadam operatione sibi applicarunt, quod Esavus & Judas applicare neglexerunt. Hoc aperte docuit Faustus Rhegiensis, De lib. arbitr. lib. 1. cap. 10. qui specialem dispensationem Dei circa certorum hominum salutem negavit: quod a Pelagio didicit, ut videre est apud Prosperum, Carm. de ingratis, cap. 10. Sed aliter Augustinus, Dominus dat quibus vult, quoniam misericors est; & non dat quibus non vult, ut notus faciat divitias gloriae suae in vasa misericordiae, De bono persever. cap. 12.
english: Second, our view makes conspicuous what Scripture presses so hard: God's free and special mercy in giving certain people both the light of the Gospel and saving grace. Prosper puts it well: "There is a certain part of the human race that is brought on to eternal salvation by special benefits" (De vocatione gentium 2.31). Those who think Christ's death has this effect—that God offers the means of saving grace to all, yet leaves it to each person's own choice whether to obey or resist the grace offered, so that if they raise no obstacle they receive grace, and if they raise one they are stripped of it—plainly cancel that special mercy. On their view God showed Jacob or Peter no special mercy he did not show Esau and Judas; Jacob and Peter merely applied to themselves by some special act what Esau and Judas neglected to apply. Faustus of Riez taught that openly (De libero arbitrio 1.10), denying any special divine dispensation for the salvation of certain people—a lesson he learned from Pelagius, as Prosper shows (Carmen de ingratis 10). Augustine speaks otherwise: "The Lord gives to whom he wills, because he is merciful; and he does not give to whom he does not will, that he may make known the riches of his glory on the vessels of mercy" (De bono perseverantiae 12).

source_text: Tertio, ex nostra sententia sequitur omnem gloriandi ansam praereptam esse hominibus, & gloriam salutis humanae Deo, qui homines ab hominibus discernit, esse totaliter tribuendam, juxta illud Apostoli, 1 Cor. iv. 7, Quis te discernit? quid habes quod non accepisti? A quo, inquit Augustinus, nisi ab illo qui te discernit ab alio, cui non donavit quod donavit tibi? De praed. Sanct. cap. 9. At si obtineat illorum sententia, qui morte Christi Deum erga universos homines ex aequo benevolum factum opinantur; atque ex hac aequali propensione erga omnes gratiam sic administrari tuentur, ut eam ad se trahat quisquis bene utatur lumine naturae, aut quisquis fecerit quod in se est; non trahat, quisquis male utatur eodem lumine, aut non fecerit quod in se est; qui gratiae evasit particeps, habet a se justam gloriandi materiam, quia suo arbitrio seipsum discrevit ab eo, a quo speciali aliquo dono Divinae misericordiae non fuit discretus.
english: Third, our view leaves human beings no handle for boasting, and assigns the glory of human salvation wholly to God, who makes one person differ from another—as the Apostle says: "Who makes you differ? What do you have that you did not receive?" (1 Corinthians 4:7). "From whom," Augustine asks, "except from him who distinguishes you from another, to whom he did not give what he gave you?" (De praedestinatione sanctorum 9). But if their view wins—that by Christ's death God has become equally kind to all people, and that from this equal bent toward all he administers grace so that whoever uses nature's light well, or does what lies in him, draws grace to himself, while whoever uses that light badly, or fails to do what lies in him, does not—then the person who ends up sharing in grace has from himself a fair ground of boasting: by his own choice he set himself apart from another whom no special gift of divine mercy had set apart.

source_text: Si supposita morte Christi, ex decreto Dei donatio aut denegatio gratiae singularibus personis, non ex absoluta libertate voluntatis Divinae, sed ex disparitate voluntatum & actionum humanarum procedat, tum facile & promptum est cuivis rationem reddere cur huic nationi denegatum fuerit Evangelium, cur alteri concessum; & cur hisce singularibus hominibus detur fides, gratia vivificans & regenerans, aliis non detur. Ex parte etenim habentium respondetur, Eos Evangelii luce donatos, quia luce naturae bene, aut minus male, usi fuerint; Ex parte non-habentium respondetur, Eos Evangelii luce destitutos manere, quia lumine naturae minus bene usi fuerint. Sic inter Christianos, si quaeratur cur hic fidem habet & gratiam regenerantem, ille non habet; ex parte habentium etiam respondetur, Quia voluerunt credere, & noluerunt obicem ponere; ex parte non-habentium, Quia noluerunt credere, quia noluerunt obicem gratiae removere. Interim de speciali & secundum propositum vocatione, qua Deus eorum quos specialiter misereri vult corda potenter flectit ad credendum, verbum nullum.
english: Suppose Christ's death is granted, and yet by God's decree the gift or denial of grace to particular persons does not proceed from the absolute liberty of the divine will, but from the disparity of human wills and actions. Then anyone can give a ready reason why the Gospel was withheld from this nation and granted to that one, and why these particular people receive faith and vivifying, regenerating grace while others do not. Of those who have it, the story runs: they got the light of the Gospel because they used nature's light well, or at least less badly. Of those who lack it: they stay without Gospel light because they used nature's light less well. Ask among Christians why this person has faith and regenerating grace and that one does not, and you hear the same human ledger—those who have it willed to believe and would not raise an obstacle; those who lack it would not believe and would not clear the obstacle away. Of the special calling according to purpose, by which God powerfully turns the hearts of those he specially chooses to pity toward belief, there is meantime not a word.

source_text: Jam addo, ex parte hominis reddere tam obviam rationem gratiae obtentae aut non obtentae, est Pelagianorum proprium, & ab omnibus orthodoxis damnatum: qui gratiae efficacis donationem aut negationem ad arcanum propositum beneplaciti Divini semper revocarunt; neque putarunt, posita Christi morte, Deum ita teneri ad gratiam suam promiscue administrandam, ut eandem habere vel non habere ex disparitate humanarum voluntatum dependeret. Non negamus eorum demeritam indignitatem & improbitatem voluntariam, qui gratiae expertes manent, sed omnes hoc morbo laborare asserimus, donec specialis gratiae remedio curentur: nec irregenitorum quenquam per voluntatem meliorem trahere ad se gratiam, sed per gratiam efficaciorem ex mero Dei beneplacito illi donatam accipere voluntatem meliorem, juxta illud Apostoli, Non est volentis, neque currentis, sed miserentis Dei, Rom. ix. 16. Deus est qui dat nobis & velle & perficere pro bona sua voluntate, Phil. ii. 13.
english: I add this: to give so ready a reason, from the human side, why grace is obtained or missed is the Pelagian trademark—and every orthodox writer has condemned it. The orthodox have always traced the gift or denial of efficacious grace back to the secret purpose of God's good pleasure. They never held that, once Christ's death is granted, God is so bound to administer his grace indiscriminately that having it or lacking it turns on the disparity of human wills. We do not deny that those who stay without grace have earned their unworthiness and choose their wickedness. We do say that everyone labors under that disease until special grace cures it; and that no unregenerate person pulls grace to himself by a better will. Rather, by a more efficacious grace given from God's mere good pleasure, he receives a better will—as the Apostle says: "It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy" (Romans 9:16). "It is God who gives us both to will and to accomplish, according to his good pleasure" (Philippians 2:13).

source_text: Huc revocat Prosper discrimen credentium & non-credentium, Ad excerpta Genuens. resp. ad Dub. 4. Multi audiunt verbum veritatis, sed alii credunt, alii contradicunt: volunt ergo isti credere, nolunt illi. Quis hoc ignoret? quis hoc neget? Sed cum aliis praeparetur, aliis non praeparetur voluntas a Domino, discutiendum est utique quod veniat de misericordia, quod de judicio. Et paulo post, Misericordia & judicium in ipsis voluntatibus facta sunt.
english: Prosper brings the difference between believers and unbelievers back to the same point (Ad excerpta Genuensium, reply to Doubt 4): "Many hear the word of truth, but some believe and others contradict—so these will to believe, and those will not. Who does not know that? Who denies it? Yet when the Lord prepares the will for some and does not prepare it for others, we must ask what comes of mercy and what of judgment." And a little later: "Mercy and judgment have been done in the wills themselves."

source_text: Ad hoc arcanum Dei beneplacitum, non ad discrimen voluntatum humanarum sese ad gratiam oblatam pro sua innata libertate applicantium vel non applicantium, ipse etiam Augustinus ubique refert gratiae actualem participationem: De bono persever. cap. 8. Ex duobus aetate jam grandibus impiis, cur iste ita vocetur ut vocantem sequatur, ille autem aut non vocetur, aut non ita vocetur ut vocantem sequatur, inscrutabilia sunt judicia Dei. Et De praed. Sanct. cap. 8. Quare, inquit, non omnes docet Deus? Si dixerimus, quia nolunt discere quos non docet, respondebitur nobis, ubi est quod dicitur, DOMINE, TU CONVERTENS VIVIFICABIS NOS.
english: Augustine too, everywhere, traces actual share in grace to this secret good pleasure of God—not to the difference among human wills that, by their native freedom, do or do not apply themselves to grace offered. De bono perseverantiae 8: of two already adult ungodly persons, why one is called so that he follows the Caller, while the other is either not called, or not called so as to follow—God's judgments are inscrutable. And De praedestinatione sanctorum 8: "Why," he asks, "does God not teach everyone? If we say it is because those he does not teach refuse to learn, the reply comes: Where then is the word, LORD, YOU TURN US AND GIVE US LIFE?"

source_text: Denique ipse Aquinas non aliam rationem reddendam putat, cur hisce singularibus personis dentur gratiae salutiferae dona, aliis non dentur, praeter simplicem Dei voluntatem; Contr. Gent. lib. 3. cap. 161. Licet, inquit, ille qui peccat, impedimentum gratiae praestet, & in quantum ordo rerum exigit gratiam non deberet recipere, tamen interdum, ex abundantia bonitatis suae, etiam eos qui impedimentum gratiae praestant, auxilio suo praevenit, avertens eos a malo, & convertens ad bonum, &c. Mox addit, Non omnes qui gratiam impediunt auxilio suo praevenit, sed aliquos in quibus vult misericordiam suam apparere, ita quod in aliis justitiae ordo manifestetur.
english: Aquinas too will give no other reason why these particular persons receive the gifts of saving grace, and others do not, than the simple will of God (Contra Gentiles 3.161). "Though the sinner," he says, "puts an obstacle in grace's way, and so far as the order of things requires ought not to receive grace, yet sometimes, from the abundance of his goodness, God also goes before with his help even those who put that obstacle there, turning them from evil and converting them to good," and the rest. He adds at once: "He does not go before with his help all who block grace, but some in whom he wills his mercy to appear, so that in others the order of justice may be shown."

source_text: Demum, ne ad disparitatem voluntatum humanarum referamus, quod hi gratiam efficacem obtinuerint & conversi sint, illi non obtinuerint & conversi maneant, subjungit ibidem & haec verba dignissima, Cum Deus hominum qui in eisdem peccatis detinentur, hos quidem praeveniens convertat, illos autem sustineat sive permittat secundum ordinem rerum procedere, non est ratio inquirenda quare hos convertat, & non illos: hoc enim ex simplici ejus voluntate dependet, sicut ex simplici ejus voluntate processit, quod, quum omnia fierent ex nihilo, quaedam facta sunt aliis digniora. Hactenus Thomas. Christi igitur morte non est stabilitum ullum decretum Divinum de gratia omnibus hominibus promiscue administranda, ea quasi lege annexa, ut singulares personae hujus gratiae participes fiant, aut non participes, prout impedimentum posituri sunt, aut non posituri: sed hoc ipsum discrimen inter ponentes & non ponentes obicem in merum Dei beneplacitum, tanquam in primam & radicalem causam, resolvendum est.
english: Finally—lest we pin on the disparity of human wills the fact that these obtained efficacious grace and were converted, while those did not and stay unconverted—he adds in the same place these weighty words: "When God, among people held in the same sins, converts some by going before them, but sustains or permits others to go on according to the order of things, we are not to ask why he converts these and not those. That hangs on his simple will—just as it was by his simple will that, when all things were made from nothing, some were made more worthy than others." So far Thomas. Christ's death, then, established no divine decree that grace should be administered promiscuously to all, with a kind of annexed law that particular persons share or do not share in that grace according as they will or will not raise an impediment. The very distinction between those who raise an obstacle and those who do not must be resolved into God's bare good pleasure as its first and radical cause.

source_text: Si Dei voluntas morte Christi intelligatur quasi determinata ad gratiam administrandam omnibus & singulis hominibus, qui Christum sibi applicent, & salventur, ita tamen ut eam accipiant & habeant illi soli, qui aut lumine naturae bene usi fuerint, aut gratiae sibi oblatae obicem minime opposuerint, caeteri omnes eandem non accipiant; tum ultima ratio gratiae & salutis obtentae & non obtentae non ex parte Divini beneplaciti, sed ex parte humani arbitrii assignaretur. Consequentia clara est & firma; Quia ab illis qui in hac opinione constituti sunt, Deus praesumitur propter Christi mortem gratiam administrare, & offerre omnibus sufficientem ad Christum sibi applicandum & salutem obtinendam; praesumitur etiam ex absoluta voluntate sive ex mero nemini gratiam salutiferam donare.
english: Suppose God's will, by Christ's death, is taken as somehow fixed to administer grace to every person who applies Christ to himself and is saved—yet so that only those receive and keep it who either used nature's light well, or raised almost no obstacle against the grace offered them, while everyone else does not receive it. Then the last account of grace obtained or missed, and of salvation gained or lost, would be charged not to the divine good pleasure but to human free choice. The consequence is plain and solid. On that view God is presumed, because of Christ's death, to administer grace and to offer everyone a grace sufficient for applying Christ and obtaining salvation; and he is also presumed, by absolute will or bare will, to give saving grace to no one specially.

source_text: Sic Remonstrantes, in Declaratione sententiae suae circa articulum tertium, Act. Synod. Dordrecht. pag. 15. Gratiae efficacitatem salutiferam pendere dicunt neque a congruitate vocationis (ut quidam Pontificii) neque ab omnipotente vi Divina, (ut Prosper, Carm. De Ingr. cap. 14. & 15. & Augustinus, Contra Julian. lib. 5. cap. 3. De praed. Sanct. cap. 2. De grat. & lib. arbit. cap. 20. & De corrept. & grat. cap. 14.) sed a tali operatione quae suum effectum certissime sortitur, cum rebellionem homo non opponit, quam ex se opponere potuisset.
english: So the Remonstrants put it in the Declaration of their view on the third article (Acts of the Synod of Dordrecht, p. 15). Saving efficacy of grace, they say, hangs neither on the fitness of the calling (as some Roman writers hold) nor on omnipotent divine force (as Prosper in the Carmen De Ingratis 14-15, and Augustine Against Julian 5.3, On the Predestination of the Saints 2, On Grace and Free Choice 20, and On Rebuke and Grace 14), but on an operation that most surely gets its effect when a person does not set rebellion against it—rebellion he could of himself have set.

source_text: Quasi dicerent, gratiam in hac vel illa persona singulari esse efficacem, quia ipse obicem non opposuit: cum dicere debuissent, ideo obicem non opposuisse, quia Deus pro beneplacito suo dederit illi gratiam efficacem. Jam vero adjungo Minorem, & affirmo, esse a Theologia & veritate prorsus alienum, si quis tueatur Christi morte tale decretum stabilitum, juxta quod, certa gratiae & salutis adeptio ab absoluta Dei voluntate ad arbitrium humanae voluntatis revocetur.
english: As if they said grace is efficacious in this or that particular person because he himself raised no obstacle—when they ought to have said he raised none because God, of his good pleasure, gave him efficacious grace. I now add the Minor, and I affirm it is wholly alien to theology and to truth for anyone to hold that Christ's death established a decree by which the sure attainment of grace and salvation is shifted from God's absolute will onto the free choice of the human will.

source_text: Haec enim obtinendae aut non obtinendae salutis ratio, quae in libertatem arbitrii humani resolvitur, fuit primae gratiae, quae data est primo Adamo: ut bene observavit Augustinus: sed haec longe potentior est quae datur in Christo omnibus salvandis, qua fit ut velint, & tantum velint, ut reapse semper vincant reluctantem carnis voluntatem.
english: For that account of gaining or missing salvation which resolves into the liberty of human choice belonged to the first grace given to the first Adam—as Augustine well noted. But the grace given in Christ to all who are to be saved is far stronger: by it they will, and will so strongly, that in fact they always overcome the flesh's unwilling will. (See Augustine, On Rebuke and Grace 11-12.)

source_text: Ergo post datum nobis Christum, non ad disparitatem humanarum voluntatum, sed ad beneplacitum Divinae voluntatis reducitur hoc discrimen, quod aliqui habeant eam gratiam qua Christum sibi applicant ad salutem, alii non habeant.
english: So after Christ has been given us, the distinction that some have the grace by which they apply Christ to themselves for salvation, and others do not, is brought back not to the unevenness of human wills, but to the good pleasure of the divine will.

source_text: Postremum nostrum argumentum petetur a testimoniis Patrum, qui ultro fatentur, quibusdam hominibus, idque ex beneplacito Divinae voluntatis, non dari ea media ac dona quibus in Christum credere et salutem obtinere queant: quod Deus nunquam facere praetermitteret, si posita Christi morte, ratio bonitatis, prudentiae aut justitiae Divinae id exigeret omnibus et singulis jam suppeditari. Neque Patres singulos percurremus, sed ex iis paucula testimonia excerpemus, quibus cum Pelagianis et Semipelagianis negotium fuit.
english: Our last argument comes from the Fathers themselves. They freely grant that some people are not given the means and gifts by which they can believe in Christ and obtain salvation—and that this denial rests on the good pleasure of the divine will. God would never leave that undone if, once Christ's death is granted, divine goodness, prudence, or justice already required those means to be supplied to every person. We will not parade every Father in turn. We will take a few passages from those who fought the Pelagians and Semi-Pelagians.

source_text: Hoc unum tamen praemitto a vobis observandum. Quando dicimus Patres orthodoxos, qui in acie steterunt contra Pelagium et Pelagianos, non admittere gratiam omnibus dari propter respectum ad mortem Christi, Gratiae vocabulum (quod Pelagiani olim faciebant) extra justos suos limites non esse extendendum. Quicquid enim gratiose hominibus conceditur a Deo, potest aliquo sensu gratia appellari.
english: One caution first. When we say the orthodox Fathers who fought Pelagius refuse to grant that grace is given to all merely because of Christ's death, we are not letting the word grace run loose past its proper bounds—the very move the Pelagians once made. Anything God freely grants to people can, in a loose sense, be called grace.

source_text: Sic illud lumen naturale quo Deus illuminat omnem hominem venientem in mundum, illa creaturarum testificatio qua Ethnici ad aliquam Creatoris cognitionem diriguntur, illa beneficia externa quibus Deus suam φιλανθρωπίαν erga totum mundum testatur, illi interni motus quibus nonnunquam afficit animos gentilium, ut eos vel coerceat ab aliquo opere malo, vel excitet ad aliquod opus bonum, possunt hoc largo sensu gratiae nomen sibi vendicare. Pelagiani sub hac generali notione gratiae pestiferi sui dogmatis venenum occultarunt. Sed neque Scripturae gratiam per Christum datam ita intelligunt, neque sancti Patres, qui post exortum Pelagium cautius loqui didicerunt.
english: Natural light by which God lights every person who comes into the world; the witness of the creatures that steers the nations toward some knowledge of the Creator; outward benefits by which God shows his love of humankind to the whole world; inward stirrings that sometimes check a Gentile from evil or move him toward good—all these can, in that wide sense, wear the name grace. Under that blanket the Pelagians hid the poison of their teaching. Scripture does not mean the grace given through Christ that way, and neither do the holy Fathers once Pelagius forced them to speak more carefully.

source_text: Nomine igitur gratiae Christi sive gratiae salutiferae, ex sensu Scripturarum acceptae, significantur solummodo ea beneficia ac dona supernaturalia quae directe ordinantur ad salutem in Christo et vitam aeternam obtinendam. Haec autem sunt in duplici discrimine constituta. Quaedam eorum sunt quae habent ordinationem ad salutem per Christum obtinendam, sed non infallibilem: qualia sunt Evangelii praedicatio, Illuminatio humanarum mentium in mysteriis fidei, et uno verbo, quicquid supernaturale eo tendit ut homines Christo conjungat et in statu salutis ponat, nondum tamen conjunxit, aut ex statu mortis in statum salutis transtulit. Hanc ipsam praedicationem et cognitionem Evangelii Apostolus gratiae nomine indigitavit, 1 Cor. i. 4. et ii. 11. Atque hinc est quod 1 Petr. iv. 10. vocat praedicatores Dispensatores ποικίλης χάριτος Θεοῦ. Sic Augustinus vocat ipsum Evangelium gratiam Christianam, De pecc. mer. et rem. l. 1. 22. Prosper vocat gratiam Salvatoris, De voc. Gent. l. 2. c. 17. (Et hoc sensu affirmat aliquas gentes extra gratiam Dei degere, quando scilicet ibi degunt, ubi nemo illis Christi Evangelium praedicat, Sentent. 10. super Capit. Gallor.)
english: So by "grace of Christ" or saving grace, in Scripture's sense, we mean only those supernatural benefits and gifts aimed straight at salvation in Christ and eternal life. They fall into two ranks. Some are ordered to salvation through Christ, but not infallibly: Gospel preaching, illumination of minds in the mysteries of the faith—in short, whatever supernatural help tends to join people to Christ and set them in a state of salvation, yet has not actually joined them or moved them from death into life. The Apostle himself calls that preaching and knowledge of the Gospel "grace" (1 Cor. 1:4; 2:11). That is why 1 Peter 4:10 names preachers stewards of God's manifold grace. Augustine calls the Gospel itself Christian grace; Prosper calls it the Savior's grace—and in that sense says some nations live outside God's grace when no one there preaches Christ to them.

source_text: Sunt etiam alia dona supernaturalia quae statum salutis habentibus apportant, qualia sunt bona Voluntas, Fides, Conversio, Regeneratio; ut dicam brevi, ea quae solis hominibus in Christum insertis et Deo reconciliatis conveniunt. Atque haec ea sunt quae Augustinus appellatione gratiae Christi proprie designanda arbitratur: priora autem illa, scilicet praedicationem et cognitionem doctrinae Christianae, ad hanc Christi gratiam proprie dictam eatenus reducit, quatenus inserviunt eidem producendae et promovendae. In libro De gratia Christi id ex professo agit ut ostendat, hoc nomine venire non illuminationem mentis aut excitationem voluntatis, sed ipsam fidem et bonae voluntatis donationem, cap. 10, 47; Epist. 99. Hanc gratiam Christi vivis coloribus depingit atque appellat, gratiam qua justificamur ab iniquitate, et qua salvamur ab infirmitate; gratiam quam cum impiis minime communem habemus, sed eam qua filii Dei sumus. Jam Patrum testimonia audiamus.
english: Other supernatural gifts actually bring the state of salvation: a good will, faith, conversion, regeneration—in short, what belongs only to people grafted into Christ and reconciled to God. Those, Augustine says, deserve the name "grace of Christ" in the proper sense. Preaching and knowledge of Christian doctrine he refers to that proper grace only so far as they help produce and advance it. In On the Grace of Christ he makes the point expressly: the name does not mean mere lighting of the mind or stirring of the will, but the gift of faith itself and of a good will. He paints that grace in bright colors—the grace by which we are justified from iniquity and saved from weakness; a grace we barely share with the ungodly, but the grace by which we are children of God. Now for the Fathers' own words.

source_text: Primo illa afferemus quae gratiam Evangelicae praedicationis, supposita Christi morte, omnibus debitam aut datam negant, imo aliquibus negatam affirmant, idque ex proposito voluntatis Divinae: quod nunquam fieret, si omnibus gratia debita esset in ordine ad mortem Christi. Augustinus, De bono persever. cap. 8. Ex duobus aetate grandibus impiis, cur iste ita vocetur ut vocantem sequatur, ille autem aut non vocetur aut non ita vocetur, inscrutabilia sunt judicia Dei. Hic aperte agnoscit quosdam omnino non vocari. Et cap. 14. docet, quibusdam qui Dei altiori judicio a perditionis massa non sunt discreti, ea media non adhiberi per quae possent credere. Utroque in loco negationem mediorum asserit, et revocat ad inscrutabilem abyssum praedestinationis Divinae, non ad discrimina voluntatum aut actionum humanarum, sicut Pelagiani et Semipelagiani solebant. Vide etiam cap. 11. ubi ad voluntatem Dei et occultam praedestinationem refert, quod quibusdam Deus nolit subvenire.
english: First, the Fathers who deny that—Christ's death granted—the grace of Gospel preaching is owed or given to all, and even say it is withheld from some by the purpose of God's will. That could not happen if grace were owed to everyone on the strength of Christ's death. Augustine, On the Gift of Perseverance, chapter 8: take two ungodly adults—why is one called so that he follows the Caller, while the other is not called, or not called that way? God's judgments are inscrutable. He plainly owns that some are not called at all. Chapter 14 adds that for some not cut out of the mass of perdition by God's higher judgment, the means by which they could believe are simply not applied. In both places he affirms that the means are denied, and he traces it to the unsearchable depth of divine predestination—not to uneven human wills or works, the Pelagian and Semi-Pelagian habit. Chapter 11 says the same: God chooses not to help some, and that rests on his will and hidden predestination.

source_text: Prosper objectionem, Quod non omnes homines vocentur ad gratiam, de illis omnibus vere dici posse agnoscit quibus sacramentum crucis Christi et redemtio sanguinis ejus non innotuit. Et Sentent. 4. super Capit. Gallor.: Non possumus dicere quod ibi sit gratiae vocatio, ubi matris Ecclesiae adhuc nulla est regeneratio. Quae loco animadvertenda sunt contra istos, qui, ut tueantur sententiam suam de gratia propter Christum omnibus parata et oblata, in mediis Paganismi tenebris nescio quam vocationem ac gratiae sufficientiam imaginantur. Nos, quod de parvulis dixit Prosper, id de natu grandioribus dicere possumus: Probentur aliquo modo vocati, quibus nec plantator praedicare, nec irrigator potuit subvenire, Resp. ad Obj. 4.
english: Prosper grants the objection that not all are called to grace, at least of everyone to whom Christ's cross and the redemption of his blood have never been made known. Sentence 4 on the Chapters of the Gauls: we cannot say there is a calling of grace where Mother Church has not yet regenerated anyone. That strikes those who, to keep grace prepared and offered to all because of Christ, invent some calling and enough-grace in the thick of pagan darkness. What Prosper said of little children we may say of adults: prove them called somehow, when neither planter could preach to them nor irrigator help them (Response to Objection 4).

source_text: Fulgentius, lib. 1. De verit. Praedest. Deus hominibus ratione utentibus congruas ad salutem personas aut procurat, aut denegat, in aliis justitiam tenens, in aliis misericordiam tribuens. Sensus est, Deum mittere vel non mittere praedicatores Evangelicos pro beneplacito suo: mittit quando vult ostendere misericordiam suam, non mittit quando vult exserere justitiam. Quinetiam et illud addo ex eodem Fulgentio, Communem illum reatum quem omnes homines contraxerunt in Adamo, sufficere ad hoc ut gratia Evangelica cuivis homini juste denegetur. Sic Fulgentius ibid.: Haec Dei gratia qua salvamur, non alicui praecedenti bono merito datur, nec tamen nisi praecedente malo merito denegatur. Primus enim homo peccati sui merita transmisit in omnes, &c. Unde patet, ex mente Fulgentii demeritum originale satis justam causam esse cur gratia Christi cuivis homini denegetur. Quod ipse Aquinas agnoscit, 2a 2ae qu. 2. art. 5. resp. ad 1., ubi ait auxilia gratiae quibusdam dari misericorditer, quibusdam ex justitia non dari, in poenam praecedentis peccati, saltem originalis. Ex hisce omnibus habemus quod primo in loco confirmandum proposuimus; nempe, Nullam esse legem decretam aut statutam, in ordine ad mortem Christi, de administrandis gratiae Evangelicae mediis toti humano generi; sed Deum, non obstante ullo ad mortem Christi respectu, negare posse de jure, et de facto negasse aliquibus ipsam vocationem gratiae.
english: Fulgentius, On the Truth of Predestination book 1: to people who use reason God either supplies or withholds the persons fitted for their salvation—holding justice toward some, showing mercy to others. Meaning: he sends Gospel preachers, or does not, by his good pleasure—sends when he means to display mercy, withholds when he means to exercise justice. From the same Fulgentius I add: the common guilt all contracted in Adam is enough for Gospel grace to be justly denied to anyone. So he says there: the grace by which we are saved is never given for a prior good desert, yet it is denied only for a prior evil desert; for the first man passed the deserts of his sin to all. So for Fulgentius original demerit is already a just reason to withhold Christ's grace from anyone. Aquinas owns the same (2a 2ae q. 2 a. 5 ad 1): helps of grace are given to some in mercy, and in justice not given to others, as punishment for prior sin—at least original sin. All this confirms what we set out first: there is no decreed law, tied to Christ's death, that the means of Gospel grace must be administered to the whole human race. God, even with Christ's death in view, can by right deny—and has in fact denied to some—the very calling of grace.

source_text: Secundo, ex iisdem Patribus ostendemus gratiam illam, quam κατ᾽ ἐξοχήν vocamus gratiam Christi, idest, quae facit hominem esse vivum membrum Christi, et salutis ac vitae aeternae participem, non in ordine ad mortem Christi omnibus praeparatam aut oblatam, multo minus donatam, sed praeparatam, oblatam et donatam aliquibus, aliis nec praeparatam nec donatam, idque secundum Dei beneplacitum absolutum. Augustinus, Contr. duas Epist. Pelag. lib. 2. cap. 7: Secundum propositum Dei vocatur alius, alius non vocatur. Vocato datur gratuitum bonum, cujus boni est vocatio ipsa principium: non vocato redditur malum, quia omnes rei sunt ex eo quod per unum hominem peccatum introivit in mundum. Ex quibus verbis patet, vocationem secundum propositum, quae fidem et charitatem infundit, hominemque in statu salutis collocat, aliquibus dari, aliquibus negari. Porro, et illud perspicuum est, hanc gratiam dari quibus datur, non ex speciali aliquo obsequio voluntatis recipientis, sed ex speciali misericordia Dei vocantis, et voluntatem ad obsequium emollientis. Denique et hoc etiam constat, ipsum communem reatum, quem in Adamo omnes contraxerunt, satis esse ad tuendam Dei justitiam, respectu eorum, quoscunque in gratiae salutaris donatione praeterierit; quod ipse Bellarminus non audet inficias ire, uti videre licet, lib. 2. De grat. et lib. arb. cap. 4.
english: Second, from the same Fathers we show that the grace we call Christ's grace by preeminence—the grace that makes a person a living member of Christ and a sharer in salvation and eternal life—is not, because of Christ's death, prepared or offered to all, still less given to all. It is prepared, offered, and given to some; to others neither prepared nor given—and that by God's absolute good pleasure. Augustine, Against Two Letters of the Pelagians 2.7: according to God's purpose one is called, another is not. To the called a free gift is given, and the calling itself is that gift's beginning; to the uncalled evil is paid back, because all are guilty since [[through one man sin entered the world >> Bible:Romans 5:12]]. So the calling according to purpose—which pours in faith and charity and sets a person in the state of salvation—is given to some and denied to others. Clear too: those who receive it receive it not because their will specially obeyed first, but because God who calls specially showed mercy and softened the will to obey. And the common guilt all contracted in Adam is already enough to uphold God's justice toward anyone he passes by in the gift of saving grace—Bellarmine himself does not dare deny it (On Grace and Free Choice 2.4).

source_text: Secundum testimonium Augustini habetur lib. 4. contra duas Epist. Pelag. cap. 6: Qui facit oves homines, ipse ad obedientiam pietatis humanas liberat voluntates. Sed quare istos homines oves facit, et istos non facit, ipsa est quaestio quae ad illam pertinet altitudinem, quam perspicere volens Apostolus expavit, et exclamavit, O altitudo. Hisce in verbis per facere oves, et non facere, nil aliud significatur, quam facere fideles et obedientes, et non facere. Utrumque Deo tribuitur, idque secundum propositum arcanae suae voluntatis. Christi ergo morte non est stabilitum tale decretum, quale nonnulli finxerunt, de praeparanda, offerenda et donanda omnibus hominibus ea gratia qua credentes et obedientes reddantur, sub conditione liberi arbitrii eandem amplexantis.
english: Augustine's second witness is Against Two Letters of the Pelagians 4.6: the One who makes people sheep is the One who frees human wills for the obedience of piety. Why he makes these sheep and not those—that is the question that belongs to the depth the Apostle feared to look into and cried, [[O the depth >> Bible:Romans 11:33]]. Making sheep or not making them means nothing but making people faithful and obedient—or not. Both acts are God's, and both run by the purpose of his hidden will. So Christ's death did not fix the decree some invent: that the grace which makes believers and the obedient is prepared, offered, and given to everyone, on condition that free choice embrace it.

source_text: Tertium testimonium depromitur ex De Praed. Sanctor. cap. 8: Fides inchoata et perfecta donum Dei est. Et hoc donum quibusdam dari, quibusdam non dari, omnino non dubitet, qui non vult manifestissimis sacris literis repugnare. Cur autem non omnibus detur, fidelem movere non debet, qui credit ex una omnes isse in condemnationem. Clare docet gratiam fidei non dari omnibus; nec opus esse ut aliquam aliam rationem non-datae hujus gratiae quaeramus, quia damnabilis iste status, in quo omnes nascimur, sufficit ad justitiam Dei asserendam, etiamsi nemini mortalium daret gratiam salvantem.
english: Third witness: On the Predestination of the Saints 8. Faith begun and faith perfected is God's gift. No one who will not fight the plainest Scripture should doubt that this gift is given to some and not to others. Why not to all should not unsettle the believer who holds that from one man all went into condemnation. Augustine teaches outright that the grace of faith is not given to all; we need no further reason for the gift withheld, because the damnable state in which we are all born already upholds God's justice—even if he gave saving grace to no mortal at all.

source_text: Quartum sumitur ex libro De corrept. et gratia, cap. 5, ubi increduli et rebelles hoc modo argutantur: Recte corriperer, si eam (id est, fidem et obedientiam) mea culpa non haberem; hoc est, si eam possem mihi dare vel sumere ipse, nec facerem; vel si dante Deo accipere noluissem: Verum cum ipsa voluntas a Domino praeparetur, cur me corripis? &c. Cap. 6. respondet Augustinus in hunc modum: Prima pravitas, qua Deo non obeditur, ab homine est, quia ex rectitudine, in qua eum Deus primitus fecit, sua mala voluntate decidens pravus effectus est. Corripiatur ergo origo damnabilis, ut ex dolore correptionis voluntas regenerationis oriatur; si tamen qui corripitur filius est promissionis, ut Deus in illo intrinsecus occulta inspiratione operetur et velle. Huic conjungo locum plane confimilem, ex Epistola 105. Ita objicit Pelagius: Quid nos fecimus qui male vivimus, quandoquidem gratiam unde bene viveremus non accepimus? Nihil aliud respondet Augustinus quam non posse eos veraciter dicere se nihil mali fecisse, qui de suo male vivunt. Et paulo post: Sibi hoc imputent, quia ex ea massa facti sunt, quam propter unius peccatum merito Deus justeque damnavit. Observandum est utroque in loco, concedere Augustinum, esse nonnullos quibus gratiam suam Deus negavit; porro, eos quibus non est data, non potuisse eam sibimetipsis sumere; denique, reatum et pravitatem originalem satis idoneam rationem esse, cur Deus gratiam Christi pro sua voluntate cuivis deneget. Denique illud quoque notandum, Augustinum non imaginari gratiam Christi salutiferam esse quiddam oblatum humanae voluntati, et pulsans ut intro mittatur, sed quiddam infusum et sanans ac vivificans voluntatem cui datur.
english: Fourth, On Rebuke and Grace 5. Unbelievers and rebels argue: I would deserve rebuke if by my fault I lacked faith and obedience—if I could give or take it myself and would not, or if when God gave it I refused. But if the Lord himself prepares the will, why rebuke me? Chapter 6 Augustine answers: the first crookedness that disobeys God is from the human, who by his own evil will fell from the uprightness God first made in him. So rebuke the damnable root, that pain may birth a will to be regenerated—yet only if the one rebuked is a child of promise, so God works inwardly in him by hidden inspiration even to will. Epistle 105 is the same case. Pelagius asks: what have we done who live badly, if we never received the grace to live well? Augustine answers only that people who live badly of themselves cannot truly claim they have done no evil. A little later: let them blame themselves; they were made from the mass God justly condemned for one man's sin. In both places Augustine grants that God has denied his grace to some; that those not given it could not take it for themselves; and that original guilt and pravity are reason enough for God, of his will, to withhold Christ's grace from anyone. Note too: he does not picture saving grace as something merely offered to the human will, knocking to be let in, but as something poured in—healing and vivifying the will that receives it.

source_text: Ultimum testimonium quod ex Augustino afferimus, erit illud quod exstat Epistola 107, ubi recenset contra Pelagianos duodecim sententias ad fidem catholicam pertinentes, quarum quarta est, Scimus gratiam Dei non dari omnibus hominibus. Ne autem quis obtendat, morte Christi id effectum esse ut omnibus praeparetur et offeratur haec gratia, quamvis habeatur aut non habeatur prout homines eam accipere aut non accipere voluerint, hoc etiam sententia quinta et sexta excluditur: Qua de re plura mox dicemus. Ab Augustino ad Prosperum descendamus. Ad Excerpta Genuens. Resp. ad dub. 7. dicit, Cum verbum veritatis praedicatur, alios voluntate credere, alios non credere; sed cum illorum corda Deus aperuerit, illorum autem non aperuerit. Quod perinde est ac si dixisset, gratiam fidei dari quibusdam, negari aliis. Et Resp. ad dub. octavum, De Tyriis et Sidoniis quid aliud possumus dicere quam, non esse eis datum ut crederent? Quare autem hoc eis negatum fuerit, dicant si possunt, &c. Duo asserit Prosper: unum, Quod donum fidei negetur quibusdam hominibus; alterum, Quod causa cur negetur sit inscrutabilis. Denique, in libro De Ingratis, cap. 6. tanquam Pelagianorum errorem proponit, Quod sine dilectu seu lex seu gratia Christi omnem hominem salvare velit; donumque vocantis sic sit propositum ut nullus non possit ad illud libertate sua proprioque vigore venire. Dein Semipelagianorum sententiam depingit, hisce coloribus, Cap. 10; quam capite 11. rejicit hisce verbis: Dic, unde probes quod gratia Christi nullum omnino hominem de cunctis qui generantur praetereat? Prospero igitur habetur Pelagianae virulentiae fibra, si quis gratiam omnibus datam defendat. Fulgentium jam audiamus. Is in libro De verit. praedest. haec habet: Sancti Patres, Apostolicae praedicationis tenentes veritatem, certissime cognoverunt, cognoscendaque libris reliquerunt, gratiam Dei non omnibus hominibus generaliter dari. Paulo post: Ipsam gratiam nullus hominum desiderare vel poscere, sed nec cognoscere poterit, nisi eam prius a Deo accipiat. Idem ibidem: Non ergo putemus gratiam Dei omnibus hominibus dari. Non enim omnium est fides, et quidam charitatem Dei non recipiunt ut salvi fiant: In quibus tamen, ut non credant, neque diligant Dominum, humanae voluntatis est vitium, quae, quandiu gratia Divini muneris non mutatur, aut praecepta Dei non intelligit, aut intellecta contemnit, &c. Quid apertius, quam, si Fulgentius audiatur, gratiam vivificantem non dari omnibus a Deo, nec posse ab ullo haberi cui non desuper data fuerit? Si clariora desiderentur, addo illud ex libro De incarnat. et grat. Jesu Christi, pag. 89: Deus qui voluntatem praeparat, ipse eam donat. Quam si Deus per suam gratiam homini non dederit, nunquam potest homo in Deum velle credere, quia ipsam voluntatem gratia non invenit, sed operatur in homine. Videtis esse concordem eorum Patrum sententiam, qui Pelagianis et Semipelagianis bellum indixerunt: Gratiam vivificantem et salutiferam non dari omnibus hominibus; ac voluntatem vitiatam cui non datur, posse quidem suo vitio gratiam fastidire, et in mediis externis oblatam repellere; non posse autem hanc vivificam gratiam pro jure innatae suae libertatis arripere, et ad se pertrahere.
english: Our last Augustine witness is Epistle 107. Against the Pelagians he lists twelve catholic sentences; the fourth is, We know God's grace is not given to all. And lest anyone claim Christ's death made this grace prepared and offered to everyone, had or missed only as people choose to take or refuse it, sentences five and six shut that door too—more on that shortly. From Augustine we come to Prosper. In the Genoese Excerpts, answer to doubt 7: when the word of truth is preached, some believe willingly and some do not—but only because God has opened some hearts and not others. That is to say, the grace of faith is given to some and denied to others. Answer to the eighth doubt: of Tyre and Sidon what can we say but that it was not given them to believe? Why denied—let them tell if they can. Prosper asserts two things: the gift of faith is denied to some, and the reason is unsearchable. In On the Ungrateful 6 he sets out the Pelagian error: that without choosing persons, law or Christ's grace wills to save every human, and the Caller's gift is so laid open that anyone can reach it by his own liberty and strength. Chapter 10 paints the Semi-Pelagian colors; chapter 11 rejects them: Tell us how you prove Christ's grace passes by none of all who are born. For Prosper, to defend grace given to all is a strand of Pelagian poison. Hear Fulgentius. On the Truth of Predestination: the holy Fathers, holding apostolic truth, knew for certain—and left it in books—that God's grace is not given generally to all. A little later: no one can desire, ask, or even know that grace unless he first receives it from God. Again: do not think God's grace is given to all. Not all have faith; some do not receive God's charity so as to be saved. That they neither believe nor love the Lord is the fault of the human will, which, until divine gift-grace changes it, either fails to understand God's commands or despises them once understood. What could be plainer? Vivifying grace is not given to all, and no one has it unless it is given from above. Clearer still, On the Incarnation and Grace of Jesus Christ, p. 89: God who prepares the will is the One who gives it. If he has not given that will by his grace, a person can never will to believe in God—because grace does not find the will ready; it works the will in the person. So the Fathers who warred on Pelagians and Semi-Pelagians speak with one voice: vivifying, saving grace is not given to all; the spoiled will that lacks it can by its own fault scorn grace and push away what is offered in outward means; but it cannot, by right of native liberty, snatch this life-giving grace and drag it to itself.

source_text: Sed quia ipsa medulla Pelagianismi sita est in modo, secundum quem fingunt gratiam vivificantem a Deo hominibus administrari, et ab hominibus acceptari, quid ea de re Pelagiana factio asserat, quid orthodoxi Patres statuant, productis in medium utrorumque testimoniis ostendemus.
