It is not credible that so great a price was spent on an outcome dangling from the uncertain dice of human choice. So the Father and Christ the Mediator meant by this precious death to redeem and save certain people infallibly and efficaciously; and those can be none other than those who are in fact saved—the elect. Therefore Christ’s intention in offering himself regarded the elect in a special way. I know Grevinchovius and others of that school boldly claim the proper end of impetration God intended was only that he might save the sinner with his justice intact, and that this redemption obtained for all might still be applied to none because of everyone’s intervening unbelief. That is as much as to say God gave the Son to death with no certain purpose of saving anyone by that death’s merit, but only a bare possibility of salvation procured for all in general, leaving efficacious share in salvation to each person’s choice—so that Christ’s death, taken in the whole breadth of its merit, might have redeemed no one from death. But whoever weighs how precious the Son’s death was in the Father’s eyes cannot even think he meant to expose the Son to death without a certain purpose of applying that death efficaciously to some. Isaiah 53:10: “The will of the Lord shall prosper in his hand.” Hear Malder, a papal writer far sounder than the Arminians here (Anti-Synod, p. 138): if you look only at the offering itself, it is equal for all; otherwise, if you look at that for whose actual obtaining he offered. For the elect obtain the perfect fruit of his passion that actually follows and is applied, as given them by the Father for this. So Christ’s blood could not run to waste; by the price of his blood, from God’s decree, he merited for the elect the fruitful application of that same price.

source_text: Quicquid boni spiritualis & salutiferi Christi Spiritus efficit in ullis hominibus, id Christi sanguis effusus promeruit iisdem hominibus: At Christi Spiritus producit in certis quibusdam personis poenitentiam & fidem, & mediante fide ac poenitentia infallibilem applicationem mortis suae: Ergo iisdem hominibus haec specialia bona promeruit: Ergo seipsum in ara crucis sacrificans promereri intendit. Neque enim temere aut casu fas est putare, Christum majora spiritualia beneficia hisce quam illis procurasse. Quid hic respondebunt adversarii? Nunquid dicent Christi Spiritum impertire beneficia hominibus, quae Christus illis minime promeruit? Non audebunt Christi meritum ita conculcare; Nunquid respondebunt, Ipsam fidem, & voluntatem, & actum fructuosae applicationis non esse Dona specialia Spiritus sancti? Pudebit tam crassi Pelagianismi. Fateantur ergo nobiscum, sicut per Christi mortem specialia bona sunt procurata electis, ita in voluntate Christi morientis, Deique Patris, hanc mortem acceptantis, fuisse efficacem intentionem de iisdem procurandis & conferendis. Atque hoc est illud singulare privilegium in morte Christi, quod solis electis vindicamus, quia ex facto apparet, Deum eos solos morte Filii sui efficaciter servandos destinasse. Unde Heb. vii. 25. statuitur Servator quorundam, id est, electorum, munus, nempe tam merito, quam efficacia.
english: Whatever spiritual, saving good Christ’s Spirit works in any people, Christ’s poured-out blood merited for those same people. But Christ’s Spirit produces in certain persons repentance and faith, and through faith and repentance an infallible application of his death. Therefore he merited these special goods for those same people; therefore, sacrificing himself on the cross’s altar, he meant to merit them. It is not right to suppose by chance that Christ procured greater spiritual benefits for these than for those. What will the adversaries say? That Christ’s Spirit gives people benefits Christ never merited for them? They will not dare so to trample Christ’s merit. That faith itself, the will, and the act of fruitful application are not special gifts of the Holy Spirit? They will blush at so crass a Pelagianism. Let them confess with us: just as through Christ’s death special goods were procured for the elect, so in the will of the dying Christ, and of the Father accepting that death, there was an efficacious intention to procure and confer those goods. And that is the singular privilege in Christ’s death we claim for the elect alone, because the fact shows God destined them alone to be saved efficaciously by his Son’s death. Hence Hebrews 7:25 establishes the office of Savior of certain ones—that is, of the elect—both by merit and by efficacy.

source_text: Quartum argumentum nobis praebebit receptissima illa inter omnes Theologos distinctio, qua dici solet, Christum pro omnibus mortuum fuisse sufficienter, pro electis mortuum efficaciter. Nam sicuti ex priore membro refutavimus illorum sententiam, qui negant Christi mortem ex decreto Dei esse omnibus hominibus remedium applicabile, ita ex hoc posteriore illi sunt refutandi, qui negant Christi mortem, idque ex decreto Dei, esse remedium electis efficaciter & infallibiliter applicandum. Quis enim potest esse alius sensus horum verborum, Mortuus est pro electis efficaciter, quam, Mortuus est absoluta intentione & efficaci voluntate servandi electos?
english: A fourth argument is the distinction most received among all theologians: that Christ died for all sufficiently, for the elect efficaciously. Just as from the first half we refuted those who deny that Christ’s death, by God’s decree, is an applicable remedy for all people, so from the second half those must be refuted who deny that Christ’s death, and that by God’s decree, is a remedy to be applied to the elect efficaciously and infallibly. What else can “He died for the elect efficaciously” mean than that he died with an absolute intention and efficacious will to save the elect?

source_text: Nam si quis eo torqueat hanc distinctionem, quasi sensus esset, Mortem Christi, quae sufficiens est pro omnibus, in eventu efficacem fieri aliquibus ex contingente actu arbitrii humani; Primo, ipsis verbis refellitur: siquidem, quando dicitur, Christus mortuus est efficaciter pro his aut illis, denotamus singularem efficaciam ex voluntate speciali morientis profluentem, non ex contingente actu credentis dimanantem. Secundo, ab ipsis Jesuitis haec efficacia (ut ita loquar) eventualis non intelligitur in hac distinctione, sed efficacia ab ipso moriente specialiter intenta & promerita. Sic Suarez, In 3. disp. 41. pag. 629. Christus non meruit omnibus remissionem peccatorum quoad efficaciam, quia non applicavit suum meritum, ut omnes infallibiliter talem effectum consequerentur. Mereri igitur efficaciter vel quoad efficaciam est, ea intentione suum meritum applicare aliquibus personis, ut infallibiliter inde effectum vitae aeternae consequantur. Paulo planius, pag. 635. Meritums Christi aequaliter se habet ad omnes quoad sufficientiam, non quoad efficaciam. Quod intelligendum est non tantum in effectibus, qui in uno sit & non in alio, sed etiam ex parte voluntatis, qua Christus ipse diverso modo obtulit sua merita pro diversis. Denique illa omnia testimonia Scripturarum, quae mortem Christi nobis proponunt complicatam cum certo proposito redimendi suas oves, Filios Dei congregandi, Ecclesiam acquirendi, populum peculiarem mundandi & servandi, atque id genus alia a nobis supra commemorata, aperte demonstrant hanc efficaciam de qua loquuntur Theologi, a voluntate morientis Christi esse arcessendam, non ex contingente actu arbitrii humani petendam. Christus speciali quadam intentione oblationis suae impetravit ut electis efficax redderetur; non autem electi in aliqua apprehensione ex libero arbitrio evagante eam sibi reddiderunt efficacem.
english: If someone twists the distinction as if Christ’s death, sufficient for all, became efficacious for some only by a contingent act of human free choice, the words themselves refute him: “Christ died efficaciously for these or those” marks a singular efficacy flowing from the dying one’s special will, not from the believer’s contingent act. Second, even the Jesuits do not take “efficacy” in this distinction as mere eventual efficacy, but as efficacy specially intended and merited by the dying one himself. So Suarez (On 3, disp. 41, p. 629): Christ did not merit remission of sins for all as to efficacy, because he did not apply his merit so that all would infallibly gain that effect. To merit efficaciously is to apply his merit to certain persons with the intention that they infallibly obtain eternal life from it. More plainly (p. 635): Christ’s merit stands equally toward all as to sufficiency, not as to efficacy—understood not only in the effects (in one, not another) but also in the will by which Christ offered his merits differently for different persons. Scripture’s witnesses that join Christ’s death to a sure purpose of redeeming his sheep, gathering God’s sons, acquiring the Church, and cleansing a peculiar people show that the efficacy theologians speak of is drawn from the dying Christ’s will, not from contingent free choice. By a special intention in his offering Christ obtained that it be made efficacious for the elect; the elect did not make it efficacious for themselves by some free-choice apprehension.

source_text: Rat. 5. A Praedestinatione Divina quintam nostram rationem sumemus: Posita siquidem praedestinatione certarum personarum ante jacta mundi fundamenta, necesse est ponere in voluntate Christi seipsum offerentis specialem quendam intuitum & respectum ad salutem eorundem merito suae passionis efficaciter producendam. Nam sive praeponamus electionem Divinam (secundum nostrum intelligendi modum) ipsius passionis decreto, sive postponamus, semper tamen illud firmum manebit, in voluntate Christi, sive passuri, sive patientis, de hisce, sive electis, sive eligendis, efficaciter salvandis fuisse efficacem quandam & singularem intentionem. Christi siquidem voluntas nunquam non conformat se Paternae voluntati. Incredibile ergo est (ut recte Suarez annotavit, In 3. disp. 41. §. 2. pag. 615.) eum aliter obtulisse Christum merita sua pro illis, quos sciebat a Patre electos, quam pro aliis, cum videret voluntatem Patris ut illi infallibiliter salvarentur, & non alii: cui voluntati ipse se in omnibus conformavit. Huc spectant verba Prophetae a nobis modo allata, Esai. liii. 10. Voluntas Domini in manu ejus dirigetur. Electio ergo quorundam ad vitam aeternam, quae est ex gratuita voluntate Dei, habet executionem suam per merita Christi: atque idcirco non est dubitandum, meritoriam Christi mortem fuisse ab ipso Redemtore hisce electis infallibiliter redimendis & servandis specialiter & efficaciter destinatam, atque Patri oblatam. Praeclarum est illud Scoti in hanc sententiam, Lib. 3. dist. 19. pag. 74. Christus praevidit passionem suam Patri offerendam pro praedestinatis & electis, & sic eam efficaciter obtulit in effectu, totaque Trinitas pro eis sic eam efficaciter acceptavit, & pro nullis aliis fuit efficaciter oblata, aut ab aeterno acceptata. Per efficacem oblationem & acceptationem nihil aliud intelligit quam oblationem & acceptationem conjunctam cum absoluto proposito servandi illos pro quibus hunc in modum oblata fuit & acceptata. Malderus Episcopus Antuerpiensis hoc argumento nixus rejicit contrariam illorum sententiam, qui opinantur Christum quoad efficaciam aeque esse mortuum pro omnibus, ac concludit, Supposita praedestinatione illud sequi, Christum hisce praedestinatis longe plus sua morte quam aliis contulisse, pag. 137.
english: Ratio 5. From divine predestination we take a fifth reason. Given the predestination of certain persons before the world’s foundations, Christ’s will in offering himself must include a special regard for producing their salvation efficaciously by the merit of his passion. Whether we place election before or after the decree of the passion (as we understand the order), this stands: in Christ’s will—whether about to suffer or already suffering—there was an efficacious, singular intention to save these elect (or to-be-elect) efficaciously. His will never fails to conform to the Father’s. So it is incredible (as Suarez notes, On 3, disp. 41, §2, p. 615) that he offered his merits one way for those he knew the Father had chosen and another way for the rest, when he saw the Father’s will that they—and not others—be saved infallibly, and conformed himself to that will in all things. Isaiah 53:10 points here: “The will of the Lord shall be directed in his hand.” Election to eternal life from God’s free will is executed through Christ’s merits; therefore the Redeemer specially and efficaciously destined his meritorious death for these elect to be redeemed and saved infallibly, and offered it to the Father. Scotus puts it well (Book 3, dist. 19, p. 74): Christ foresaw his passion offered to the Father for the predestinate and elect, and so offered it efficaciously in effect; the whole Trinity accepted it efficaciously for them, and for no others was it efficaciously offered or accepted from eternity. By efficacious offering and acceptance he means offering joined to an absolute purpose to save those for whom it was so offered and accepted. Malderus, Bishop of Antwerp, on this argument rejects those who think Christ died equally for all as to efficacy, and concludes (p. 137) that, given predestination, Christ by his death conferred far more on these predestinate than on others.

source_text: Rat. 6. Sexto, argumentari possumus ab illa proportione quae est retinenda inter oblationem Christi pro hominibus, & orationem sive intercessionem pro eisdem. Orasse Christum sive intercessisse apud Patrem suum pro electis, ut fidem firmam & invictam usque ad extremum retinerent, & salutem efficaciter obtinerent, ex Ioann. xvii. atque ex oratione nominatim pro Petro facta, ne fides ejus deficeret, promptum est colligere. Et sane qui eximium illud donum perseverantiae specialibus personis speciali oratione Christi impetratum negaverit, is beneficium omnium beneficiorum spiritualium longe maximum libero arbitrio acceptum referret. Jam hoc posito, illud addam, Sicuti Christus specialiter oravit pro specialibus beneficiis in electos conferendis, ita specialiter seipsum obtulit pro eisdem beneficiis promerendis. De hac oratione & oblatione speciali Suarez ait, In 3. disp. 41. p. 635. Sicut Christus diversimode pro hominibus oravit, ita diversimode meruit: propter quod, licet omnium sit universalis Redemptor, & sufficiens causa salutis, speciali tamen modo est causa efficax salutis eorum quos sibi facit obedientes. Oratio igitur, qua Christus specialiter & efficaciter oravit pro electis, fundamentum habuit in oblatione, qua pro eisdem specialiter & efficaciter sese obtulit. Videtis vim argumenti; Quicquid Christus impetrat singularibus personis per specialem intercessionem, id promeruit iisdem apud Patrem per oblationem suiipsius ad eos specialiter pertinentem: Sed per intercessionem impetrat electis fidem, perseverantiam, ipsam denique salutem: Ergo, ut haec bona illis infallibiliter procuraret, specialiter sese pro iis obtulit. Non dubitat, inquit Vasquez, Christum peculiari oratione & voluntate merita sua illis applicasse qui praedestinati & electi fuerunt, In 1. qu. 23. art. 5. disp. 94. cap. 3.
english: Ratio 6. Sixth, keep the proportion between Christ’s offering for people and his prayer or intercession for them. From John 17, and from his named prayer for Peter that Peter’s faith not fail, it is plain that Christ interceded with the Father for the elect to keep a firm, unconquered faith to the end and obtain salvation efficaciously. Anyone who denies that the gift of perseverance was won for special persons by Christ’s special prayer would credit free choice with the greatest of all spiritual benefits. That granted, I add: just as Christ specially prayed for special benefits for the elect, so he specially offered himself to merit those same benefits. On this special prayer and offering Suarez says (On 3, disp. 41, p. 635): as Christ prayed in different ways for people, so he merited in different ways; though he is universal Redeemer of all and a sufficient cause of salvation, in a special mode he is the efficacious cause of salvation for those he makes obedient. So the prayer by which he specially and efficaciously prayed for the elect rests on the offering by which he specially and efficaciously offered himself for them. See the force: whatever Christ obtains for particular persons by special intercession, he merited for them with the Father by an offering specially pertaining to them. By intercession he obtains for the elect faith, perseverance, and salvation itself; therefore, to procure those goods for them infallibly, he specially offered himself for them. Vázquez does not doubt (On 1, q. 23, art. 5, disp. 94, ch. 3) that by peculiar prayer and will Christ applied his merits to those who were predestinate and elect.

source_text: Rat. 7. Christi mors meritumque est medium a Deo ordinatum ad exequendum & implendum aeternum Dei consilium de salute hominum. Si igitur Dei voluntas diversimode se habeat ad salutem hominum efficiendam, tum & mors Christi ab eodem diversimode intendetur in salutem humanam, diversimode applicabitur. Media siquidem semper adhibentur in ordine ad finem: & juxta intentionem agentis erit modus applicationis. Jam certum est & in confesso apud omnes sanos Theologos, Deum non eo modo velle salutem omnium quo vult salutem aliquorum: Ergo neque medium quo salutem humanam procurandam decrevit, scilicet mortem Christi, ita omnibus applicatum voluit sicut aliquibus. Unde liquet iis quibus Deus efficaci voluntate salutem decrevit, Christi mortem fuisse ita destinatam, ut merito ejusdem omnia ad salutem infallibiliter producendam necessaria ex eadem ad eos redundarent: Et e contra, quibus tali voluntate salutem minime decrevit, iis neque mortem Christi fuisse ad eundem modum destinatam. Mors igitur Christi ex speciali intentione Dei Patris illud sacrificium ad salutem hominum ordinantis, & Christi seipsum offerentis, ac Paternae voluntati conformantis, aliter electis destinata & applicata intelligitur, quos Deus decrevit per hanc mortem infallibiliter servare, aliter ceteris, quos Deus non impedit quin hac morte permittit suo vitio perire. Quisquis negat mortem Christi hoc discrimine oblatam pro hominibus, & applicatam ipsis hominibus, ille eadem opera negare potest Deum sapientissimum & potentissimum aut nosse aut posse media a se instituta, prout diversa ratio voluntatis suae exigit, diversimode diversis hominibus intendere & accommodare.
english: Ratio 7. Christ’s death and merit is the means God ordained to carry out his eternal counsel for human salvation. If God’s will stands differently toward effecting people’s salvation, then Christ’s death is likewise intended and applied differently toward that end. Means always serve the end, and the mode of application follows the agent’s intention. All sound theologians confess that God does not will everyone’s salvation in the same mode in which he wills some people’s. Therefore he did not will the means—Christ’s death—applied to all as it is applied to some. So for those for whom God by efficacious will decreed salvation, Christ’s death was destined so that by its merit everything needed to produce salvation infallibly would flow to them; for those for whom he did not so decree salvation, Christ’s death was not destined in that same mode. From the Father’s special intention in ordaining that sacrifice, and from Christ’s self-offering conformed to the Father’s will, the death is understood as destined and applied one way to the elect, whom God decreed to save infallibly through it, and another way to the rest, whom he allows to perish by their own fault even with this death. Whoever denies that discrimination in the offering and application can as easily deny that the wisest and most powerful God knows how—or is able—to intend and fit the means he instituted to different people as his will’s different reason requires.

source_text: Rat. 8. Certum est ex eventu, quosdam homines mortem Christi cum infinito ejusdem merito realiter & efficaciter ad salutem sibi applicare. Quaero igitur utrum haec applicatio facta sit secundum antecedaneam & efficacem intentionem Christi in cruce seipsum offerentis, an contra eandem, sive absque eadem praecedente. Si concesserint in Christo moriente antecedaneam & specialem voluntatem de hac efficaci applicatione quae omnibus electis, & solis electis contingit, habemus id ipsum quod evincere conamur, nempe hanc mortem ex speciali intentione Dei & Christi electis ut efficaciter applicandam destinari. Jam vero, contra Christi intentionem posse ullum hominem mortem ejus sibi efficaciter applicare, nemo dixerit. Id unum reliquum est, ut dicant fieri hanc applicationem efficacem ab iisdem hominibus pro libertate suae voluntatis absque praecedente ulla speciali & efficaci intentione Divinae voluntatis. At pietas vetat hoc asserere: Primo, quia in actibus bonis & salutiferis efficax Dei voluntas se habet antecedenter ad efficacem voluntatem humanam. Deus enim est qui in nobis operatur & velle & perficere, Phil. ii. 13. nec quicquam operatur in nobis antecedenter, quod non antecedenter decrevit operari. Secundo, quia in operibus hisce ad salutem pertinentibus nihil possumus sine Christo: Ioann. xv. 5. Sine me nihil potestis facere. At quod possumus per Christum, ejus rei faciundae potestatem accipimus propter Christi meritum: quod absque antecedanea & speciali intentione Christi morientis & merentis nemini assignatur. Quicunque igitur eximiam hanc gratiam obtinuit, meritum Christi sibi jam efficaciter applicaverit, fateri debet, se hanc ipsam applicandi facultatem prae aliis accepisse a speciali benignitate Dei Christique hoc suum meritum specialiter illi intendentis, destinantis, applicantis. Sic ipse eventus fructuosae applicationis in praedestinatis demonstrat fuisse in Christo offerente seipsum, & Deo acceptante hoc sacrificium, specialem & efficacem intentionem ejusdem applicationis quoad praedestinatos. Atque hoc est illud ipsum singulare privilegium electorum in morte Christi quod hac thesi nostra conamur stabilire.
english: Ratio 8. The event shows that some people really and efficaciously apply Christ’s death, with its infinite merit, to themselves for salvation. Was that application made according to Christ’s antecedent, efficacious intention in offering himself on the cross—or against it, or without it preceding? If they grant in the dying Christ an antecedent special will for this efficacious application that falls to all the elect and to them alone, we have what we aim to prove: that by God’s and Christ’s special intention this death is destined for the elect as to be applied efficaciously. No one will say a person can apply Christ’s death to himself efficaciously against Christ’s intention. The only remaining claim is that people make the application efficacious by free will without any preceding special, efficacious intention of the divine will. Piety forbids that. First, in good and saving acts God’s efficacious will stands before the human: “It is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish” (Phil. 2:13), and he works nothing in us antecedently that he did not antecedently decree to work. Second, in works that belong to salvation we can do nothing without Christ: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). What we can do through Christ we receive power to do because of Christ’s merit—which, without the dying and meriting Christ’s antecedent special intention, is assigned to no one. So whoever has obtained this excellent grace and already applied Christ’s merit to himself efficaciously must confess he received that applying faculty above others from the special kindness of God and of Christ, who specially intended, destined, and applied his merit to him. The fruitful application in the predestinate itself shows that in Christ offering himself, and in God accepting the sacrifice, there was a special efficacious intention of that application for the predestinate. And that is the singular privilege of the elect in Christ’s death this thesis aims to establish.

source_text: Rat. 9. Si ponamus Christi mortem ex ordinatione Dei & intentione Christi non meruisse praedestinatis efficacem applicationem, & infallibilem salutis consecutionem inde emanantem, illud incommodi sequetur, hoc meritum Mediatoris, juxta voluntatem & intentionem Patris illud acceptantis Filiiique illud exhibentis, non magis spectare ad electos quam praeteritos, sed ex aequo ad utrosque pertingere. Patet consequentia, quia concessum est, Ex voluntate Dei meritum Christi morientis ad omnes homines se extendere sub hac conditione, Si per fidem illud sibi applicaverint. Nisi ergo Christus morte sua intenderit electis hoc insuper mereri, ut per Fidem donatam fiat in illis haec fructuosa applicatio, nullum singulare privilegium in merito Christi illis assignatur. Nam Christi mors ex ordinatione Dei Iudae hoc meruit, ut potuerit sub conditione Fidei ad vitam aeternam pervenire: Petro igitur & illud insuper obtinuit, ut propter meritum Christi fidem perseverantem acciperet, caeteraque omnia spiritualia beneficia quae ad vitam aeternam infallibiliter consequendam requiruntur. Atque huc spectat illa Apostoli ratiocinatio, Rom. viii. 32. Ubi de praedestinatorum privilegiis disserit, Qui proprio Filio non pepercit, sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit eum, quomodo non etiam cum eo omnia nobis donabit? Quo in loco sicut specialem quandam vocationem praedestinatorum antea innuuerat, quam appellavit vocationem secundum propositum, ita & specialem quandam oblationem Christi pro eisdem praedestinatis designat, quam licet appellare oblationem secundum propositum, id est, cum proposito certo gratiam efficacem conferendi electis, eosdemque merito hujus mortis ad vitam infallibiliter perducendi. Qui tollunt hoc discrimen intentionis Divinae, quoad mortem Christi, in relatione ad electos & praeteritos consideratam, illi, (ut vere Bannesius In 1. quaest. 23. art. 5. pag. 296. 297.) faciunt meritum Christi nihilo perfectius esse causam salutis praedestinatorum quam reproborum. Quia quod attinet ad sufficientiam meriti, aeque respicit omnes; sed differentia est in hoc, quod quibusdam applicatur illud meritum, quibusdam vero non. Ergo (si applicatio ipsa quoad electos non cadat sub merito Christi) meritum Christi aequaliter respiciet praedestinatos & reprobes. Haec ille.
english: Ratio 9. Suppose Christ’s death, by God’s ordination and Christ’s intention, did not merit for the predestinate an efficacious application and the infallible obtaining of salvation that flows from it. Then this follows: the Mediator’s merit, under the Father’s accepting will and the Son’s exhibiting will, regards the elect no more than the passed-by, but reaches both alike. The consequence is clear, since it is granted that by God’s will the dying Christ’s merit extends to all under the condition: if by faith they apply it to themselves. Unless Christ by his death also meant to merit for the elect that, through faith given, this fruitful application be made in them, no singular privilege in his merit is assigned to them. By God’s ordination Christ’s death merited for Judas that he could, under the condition of faith, reach eternal life; for Peter it obtained besides that, because of Christ’s merit, he receive persevering faith and all other spiritual benefits required to obtain eternal life infallibly. Paul’s reasoning in Romans 8:32 looks here, treating the predestinate’s privileges: “He who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how will he not also with him give us all things?” Just as he had hinted a special calling of the predestinate—“according to purpose”—so he marks a special offering of Christ for those same predestinate, an offering according to purpose: with a sure purpose to confer efficacious grace on the elect and lead them infallibly to life by this death’s merit. Those who erase that discrimination of divine intention in Christ’s death toward elect and passed-by, as Báñez truly says (On 1, q. 23, art. 5, pp. 296–297), make Christ’s merit no more perfect a cause of the predestinate’s salvation than of the reprobate’s. As to sufficiency the merit regards all equally; the difference is that it is applied to some and not to others. So if application itself for the elect does not fall under Christ’s merit, that merit regards predestinate and reprobate alike. So Báñez.

source_text: Rat. 10. Si Christus non obtulerit seipsum Deo Patri cum peculiari quadam, & absoluta voluntate redimendi & efficaciter salvandi electos merito mortis suae; tum gratia efficax & vita aeterna non aliter praeparata esset, aut donata ullis hominibus in Christo, quam fuit in Adamo. Possibilitas enim habendi gratiam & vitam aeternam sub conditione ex libero arbitrio nostro pendente, in primo Adamo fuit concessa humano generi.
english: Ratio 10. If Christ did not offer himself to the Father with a peculiar absolute will to redeem and save the elect efficaciously by his death's merit, then efficacious grace and eternal life would be prepared or given to no one in Christ on any better footing than they were in Adam. The first Adam already gave the race the chance of grace and eternal life under a condition that hangs on our free choice.

source_text: Si ergo Christus morte sua non meruerit gratiam vitamque ullis hominibus absolute, sed omnibus promiscue sub hac incerta conditione, Si voluerint oblatam gratiam admittere, in ipsum credere, & in Fide perseverare, atque interim libero uniuscujusque arbitrio committat & relinquat, utrum velit credere, velit perseverare necne; profecto quod attinet ad ipsum modum & certitudinem obtinendae gratiae efficacis & vitae aeternae, nihilo meliore conditione uteremur in Christo, quam usi fuimus in Adamo.
english: So if by his death Christ did not merit grace and life for anyone absolutely, but only for all alike under the uncertain condition that they choose to receive the offered grace, believe in him, and persevere in faith, leaving to each person's free choice whether to believe and persevere, then we would be no better off in Christ than we were in Adam. That is so as to how and how surely we obtain efficacious grace and eternal life.

source_text: At hoc repugnat sacrae Scripturae, quae gratiam & vitam aeternam in Christo omnibus salvandis praeparatam & donandam suspendit ex certo proposito beneplaciti Divini, non ex contingente motu arbitrii humani; quod in controversia De Electione & Praeteritione ostendetur.
english: But that clashes with Scripture. Scripture hangs the grace and eternal life prepared and to be given in Christ to all who will be saved on God's sure purpose of good pleasure, not on a contingent turn of human choice. The treatise on Election and Passing-by will show this.

source_text: Repugnat etiam orthodoxorum Patrum sententiae, qui Pelagianis sese opposuerunt, ac nominatim Augustini, De corrept. & grat. cap. 11. ubi cum ostendisset, qualis ea gratia fuerit quae primo Adamo data fuit, De gratia praedestinatis in Christo praeparata & donata sic loquitur, Tanto amplius datur adjutorium gratiae per Jesum Christum, quibus id dare Deo placuit, ut non solum adsit sine quo permanere non possumus, etiamsi velimus, verum etiam tantum ac tale sit ut velimus. Est quippe in nobis per hanc Dei gratiam in bono recipiendo & perseveranter tenendo non solum posse quod volumus, verum etiam velle quod possumus.
english: It also clashes with the orthodox Fathers who opposed the Pelagians—above all Augustine, On Rebuke and Grace chapter 11. After showing what grace was given to the first Adam, he says of the grace prepared and given to the predestinate in Christ: “So much more largely is the help of grace given through Jesus Christ to those to whom God was pleased to give it, that it not only is present—without which we cannot remain even if we will—but also is so great and of such a kind that we will. For through this grace of God, in receiving the good and holding it perseveringly, there is in us not only the ability to do what we will, but also the will to do what we can.”

source_text: Haec gratia quae datur propter Christum solis electis, quaeque in illis solis producit effectum fructuosae applicationis & salutis, non ex speciali aliqua operatione arbitrii humani, sed ex speciali decreto voluntatis Divinae ad eos dimanat, idque mediante merito Christi. Ergo Christi meritum fuit iisdem speciali quodam modo a Deo destinatum, ab ipso Christo applicatum.
english: This grace, given for Christ's sake to the elect alone, and producing in them alone the fruitful application that saves, flows to them not from some special act of human choice but from a special decree of God's will, and that through Christ's merit. So Christ's merit was destined for those same persons in a special way by God, and applied by Christ himself.

source_text: Rat. 11. Est ea sententia a nobis rejicienda quae aut plane eadem est, aut saltem arctam habet cognationem cum damnato Pelagianorum dogmate: Illorum autem opinio, qui statuunt mortem Christi ex parte voluntatis & intentionis Divinae aequaliter se habere ad omnes quoad efficaciam, ex parte autem voluntatis humanae evenire, quod in eventu fiat efficax & fructuosa quibusdam, ad Pelagium quam proxime accedit. Orthodoxi autem, ad accuratam hujus rei considerationem a Pelagio expergefacti, & contra semper docuerunt, Fructuosam sive efficacem applicationem meritorum Christi a gratia praedestinationis pendere, per quam quibusdam misericorditer confertur Fides & ipsa bona voluntas, quae aliis justo Dei judicio denegatur.
english: Ratio 11. We must reject any view that is the same as—or at least close kin to—the condemned Pelagian dogma. Those who hold that on God’s will and intention Christ’s death stands equally efficacious toward all, while on the human will’s side it happens that in the event it becomes fruitful for some, come as near Pelagius as can be. The orthodox, roused by Pelagius to weigh this carefully, have always taught against him that fruitful application of Christ’s merits hangs on the grace of predestination, by which faith and even the good will itself are mercifully given to some and, by God’s just judgment, denied to others.

source_text: Quod Pelagianum sit, fructum mortis Christi, id est, vitam aeternam, a speciali intentione Dei ad specialem operationem liberi arbitrii transferre, patet ex Prosperi Epistola ad Augustinum. Patet etiam ex Hilarii ad eundem Augustinum Epistola, ubi Reliquiae Pelagianorum in morte Christi vitam aeternam sic omnibus propositam & expositam opinantur, ut singulare aliquod sive speciale propositum Dei de salvandis electis per hanc mortem Christi prorsus pernegent, & totum hoc discrimen servatorum per mortem Christi & non-servatorum ad humanas voluntates revocent. Jam & contra, orthodoxos speciale & arcanum propositum agnovisse in Deo acceptante sacrificium mortis Christi, Christoque illud offerente, de applicatione ejusdem efficaci & fructuosa ad certas personas, non minus clarum est ex libris Augustini De Praedestinatione sanctorum, De Bono perseverantiae, aliisque contra Pelagianos & Semipelagianos conscriptis, in quibus haec, de speciali voluntate salvandi electos per Christum, si non unica, primaria tamen conclusio est. De Prospero & Fulgentio idem dici potest, qui passim asserunt efficacem salutis consecutionem in Christo ab efficaci & speciali voluntate Divina Christum electis speciali modo destinante, non a libero hominum arbitrio Christi mortem ac merita sibi, prout contigerit, applicante.
english: That it is Pelagian to shift the fruit of Christ’s death—eternal life—from God’s special intention to a special act of free choice is plain from Prosper’s Letter to Augustine. Hilary’s Letter to Augustine shows the same: the Pelagian remnants treat eternal life in Christ’s death as so set before all that they flatly deny any singular purpose of God to save the elect by that death, and put the whole divide between the saved and the unsaved down to human wills. Against them, the orthodox saw a special hidden purpose in God accepting Christ’s death-sacrifice and in Christ offering it—toward efficacious fruitful application to certain persons. That is clear from Augustine’s On the Predestination of the Saints, On the Good of Perseverance, and his other anti-Pelagian and anti-Semipelagian books, where the special will to save the elect through Christ is if not the only then the chief conclusion. Prosper and Fulgentius say the same throughout: efficacious obtaining of salvation in Christ comes from God’s efficacious special will destinating Christ to the elect in a special way, not from human free choice applying Christ’s death and merits to itself as chance may have it.

source_text: Sed ne nudis nominibus pugnare videamur, ultimum nostrum argumentum petetur ab expressis testimoniis Patrum & modernorum, qui praedestinatis in hac morte Christi specialem praerogativam assignant, quae alia non est quam infallibilis consecutio gratiae & gloriae secundum specialem Dei ordinationem a merito Christi morientis, & pro illis speciali quodam intuitu sese offerentis, derivata. Prodeat primo S. Augustinus. 1. Praeclarum est illud testimonium, In Joh. tract. 48. pag. 352. tom. 9. Quomodo istos dixit, NON ESTIS EX OVIBUS MEIS? Quia videbat eos ad sempiternum interitum praedestinatos, non ad vitam aeternam sui sanguinis pretio comparatos. Paulo post, De ovibus illis nec lupus rapit, nec fur tollit, nec latro interficit. Securus est de numero earum, qui pro eis novit quid dedit. Ex quibus verbis duo colligimus: Unum, Servatorem nostrum pro praedestinatis redimendis pretium sui sanguinis obtulisse speciali quodam modo, eo nimirum ex quo infallibilis salus eorundem consequatur. Alterum, pro praeteritis sive non-praedestinatis haud obtulisse sanguinem suum eo modo: unde negantur ad vitam aeternam sui sanguinis pretio comparati: quod intelligendum est de absoluta & efficaci ordinatione ad vitam aeternam per Christi mortem implenda, & in actum deducenda.
english: Lest we seem to argue by empty labels, our last proof comes from the express witnesses of the Fathers and of later writers who give the predestined, in this death of Christ, a special privilege — nothing other than the sure attainment of grace and glory by God's special ordination, drawn from the dying Christ's merit and from his offering himself for them with a particular regard. Let Augustine speak first. 1. Outstanding is the word in In John, tractate 48 (vol. 9, p. 352): How did he say of those, YOU ARE NOT OF MY SHEEP? Because he saw them appointed to everlasting ruin, not bought for eternal life by his blood's price. Soon after: Of those sheep neither wolf snatches, nor thief carries off, nor robber kills. He who knows what he gave for them is sure of their number. Two points follow: first, our Savior offered his blood's price for redeeming the predestined in a special way — the way from which their sure salvation follows; second, for the passed-over or non-predestined he did not offer it that way, so they are denied to have been bought for eternal life by that price — meaning an absolute, efficacious ordering to eternal life that Christ's death is to carry out and bring into act.

source_text: 2. Huic affine est illud alterum, Serm. 56. De verbis Domini, pag. 194. tom. 10. Erant praedestinati nondum congregati. Hos tamen noverat qui praedestinaverat, noverat qui redimere sanguine suo venerat. Videbat eos nondum videntes eum; noverat eos nondum credentes in eum. Quid apertius quam Christum venisse in mundum ut praedestinatos sanguine suo redimeret, atque redimeret efficaciter & infallibiliter ad participationem vitae aeternae perducendos; quo modo nunquam apud se decrevit redimere non-electos.
english: 2. Closely related is Sermon 56 On the Lord's words (vol. 10, p. 194): The predestined were not yet gathered. Still, he who had predestined them knew them, and he who had come to redeem them with his blood knew them. He saw them while they did not yet see him; he knew them while they did not yet believe in him. Nothing is clearer: Christ came into the world to redeem the predestined by his blood — and to redeem them efficaciously and infallibly as people to be brought through to share eternal life. He never resolved with himself to redeem the non-elect in that way.

source_text: 3. Tertium ejusdem Augustini testimonium proferemus ex libro De natura & grat. cap. 5. quod ita se habet, Qui liberantur, non vasa meritorum suorum, sed vasa misericordiae nominantur. Cujus misericordiae, nisi illius qui Christum Jesum misit in hunc mundum peccatores salvos facere? Quos praescivit, & praedestinavit, & vocavit, & justificavit, & glorificavit. Quasi dixisset, Deum ex specialis misericordiae decreto misisse Christum pro liberandis & salvandis praedestinatis efficaciter & infallibiliter; quo sensu illi soli dicuntur vasa misericordiae. Supervacaneum esset ex Augustino plura congerere, cujus sententia de absoluta praedestinatione quorundam ad vitam aeternam, deque aeterna datione eorundem Christo Mediatori, ut ab eo infallibiliter perducantur ad eandem, est omnibus in Augustino versatis notissima. Quae praedestinatio, donatio, perductio ad vitam aeternam, absque hac speciali intentione mortem ac merita sua illis applicandi, neque intelligi, neque cogitari potest. Videte caput 18. De Praed. Sanct. De bono persev. cap. 7. De cor. & grat. cap. 9.
english: 3. A third witness from the same Augustine is On nature and grace, chapter 5: Those who are delivered are called not vessels of their own merits, but vessels of mercy. Whose mercy, if not his who sent Christ Jesus into this world to save sinners? Whom he foreknew, predestined, called, justified, and glorified. As if to say: by a decree of special mercy God sent Christ to deliver and save the predestined efficaciously and infallibly — and in that sense they alone are vessels of mercy. Piling up more Augustine would be wasted work. Anyone at home in him knows his teaching on the absolute predestination of some to eternal life, and on the eternal gift of those same persons to Christ the Mediator so that he may lead them to that life without fail. That predestination, gift, and leading cannot be understood — or even thought — without this special intention of applying his death and merits to them. See On the Predestination of the Saints 18; On the gift of perseverance 7; On rebuke and grace 9.

source_text: 4. Quartum testimonium ex Ambrosio peti potest, cujus haec sunt verba, Et Christus passus est pro omnibus, pro nobis tamen specialiter passus est, quia pro Ecclesia passus est. Itaque non est dubium quod plus debeat quae plus accepit, lib. 6. cap. 7. Lucae. Hic videmus ex mente Ambrosii fuisse specialem Christi patientis ad Ecclesiam suam intuitum, unde factum est ut ea ex passione Christi specialem fructum perceperit. Ita igitur Christum pro omnibus passum asserit, ut tamen voluntas & intentio Christi patientis haud omnes ex aequo respiciat, sed singulari quodam modo feratur in corpus suum mysticum, id est, primogenitorum Ecclesiam, quam sanguine suo voluit sibi acquirere, Spiritu conjungere ad infrustrabilem vitae aeternae participationem. Non passus est pro omnibus speciali hac intentione.
english: 4. Ambrose supplies a fourth witness: And Christ suffered for all, yet for us he suffered specially, because he suffered for the Church. So she who received more doubtless owes more (On Luke, book 6, chapter 7). On Ambrose's reading, the suffering Christ had a special regard for his Church, and from that she drew a special fruit of the passion. He can say Christ suffered for all, and still hold that the will and intention of the suffering Christ does not regard everyone alike, but turns in a singular way upon his mystical body — the Church of the firstborn — which he meant by his blood to make his own and by the Spirit to join to a share in eternal life that cannot fail. He did not suffer for all under that special intention.

source_text: 5. Ambrosium sequatur Remigius Episcopus Rhemensis, qui haec scribit, in Rom. viii. Quos praedestinavit sive praefinivit secum regnaturos in aeterna beatitudine, hos vocavit, hos & justificavit per passionem suam, per baptismum & fidem exornatam bonis operibus, & justificavit usque ad finem seculi. Paulo post, in haec verba, Qui proprio Filio non pepercit, id est, inquit Remigius, a morte non servavit, sed pro nobis omnibus praedestinatis ad vitam aeternam illum tradidit. Quae omnia demonstrant Christum pro electis, & solis electis, cum proposito certo eosdem salvandi passum: quae est ipsissima specialis intentio, quam nos stabilire conamur, quamque ad solos electos restringendam tuemur, in hac Christi oblatione.
english: 5. After Ambrose comes Remigius of Rheims on Romans 8: Those he predestined — or marked out beforehand — to reign with him in eternal blessedness he also called and justified through his passion, through baptism and faith adorned with good works, and he justified them to the world's end. Soon after, on Who did not spare his own Son, Remigius says: he did not keep him from death, but delivered him for all of us predestined to eternal life. That shows Christ suffered for the elect, and for them alone, with a fixed purpose to save them — the very special intention we are establishing, and which we insist must be limited to the elect alone in this offering of Christ.

source_text: 6. Fulgentius, De Incarn. & grat. Jesu Chr. cap. 29. p. 92. Biblioth. Patr. tom. 6. Hi qui voluntatem Dei, qua omnes homines vult salvos fieri, aequalem circa redimendos & damnandos existimant, cum interrogati fuerint cur Deus velit omnes homines salvos fieri, nec tamen omnes salvi fiant, quid respondebunt? Innuit doctissimus Fulgentius, Deum speciali voluntate illorum salutem per Christum procurandam decrevisse qui de facto salvantur; eosque qui contrarium affirmant, nihil solidi habere quod respondeant, quando urgentur ut ostendant, unde hoc discrimen oriatur, quod quidam morte Christi reapse salvantur, alii non salvantur. Ad humanarum voluntatum discrimen hoc revocari non posse demonstrat. cap. 30. & 31. 7. Adjungo aliud testimonium ejusdem Fulgentii, lib. 3. De verit. Praedest. Quos Deus praedestinavit in adoptionem Filiorum, hos non solum ad praemium glorificationis sed ad gratiam justificationis ante mundi constitutionem in Christo praedestinatos, & hujus praedestinationis beneficio secundum propositum vocatos & justificatos, nullus debet ambigere Christianus. Qui non ambigit electos Dei filios fuisse in Christo tam ad gratiam, quam ad gloriam ante mundi constitutionem praedestinatos, ille ultro fatebitur, mortem meritumque Christi fuisse speciali quadam ratione pro eisdem electis ordinatum & acceptatum, ut inde possent hanc gratiam & gloriam sibi destinatam infallibiliter obtinere.
english: 6. Fulgentius, On the Incarnation and grace of Jesus Christ 29 (Bibliotheca Patrum, vol. 6, p. 92): Those who treat God's will that all be saved as the same toward the redeemed and the damned — when asked why God wills all to be saved and yet not all are — what answer have they? Fulgentius implies that God by a special will decreed to procure, through Christ, the salvation of those who are in fact saved; and that their opponents have nothing solid left when pressed to explain why some are actually saved by Christ's death and others are not. He shows this difference cannot be reduced to a difference of human wills (chs. 30-31). 7. Another from the same Fulgentius, On the truth of Predestination, book 3: No Christian should doubt that those God predestined to the adoption of sons were predestined in Christ before the world's foundation not only to the reward of glory but to the grace of justification, and by that predestination's benefit called and justified according to purpose. Anyone who grants that God's elect sons were so predestined in Christ to grace and glory will freely admit that Christ's death and merit were ordained and accepted in a special way for those same elect, so that from them they might obtain without fail the grace and glory marked out for them.

source_text: 8. Paschasius, Biblioth. Patr. tom. 9. pag. 930. in illa verba Matth. i. 21. Saluum faciet populum suum a peccatis, sic scribit, Hinc Zacharias inquit, Et fecit REDEMPTIONEM PLEBIS SUAE IN DOMO DAVID PUERI SUI. Ergo quam sua praescivit, illam proculdubio venit salvare; reliquos omnes occulto suo judicio in massa damnationis reliquit. Quibus verbis docet Christum venisse in mundum, ac mortem subiisse, speciali quadam intentione salvandi praedestinatos, quam specialem intentionem de aliorum salute efficienda minime habuit, utcunque omnibus sub conditione Fidei salutem parabilem reddere voluerit. 9. Gregorius Magnus, moral. lib. 22. cap. 18. pag. 132. Unigenito Dei Filio pro homine interpellare, est apud coaeternum Patrem seipsum hominem demonstrare: eique pro humana natura rogasse, est eandem naturam in Divinitatis suae celsitudine suscepisse. Interpellat igitur pro nobis non voce, sed miseratione, quia quod damnari in electis noluit, suscipiendo liberavit. Notanda sunt imprimis illa ultima verba, quibus clare indicatur, Christum in toto suo officio Mediatorio specialem intuitum habuisse ad electos infallibiliter liberandos. 10. Bernardus in Psalmum, Qui habitat in adjutorio Altissimi, vers. 9. Christus, inquit, pro amicis mortuus est, hoc est acquirendis, videlicet ut amicos faceret ex inimicis. Paulo post, Sic ergo Christus secundum tempus pro impiis mortuus est, secundum praedestinationem autem pro fratribus & amicis. Quod perinde est ac si dixisset, Christum morientem in cruce ad praedestinatos suos fratres & futuros amicos singularem respectum habuisse.
english: 8. Paschasius (Bibliotheca Patrum, vol. 9, p. 930) on Matthew 1:21, He shall save his people from their sins: Hence Zechariah says, And he made REDEMPTION OF HIS PEOPLE IN THE HOUSE OF DAVID HIS SERVANT. So the people he foreknew as his he surely came to save; all the rest he left, by his hidden judgment, in the mass of damnation. That teaches Christ came and died with a special intention to save the predestined — an intention he did not have for making others' salvation actual, even while he willed to make salvation obtainable for all under the condition of faith. 9. Gregory the Great, Morals 22.18 (p. 132): For the Only-begotten to intercede for man is to present himself as man before the coeternal Father; to ask for human nature is to have taken that nature up into his Divinity's height. So he intercedes for us not by voice but by compassion, because what he would not have damned in the elect he set free by taking it up. Those last words show plainly that in his whole Mediator's work Christ kept a special eye on freeing the elect without fail. 10. Bernard on Psalm He who dwells in the help of the Most High, verse 9: Christ died for friends — that is, for friends to be won, to make friends out of enemies. A little later: So according to time Christ died for the ungodly, but according to predestination for brothers and friends — as much as to say that Christ dying on the cross had a singular regard for his predestined brothers and future friends.

source_text: Sed missis antiquioribus, ad Scholasticos & modernos Pontificios descendamus: Qui sic defendunt Christum pro omnibus mortuum, ut interim agnoscant pro Electis solis mortuum cum speciali intentione mortem suam eisdem applicandi ad infallibilem consecutionem vitae aeternae. 1. Ordiamur a Magistro Scholasticorum Petro Lombardo; Christus se in ara crucis obtulit pro omnibus, quantum ad pretii sufficientiam; sed pro electis tantum, quantum ad efficaciam, quia praedestinatis tantum salutem efficit, lib. 3. dist. 20 litt. c. Ratio quam subnectit Magister, cur Christus pro solis electis mortuus dicatur quantum ad efficaciam, est observatione dignissima. Non enim illam affert quam Pelagiani & Arminiani attulissent, scilicet quod illi tantum praevidebantur, pro libertate arbitrii sui per gratiam excitati, ut Christum sibi applicaturi, sed quod in illis tantum pro benignitate specialis suae misericordiae salutem effecerit. Quod autem morte sua in Electis effecit, proculdubio efficere decrevit. Atque haec est illa specialis intentio sub qua mortem Christi ad solos electos relatam, & ordinatam profitemur.
english: Setting the older writers aside, we come down to the Scholastics and modern Romanists. They defend Christ as having died for all, yet they also grant he died for the elect alone with a special intention to apply that death to them so that eternal life follows without fail. 1. Start with Peter Lombard, master of the Scholastics: Christ offered himself on the cross's altar for all as to the price's sufficiency, but for the elect only as to efficacy, because he effects salvation only for the predestined (Sentences 3, dist. 20, litt. c). The reason he gives for calling Christ's death efficacious for the elect alone is worth marking. He does not say what Pelagians and Arminians would say — that only those were foreseen who, stirred by grace in free choice, would apply Christ to themselves — but that in them alone, by the kindness of special mercy, he wrought salvation. What his death wrought in the elect he surely decreed to work. That is the special intention under which we say Christ's death is related and ordained to the elect alone.

source_text: 2. Aquinas, part. 3. qu. 24. art. 4. Deus praeordinavit nostram salutem, ab aeterno praedestinando ut per Jesum Christum compleretur. Loquitur Aquinas de hominibus electis, atque asserit Deum ab aeterno ordinasse, ut eorum salus per Jesum Christum infallibiliter compleretur. Quaero igitur quomodo Christus huic aeternae ordinationi Patris sui sese conformem exhibuerit, si in passione sua salutifera ad electorum salutem infallibiliter efficiendam & complendam merita sua peculiari modo non applicaverit? Concedenda est itaque specialis intentio Dei hanc hostiam acceptantis, & Christi seipsum offerentis, restricta ad solos electos, quatenus passio Christi cum infallibili effectu salutis in singularibus personis conjungitur.
english: 2. Aquinas (ST III q.24 a.4): God preordained our salvation by eternally predestining that it be completed through Jesus Christ. He is speaking of the elect, and he holds that from eternity God ordained their salvation to be finished through Christ without fail. How then could Christ have matched that eternal ordination of his Father if, in his saving passion, he did not apply his merits in a peculiar way to effect and complete the elect's salvation without fail? So we must grant a special intention — God accepting this victim, Christ offering himself — restricted to the elect alone, so far as Christ's passion is joined to an infallible saving effect in particular persons.

source_text: 3. Idem, Quaest. Disp. De grat. Christi, art. 7. resp. ad 4. Meritum Christi quantum ad sufficientiam aequaliter se habet ad omnes, non autem quantum ad efficaciam: quod accidit partim ex libero arbitrio, partim ex Divina electione, per quam quibusdam misericorditer effectus meritorum Christi confertur, quibusdam vero justo judicio subtrahitur. Quod ait Aquinas, partim ex libero arbitrio accidere quod merita Christi, quantum ad efficaciam, non se habeant aequaliter ad omnes, id intelligendum est ex parte perditorum, qui libero arbitrio se avertunt a fonte salutis: Quod autem dixit, hanc inaequalitatem partim ex Divina electione accidere, id intelligendum est ex parte servatorum, qui, Deo secundum beneplacitum electionis specialiter illorum miserante, accipiunt a fonte salutis, quicquid necessarium est ad salutem illorum efficiendam. Hanc fuisse mentem Aquinatis patet ex responsione ad argumentum ultimum, ubi dicit, Hoc ipsum hominibus a Deo conferri gratis, quod effectum meriti Christi consequantur. Si effectus meritorum Christi ex Divina electione certis quibusdam personis misericorditer confertur, aliisque interim denegatur, quis dubitet Christum, Divinae electionis & suae vocationis optime conscium, pro iisdem personis seipsum & merita sua specialiter obtulisse, & pretio mortis in se sufficientissimo addidisse insuper efficacissimam & singularem voluntatis intentionem pro salute horum electorum operanda? Huc spectant illa, Johann. x. 15. Animam meam pono pro ovibus meis — nempe singulari quadam intentione eas efficaciter redimendi, liberandi, & ad vitam perducendi, uti ex toto discursu Servatoris eo in loco colligi potest.
english: 3. The same Aquinas, On the Grace of Christ (disp. q.), art. 7 ad 4: Christ's merit stands equally toward all as to sufficiency, not as to efficacy. That inequality comes partly from free choice, partly from divine election, by which the effect of Christ's merits is mercifully given to some and justly withheld from others. When he says free choice partly explains unequal efficacy, read that of the lost, who turn themselves from the fountain of salvation. When he says divine election partly explains it, read that of the saved, who, under God's special mercy according to election's good pleasure, receive from that fountain whatever is needed to effect their salvation. His reply to the last objection shows the mind: God freely confers on people that they obtain the effect of Christ's merit. If election mercifully gives that effect to some and denies it to others, who can doubt that Christ — knowing election and his own calling — specially offered himself and his merits for those persons, and added to a price already sufficient in itself a most effectual, singular will to work their salvation? John 10:15 points the same way: I lay down my life for my sheep — with a singular intention to redeem, free, and bring them to life, as the whole discourse there shows.

source_text: 4. Scotus in 3. Sentent. dist. 19. quest. unica, multa habet quae valde conducunt ad sententiam nostram illustrandam, illud inprimis, Sicut Verbum praevidit passionem suam Patri offerendam pro electis, sic eam efficaciter obtulit in effectum, & tota Trinitas pro eis passionem efficaciter acceptavit, & pro nullis aliis fuit efficaciter oblata, nec ab aeterno acceptata. Agnoscit Scotus, ex aeterno decreto totius Trinitatis passionem Christi fuisse singulari quodam modo & speciali intentione oblatam & acceptatam pro electis. 5. Hugo de S. Victore, De Sacr. fid. lib. 1. part. 8. cap. 7. Ubi tractationem instituit De passione Christi, sic scribit, Natura humana per peccatum corrupta fuit, & tota per peccatum damnationi debita erat, & idcirco, si tota damnata fuisset, injustitia non fuisset. Venit autem gratia, & elegit quosdam de massa universitatis per misericordiam ad salutem, quosdam autem per justitiam deseruit ad damnationem. Aperte docet Hugo, Christum in mundum venientem, & pro peccatis humani generis sese offerentem, habuisse respectum singularem ad electos, quos de massa universitatis elegit, quosque ad salutem pro aeterno Dei beneplacito per merita mortis suae perducere decrevit, & de facto semper perducit.
english: 4. Scotus (Sentences III, dist. 19, single q.) has much that illustrates our view. First: just as the Word foresaw his passion to be offered to the Father for the elect, so he offered it effectually unto its effect, and the whole Trinity effectually accepted that passion for them; for no others was it effectually offered or eternally accepted. So Scotus grants that by the Trinity's eternal decree Christ's passion was offered and accepted for the elect in a singular way, with special intention. 5. Hugh of St Victor (On the Sacraments I.8.7), treating Christ's passion: Human nature was corrupted by sin and wholly owed to damnation; if all had been damned, that would not have been injustice. But grace came and chose some from the mass of the whole by mercy unto salvation, and left some by justice unto damnation. Hugh teaches plainly that Christ, coming and offering himself for the race's sins, kept a singular eye on the elect he chose from that mass, whom he decreed — and in fact always does — to bring to salvation by his death's merits according to God's eternal good pleasure.

source_text: 6. Cajetanus, in Rom. viii. explicans haec verba, Qui proprio Filio suo non pepercit, sed pro nobis omnibus eum tradidit, quomodo non cum illo omnia nobis donabit? sic scribit, Animadverterat Paulus, quod praeallegata ratio tot donorum non efficaciter inferebat Deum omnia in bonum electis cooperari, sed Deum illis cooperari in bonum, & propterea ut efficaciter concluderet quod OMNIA, adjinxit, quod Deus liberaliter donavit etiam Filium pro electis, ut hinc inferret quod omnia cum Filio electis donata sunt. Non possunt haec dicta Cajetani ad illam universalem Christi donationem accommodari, qua toti mundo datus ex aequo intelligitur: nam hoc posito, Deus omnia omnibus hominibus ex aequo daret: quod manifeste falsum est. Specialis ergo quaedam donatio necessario concedenda est, juxta quam Christus solis electis datus intelligatur, & quae sola trahat post se infallibilem & certissimam donationem omnium rerum ad salutem necessariarum.
english: 6. Cajetan on Romans 8: He who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how will he not also with him give us all things? Paul saw that the earlier chain of gifts did not yet prove effectually that God works all things for the elect's good — only that he works with them unto good. So, to conclude ALL THINGS effectually, he added that God freely gave even the Son for the elect, and from that inferred that with the Son all things are given to them. Cajetan's words cannot be bent to a universal gift of Christ given equally to the whole world: if that were so, God would give all things equally to every human being — which is plainly false. A special donation must be granted, under which Christ is given to the elect alone, and which alone carries after it an infallible, most certain gift of everything needed for salvation.

source_text: 7. Stapletonus, Promptuar. Moral. Dominic. 2. post Pasch. pag. 254. Christus moriens efficaciter quidem pro solis amicis mortuus est, idque pro futuris amicis post conversionem singulorum, non pro iis qui antea amici fuerant. Non veretur hic Papista singularem Christi morientis intentionem quoad Electos agnoscere. Nam hi sunt illi amici post conversionem futuri, pro quibus efficaciter redimendis Christus animam suam posuit, quando cum caeteris impii, inimici, peccatores, in peccatis mortui exstiterunt. Mortuus quidem dicitur pro omnibus hominibus, sed quoad sufficientiam: pro ovibus autem, sive electis suis, quoad hanc efficaciam, id est, cum singulari intentione ex merito mortis suae dandi illis gratiam illam efficacem unde credant & salventur. 8. Estius, ad illa verba, Tit. ii. 14. Qui dedit semetipsum pro nobis, Hoc est, inquit, qui in assumpta carne tradidit semetipsum, sive pro omnibus hominibus, sive speciatim pro electis, in quorum persona Paulus saepe loquitur. Nam pretium mortis Christi sufficit quidem omnibus redimendis & salvandis, sed solis ad salutem applicatur electis. Hactenus ille. Duo hic innuit Estius: Unum, Christi oblationem generalem respectum ad omnes, ac specialem ad electos habuisse; Alterum, Hunc specialem respectum in eo constitui oportere, quod cum intentione certi applicandi sit conjunctus. Non enim dixit, Soli Electi hanc mortem Christi viribus liberi arbitrii sibi applicant ad salutem, sed, Hisce solis applicatur ad salutem, Dei scilicet eligentis, & hoc tantum bonum electis suis ex Christi morte intendentis, favore speciali.
english: 7. Stapleton (Moral Promptuary, Second Sunday after Easter, p. 254): Dying, Christ died effectually for friends alone — for friends-to-be after each one's conversion, not for those who were already friends. This Romanist does not shrink from granting Christ's dying a singular intention toward the elect. They are the future friends after conversion for whose effectual redemption he laid down his life while, with the rest, they were still ungodly, enemies, sinners, dead in sins. He is said to have died for all humans as to sufficiency; for his sheep — his elect — as to this efficacy, that is, with a singular intention, from his death's merit, to give them the effectual grace by which they believe and are saved. 8. Estius on Titus 2:14, Who gave himself for us: that is, who in assumed flesh delivered himself up, whether for all humans or specially for the elect, in whose person Paul often speaks. Christ's death-price suffices to redeem and save all, yet is applied unto salvation to the elect alone. Estius thus hints two things: Christ's offering had a general respect to all and a special to the elect; and that special respect must be defined as joined to an intention of applying it with certainty. He did not say the elect alone apply Christ's death to themselves by free choice's powers, but that it is applied unto salvation to them alone — by electing God, intending this good for his elect from Christ's death by special favor.

source_text: 9. Venio ad Jesuitas, qui utcunque universalem gratiam, & universalem redemtionem defendant, tamen hanc specialem & efficacem salutiferae passionis ordinationem & intentionem quoad solos electos non audent inficiari. Pro reliquis loquantur duo ex antesignanis, Suarez, & Vasquez. Suarez, in 3. Aquin. qu. 19. Disp. pag. 635. §. 41. Sicut Christus diversimode pro hominibus oravit, ita diversimode meruit, aliis sufficienter, aliis efficaciter. Propter quod, licet omnium sit universalis Redemtor, & sufficiens causa salutis, speciali tamen modo est causa efficax salutis eorum, quos sibi facit obedientes. Incredibile enim est, non aliter obtulisse Christum sua merita pro illis, quos sciebat esse electos a Patre, quam pro aliis, cum videret esse Patris voluntatem ut illi infallibiliter salvarentur, & non alii. Largitur nobis Suarez, Christi mortem ac merita esse efficacia ad salutem electorum ex speciali modo oblationis & voluntate offerentis, non ex casuali seu contingente actu humanae voluntatis eam apprehendentis. 10. Vasquez hanc specialem Christi intentionem quoad electos in applicatione meritorum suorum clare agnoscit, in 1. Aquinat. qu. 23. disp. 49. cap. 3. pag. 687. Ego non dubito Christum peculiari oratione & voluntate merita sua illis applicasse, qui praedestinati & electi fuerunt. Idem, in 3. Aquinat. qu. 19. disp. 77. cap. 5. pag. 384. inducit Andream Vegam asserentem, merita Christi non omnibus efficaciter prodesse, quia pro illis (quibus non prosunt) efficaciter Christus non oravit, nec obtulit suam passionem. Habemus igitur non solum antiquos Patres, sed ipsos etiam Papistas neotericos fatentes, quod nos demonstrare conamur, nimirum, Christi mortem sic a Deo constitutam universalem causam salutis omnibus applicabilem, ut interim, per specialem quandam intentionem offerentis & acceptantis, constituatur particularis causa salutis omnibus & solis electis infallibiliter & singulariter applicanda. Vide etiam Malderi Antisynod. pag. 138.
english: 9. Next the Jesuits. However they defend universal grace and universal redemption, they dare not deny this special, effectual ordination and intention of the saving passion toward the elect alone. Let two chiefs speak: Suarez and Vasquez. Suarez on Aquinas III q.19 (Disp. p. 635 §41): as Christ prayed diversely for humans, so he merited diversely — for some sufficiently, for others effectually. So though he is everyone's universal Redeemer and a sufficient cause of salvation, in a special way he is the effectual cause of salvation for those he makes obedient. It is incredible he offered his merits no differently for those he knew the Father had elect than for others, when he saw the Father's will was that they be saved without fail, and not others. Suarez thus grants that Christ's death and merits save the elect from the special mode of offering and the offerer's will — not from a chance act of human will laying hold of them. 10. Vasquez clearly owns this special intention toward the elect in applying his merits (on Aquinas I q.23, disp. 49, c.3, p. 687): I do not doubt Christ by peculiar prayer and will applied his merits to those predestined and elect. The same on Aquinas III q.19, disp. 77, c.5, p. 384, cites Andreas Vega: Christ's merits do not profit all effectually, because for those they do not profit he did not pray effectually or offer his passion. So not only the old Fathers but even newer Romanists confess what we aim to prove: God constituted Christ's death a universal saving cause applicable to all, yet by a special intention of offerer and accepter it is also a particular saving cause to be applied without fail, and singularly, to all and only the elect. See also Malderus, Antisynod, p. 138.

source_text: 11. Postremo, Theologi nostri, qui Christum pro omnibus passum non diffitentur, tamen illum in morte sua peculiari quodam intuitu electos redemisse simul profitentur: Bucerus sententiam suam expressit in Math. i. ad illa verba, Populum suum salvum faciet, Hoc est, electos, quos ipsi Pater adducit. Morte sua omnium electorum peccata expiavit, meruitque ut illis Pater propitius suum Spiritum donet. Hic videtis Christum morte sua meruisse aliquid electis quod aliis non meruit. At quicquid cuiquam meruit Christus, id meruit secundum ordinationem & acceptationem Patris sui: Ex Patris igitur voluntate & ordinatione Christi mors pertinet ad electos speciali quadam ratione, sub qua ad alios non extenditur.
english: 11. Last, our own theologians. They do not deny that Christ suffered for all, yet they also confess that in his death he redeemed the elect under a peculiar regard. Bucer states it on Matthew 1 at He shall save his people — that is, the elect whom the Father himself brings to him. By his death he expiated all the elect's sins and merited that the propitious Father give them his Spirit. So Christ's death merited something for the elect that he did not merit for others. Whatever he merited for anyone, he merited under the Father's ordination and acceptance. From that Fatherly will and ordination, then, Christ's death belongs to the elect in a special way that does not reach the rest.

source_text: Musculus, qui in locis communibus acriter illud urget, Christum pro universali Redemtore habendum, tamen specialem Christi intentionem de redimendis electis agnoscit, in Rom. viii. ubi dicit, Electorum gratia Christum in hunc mundum venisse. Quod aliter intelligi non potest, quam peculiari intentione electorum infallibiliter servandorum in mundum venisse. Quae specialis intentio obtinendi ipsis electis fructum applicatum suae passionis est ita illorum propria, ut ad alios se haud extendat.
english: Musculus, who in the Common Places presses hard that Christ must be held universal Redeemer, still grants Christ's special intention to redeem the elect. On Romans 8 he says Christ came into this world for the elect's sake — which can only mean he came with a peculiar intention to save the elect without fail. That special aim, securing for the elect the applied fruit of his passion, belongs to them so properly that it does not stretch to others.

source_text: Calvinus in Hebr. ii. ad illa verba, Ecce ego & pueri quos mihi dedit Deus, Nullos, inquit, adducit Christus ad Patrem, nisi ab ipso sibi datos. Hanc vero donationem ex aeterna electione pendere scimus: quia quos Pater destinavit ad vitam, eos in custodiam Filio suo tradit, ut ipsos tueatur. Tria hic notanda: Primum est, Deum Patrem quosdam ex decreto electionis singulariter ad vitam destinasse: Secundum, Christum Mediatorem hosce electos quasi peculiariter sibi commendatos a Patre accepisse: Tertium, singularem curam horum electorum Christum gerere, eosque ita tueri & regere in hac vita, ut tandem perducat ad aeternam. Quibus positis, ab omni ratione & religione abhorrerer, qui iret inficias, Christum, in ipso opere oblationis suae & redemtionis humanae, horum electorum salutem peculiari intentione, id est, absoluta & efficaci, intendisse.
english: Calvin on Hebrews 2 at Behold I and the children God has given me: Christ brings none to the Father, he says, except those the Father himself has given him. That gift hangs on eternal election: those the Father destined for life he places in the Son's keeping to guard them. Mark three points. First, the Father from the election decree has singularly destined some for life. Second, Christ the Mediator received those elect as peculiarly entrusted to him by the Father. Third, Christ keeps a singular care of them, guarding and ruling them in this life until he brings them to eternal life. With that set down, it would offend all reason and piety to deny that, in the very work of his offering and of mankind's redemption, Christ intended these elect's salvation by a peculiar intention — absolute and effectual.

source_text: Zanchius, in Miscellaneis, tract. De praedest. san. pag. 14. Falsum non est, Christum mortuum pro omnibus hominibus: Omnibus enim passio Christi offertur in Evangelio. Sed pro electis tantum efficaciter mortuus est: quia scilicet ipsi tantum efficacitatis passionis Christi participes fiunt. Quod autem illi soli fiant participes hujus passionis efficaciter, id referendum est ad specialem & efficacem voluntatem Christi patientis, Deique Patris hanc hostiam acceptantis, pro electis magis peculiari modo quam pro aliis. In boni enim salutiferi participatione voluntas Divina praecedit humanam.
english: Zanchi (Miscellanies, On the Predestination of the Saints, p. 14): it is not false that Christ died for all men — his passion is offered to all in the Gospel. Yet he died efficaciously only for the elect, because they alone share the passion's efficacy. That they alone so share it must be referred to the special, effectual will of Christ suffering and of the Father accepting this victim — for the elect in a more peculiar way than for others. In sharing saving good, the divine will goes before the human.

source_text: Denique, ne taedio sim plures autores congerendo, Vorstius ipse non potuit negare, redemtionem in cruce peractam peculiari quadam ratione ad electos pertinere. Sic enim loquitur, in Amica duplic. pag. 230, Constat redemtionis vocem diverso sensu ad plures ejusdem generis species aptari posse; ac proinde aliquos tantum, & non omnes, quadam speciali ratione seu peculiari sensu redemtos dici commode posse, inque sacris literis sic appellari solere. Idem, pag. 235. respondens loco adducto ex Heb. xiii. 20, in quo Christus magnus Pastor ovium per sanguinem foederis aeterni appellatur, concedit nobis, Christum esse harum ovium, & quidem harum tantum, Pastorem peculiari modo, puta quoad salvificam & spiritualem illas pascendi actum, qui actualem Spiritus sancti donationem continet, item quoad specialem quandam harum ovium acquisitionem. Hactenus ille.
english: Finally — not to weary by stacking more writers — even Vorstius could not deny that the redemption finished on the cross belongs to the elect in a peculiar sense. In the Friendly Duplicate (p. 230) he grants that redemption can be taken in different senses for several species of the same kind, so that some only, not all, may fitly be called redeemed in a special reason or peculiar sense, as Scripture often names them. On p. 235, answering Hebrews 13:20 (Christ the great Shepherd of the sheep through the blood of the eternal covenant), he concedes Christ is Shepherd of these sheep, and of these alone, in a peculiar way: as to the saving, spiritual act of feeding them (which includes the actual gift of the Holy Spirit), and as to a special acquisition of those sheep. So far Vorstius.

source_text: Quaero quid hoc sit quod nobis Vorstius largitur, quando dat, non omnes sed aliquos speciali ratione & peculiari sensu fuisse morte Christi redemtos; quando ait Christum esse ovium suarum Pastorem peculiari modo, & quoad specialem quandam acquisitionem. Si nihil aliud vult, quam in ipso eventu, pro diversis actibus voluntatum humanarum, fructum redemtionis ad aliquos, hoc est, ad credentes, speciali & peculiari modo pertinere, nugas agit, & testimoniis contra eum allatis omnino non satisfacit. Nam illa omnia, Ecclesiam acquisivit sanguine suo; Dat salutem corpori suo; Animam ponit pro ovibus suis; Mortuus est ut filios Dei congregaret: haec, inquam, & consimilia, non specialem aliquam operationem Ecclesiae, corporis, ovium designant; sed specialem intentionem & operationem sponsi, Capitis, Pastoris circa hanc Ecclesiam, hoc corpus, hasce oves versantis, & eorundem salutem virtute & merito mortis suae speciali voluntate decernentis & procurantis.
english: What exactly does Vorstius grant us when he allows that not all but some were redeemed by Christ's death in a special reason and peculiar sense, and that Christ is Shepherd of his sheep in a peculiar way as to a special acquisition? If he means only that, in the outcome, by diverse acts of human wills, redemption's fruit reaches some — that is, believers — in a special way, he trifles and never answers the texts brought against him. For He purchased the Church with his blood; He gives salvation to his body; He lays down his life for his sheep; He died to gather God's children — these and like sayings do not mark some special act of the Church, body, or sheep. They mark the Bridegroom's, Head's, and Shepherd's special intention and work toward this Church, this body, these sheep, decreeing and securing their salvation by his death's virtue and merit under a special will.

source_text:
Contra haec omnia quae disputavimus de speciali intentione Christi morientis relata & restricta ad electos, & de salutifera applicatione mortis Christi ab eadem intentione dependente & dimanante, objici possunt.

1. Si in oblatione Christi detur talis intentio ad electos limitata, unde pro illis obtineatur efficacitas applicationis, & infallibilitas salutis, tum videmur illorum justificationem & salutem non tam ad eudokian, & specialem Dei misericordiam, quam ad rationem quandam justitiae revocare. Nam si quaeratur cur Petrus potius quam Judas gratiam efficacem & salutem ex merito mortis Christi acceperit, juxta nostram sententiam respondendum erit, Quia Christus speciali intentione & applicatione meritorum suorum id nomine Petri promeruit, quod pro Juda mereri noluit. Quod autem datur ex meritis Christi peculiariter applicatis huic personae, non videtur dari ex sola misericordia beneplaciti Divini, sed potius ex justitia: quia justum est ut quod Christus hisce aut illis personis promeruit, eisdem specialiter assignetur. Hoc autem videtur contravenire Apostolo, qui gratiam & salutem infallibilem praedestinatorum a pura Dei gratia arcessit.
english:
Against all we have argued about Christ's special dying intention toward the elect, and about the saving application of his death that hangs on and flows from that intention, objections can be raised.

1. If Christ's offering carries an intention limited to the elect, and from it they receive efficacious application and sure salvation, then we seem to ground their justification and salvation less in God's eudokia and special mercy than in a kind of justice. Ask why Peter rather than Judas received efficacious grace and salvation from Christ's death, and on our view the answer must be: because by special intention and application of his merits Christ merited for Peter what he refused to merit for Judas. Yet what comes from Christ's merits peculiarly applied to one person seems to come not from bare mercy of Divine good pleasure, but from justice — for it is just that what Christ merited for these or those persons be specially assigned to them. That seems to clash with the Apostle, who traces the grace and sure salvation of the predestined to God's pure grace alone.
