source_text: Nulla pugna est inter haec duo pronunciata, Deus justificat & salvat Petrum ex pura gratia sive mera sua eudokia, & Deus justificat & salvat Petrum intuens merita Christi pro Petri salute specialiter ordinata & acceptata. Ratio hujus rei in promptu est; nempe, Quod ipse Deus, qui ex mero suo beneplacito & pura misericordia decrevit dare Petro fidem & salutem, decrevit simul non aliter illi haec dare quam per & propter merita Christi Petro singulari quadam ratione destinata & donata, idque ex eadem eudokia & pura misericordia. Quae Dei eudokia opponitur meritis nostris; sed per merita Christi nobis applicata impletur, non evacuatur. Unde Apostolus Heb. xiii. 21. dicit ipsum Deum efficere in nobis beneplacitum suum per Jesum Christum. Quamvis igitur sit mera Dei eudokia, quod Deus velit Petrum efficaci gratia donare & salvare, tamen hujus beneplaciti executio non aliter fit quam per merita Christi. Huc igitur redit summa responsionis nostrae; Quamvis omne opus specialis gratiae quod fit in electis, fiat propter merita Christi specialiter illis applicata, tamen in illorum justificatione & salute veram rationem misericordiae, non justitiae conspici, quia Christus cum meritis suis, cum hoc ipso modo merendi, & offerendi sua merita speciali quodam intuitu habito ad electos, totum, inquam, hoc ex gratuita Dei erga illos voluntate duxit originem.
english: These two claims do not clash: God justifies and saves Peter by pure grace — his mere eudokia — and God justifies and saves Peter with an eye to Christ's merits specially ordained and accepted for Peter's salvation. The reason is plain. The same God who, from bare good pleasure and pure mercy, decreed faith and salvation for Peter also decreed to give them only through and because of Christ's merits, destined and granted to Peter in a singular way — and that from the same eudokia and pure mercy. God's eudokia stands against our merits; yet through Christ's merits applied to us it is filled out, not voided. So the Apostle says (Hebrews 13:21) that God himself works his good pleasure in us through Jesus Christ. It is therefore mere Divine eudokia that God wills to give Peter efficacious grace and save him; still that good pleasure is carried out only through Christ's merits. Our whole answer comes to this: every work of special grace in the elect is for Christ's merits specially applied to them, yet their justification and salvation show true mercy, not justice — because Christ, with his merits and with this very way of meriting and offering them under a special regard for the elect, drew the whole plan from God's free will toward them.

source_text: Si ponamus electos obtinere gratiam efficacem, sive fidem salutiferam, exinde quod mors meritumque Christi in cruce patientis speciali quadam intentione illis applicabatur, tum videmur admittere merita passionis Christi quibusdam hominibus imputata sive applicata ante fidem ipsorum: At hoc receptae Theologorum sententiae adversatur, quae ponit fidem esse instrumentum sive medium, sine quo merita passionis Christi singularibus personis non applicantur: Necesse est igitur ut is actu fidelis exstet, qui Christi merita habeat sibi singulariter applicata aut imputata. Quomodo igitur defendi potest specialis haec applicatio meritorum Christi ad electos, nondum factos fideles & credentes?
english: Suppose the elect gain efficacious grace — saving faith — because Christ's death and merit on the cross were applied to them by a special intention. Then we seem to allow the merits of his passion to be imputed or applied to some people before they believe. That clashes with the received theological rule that faith is the instrument or means without which Christ's passion-merits are not applied to particular persons. So whoever has Christ's merits singularly applied or imputed must already stand as a believer. How then can we defend this special application of Christ's merits to the elect before they are made faithful and believing?

source_text: Ut huic objectioni occurratur, fundamenti loco ponendum est illud Apostoli, Ephes. i. 3. Benedixit nobis Deus omni benedictione spirituali in Christo. Id est, Quicquid boni salutiferi ad nos a Deo descendit, id nobis per Christum & propter merita Christi donatur. Cum igitur ipsa fides salutifera, quae propria est electorum, sit inter praecipuas spirituales benedictiones reponenda, propter merita Christi illam donari iis omnibus, quibus de facto donatur, in confesso est. Quod igitur vulgo dicunt Theologi, fidem esse illud instrumentum, quo mediante merita Christi nobis applicantur, id intelligendum est de applicatione ex parte hominum considerata: Ipsi enim electi non possunt sibi applicare merita Christi ad perceptionem beneficiorum quorumcunque spiritualium, nisi fide in iis praesupposita. At si applicationem aut imputationem ex parte solius Dei consideremus, tum dicendum est, Deum & posse & solere applicare, id est, imputare & communicare, hominibus merita Christi, ita ut intuitu horum meritorum det illis bona spiritualia, etiam cum impii & infideles censeantur. Fides enim ipsa, cum primum datur, non fideli datur, sed infideli: datur autem electis propter merita Mediatoris. Necesse est ergo ut fateamur, neminem ex electis potuisse credendo sibi applicare merita Christi ad fructum vitae aeternae, nisi Deus ex speciali misericordia, propter hoc meritum Christi, fidem qua crederent illis prius infudisset. Atque haec est illa specialis applicatio meritorum Christi quam ex speciali voluntate Christi seipsum offerentis, Deique Patris hoc sacrificium acceptantis, ad electos peculiari quodam privilegio pertinere affirmamus. Scotus huc respexit, illo dicto observatione dignissimo, Haec fuit potissimum in merito Christi, quod meruit non-conjunctos conjungi, lib. 3. dist. 19. qu. unica, pag. 75. Quod perinde est ac si dixisset, praecipuam efficaciam meritorum Christi in eo sitam, quod meruit ut quidam ex infidelibus reapse fierent fideles, Christoque per fidem conjuncti vitam aeternam consequerentur. Haec est illa specialis ordinatio meritorum Christi, atque applicatio, quae tota pendet ex Dei beneplacito, non ex hominum arbitrio.
english: To meet the objection, take Ephesians 1:3 as foundation: God has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in Christ — that is, every saving good that comes down from God is given through Christ and for his merits. Saving faith, proper to the elect, ranks among the chief spiritual blessings; so it is granted, for Christ's merits, to all who in fact receive it. When theologians say faith is the instrument by which Christ's merits are applied to us, they mean application on the human side: the elect cannot apply those merits to themselves for any spiritual benefit unless faith is already presupposed in them. But if we view application or imputation from God's side alone, God can and does apply — impute and communicate — Christ's merits to people so that, with regard to those merits, he gives spiritual goods even while they still count as ungodly and unbelieving. Faith, when first given, is not given to a believer but to an unbeliever; yet it is given to the elect for the Mediator's merits. So we must confess: no elect person could, by believing, apply Christ's merits to himself for eternal life's fruit unless God, from special mercy and for that merit of Christ, had first infused the faith by which they would believe. That is the special application of Christ's merits which, from Christ's special will in offering himself and the Father's in accepting the sacrifice, we say belongs to the elect by a peculiar privilege. Scotus saw this in a saying worth marking: the chief thing in Christ's merit was that he merited the joining of the unjoined (lib. 3, dist. 19, unique q., p. 75) — as if to say the main force of those merits is that some from among unbelievers should become believers and, joined to Christ by faith, obtain eternal life. That special ordination and application of Christ's merits hangs wholly on God's good pleasure, not on human choice.

source_text:
Obj. 3. Si in Christo seipsum offerente, Deoque illud sacrificium acceptante, sit specialis quaedam intentio de vivificandis & infallibiliter salvandis electis omnibus virtute & merito ejusdem sacrificii, videmur ab hoc speciali privilegio excludere electos sub Veteri Testamento, qui nati ac denati fuerunt ante hoc sacrificium Christi in cruce exhibitum.

Sol. Quoad rationem sufficientiae generalis sive efficaciae specialis, respondeo, Christi sacrificium eandem virtutem habuisse sub Veteri Testamento, ante externum actum exhibitionis, quam habuit & habet sub Novo, post Christum realiter in cruce exhibitum & oblatum. Sicuti igitur ad electos sub N. T. ex speciali intentione Dei derivatur gratia specialis a merito hujus sacrificii jam actu exhibiti, ita ad electos sub V. T. ex speciali ejusdem Dei voluntate dimanavit gratia specialis a merito ejusdem sacrificii postmodum exhibendi. Christus enim erat Agnus occisus ab origine mundi, tam in praeparatione voluntatis suae, quam in acceptatione voluntatis Paternae. Est itaque hic observandum, aliam esse rationem causae ejus quae operatur Physice sive naturaliter, aliam ejus quae operatur meritorie sive moraliter. Causa physice agens, actu ponatur est necesse, priusquam ejus virtute effectum aliquod producatur: at causa agens meritorie sive moraliter, qualis est passio Christi, potest effectum producere priusquam actu exsistat, si praecedat saltem in ejus cognitione & acceptatione ad quem spectat ejusdem intuitu beneficia gratiae suae hominibus dispensare. Nam hac in re causa Meritoria habet cognationem quandam cum causa Finali, quae nondum actu exsistens, sed tantummodo praevisa & praeconsiderata, valide movet agentem ad hoc vel illud agendum. Hoc modo dicimus passionem Christi, meritaque ab eadem dependentia, praevisa ut Deo offerenda & applicanda specialiter Jacobo, & non Esavo, habuisse rationem causae moventis Deum ad donandum Jacobo illam specialem gratiam, quam Esavo negavit. Recte Suarez, in 3. qu. 49. art. 4. in comm. Illa specialis dilectio, qua propter merita Christi, sive exhibita sive praevisa, Deus homines sanctificat, & sibi reconciliat, potest cadere sub meritis Christi, sive promerendo nobis effectum illius dilectionis, sive dilectionem (vel electionem) Dei ad nos libere terminatam.
english:
Obj. 3. If Christ in offering himself, and God in accepting that sacrifice, had a special intention to vivify and surely save all the elect by that sacrifice's virtue and merit, we seem to shut Old Testament elect out of the privilege — those born and dead before Christ's sacrifice was shown on the cross.

Sol. On general sufficiency or special efficacy I answer: Christ's sacrifice had the same virtue under the Old Testament, before the outward act of exhibition, that it has under the New after Christ was really shown and offered on the cross. Just as special grace reaches New Testament elect from God's special intention by the merit of this sacrifice already actually exhibited, so special grace flowed to Old Testament elect from the same God's special will by the merit of that same sacrifice still to be exhibited. For Christ was the Lamb slain from the world's beginning, both in the readiness of his will and in the Father's acceptance. Note the difference: a cause that works physically or naturally must already be in act before its power yields an effect; a cause that works meritoriously or morally — such as Christ's passion — can yield an effect before it actually exists, if it at least stands beforehand in the knowledge and acceptance of him who, with regard to it, dispenses the benefits of his grace. Here a meritorious cause is kin to a final cause: not yet existing in act, but only foreseen and weighed, it still moves the agent to act. So we say Christ's passion and its dependent merits, foreseen as to be offered to God and applied specially to Jacob, not Esau, moved God to give Jacob the special grace he denied Esau. Suarez puts it well (In 3, q. 49, art. 4, comm.): that special love by which, for Christ's merits — exhibited or foreseen — God sanctifies and reconciles people can fall under Christ's merits, whether by meriting for us the effect of that love, or God's love (or election) freely fixed on us.

source_text: Obj. 4. Ultimo in loco & illud objici potest, Parum consentaneum, imo plane incongruum esse, ut Deus, qui Christi mortem, cum divite thesauro meritorum eodem incluso, omnibus voluerit esse ex aequo sub Fidei conditione applicabilem ad consecutionem vitae aeternae, noluerit interim ex aequo hanc ipsam fidem propter eadem Christi merita omnibus praeparare & donare, sed ipsam fidem perseverantem & salutiferam solis electis dederit, idque propter Christi merita speciali quadam Dei intentione, speciali quodam intuitu ad eos restricta & ordinata.
english: Obj. 4. Last comes this charge: it is hardly fitting — indeed plainly incongruous — that God, who willed Christ's death, with its rich treasury of merits, to be equally applicable to all under the condition of faith for obtaining eternal life, should meanwhile refuse to prepare and give that same faith, for those same merits, equally to all, and should give persevering saving faith to the elect alone — and that for Christ's merits by a special Divine intention, a special regard restricted and ordained toward them.

source_text: Respondeo, ubi de facto aliquo Divino constat, temerarium est (ne dicam impium) de aequitate aut congruitate ejusdem dubitare. Jam vero Christi morte esse stabilitum illud pactum cum humano genere, ex cujus tenore vita aeterna cuivis homini sub Fidei conditione promittitur, jam pridem a nobis demonstratum est. De hoc pacto Rupertus, in 4. Genes. cap. 34, Dicimus pactum multoties quidem promissum, sed semel initum, quo solo inimicitiae solvuntur, quae erant inter Deum & homines, passio scilicet Christi Filii Dei. Illic enim absque ulla contradictione certa est constitutio pacis, dum accepta Deus Fide hominum dat hominibus eundem Christum Filium suum, ut salventur per ipsum. De hac itaque Dei ordinatione in Christi morte meritisque fundata, atque ad omnes & singulos spectante, non est ambigendum. Verum illud adhuc in dubium vocatur, utrum posito hoc universali pacto dandae vitae aeternae omnibus, si crediderint, Deus exerceat libertatem, & exserat specialem misericordiam in danda hac Fide salutifera electis qua credant; idque per Christum, & propter merita Christi peculiari quodam privilegio ad eos applicata. Res ipsa loquitur. Videmus enim electos, & solos electos, in eventu obtinere a Deo fidem perseverantem & salutiferam: Putare autem tantum ac tale donum illis specialiter donatum alio modo, aut intuitu quam propter merita Christi illis speciali quadam intentione Dei ordinata & applicata, plane nefas est. Nam, ut pie Ambrosius, Omne donum gratiae in Christo est, ad illud Apostoli, Ephes. i. 3. Benedixit nobis omni benedictione spirituali in Christo. Hisce constitutis, quamvis (ut dixi) supervacaneum est de congruitate Divinorum factorum disceptare ubi de ipsis factis constat, tamen, ne quid scrupuli relinquatur, primo dicimus, Hanc specialem Dei intentionem, juxta quam apud se decrevit propter merita Christi dare electis specialia beneficia gratiae efficacis & salutis, non pugnare cum pacto illo conditionato, Quisquis crediderit salvus erit, sed potius esse speciale quoddam consilium, ad universalis hujus pacti infallibilem impletionem subordinatum. Qui enim suo arbitrio committuntur sub quibusvis gratiae adminiculis, aut Fidem repellunt, aut excutiunt. Ne itaque pactum illud universale nemini effectum salutis apportaret, Deus speciali hac & arcana sua intentione curavit aliquibus applicatum iri mortis Christi meritum, ad Fidei vitaeque aeternae infallibilem consecutionem. Secundo, dicimus, Nihil iniqui aut incongrui esse, quod haec specialis intentio de efficaci applicatione meritorum Christi in aliquibus, non in omnibus vim suam exserat; quia cum mors Christi sit gratuitum Dei donum humano generi impensum, libera distributio & applicatio meritorum inde redundantium omni jure ex mera Dei voluntate dependere debeat. Tertio, & illud addimus, Deum, qui in Evangelio promisit omnibus & singulis vitam aeternam propter merita Christi, si crediderint, nulli tamen infidelium promisisse se illi propter merita Christi daturum ut infallibiliter & perseveranter credat. Quaero igitur, Ex qua parte versatur haec incongruitas? Non ex parte credentium & servatorum: Nam dare propter merita Christi singularibus personis quod illis singulariter minime promissum fuit, non est culpandae iniquitatis, sed celebrandae bonitatis. Non ex parte incredulorum & perditorum: Nam illud beneficium negare alicui, quod constat te nulla ratione illi debere, nec in se iniquum, nec summae bonitati Divinae incongruum judicari potest.
english: I answer: once a Divine fact stands, it is rash — not to say impious — to quarrel with its equity or fittingness. We have long shown that by Christ's death that covenant with the human race was fixed, by whose terms eternal life is promised to anyone under the condition of faith. On that covenant Rupert of Deutz (on Genesis 4.34) says: we call it a covenant many times promised but once struck, by which alone the enmities between God and humankind are dissolved — namely the passion of Christ the Son of God. There peace is settled without contradiction when God, receiving human faith, gives people the same Christ his Son that they may be saved through him. So there is no doubt about this Divine ordination, founded in Christ's death and merits and looking to every person. What is still doubted is whether, given this universal covenant of eternal life for all who believe, God may freely show special mercy in giving the elect the saving faith by which they believe — and that through Christ, for his merits applied to them by a peculiar privilege. The fact itself speaks. We see the elect alone, in the outcome, receive from God persevering saving faith. To imagine so great a gift given them in any other way or regard than for Christ's merits, ordained and applied by a special Divine intention, is plainly unlawful. As Ambrose says devoutly, every gift of grace is in Christ — pointing to Ephesians 1:3, He has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in Christ. That settled, though it is needless to debate the fittingness of Divine deeds when the deeds themselves are clear, still, to leave no scruple: first, this special intention by which God decreed, for Christ's merits, to give the elect the special benefits of efficacious grace and salvation does not fight the conditioned covenant Whoever believes will be saved; it is rather a special counsel subordinated to that universal covenant's sure fulfillment. Those left to their own choice under any helps of grace either push faith away or shake it off. Lest that universal covenant bring salvation's effect to no one, God by this special and secret intention saw to it that Christ's death-merit would be applied to some for the sure obtaining of faith and eternal life. Second, nothing unjust or incongruous follows if this special intention of efficacious application of Christ's merits puts forth its force in some, not in all: Christ's death is God's free gift to the human race, so free distribution and application of the overflowing merits ought by every right to hang on God's mere will. Third, God, who in the Gospel promised every person eternal life for Christ's merits if they believe, never promised any unbeliever that for those merits he would make him believe surely and perseveringly. So where is the incongruity? Not on the side of believers and the saved: to give singular persons, for Christ's merits, what was never singularly promised them is not blameworthy injustice but goodness to praise. Not on the side of the unbelieving and lost: to deny someone a benefit you owe him by no title is neither unjust in itself nor unfit for God's highest goodness.

source_text: Sit itaque haec totius hujus controversiae De Morte Christi summa & conclusio; Mediatorem Dei ac hominum, Jesum Christum, in foedere illo Evangelico sanciendo, ex cujus tenore omni credenti debetur vita aeterna, nullam partitionem hominum vel discretionem instituisse, ut quenquam dicere possimus a mortis suae beneficio exclusum, si crederet: Atque hoc sensu, suffragantibus Scripturis, Patribus, ac solidis rationibus, tuemur, Christum pro omnibus hominibus, sive pro toto humano genere, in cruce passum ac mortuum fuisse. Quinetiam addimus & hoc, Eundem Mediatorem, cum animam suam pro peccato decrevisset ponere, habuisse insuper hanc singularem intentionem, quod virtute meritorum suorum efficaciter & infallibiliter quosdam sibi a Patre singulariter datos esset vivificaturus & ad vitam perducturus: Atque hoc sensu defendimus, Christum pro solis Electis, vel pro Ecclesia sua acquirenda, animam suam posuisse, id est, pro illis solis mortuum fuisse cum hoc singulari & certo proposito per meritum mortis suae eos efficaciter regenerandi & salvandi. Quamvis ergo meritum Christi aequaliter se habeat ad omnes quoad sufficientiam, non tamen quoad efficaciam: quod intelligendum est non tantum ex parte effectus, qui in uno fit & non in alio, sed etiam ex parte voluntatis, qua ipse Christus meruit, & diverso modo obtulit sua merita pro diversis. Prima autem radix hujus diversitatis fuit electio & voluntas Divina, cui se voluntas humana Christi conformavit. Atque hinc recte deducit Suarez, Meritum hoc Christi esse causam ipsius spiritualis regenerationis, & dare illi efficaciam, & influere in effectum ejus, & simul causam esse ut hic homo regeneretur, propter quem specialiter suum obtulit meritum, In 3. qu. 19. disp. 41. S. 2. pag. 635. Pro nostris loquatur vir eximiae eruditionis & piae memoriae Robertus Sarisburiensis; sic igitur ille, in Thomson. Diatrib. pag. 94. Nos etsi Christum pro omnibus mortuum non negamus, specialiter tamen & proprie credimus mortuum esse pro Ecclesia, neque ad omnes homines beneficium redemtionis pari jure pertinere. Atque ab hujus beneficii proprietate, non ab humana aliquatenus voluntate pendet efficacia mediorum omnium, ut illis tantum sint, & ex usu sint, quos Christus in se electos peculiari quodam intuitu redemit: neque ex eo effectum sortiantur, quia nos volumus, sed ex eo quod in electis & redemtis secundum propositum gratiae suae operatur Deus hoc velle ad quod elegit. Qui igitur morte sua omnibus sufficientissime promeruit vitam aeternam, donandam utique omnibus ex pacto Evangelico, si crederent; is aliquibus ex peculiari meritorum suorum applicatione promeruit efficacissime ut crederent, ut vitam aeternam ex gratuito Dei dono per & propter Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum acciperent. Atque haec est sors electorum peculiaris: Cujus nos omnes participes faciat Pater misericordiarum, cui cum Filio & Spiritu Sancto sit honor, laus & gloria nunc & in secula sempiterna. Amen.
english: Let this be the sum and close of the whole controversy On the Death of Christ. The Mediator between God and humankind, Jesus Christ, in sealing that evangelical covenant by which eternal life is due to every believer, made no partition or sorting of people by which we could say anyone was shut out from the benefit of his death if he believed. In that sense — with Scripture, the Fathers, and solid reasons agreeing — we hold that Christ suffered and died on the cross for all human beings, for the whole human race. We add this too: the same Mediator, when he decreed to lay down his life for sin, also had this singular intention — that by the virtue of his merits he would efficaciously and surely vivify and bring to life certain ones singularly given him by the Father. In that sense we defend that Christ laid down his life for the elect alone, or to acquire his Church — that is, he died for them alone with this singular, fixed purpose of efficaciously regenerating and saving them through the merit of his death. So Christ's merit stands equally toward all as to sufficiency, yet not as to efficacy — and that not only from the effect, which lands in one and not another, but from the will by which Christ himself merited and offered his merits in different ways for different people. The first root of that diversity was Divine election and will, to which Christ's human will conformed. From this Suarez rightly draws that this merit of Christ is the cause of spiritual regeneration itself, gives it efficacy, influences its effect, and is at once the cause that this person is regenerated for whom he specially offered his merit (In 3, q. 19, disp. 41, §2, p. 635). Let Robert of Salisbury, of rare learning and pious memory, speak for our side (in Thomson's Diatribe, p. 94): though we do not deny that Christ died for all, yet we specially and properly believe he died for the Church, and that redemption's benefit does not belong to all by equal right. On that benefit's peculiarity — not on human will — hangs the efficacy of every means, so that they are and are useful only for those whom Christ redeemed in himself as elect under a peculiar regard; nor do they take effect because we will, but because in the elect and redeemed, according to the purpose of his grace, God works the willing for which he chose them. He who by his death most sufficiently merited eternal life for all — to be given to all under the evangelical covenant if they believed — also, by a peculiar application of his merits, most efficaciously merited for some that they should believe and receive eternal life as God's free gift through and for our Lord Jesus Christ. That is the elect's peculiar lot. May the Father of mercies make us all partakers of it; to him, with the Son and the Holy Spirit, be honor, praise, and glory now and forever. Amen.

source_text: DISSERTATIO DE PRAEDESTINATIONE ET REPROBATIONE. Per Reverendissimum virum JOANNEM DAVENANTIUM, Nuper Episcopum SARISBURIENSEM, Ante aliquot annos in celeberrima Academia Cantabrigiensi Theologiae Professorem in Scholis Theologicis auditoribus suis dictata. Rom. IX. 18. Cujus vult, miseretur: & quem vult, indurat. Calvin. in Rom. IX. 18. Minime dubium est, Paulum e suo ipsius sensu haec loqui, Deum scilicet PRO ARBITRIO SUO, quem visum illi fuerit, misericordia dignari: in quemcunque libuerit judicii severitatem stringere. Ex Officina Rogeri Danielis, Alma Academiae Cantabrigiensis Typographi, 1650.
english: A DISSERTATION ON PREDESTINATION AND REPROBATION. By the Most Reverend John Davenant, lately Bishop of Salisbury, formerly Professor of Theology in the University of Cambridge, delivered in the Theological Schools to his hearers. [[Romans 9:18 >> Bible:Romans 9:18]]. Of whom he wills, he has mercy; and whom he wills, he hardens. Calvin on Romans 9:18: There is scarcely any doubt that Paul speaks here in his own sense — that God, by his own free decision, shows mercy to whom he chooses, and draws the severity of judgment against whomever he pleases. Printed at Cambridge by Roger Daniel, University Printer, 1650.

source_text: Prefatio habita ad Academicos. Quod de agricolis dixit Poeta, Redit agricolis labor actus in orbem, Georg. 2, id Theologis verius convenit; ac praesertim illis quibus ipsa Cathedra laboris & sudoris necessitatem, non otii aut quietis opportunitatem subministrat. Hos igitur circulos orbesque laboris Theologici, quos mihi pro officii mei ratione conficiendos video, alacri & lubenti animo ingrediar: Deumque inprimis precabor, ut me sic dirigat in toto hoc operis suscipiendi curriculo, ne vel tantillum deflectam ab immobili illo centro sacrae veritatis. Est autem opus quod aggredior in se arduum, multisque difficultatibus obstructum. Quid enim altius, aut ab humanis sensibus remotius, quam illud aeternum decretum praedestinationis Divinae, quo ante jacta mundi fundamenta quosdam prae aliis, imo aliis plane praeteritis, ad vitam aeternam in Christo participandam electos confitemur? Huic negotio explicando operam nostram addiximus; ea tamen lege, ne quis vestrum exspectet ut vel omnes quaestiones, quae in hac materia tractantur a Theologis, attingam (immensi hoc, addo etiam, & supervacui laboris esset), vel ullas omnino ex illis curiosis quaestiunculis, quibus malesani homunciones seipsos torquere, alios vexare, fidem denique Christianam obscurare solent & pervertere. Respuit enim captiosas & inutiles quaestiones fides constans; &, quisquis fidelis vere audit, Divinae sapientiae se religiosum ostendit, non libidinosum suae, Hilar. 1. De Trinit. ut graviter Tertullianus, De Resurr. Proponemus ergo nobis in hac disquisitione nostra paucula quaedam ex maxime necessariis tractanda; eaque non rimabimur altius quam quo Scriptura praelucente penetremus. Huic regulae si adhaerescamus, doctrinam hanc praedestinationis non modo inter eruditos proponendam, sed ipsi populo divulgandam, recte & sapienter judicavit Augustinus, De persev. sanctor. lib. 2. cap. 16. idque ita fieri posse docuit, ut id quod dicitur, & parvulis lac, & grandibus esca sit.
english: Preface delivered to the University. What the poet said of farmers — "The finished labor returns for farmers in a circle" (Georgics 2) — fits theologians still more truly, especially those whose chair itself demands labor and sweat, not leisure or quiet. So I will enter these rounds of theological work that my office requires, eager and willing; and I will ask God first to steer me through the whole course of this undertaking so that I do not swerve even a little from the fixed center of sacred truth. The work I take up is steep in itself and blocked with many difficulties. For what is higher, or farther from human sense, than that eternal decree of Divine predestination by which, before the world's foundations were laid, we confess that certain ones were chosen before others — indeed with others plainly passed by — to share eternal life in Christ? We have given our labor to explaining that business, yet under this rule: let no one of you expect that I will touch every question theologians treat in this matter (that would be immense labor, and superfluous too), or any of those curious little puzzles by which unhealthy little men torture themselves, vex others, and finally obscure and twist the Christian faith. Steady faith rejects captious and useless questions; and whoever truly hears as a believer shows himself devout toward Divine wisdom, not craving his own (Hilary, On the Trinity 1; so also Tertullian, On the Resurrection). In this inquiry, then, we will set ourselves only a few of the most necessary points, and we will not dig deeper than Scripture's light lets us go. If we keep to that rule, Augustine rightly judged that this doctrine of predestination should be taught not only among the learned but also to the people (On the Perseverance of the Saints 2.16), and that it can be said so as to be milk for little ones and solid food for the grown.

source_text: Si Pauli vestigia premamus, si sancti Augustini exemplum imitemur, si doctrinae in hac Ecclesia nostra receptae adhaerescamus, nullum scandali periculum est. E contra, si obrui & sepeliri patiamur doctrinam gratuita electionis, aut (quod turpius est) si illam a quibusdam Pontificiis aliisque pessime corruptam & in contrarium detortam aequo animo feramus, non carebit utique suspicione haec iners taciturnitas: occurreret enim nobis expedita defensio veritatis, si falsitas promulgata displiceret. Neminem vestrum latere arbitror, ex Pontificiis scriptoribus multos, totum hoc mysterium electionis & reprobationis, in quo Paulus obstupuit, ad nimis claram facilemque discriminis rationem revocasse, dum alios ex praescientia meritorum electos, alios autem ex praescientia demeritorum rejectos philosophorum.
english: If we follow Paul's steps, imitate holy Augustine, and hold the doctrine received in this our Church, there is no danger of scandal. But if we let the doctrine of free election be overwhelmed and buried — or, worse, if we calmly endure it when certain Papal writers and others have badly corrupted it and twisted it the other way — that lazy silence will not escape suspicion. A ready defense of the truth would meet us if published falsehood displeased us. None of you, I think, fails to see that many Papal writers have reduced this whole mystery of election and reprobation — at which Paul stood astonished — to an all-too-clear and easy account of the difference, teaching that some are chosen from foreknowledge of merits, others rejected from foreknowledge of demerits.

source_text: Et quod magis dolendum est, e schola Arminiana prodierunt novelli doctores, qui fundatissimam Ecclesiae catholicae doctrinam labefactare conantur, & novam nescio quam atque orthodoxis Ecclesiis plane incognitam electionis & reprobationis fabricam exstruere. Quod Papistae praevisis operibus, id isti fidei & infidelitati praevisae assignandum putant: Et sic demum Divinae justitiae prospectum opinantur, si ante jacta mundi fundamenta eos tantum elegisse dicatur, quos ad oblatam vocationis gratiam credituros, & in fide ad extremum usque perseveraturos praeviderit; Ex adverso eos solos statuatur reprobasse, quos gratiam repulsuros, incredulos, & in incredulitate morituros praesciverit. Bellos scilicet Theologos, qui hominem fide prius justificatum, & in adoptionis & salutis statu positum, quam a Deo praedestinatum, aut ad salutem in Christo electum introducunt! Praeclaros gratiae Divinae praecones, qui discrimen bonarum & malarum voluntatum in credendo aut non credendo nolunt ad Dei eligentis specialem erga credentes misericordiam reducere: Sed quicquid hoc discriminis est, satagunt ad contingentem liberi arbitrii actum in admittenda, retinenda & exercenda gratia revocare. Quanto melius, & ad mentem Apostoli accommodatius Pelagianorum flagellum Augustinus de praedest. Sanct. lib. 1. cap. 17. Elegit Deus fideles, sed ut fiant, non quia jam erant. Eligendo facit divites in fide, sicut heredes regni. Fuit igitur post Pelagium exortum Augustini atque omnium adeo Catholicorum explicata ac rata sententia, homines fuisse electos non ex operibus, sed ad opera bona, non ex fide, sed ad fidem. Hoc est, qui electi sunt fideles & bonorum operum studiosi evaserunt; non quia tales futuri praevidebantur a Deo, electi fuerunt. Hanc doctrinam in Scholis propugnare, hanc in Ecclesiis praedicare oportet. Nam cum Pontificii alii errorum suorum venena passim diffundunt, nos etiam haud minore industria paremus nostris salutaria antidota. Notum est illud Aristotelis, &c. Nos etiam turpe ducamus in causa Dei obmutescere, cum hostes veritatis scriptis & clamoribus suis undique nobis obstrepant. Ne igitur vicini erroris contagio & nostros tandem corripiat, pro meae tenuitatis modulo suscipiam explicationem verissimae ejus doctrinae, quam Ecclesia haec Anglicana in praedestinationis negotio suis omnibus amplectandam commendavit. Refellam etiam pro virili illa sophismata, quibus adversarii sanam Ecclesiae doctrinam subvertere, atque nova sua commenta stabilire moliuntur.
english: And what hurts more: from the Arminian school new teachers have come out who try to shake the catholic Church's most settled doctrine, and to raise I know not what new fabric of election and reprobation, wholly unknown to orthodox churches. What Papists assign to foreseen works, these assign to foreseen faith and unbelief. So they think they have secured Divine justice if, before the world's foundations were laid, God is said to have chosen only those he foresaw would believe the offered call and persevere in faith to the end; and, on the other side, to have reprobated only those he foreknew would refuse grace, remain unbelieving, and die in unbelief. Fine theologians indeed — who bring in a man already justified by faith, already set in adoption and salvation, before God has predestined him or chosen him to salvation in Christ! Splendid heralds of Divine grace — who will not trace the difference of good and bad wills in believing or not believing to the electing God's special mercy toward believers, but strain to refer whatever difference there is to a contingent act of free choice in admitting, keeping, and exercising grace. How much better — and closer to the Apostle's mind — is Augustine, scourge of the Pelagians (On the Predestination of the Saints 1.17): "God chose the faithful, but that they might become so, not because they already were. By choosing he makes them rich in faith, as heirs of the kingdom." So after Pelagius arose, Augustine and Catholics generally held and ratified this: people were chosen not from works but unto good works, not from faith but unto faith. That is: the elect became faithful and eager for good works; they were not chosen because God foresaw they would be such. This doctrine must be defended in the schools and preached in the churches. When Papal writers pour out their error's poisons everywhere, let us with no less care prepare antidotes for our own. Aristotle's saying is known. Let us also count it shameful to fall silent in God's cause while enemies of the truth shout against us on every side with writings and noise. Lest neighboring error's contagion seize ours too, I will, according to my slender measure, undertake to explain that most true doctrine which this Church of England has commended to all her people to embrace in the matter of predestination. And as far as I can I will refute those sophisms by which adversaries try to overturn the Church's sound teaching and to settle their new inventions.

source_text: Cap. I. Prolegomena. Sed quo tota haec res in lucem proferatur facilius, non abs re erit ipsi disputationi praemittere nonnulla, quorum explicatio viam sternet huic controversiae intelligendae. Primo igitur, quia in illis quaestionibus quae de praedestinatione aguntur, aut reprobatione, maximas lites parit ipse ordo considerationis nostrae, dum alius contendit in intellectu & decretis Divinis illud esse prius, quod alius opinatur esse posterius, de tota hac ratione prioritatis & posterioritatis quoad diversa signa rationis, paucis differendum est. Secundo, quia ipsa vocabula Electionis, Praedestinationis, Reprobationis, diversimode a diversis usurpantur, necesse erit ipsam vocabulorum vim explanare, & quo sensu ab aliis, quo a nobis accipiantur, ostendere. Tertio, quia de qualitatibus sive conditionibus subjecti, diversi diverso modo philosophantur, operae pretium erit exponere, quid absolute requiratur & praesupponitur in ipso subjecto praedestinationis aut reprobationis promiscue considerato. Ultimo, quia praeter conditiones communes, quae ex aequo & indiscriminatim requiruntur, sive quis praedestinationis sive reprobationis subjectum statuatur, nonnulli insuper qualitates sive conditiones distinguentes ponunt, pro quarum discrimine actus praedestinationis Divinae in unum cadat, actus reprobationis in alterum, de hisce etiam, quam vim habeant, dispiciendum erit. Nam aliqui qui discrimen electionis & reprobationis ad hujusmodi, sive qualitates sive actus nostros, referunt, non patiuntur tamen ut causae appellentur, multo minus ut merita, imo non nisi gravate concedunt, ut vel conditiones praedestinationis nostrae nuncupentur. Sed ad rem accingamur: & ordiamur ab illis signis sive diversis instantibus, quae a Theologis assignari & distingui solent secundum ordinem prioris & posterioris, in actibus tum intellectus tum voluntatis Divinae.
english: Chapter I. Prolegomena. But so that this whole matter may come into the light more easily, it will not be out of place to set a few things before the dispute itself — things whose explanation will open the way into this controversy. First: in questions of predestination or reprobation the very order of our thought breeds the sharpest fights, while one claims that in God's intellect and decrees this is prior which another holds is posterior. So we must speak briefly of this whole account of priority and posteriority under the diverse signs of reason. Second: because the words Election, Predestination, and Reprobation are used differently by different writers, we must explain the force of the words themselves, and show in what sense others take them, and in what sense we do. Third: because writers argue differently about the qualities or conditions of the subject, it will be worth setting out what is absolutely required and presupposed in the subject of predestination or reprobation when that subject is considered in common. Last: besides the common conditions required equally and without distinction whether someone is made the subject of predestination or of reprobation, some place further distinguishing qualities or conditions, by whose difference the act of Divine predestination falls on one and the act of reprobation on another. Those too must be weighed for what force they have. For some who refer the difference of election and reprobation to such things — whether our qualities or our acts — still will not let them be called causes, much less merits, and only grudgingly allow them even to be named conditions of our predestination. But let us gird for the work, and begin from those signs or distinct instants that theologians usually assign and separate according to prior and posterior order in the acts of both the Divine intellect and the Divine will.

source_text: Primo igitur sciendum & tenendum est, si Dei naturam & perfectionem in se consideremus, illum non prius unum videre, dein aliud; neque prius hoc decernere aut velle, deinde illud; sed unico & simplicissimo actu ab aeterno omnia simul vidisse, omnia simul in se decrevisse. Ratio firmissima petitur ab immutabilitate Divina, Jacob. 1. 17. Apud Deum non est transmutatio, aut vicissitudinis obumbratio. Quae verba omnem mutationem sive in essendo, sive in operando a Divina natura excludunt. Nam si fingamus Deum quasi per vices agere in illis operationibus quae in Deo immanentes intelliguntur, ita ut prius hoc intelligat, deinde illud, prius hoc velit, deinde aliud; ponimus in Deo mutationem a potentia in actum: quae ejus absolutissimae simplicitati adversatur. Recte igitur Ambrosius, sed quicunque alius Autor fuerit, lib. 2. De vocat. Gent. cap. 10. Non est in Deo accidens, motus, aut nova voluntas, aut temporale consilium, nec cogitatio ejus cum rerum mutabilium inaequalitate variatur, sed cuncta pariter tempora & temporalia sempiterno ac stabili comprehendit intuitu. Adstipulatur etiam Hilarius, qui negat in Deo particulatas rerum cogitationes, atque asserit omnia penes Deum aequabili aeternitatis infinitate consistere, de Trin. 12. pag. 193. Assentiuntur Scholastici & Theologi omnes quos ego viderim, extra unum Vorstium, cujus deliria indigna sunt quae vel refutentur in Schola Theologica.
english: First, then, this must be known and held: if we consider God's nature and perfection in itself, he does not first see one thing and then another, nor first decree or will this and then that. By one most simple act from eternity he has seen all things at once and decreed all things at once in himself. The firmest ground is Divine immutability — [[James 1:17 >> Bible:James 1:17]]: with God there is no change, or shadow of turning. Those words shut every change — in being or in working — out of the Divine nature. If we imagine God acting by turns in those operations understood as immanent in him, so that he first understands this then that, first wills this then another, we place in God a move from potency into act — which contradicts his most absolute simplicity. So Ambrose is right (or whoever wrote book 2 of On the Calling of the Gentiles, chapter 10): In God there is no accident, motion, new will, or temporal counsel; his thought is not varied by the inequality of changeable things; he comprehends all times and temporal things together with an everlasting, steady gaze. Hilary agrees: he denies piecemeal thoughts of things in God, and holds that all things stand with God in the even infinity of eternity (On the Trinity 12, p. 193). Every Scholastic and theologian I have seen assents — except one Vorstius, whose ravings are not even worth refuting in a theological school.

source_text: Secundo, utcunque omnes actus in mente & voluntate Divina sint aeterni, & proinde ne levissimo quidem prioritatis & posterioritatis momento separemur; tamen, ex parte ipsarum rerum quas Deus intelligit & decrevit, signa quaedam prioritatis & posterioritatis distingui possunt, secundum nostrum modum intelligendi. Et hoc sensu quaeritur inter Theologos, utrum Deus prius decreverit dare electis vitam aeternam, an fidem & obedientiam, quae ducant ad vitam aeternam; & utrum prius aliquos reprobaverit & rejecerit a vita aeterna, quam lapsos & peccato contaminatos praeviderit. Atque hinc est quod fere omnes qui de praedestinatione & reprobatione scripserunt, seriem quandam, & quasi tabellam describunt, in qua ordinem decretorum Divinorum conantur delineare: non quod secundum rem in ipso Deo unum altero prius aut posterius esse judicent, sed quod juxta ordinatam rerum dependentiam in seipsis, unum ab intellectu nostro prius alio concipi debeat. Hic tamen observandum est inter ipsos Scholasticos, non admodum certam & constantem esse hanc doctrinam de hisce signis sive instantibus prioritatis & posterioritatis, quibus imbecilla nostra ratio sustentat se in consideratione decretorum Divinorum. Scotus, qui primarius est ad haec signa fabricanda artifex, videtur nonnullis non solum eadem posuisse priora & posteriora secundum nostrum intelligendi modum, sed insuper statuisse unum esse in ipso Deo prius natura alio; quasi hic ordo prioris & posterioris ex natura rei in ipsis Divinis actibus posset assignari. Sed cum attente lego quae Scotus de hisce signis tradit lib. 1. dist. 41. qu. unica, & lib. 3. dist. 7. qu. 4. & dist. 19. qu. unica, nihil aliud mihi docuisse videtur, quam esse in ipsis rebus aliquod fundamentum, unde nos concipiamus unum Dei decretum ordine quodam rationis nostrae alteri esse praeponendum. Jam vero ex adversa parte Occamus noster haec signa, quocunque modo considerata, negavit; In 1. dist. 9. qu. 3. & Bielus sententiam amplexus, haec signa oppugnavit, In 3. dist. 2. qu. 1. dub. 3. Prioritates in Divinis non sunt ponendae, sicut nec pluralitates actuum ordinatorum. Unus est enim actus in Divinis, re & ratione indistinctus, qui est ipsa essentia Divina; qua unica cognitione Deus praevidit Christi incarnationem, omnium electorum futuram beatitudinem, casum & reparationem; nec unum prius, aliud posterius: & mox addit, ne secundum nostram quidem considerationem talem ordinem prioritatis & posterioritatis concipi posse in decretis Divinis, ut talis consideratio non sit falsa speculatio. Dominicus Bannes, quamvis non omnino explodat haec signa cum Biele, perpendens tamen discordiam Theologorum in illis assignandis, Animadvertendum est, inquit, quam pro libito in negotiis praedestinationis & reprobationis multiplicentur instantia a Theologis, & quam parum illa conferant ad assignandam rationem differentiae inter praedestinatos & reprobos. Liceat itaque hic paucis monere, non esse nimis confidendum, aut tanquam certo dogmati adhaerescendum, ulli certo ordini decretorum Divinorum, sive a Protestantibus sive Pontificiis assignato, cum difficile sit duos reperire, sive inter nostros, sive inter adversarios, qui ad amussim per omnia consentiant in hac serie decretorum Divinorum describenda. Caveat itaque unusquisque ne talem considerationem praedestinationis & reprobationis inducat, quae vel Divinae justitiae, vel gratiae gratuitae adversatur: & cum non multum refert quo ordine prioritatis & posterioritatis haec decreta, quae reapse in Deo omnino simul sunt, secundum nostrum intelligendi modum distribuantur & disponantur.
english: Second: although every act in God's mind and will is eternal, and so not parted even by the lightest instant of before and after, still, from the side of the things God understands and has decreed, certain signs of priority and posteriority can be marked — according to our way of understanding. In that sense theologians ask whether God first decreed to give the elect eternal life, or faith and obedience that lead to eternal life; and whether he first reprobated some and cast them from eternal life before he foresaw them fallen and stained by sin. Hence nearly everyone who has written on predestination and reprobation draws a kind of series, almost a little table, trying to sketch the order of the Divine decrees — not because they judge that in God himself one decree is really before or after another, but because, given the ordered dependence of the things in themselves, our intellect ought to conceive one before another. Yet among the Scholastics themselves this teaching about those signs or instants of before and after — props by which our weak reason steadies itself when it thinks of God's decrees — is not very fixed or constant. Scotus, the chief craftsman of these signs, seems to some not only to have set them as prior and posterior in our mode of understanding, but also to have held that one is prior by nature to another in God himself — as if that before-and-after order could be assigned from the nature of the thing in the Divine acts themselves. But when I read carefully what Scotus teaches on these signs (1 Sent. dist. 41 q. unica; 3 Sent. dist. 7 q. 4 and dist. 19 q. unica), he seems to me to teach only this: that in the things themselves there is some foundation from which we conceive that one decree of God is to be set before another by a certain order of our reason. From the other side our Occam denied these signs however considered (1 Sent. dist. 9 q. 3); and Biel, taking that view, attacked them (3 Sent. dist. 2 q. 1 dub. 3): "Priorities are not to be placed in Divine things, any more than pluralities of ordered acts. For there is one act in Divine things, indistinct in reality and in reason, which is the Divine essence itself; by that one cognition God foresaw Christ's incarnation, the future beatitude of all the elect, the fall and the repair — not one before, another after." And he adds at once that not even according to our consideration can such an order of before and after be conceived in the Divine decrees without that consideration becoming a false speculation. Dominic Báñez, though he does not wholly explode these signs with Biel, still weighs the theologians' discord in assigning them and says: notice how freely, in the business of predestination and reprobation, theologians multiply instants, and how little those help assign the account of the difference between the predestined and the reprobate. So let this brief warning stand: do not trust too much, or cling as to fixed dogma, to any certain order of the Divine decrees, whether drawn by Protestants or by Papal writers. It is hard to find two — among ours or among adversaries — who agree to the line in every point when they describe this series of Divine decrees. Let each take care not to bring in a view of predestination and reprobation that runs against Divine justice or free grace; and since these decrees are in reality altogether simultaneous in God, it matters little in what order of before and after we distribute and arrange them according to our mode of understanding.

source_text: Tertio, quia propter imbecillitatem intellectus nostri cogimur saepenumero in materia praedestinationis explicanda, aliquid concipere ut prius, aliquid ut posterius (ut cum cogitamus Deum prius considerasse hominem ut lapsum, quam ut in Christo electum; vel cum affirmamus Deum prius hominem destinare ad vitam aeternam, quam ad gratiam efficacem) videamus qua in re fundetur hic ordo prioritatis & posterioritatis, quem consideramus in actibus Divinis. Non in ipsa scientia vel voluntate Dei secundum se: nam in Divinis, omnia sunt simul duratione. Fundatur itaque in ipsa rerum habitudine, prout una ex altera dependet. Quocirca secundum modum considerationis nostrae illud prius intelligitur in mente & voluntate Divina, a quo aliud pendet secundum ordinem causalitatis; illud posterius, quod pendet ab alio: si autem unum se habeat prorsus independenter ad aliud, neutrum dicendum est altero prius aut posterius. Dein, diligenter animadvertendum est, idem in diverso genere causae posse esse prius & posterius altero. Quod evidenter apparebit si causam effectivam seu dispositivam cum finali comparemus. Nam in genere causae finalis sanitas est prior pharmaco: movet etenim tum medicum ut det, tum aegrotum ut illud accipiat: At in genere causae effectivae pharmacum est prius sanitate: nam ejus virtute & efficacia aegrotus ad sanitatem reducitur. Sic in negotio praedestinationis, voluntas dandi vitam aeternam concipitur prior voluntate dandi efficacem gratiam in ordine causae finalis: nam ex intentione dandi vitam oritur decretum dandi talem gratiam: At in ordine causae effectivae prior est voluntas dandi gratiam, quae ideo datur ut ejus virtute & efficacia praeeunte homo perducatur ad gloriam. Atque hoc est quod a Philosopho innuitur, Ethic. 3. cap. 8. ubi docet, illud quod est ultimum in intentione, esse primum in executione; & e contra. Ratio hujus discriminis manifesta est; Quia in actu volendi & intendendi illud habet rationem causae, quod sui desiderio & amore movet efficientem ad talia media quaerenda & applicanda; in actu autem exsequendi illud habet rationem causae quod ipsum finem promovet, & operatur ad finis consecutionem. Sic Bannesius, Finis qui in intentione operantis habet rationem causae respectu mediorum, in exsecutione positus habet rationem effectus, & ipsa media habent rationem efficientis respectu ejus. Hoc valde observandum: nam cum secundum rem sit unicus & idem actus voluntatis in Deo, quo vult tam media quam finem, & finem per media, & media propter finem; tamen secundum nostrum intelligendi modum haec omnia distinguuntur: & hinc perplexae quaestiones, quid horum prius, quid posterius in voluntate Divina. Ut hisce occurratur, semper perpendendum est quem ordinem causalitatis res ipsae inter se habeant: nam eundem prioritatis habere intelliguntur. Hoc etiam addendum est, licet in actibus Divinae voluntatis quoad rem nulla sit prioritas vel posterioritas, tamen Deus non vult res creatas confuse & inordinate. Verum est quidem, in Deo non esse volitiones multas, nec unam alia priorem: sed unico tamen simplicissimo actu voluntatis suae voluit unam rem esse propter aliam, unam esse dependentem ab alia. Et hinc illa consideratio prioritatis & posterioritatis, quae proprie competit ipsis rebus, a nobis tribuitur ipsis decretis Divinis. Quapropter, quoties disceptatur sive de scientia Dei, quaerendo, ex duobus utrum hoc an illud prius sciverit; sive de voluntate, quaerendo ex duobus utrum hoc an illud prius decreverit; semper meminisse debetis, hanc prioritatem aut posterioritatem non inesse reapse, vere, & formaliter, ipsis actibus mentis & voluntatis Divinae, sed considerari ex parte rerum a Deo cognitarum & decretarum, inter quas Deus voluit esse veram & realem quandam prioritatem & posterioritatem. Atque haec pro instituto nostro, hac de re dixisse sufficiat.
english: Third: because our intellect is weak, we are often forced, when explaining predestination, to conceive something as before and something as after — as when we think God first considered the human being as fallen, before as elect in Christ; or when we say God first destines a person to eternal life, before to efficacious grace. So let us see where this order of before and after, which we mark in the Divine acts, is founded. Not in God's knowledge or will considered in itself: in Divine things all are simultaneous in duration. It is founded in the relation of the things themselves, insofar as one depends on another. Therefore, in our mode of consideration, that is prior in the Divine mind and will from which another hangs in the order of causality; that is posterior which hangs from another. If one stands wholly independent of another, neither is prior or posterior to the other. Next, mark carefully: the same thing can be prior and posterior to another in different kinds of cause. Compare an efficient or dispositive cause with a final one. In the kind of final cause, health is prior to the drug: it moves the physician to give it and the sick person to take it. But in the kind of efficient cause the drug is prior to health: by its virtue and efficacy the sick person is brought back to health. So in predestination: the will to give eternal life is conceived prior to the will to give efficacious grace in the order of final cause — for from the intention of giving life arises the decree to give such grace. But in the order of efficient cause the will to give grace is prior, and grace is given so that by its virtue and efficacy going before, the person may be led through to glory. That is what the Philosopher hints (Ethics 3.8): what is last in intention is first in execution, and the reverse. The reason is plain. In the act of willing and intending, that has the account of a cause which by desire and love of itself moves the agent to seek and apply such means; but in the act of executing, that has the account of a cause which advances the end itself and works toward obtaining it. So Báñez: the end which in the agent's intention has the account of a cause with respect to the means, when set in execution has the account of an effect, and the means themselves have the account of an efficient cause toward it. Mark this well: although in reality there is one and the same act of will in God by which he wills both means and end, the end through the means, and the means for the end, still in our mode of understanding all these are distinguished — and hence the tangled questions which of them is prior or posterior in the Divine will. To meet those questions, always weigh what order of causality the things themselves have among themselves: they are understood to carry the same order of priority. Add this too: although in the acts of the Divine will as to the thing there is no before or after, God does not will created things in a confused, unordered heap. It is true that in God there are not many volitions, nor one prior to another; yet by one most simple act of his will he willed one thing to be for another, and one to depend on another. Hence that consideration of before and after which properly belongs to the things themselves is attributed by us to the Divine decrees. So whenever the dispute is about God's knowledge — asking of two which he knew first — or about his will — asking of two which he decreed first — always remember: this priority or posteriority does not inhere really, truly, and formally in the acts of the Divine mind and will themselves, but is considered from the side of the things God has known and decreed, among which he willed a true and real before and after. And for our purpose, that is enough on this point.

source_text: 2. Jam veniamus ad explicationem illorum trium vocabulorum, quae subinde recurrent in tota nostra futura disputatione. Primum est Electio: Quod vocabulum in sacris Scripturis diversimode usurpatur. Nam aliquando designat separationem alicujus gentis, ad participationem communem verbi & aliorum mediorum, quibus homines ordinare perducuntur ad salutem. Sic Deus elegisse dicitur nationem Judaeorum, aliis gentibus praeteritis. Te elegit Jehovah Deus tuus, ut sis populus peculiaris prae omnibus populis, &c. Deut. vii.6. Aliquando vox haec denotat separationem certae alicujus personae ad munus aliquod sive officium vel in Republica vel in ecclesia. Sic Deus dicitur Saulum elegisse in regem Judaeorum: Videte quem elegerit Jehovah, 1 Sam. x.24. & Christus duodecim sic elegit in Apostolos: Nonne ego vos duodecim elegi, Johan. vi.70. De hisce electionibus non jam quaeritur: quamvis & in his ac caeteris ejusmodi, observare liceat electionem semper significare alicujus aut aliquorum e numero plurium separationem ad specialem finem ab agente intentum.
english: 2. Let us now explain the three words that will keep returning through the whole dispute ahead. First is Election. Scripture uses that word in more than one way. Sometimes it means setting a people apart to share the word and the ordinary means by which people are led to salvation. So God is said to have chosen the Jewish nation and passed by the other nations. "The Lord your God has chosen you to be a people for his own possession, out of all the peoples," and so on ([[Deuteronomy 7:6 >> Bible:Deuteronomy 7:6]]). Sometimes the same word means setting a particular person apart for an office in the state or in the church. So God is said to have chosen Saul as king of the Jews: "See whom the Lord has chosen" ([[1 Samuel 10:24 >> Bible:1 Samuel 10:24]]); and Christ chose the Twelve as apostles: "Did I not choose you, the twelve?" ([[John 6:70 >> Bible:John 6:70]]). Those elections are not our question now. Still, in them and in every case of the same kind, election always means taking someone — or some — out of a larger number for a special end the agent intends.

source_text: Electio igitur, de qua nobis agendum erit, denotat singularem actionem voluntatis Divinae ab aeterno separantis quosdam ad finem gloriae seu vitae aeternae, aliis praeteritis. Atque haec electio, sicuti etiam & dilectio, praesupponitur praedestinationi, ut recte annotavit Thomas. Nam omnes praedestinati intelliguntur electi & dilecti: Dilecti, quatenus Deus vult illis bonum aeternae vitae; electi, quatenus vult illis hoc bonum quod non vult aliis. Proprie igitur & recte sumpta electio solum finem respicit, & est voluntas Divina conferendi gloriam singularibus quibusdam personis, cum praeteritione aliorum. Quanquam fatendum est, a Theologis nonnunquam confundi electionem cum praedestinatione: Quando vero distinguuntur, electio praecipue & proprie refertur ad ipsum finem, uti dictum est; praedestinatio ad media, uti nunc ostendetur.
english: The election we must treat, then, is the singular act of the Divine will that from eternity sets certain ones apart for the end of glory — eternal life — and passes others by. Thomas rightly notes that this election, like love, is presupposed to predestination. All the predestined are understood as elect and beloved: beloved insofar as God wills them the good of eternal life; elect insofar as he wills them that good and does not will it to others. Taken properly, election looks only to the end: it is God's will to confer glory on particular persons while passing others by. Theologians do sometimes blur election with predestination. When the words are kept apart, election belongs chiefly to the end itself; predestination belongs to the means — as we will now show.

source_text: Venio igitur ad vocabulum Praedestinationis, quod aliquando, licet raro, in malam etiam partem usurpatur a Theologis, nimirum pro destinatione ad mortem. Sic Augustinus Tract. 48. in Johan.: Quomodo, inquit, istis dixit, Non estis ex ovibus meis? quia videbat eos ad sempiternum interitum praedestinatos, non ad vitam aeternam sui sanguinis pretio comparatos. Et 15. De civit. cap. 1. Duo dicit esse civitates vel societates hominum; quarum una praedestinata est in aeternum regnare cum Deo, altera aeternum supplicium subire cum diabolo. Sic etiam nonnunquam loquuntur Augustini discipuli, Prosper, & Fulgentius. Quinetiam Patres in Concilio Valentino confitentur praedestinationem electorum ad vitam, & praedestinationem impiorum ad mortem. Sed nos (quod jam fere obtinuit in Schola Theologorum) praedestinationis & praedestinatorum vocabula arctamus ad illam providentiam Dei specialem, qua ab aeterno proposuit illorum salutem efficacibus mediis procurare, quos in Christo elegit: & conformiter huic aeterno proposito, eorundem salutem in tempore efficaciter & infallibiliter operatur.
english: I turn next to Predestination. Theologians sometimes — though rarely — use that word for a bad end too: destination to death. So Augustine on John, Tractate 48: How did he say to them, "You are not of my sheep"? Because he saw them predestined to everlasting ruin, not purchased for eternal life by the price of his blood. And in City of God 15.1 he says there are two cities or societies of human beings: one predestined to reign forever with God, the other to suffer eternal punishment with the devil. Augustine's disciples Prosper and Fulgentius sometimes speak the same way. The Fathers at the Council of Valence even confess a predestination of the elect to life and a predestination of the ungodly to death. We, following what has nearly become school usage, narrow "predestination" and "the predestined" to that special providence of God by which from eternity he proposed to secure, by efficacious means, the salvation of those he chose in Christ — and, matching that eternal purpose, he works their salvation in time efficaciously and without fail.

source_text: In praedestinatione ergo considerare possumus duos actus, unum voluntatis Divinae, alterum intellectus. Ad voluntatis actum pertinet, velle huic singulari personae salutem, eligere illum prae aliis, misereri ejus, & aliorum non misereri: quem tamen actum (ut antea observavimus) Aquinas putat esse praevium praedestinationi, & electionem appellat. Ad intellectus actum pertinet, praescire, & dirigere per media infallibilia hasce certas personas ad finem illis destinatum. Atque in hoc potissimum proprius & peculiaris praedestinationis actus versatur. Huc facit Augustiniana illa praedestinationis descriptio, Praedestinatio nihil aliud est quam praescientia & praeparatio beneficiorum Dei, quibus certissime liberantur quicunque liberantur. Nos igitur per praedestinationem semper intelligimus hanc providentiae Divinae partem quae electos suos per media infallibilia dirigit & perducit ad finem aeternae beatitudinis. Quanta sit necessitas hujus praedestinationis exinde patet, quod cum vita gloriae sit finis superans virtutem naturae humanae, non sufficit ad ejus consecutionem quod ex Dei gratuita bonitate eligamur solummodo ad hunc finem, nisi insuper per Divinam sapientiam & potentiam media apta & infallibilia nobis suppeditentur, quorum adminiculo dirigamur ad eundem. Similitudine non inepta hoc illustratur ab Aquinate. Sicut sagitta, quae primo ex proposito sagittarii destinatur ad certum scopum, mox virtute ejusdem, mediante arcu, ad eundem dirigitur & quasi transmittitur: sic quaelibet persona, quae ab aeterno ex proposito Dei destinatur ad scopum vitae aeternae, in tempore, ejusdem virtute, mediante gratia efficaci, ad hanc metam gloriae dirigitur, & tandem perducitur. Atque haec ratio transmittendi electos in vitam aeternam, quatenus ab omni aeternitate in mente Divina existere intelligitur, praedestinatio nominatur.
english: In predestination, then, we can mark two acts: one of the Divine will, one of the intellect. The will's act is to will salvation for this particular person, to choose him before others, to show him mercy and not show mercy to others — an act Aquinas (as we noted earlier) treats as prior to predestination and calls election. The intellect's act is to foreknow, and to direct these particular persons by infallible means to the end destined for them. That second act is where predestination proper chiefly lives. Augustine's description fits here: Predestination is nothing other than God's foreknowledge and preparation of the benefits by which whoever are set free are set free with certainty. So by predestination we always mean that part of Divine providence which directs its elect by infallible means and leads them through to eternal blessedness. How necessary this is becomes clear once you see that the life of glory surpasses what human nature can reach: free election to that end is not enough unless Divine wisdom and power also supply fit, infallible means that guide us there. Aquinas's likeness is not strained. An arrow is first aimed at a mark by the archer's purpose; then by his power, through the bow, it is sent toward that same mark. So every person destined from eternity by God's purpose for the mark of eternal life is, in time, by that same power, through efficacious grace, directed to glory's goal and at last brought there. That whole account of transmitting the elect into eternal life — as it is understood to stand from all eternity in the Divine mind — is what we call predestination.

source_text: De opposito Reprobationis vocabulo jam paucis dicemus. Ad vocem quod attinet, in sacris Scripturis reprobus & reprobare referuntur potius ad praesentem hominum impiorum conditionem, quam ad aeternam Dei de illis ordinationem. Nam ἀδόκιμος sive reprobus appellatur qui impie vivit, nec gerit se pro filio Dei, sed factis ostendit se esse rejectitium, spurium & adulterinum: Atque Deus tales repellere, rejicere sive reprobare dicitur propter illorum impuritatem, sicut aurifices rejiciunt nummos adulterinos. Quinetiam apud Augustinum (qui hanc materiam uberius & dilucidius quam caeteri Patres tractavit) reproborum & reprobandi vocabula, eo sensu quo nunc in Schola Theologorum frequentantur, aut raro, aut non omnino occurrunt. Sed tamen sciendum est rem ipsam in sacris Scripturis aperte contineri. Primo, quando ea affirmantur in sacris Scripturis unde clara & necessaria consecutione deducitur quorundam reprobatio: Ut cum certae quaedam & signatae personae dicuntur electi & praedestinati a Deo ante jacta mundi fundamenta. Electio enim aliquorum praeteritionem sive rejectionem aliorum infert. Secundo, quando verbis aequivalentibus reprobationis decretum exprimitur: ut cum Deus dicitur quosdam nunquam nosse, non dedisse Christo, nolle quorundam misereri, non scripsisse quorundam nomina in libro vitae, & id genus alia, quae liquido probant, apud Divinam mentem & voluntatem fuisse discrimen electorum & non-electorum ab aeterno. Postremo, licet Augustinus, aliique Patres non multum utantur hoc vocabulo reprobationis, tamen aliis utuntur quae perinde valent. Nam quos Schola appellat reprobatos, illi vocant praescitos & praedestinatos ad interitum.
english: On the opposite word, Reprobation, a few points. As for the bare term, Scripture's "reprobate" and "to reprobate" point more to the present state of the ungodly than to God's eternal decree about them. ἀδόκιμος — a reprobate — is one who lives ungodly, does not carry himself as a son of God, and by his deeds shows himself counterfeit, spurious, adulterate. God is said to reject or reprobate such people because of that impurity, as goldsmiths throw out counterfeit coins. Even in Augustine — who treated this matter more richly and clearly than the other Fathers — "reprobate" and "reprobating" in the school sense barely appear, or do not appear at all. Still, the thing itself is plainly in Scripture. First, when Scripture affirms what forces the reprobation of some by clear necessary consequence: as when certain named persons are said elect and predestined by God before the world's foundations were laid. Election of some imports passing by — rejecting — others. Second, when equivalent phrases express the decree: God is said never to have known some, not to have given them to Christ, to refuse mercy to some, not to have written some names in the book of life — and the like, which plainly prove that from eternity the Divine mind and will marked a difference between elect and non-elect. Finally, though Augustine and the other Fathers seldom use the school word "reprobation," they use other words that mean the same. Those the School calls reprobates, they call foreknown and predestined to destruction.

source_text: Sed misso vocabulo, veniamus ad rem. Sicuti igitur eligere & praedestinare denotat illum aeternum actum Divinae voluntatis, quo decrevit quasdam personas dirigere ad beatitudinem infallibiliter consequendam; sic reprobare denotat oppositum actum Divinae voluntatis, quo decrevit permittere quasdam personas ab hoc fine beatitudinis deficere & excidere. Atque hoc vel maxime convenit providentiae Divinae, ut permittat aliquem defectum in rebus quae providentiae ejus subduntur. Videte Aquinatem, part. 1. qu. 23. art. 6. In hac reprobatione duos quasi actus Divinae voluntatis consideramus. Prior est, nolle eligere ad beatitudinem infallibiliter consequendam. Atque cur hic actus potius ad Judam quam ad Petrum terminetur, nulla datur ratio ex parte reprobati, sed referendum est ad libertatem Divinae voluntatis. Sic Bannes: In singulari, quare Deus hos elegerit, illos reprobaverit, non habet causam adaequatam, nisi Divinam voluntatem. Et eodem in articulo dicit, hanc praedestinationem aliquorum, & reprobationem aliorum esse manifestationem maximae libertatis, quam habet Divina voluntas circa dispensationem bonorum supernaturalium: quae libertas est magna perfectio Divina. Hunc actum, quem nos appellamus praeteritionem sive non-electionem, Bellarminus vocat actum negativum reprobationis. Sed illud hic cavendum est, ne cum Scoto putemus Dei voluntatem respectu reproborum, quos non eligit, sed praeterit, habere se mere negative. Nam in hoc actu, quem per negationem significamus, continetur expressa & affirmata voluntas Dei, non innuitur negata aut suspensa actio volendi circa reproborum deficientiam a beatitudine. Affirmative ergo explicari debet & intelligi hic actus Divinae voluntatis, & non solum negative. Nam praeteritio sive non-electio involvit hosce actus affirmativos: volo permittere Judam deficere a vita aeterna: volo & decerno Judae non dare eam gratiam specialem, quam si reciperet, perveniret ad vitam aeternam. Haec de priori actu reprobationis. Posterior est, destinare ad poenam. Atque hic actus terminatur ad reprobatum, sicuti praecognitus & praevisus est peccato contaminatus, idque ex vitio propriae voluntatis. Hanc Scotus vocat privativam reprobationem; Bellarminus, actum positivum reprobationis. Et designat voluntatem damnandi personam reprobatam. Porro, notandum est, erga ipsos reprobatos exhiberi a Deo quaedam effecta quae non fluunt a reprobatione illorum; ut quod creentur, quod vocentur ad cognitionem Evangelii, quod illustrentur cognitione supernaturali: nam haec, & alia ejusmodi, effecta sunt communis amoris, & communis providentiae Divinae, non reprobationis.
english: Drop the bare word; come to the thing. As to elect and to predestinate name that eternal act of the Divine will by which God decreed to direct certain persons to blessedness they will infallibly reach, so to reprobate names the opposite act: the decree to permit certain persons to fail and fall short of that end. That fits providence itself — which allows some defect in the things under its care. See Aquinas, ST I q.23 a.6. In reprobation we mark two quasi-acts of the Divine will. The first is unwillingness to elect someone to blessedness obtained without fail. Why that act lands on Judas rather than Peter has no reason on the reprobate's side; it is referred to the liberty of the Divine will. So Báñez: in the particular case, why God chose these and reprobated those has no adequate cause but the Divine will. In the same article he says this predestination of some and reprobation of others manifests the greatest liberty the Divine will has in dispensing supernatural goods — and that liberty is a great Divine perfection. The act we call passing-by or non-election, Bellarmine calls the negative act of reprobation. Guard this point: do not follow Scotus in treating God's will toward the reprobate — whom he does not choose but passes by — as merely negative. In the act we name by a negation there is an expressed, affirmative will of God; it does not mean God simply suspends willing about their falling short of blessedness. Read that act affirmatively, not only negatively. Passing-by / non-election involves affirmative decrees: I will to permit Judas to fall short of eternal life; I will and decree not to give Judas that special grace which, if he received it, would bring him to eternal life. So much for the first act. The second is to destine to punishment. That act terminates on the reprobate as foreknown and foreseen stained by sin — and that from the fault of his own will. Scotus calls this privative reprobation; Bellarmine, the positive act of reprobation. It designates the will to damn the reprobate person. Note also: God shows the reprobate certain effects that do not flow from their reprobation — that they are created, called to know the Gospel, illuminated with supernatural knowledge. Those are effects of common love and common providence, not of reprobation.

source_text: Propria autem & vera effecta reprobationis negativae haec sunt: Nolle decernere efficacem liberationem personae in statu damnationis jacentis; Velle negare tali personae auxilia efficacia quibus de facto converteretur. Ultimus effectus est aeterna punitio obstinati peccatoris: qui non proprie oritur ex mera praeteritione vel non-electione, sed ex illo altero reprobationis actu, quem praedamnationem licet appellare; atque peccati praevisionem supponit, & derelictionem in eodem. Jam & illud perpendendum, effecta reprobationis non habere illam connexionem inter se, quam habent effecta praedestinationis. Nam in praedestinatione prior effectus solet esse causa posterioris; ut vocatio efficax parit fidem, fides justificationem, &c.; sed in reprobatione effectus non sunt hoc modo invicem ordinati, quamvis omnes junctim sumpti ordinentur ad unum & eundem finem, relucentiam scilicet justitiae Divinae. Ultimo, & illud contra quorumdam malevolas calumniationes animadvertendum est: Licet peccata, qualia sunt infidelitas, improbitas, obduratio, & poena hisce debita, hoc est, aeterna damnatio, in homine lapso aeque infallibiliter consequantur reprobationem, atque fides, sanctitas, perseverantia consequuntur praedestinationem, tamen non eodem modo consequuntur. Nam Deus agens ex decreto praedestinationis operatur haec priora per influxum gratiae efficacis: at ex decreto reprobationis nihil agit quo deterior efficiatur reprobatus, nihil quo vel impediatur a credendo & sancte vivendo, vel impellatur ad infidelitatem aut improbitatem. Hoc diligenter observandum est, quia tam veteres Pelagiani, quam novi, cum videant, posita reprobatione tali qualem descripsimus, neminem reproborum aut credere perseveranter, aut sancte vivere, illico clamant, nos facere Deum autorem peccati, & causam cur vel non credant, vel resilant a fide & sanctitate; Sed cum Propheta respondemus cuivis reprobo, perditio tua ex te, licet auxilium ex solo Deo. Nam reprobatio nil subtrahit de potentia ipsius reprobati, quamvis Deus erga illum non exserat illam potentiam efficacem, quam posset si vellet. Sic olim Prosper, Deus neminem boni possibilitate desoliat. Non est ergo consequens, sicut putant qui talia objiciunt, ut Deus quibus poenitentiam non dederit, resipiscentiam abstulerit; & quos non levaverit, alliserit, &c. haec ille. Longe aliter igitur se habet reprobatio in causando, quam praedestinatio. Deus praedestinans operatur omnia bona in praedestinatis per influxum gratiae, & causa efficiens proprie nominatur: sed Deus reprobans nulla operatur mala in reprobis per subtractionem gratiae, sed mala consequenter erumpunt ex corruptione naturae, quorum Deus non magis causa est, quam sol tenebrarum, quando non illuminat aerem. Haec de electione, Praedestinatione & reprobatione praefanda putavi.
english: The proper effects of negative reprobation are these: unwillingness to decree the efficacious liberation of a person lying under damnation; and the will to deny that person the efficacious helps by which he would in fact be converted. The last effect is the eternal punishment of the obstinate sinner. That does not properly rise from mere passing-by or non-election, but from the other reprobation-act one may call pre-damnation — which presupposes foresight of sin and leaving the person in it. Weigh this too: reprobation's effects are not chained to one another the way predestination's are.
