In predestination the earlier effect usually causes the later — efficacious calling begets faith, faith justification, and so on. In reprobation the effects are not ordered that way, though taken together they serve one end: the shining of Divine justice. Finally, against certain malevolent slanders, mark this: In the fallen human being, sins such as unbelief, wickedness, and hardening — and the penalty due them, eternal damnation — follow reprobation as infallibly as faith, holiness, and perseverance follow predestination; yet they do not follow in the same way. Acting from the decree of predestination, God works those earlier goods by the influx of efficacious grace. From the decree of reprobation he does nothing that makes the reprobate worse, nothing that blocks believing and holy living, nothing that drives him into unbelief or wickedness. Watch that carefully. Old Pelagians and new alike see that, given reprobation as we have described it, none of the reprobate perseveres in faith or holy life — and they cry at once that we make God the author of sin and the cause why people do not believe or spring back from faith and holiness. With the Prophet we answer every reprobate: your destruction is from you, though help is from God alone. Reprobation takes nothing from the reprobate's own power; God simply does not put forth toward him the efficacious power he could put forth if he willed. So Prosper long ago: God despoils no one of the possibility of the good. It does not follow — as the objectors think — that those to whom God has not given penitence he has robbed of repentance, or that those he has not lifted he has struck down, and so on. Reprobation causes in a far different way from predestination. God predestinating works every good in the predestined by grace's influx, and is properly called an efficient cause. God reprobating works no evils in the reprobate by subtracting grace; the evils break out from nature's corruption — and God is no more their cause than the sun is cause of darkness when it does not light the air. So much I thought should be set down first on election, Predestination, and reprobation.

source_text: III. Tertio in loco jam accedamus ad qualitates sive conditiones subjecti communiter & indistincte considerati; hoc est, ad inquirendum, quibus qualitatibus necesse sit ut vestiatur, & quasi induatur illud subjectum, in quod hic actus Divinus sive praedestinationis sive reprobationis indiscriminatim terminetur. Primo, extra controversiam est, ut actus praedestinationis aut reprobationis cadat in subjectum quodcunque, hanc qualitatem sive conditionem requiri, ut illud subjectum sit natura rationali praeditum. Rationalitas ergo est necessaria conditio semper supponenda in subjecto vel praedestinato, vel reprobato. In promptu & cuivis obvia est hujus rei ratio; quia scilicet tam praedestinatio quam reprobatio est decretum Dei circa finem supernaturalem aeternae beatitudinis; cujus finis natura bruta nullo modo capax esse potest. Quando igitur dicimus aliquem ad beatitudinem ordinatum per praedestinationem, aut a beatitudine exclusum per reprobationem, necesse est ut utrumque de rationali creatura intelligatur. Sed quae perspicua sunt, longa esse non debent.
english: III. Third: the qualities or conditions of the subject taken commonly and without distinction — what must clothe that subject on which the Divine act of predestination or reprobation, taken without discrimination, terminates. First, beyond dispute: for either act to fall on any subject at all, that subject must be endowed with a rational nature. Rationality is therefore a necessary condition always to be supposed in the predestined or the reprobate. The reason is plain to anyone. Both predestination and reprobation are God's decree about the supernatural end of eternal blessedness, and brute nature cannot be capable of that end. So when we say someone is ordered to blessedness by predestination, or shut out of it by reprobation, both must be understood of a rational creature. What is clear need not be long.

source_text: Est altera qualitas sive conditio quam plerique arbitrantur necessario prerequiri & praesupponi in actu Praedestinandi & Reprobandi, sed non est tam in confesso apud omnes: Haec autem est Peccati infectio, quam a Deo praevisam putant in subjecto, priusquam vel praedestinari vel reprobari possit. Ex horum igitur sententia, ut actus hi terminentur ad creaturam, non sufficit quod rationalis sit, sed etiam praesupponitur quod peccatrix, sive peccato coinquinata sit. Haud lubens hanc litem meam fecerim; paucis tamen quid ab aliis sentiatur, & quid ipse sentiam, aperiam. Est itaque nobis necessario fatendum, non esse nuper natam, aut ignobilium Theologorum sententiam, quae ponit praedestinationem priorem praevisione peccati. Imo omnes fere qui per praedestinationem intellexerunt non tam mediorum praeparationem, quam meram designationem ad ipsum finem, hoc modo philosophati sunt. Scotus ubi assignat ordinem instantium in mente & voluntate Divina, semper statuit priorem esse voluntatem dandi beatitudinem praevisione lapsus, Lib. 1. dist. 41. qu. unica; & lib. 3. dist. 19. qu. 1. ponit Deum in primo instanti voluisse gloriam determinato numero electorum, in secundo ordinasse illis gratiam, in tertio praevidisse eos lapsuros in Adamo. Jam cum dico Scotum in hac sententia fuisse, intelligitis & alios quam plurimos, qui Scotistae haberi volunt, idem sensisse. Maclantus, Galatinus, Alfonfus Mendoza, aliique innumeri decretum praedestinationis, non solum decreto lapsus permittendi, sed etiam hominis creandi, prius esse docent. Hi ergo non putant peccatum praevisum esse conditionem, aut qualitatem subjecti, in quod cadere debet actus praedestinationis. Postremo, ex Jesuitis neotericis, ipse Suarez hanc sententiam sequitur, & communem esse testatur, hisce verbis: Probabiliorem existimo communem sententiam Theologorum asserentium, electionem hominum praedestinatorum antecessisse permissionem originalis peccati.
english: Another quality most writers treat as necessarily presupposed in predestinating and reprobating — though not all agree: the infection of sin, which they think God foresaw in the subject before it could be predestined or reprobated. On their view rationality is not enough; the creature must also be presupposed a sinner, stained with sin. I do not gladly make this quarrel my own; still I will open briefly what others hold and what I hold. We must admit that the opinion which puts predestination before foresight of sin is neither new nor the property of obscure theologians. Nearly everyone who took predestination as bare designation to the end itself, rather than preparation of means, reasoned this way. Scotus, ordering instants in the Divine mind and will, always set the will to give beatitude before foresight of the fall (I dist. 41; III dist. 19 q.1): God first wills glory for a fixed number of elect, next orders grace for them, then foresees their fall in Adam. With Scotus stand many who claim the Scotist name. Maclantus, Galatinus, Alfonso Mendoza, and countless others teach the decree of predestination prior even to permitting the fall — and prior to creating man. So they do not treat foresight of sin as a condition of the subject on which predestination falls. Among recent Jesuits Suarez follows the same line and calls it the common opinion: I judge more probable the theologians' common view that the election of the predestined preceded permission of original sin.

source_text: Posse Deum eligere & reprobare ante omnem praevisionem peccati, manifestum est in Angelorum electione & reprobatione. Nam qui steterunt, proculdubio electi fuerunt; & qui ceciderunt, praeteriti sive reprobati, idque ante praevisum discrimen standi & labendi. Quod hac ratione ostendo. Necesse est ut concedamus, Deum intellexisse ante voluntarium decretum creandi aut salvandi Angelos, eos, quos tali gratia donaret, de facto in sanctitate perseveraturos, & aeternam beatitudinem adepturos; e contra, vidisse eos qui perierunt, infallibiliter casuros, si illam solam gratiam iis daret, quam de facto postea dedit. Quaero, Cur dedit bonis Angelis illam gratiam, quam sciebat illos ad gloriam perducturam? Aliud fingi non potest, nisi quod antecessit voluntas illos salvandi, quam appellamus Electionem vel Praedestinationem. Quaero itidem, Cur dedit malis illam gratiam, qua sola accepta intellexit illos infallibiliter perituros? Respondemus necesse est, Quia antecessit voluntas permittendi illos deficere a beatitudine: nam alioquin novit, & potuit Deus non minus illis quam aliis dedisse gratiam, quae infallibiliter eos provexisset ad gloriam. Videtis erga Angelos habuisse Deum voluntatem eligendi quosdam ad gloriam, & non eligendi alios, non ortam post praevisionem standi in his, labendi in illis; sed causam potius hujus discriminis & diversi eventus, ac proinde ordine priorem. Electio igitur & praeteritio non praesupponunt necessario ex ipsa natura actuum praevisionem peccati in subjecto; quia non in Angelis. Sed videtur etiam quod nec in hominibus necessarium est ponere praevisionem peccati, ut conditionem in subjecto praedestinato & reprobato, priorem ipso decreto Praedestinationis & reprobationis. Nam (ut recte annotavit Thomas) metus non accipit speciem a termino a quo, sed a termino ad quem. Sicut ergo nihil refert quantum ad rationem dealbationis, utrum ille qui dealbatus fuerit niger, aut pallidus, aut rubens; sic nihil refert ad rationem praedestinationis, utrum aliquis praedestinetur in vitam aeternam, a statu miseriae, vel non. Haec ille. Potest itaque (secundum Thomam) actus praedestinationis cadere in subjectum peccati miseria nondum implicatum.
english: That God can elect and reprobate before any foresight of sin is plain in the angels. Those who stood were elect; those who fell were passed by or reprobated — and that before any foresight of standing versus falling. Before the decree to create or save them, God knew which angels, given such grace, would in fact persevere and reach eternal blessedness, and knew which would infallibly fall if given only the grace he later in fact gave. Why give the good angels grace he knew would bring them to glory? Only because a will to save them — election or predestination — came first. Why give the wicked angels grace he knew, taken alone, would leave them to perish? Because a will to permit their falling short of blessedness came first: otherwise he knew and could have given them, no less than the others, grace that would have carried them infallibly to glory. So toward the angels God's will to elect some and not others did not arise after foresight of who would stand or fall; it is rather the cause of that different outcome, and prior in order. Election and passing-by therefore do not, from the nature of the acts themselves, necessarily presuppose foresight of sin in the subject — not in angels. Nor does it seem necessary in humans to place foresight of sin as a condition in the subject prior to the decree of predestination and reprobation. Thomas notes rightly: motion takes its species from the terminus to which, not from the terminus from which. As whitening does not care whether the thing whitened was black, pale, or red, so predestination does not care whether someone is destined to eternal life from a state of misery or not. On Thomas's showing the act of predestination can fall on a subject not yet tangled in sin's misery.

source_text: Imo videtur Aquinas magis inclinare in illam sententiam, quae asserit ipsam reprobationem de facto antecessisse praevisionem originalis peccati. Nam cum dicit reprobare esse illam partem Divinae providentiae, quae permittit aliquos a fine beatitudinis deficere, innuit ipsam permissionem deficiendi a mediis ad beatitudinem ducentibus fluere a reprobatione, & proinde esse illa posteriorem secundum nostrum modum intelligendi. Quod si ipsa permissio deficiendi sequatur Reprobationem, tum multo magis praevisio actualis defectionis sive lapsus: praevidetur enim non nisi ex hypothesi permissionis. Haec a me in eum finem adducuntur, non quod huic sententiae adhaerescam, sed ut obiter perstringam illorum inscitiam dicam, an malitiam? qui Calvinum aut Bezam lacerant maledictis, quasi primarios autores hujus sententiae, quae inter Scholasticos & ipsos Pontificios non minus recepta est, quam illa contraria, quae ponit hominem peccato infectum subjectum praedestinationis. Atque ad Calvinum quod attinet, (quantum ego possum judicare) quamvis recte neget praescientiam peccati esse causam praedestinationis aut reprobationis; tamen cum Augustino semper statuit, praevisi peccati considerationem obversari Deo praedestinanti aut reprobanti, tanquam communem conditionem subjecti. Clara sunt illa verba, Si judicio mortis obnoxii sunt omnes naturali conditione, quos ad mortem Dominus praedestinat, si ex corrupta massa desumpti sunt omnes, non mirum si damnationi subjacent. Sed adhuc clariora audite. Postquam Paulus Deum ex perdita massa eligere & reprobare quos illi visum est, docuit, quare & quomodo id fiat adeo non expedit, ut potius expavescens in clamorem illum erumpat, O altitudo! Tract. De aeterna Dei praedestinatione, pag. 711. Scio Bezam, & Zanchium, aliosque viros perdoctos paulo durius loqui, & massae corruptae considerationem decreto praedestinationis omnino postponere, nunquam tamen damnationem alicujus decerni putant nisi ex praesupposito peccato.
english: Aquinas even seems to lean toward saying reprobation in fact preceded foresight of original sin. When he calls reprobation that part of Divine providence which permits some to fall short of beatitude, he implies that permission to fail from the means that lead to beatitude flows from reprobation — and so, in our way of understanding, is posterior to it. If permission to fail follows reprobation, then foresight of the actual fall follows all the more: it is foreseen only on the hypothesis of permission. I bring this in not because I cling to that opinion, but to touch in passing the ignorance — or malice? — of those who curse Calvin or Beza as if they invented a view no less current among Scholastics and even Pontificians than the contrary view that puts the sin-infected human as predestination's subject. As for Calvin (so far as I can judge): he rightly denies that foresight of sin is the cause of predestination or reprobation; yet with Augustine he always holds that consideration of foreseen sin stands before God as he predestinates or reprobates — as a common condition of the subject. Clear words: If all whom the Lord predestines to death are by natural condition liable to death's judgment, if all are taken from a corrupted mass, no wonder they lie under damnation. Hear clearer still. After Paul taught that God from a lost mass elects and reprobates whom he wills, why and how so little helps that, terrified, he breaks into O the depth! (Tractate on God's eternal predestination, p. 711). Beza, Zanchi, and other learned men speak more harshly and set consideration of the corrupted mass wholly after the decree of predestination — yet they never think anyone's damnation decreed except on presupposed sin.

source_text: Sed ut paucis expediam quid mei judicii sit hac in re. Primo, si per Praedestinationem quis intelligat solam designationem ad finem gloriae (sicuti multi intelligunt ex antiquioribus Scholasticis) & per Reprobationem solam negationem hujus actus, vel ipsum decretum praetereundi & non-eligendi, puto non esse necessarium ut supponamus peccatum fuisse praevisum in subjecto sic praedestinato aut reprobato, tanquam praecedaneum. Ratio haec est; Quia in actibus mentis & voluntatis Divinae unus non est realiter prior alio, sed tota haec prioritas & posterioritas desumitur ex mutua rerum dependentia: ubi ergo nulla est dependentia causalitatis inter res ipsas, nulla debet aut potest esse consideratio prioritatis aut posterioritatis in decretis Divinis, quae circa easdem versantur. Jam vero peccatum ad actum Divinae electionis vel non-electionis omnino impertinenter se habet: non est enim ratio actus sive hujus sive illius (ut omnes fatentur) neque est talis subjecti qualificatio, absque qua hi actus in subjectum cadere non possunt, sicuti est rationalitas; quod exemplo Angelorum antea demonstratum est. Cum itaque peccatum nec causa sit cur aliquis eligatur ad gloriam, aut permittatur deficere a gloria, nec dispositio subjecti sive ad hunc actum, sive ad illum necessaria, improprie loquitur, qui dicit hoc decretum eligendi aut non eligendi esse prius in mente Divina praevisione peccati; improprie etiam loquitur qui dicit praevisionem peccati fuisse priorem hoc decreto, cum inter res independentes nulla sit ponenda aut prioritas aut posterioritas, sive in mente, sive in voluntate Dei. Atque hinc colligere potestis, illos qui conantur horrendis nescio quibus consequentiis illorum sententiam deturpare, qui considerant decretum electionis & praeteritionis absque praevisione peccati, funiculos ex arena nectere.
english: My judgment in brief. First: if by Predestination you mean bare designation to the end of glory (as many older Scholastics do), and by Reprobation only the negation of that act — the decree to pass by and not elect — I do not think foresight of sin must be supposed as something prior in the subject so predestined or reprobated. Why? In God's mind and will no act is really prior to another; all before-and-after is taken from the mutual dependence of the things themselves. Where the things have no causal dependence, Divine decrees about them admit no before or after. Sin is altogether beside the point for the act of Divine election or non-election. It is not the reason of either act (all confess that), nor a qualification of the subject without which those acts cannot fall — as rationality is; the angels already showed that. Since sin is neither cause why someone is elect to glory or permitted to fall short of it, nor a disposition required for either act, it is improper to say the decree to elect or not elect is prior in God's mind to foresight of sin — and improper to say foresight of sin was prior to that decree — for among independent things there is no before or after in God's mind or will. Those who try to blacken, with I know not what horrid consequences, the view that considers election and passing-by without foresight of sin are twisting ropes out of sand.

source_text: Veruntamen, quia sacra Scriptura, & decus Patrum Augustinus, videntur per praedestinationem & reprobationem, non meram & solam electionem ad finem, nec meram praeteritionem sive non-electionem ad talem finem intelligere, sed simul conjungere cum decreto dandi finem, decretum praeparandi & dandi certa, designata, & infallibilia media ad finem; & cum decreto permittendi aliquem deficere a fine, aliud decretum copulare, puniendi & in aeternum damnandi ipsum qui defecit; ob hanc, inquam, causam puto melius & commodius, addo etiam verius hoc sensu, praevisum peccatum praesupponi ut conditionem subjecti, in quod cadit decretum talis praedestinationis & reprobationis. Ad Scripturam quod attinet, per praedestinationem solet denotare non nudam designationem ad finem gloriae, sed destinationem ad gloriam per media; nec per media quaelibet, sed per media gratiae efficacis derivatae a Christo Capite & Mediatore nostro. Huc faciunt illa loca; Eph. i.4. Vos elegit in ipso ut essemus sancti. 2 Tim. i.9. Servavit nos ex suo proposito & gratia, quae data est nobis in Christo ante tempora secularia. Ex quibus locis, aliisque multis quae accumulari possent, perspicuum est, Apostolum per praedestinationem intelligere destinationem & directionem ad finem gloriae per infallibilia media gratiae efficacis a Christo derivandae. De Augustino notius est quam ut multis egeat, illum per praedestinationem designare praeparationem gratiae infallibiliter perducentis ad gloriam. Celebris est illa definitio, Praedestinatio est praeparatio beneficiorum Dei, quibus certissime liberantur, quicunque liberantur. Unde Aquinas describit praedestinationem esse actum providentiae specialis ordinantis & dirigentis electos ad finem salutis, non per media quaelibet, sed per talia quae ipsum eventum infallibiliter producent. Sumatur itaque hoc: Praedestinationem prout usurpatur in Scripturis, designare non decretum abstractum, de solo fine, sed decretum quasi complicatum, de dando fine vitae aeternae per media gratiae in Christo. Jam ad Reprobationem quod attinet, ex usu Scripturarum designat non nudam praeteritionem aut non-electionem, sed praedamnationem sive deputationem ad interitum, quae inseparabili nexu cohaeret cum non-electione sive praeteritione, saltem quoad eventum. Hoc inde patet, quod reprobati vocentur in Scripturis vasa irae coagmentata ad interitum, Rom. ix.22. Olim descripti ad damnationem, Judae 4. Et Augustinus reprobationem appellat praedestinationem ad interitum. Sub reprobationis itaque vocabulo comprehendere debemus non nudum decretum praetereundi, aut non-eligendi aliquos, sed insuper voluntatem illos praedamnandi. His positis, dico talem praedestinationem & reprobationem non recte concipi aut explicari posse, nisi praeconcepto peccato, ut communi conditione in ipso subjecto.
english: Yet Scripture and Augustine, glory of the Fathers, do not take predestination and reprobation as bare election to the end, or bare passing-by. With the decree to give the end they join the decree to prepare and give certain, designated, infallible means; with the decree to permit falling short of the end they couple another — to punish and damn forever the one who fell short. For that reason I judge it better, fitter, and in this sense truer that foresight of sin be presupposed as a condition of the subject on which such a decree of predestination and reprobation falls. In Scripture predestination usually means not bare designation to glory's end, but destination to glory through means — and not any means, but means of efficacious grace derived from Christ our Head and Mediator. So Ephesians 1:4: he chose us in him that we should be holy; 2 Timothy 1:9: he saved us according to his purpose and the grace given us in Christ before the ages. From these and many like them it is plain the Apostle means destination and direction to glory's end by infallible means of efficacious grace from Christ. Augustine, as everyone knows, takes predestination as preparation of the grace that leads infallibly to glory: Predestination is the preparation of God's benefits by which whoever are set free are set free with certainty. So Aquinas describes it as special providence ordering and directing the elect to salvation's end not by any means, but by means that produce the event infallibly. Take it thus: Predestination in Scripture is not an abstract decree about the end alone, but a compounded decree — to give eternal life through means of grace in Christ. Reprobation in Scripture's use is not bare passing-by or non-election, but pre-damnation — appointment to destruction — bound inseparably to non-election, at least as to the event. Scripture calls the reprobate vessels of wrath fitted for destruction ([[Romans 9:22 >> Bible:Romans 9:22]]); formerly marked out for condemnation ([[Jude 4 >> Bible:Jude 4]]). Augustine calls reprobation predestination to destruction. Under "reprobation" we must include not only the bare decree to pass by, but also the will to pre-damn. That kind of predestination and reprobation cannot be conceived or explained rightly unless sin is preconceived as a common condition in the subject.

source_text: Quod hisce rationibus ostendi potest. Primo, Praedestinatio hominum ad vitam aeternam continet in se donationem quorundam ipsi Christo, tanquam Medico aut Vivificatori; & exemptionem eorundem e stipite & capite veteris Adami, tanquam corruptoris & occisoris posterorum suorum. Huc spectant illa loca Scripturarum. Quos dedisti mihi, ego custodivi, Johan. xvii.12. Ecce ego & pueri quos dedisti mihi, Heb. ii.13. Elegit nos in Christo, Ephes. i.4. Non egent qui sani sunt medico, Luc. v.31. Christus cum adhuc infirmi essemus pro impiis mortuus est, Rom. v.6. Si unius delicto multi mortui sunt, multo magis gratia Dei, & donum per gratiam, quae est unius Jesu Christi, in multos redundavit, Rom. v.15. Ex hisce Scripturarum locis colligimus, In decreto praedestinationis omnes electos fuisse datos Christo ut Redemptori, ut Vivificatori, ut Medico eorundem futuro. At redemptor supponit captivum, vivificator mortuum, medicus aegrotum: ergo ut tales a Deo considerantur qui in Christo Redemptore praedestinantur. Nam ut quivis actus praesupponit objectum, sic talis actus tale objectum: actus igitur redemptionis, vivificationis, sanationis, qui omnes includuntur ut futuri in actu praedestinationis sive electionis nostrae in Christo, supponunt objectum redimendum, vivificandum, sanandum: quod nihil aliud est quam peccato corruptum. Hinc Augustinus, Serm. 9. De verb. Apost. Nulla causa fuit veniendi Christo Domino, nisi peccatores salvos facere. Tolle morbos, tolle vulnera, nulla causa est medicinae. Si Christus in tempore fuit incarnatus ut peccatores salvos faceret, tum etiam ab aeterno ut peccatores considerati sunt qui per praedestinationem Christo incarnando donabantur salvandi. Secundo, Praedestinatio non modo designat donationem quorundam Christo tanquam Redemptori & Liberatori, sed etiam praeparationem aeternam in mente Divina illorum mediorum per quae certissime liberentur. Ac omnia haec media, quae praeparantur electis, ejusmodi sunt quae propriam suam vim exercere nequeunt nisi circa subjectum peccato inquinatum: Tale igitur subjectum supponit praedestinatio. Nam ut ordinemur ab efficaci vocatione ad resipiscentiam & fidem: quis, quaeso, resipiscentiae usus nisi in homine peccatore? quae vis fidei nisi ad justificandum hominem peccatorem? quid facit spiritus regenerationis, nisi quod refingat peccatorem ad imaginem sanctitatis Divinae in Adamo amissam? Cum igitur praedestinatio haec aliaque ejusmodi media praeparet electis, manifestum est illos a Deo praedestinante considerari ut peccato corruptos, atque ex hac corruptione per media haec efficacia eruendos. Porro, quod ad reprobationem attinet, hoc unico argumento mihi videtur evinci, non cadere illam nisi in hominem consideratum ut peccatorem: Nimirum, quia scopus ejus est illustrare gloriam Divinam per modum vindicantis justitiae, sicuti scopus praedestinationis est illustrare gloriam Divinam per modum parcendi misericordiae. Non autem facit ad gloriam Dei illustrandam, si mente concipiamus illum destinasse poenae aeternae suam creaturam nondum poena dignam. Nam utcunque Deus, pro absoluta sua libertate, potest apud se decernere, quod creaturae, quantumvis innocenti, hoc aut illud bonum non sit communicaturus quod aliis communicabit, tamen non potest decernere, stante sua justitia, creaturae innocenti poenam infligendam. Quandoquidem ergo in reprobatione continetur voluntas inferendi poenam reprobato, necesse est ut ex hac parte Deo objiciatur ut peccato constrictus & contaminatus. Loquantur Scripturae, quae semper iram & vindictam Dei peccato provocatam docent: Tribulatio & angustia adversus omnem animam hominis perpetrantis malum, Rom. ii.9. Stipendium peccati mors, Rom. vi.23. Propter quae (id est, peccata sua) venit ira Dei super filios incredulitatis, Coloss. iii.6. Patres etiam universi solicite cavent, ne Deo tribuant voluntatem puniendi aut damnandi quemlibet, nisi ex occasione peccati praecedentis exortam. Tertullianus, De resurrect. Deus de suo bonus, de nostro justus. Intelligit justitiam vindicativam. Augustinus, potest Deus sine bonis meritis liberare, quia bonus est: non potest quenquam sine malis meritis damnare, quia justus est, Lib. 3. Advers. Jul. cap. 18. Prosper Ad Obj. Vincent. Respons. 2. Quod multi pereunt, pereuntium est meritum: quod multi salvantur, salvantis est donum. Et Respons. ad undecim, Ad praedestinationem Dei nihil aliud referri potest, nisi quod aut ad debitam justitiae retributionem, aut ad indebitam pertinet gratiae largitatem. Ex hisce omnibus quae disputata sunt, arbitror satis liquere, non modo rationalem naturam, sed peccatricem substare actui Divino sive praedestinationis sive reprobationis, tanquam communes subjecti conditiones, absque quibus neuter horum actuum posset in homines competere, eo modo quo praedestinatio & reprobatio in Scripturis describuntur.
english: That can be shown by these reasons. First: predestination of humans to eternal life includes giving certain ones to Christ as Physician and Life-giver, and freeing them from the stock and head of old Adam, corrupter and killer of his posterity. So Scripture: "Those you gave me I have kept" ([[John 17:12 >> Bible:John 17:12]]); "Behold, I and the children God has given me" ([[Hebrews 2:13 >> Bible:Hebrews 2:13]]); "He chose us in Christ" ([[Ephesians 1:4 >> Bible:Ephesians 1:4]]); "Those who are well have no need of a physician" ([[Luke 5:31 >> Bible:Luke 5:31]]); "While we were still weak, Christ died for the ungodly" ([[Romans 5:6 >> Bible:Romans 5:6]]); "If many died through one man's trespass, much more have the grace of God and the free gift by the grace of that one man Jesus Christ abounded for many" ([[Romans 5:15 >> Bible:Romans 5:15]]). From these we gather: in the decree of predestination all the elect were given to Christ as Redeemer, Life-giver, and their future Physician. But a redeemer presupposes a captive, a life-giver a dead person, a physician a sick one — so those predestined in Christ the Redeemer are considered by God as such. As any act presupposes an object, such an act presupposes such an object: the acts of redemption, vivification, and healing, all included as future in our predestination or election in Christ, presuppose an object to be redeemed, made alive, healed — which is nothing other than one corrupted by sin. So Augustine (Serm. 9 on the Apostle's words): There was no cause for the Lord Christ's coming except to save sinners. Take away diseases and wounds, and medicine has no cause. If Christ was incarnate in time to save sinners, then from eternity too those given by predestination to the incarnate Christ to be saved were considered as sinners. Second: predestination means not only giving some to Christ as Redeemer and Liberator, but also the eternal preparation in God's mind of the means by which they are most certainly set free. All those means prepared for the elect can exercise their proper force only on a subject stained with sin — so predestination presupposes such a subject. Begin with efficacious calling to repentance and faith: what use is repentance except in a sinner? what force has faith except to justify a sinner? what does the Spirit of regeneration do but reshape the sinner to the image of Divine holiness lost in Adam? Since predestination prepares these and like means for the elect, God clearly considers them corrupted by sin and to be drawn out of that corruption by those efficacious means. As for reprobation, one argument seems enough: it falls only on a human considered as a sinner. Its aim is to display Divine glory by way of vindicating justice, as predestination's aim is to display that glory by way of sparing mercy. It does not serve God's glory to conceive him as destining to eternal punishment a creature not yet worthy of punishment. By absolute liberty God may decree not to communicate to an innocent creature some good he will give others; yet standing in his justice he cannot decree to inflict punishment on an innocent creature. Since reprobation includes the will to inflict punishment on the reprobate, on that side the person must be set before God as bound and stained by sin. Scripture always teaches wrath and vengeance provoked by sin: tribulation and anguish on every soul that does evil ([[Romans 2:9 >> Bible:Romans 2:9]]); the wages of sin is death ([[Romans 6:23 >> Bible:Romans 6:23]]); because of these (their sins) the wrath of God comes on the sons of disobedience ([[Colossians 3:6 >> Bible:Colossians 3:6]]). The Fathers carefully refuse to attribute to God a will to punish or damn anyone except as arising from preceding sin. Tertullian (On the resurrection): God is good from his own, just from ours — meaning vindicative justice. Augustine (Against Julian 3.18): God can free without good merits, because he is good; he cannot damn anyone without evil merits, because he is just. Prosper (Reply to Vincent's objections 2): That many perish is the merit of those perishing; that many are saved is the gift of the one who saves. And in the Reply to the eleven: Nothing can be referred to God's predestination except what belongs either to due retribution of justice or to undue largess of grace. From all this I judge it clear enough: not only a rational nature but a sinful one underlies the Divine act of predestination or reprobation — as common conditions of the subject without which neither act can fall on humans in the way Scripture describes those acts.

source_text: Jam de conditionibus distinguentibus pauca etiam dicenda sunt. IV. Conditiones distinguentes appello, contrarios actus aut qualitates, quibus in subjecto praevisis & praeconsideratis, contrarii actus etiam in Deo circa idem subjectum exercentur. Verbi causa, bonus usus liberi arbitrii, & malus usus liberi arbitrii sunt actus contrarii: Si quis ergo sentiat ex praevisione boni usus secundum Dei ordinationem homines semper praedestinari, ex praevisione mali usus reprobari, is facit bonum & malum usum liberi arbitrii conditiones distinguentes in subjecto praedestinationis aut reprobationis requisitas.
english: A few words now on distinguishing conditions. IV. By distinguishing conditions I mean contrary acts or qualities which, when foresight and weighed beforehand in the subject, bring about contrary acts in God toward that same subject. Take free choice: its good use and its bad use are contrary acts. If someone holds that, by God's ordination, foresight of the good use always means predestination, and foresight of the bad use means reprobation, then that person makes the good and bad use of free choice into distinguishing conditions required in the subject of predestination or reprobation.

source_text: Sic etiam, si quis tueatur illos solos eligi ad gloriam, quos Deus praevidet meritis sive bonis operibus ornatos usque ad finem vitae suae, atque eos solos reprobari sive non-eligi, quos praevidet demeritis sive malis operibus perseveranter adhaerescentes, is praevisa opera, prout bona fuerint vel mala, ponit conditiones distinguentes, pro quarum differentia differentes actus Divinae praedestinationis & reprobationis diversis hominibus conveniunt. Item, si quis doceat Deum illos solos eligere quos praevidet perseveraturos in fide, illos solos praeterire & rejicere quos praevidet perseveraturos in infidelitate, is hanc fidem & infidelitatem constituit conditiones distinguentes, pro quarum discrimine distincti actus praedestinationis & reprobationis cadunt in distinctas personas.
english: So too if someone maintains that only those are elected to glory whom God foresees clothed with merits or good works to the end of life, and that only those are reprobated or not elected whom he foresees clinging perseveringly to demerits or evil works — then that person makes foresight works, good or evil, into distinguishing conditions, and by their difference different Divine acts of predestination and reprobation are assigned to different people. Likewise if someone teaches that God elects only those he foresees will persevere in faith, and passes by and rejects only those he foresees will persevere in unbelief — then faith and unbelief become the distinguishing conditions by whose discrimination the distinct acts of predestination and reprobation fall on distinct persons.

source_text: Videtis jam magnum discrimen inter priores illas conditiones subjecti, quas communes appellavimus, & has posteriores, quas distinguentes nuncupamus. Nam natura Rationalis, & Peccato subdititia, praesupponitur in subjecto praedestinato & reprobato, ut in illis nulla ponatur causa, ratio, aut occasio discriminis; sed Bona opera & Mala, Fides & Infidelitas, ita ponuntur praevisae condiciones in hominibus, ut secundum illas procedat ipsum discrimen hominum praedestinatorum aut reprobatorum. Quanquam ergo concedamus priores conditiones praerequisitas, ut subjectum communiter & promiscue possit subjacere Deo praedestinanti & reprobanti, tamen hasce posteriores, quas multi stabilire conantur, prorsus pernegamus praesupponi & praevideri a Deo in homine praedestinando aut reprobando, aut pro earum diversitate praevisa diversos actus praedestinationis atque reprobationis tendere semper in diversas personas.
english: You already see the great difference between those earlier subject-conditions we called common, and these later ones we call distinguishing. Rational nature, and nature under sin, is presupposed in the predestined and the reprobate so that nothing in them is set as cause, reason, or occasion of the divide. Good and evil works, faith and unbelief, are instead set as foresight conditions in people so that the very divide between the predestined and the reprobate proceeds according to them. We grant the earlier conditions as prerequisites — so that a subject can, commonly and without distinction, lie under God as he predestines and reprobates. But these later ones, which many try to fix in place, we flatly deny: they are not presupposed or foreseen by God in the person to be predestined or reprobated, nor do different foresight varieties of them always drive different acts of predestination and reprobation onto different persons.

source_text: Hisce adhuc praeludam: Pontificios scriptores, qui contendunt bona opera aut peccata praevisa esse conditiones, quas Deus intueatur in praedestinatione ad gloriam & reprobatione, ingenue etiam largiuntur esse causas cur alii eligantur ad gloriam, alii non eligantur; sicuti causae sunt, cum ad executionem decreti ventum fuerit, cur alii admittantur in regnum gloriae, alii excludantur. Sed nuperi Doctores e Schola Arminiana, qui urgent nullam esse electionem aut reprobationem hominum nisi secundum discrimen praevisae in illis fidei aut infidelitatis, negant tamen obstinate fidem esse causam electionis. Dicunt esse Modum secundum quem Deus spectat hominem eligendum, esse antecedens electionis; sed negant esse causam electionis, & simul negant esse effectum, ab electione manentem. Sed hac tergiversatione produnt infirmitatem causae suae. Nam si ponerent fidem solummodo conditionem antecedentem, sine qua non fieret electio hujus aut illius singularis personae, possent probabiliter affirmare se non statuere fidem hujus electionis causam: sed cum insuper doceant, ad positionem fidei poni electionem, ad negationem fidei praevisae negari electionem, aperte tribuunt fidei non nudam antecessionem, sed etiam causalitatem.
english: One more prelude. Pontifical writers who hold that foresight works or sins are conditions God looks to in predestination to glory and in reprobation also frankly grant that those conditions are causes why some are elected to glory and others are not — just as, once the decree is executed, they are causes why some are admitted to the kingdom of glory and others shut out. Recent doctors of the Arminian school press hard that there is no election or reprobation of humans except by the foresight divide of faith or unbelief in them, yet they stubbornly deny that faith is the cause of election. They call it a Mode by which God regards the person to be elected, an antecedent of election; but they deny it is election's cause, and at the same time deny it is an effect flowing from election. That dodge shows how weak their case is. If they set faith only as an antecedent condition without which this or that person's election would not occur, they could fairly say they do not make faith the cause of that election. But when they further teach that faith posited means election posited, and foresight faith denied means election denied, they openly give faith not bare precedence but causality as well.

source_text: Ausim affirmare Augustinum reliquosque Patres, quandocunque qualitas aut actio aliqua humana ita praerequiritur, ut illa posita ponatur simul consequens aliquod Dei beneficium, illa absente negetur, habere talem qualitatem aut actum causae loco, causae (ut illi loquuntur) suo modo meritoriae. Conditio enim secundum ordinationem Dei postulata, & per gratiam Dei ab homine praestita, habet apud Patres vim & naturam causae meritoriae motivae, quoad beneficium sub tali conditione conferendum. Sic loquitur Augustinus Epist. 105. ubi dicit, ipsam remissionem peccatorum non esse sine aliquo merito, si fides hanc impetrat. Pari ratione electio ad gloriam non erit sine aliquo merito ex parte electi, si fides illam impetrat. Nam meritum apud Patres nihil aliud est, quam opus ex Dei ordinatione alicujus beneficii impetratorium. Si ergo ex praeviso nostro actu credendi conferatur in nos beneficium electionis, non est conditio sine qua non, sed est causa, imo meritum sequentis beneficii, eo sensu quo Patres usurpant hoc meriti vocabulum.
english: I dare say Augustine and the other Fathers treat it this way: whenever some human quality or act is so required beforehand that when it is present some following gift of God is present with it, and when it is absent that gift is denied, they set that quality or act in the place of a cause — a cause, as they put it, meritorious in its own way. A condition demanded by God's ordination and performed by the person through God's grace has, for the Fathers, the force and nature of a meritorious motive cause with respect to the benefit conferred under that condition. So Augustine in Epistle 105: the very remission of sins is not without some merit, if faith obtains it. By the same reason, election to glory will not be without some merit on the elect person's side, if faith obtains it. For among the Fathers merit is nothing but a work which, by God's ordination, obtains some benefit. So if the benefit of election is conferred on us from our foresight act of believing, that is not a mere condition sine qua non — it is a cause, indeed the merit of the following benefit, in the sense in which the Fathers use the word merit.

source_text: Nam quando contra Pelagianos disputant, gratiam non dari aut negari secundum merita liberi arbitrii, nihil aliud volunt, quam non dari secundum praevisam conditionem boni aut mali usus ejusdem liberi arbitrii. Si enim Pelagiani hoc evicissent, Patres nunquam negassent esse veram causam gratiae collatae. Sic etiam cum Theologi nostri contra Scholasticos nonnullos contendunt, Deum non praedestinare homines ex praevisis meritis congruis, nihil aliud volunt, quam haec quae appellantur merita congrua non esse conditiones antecedentes ac distinguentes, secundum quas eligantur omnes in quibus illae praevisae fuerant, rejiciantur omnes in quibus non fuerant. Nam si tales conditiones esse demonstraverint, rem confectam habent Scholastici, & nos ultro fatebimur esse causas discriminis electorum & reprobatorum, eo sensu quo causae & meriti vocabulum usurpatur.
english: When the Fathers argue against the Pelagians that grace is not given or withheld according to free choice's merits, they mean simply this: it is not given according to a foresight condition of free choice's good or bad use. Had the Pelagians proved that, the Fathers would never have denied it was a true cause of the grace conferred. So too when our theologians contend against some Scholastics that God does not predestine people from foresight congruent merits, they mean that these so-called congruent merits are not antecedent distinguishing conditions by which everyone in whom they were foresight is elected and everyone in whom they were not is rejected. If the Scholastics ever prove such conditions, their case is finished — and we will freely admit that those conditions are causes of the divide between elect and reprobate, in the sense in which cause and merit are spoken of.

source_text: Sunt ergo merae verborum praestigiae, cum aiunt praevisam fidem & infidelitatem esse conditiones, non modo quae antecedunt praedestinationem & reprobationem communiter & promiscue consideratam, sed etiam ex quibus oritur ipsa distinctio electorum & reprobatorum, & tamen negant habere aliquam causalitatem. Nam omnes Theologi qui unquam disputarunt de ratione aut causa electionis, praesumunt id vim causae obtinere, qua posita & a Deo praevisa sequitur; qua negata aut non praevisa non sequitur electio. Atque haec ea sunt quae praefationis loco praemittenda putavi. Totam, quae futura est, disputationem nostram deinceps ad certas quasdam theses revocabimus.
english: So it is mere word-trickery when they say foresight faith and unbelief are conditions — not only ones that precede predestination and reprobation taken commonly and without distinction, but ones from which the very distinction of elect and reprobate arises — and yet deny those conditions any causality. Every theologian who has ever argued the reason or cause of election assumes this: whatever, when posited and foresight by God, brings election with it, and when denied or not foresight leaves election absent, has the force of a cause. These are the points I thought should stand as a preface. From here our whole coming dispute will be drawn into certain fixed theses.

source_text: CAP. II. Variae illorum sententiae referuntur, qui electionem praevisis nostris meritis inniti docuerunt. Accedamus tandem ad ipsum negotium cui hanc operam nostram destinavimus. Et primo de Electione sive Praedestinatione ad salutem & aeternam beatitudinem disputabimus: dein ad illam alteram hujus controversiae partem, de Non-electione, Praeteritione, sive reprobatione deveniemus.
english: CAP. II. Here I set out the various opinions of those who teach that election rests on our foresight merits. We come at last to the business this labor was meant for. First we will argue election — or predestination — to salvation and eternal blessedness; then the other half of the controversy: non-election, passing-by, or reprobation.

source_text: Principale quaesitum quod attinet ad prius membrum futurae disceptationis, hoc est; Utrum in illis qui eliguntur & praedestinantur ad gloriam, detur aliquis actus aut qualitas a Deo praevisa & praeconsiderata, aut aliud quodcunque, quod sit meritum, causa, ratio, conditio, aut antecedens quolibet modo ita praesuppositum decreto electionis, ut ex positione talis praecedanei in praevisione Divina ponatur electio, ex negatione, negetur. Quid sentiant hac de re Pelagiani, quid Scholastici, quid nuperi quidam Doctores, videamus.
english: The chief question for the first half of the coming dispute is this: in those elected and predestined to glory, is there some act or quality God foresaw and weighed beforehand — or anything at all — that stands as merit, cause, reason, condition, or antecedent so bound to the decree of election that when that prior thing is set in the Divine foresight election follows, and when it is denied election is denied? Let us see what Pelagians, Scholastics, and certain recent doctors hold on this.

source_text: Dari tale aliquod praecedaneum, cui semper innitatur decretum electionis, humana ratio amore sui occaecata praetendit, Scriptura reclamante. Britannus ille coluber hoc plenum veneni & pestilentiae dogma evomuit, Posse hominem solis viribus liberi sui arbitrii legem Dei servare, ad vitam aeternam pervenire. Huic & illud alterum conjunxit ejusdem virulentiae, Deum scilicet praevidentem quinam essent per voluntatis suae arbitrium sancte victuri, eos omnes ante jacta mundi fundamenta ad gloriam elegisse.
english: Blinded self-love in human reason claims there is always some prior ground on which the decree of election rests — and Scripture cries against it. That British serpent spat out this poison: that a person can keep God's law and reach eternal life by free choice alone. He joined to it another venom of the same kind: that God, foresighting who would live holy by their own will's choice, elected them all to glory before the world's foundations were laid.

source_text: Utrumque colligitur ex Augustino: prius ex Epist. 89. Ubi Anathema vibrat contra Pelagianos ob haeresin praedictam, Illud quod dicunt, sufficere homini liberum arbitrium ad dominica praecepta implenda, omnino anathematizandum est, & omnibus exsecrationibus detestandum. Posterius ex De praedestin. Sanctor. lib. 1. cap. 18. Praesciebat ergo, ait Pelagianus, qui futuri erant sancti per liberae voluntatis arbitrium, & ideo eos ante mundi constitutionem in ipsa sua praescientia, qua tales futuros esse praescivit, elegit. Sed quia Pelagium atque Pelagianum hoc dogma omnes omnium sectarum Theologi jam rejiciunt, aut saltem videri volunt rejecisse, non facessam mihi negotii in illis refellendis, quae nemo audet aperte propugnare.
english: Augustine supplies both. First, Epistle 89, where he hurls anathema at the Pelagians for that heresy: their claim that free choice alone is enough to keep the Lord's commands is to be anathematized and cursed outright. Second, On the Predestination of the Saints 1.18: God foresaw, says the Pelagian, who would be holy by free will's choice, and so before the world's founding he elected them in that very foresight by which he foresaw them to be such. But since theologians of every party already reject Pelagius and this Pelagian dogma — or at least want to look as if they have — I will not waste effort refuting what no one dares openly defend.

source_text: Pelagii venenatum dogma Semipelagiani ex parte amplexi sunt; in queis numero Faustum Regiensem, Cassianum Collatorem, Massilienses, aliosque omnes, qui confitentes gratiae necessitatem ad pie vivendum, in pietate perseverandum, & vitam aeternam consequendam, defendunt tamen ex nobis praecedere quoddam initium laboris & conatus, quod Divina gratia subsequitur, & cujus intuitu haec gratia salutaris nobis donatur. Tenent etiam consequenter, postquam homo conando & laborando Dei gratiam adeptus est, non per donum aliquod quod manat ab electione, sed per liberum arbitrium suum perseverare in hac gratia, fide, & bonis operibus; atque ex praescientia talis voluntatis eligi ad vitam aeternam.
english: The Semipelagians took up part of Pelagius's poison. Count among them Faustus of Riez, Cassian the Conferencer, the Massilians, and all who admit grace is needed to live godly, persevere, and reach eternal life — yet still claim that from us there first comes a beginning of labor and effort, which God's grace then follows, and for the sake of which saving grace is given. Consequently they hold that once a person has gained God's grace by striving and labor, he stays in that grace, faith, and good works not by any gift flowing from election, but by his own free choice; and that election to eternal life rests on foresight of that will.

source_text: De praevio conatu & labore scribit Faustus lib. 1. cap. 12. Sicut sui criminis est, quod filius prodigus longe pii parentis fugit oculos, ita suae est devotionis, quod per insitum sibi bonum deliberans & assurgens, ad paternos recurrit amplexus. Et cap. 17. Dominus invitat volentem, attrahit desiderantem, erigit adnitentem. Et cap. ult. Voluntatem ejus qui est purgandus, exspectat. De progressu & perseverantia per vires liberi arbitrii, non per donum aliquod speciale manans a decreto praedestinationis, sic philosophatur, Lib. 2. sect. 5. Salutem hominis non in praedestinatione Factoris, sed in operatione famulantis largitor gratiae collocavit. Et Cap. 12. Status hominis in diversa, non pro constitutione Dei, sed pro arbitrii libertate potest versari. Denique electionem nostram ex praescientia hujusmodi bonae voluntatis & operationis nostrae, non ex Dei decreto aliquo antecedente, aperte docet lib. 2. sect. 2. Praescientia Dei de materia humanorum actuum sumit exordium. Et paulo post, Aliud est praescire, aliud praedestinare. Praescientia gerenda praenoscit, postmodum praedestinatio retribuenda describit. Illa praevidet merita, haec praeordinat praemia. Praescientia ad potentiam, praedestinatio ad justitiam pertinet. Nisi praescientia exploraverit, praedestinatio nihil decernit. Hisce verbis non a gratia praedestinationis arcessit merita, sed a praevisis meritis praedestinationem.
english: On that prior effort and labor Faustus writes (1.12): just as the prodigal's flight from a pious father's eyes is his own crime, so his return to the father's embrace — deliberating and rising by the good planted in him — is his own devotion. Chapter 17: the Lord invites the willing, draws the desiring, raises the striving. The last chapter: he waits for the will of the one to be cleansed. On progress and perseverance by free choice's powers — not by any special gift flowing from the predestination decree — he reasons (2.5): human salvation is set not in the Maker's predestination, but in the working of the one who serves the Giver of grace. Chapter 12: a person's state can turn this way or that not by God's constitution, but by liberty of choice. At last he openly teaches election from foresight of such good will and working of ours, not from any prior decree of God (2.2): God's foresight begins from the matter of human acts. A little later: to foresee is one thing, to predestine another. Foresight knows beforehand what is to be done; then predestination marks out what is to be repaid. That foresights merits; this preordains rewards. Foresight belongs to power, predestination to justice. Unless foresight has searched, predestination decides nothing. In these words he does not draw merits from the grace of predestination — he draws predestination from foresight merits.

source_text: Sed horum Semipelagianorum sententia clarissime intelligi potest ex Epistola Prosperi & Hilarii ad Augustinum, quae ambae praefiguntur libro quem inscripsit Augustinus De praedestinatione sanctorum. De istis sic scribit Prosper, Haec ipsorum definitio est; Qui credituri sunt, quive in ea fide, quae deinceps per Dei gratiam sit juvanda, mansuri sunt, praescisse ante mundi constitutionem Deum, & eos praedestinasse in regnum suum, quos gratis vocatos, dignos futuros electione, & de hac vita bono fine excessuros praeviderit. Et Hilarius, Massilienses inutile esse praedicationi dicant, quod quidam secundum propositum eligendi dicantur, &c. Et pauculis interjectis, Asserunt eo merito, quo voluerit & crediderit unusquisque, a suo morbo se posse sanari, & ipsius fidei augmentum, & totius sanctitatis suae consequi effectum. De compendio, putant rationem reddi electorum vel rejectorum in eo, quod unicuique meritum propriae voluntatis adjungitur. Concedunt Deum non eligere opera cujusquam in praescientia quae ipse donaturus est; sed affirmant, fidem eligere in praescientia, ut quem crediturum esse praescivit, ipsum elegerit, cui spiritum sanctum donet, ut bene operando aeternam vitam consequeretur. Denique, nemini dari talem perseverantiam putant, a qua non permittitur praevaricari; atque idcirco non admittunt eligendorum & rejiciendorum esse numerum definitum. Haec paulo latius recitanda putavi, ut videatis, quam prope absint a Pelagianis aut Semipelagianis, qui nostro hoc saeculo Augustini doctrinam, in sacris Scripturis fundatam, & catholicae Ecclesiae testimonio olim confirmatam, explosum eunt.
english: These Semipelagians are clearest in the letters of Prosper and Hilary to Augustine — both prefixed to Augustine's On the Predestination of the Saints. Prosper reports their definition: God foresaw before the world's founding who would believe, or who would stay in the faith later helped by his grace, and predestined to his kingdom those he foresaw, once called by grace, would be worthy of election and would leave this life with a good end. Hilary: the Massilians say it empties preaching to speak of some as elect according to purpose, and so on. A few lines later: they claim that by the merit of each person's willing and believing, one can be healed of disease and gain both the increase of that faith and the full effect of one's holiness. In short, they put the reason for elect or reject in this: each is paired with the merit of his own will. They grant God does not elect anyone's works in foresight of gifts he himself will give; yet they affirm he elects faith in foresight — so that whom he foresaw would believe, he elected, and to him gives the Holy Spirit so that by good works he may reach eternal life. Finally they hold that no one is given such perseverance that falling away is impossible; and so they deny any fixed number of those to be elected and rejected. I thought this worth quoting a little more fully, so you may see how near they stand to the Pelagians or Semipelagians who in our own age try to explode Augustine's teaching — rooted in Scripture and long confirmed by the catholic Church's witness.

source_text: Sed descendamus a Semipelagianis ad Scholasticos. Ex hisce nonnulli docent causam dari praedestinationis seu electionis, quatenus cadit super hunc hominem potius quam super illum. Atque hic quidam obtendunt opera bona moralia, quae antecedunt gratiam justificationis; alii, opera bona quae subsequuntur; alii praevisum bonum usum gratiae Divinae. Verum haud necesse est ut in hisce sententiis refellendis inhaeream, quae omnes unico illo Apostoli ictu prosternuntur Rom. ix. 11. Nondum natis pueris, cum nihil fecissent boni vel mali, ut propositum Dei secundum electionem maneret, non ex operibus, sed ex vocante, dictum est, &c.
english: Next, down from the Semipelagians to the Scholastics. Not a few of them teach that predestination — or election — has a cause insofar as it falls on this man rather than that. Some plead good moral works before justifying grace; others good works after it; others foresight of a good use of God's grace. I need not linger refuting these views: one blow from the Apostle flattens them all (Rom. 9:11) — the children not yet born, having done nothing good or evil, so that God's purpose according to election might stand, not from works but from the One who calls.

source_text: Jam si quis quaerat unde hoc, quod tanto consensu Pelagiani, Semipelagiani, Scholastici, aliique multi electionem ad gratiam & gloriam inniti volunt alicui rei quod sit penes nos habere vel non habere, facere vel non facere, facile est hujus erroris causas designare. Prima est, innata humano generi superbia & philautia, quae aegerrime patitur omnem gloriandi causam eripi hominibus. Altera, crassa inscitia & ignorantia corruptionis nostrae, & voluntatis sub jugo peccati captivatae. Tertia, quia posita quacunque causa electionis in nobis, facile expediuntur omnes illae difficultates, quas alioqui cogemur ad altitudinem quandam inscrutabilem referre; quod curiositati humanae rationis valde adversatur. Nam posita electione juxta praescientiam alicujus operis humani, si quaeratur cur unus gratiam recipiat, alius non, illico occurrit: Quia unus se disposuit per liberum arbitrium, alius non. Si quaeratur cur unus perseveret in gratia, alius non perseveret, in promptu est responsio, Quia scilicet unus vult perseverare, alter non vult. Denique, si quaeratur cur hic ante constitutionem mundi electus fuerit ad gloriam, ille non fuerit, solvitur hic nodus facillime; Quia Deus praevidit ab aeterno unum admissurum oblatam gratiam, & bene illa usurum, & ad extremum usque vitae ex libero suo arbitrio in gratia permansurum, alterum aut repulsurum ab initio, aut saltem ante obitum excussurum.
english: Why do Pelagians, Semipelagians, Scholastics, and so many others agree that election to grace and glory rests on something in our power to have or do? The causes of the error are plain. First: pride and self-love native to the race, which hates having every ground of boasting torn away. Second: thick ignorance of our corruption and of the will captive under sin's yoke. Third: put any cause of election in us, and the hard questions that otherwise force us up to an unsearchable height are easily waved off — and human curiosity hates that height. Once election tracks foresight of some human act, ask why one gets grace and another does not: because one disposed himself by free choice, the other did not. Why one perseveres and another not: because one wills to persevere, the other will not. Why this one was elect to glory before the world, that one not: God foresaw from eternity that one would admit offered grace, use it well, and stay in it by free choice to life's end — the other reject it at once, or at least shake it off before death.

source_text: Postrema causa, qua moti sunt quamplurimi ut nullam admitterent electionem, nisi praescientia nixam alicujus actus eliciendi ex potestate liberi arbitrii, hac mihi fuisse videtur, Quod tanquam necessarium postulatum praesumpserunt, quod est fallissimum, scilicet, Deum crudelem fore, nisi in cujusvis hominis potestate constituat ut salutem possit, quam in Adamo emisit, per seipsum recuperare. Sed missis veteribus Pelagianis & Scholasticis, congrediamur cum illis qui nostro hoc seculo perturbant Ecclesiam, dum veteres errores interpolare & sub novis verborum formulis obtrudere conantur. Atque primo agemus contra Pontificios quosdam, dein contra Arminianos: qui in hoc consentiunt, quod electionem nullam ad salutem admittunt nisi nixam praescientia actuum humanorum eliciendorum, ex libero arbitrio per gratiam praevento.
english: A last motive for many who will admit no election except one resting on foresight of some act free choice can elicit: they took as a necessary postulate what is utterly false — that God would be cruel unless he put it in every person's power to recover by himself the salvation lost in Adam. Leave the old Pelagians and Scholastics. Engage those who disturb the Church in our age by dressing old errors in new formulas. First certain Papal doctors, then the Arminians: both refuse any election to salvation that does not rest on foresight of human acts elicited from free choice, grace having gone before.

source_text: In arenam primo prodeant Papistae: atque pro caeteris omnibus qui hanc sententiam sequuntur (nam ex sanioribus multi non sequuntur) loquatur Vasques: Qui hanc thesin multis argumentis stabilire conatur, in 1. quaest. 23. art. 3. disp. 89. Nulla est electio efficax singularium personarum ad gloriam ex sola Dei voluntate; sed quilibet ad gloriam eligitur ex meritis praevisis, quae Dei gratia est facturus. Pauca praemitto, ut ipsa thesis melius intelligatur, dein argumenta adversariorum proponam & dissolvam.
english: First into the arena: the Papists. For all who hold this view (many of the sounder sort do not), let Vasquez speak. He tries to prop this thesis with many arguments (on ST 1.23.3, disp. 89): There is no efficacious election of particular persons to glory from God's will alone; each is elect to glory from foresight merits which God's grace will bring about. A few notes first so the thesis is clear; then the adversaries' arguments, stated and dissolved.

source_text: Primo, per electionem efficacem videtur Vasques designare absolutam & peculiarem Dei voluntatem quae ad singulares & certas personas certo beandas terminatur, puta ad Petrum & Paulum reliquosque electos sigillatim. Hanc autem vocat efficacem electionem, vel efficacem voluntatem dandi gloriam, ut distinguatur ab illa communi & antecedente voluntate, sive simplici desiderio, aut affectu, quo statuunt Deum velle omnibus communicare etiam ipsis reprobis, vitam aeternam. Secundo, quando affirmat ex meritis praevisis esse hanc efficacem electionem ad gloriam, non illud vult, praevisa merita humana esse causam ipsius volitionis Divinae, cujus nulla causa extra Deum quaerenda est; sed esse rationem propter quam Divina voluntas libere terminetur ad hanc personam glorificandam. Tertio, quando addit, quae Dei gratia facturus est, vult suam sententiam a Pelagianis sejungere, qui merita, sive bona opera, ex libero arbitrio dimanare putabant absque illa gratia Christi, quam passim Augustinus ex sacris Scripturis esse necessariam demonstravit. Postremo, animadvertendum est, quamvis Jesuita tueatur, electionem efficacem ad gloriam non esse, nisi ex praevisione meritorum; lubenter tamen eundem concedere praedestinationem ad gratiam specialem, quae infallibiliter ducit ad gloriam, nulla niti praevisione meritorum, neque ex parte praedestinati excogitari posse ullam causam, ullum initium, ullam occasionem, cur Deus illi talem gratiam donaverit, aut in praescientia dare decreverit: Part. 1. quaest. 23. disp. 91. cap. 11. Hac igitur ex parte, de praedestinatione singularium personarum ad gratiam specialem multo rectius sentit Jesuita quam qui ex Schola Arminiana & Vorstiana prodierunt. Sed jam quibus argumentis praedictam thesin adstruant, dispiciamus. A Scripturis auspicantur, atque inde haec testimonia afferre solent pro electione ex praevisis operibus.
english: First: by efficacious election Vasquez means God's absolute, particular will that settles on certain persons to be blessed — Peter, Paul, and the rest one by one. He calls it efficacious election, or an efficacious will to give glory, to mark it off from the common antecedent will (a bare desire or affection) by which they say God wills eternal life for all, even the reprobate. Second: when he says this efficacious election to glory is from foresight merits, he does not make those merits the cause of God's willing — no cause of that is sought outside God — but the reason why the divine will freely terminates on glorifying this person. Third: adding "which God's grace will bring about" cuts him off from Pelagians who let merits flow from free choice without Christ's grace, which Augustine everywhere proved from Scripture necessary. Last: though the Jesuit holds there is no efficacious election to glory except from foresight of merits, he gladly grants predestination to special grace that infallibly leads to glory rests on no foresight of merits, and no cause, start, or occasion can be invented on the predestinate's side why God gave that grace or decreed in foresight to give it (ST I q.23, disp. 91.11). On predestination of particular persons to special grace, then, the Jesuit is far sounder than the Arminian and Vorstian school. Now their arguments for the thesis: they start from Scripture and usually cite these for election from foresight works.

source_text: Primo, Ex illis verbis Matth. xxv. 34, &c. Venite benedicti Patris, possidete regnum paratum vobis ab initio mundi. Esurivi enim, & dedistis mihi, &c. sic argumentatur Vasques, Hoc in loco Christus offert regnum praeparatum ab origine mundi, id est, ab aeternitate; atque reddit simul rationem cur debeant accipere praeparatum & destinatum, quod est causam ipsius praeparationis indicare. Nam si praeparatio sit alia ratione, & non propter haec ipsa opera quae nominantur, inanis & nulla plane esset causa quam hic ipse Christus assignavit. Ergo homines eliguntur ad gloriam caelestem ex praevisione operum suorum bonorum. In 1. quaest. 23. art. 3. cap. 2. disp. 89.
english: First argument (Matt. 25:34ff.): "Come, you blessed of the Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the world's beginning. For I was hungry, and you gave me…" Vasquez: here Christ offers a kingdom prepared from the world's origin — that is, from eternity — and at once gives the reason they should receive what was prepared and destined, which is to mark the cause of that preparation. If the preparation rested on some other ground, and not on these very works named, the cause Christ himself assigns would be empty and none. Therefore people are elect to heavenly glory from foresight of their good works (ST I q.23 a.3, disp. 89.2).

source_text: Ex his verbis nihil aliud colligi potest, quam Dei filios, ab aeterno ad gloriam gratis praedestinatos, tandem illud adire, vel in illud intromitti, exclusis aliis, quia hi soli per rectam & a Deo ordinatam viam eo perrexerunt. Quod autem Vasques urget praedicta opera hoc in loco nominari ut causas ipsius praeparationis, sive aeternae destinationis Divinae, falsissimum est. Nam vera causa innuitur, quando benedicti Patris appellantur. Ideo siquidem haereditati caelesti illos destinavit quia ex gratia sua voluit effici illorum Pater in Christo. Opera autem illorum, neque ut praevisa, neque ut in tempore facta, erant causa praedestinationis ad gloriam, sed introductionis: neque hujus sunt causae meritoriae, sed causae solummodo subordinatae, eodem sensu quo motus in via causa dicitur perveniendi ad terminum viae. In hoc igitur lapsus est Vasques, quod non animadvertit, actum decernendi vel praedestinandi ad gloriam posse esse mere gratuitum in Deo, & nulla niti praevisione actuum humanorum: cum tamen modus perveniendi ad gloriam quoad hominem sit laboriosus, & requirat multos actus, sine quibus Deus ordinavit ac praevidit illum ad gloriae regnum nunquam appulsurum. Scotus hanc solutionem indicavit Lib. 1. dist. 41. ubi scribit, hanc propositionem, DEUS VULT PETRO DARE AETERNAM GLORIAM PROPTER MERITA, esse falsam, si illa verba, PROPTER MERITA, construantur cum verbo, VULT: non enim Deus ex praevisione meritorum concepit voluntatem glorificandi Petrum. Esse veram, si construantur cum verbo, DARE: non enim vult introducere in possessionem gloriae, nisi postquam praevisum est ambulasse in illis bonis operibus, quae Deus illi praescripsit & praeordinavit. Bellarminus eadem responsione utitur lib. 2. De grat. & libero arb. cap. 13. Haec propositio, DEUS AB AETERNO PRAEDESTINAVIT HOMINIBUS DARE REGNUM PER BONA OPERA PRAEVISA, potest & vera esse & falsa. Nam si illud, PER OPERA PRAEVISA, referatur ad verbum, PRAEDESTINAVIT, falsa erit: significabit enim Deum praedestinasse homines, quia opera illorum bona praeviderat; Si referatur ad verbum, DARE, vera erit: quia significabit glorificationem in exsecutione, esse effectum justificationis & sanctificationis sive operum bonorum. Sed hoc argumentum rursus urgebitur, & aliquanto fortius; ubi nos etiam plenius respondebimus.
english: From these words you may gather only this: God's children, freely predestined from eternity to glory, at last enter it — others shut out — because they alone took the straight road God ordained. Vasquez's claim that the works named here are causes of the preparation itself, or of God's eternal destination, is utterly false. The true cause is hinted when they are called the Father's blessed: he destined them to the heavenly inheritance because by grace he willed to be their Father in Christ. Their works, neither as foresight nor as done in time, caused predestination to glory — only introduction into it; and even of that they are not meritorious causes, only subordinate ones, as motion on a road is a "cause" of reaching the end. Vasquez's slip: he missed that decreeing or predestining to glory can be purely gratuitous in God and rest on no foresight of human acts, while the way of arriving at glory for man is laborious and needs many acts without which God ordained and foresaw he would never put in to glory's kingdom. Scotus (I dist. 41) marks the solution: "God wills to give Peter eternal glory on account of merits" is false if "on account of merits" construes with "wills" — God did not form the will to glorify Peter from foresight of merits — and true if it construes with "to give": he will not bring into possession of glory until it is foresight that Peter walked in the good works God prescribed and preordained. Bellarmine uses the same reply (De grat. et lib. arb. 2.13): "God from eternity predestined to give men the kingdom through foresight good works" is false if "through foresight works" hangs on "predestined," true if it hangs on "to give" — glorification in execution as the effect of justification, sanctification, or good works. This argument will be pressed again, harder; we will answer more fully then.

source_text: Secundo, urgentur illa loca in quibus electio sive praedestinatio ad gloriam expressis verbis conjungitur cum praescientia. Ut Rom. viii. 29, 30. Quos praescivit, eos & praedestinavit ut conformes fiant imagini Filii sui, &c. Et Rom. xi. 2. Non repulit Deus plebem suam quam praescivit. Et 1. Pet. i. 2. Electis advenis secundum praescientiam Dei Patris in sanctificationem spiritus, &c. Ex hisce & hujusmodi locis inferunt adversarii, Deum eos ad gloriam elegisse, quos praescivit futuros conformes imagini Filii sui, id est, sanctos & bonos; ita ut haec praescientia futurae bonitatis sive sanctitatis fuerit causa electionis ad gloriam.
english: Second: they press the places where election or predestination to glory is joined in so many words with foreknowledge — Rom. 8:29–30 ("Whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to his Son's image…"); Rom. 11:2 ("God has not cast off his people whom he foreknew"); 1 Pet. 1:2 ("elect strangers according to the Father's foreknowledge, unto sanctification of the Spirit…"). From these they infer that God elected to glory those he foreknew would be conformed to the Son's image — holy and good — so that foresight of future goodness or holiness was the cause of election to glory.

source_text: In locis allegatis non dicitur Deus elegisse aut praedestinasse certos homines ad gloriam quia praescivit eos fore conformes imagini Christi, id est, sanctos & bonos, sed dicitur eos elegisse quos praescivit, atque praedestinasse ut conformes fierent, vel elegisse in sanctificationem. Praescientia igitur futurae sanctitatis non fuit causa praedestinationis, sed praedestinatio causa praevisae sanctitatis. Deus enim nullum bonum salutiferum & spirituale in hominibus praevidet, nisi quod ipse in illis operatur; nullum bonum operatur, nisi quod decrevit operari. Decretum igitur operandi gratiam & sanctitatem, quod in praedestinatione includitur, semper praecedit praevisionem gratiae & sanctitatis, quae hominibus inesse intelligitur.
english: Reply: those texts do not say God elected or predestined certain people to glory because he foresaw they would be conformed to Christ's image — holy and good. They say he elected those he foreknew, and predestined them to become conformed, or elected them unto sanctification. So foresight of future holiness was not the cause of predestination; predestination was the cause of the holiness foreseen. God foresees no saving spiritual good in people except what he himself works in them; he works none except what he decreed to work. The decree to work grace and holiness — already wrapped into predestination — always comes before any foresight of grace and holiness as in them.

source_text: Sed ipsa verba expendamus paulo accuratius. Non dixit Apostolus, quos praevidit; sed, quos praescivit, οὓς προέγνω. At haec praescientia practica est, non intuitiva: & scientia approbationis vocatur a Theologis. Sensus igitur est; Quos Deus dilexit, & ab aeterno suo beneplacito secretos ab aliis comprobavit, hos praedestinavit, &c. Nihil usitatius in Scripturis quam ut scire sive cognoscere ponatur pro amare sive approbare; sicuti nescire pro odisse & improbare. Non novi vos, Matth. vii. 23. Novit Dominus viam justorum, Psal. i. 6. Hinc Catharinus in hunc ipsum locum, Quid est quod praescivit, nisi predilexit?
english: Weigh the words more closely. Paul did not say "whom he foresaw," but "whom he foreknew" (οὓς προέγνω). This foreknowledge is practical, not bare intuition — what theologians call the knowledge of approbation. Sense: those God loved and, by his eternal good pleasure, set apart from others and approved — those he predestined. Scripture often uses "know" for love or approval, and "not know" for hate or rejection ("I never knew you," Matt. 7:23; "The Lord knows the way of the righteous," Ps. 1:6). So Catharinus on this place: What is "he foreknew," if not "he foreloved"?

source_text: Secundo, non dixit Apostolus, quos praescivit futuros conformes praedestinavit; sed, quos praescivit (hoc est, predilexit) praedestinavit conformes fieri, ut vulgata versio recte supplevit, quod in Graeco contextu deest. Non itaque Deus praedestinare dicitur ex praescientia operum nostrorum, sed praescire bona nostra opera quae praedestinatis praeparavit.
english: Second: Paul did not write "whom he foreknew would be conformed, he predestined," but "whom he foreknew" (that is, foreloved) "he predestined to become conformed" — as the Vulgate rightly supplies what the Greek leaves open. So God is not said to predestine from foresight of our works, but to foreknow the good works he prepared for those already predestined.

source_text: Audiamus Augustinum; qui lib. 2. De bono persever. c. 14. praedestinationem definivit, Praescientia & praeparatio beneficiorum Dei quibus certissime liberantur quicunque liberantur. Et apertius, cap. 17. Quibuscunque Deus sacra dona donat, proculdubio donaturum se esse praescivit, & in sua praescientia praeparavit. Nam in sua praescientia opera sua futura disponere, id omnino, nec aliud quicquam, est praedestinare. Ex quibus verbis facile videtis quam dolose & impie agant, qui gratuitam praedestinationem praescientia operum conentur obscurare, cum Deus nulla in nobis bona opera praeviderit, nulli praesciverit fidem aut sanctitatem, nisi eam quam in ipso decreto praedestinationis nobis praeparavit. Non igitur exinde praedestinavit nos quod praevidit bona opera facturos; sed ex eo praevidit bona opera facturos, quia in praedestinatione nostra praeparata sunt nobis bona opera, ut in illis ambulemus; Ephes. ii. 10.
english: Hear Augustine (On the Gift of Perseverance 2.14): predestination is the foreknowledge and preparation of God's benefits by which whoever is freed is most surely freed. More plainly still (ch. 17): to whom God gives his holy gifts, he without doubt foresaw he would give them, and in that foreknowledge prepared them — for to arrange his own future works in his foreknowledge is exactly, and nothing else, to predestine. So you see how craftily and wickedly they cloud free predestination with foresight of works: God foresaw no good works in us, foresaw faith or holiness for no one, except what he prepared for us in the decree of predestination itself. He did not predestine us because he foresaw we would do good works; he foresaw we would do them because in our predestination good works were prepared for us to walk in (Eph. 2:10).

source_text: Tertio, affertur illud ex 1. Cor. ii. 9. Oculus non vidit, &c. quae praeparavit Deus iis qui diligunt illum. Verba illa, iis qui diligunt illum, secundum communem loquendi modum ipsam causam praeparationis indicant. Nam si quis diceret Regem praeparasse aut destinasse coronam adscendentibus muros oppugnatae alicujus civitatis, hoc dicto significaret ex praevisione adscensionis hanc coronam esse huic vel illi destinatam, & non aliter.
english: Third: they bring 1 Cor. 2:9 — "Eye has not seen… the things God prepared for those who love him." On ordinary speech, "for those who love him" looks like the cause of the preparation. Say a king prepared a crown for whoever scales a besieged city's walls: that would mean the crown was destined to this or that man from foresight of the climb — and no other way.

source_text: Verba illa, iis qui diligunt eum, ostendunt nobis quales tandem illi omnes sint, quibus ab aeterno gloriam praeparavit: sed non indicant hanc dilectionem praevisam fuisse causam aut rationem cur gloria fuit illis destinata. Idem amor Dei qui eos destinavit gratuito ad gloriam, destinavit etiam eos ad hanc dilectionem Dei, qua impellente viam ineunt quae recte ducit ad gloriam. Est itaque nostra Dei dilectio effectum amoris Divini quo nos elegit & praedestinavit ad salutem, atque idcirco inepte supponitur causa nostrae electionis. Huc spectant illa Apostoli verba, Nos diligimus Deum quia ipse prior dilexit nos. 1 Joan. iv. 19.
