english: Reply: "for those who love him" tells what sort of people finally receive the glory he prepared from eternity — it does not make foresight of that love the cause why glory was destined to them. The same love that freely destined them to glory also destined them to love God, and by that love they take the road that leads to glory. So our love of God is an effect of the divine love that elected and predestined us to salvation — foolishly taken as election's cause. So the Apostle: "We love God because he first loved us" (1 John 4:19).

source_text: Optime Augustinus, in Johan. tract. 86. Praescientiam Dei defendunt contra gratiam Dei, qui dicunt nos electos ante mundi constitutionem quia praescivit nos Deus futuros bonos. Non enim electi sunt quia boni fuerunt, qui boni non essent nisi electi essent. Quidni igitur & nos dicamus, eos praescientiam Dei defendere contra gratiam Dei, qui dicunt nos electos, quia Deus praescivit nos ut illum diligentes? cum utique Dei amantes nunquam essemus nisi electi fuissemus.
english: Augustine (In John, tract. 86) puts it best: they defend God's foreknowledge against his grace when they say we were elect before the world's foundation because God foresaw we would be good. They were not elect because they were good — they would not have been good unless elect. So we may say the same of those who claim we were elect because God foresaw us as loving him: we would never love God unless we had been elect.

source_text: Postremo, quod attinet ad similitudinem allatam de Rege terreno coronam destinante adscendentibus muros civitatis; ingentem habet dissimilitudinem in illa ipsa re, unde tota vis argumenti dependet. Nam si nemo possit suis viribus adscendere, & Rex ille possit vires hasce quibus visum fuerit inspirare, non jam illis quibus hasce vires tribueret, destinata fuisset corona ex praevisione adscensionis; sed praevisa adscensio & vires inspiratae, ex destinatione coronae. At sic res habet planissime inter Deum & homines.
english: Last: the earthly-king crown analogy fails at the very hinge of the argument. If no one could climb by his own strength, and the king could breathe that strength into whomever he chose, the crown would not be destined from foresight of the climb — the climb foreseen, and the strength given, would flow from the crown's destination. That is exactly how it stands between God and men.

source_text: Nemo Deum diligeret, nisi Deus charitatem illi infunderet; nemini charitatem salutiferam infunderet, nisi eum prius ad salutem destinasset. Non ergo ex praevisione dilectionis nostrae destinat nobis vitam aeternam, sed ex proposito electionis ad vitam aeternam infundit nobis hanc dilectionem. Concludamus hoc responsum nostrum verbis Augustini, qui mallei instar ubique contundit Pelagianos. Sic ergo ille, Ut acciperemus dilectionem qua diligeremus, dilecti sumus, cum eam nondum haberemus. De grat. Christi contr. Pelag. cap. 26.
english: No one would love God unless God poured charity into him; God would pour saving charity into no one unless he had first destined him to salvation. So he does not destine eternal life from foresight of our love — from the purpose of election to eternal life he infuses that love. Close with Augustine, who hammers the Pelagians everywhere: "That we might receive the love with which we should love, we were loved when we did not yet have it" (On the Grace of Christ against Pelagius, ch. 26).

source_text: Quarto, objicitur ille locus 2 Timoth. ii. 21, Si quis emundaverit se ab istis, erit vas in honorem sanctificatum & utile Domino. Vasa igitur electionis sive misericordiae illa sunt, quos Deus praevidit & praescivit sese emundaturos: Electio igitur nititur praevisione sanctorum operum.
english: Fourth: they bring 2 Tim. 2:21 — "If anyone cleanses himself from these, he will be a vessel unto honour, sanctified and useful to the Lord." So the vessels of election (or mercy) are those God foresaw would cleanse themselves: election, they say, rests on foresight of holy works.

source_text: Non est negandum Deum praescire illorum sanctitatem quos elegit ad gloriam: impossibile enim est ut Deus non praesciat ea quae ipse facturus est; ipse autem omnia nostra bona in nobis operatur. Sed non satis est ad causam hanc obtinendam, ut probetur Deum praevidere bona opera, aut sanctitatem electorum, nisi insuper ostendatur ex hac praevisione antecedente Deum procedere ad eligendum. At hoc nunquam extorquere possunt ex verbis Apostoli.
english: Reply: of course God foreknows the holiness of those he elects to glory — he cannot fail to foreknow what he himself will do, and he works all our good in us. But proving that he foresees the elect's good works is not enough for their cause, unless they also show he elects from that prior foresight. And that they can never force out of Paul's words.

source_text: Nam ille, in loco praedicto, non docet ex qua causa eligantur vasa ad gloriam, sed qua nota discernantur. Duplicem autem notam illis impressam dicit: Unam, quae Deo soli perceptibilis est, nempe signaculum aeternae adoptionis, Novit Deus qui sunt sui. Alteram, quae hominibus patet, fugam scilicet impietatis, & praxim sanctitatis & justitiae; Recedat ab iniquitate: Si se emundaverit, erit vas in honorem.
english: In that place Paul does not teach why vessels are elect to glory, but by what mark they are known. He stamps a double mark on them: one God alone can read — the seal of eternal adoption ("The Lord knows who are his"); the other men can see — flight from impiety and the practice of holiness and justice ("Let him depart from iniquity"; "If he cleanses himself, he will be a vessel unto honour").

source_text: Huc adde, vas in honorem dupliciter dici: Vel ex proposito aeterno Dei eligentis ad honorem: & sic, ut quis sit vas in honorem, non pendet ex sanctificatione praevisa, sed sanctificatio postmodum fluit ab hoc decreto. Vel ex actuali sanctificatione: & hoc sensu tum fit aliquis vas in honorem, quando spiritu Dei purificatus & renovatus incipit inter honoratos Dei servos honori Divino in sanctitate vitae inservire.
english: Add: "vessel unto honour" is said two ways. From God's eternal electing purpose to honour — and then being such a vessel does not hang on foresight of sanctification; sanctification afterward flows from that decree. Or from actual sanctification — and in that sense someone becomes a vessel unto honour when, purified and renewed by God's Spirit, he begins among God's honoured servants to serve the divine honour in a holy life.

source_text: Sic videtur hunc locum intellexisse Lyranus, qui exponit haec verba, erit vas in honorem id est, erit vas Divino cultui applicatum. Sed quocunque modo intelligatur hic locus, non probat Deum nos eligere ad gloriam ex praevisione nostrae sanctitatis, sed electos ad gloriam imbui vera sanctitate, & ex hac nota pro vasis ad honorem destinatis agnosci, & actualiter ad usum honorabilem per hanc sanctitatem applicari.
english: So Lyranus seems to take the place: "he will be a vessel unto honour" means a vessel set apart for divine worship. However you read it, the text does not prove God elects us to glory from foresight of our holiness. It proves the elect to glory are filled with true holiness, known by that mark as vessels destined to honour, and actually put to honourable use through that holiness.

source_text: Quinto, ex 1 Timoth. ii. 4. Deus vult omnes homines salvos fieri, hunc in modum argumentantur, Deum ex hac communi voluntate salvandi omnes, dare omnibus sufficientem gratiam qua ad salutem perducantur. Quod itaque quosdam eligit ad gloriam, quosdam praeterit, id inde evenire, quod praevideat quosdam cooperaturos huic gratiae & in sanctitate perseveraturos, quosdam aut non omnino cooperaturos, aut in bonis operibus & fide non permansuros: Ergo nulla est electio ad gloriam nisi ex praescientia meritorum.
english: Fifth: from 1 Timothy 2:4 — "God wills all men to be saved" — they argue that from this common will to save all, God gives everyone sufficient grace to reach salvation. So some are elect to glory and others passed by only because he foresaw who would cooperate with that grace and persevere in holiness, and who would not cooperate at all, or would not remain in good works and faith. Therefore, they say, there is no election to glory except from foresight of merits.

source_text: Voluntas haec Divina de salute omnium hominum, non aliter concipienda, quam illa quae conjungitur de eruditione omnium hominum. Connectuntur enim ab Apostolo; Deus vult omnes salvos fieri, & ad agnitionem veritatis venire. Est autem certissimum, tum ex verbo Dei, tum ex ipso eventu, Deum non habuisse aut habere voluntatem erudiendi omnes, sive perducendi omnes singulatim ad salutiferae veritatis cognitionem: Rom. x. 14. Quomodo invocabunt eum in quem non crediderint? quomodo autem credent ei de quo non audierint? quomodo audient absque praedicante? aut quomodo praedicabunt si non mittantur? At Deus praeteritis generationibus dimisit omnes gentes suis ipsarum viis incedere; Act. xiv. 16. Ac veritatis agnitionem soli nationi Judaeorum concessit. Post Christi adventum lux veritatis non statim omnibus ex voluntate Dei affulsit. Ad tempus prohibiti sunt Apostoli in viam gentium abire, Matth. x. 5. Aliquanto post vetiti sunt etiam ne praedicarent verbum in Asia, Actor. xvi. 6. Atque ut ad nostra secula descendamus, quot nationes in Novo orbe detectas habemus, ad quas salutiferae veritatis per multa secula ne tenuissima quidem aura pervenit? An dici potest Deus voluisse illos ad agnitionem veritatis venire, ad quos noluit praecones veritatis mittere? Videte Prosperum Aquitanicum, ad Capit. Gall. Respons. 4. & Sent. 4. Si itaque sic intelligunt verba Apostoli, ut sentiant Deum, quantum in se est, velle omnes & singulos mortales in Adamo lapsos propter Christum donare salutiferae veritatis cognitione & ipsa salute, aut in hac illorum sententia manifestum errorem, aut in Divina voluntate manifestam infirmitatem agnoscere est necesse; nam volens potens operatur.
english: This divine will for the salvation of all men must be read with the will joined to it — the will to teach all men. Paul binds them: God wills all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Timothy 2:4). Yet it is certain from God's word and from history that he has not willed to teach all, or to lead every person one by one to saving truth. Romans 10:14: how will they call on him in whom they have not believed? how believe without hearing? how hear without a preacher? how preach unless they are sent? In past generations God let the nations walk in their own ways (Acts 14:16) and gave knowledge of the truth to Israel alone. After Christ's coming the light did not at once shine on all by his will: for a time the apostles were barred from the Gentile road (Matthew 10:5), and later forbidden to preach in Asia (Acts 16:6). Come to our own age: how many nations found in the New World have for centuries not felt even a breath of saving truth? Can God be said to have willed them to know the truth when he would not send them heralds of it? See Prosper of Aquitaine on the Gallic chapters (Response 4 and Sentence 4). If they take Paul to mean that God, as far as in him lies, wills to give every fallen child of Adam saving knowledge and salvation itself for Christ's sake, you must either call their reading a clear error or confess weakness in the divine will — for the one who wills, and can, acts.

source_text: Sed nonnulli, ut tueantur hanc sententiam, urgent Deum per omnia secula voluisse omnes singulatim ad veritatis cognitionem venire, & salvos fieri, quatenus in foedere Dei comprehendebantur, non vero quatenus ab illo foedere in se, aut in parentibus exciderant: Vocasse etiam Deum universos ad veritatis agnitionem, vel in sua persona, vel saltem in persona parentum, avorum, abavorum, &c. Sed hoc commento nihil stultius. Nam primo, qui ob aliquam causam antecedentem decrevit, antequam nascerentur, innumeras singulares personas ad veritatis agnitionem nunquam vocare, is non habuit voluntatem vocandi hasce easdem singulatim. Dein, quam a sensu communi alienum est, Deum vocare voluisse hanc singularem personam ad cognitionem salutiferae veritatis in persona avorum aut abavorum suorum? Haeccine est illa universalis & sufficiens gratia ex qua probant Deum velle omnium salutem sigillatim? An quilibet ex majoribus una persona esse praesumitur cum suis nepotibus? Aut Deus ideo nepoti aliquid dare voluisse dicetur sigillatim & personaliter, quia id dederit impiis & ingratis avis ejus aut abavis qui illud rejecerunt? Qui hoc sensu sufficientem gratiam & generalem Dei voluntatem quoad omnium salutem velit defendere, non ad avos aut abavos, sed ad primum parentem humani generis se recipere debet. Nam in Adamo, qui fuit radix, & sustinuit quasi communem personam humani generis, non incommode dicere possumus, Deum voluisse salutem omnium: Sed dicere Deum sigillatim voluisse salutem hujus Indi aut Americani, atque insuper voluisse ut is ad veritatis salutiferae cognitionem sufficienter vocaretur, cui nunquam misit praeconem aliquem gratiae salutiferae, nec alia ratione id asserere quam quod avus ejus aut abavus, aut quisquis tandem ille fuerit majorum ejus, quingentis aut mille fortasse abhinc annis sua culpa Evangelium rejecit, & hoc suo facto posteros a gratiae foedere exclusit, hoc, inquam, tueri, est ejus qui nihil aliud habet quod dicat; refellere autem illius, qui nihil aliud habet quod agat.
english: Some, to save the opinion, press that through every age God willed each person to come to truth and be saved insofar as they stood in his covenant, not insofar as they fell from it in themselves or in their parents — and that he called everyone to the truth either in their own person or at least in parents, grandparents, and great-grandparents. Nothing is more foolish. First: if for some prior cause God decreed, before they were born, never to call countless particular persons to the truth, he did not will to call those same people one by one. Next: how far from common sense is it that God called this one person to saving truth in the person of his grandparents? Is that the universal sufficient grace by which they prove he wills everyone's salvation person by person? Is each ancestor one person with his grandchildren? Or did God will to give something personally to a grandson because he once gave it to impious grandparents who threw it away? Anyone who wants to defend sufficient grace and a general will to save all this way should go not to grandparents but to the first parent of the race. In Adam — the root, the common person of humankind — we may fairly say God willed the salvation of all. But to say he personally willed the salvation of this Indian or American, and that he was sufficiently called to saving truth, though God never sent him a herald of saving grace — and to rest that only on some ancestor five hundred or a thousand years ago who by his own fault rejected the Gospel and cut his line out of the covenant of grace — that defense belongs to someone with nothing left to say; refuting it belongs to someone with nothing better to do.

source_text: Verum si non placet haec sententia, quis tandem sensus verborum Apostoli? Primo, animadvertendum est, non dixisse Apostolum, Deus vult omnes homines salvos facere, & ad agnitionem veritatis efficacia praedicationis & Spiritus pertrahere; sed, vult omnes salvos fieri, & venire ad cognitionem veritatis. Nam Deo volenti salvum facere nullum hominum resistit arbitrium, ut vere Augustinus De corrept. & grat. cap. 14. Hisce igitur verbis exprimitur potius quid Deus velit ab hominibus fieri, quam quid velit in hominibus facere. Vult Deus, ut Ministri Evangelici teneantur, quantum in illis est, niti ut omnes salvi fiant, & ad Christum veniant; vult ut singuli Christiani orando, aliisque quibus possunt modis, promoveant salutem omnium hominum. Nostrum est, inquit Augustinus, qui nescimus quisnam pertineat ad numerum praedestinatorum, velle omnes salvos fieri, cap. 15. Ad voluntatem igitur praecipientem, quae homines dirigit, haec verba pertinent; non ad voluntatem decernentem, quae bonum homini destinatum infallibiliter largitur.
english: If that reading fails, what do Paul's words mean? First notice: he did not say God wills to make all men saved and drag them to the truth by the force of preaching and the Spirit. He said he wills all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Timothy 2:4). When God wills to make someone saved, no human will blocks him — so Augustine, On Rebuke and Grace 14. These words show what God wills people to do, more than what he wills to work inside them. He wills gospel ministers, as far as they can, to labor that all may be saved and come to Christ; he wills each Christian, by prayer and every means he can, to further the salvation of all. It is ours, Augustine says, who do not know who belongs to the number of the predestined, to will that all be saved (On Rebuke and Grace 15). So the text belongs to the preceptive will that directs us — not to the decretive will that infallibly gives the good God has destined for a person.

source_text: Secundo, notandum est Deum dici velle aliquid voluntate affectionis, vel voluntate effectus, ut distinguit Thomas, Quaest. Disp. De voluntate Dei, art. 1. vel ut alii loquuntur, Deus dicitur velle aliquid approbative, ut quod est in se bonum & amabile, vel efficaciter, ut quod decrevit propter gloriam suam in singulari aliquo subjecto efficere. Prior voluntas nihil aliud designat quam simplicem complacentiam Divinae voluntatis in re aliqua, tanquam Divinae naturae consentanea: Posterior denotat absolutum decretum communicandi hoc bonum singulariter alicui personae. Verbi causa, Castitas, Sapientia, Fides, Salus, sunt bona amabilia, & considerata in se Divinae voluntati consentanea: Recte igitur dicimus Deum velle ut omnes homines casti, sapientes, fideles, salvi fiant. Sed hoc intelligendum de voluntate approbante, quae tendit in rem secundum se consideratam, non de voluntate efficiente, quae statuit rem talem in tali persona operari. Frustra igitur ab illa priori voluntate, quae per se nihil decernit de singularibus personis, moliuntur illud deducere, Deum velle cuivis singulari personae concedere quod sufficit ad salutem ejus procurandam. Frustra etiam huic subnectunt, Deum ex praevisione quinam sint recte usuri hisce mediis, quinam minime, alios eligere ad salutem, alios praeterire & reprobare.
english: Second: God is said to will something by a will of affection or of effect — so Thomas in the Disputed Questions on the will of God, art. 1 — or, as others put it, approbatively (what is good and lovable in itself) or efficaciously (what he has decreed to work for his glory in some particular person). The first is only the divine will's simple delight in a thing as fitting God's nature; the second is an absolute decree to give that good to someone in particular. Chastity, wisdom, faith, salvation are lovable goods, and in themselves agreeable to God's will — so we rightly say God wills all people to be chaste, wise, faithful, and saved. Hear that of the approving will, which looks at the thing as such, not of the effecting will, which decides to work it in this or that person. From that prior will — which of itself settles nothing about particular persons — they cannot force the claim that God wills to grant each person whatever suffices for his salvation. Still less can they hang on it that, from foresight of who will use those means well and who will not, he elects some to salvation and passes by and reprobates others.

source_text: Postremo, si quis obstinate contendat verba Apostoli de efficaci voluntate Dei esse intelligenda, is nunquam se expediet, si aliter locum capiat quam ab Augustino, Gregorio & Scholasticis olim fuit explicatus. Sic Augustinus de corrept. & grat. cap. 14. Deus vult omnes homines salvos fieri, ut intelligantur omnes praedestinati, quia omne genus hominum est in iis. Et Gregorius, Omnes homines vult salvos fieri, quia ex omni hominum genere eligit, quos ad gaudium aeternae salutis trahit. In 1. Reg. lib. 5. cap. 4. Aquinas denique in Commentariis ad haec ipsa verba, Est distributio pro generibus singulorum, non pro singulis generum. Quandoquidem ergo hic locus non probat Deum voluntate beneplaciti velle salutem omnium & singulorum, multo minus probat Deum eligere homines ad salutem ex praescientia futurae cooperationis, qua se accommodent huic voluntati Dei.
english: Last: if someone still insists Paul's words mean God's efficacious will, he will never get free unless he reads the place as Augustine, Gregory, and the scholastics long did. Augustine, On Rebuke and Grace 14: "God wills all men to be saved" — understand all the predestined, because every kind of human being is among them. Gregory: he wills all men to be saved because from every kind of people he elects those he draws to the joy of eternal salvation (on 1 Kings, book 5, ch. 4). Aquinas on the same words: the distribution is for the kinds of individuals, not for the individuals of the kinds. So this text does not prove that by the will of good pleasure God wills the salvation of every single person — and far less that he elects people to salvation from foresight of the future cooperation by which they would fit themselves to that will.

source_text: Sextum testimonium quo nititur Vasques, habetur Jacob. ii. 5. Nonne Deus elegit pauperes in hoc mundo, divites in fide, & heredes regni, quod promisit Deus diligentibus se? Hoc est, interprete Jesuita, Deus eos qui in hoc mundo pauperes erant, quia erant in fide & charitate divites, elegit ad gloriam, sive regni hereditatem. Electio igitur ad gloriam est ex praescientia Dei, qui videt quinam tandem futuri sunt divites in fide & operibus.
english: Sixth: Vasquez leans on James 2:5 — "Has not God chosen the poor in this world, rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom he promised to those who love him?" The Jesuit reads it: God chose those who were poor in this world because they were rich in faith and charity — chose them to glory, the inheritance of the kingdom. So, they say, election to glory hangs on God's foresight of who will finally be rich in faith and works.

source_text: Scopus verborum hic est; Pauperes non esse a nobis contemnendos, quia tantum abest ut negligantur a Deo, ut in dispensatione rerum spiritualium maximam ob partem praeferantur ditioribus: Divites e contra non esse nimis suspiciendos, & cum neglectu pauperum honorandos, quia Deus saepenumero vacuos dimittit divites, cum pauperes impleat bonis. Non absimilis huic est ille alter locus 1 Cor. i. 26. Non multi sapientes secundum carnem, non multi potentes, non multi nobiles: Sed quae stulta sunt mundi elegit Deus, ut confundat fortia, &c. Ostendit ergo Apostolus Deum ex classe pauperum plures elegisse, quos tum fide tum hereditate caelesti donaret, quam ex numero divitum.
english: Reply: James's point is that we must not despise the poor. Far from neglecting them, God in spiritual gifts mostly prefers them to the richer. The rich, for their part, are not to be overrated and honored while the poor are ignored — God often sends the rich away empty and fills the poor with goods. 1 Corinthians 1:26 runs the same way: not many wise by flesh, not many mighty, not many noble — God chose what the world calls foolish to shame the strong. So the Apostle shows God has chosen more from the poor, to give them faith and the heavenly inheritance, than from the rich.

source_text: Atque hinc est quod conjungit haec duo, divites in fide, & heredes regni. Non dixit electos heredes regni, quia praevisi erant futuri divites in fide, sed electi erant ut fierent divites in fide, atque heredes regni.
english: That is why he binds the two phrases: rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom. He did not say the elect are heirs because they were foreseen as going to be rich in faith. He said they were elect so they would become rich in faith — and heirs of the kingdom.

source_text: Hanc expositionem frivola calumniatione Vasques conatur evertere: Si, inquit, eligere divitem in fide est facere divitem in fide, eligere etiam pauperes in hoc mundo, erit facere pauperes in hoc mundo: at Jacobus non significavit Deum fecisse pauperes, sed eos qui pauperes erant, quia fuerunt divites in fide, elegisse ad gloriam. Respondeo, nullum absurdum inde sequi si dicamus Deum fecisse pauperes in hoc mundo, cum ipsa distinctio pauperum & divitum fiat ex decreto voluntatis Divinae; sed fatemur non ea spectare verba Apostoli; neque hoc obstat interpretationi nostrae;
english: Vasquez tries a cheap jab at that reading: if "choosing the rich in faith" means making them rich in faith, then "choosing the poor in this world" would mean making them poor — yet James does not say God made people poor; he says those who already were poor, because they were rich in faith, God chose to glory. Reply: no absurdity if we say God made people poor in this world — the rich/poor split itself comes from the divine decree. We grant James's words are not about that. And that does not hurt our reading;

source_text: quod exemplo non dissimili patebit. Si dicamus Deum elegisse piscatores Apostolos suos, in hac loquendi formula eligere est idem quod facere Apostolum; non autem significat facere piscatores, quia prius sua voluntate erant facti piscatores, quam electi Apostoli: Sic cum dico Deum elegisse pauperes divites in fide & heredes regni, eligere est idem quod facere fideles & regni heredes, sed non est idem quod facere pauperes; quia tum supponuntur pauperes cum donantur fide & adoptione ad regnum coeleste.
english: a near parallel shows why. If we say God chose fishermen as his Apostles, "choose" there means make them Apostles — not make them fishermen. They were already fishermen by their own trade before they were elect Apostles. So when I say God chose the poor who are rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom, "choose" means make them believers and kingdom-heirs — not make them poor. Poverty is already assumed when faith and adoption to the heavenly kingdom are given.

source_text: Denique ad pleniorem verborum intelligentiam accedat & hoc quoque; Quamvis Deus non eligat homines ex praescientia fidei, recte tamen dicitur elegisse divites in fide, quia tales facit in tempore eos omnes, quos elegit ab aeterno; & quia tales factos jam actualiter & quasi visibiliter eligit, & ab infidelibus secretos in peculium suum transfert. Concludamus hoc responsum verbis illis quibus Augustinus hunc ipsum locum explicavit; Elegit Deus fideles, sed ut fiant, non quia jam erant. Eligendo ergo facit divites in fide, sicut heredes regni. Recte quippe in eis hoc eligere dicitur, quod ut in eis faciat, eos elegit. Haec ille, De Praedest. Sanct. lib. 1. cap. 17.
english: Add this for the full sense: God does not elect from foresight of faith, yet he is rightly said to have chosen the rich in faith — because in time he makes such everyone he elected from eternity; and because, once made such, he already actually and almost visibly elects them, sets them apart from unbelievers, and takes them as his own. Close with Augustine on this very text (On the Predestination of the Saints 1.17): "God chose the faithful, but that they might become so, not because they already were. By electing he makes them rich in faith, just as he makes them heirs of the kingdom." That choosing is rightly said of them: he chose them so that he might do this in them.

source_text: Non ergo Deus elegit quia praevidit illos futuros fideles, sed praevisi sunt fideles quia eligendo eos tales facit.
english: Bottom line: foresight of future faith is not why God elects. He foresaw them faithful because election itself is what makes them faithful.

source_text: Ultimum testimonium petitur ex Apoc. iii. 11. Tene quod habes, ne alius accipiat coronam tuam. Ex hisce verbis patet coronam gloriae amitti posse vita impia: Deus ergo neminem praedestinat ad hanc coronam gloriae, nisi quia videt illum ad extremum in pietate & fide perseveraturum. Si enim absque hac praevisione quenquam praedestinaret, incerta redderetur praedestinatio, & posset per suam infirmitatem aut pravitatem a gloria excidere, quem Deus voluit ad gloriam praedestinare.
english: Last: they take Revelation 3:11 — "Hold what you have, lest another take your crown." From that they say the crown of glory can be lost by an ungodly life, so God predestines no one to that crown unless he sees the person will persevere to the end in piety and faith. Without that foresight, they argue, predestination would be unsure — someone God meant for glory could drop out by weakness or wickedness.

source_text: Respondeo, haec verba non minore probabilitate ad coronam ministerii accommodari posse quam ad coronam caelestis gloriae, hoc nimirum sensu; Tene quod habes, id est, Episcopale officium constanter & diligenter exerce: ne alius accipiat coronam tuam, hoc est, ne, si tu negligentem te ostenderis, alius, te rejecto, in locum tuum sufficiatur. Sed quia eadem verba possunt haud incommode, & solent a multis, ad coronam caelestis gloriae referri, hoc sensu admisso, respondemus.
english: Reply: the words fit the crown of ministry at least as well as heavenly glory — "Hold what you have" as keep the bishop's office steadily and carefully; "lest another take your crown" as lest, if you prove negligent, someone else is put in your place after you are set aside. Still, many read them of the heavenly crown without strain. Take that sense, and we answer as follows.

source_text: Primo, Non posse praedestinatos amittere coronam gloriae: hanc tamen certitudinem adipiscendi coronam non oriri ex necessitate cogente illos ad vitam aeternam, neque niti mera Dei praescientia intuente quid illi ex libero suo arbitrio facturi sint; sed fundatam esse in illo causarum ordine quem specialis quaedam Divina providentia ad salutem electorum infallibiliter producendam concatenavit. Hanc certitudinem, non nudae praescientiae, sed causalitatis Apostolus indicavit Rom. viii. ubi docet ita Deum instituisse & gubernare ordinem causarum ad promovendam salutem electorum, ut omnia etiam illa quae saluti illorum infesta videntur, tamen cooperentur illis in aeternum bonum animarum; versu 28. & seq. usque ad finem capitis.
english: First: the predestined cannot lose the crown of glory. That certainty does not come from a force that drags them into eternal life, nor from bare foresight of what free will will do. It rests on the chain of causes special providence has linked so the elect's salvation is produced without fail. Paul marks that as causality, not naked foresight — Romans 8: God so set and steers the order of causes for the elect that even what looks hostile still works for their souls' eternal good (vv. 28ff to the chapter's end).

source_text: Atque hinc est quod Augustinus infert, si aliquis electorum a Deo discederet mutabilitate liberi sui arbitrii, quod non modo falleretur Deus, sed vinceretur, quia scilicet non modo praevidit electos fore glorificandos, sed invicta causarum concatenatione hoc efficere decrevit. Horum (id est, electorum) si quisquam perit, fallitur Deus; sed nemo eorum perit, quia non fallitur Deus: horum si quisquam perit vitio humano, vincitur Deus; sed nemo eorum perit, quia nulla re vincitur Deus, De corrept. & grat. cap. 7. Cur Deus vinceretur si electus periret vitio propriae voluntatis? Quia scilicet in se Deus suscepit, ut omnibus electis non nudam & languidam possibilitatem, sed firmam, certam & invictam perseverandi voluntatem ingeneraret.
english: That is why Augustine says: if any elect left God by free will's changeableness, God would not only be deceived but beaten — he not only foresaw their glorification; he decreed to bring it about by an unbeatable chain of causes. On Rebuke and Grace 7: if any of them perishes, God is deceived — but none does, for God is not deceived; if any perishes by human fault, God is overcome — but none does, for nothing overcomes God. Why "overcome" if an elect fell by his own will's fault? Because God undertook to plant in every elect not a thin bare possibility, but a firm, sure, unconquered will to persevere.

source_text: Quamvis igitur, si spectentur electi ex propriae voluntatis infirmitate, possunt amittere coronam; tamen si spectentur, qua subjacet haec illorum voluntas efficacissimae directioni Divinae, non possunt illam amittere.
english: So if you look only at the elect's weak will, they can lose the crown. Look at that same will under God's most effective direction, and they cannot.

source_text: Secundo, quod dicunt adversarii, Deum neminem praedestinare ad coronam nisi quem praevidet perseveraturum, eatenus pro vero admittendum, quatenus ponit easdem singulares personas quae praedestinantur ad gloriam, esse praevisas simul a Deo ut perseveraturas in gratia. Sed quatenus supponit hanc praevisionem esse causam praedestinationis, & secundum nostrum modum intelligendi illa priorem, est omnino repudiandum.
english: Second: when opponents say God predestines to the crown only those he foresees will persevere, grant it this far — the same people predestined to glory are also foreseen as going to persevere in grace. Reject it when they make that foresight the cause of predestination, and prior to it in our order of thought.

source_text: Postremo, quod attinet ad ipsorum verborum formulam, recte Augustinus, De corrept. & grat. cap. 13. Perseveraturis sanctis sic ista dicuntur, quasi eos perseveraturos habeatur incertum: non aliter enim hoc audire debent, quibus expedit non altum sapere, sed timere. Hujusmodi ergo hortationes ipsis electis adhibentur, non quod incerta sit illorum praedestinatio, aut ex mutabilitate arbitrii illorum pendula, sed quod hoc medio hortationum, aliisque quae Deus apta esse novit, efficiat ut in gratia & sanctitate perseverent. Atque haec praecipua testimonia Scripturarum sunt, quae ad probandam electionem ex praevisione meritorum afferuntur. Si quae alia occurrant, ex hisce quae explicata sunt veram illorum sententiam desumere in promptu erit. A testimoniis ergo ad rationes adversariorum veniamus.
english: Last, on the wording itself: Augustine (On Rebuke and Grace 13) says these lines are spoken to saints who will persevere as if their perseverance were unsure — they need to hear it that way, not to be proud but to fear. So the elect get such warnings not because their predestination is shaky or hangs on free will's change, but because by exhortation and other means God knows fit, he makes them persevere in grace and holiness. Those are the main Scripture proofs used for election from foresight of merits. Any further texts take their sense from these. From the texts, then, to the adversaries' reasons.

source_text:
CAP. III. Argumenta adversariorum expenduntur & dissolvuntur.

Jam rationes adversariorum ventilemus. Primo igitur conantur demonstrare, neminem esse efficaci Dei voluntate electum ad gloriam nisi ex meritis praevisis, hujusmodi argumentatione:

Rat. 1. Voluntas dandi vitam aeternam, quae antecedit praevisionem meritorum, est quaedam voluntas communis & inefficax, quae ex aequo respicit omnes homines, tam praeteritos quam praedestinatos: Ergo quod vult Deus alicui efficaciter dare gloriam, pendet ex praevisione meritorum.
english:
Cap. III — the adversaries' arguments weighed and answered.

Now to their reasons. First they try to prove no one is chosen for glory by God's efficacious will except from foreseen merits, like this:

Rat. 1. The will to give eternal life that comes before foresight of merits is only a common, inefficacious will, looking equally at all — reprobate and predestinate alike. So if God efficaciously wills glory for someone, that hangs on foresight of merits.

source_text: Rej. Communis illa voluntas dandi vitam aeternam omnibus, (ut optime Bannes) secundum nostrum modum intelligendi concipitur ante praescientiam peccati. Eo igitur tantum valebit, ut inde probetur, Deum in Adamo integro voluisse communem omnium hominum salutem, atque in hunc finem dedisse Adamo sufficientia media, quibus si uti voluisset, neque seipsum, neque posteros in aeternae mortis reatum praecipitasset. Posito autem primi Adami lapsu, nego Deum unquam habuisse communem & indifferentem illam voluntatem dandi omnibus vitam aeternam in Christo Jesu.
english: Rejection. That "common will to give eternal life to all" (Bannes is right) is only how we picture things before foreknowledge of sin. It proves at most that in intact Adam God willed everyone's salvation and gave him enough means — if Adam had used them, neither he nor his line would have fallen into eternal death's guilt. Once Adam fell, I deny God ever had a common, indifferent will to give eternal life to all in Christ Jesus.

source_text: Quoad reprobandos, non habuit voluntatem quae proxime referebatur ad eorum salutem: nam qui id defendunt, coguntur hoc additamentum apponere, Si ipsi voluerint. Cum ergo Deus praevideat hoc ipsorum Nolle, & nolit illis dare id, quod revera dat electis, manifestum est hanc voluntatem Dei non ex aequo terminari ad salutem electorum & non-electorum.
english: Toward the reprobate he had no will aimed next at their salvation: defenders must tack on "if they themselves will." Since God foresees their Not-willing and will not give them what he really gives the elect, that will clearly does not terminate equally on elect and non-elect salvation.

source_text: Porro, qui Deo tribuunt hanc voluntatem beneplaciti circa omnium salutem, id inde colligunt, quod omnibus det sufficientia auxilia ad salutem obtinendam: quod tamen nec de Paganis, quibus Christi nomen & Evangelii lumen nunquam innotuit, nec de infantibus illorum qui absque baptismo moriuntur, (ut de aliis nihil dicam) unquam probabunt. Augustinus diserte docet, damnari multos qui justificari & salvari non potuerint, De Nat. & grat. cap. 8. & 9.
english: Those who put on God a good-pleasure will for everyone's salvation infer it from "sufficient helps for all" — yet they never prove that of pagans who never heard Christ's name or Gospel light, nor of their infants dying unbaptized (never mind the rest). Augustine says plainly many are damned who could not be justified and saved (On Nature and Grace 8–9).

source_text: Et Epist. 107. inter duodecim sententias quae ad fidem rectam & catholicam pertinere affirmat, haec quarta est, Scimus gratiam non omnibus hominibus dari, & quibus datur, non solum secundum merita operum non dari, sed nec secundum merita voluntatis eorum quibus datur: quod maxime apparet in parvulis. Et non multo post, hanc ipsam objectionem respiciens, quae obtendi solet de voluntate communi & indifferenti quoad salutem omnium, haec verba adjungit, recitatione nostra & observatione vestra dignissima: Manifestum est eos qui huic resistunt tam perspicuae veritati, non intelligere omnino qua locutione sit dictum, quod omnes homines vult Deus salvos fieri, cum tam multi salvi non fiant. Non quia ipsi, sed quia Deus non vult: quod sine ulla caligine manifestatur in parvulis. Quod igitur dictum est, OMNES HOMINES VULT DEUS SALVOS FIERI, cum tam multos nolit salvos fieri, ideo dictum est, quia omnes qui salvi fiunt, nisi ipse velit non fiunt; & si quae alio modo intelligi possunt, ut tamen huic apertissimae veritati, in qua vides tam multos, volentibus hominibus, sed Deo nolente, salvos non fieri, contraria esse non possunt. Hactenus Augustinus.
english: Epistle 107's fourth of twelve catholic sentences: we know grace is not given to all; and where it is given, not by works' merits, nor even by the will's merits of those who get it — clearest in infants. Soon after, on the usual "common indifferent will to save all" objection, he adds words worth quoting: those who fight this plain truth miss how "God wills all to be saved" is said when so many are not. Not because they refuse, but because God does not will — obvious in infants. So "GOD WILLS ALL MEN TO BE SAVED," though he does not will so many saved, means all who are saved are saved only if he wills; any other reading must not contradict that open truth: many are not saved though men will it, if God does not. So Augustine.

source_text: Ipse Vasques ante rei evidentiam coactus, concedit nobis, quibusdam parvulis nec sufficiens remedium per Christum humana diligentia potuisse applicari. Ego addo, nec Divina providentia fuisse applicatum. Atque hinc a posteriori colligimus, Deum non habuisse hanc communem, quam comminiscuntur, salvandi omnes & singulos beneplaciti voluntatem. Postremo, quod maxime facit ad argumentationis propositae nervos incidendos, nego illam Dei voluntatem, quae ante praescientiam meritorum decrevit dare vitam aeternam electis, fuisse solummodo hanc communem, inefficacem, & quam vocant, simplicis affectus sive complacentiae; atque affirmo fuisse specialem quandam & efficacissimam voluntatem.
english: Even Vasquez, pressed by the facts, grants that for some infants no sufficient Christ-remedy could be applied by human care. I add: nor was it applied by divine providence. So a posteriori God never had that invented common good-pleasure will to save every single person. Finally — and this most cuts their argument's nerve — I deny that the will by which God, before foreknowledge of merits, decreed eternal life for the elect was only that common, inefficacious "simple affection / complacency" will; I affirm it was a special, most efficacious will.

source_text: Hoc ex eo liquet, quia haec ipsa gratuita voluntas Dei, quae praecedit merita sive bona opera nostra, est causa horum meritorum: Quomodo igitur dicamus illam Dei voluntatem quae meritis praesupponitur esse communem, aequalem & indifferentem quoad omnes, cum in aliquibus efficiat haec ipsa quae vocantur merita, in aliis non efficiat? Manifestum apparet discrimen in effectu; ergo intelligitur etiam in ipsa causa. Audiamus iterum (quem nunquam satis audire possumus) loquentem Augustinum: Vera Dei gratia est, quae non secundum merita nostra datur, sed quae dat merita ipsa cum datur, quia praevenit hominis voluntatem bonam, nec eam cujusquam invenit in corde, sed facit. Sic itaque haec summa responsionis nostrae: Non esse aequalem aut indifferentem de omnium salute illam Dei voluntatem, quae antecedit praescientiam bonorum operum, quandoquidem in aliquibus vult Deus producere haec opera gratiae, quae ducant ad gloriam, in aliis non vult: Male ergo inferunt, ex praevisione meritorum incipere efficacem Dei voluntatem de danda salute electis, cum ea manifeste se exerat in illa voluntate dandi haec ipsa merita, quae voluntas praevisionem meritorum praecessit, atque ad salutem haec ipsa illorum merita ordinavit.
english: Clear why: that free will of God before our merits or good works is itself their cause. How then call the will presupposed to merits common, equal, and indifferent to all, when in some it effects those "merits" and in others not? Effect differs; so does the cause. Hear Augustine again (never enough): true grace is not given by our merits but gives the merits when given — it goes before a good will, finds it in no heart, and makes it. Sum of our answer: the divine will before foresight of good works is not equal or indifferent about everyone's salvation, since in some God wills grace-works that lead to glory and in others he does not. So they wrongly start the efficacious saving will for the elect from foresight of merits — that will already shows itself in willing to give those merits, which will came before merit-foresight and ordered those merits to salvation.

source_text: Rat. 2. Secundo, argumentatur Vasques a discrimine mediorum Physicorum & Moralium. In Physicis mediis concedit efficacem intentionem finis praecedere intentionem mediorum: at quoties medium ad aliquem finem est morale (qualia sunt opera bona relata ad vitae aeternae consecutionem) negat ullam esse posse efficacem voluntatem in Deo conferendi talem finem ante praescientiam mediorum: Deus ergo non eligit ad gloriam nisi ex praevisione operum, In 1. quaest. 23. art. 3. disp. 89. cap. 9. Vide etiam disp. 81. cap. 5. Esse autem talem differentiam inter media moralia & physica, hinc putat se posse ostendere; quod media physica in se habeant naturalem virtutem causandi finem sine relatione ad voluntatem alterius: ideo licet finis efficaciter intendatur ante praescientiam eorum, ex sua nihilominus virtute, cum adhibentur, conducunt ad finem obtinendum. Jam vero, quia media moralia non producunt finem infra & naturali virtute, sed ex ordinatione alterius, nisi per praescientiam ejus ordinentur & acceptentur ad finem prius quam ille finis efficaciter alicui intentus fuerit, nullius momenti erunt ad finis consecutionem: ut autem acceptentur & ordinentur, praevideri est necesse. Nulla igitur praedestinatio est cujuscunque ad hunc gloriae finem, nisi post praevisionem operum, quae sunt media moralia a Deo ordinata ad eundem.
english: Rat. 2. Second, Vasquez argues from the split between physical and moral means. With physical means he grants that an efficacious intention of the end comes before intending the means. But whenever the means to an end is moral (good works ordered to eternal life), he denies God can have any efficacious will to confer that end before foreknowing the means. So God elects to glory only from foresight of works (In 1. q. 23 art. 3 disp. 89 ch. 9; also disp. 81 ch. 5). He thinks he can prove the difference: physical means carry in themselves a natural power to cause the end, without depending on another's will — so even if the end is intended before they are foreknown, when applied they still tend to the end by their own virtue. Moral means, he says, do not produce the end by any inward natural power but only by another's ordination; unless foresight ordains and accepts them to the end before that end is efficaciously intended for someone, they count for nothing toward obtaining it — and to be accepted and ordained they must be foreseen. Hence no one is predestined to glory's end except after foresight of works that are moral means God ordained to that end.

source_text: Resp. Hoc discrimen inter media physica & moralia, quod Vasques cupit stabilire, nullo modo admittimus. Nam secundum ordinem intentionis (de quo jam quaeritur) finis est causa mediorum tam moralium quam physicorum: atque ex praecedente finis desiderio media haec tum eliguntur tum adhibentur. Nota est regula, Media adhibentur in ordine ad finem. Finis itaque intentio semper praecedit suppeditationem mediorum. Non enim Deus destinasset Paulo efficacem gratiam, nisi prius efficaciter destinasset dare illi gloriam.
english: Resp. We do not grant Vasquez's physical/moral split at all. In the order of intention (the real question) the end causes the means — moral as well as physical — and from desiring the end first those means are chosen and applied. Known rule: means are applied toward the end. So intending the end always comes before supplying the means. God would not have destined efficacious grace to Paul unless he had first efficaciously destined to give him glory.

source_text: Quod autem attinet ad diversum modum operandi, quem Vasques annotavit in mediis physicis & moralibus, concedimus modo differre; sed negamus hoc causae nostrae obesse. Nam primo, illa sua consideratione aberrat a scopo controversiae. Quaeritur enim non de ordine exsecutionis, in quo fatemur media relata ad finem habere rationem causae ad effectum; sed de ordine intentionis, in quo media comparantur ad finem tanquam effecta ad causam. Quae autem ille philosophatur de diversitate operandi inter media physica & moralia, spectant ad finem, non qua consideratur in voluntate & mente agentis, sed qua consideratur ut posita in exsecutione externa: quo sensu, perspicuum est media praecedere finem: Sed ad rem non facit.
english: As for Vasquez's different operating mode in physical vs moral means: we grant they differ in mode, but deny that hurts our case. First, that angle misses the controversy's aim. We are not asking about execution-order — where we admit means related to the end act as cause toward the effect — but about intention-order, where means stand to the end as effects to a cause. His philosophy about how physical and moral means operate looks to the end as already out in external execution, not as in the agent's will and mind. In that sense means do precede the end — but that is beside the point.

source_text: Secundo, quod urget nullius momenti fore media moralia ad ipsam consecutionem finis, nisi fuissent praevisa & acceptata a Deo ante efficacem intentionem finis, fatemur talia media habere suam vim causandi finem, sive operandi ad consecutionem finis, a praecedente voluntate Dei, qui ea ordinavit & acceptavit ad talem finem: sed simul affirmamus, haec media praecognosci & praevideri a Deo antequam finis intendatur, solummodo tanquam apta & conducentia ad finem, tanquam possibilia & communicabilia illis omnibus quibus vult finem; sed non praesciuntur & praevidentur tanquam absolute futura in hoc aut illo singulari homine, priusquam sit efficaciter ad gloriam electus, id est, ad finem destinatus.
english: Second, he presses that moral means would be worthless for obtaining the end unless foreseen and accepted by God before an efficacious intention of the end. We grant such means get their power to cause — or work toward — the end from God's prior will that ordained and accepted them to that end. But we also affirm: before the end is intended, God foreknows those means only as apt and helpful to it, as possible and shareable with all for whom he wills the end — not as absolutely going to happen in this or that particular person before that person is efficaciously elected to glory (destined to the end).

source_text: Postremo, in hoc suo argumento Vasques transit in castra Semipelagianorum, & Augustinum deserit, qui passim docet, non eligi homines ad vitam aeternam ex praescientia fidei aut bonorum operum, sed inde potius oriri omnia nostra bona opera, quod fuimus praedestinati ad vitam aeternam. Hinc fides: Non eliguntur quia crediderunt, sed eliguntur ut credant, De Praedest. sanct. lib. 1. cap. 17. Hinc sanctitas: Certum & manifestum est, ideo nos sanctos futuros, quia elegit nos Deus, praedestinans ut per gratiam tales essemus: ibid. cap. 18. Hinc perseverantia: Sanctis in regnum Dei per gratiam praedestinatis, donatur ipsa perseverantia, De corr. & gratia, cap. 12. Post electionem igitur omnia nostra bona praevidentur, quia ab electione ipsa proficiscuntur.
english: Finally, in this argument Vasquez crosses into the Semipelagian camp and leaves Augustine, who everywhere teaches men are not elected to eternal life from foresight of faith or good works — rather all our good works arise because we were predestined to eternal life. Faith: not elected because they believed, but elected that they may believe (De praed. sanct. 1.17). Holiness: certain and plain we will be holy because God elected us, predestining that by grace we should be such (ibid. 18). Perseverance: to saints predestined by grace into God's kingdom, perseverance itself is given (De corr. et grat. 12). So after election all our goods are foreseen, because they spring from election itself.

source_text: Rat. 3. In Divina voluntate ordo actuum consideratur non per se, sed ex analogia quadam ad voluntatem humanam: unde secundum nostrum intelligendi modum aliquid prius, aliquid posterius a Deo volitum sive praevisum affirmamus. Hoc posito contendit Vasques, Sicuti cum Rex aliquis proponit premium bene certantibus, ea lege ut nullus illo potiatur nisi qui victor sit, nunquam decernit alicui, quantumvis amato, dare illud premium, antequam illum videat victoria potitum; ita de Deo sentiendum, nunquam illum decernere alicui premium aeternae gloriae, quod tanquam coronam promisit legitime certantibus, nisi post intuitum victoriae, hoc est, perseverantiae in bonis operibus. Jam vero quia Deus est praescius omnium futurorum, ab aeterno praevidit quinam victoriam reportabunt, atque idcirco ab aeterno ex hac praevisione decrevit illis dare gloriam: sicuti princeps, cum videt aliquem vicisse, tum demum statuit illi premium assignare.
english: Rat. 3. In God’s will the order of acts is not read in itself but by analogy to human willing — so in our way of speaking we call one thing prior and another later as willed or foreseen by God. On that footing Vasquez presses: as a king who sets a prize for those who contend well, on the rule that only the victor takes it, never decrees to give that prize to anyone — however loved — before he sees him possessed of the victory, so of God: he never decrees to anyone the prize of eternal glory (promised as a crown to those who contend lawfully) except after intuition of victory, that is perseverance in good works. And since God foreknows all futures, from eternity he foresaw who would win, and from that foresight decreed to give them glory — as a prince, seeing someone has conquered, only then resolves to assign the prize.

source_text: Sol. Concedimus illud postulatum, nimirum, Non esse aliquem ordinem prioritatis & posterioritatis in actibus sive voluntatis sive mentis Divinae; sed hunc ordinem desumi ex analogia ad voluntatem humanam; & ex dependentia obiectorum, quam habent inter se. Ad inductam autem comparationem respondemus, Primo, posse nos manifestam causam afferre cur Princeps terrestris non designat aliquem singulariter ad premium, nisi ex precedente intuitu Victoriae, & Deus tamen possit e contra primo ex mera gratia destinare aliquem singulariter ad coronam, & consequenter praeparate & dare illi ea dona, per quae praevidebitur producendus ad coronam.
english: Sol. We grant the postulate: there is no priority/posteriority in the acts of the divine will or mind themselves; that order is borrowed from analogy to human willing and from how the objects depend on one another. To the comparison itself: first, we can show why an earthly prince does not mark someone out for the prize except after seeing the victory — and yet God, on the contrary, can first from mere grace destine someone singularly to the crown, and then prepare and give the gifts through which that person will be foreseen as brought to the crown.

source_text: Ratio autem haec est; Quia non est penes Regem mortalem inspirare & infundere illam voluntatem, & illas vires ex quibus infallibiliter haec singularis persona prae aliis obtineat victoriam. Si hoc posset, nihil impediret, quin cuicunque amico suo ex primaria & gratuita voluntate intenderet & decerneret dare illud premium, ita tamen ut perveniret ad illud secundum legem positam, nimirum vincendo, idque ex viribus illi inspiratis virtute primariae illius intentionis. Si ita res se haberet in terreno Principe, non ex praevisione meritorum elegisse diceretur amicum suum ad premium obtinendum, sed ex antecedente proposito & intentione dandi premium, dedisse merita, & in hac sua donatione praevidisse. At sic agere Deum cum omnibus glorificandis in confesso est.
english: The reason: a mortal king cannot inspire and pour in the will and powers by which this one person rather than others infallibly wins. If he could, nothing would stop him intending and decreeing from a primary, gratuitous will to give that prize to any friend — yet so the friend reaches it by the stated law, namely by winning, and from powers inspired by that primary intention. Were an earthly prince so able, we would not say he elected his friend to the prize from foresight of merits, but that from an antecedent purpose to give the prize he gave the merits and in that gift foresaw them. And that God so deals with all who are to be glorified is confessed.

source_text: Secundo, quod assumit Vasques, non posse Principem intendere efficaciter ut aliquis consequatur premium, nisi ex praeviso intuitu meritorum, non est tam exploratae veritatis, atque ille opinatur. Est enim efficax intentio finis, quae movet agentem ut efficaciter adhibeat quaecunque potest media ad eiusdem consecutionem: licet non sit in eius potestate certo praevidere eventum, aut infallibiliter ipsum finem consequi. Potest igitur Princeps ex speciali benevolentia serio & efficaciter intendere praemium amico suo ante intuitum victoriae; atque ex hac intentione non modo optare, sed quantum in illo est, parare & dare illi omnia quae conducunt ad victoriam; quamvis ut judex & agonothetes non possit illum actu coronare, nisi intuitu victoriae obtentae. Deus ergo multo magis (cui velle & facere aeque in promptu sunt) potest efficaciter intendere Petro aut Paulo coronam aeternae gloriae, atque ex vi hujus intentionis praeparate & dare illis ea omnia quae merita coronae dicuntur; atque in hac sua praedestinatione ab aeterno praevidere illorum merita, atque tandem intuitu pugnae praeclare depugnatae coronam destinatam illorum capitibus imponere.
english: Second, Vasquez’s claim that a prince cannot efficaciously intend someone’s prize except from foresight of merits is not as settled as he thinks. Efficacious intention of an end moves the agent to apply every means in his power toward obtaining it — even when he cannot certainly foresee the event or infallibly secure the end. So a prince from special goodwill can seriously and efficaciously intend the prize for his friend before seeing the victory, and from that intention not only wish but, as far as he can, prepare and give all that helps toward victory — though as judge and agonothetes he cannot actually crown him except upon the victory won. God much more (for whom to will and to do are ready alike) can efficaciously intend for Peter or Paul the crown of eternal glory, and by that intention’s force prepare and give all that are called merits of the crown; and in this predestination from eternity foresee their merits, and at last, upon the fight nobly fought, set the destined crown on their heads.

source_text: Postremo, dicimus hanc esse ipsissimam sententiam quam Augustinus passim propugnat contra Pelagianos, nimirum, Eligi homines gratuito, & ante omnem praescientiam meritorum, non modo ad dona gratiae, sed etiam ad regnum gloriae: utcunque perducantur ad regnum gloriae per viam bonorum operum, sive meritorum, ut loqui solent antiqui Patres. Unicum tantummodo locum citabo, qui sic se habet, De damnabili humani generis massa Deus praescivit misericordia, non meritis, quos ex electione gratiae praedestinavit ad vitam, Contra Pelag. Hypognost. lib. 6. Ubi videtis praescientiam illam, qua nititur praedestinatio ad vitam, non esse meritorum nostrorum, sed misericordiae Divinae, qui decrevit nos eligere ex massa damnabili ad participationem vitae aeternae, atque meritis ornare.
english: Finally, this is the very sentence Augustine everywhere defends against the Pelagians: men are elected gratuitously and before all foresight of merits — not only to gifts of grace but also to the kingdom of glory — however they are brought there by the path of good works or merits, as the ancient Fathers usually speak. One place only: From the damnable mass of the human race God foresaw by mercy, not merits, those whom by election of grace he predestined to life (Contra Pelag. Hypognost. 6). So the foresight on which predestination to life rests is not of our merits but of divine mercy, who decreed to elect us from that damnable mass to share eternal life and to adorn us with merits.

source_text: Rat. 4. Aequum est ut statuamus Deum optimo modo homines ad gloriam designare: Sed optimus modus est ex praevisione meritorum id facere: sic enim decernitur tanquam corona Justitiae.
english: Rat. 4. It is fair to hold that God marks people out for glory in the best way. But that best way, they say, is to do it from foresight of merits — for so the decree is cast as a crown of justice.

source_text: Sol. Deum optimo modo omnia facere, nemo nisi pessimus audet negare: sed negamus tamen optimum modum eligendi homines ad vitam aeternam esse illum, qui nititur praescientia meritorum. Non est optimus, quia non optime facit ad illustrandam gloriam purae misericordiae Divinae erga electos. Nam tollit illud quod Augustinus passim inculcat, Detur totum Deo. Tollit etiam illud Cypriani, ab Augustino nunquam satis laudatum, In nullo gloriandum; quia nihil est nostrum.
english: Sol. That God does all things in the best way no one but the worst would deny — yet we deny that the best way of electing people to eternal life is the one that rests on foresight of merits. It is not best, because it does least to display the glory of God’s pure mercy toward the elect. It strips what Augustine everywhere presses: Let the whole be given to God. It also strips Cyprian’s line, which Augustine never praised enough: In nothing is one to glory, because nothing is ours.

source_text: Porro, non est optimus modus eligendi, quia hominem inflat superbia, dum supponit unumquemque suis operibus semet a non-electis discrevisse. Demum addo, tantum abest ut sit optimus, ut ne possibilis quidem sit in hoc statu peccati. In homine enim per peccatum corrupto nulla possunt praesciri merita ad vitam aeternam efficacia, nisi Deus gratuito illa dederit. Deus nulli dat talia, nisi cui decrevit dare ab aeterno. Nemini decrevit dare gratiam efficacem ad salutem, nisi illis quos praedestinavit ad salutem. A primo igitur ad ultimum, merita talium non possunt praevideri in nondum electis ad vitam aeternam: Non igitur ex praescientia meritorum praecedente ad vitam eliguntur.
english: Further, it is not the best mode of electing, because it puffs a person up with pride by assuming each has by his own works set himself apart from the non-elect. Finally: it is so far from best that it is not even possible in this state of sin. In a person corrupted by sin no merits efficacious for eternal life can be foreknown unless God has freely given them. God gives those only to whom he decreed from eternity to give. He decreed efficacious grace unto salvation only to those he predestined to salvation. From first to last, then, such merits cannot be foreseen in those not yet elected to eternal life — so they are not elected to life from a preceding foresight of merits.

source_text: Sed illud etiam adjungamus, Jesuitas hunc ab aliis Pontificiis diffidere; qui virginem Mariam, beatos Apostolos, aliosque eximie sanctos, ad gloriam absolute praedestinatos docent ante omnem praescientiam meritorum: Verisimile autem est optimos fuisse optimo modo praedestinatos. De illis igitur eximie sanctis sic scribit Valentia, Tales ante respectum Divinae praescientiae ad finalem eorum cooperationem, praedestinantur ad vitam aeternam, In 1. qu. 23. Sed linquamus Jesuitas compugnantes:
english: Add also: the Jesuits themselves diverge here from other Roman doctors, who teach that the virgin Mary, the blessed Apostles, and other eminently holy persons were absolutely predestined to glory before any foresight of merits — and it is likely the best were predestined in the best way. Of those eminently holy ones Valentia writes: such are predestined to eternal life before any regard of God’s foresight to their final cooperation (In 1. q. 23). But leave the Jesuits fighting one another:

source_text: et illud denique respondeamus, Eligi posse homines gratuito ad vitam aeternam, quamvis corona vitae aeternae decernatur electis imponenda, ut premium vitae laudabiliter justeque transactae. Nam voluntas Dei de modo perducendi ad premium per opera sanctitatis, non evertit gratuitam et misericordem electionem ad vitam aeternam ex proposito primario et beneplacito mero eligentis. Quando enim Deus decernit perducere aliquem ad gloriam per talia opera, primarium decretum dandi gloriam non oritur ex praevisione illorum operum, sed ex hoc decreto fluit voluntas dandi gratiam efficacem ad talia opera justitiae facienda. Illorum igitur praevisio electione posterior.
english: and finally: people can be elected gratuitously to eternal life even when the crown of eternal life is decreed to be set on the elect as the prize of a life lived laudably and justly. God’s will about the way of bringing them to that prize through holy works does not overturn gratuitous, merciful election to eternal life from the elector’s primary purpose and mere good pleasure. When God decrees to bring someone to glory through such works, the primary decree to give glory does not rise from foresight of those works — rather, from that decree flows the will to give efficacious grace for doing such works of justice. So foresight of them is after election.

source_text: Rat. 5. Si Deus ex meritis praevisis eligeret quosdam ad gloriam, aliis praeteritis, esset acceptor personarum. Nam electio justa et rationabilis disparitatem quandam inter electos et non-electos praesupponit; et prudens semper quod est melius eligit. Cum ergo nulla excogitari possit differentia inter homines absque hac praevisione meritorum in aliquibus, quae non praevidentur in aliis, consequens est ut dicamus, electionem Dei semper inniti hujusmodi praescientiae humanorum meritorum.
english: Rat. 5. If God elected some to glory from foresight of merits and passed others by, he would be an acceptor of persons. A just, rational election presupposes some disparity between elect and non-elect, and the prudent always chooses what is better. Since no difference among people can be imagined apart from foresight of merits in some that are not foreseen in others, it follows that God's election always rests on that kind of foresight of human merits.

source_text: Sol. Hoc argumentum ab antiquis Pelagianis urgeri solitum, patet ex Augustino multis in locis: Contra 2 Epist. Pelag. lib. 2. cap. 7. Et epist. 105. ad Sixtum, Hypogn. contra Pelag. lib. 6. et alibi. Quinetiam antesignanus Semipelagianorum Faustus Regiensis sic argumentatur lib. 2. cap. 4. Si ambo res sunt in natura, in isto justitia periclitabitur, qui sine merito indignus eligitur. Sed respondemus cum doctissimo Bannesio, Deum posse absque ulla injustitia, aut vitiosa personarum acceptione non modo ex duobus hominibus prorsus aequalibus unum eligere ad vitam aeternam, alio praeterito, sed etiam illum eligere quem praescivit pluribus et gravioribus peccatis implicandum, illo relicto quem praevidit pauciora et leviora admissurum, In 1. quest. 23. art. 5.
english: Sol. This argument was the old Pelagian press — Augustine shows it in many places (Contra 2 Epist. Pelag. 2.7; Ep. 105 to Sixtus; Hypogn. contra Pelag. 6; and elsewhere). Even Faustus of Riez, champion of the Semipelagians, argues (lib. 2.4): if both are equal in nature, justice is at risk when the one without merit is elected unworthy. We answer with Banez: without injustice or vicious respect of persons God can not only elect one of two wholly equal people to eternal life and pass the other by, but even elect the one he foresaw would be entangled in more and heavier sins, leaving the one he foresaw would commit fewer and lighter (In 1. q. 23 art. 5).

source_text: Hujus autem rei hanc rationem afferre licet, Quia Deus diligendo et eligendo facit eos digniores et meliores, quos diligit et eligit. Humana electio, quae facere non potest disparitatem dignitatis in rebus electis, tenetur tendere in illud objectum in quo praesupponitur major dignitas: sed ad Divinae electionis justitiam et sapientiam statuendam sufficit quod cum omnes homines sint indignissimi hoc electionis beneficio, Deus eligendo facit illos quos ad gloriam eligit prae aliis dignos et idoneos ad participandam sortem sanctorum in lumine, Coloss. i. 12.
english: The reason: by loving and electing, God makes those he loves and elects worthier and better. Human choice cannot create disparity of worth in what it chooses, so it must aim at the object where greater dignity is already assumed. For divine election's justice and wisdom it is enough that, though all people are most unworthy of this electing gift, God by electing makes those he elects to glory fit and worthy ahead of others to share the saints' lot in light (Colossians 1:12).

source_text: Hoc Thomas annotavit, Necesse est dicere quod Deus quosdam aliis magis amet. Nam cum amor Dei sit causa bonitatis rerum, non esset aliquid alio melius, si Deus non vellet uni majus bonum quam alteri. Part. I. qu. 20. art. 3. Et in commentariis ad Rom. cap. 9. Electio non respicit bonum in homine, sed facit. Quod ab Augustino didicit, qui contra Jul. Pelag. lib. 5. cap. 3. docet, Deum non elegisse quos praevidit dignos, sed eligendo effecisse dignos. Uterque hanc doctrinam hausit ab Apostolo, qui dicit, Deum elegisse nos ut sancti essemus; non quia sancti praevisi fuimus.
english: Thomas notes: we must say God loves some more than others — for God's love is the cause of things' goodness, and nothing would be better than another if he did not will a greater good to one than to another (ST I q.20 a.3). On Romans 9: election does not look to a good already in the person but makes it. He learned that from Augustine (Contra Jul. Pelag. 5.3): God did not elect those he foresaw as worthy, but by electing made them worthy. Both drew it from the Apostle: God elected us that we should be holy — not because we were foreseen holy.

source_text: Ad haec; injusta personarum acceptio locum non habet, ubi quis ex mera liberalitate de suo dat inaequaliter aequalibus, sed ubi, in dispensatione rerum debitarum, quis uni faveat prae altero, ex respectu ad aliquam personae circumstantiam quae est extra causam meriti: ut si Praelatus in collatione beneficii praeferat divitem aut consanguineum suum doctoribus et melioribus viris, est personarum acceptor, quia respicit circumstantias, quae nihil faciunt ad meritum vel dignitatem talis praemii. Jam vero Deus eligens ad regnum gloriae unum prae alio, non agit ex debito justitiae, sed ex dono munificentiae: neque respicit nobilitatem, divitias, ingenium, aut aliam qualitatem quamcunque extra rem, unde personarum nomen invenit; sed liberalitatem et bonitatem suam, juxta illud, Matth. xx. 15. Licet mihi quod volo facere de eo. Videte Augustinum, Epist. 106. et De bono persever. lib. 2. cap. 8. Et contr. 2. Epist. Pelag. cap. 3. lib. 2.
english: Further: unjust respect of persons has no place where someone from mere liberality gives unequally of what is his own to equals — only where, in dispensing what is owed, he favors one over another for a personal circumstance outside the cause of merit (as when a prelate, conferring a benefice, prefers a rich man or kinsman to better and more learned men: that is respect of persons, because those circumstances do nothing for the merit or dignity of such a prize). God electing one to the kingdom of glory ahead of another does not act from a debt of justice but from a gift of munificence; he does not regard nobility, riches, talent, or any quality outside the matter that earns the name "respect of persons," but his own liberality and goodness — Matthew 20:15: Is it lawful for me to do what I will with my own? See Augustine, Ep. 106; De bono persever. 2.8; Contra 2 Epist. Pelag. 2.3.

source_text: Rat. 6. In omnibus operibus Dei misericordia concurrit cum justitia: Ergo ponere debemus ex parte electi aliquam convenientiam sive congruitatem, quae non fuit ex parte reprobi; secus nullum justitiae vestigium in hac Dei electione apparebit: Et quod elegit ex praevisione, et non ex mero beneplacito voluntatis suae. Est argumentum Javelli in Quaestionibus adjunctis primae parti Aquinatis.
english: Rat. 6. In all God's works mercy concurs with justice — so, they say, we must posit on the elect's side some fittingness or congruity that was not on the reprobate's; otherwise no trace of justice will show in this election of God — and that he elects from foresight, not from the mere good pleasure of his will. So argues Javellus in the Questions annexed to Aquinas's Prima Pars.

source_text: Sol. Sed respondeo; Si justitiam aliam Javellus intelligat, praeter illam quae sita est in hoc, quod Deus agat prout convenit bonitati suae et fidelitati, nego justitiam reperiri in omnibus illis actionibus, in quibus miseris hominibus facit benigne. Cum igitur Javellus ita justitiam Dei intelligat, ut juste agere inde dicatur, quod in beneficio electionis respiciat ad aliquod meritum congruum hominis; hoc sensu, justitiam concurrere cum misericordia in omni actione erga homines, dico non solummodo esse, sed impossibile.
english: Sol. I answer: if Javellus means some justice other than that God acts as befits his own goodness and faithfulness, I deny that justice is found in every act where he deals kindly with wretched people. And if he so takes God's justice that acting justly means, in the gift of election, looking to some congruent human merit — then, in that sense, justice concurring with mercy in every dealing with people is not only false but impossible.

source_text: Nam, ut optime Aquinas Part. I. qu. 21. art. 4, Omne opus Divinae justitiae semper praesupponit opus misericordiae, in quo fundatum sit. Nil igitur procedere velimus in infinitum, deveniamus necesse est ad aliquod primum, quod ex sola misericordia et bonitate Divinae voluntatis dependet. Hoc autem quid aliud esse potest, quam gratuita illa adoptio et destinatio electorum ad vitam aeternam?
english: For as Aquinas puts it best (ST I q.21 a.4): every work of divine justice always presupposes a work of mercy on which it is founded. So we must not run to infinity — we have to arrive at some first thing that depends on the mercy and goodness of the divine will alone. And what else can that be than the gratuitous adoption and destination of the elect to eternal life?

source_text: Ad hoc igitur primum beneficium, ut appareat in eo ratio quaedam justitiae, non debemus requirere praevisam aliquam congruentiam in electis: sed eatenus hoc justum est, quatenus convenit voluntati et bonitati Divinae sic agere velle, juxta illud, Miserebor cujus misertus fuero; non autem, Miserebor illorum in quibus, ut hoc juste simul faciam, merita quaedam congrua praevidero.
english: So for this first benefit, if some reason of justice is to appear in it, we must not require a foreseen congruity in the elect. It is just insofar as it befits the divine will and goodness to will to act so — according to I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy — not I will have mercy on those in whom, that I may do this justly at once, I shall have foreseen certain congruent merits.

source_text: Rat. 7. Si Deus praedestinaret ad gloriam ex mero beneplacito voluntatis suae, et non ex praevisione operum, tum omnes ex aequo praedestinaret, quia omnes aeque dispositi sunt ad illud donum recipiendum. Nam si Deus non eligat homines quatenus praevidentur ut bene operantes, et in bonis operibus perseverantes, consequens est ut eligantur quatenus praesciuntur esse homines, vel peccatores: at hoc omnibus convenit; omnes ergo eligerentur. Habetur hoc argumentum apud Gregorium de Valentia, In 1. qu. 23.
english: Rat. 7. If God predestined to glory from the mere good pleasure of his will and not from foresight of works, then he would predestine all alike, because all are equally disposed to receive that gift. For if he does not elect people as foreseen working well and persevering in good works, they must be elected as foreknown to be human beings or sinners — which belongs to all; so all would be elected. So argues Gregory of Valencia (In 1. q. 23).

source_text: Sol. Vacillat Majoris consequentia. Neque enim sequitur, ut in quibus Deus agit ex mero suo beneplacito, semper aequaliter agere cum aequalibus teneatur: Imo e contra, quia agit ex beneplacito, potest discrimen facere in collatione suorum beneficiorum ubi nullum fuit discrimen in qualitatibus aut statu personarum. Quod autem affertur primo in loco ad confirmationem Majoris, scilicet Exclusa praescientia operum, omnes esse aeque dispositos ad donum electionis recipiendum, falso et imperite a Gregorio asseritur. Dicere debuisset omnes esse prorsus indispositos ad gloriam recipiendam, atque dispositos ad poenas gehennae subeundas. Quae enim dispositio, ut eligatur ad gloriam, in illo reperitur, qui naturae irae filius, et labe originali contaminatus consideratur?
english: Sol. The Major's consequence fails. It does not follow that wherever God acts from mere good pleasure he must always deal equally with equals — on the contrary, because he acts from good pleasure he can discriminate in conferring his gifts where there was no difference in persons' qualities or state. And Gregory's first support for the Major — that with foresight of works excluded all are equally disposed to receive election — is false and unskillful. He should have said all are wholly undisposed to receive glory and disposed to undergo hell's pains. What disposition for election to glory is found in one reckoned a child of wrath by nature, stained with original corruption?

source_text: Sicuti ergo inepta esset haec argumentatio, Si Christus in terris agens mortuum Lazarum resuscitavit ad vitam ex mero beneplacito voluntatis suae, et non ex praevisione alicujus cooperationis ex parte Lazari, tum omnes mortuos ex aequo resuscitasset, quia omnes aeque dispositi fuerant ad hoc donum resuscitationis recipiendum; sic etiam et prior illa Gregorii invalida et inepta est; quia supponit obligationem in Deo, ut quoties agit ex beneplacito, agat pariter cum paribus; et quia ponit communem dispositionem in hominibus ad recipiendum donum electionis, qui sunt communiter dispositi ad recipiendam poenam damnationis.
english: Just as it would be inept to argue: if Christ on earth raised dead Lazarus from mere good pleasure of his will, not from foresight of any cooperation on Lazarus's part, then he would have raised all the dead alike, because all were equally disposed to receive that gift of raising — so Gregory's prior argument is invalid and inept. It assumes God is bound, whenever he acts from good pleasure, to deal alike with equals; and it posits a common disposition to receive election in people who are commonly disposed to receive damnation's punishment.

source_text: Quod autem attinet ad posteriorem partem confirmationis, ubi colligit Gregorius, Si homines non eligantur ad gloriam quatenus praevisi sunt bene operantes, tum electi sunt quatenus praesciuntur homines, vel quatenus peccatores; quod cum omnibus convenit, electio etiam omnibus conveniret; haec etiam argumentatio frivola est. Nam cum recte Philosophi statuunt, Quod convenit rei quatenus tali, convenit omni tali, certum est electionem Dei non cadere in hominem quatenus hominem, neque in peccatorem quatenus peccatorem, quia ex eventu liquet, non omnibus hominibus, neque omnibus peccatoribus contingere ut eligantur. Negamus ergo illam distinctionem, Aut Deus eligit homines quatenus praevidentur cooperaturi gratiae suae, aut quatenus praesciuntur ut homines vel peccatores, et dicimus Deum eligere homines quatenus sibi prae aliis fuerunt gratis dilecti. Siquis porro quaerat, Cur hi prae aliis gratis dilecti? ridicula quaestio est: nam prima causa voluntatis Divinae in diffusione suorum bonorum, est ipsa voluntas; cujus ulterior causa non est indaganda. Non male Aquinas; Part. 1. qu. 23. art. 4. Praedestinatio aliquorum in salutem aeternam praesupponit secundum rationem quod Deus velit eorum salutem. Ad quod pertinet Electio et Dilectio: Dilectio quidem, in quantum vult eis hoc bonum salutis aeternae; Electio autem, in quantum hoc bonum eis vult prae aliis. Et haec voluntas Dei qua vult bonum alicui diligendo, est causa quod illud bonum ab eo prae aliis habeatur. Et sic patet, quod Dilectio praesupponitur Electioni, et Electio praedestinationi. Hactenus ille.
english: As for Gregory's second support — if people are not elected to glory as foreseen working well, then they are elected as foreknown humans or as sinners, and since that belongs to all, election would belong to all — that too is frivolous.
