Philosophers rightly hold that what belongs to a thing as such belongs to every such; yet God's election does not fall on a person as human, nor on a sinner as sinner, because the event shows not all humans and not all sinners are elected. So we deny the fork Either God elects as foreseen cooperators with his grace, or as foreknown humans/sinners — and say he elects people as freely loved by him ahead of others. Why these freely loved ahead of others? A ridiculous question: the first cause of the divine will in pouring out its goods is the will itself; no further cause is to be hunted. Aquinas is not wrong (ST I q.23 a.4): predestination of some to eternal salvation presupposes that God wills their salvation. To that belong Love and Election: Love, inasmuch as he wills them this good of eternal salvation; Election, inasmuch as he wills them that good ahead of others. And that willing-by-loving is why they have the good from him ahead of others. So Love is presupposed to Election, and Election to predestination. So far Aquinas.

source_text: Ex quibus videtis, non praescientiam humanae cooperationis, sed gratuitum affectum Dei solummodo praesupponi ut antecedens ad electionem et praedestinationem singularum personarum. Quod Apostolus illustravit in illo celeberrimo exemplo Jacobi et Esavi, quod proponitur Rom. ix. 12. Et etiam disertis verbis expressit Ephes. i. 5. Qui praedestinavit nos, quos adoptaret in filios per Jesum Christum in sese, pro beneplacito affatus voluntatis suae. Atque hic huic argumento factum est satis.
english: From this you see: not foresight of human cooperation, but God's gratuitous affection alone is presupposed as antecedent to the election and predestination of particular persons. The Apostle illustrated it in that famous example of Jacob and Esau (Romans 9:12), and said it in plain words in Ephesians 1:5: who predestined us to adoption as sons through Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his will. And here enough for this argument.

source_text: Rat. 8. Si Deus absque operum nostrorum praescientia praedestinaret, majorem saltem partem hominum praedestinasset ad vitam, cum sit natura bonus, et misericordia ejus sit super omnia opera ejus: At pauci sunt qui salvantur: Ergo non praedestinat Deus nisi secundum praevisionem operum sive boni aut mali usus liberi arbitrii.
english: Rat. 8. Without foresight of our works, they argue, a God good by nature — whose mercy is over all his works — would have marked at least most of humankind for life. Yet few are saved. So predestination must track foresight of works, that is of free choice used well or badly.

source_text: Sol. Ex eo quod Deus sit natura bonus, recte infertur, illum velle bonum omni suae creaturae; sed non recte, illum velle quodvis bonum cuivis creaturae, aut aequalia et eadem bona aequalibus creaturis. Nec in Naturae quidem aut Fortunae falso dictis bonis dispensandis tenetur Deus aut haec dispensare ex praeviso bono usu eorum, aut ea majori parti hominum impertire. Videmus siquidem neque robur corporis, neque acumen mentis, neque formae venustatem, neque divitiarum affluentiam dari ex boni usus praescientia. Nam, ut plurimum, dantur illis, qui hisce omnibus pessime abutuntur, ad injuriam, ad fraudem, ad libidinem, ad luxuriam. Haec tamen ipsa bona non nisi paucis conceduntur.
english: Sol. From God's being good by nature it rightly follows that he wills some good to every creature of his — not that he wills every good to every creature, or the same equal goods to equal creatures. Even in dispensing so-called goods of Nature or Fortune he is not bound to give them from foresight of good use, nor to impart them to the majority. We see strength of body, sharpness of mind, beauty of form, and abundance of riches are not given from foresight of good use — for the most part they go to those who abuse them worst: to injury, fraud, lust, luxury. And even those goods are granted only to few.

source_text: Porro, illud quoque observandum nos loqui de electione eorum ad vitam, qui sunt omnes morte aeterna dignissimi. Quamvis igitur admittamus Deum ex bonitate suae naturae velle omnibus hominibus, quatenus considerantur ante lapsum justitia et sanctitate ornati, donum illud aeternae vitae; nulla tamen ratio cogit ut dicamus, ex hominibus corruptis et in massa damnabili obrutis, Deum pro bonitate sua debere vel omnes, vel majorem partem eligere ad gloriam.
english: Further: we are speaking of election to life of people who are all most worthy of eternal death. We may grant that from the goodness of his nature God wills the gift of eternal life to all humans as considered before the fall, adorned with justice and holiness — yet no reason forces us to say that, from humans corrupted and sunk in the damnable mass, his goodness obliges him to elect either all or the greater part to glory.

source_text: Ad extremum, quod urgetur, misericordiam ejus esse super omnia opera ejus, ad rem non facit. Nam primo, potest Deus misericordiam exhibere omni homini (quod revera facit) et tamen non hanc specialem et eximiam misericordiam, ut illum adoptet in haeredem vitae aeternae. Secundo, magnitudo misericordiae Divinae non pensanda est ex multitudine individuorum quibus impertitur, sed ex magnitudine beneficiorum quae hominibus impertiuntur, et indignitate illorum quibus impertiuntur. Nam quod Deus ex inimicis suis, peccati labe contaminatissimis, et aeterna morte dignissimis, per mortem dilectissimi sui filii, quantumvis paucos voluerit liberare, et regno caelesti destinare, illustrius est specimen misericordiae, quam justitiae illud, quod totum mundum improbum relinquat merito exitio.
english: Finally, the press that his mercy is over all his works misses the point. First, God can show mercy to every person (and he does) without that special, outstanding mercy of adopting them as heir of eternal life. Second, the greatness of divine mercy is not weighed by how many individuals receive it, but by the greatness of the benefits given and the unworthiness of those who receive them. That God from his enemies — most stained with sin and most worthy of eternal death — through the death of his most beloved Son has willed to free even a few and destine them to the heavenly kingdom is a more illustrious specimen of mercy than the justice of leaving the whole wicked world to deserved ruin.

source_text: Postremo, cur Deus qui posset omnes, paucos tamen prae multitudine rejectorum voluerit ad vitam praedestinare, duae rationes ab Augustino afferuntur, ut minime opus sit ad praescientiam bonorum et malorum operum confugere. Sic igitur ille, Hoc voluit Deus, ut ipsa rejectorum multitudine ostenderetur, quam nullius momenti sit apud Deum justum quantalibet numerositas justissime damnatorum: Atque ut suaderet ut hinc intelligant qui ex ipsa damnatione redimuntur, hoc fuisse debitum massae illi universae, quod tam magnae parti ejus redditum cernerent, Epist. 190.
english: Finally: why God, who could save all, yet willed to predestine few to life against the multitude of the rejected — Augustine gives two reasons, so there is little need to take refuge in foresight of good and bad works. Thus he: God willed this, that by the very multitude of the rejected it might be shown how little moment any number of those most justly damned has with the just God — and that those redeemed from that damnation might understand from this that what they see rendered to so great a part of it was due to that universal mass (Epist. 190).

source_text: Rat. 9. Quorum gloria dependet ex peccatis aliorum, iis non potest decerni nisi ex praevisione: ut verbi causa, quia gloria Stephani aliquo modo pendebat ex impietate Judaeorum qui illum erant lapidaturi, non potuit Deus gloriam illi decernere, saltem non in eo gradu quo tam glorioso martyrio danda fuit, nisi praeviso peccato quod occasionem praebebat ejus martyrio, et simul praevisa ejus patientia et fide quibus mediantibus ex illorum crudelitate eximiam martyrii gloriam sibi acquirebat. Si non omnibus ergo, at aliquibus saltem destinatur gloria ex praescientia meritorum.
english: Rat. 9. Where someone's glory hangs on others' sins, they say it cannot be decreed except from foresight. Take Stephen: his glory somehow depended on the impiety of the Jews who would stone him — so God could not decree him glory, at least not in the degree that so glorious a martyrdom would give, unless that sin (which occasioned the martyrdom) was foreseen, and with it his patience and faith, by which he won outstanding martyr's glory from their cruelty. So if not to all, at least to some glory is destined from foresight of merits.

source_text: Sol. Aliud est considerare gloriam ante jacta mundi fundamenta electis destinatam secundum Dei intentionem, aliud considerare eandem ipsis in tempore collatam per ejusdem decreti exsecutionem. In ipsa Dei intentione praedestinata fuit gloria, et tanta gloria Stephano, ante praescientiam patientiae et fidei ejus: Imo in praedestinationis decreto tantam fidem et patientiam Deus illi praeparaverat, quia ad tantam gloriam illum elegerat.
english: Sol. One thing is glory destined to the elect before the world's foundations, according to God's intention; another is that same glory conferred on them in time by executing the decree. In God's intention itself glory — and so great a glory — was predestined to Stephen before foresight of his patience and faith. Indeed, in the decree of predestination God had prepared him that faith and patience because he had elected him to that glory.

source_text: Sed in exsecutione hujus decreti Deus praevidebat Judaeorum crudelitatem, ipso permitente, martyrii occasionem Stephano praebituram. Praevidebat simul Stephanum tanta fide et constantia armatum cupide et libenter pro Christo moriturum. Praevidebat denique se, post certamen hoc tam praeclare certatum, eximiam coronam gloriae huic fortissimo militi donaturum.
english: But in executing that decree God foresaw the Jews' cruelty — which he permitted — that would give Stephen occasion for martyrdom. He foresaw Stephen, armed with such faith and constancy, about to die eagerly and willingly for Christ. And he foresaw himself, after that fight so nobly fought, about to give this bravest soldier an outstanding crown of glory.

source_text: Praevisa igitur fuit fides et patientia Stephani ut antecedens ipsam coronae adeptionem; sed non fuit praevisa ut antecedens hujus coronae destinationem. Nam praescientia Divina de illa gratiae mensura quam largitus est Stephano, quamque ille exercuit tam gloriose, fundata fuit in praecedente decreto electionis; et non ipsum decretum electionis ad tantam gloriam, in praescientia fidei, quam accepturus a Deo et in certamine postmodum exseruit, fuit.
english: So Stephen's faith and patience were foreseen as going before his actually receiving the crown — not as going before the destinating of that crown. Divine foresight of the measure of grace God gave him, and which he exercised so gloriously, rested on the prior decree of election; the decree electing him to that glory did not rest on foresight of the faith he would receive from God and later show in the fight.

source_text: Falsum ergo fuit quod in argumento assumptum erat, nempe, non posse eam gloriam, quae aliquo modo dependet ex peccatis aliorum, decerni nisi ex tali praescientia. Decerni enim vel destinari potest, quamvis non conferri, nisi hujusmodi praescientia praeeunte.
english: So the argument's assumption was false — that glory which somehow depends on others' sins cannot be decreed except from such foresight. It can be decreed or destined without that; it is only the conferring that cannot happen unless foresight of that sort goes first.

source_text: Rat. 10. Si Deus non habens rationem meritorum, ex solo suo beneplacito decrevisset singulares personas, puta Paulum et Petrum, beare, cum bona opera nihil prorsus operarentur ad gloriam consequendam, Fac igitur Petrum in bonis operibus ambulare, tamen gloria non tribuetur illi ex ullo merito ad talia opera: fac eum bona opera prorsus negligere, Deus tamen virtute beneplaciti sui dabit illi gloriam destinatam: At hoc est valde absurdum, et propendet in errorem Praedestinatorum, quos Sigebertus in Chronico suo ostendit docuisse, Pie viventibus non prodesse bona opera ad gloriam, si Praedestinati non sint; flagitiose viventibus non obesse ulla scelera, si sint ex praedestinatis.
english: Rat. 10. If God, ignoring merits, had from mere good pleasure decreed to bless particular persons — say Paul and Peter — then good works would do nothing toward obtaining glory. So let Peter walk in good works: still glory is not credited to him from any desert of those works. Let him neglect good works entirely: God will still give him the destined glory by the force of his good pleasure. That is highly absurd, and leans toward the Predestinarian error Sigebert's Chronicle reports: pious living's good works do not help toward glory if one is not predestinated; flagrant living's crimes do not hurt if one is.

source_text: Hoc argumentum urgetur a Gregorio de Valencia. Vasques etiam eodem argumento utitur. Quinetiam antiqui Pelagiani Catholicos hoc argumento oppugnabant: Sic enim Faustus Regiensis, Praedestinatis ad vitam necessaria non erit oratio; deputatis ad mortem prodesse non poterit: in istis supervacua, in illis infirma judicabitur; lib. 1. De lib. arb. c. 4. Quod de oratione, id de caeteris omnibus bonis operibus eadem argumentandi formula concludi potuit, esse nimirum supervacua, posito antecedente et gratuito decreto electionis Divinae. Electio igitur ponenda ex praescientia operum.
english: Gregory of Valencia presses this; Vasquez uses it too. Even the old Pelagians turned it on the Catholics — so Faustus of Riez (De lib. arb. 1.4): for those predestined to life prayer will not be necessary; for those appointed to death it cannot help — superfluous in the one case, powerless in the other. What they say of prayer they could conclude of every other good work: superfluous once an antecedent, gratuitous decree of divine election is posited. Therefore election must be set on foresight of works.

source_text: Sol. Consequentia praedictae argumentationis plane nulla est. Nam quamvis recte statuamus decretum dandi gloriam esse gratuitum, atque esse etiam prius, secundum nostrum intelligendi modum, quam decretum dandi gratiam, aut bona opera, quia illud praestituit finem, hoc media ad finem ordinat; tamen recte negamus gratiam Dei aut opera bona, quae sunt effecta gratiae, nihil operari ad gloriae consecutionem. Ratio in promptu est: Quia quando ponimus absolutum et efficax Dei decretum de quocunque eventu futuro, intelligimus simul Deum propter hanc intentionem adimplendam velle adhibere et applicare illa media, quibus tale effectum producatur. In antecedente ergo decreto dandi gloriam, virtualiter includitur consequens decretum dandi bona opera caeteraque media quae via sunt ad regnum gloriae. Operantur itaque haec media ad finis consecutionem isto modo, licet huic personae singulari finis non fuerit destinatus ex antecedente illorum praevisione. Facito ut appositione exempli hoc magis illucescat: Sumatur Deum antecedente decreto, et gratuito praestituisse magnam frugum ubertatem anno insequente nobis donare: Si quis hinc inferat, Ergo nihil bona aeris temperies, nihil tempestivae pluviae, nihil labor agricolarum operabuntur ad hanc ubertatem efficiendam, ridicule concluserit; quia in illo priori decreto de dando fructu non excluditur voluntas exsequendi per media, sed ut ab eo dependens includitur.
english: Sol. That argumentation's consequence is plainly none. We rightly hold the decree to give glory gratuitous, and prior (in our way of understanding) to the decree to give grace or good works — because the first sets the end, the second orders means to the end — yet we deny that God's grace or the good works that are grace's effects do nothing toward obtaining glory. The reason is ready: an absolute, efficacious decree of any future event already means God wills to employ and apply the means that produce that effect. So in the antecedent decree to give glory is virtually included the consequent decree to give good works and the other means that are the way to glory's kingdom. Those means therefore work toward obtaining the end this way, even if for this particular person the end was not destined from prior foresight of them. Take an example: suppose God by an antecedent, gratuitous decree had set to give us a great harvest next year. To infer Therefore neither fair weather, nor seasonable rains, nor farmers' labor will do anything toward that abundance is ridiculous — for in that prior decree to give the fruit the will to execute through means is not shut out but included as depending on it.

source_text: Idem prorsus cogitandum de absoluto et efficaci decreto quoad Petri glorificationem, et de mediis gratiae bonorumque operum per quae ad gloriam perducetur. Vide hoc doctissimus Bannes, et hujusmodi consequentias explosit: In istis consequentiis, inquit, ex prioritate nostrae rationis quantum ad modum intelligendi in uno genere causae, colligitur absque ulla apparentia prioritas realis in ipsis rebus, vel Independentia unius rei ab altera secundum ordinem statutum a Deo: sicuti quis diceret, Prius a Deo volita est forma quam materia, ergo etiamsi non esset futura materia, fieret forma. Haec ille, In 1. qu. 23. art. 2. Par illorum stultitia qui argumentantur: Si prius Petro volita sit gloria quam gratia, aut quam praevisa sunt bona opera quae fluunt ex gratia, tum etiamsi Petrus maneret expers gratiae et bonorum operum, gloriam tamen consequeretur. Apage has ineptias! Nam licet Deus non velit gloriam huic singulari homini ex intuitu antecedente operum ejus, sed ex beneplacito voluntatis suae gratuito, vult tamen illi gloriam cum intuitu bonae operationis futurae, tanquam modi necessarii, per quem ipse Deus ordinavit ut ad hunc finem obtinendum homo procederet.
english: Think the same of the absolute, efficacious decree for Peter's glorification, and of the means of grace and good works by which he is brought to glory. Báñez saw this and exploded such consequences (In 1. q.23 a.2): from a priority in our way of understanding one kind of cause, people infer without any show a real priority in the things themselves, or independence of one from another in the order God set — as if: Form was willed by God before matter, therefore form would come to be even if matter never would. Equal folly: If glory was willed to Peter before grace, or before foresight of the good works that flow from grace, then even if Peter stayed devoid of grace and good works he would still get glory. Away with that nonsense! Though God does not will glory to this particular person from prior intuition of his works, but from the gratuitous good pleasure of his will, he still wills him glory with intuition of future good working as the necessary mode by which God ordained that the person proceed to that end.

source_text: Praedestinatorum igitur haeresis nihil ad nos, qui pleno ore docemus opera pietatis prodesse ad consecutionem gloriae; Flagitia etiam praedestinatis ipsis ita obstare, ut nisi per poenitentiam et vitae novitatem abjicerentur, non possent ad regnum gloriae pervenire. Sed idem caelestis Pater, qui gratuito illis gloriam destinavit, hanc poenitentiam et vitae novitatem infallibiliter etiam iisdem praeparavit.
english: So the Predestinarian heresy is nothing to us — we teach outright that works of piety profit toward obtaining glory, and that crimes block even the predestinated so that, unless cast off by repentance and newness of life, they cannot reach the kingdom of glory. Yet the same heavenly Father who gratuitously destined them glory has also infallibly prepared for them that repentance and newness of life.

source_text: Deus non rejicit nisi ex praevisione peccati: Nam rejectio sive reprobatio est opus justitiae Divinae, quod semper supponit hominem peccato inquinatum. Non igitur eligit nisi ex praescientia bonorum operum; quoniam qui non est rejectus, hoc ipso est electus.
english: God rejects only from foresight of sin — for rejection or reprobation is a work of divine justice, which always presupposes a person stained with sin. Therefore he elects only from foresight of good works, since whoever is not rejected is by that very fact elected.

source_text: Sol. Revocandum est in memoriam, quod de duplici actu reprobationis in Prolegomenis dictum fuit; nimirum, Reprobationem duos hosce actus involvere: unum negativum, quem appellare licet Praeteritionem sive non-electionem; alterum affirmativum, quem vocare possumus praedamnationem, sive Deputationem ad poenam: Respondeo igitur, si per reprobationem prior ille actus intelligatur, quamvis supponamus peccatum in subjecto reprobato, tamen non debemus cogitare Deum ex intuitu peccati hujus decrevisse apud se non eligere aut non liberare hanc personam singularem. Nam idem peccatum in illis etiam intuitus est, quos voluit eligere et liberare.
english: Sol. Recall what the Prolegomena said of reprobation's twofold act: a negative act — Passing-by or non-election — and an affirmative — praedamnation, or deputing to punishment. If reprobation means that prior act, we may grant sin in the reprobated subject, yet we must not think God from intuition of that sin decreed not to elect or not to free this particular person. He looked on the same sin in those he willed to elect and free.

source_text: Verum si per reprobationem intelligatur actus praedamnandi, sive deputandi ad interitum, lubens agnosco hunc actum Divinum inniti praescientiae peccati humani. Sed tum dico non esse paris rationis electionem ad gloriam, et deputationem ad poenam: Nam Deus potest immerentem destinare ad gloriam ex mero beneplacito voluntatis suae, quia bonus est, sed non potest immerentem destinare ad poenam absque intuitu peccati, quia justus est. Observavit hoc discrimen Augustinus advers. Julian. lib. 3. cap. 18. Bonus est Deus, justus est Deus: potest sine bonis meritis liberare, quia bonus est; non potest sine malis meritis damnare, quia justus est.
english: But if reprobation means praedamning — deputing to destruction — I gladly grant that divine act rests on foresight of human sin. Election to glory and deputation to punishment are not on equal footing: God can destine the undeserving to glory from mere good pleasure, because he is good; he cannot destine the undeserving to punishment without intuition of sin, because he is just. Augustine marked that difference (Contra Jul. 3.18): God is good, God is just — he can free without good merits because he is good; he cannot damn without evil merits because he is just.

source_text: Illustremus hoc quod dictum est hujusmodi exemplo: Sumamus duos homines latrocinii, aut proditionis in Principem suum reos: Utrumque igitur ut ex aequo nocentem Princeps intuetur: vult tamen unum ex iis morte capitis afficere; vult alterum non modo a supplicio absolvere, sed in famulitium suum adsciscere, et honoribus eximiis cumulare. Hic siquis argutetur, Rex horum unum damnavit ex intuitu sceleris commissi, quia nempe et latro fuit et proditor, ergo alterum elegit ad honores ex intuitu innocentiae sive virtutis, quia scilicet bonus et justus erat; falso et ridicule concluserit. Perinde ergo et illi falluntur, qui ab intuitu peccati in voluntate damnandi arguunt ad intuitum meritorum in voluntate liberandi, et ad gloriam eligendi.
english: Illustrate it so: take two men guilty of robbery or treason against their prince. The prince sees each as equally harmful — yet he wills to put one to death, and the other not only to free from punishment but to take into his household and heap with high honors. If someone argues The king condemned one from intuition of the crime (robber and traitor), therefore he elected the other to honors from intuition of innocence or virtue — that conclusion is false and ridiculous. So too are they deceived who from intuition of sin in the will to damn argue to intuition of merits in the will to free and elect to glory.

source_text: Porro, et illud adjiciam: Si quaeratur, Cur miser iste sententiam mortis subiit? recte respondetur, Quia latro et proditor erat. At si quaeratur, Cur noluit Rex perinde illi ignoscere atque alteri qui in eadem causa fuit? cur non iisdem honoribus afficere? Hic non possumus nisi inepte respondere, Quia latrocinii et laesae majestatis reus erat; sic enim et ille alter quem cogitatione informavimus. Sed respondendum est, Quia visum est Regi pro suo beneplacito alterius misereri, alterius non misereri. Hujus autem discriminis ratio latet in scrinio Regii pectoris, non fundatur in personarum diversis meritis. Obsigno hanc responsionem illo Augustini dicto, Cur istum potius quam illum liberet, an non liberet, scrutetur, qui potest, judiciorum ejus tam magnum profundum, veruntamen caveat praecipitium; Epist. 190. Sed cum ad alteram thesin nostram, De Reprobatione, ventum fuerit, haec explicabimus magis enucleate.
english: Add this: ask why the wretched man suffered death — rightly, Because he was robber and traitor. Ask why the king would not pardon him as he did the other in the same case, or heap the same honors on him — here to answer Because he was guilty of robbery and treason is inept (so was the other we imagined). The answer is: it seemed good to the king, of his good pleasure, to pity the one and not the other. The reason of that discrimination lies in the king's breast, not in diverse merits. I seal it with Augustine (Epist. 190): why he frees this one rather than that, or does not free — let whoever can sound that great depth of his judgments, yet beware the precipice. When we reach our other thesis, On Reprobation, we will unpack this more clearly.

source_text: Rat. 12. Si ponamus Deum efficaciter eligere quosdam ad gloriam ex mero beneplacito voluntatis suae, et non ex praescientia meritorum, tolletur plane liberum arbitrium. Nam cum nemo potest resistere efficaci voluntati Dei, non manebit in eorum libera potestate gloriam amittere, qui hoc modo sunt ad gloriam praedestinati. Posita itaque tali antecedente voluntate Dei de salute Petri et Pauli, aut erit in illis absoluta necessitas operandi ea quae sunt necessaria ad salutem, puta credendi, pie vivendi, in fide et pietate perseverandi, atque adeo perveniendi ad ipsam salutem, aut Dei decretum efficax potest fieri irritum. Utrumque absurdum et impossibile. Ergo non debemus ponere electionem aliquorum efficacem ad gloriam, nisi ex praescientia meritorum quae orientur ex libero arbitrio per gratiam Dei praevento.
english: Rat. 12. If God efficaciously elects some to glory from mere good pleasure of his will, not from foresight of merits, free choice is plainly destroyed. No one can resist God's efficacious will — so those so predestined to glory will not keep free power to lose it. Posit that antecedent will for the salvation of Peter and Paul: either they are under absolute necessity to do what salvation requires (believe, live piously, persevere in faith and piety, and so arrive at salvation), or God's efficacious decree can be made void. Both absurd and impossible. Therefore we must not posit efficacious election of some to glory except from foresight of merits that will arise from free choice preceded by God's grace.

source_text: Sol. Antiqua fuit Pelagianorum cantilena, eos fatum inducere et liberum arbitrium perimere, qui statuunt absolutam et efficacem certorum hominum praedestinationem ante praescientiam meritorum. Id videre licet apud Prosperum, qui scribit Pelagianos infamasse Augustinum, dicentes Eum liberum arbitrium penitus submovere, et sub gratiae nomine necessitatem praedicare fatalem, De lib. arbit. pag. 223. Eadem objectio occurrit etiam in Responsionibus ejusdem ad capitula Gallorum Obj. 6. Porro Faustus Regiensis Semipelagianorum coryphaeus oblique perstringit Augustinum, et appellat liberi arbitrii interemtorem, qui omnia alterutram partem ex praedestinatione statuta et definita esse pronunciat, De lib. arbit. lib. 1. sect. 11. Atque dicit sub gratiae vocabulum absconditum esse ab illo fatale decretum, ibidem. Postremo, ipse Augustinus multis in locis cogitur hanc iniquissimam calumniam eluere: Contra 2 Epist. Pelag. lib. 2. cap. 7. et De bono persever. lib. 2. cap. 12. et alibi passim. Haec praemittere volui responsioni nostrae, ut ex quorum lacunis omnia fere adversariorum argumenta hauriantur intelligatis.
english: Sol. An old Pelagian refrain: those who hold absolute, efficacious predestination of certain people before foresight of merits induce fate and destroy free choice. Prosper records Pelagians defaming Augustine as utterly removing free choice and preaching fatal necessity under the name of grace (De lib. arb. p. 223). The same charge is in his Responses to the Gallic chapters, Obj. 6. Faustus of Riez, Semipelagian champion, obliquely strikes Augustine as destroyer of free choice for saying everything on either side is fixed by predestination (De lib. arb. 1.11), and claims a fatal decree is hidden under the word grace. Augustine himself must often wash off that foul calumny (Contra 2 Epist. Pelag. 2.7; De bono persever. 2.12; and elsewhere). I premise this so you see from whose cisterns almost all the adversaries' arguments are drawn.

source_text: Jam ad rem. Nego posita antecedente Dei voluntate de danda Petro aeterna salute, tolli aut impediri liberum ejus arbitrium circa salutis consecutionem: et tamen illud simul assero, non posse illum, posita hac hypothesi, a salute excidere, ac per consequens, Divinum decretum non posse fieri irritum. Quod ad prius; Efficax Dei voluntas non modo operatur omnia quae vult Deus, sed eo modo, et per illa media quae vult. Ex efficaci igitur et antecedente proposito salvandi Petrum, non tenetur Deus uti mediis coactivis, aut necessitantibus voluntatem humanam, sed sufficit ut utatur illis, quae sapientia Divina novit efficaciter, infallibiliter, et tamen libere posse movere, et flectere ejus voluntatem. Imo et hoc etiam addo, Dum Deus ex antecedente decreto dandae salutis movet liberum arbitrium electorum ad salutem acquirendam, tantum abest ut inde amittatur, ut potius augeatur et roboretur humanae voluntatis libertas. Nam ut optime Bannes, In 1. qu. 22. art. 4, Liberum creaturae arbitrium accipit libertatem participatam ex Divino libero arbitrio, movente illud fortiter et suaviter juxta modum suae naturae.
english: Now to the point. I deny that God's antecedent will to give Peter eternal salvation takes away or hinders his free choice about obtaining it — and yet I affirm that, on that hypothesis, he cannot fall from salvation, so the divine decree cannot be made void. First: God's efficacious will works all he wills, but in the manner and by the means he wills. From an efficacious, antecedent purpose to save Peter he need not use coercive means that necessitate the human will; it is enough to use those Divine wisdom knows can move and bend the will efficaciously, infallibly, yet freely. Indeed, when from the antecedent decree to give salvation God moves the elect's free choice toward acquiring it, liberty is not lost but rather increased and strengthened. As Báñez puts it (In 1. q.22 a.4): the creature's free choice receives participated liberty from Divine free choice, moving it strongly and sweetly according to its nature.

source_text: Sed Augustinum audiamus: Cum Deus vult fieri aliquid, quod non nisi volentibus hominibus oportet fieri, inclinantur eorum corda ut hoc velint eo inclinante, qui in nobis mirabili modo et ineffabili operatur et velle, De praed. Sanct. lib. 1. cap. 20. Falsum ergo fuit illud prius assumptum Jesuitae, Posita, scilicet efficaci voluntate Divina de salute electorum, eos necessario, et non libere velle ac facere ea per quae perducuntur ad salutem: libere enim agunt, quia ut sic agant, ipse Deus inspirat illis liberrimum velle.
english: Hear Augustine: when God wills something that must be done only by willing people, their hearts are inclined to will it by him who works in us, wonderfully and ineffably, even the willing (De praed. Sanct. 1.20). So the Jesuit's first assumption was false — that once God's efficacious will for the elect's salvation is posited, they necessarily and not freely will and do what brings them to salvation. They act freely, because God himself inspires in them a most free willing so to act.

source_text: Accedo ad illud posterius dictum Jesuitae, nimirum, Posse electum a salute excidere, et decretum Dei irritum fieri, si modo dicamus post efficax Dei decretum electos libere operari ad consecutionem salutis. Nam qui libere perseverat, potest non perseverare; potest ergo non salvari, et sic sequetur quod est impossibile, decretum Dei irritum reddi posse. Respondeo, Haec pronunciata, Qui libere operatur, potest non operari; Qui libere salvatur, potest non salvari; unde infertur decretum Dei efficax posse fieri irritum: haec, inquam, pronunciata, si respiciant possibilitatem non operandi, et non perveniendi ad salutem, quatenus ex humana fragilitate per se considerata nasci et oriri possit, agnoscimus ipsis electis adhaerescere talem pereundi, et a vita aeterna excidendi possibilitatem: Sed si referantur ad possibilitatem non operandi aut pereundi, quasi, non obstante manutinentia Divina, possit haec imbecillitas electorum in actum exire, atque sic eos quoad eventum posse non perseverare in fide et sanctitate, posse non pervenire ad vitam aeternam, negamus prorsus, posito decreto Dei efficaci de illorum salute, talem possibilitatem pereundi illis competere. Exemplo Petri hoc declaravit Augustinus; Potuit ille, ut homo infirmus et mutabilis, a fide et sanctitate et a salute deficere: sed hoc posito, quod Deus decreverat illi propter Christi orationem inspirare liberrimam, fortissimam, invictissimam, perseverantissimam in fide voluntatem, ex hac hypothesi non potuit perire, non potuit non liberrime perseverare; Vide De corr. et grat. c. 8.
english: Next the Jesuit's later claim: if after God's efficacious decree the elect freely work toward salvation, an elect person can fall from salvation and God's decree can be made void — for whoever freely perseveres can fail to persevere, so can fail to be saved. I answer: the sayings Whoever freely acts can fail to act and Whoever is freely saved can fail to be saved, if they mean a possibility of not acting and not reaching salvation that can arise from human fragility considered in itself, we grant such a possibility of perishing still clings to the elect. But if they mean that, despite God's upholding hand, that weakness can go into act so that in the event they might not persevere in faith and holiness or reach eternal life — we deny entirely that, once God's efficacious decree for their salvation is posited, such a possibility of perishing belongs to them. Augustine shows it by Peter (De corr. et grat. 8): as a weak, changeable man he could fall from faith, holiness, and salvation — but given that God had decreed, for Christ's prayer, to inspire in him a most free, strong, unconquered, persevering will in the faith, on that hypothesis he could not perish and could not but most freely persevere.

source_text: Manus igitur Dei est, non nostra, ut non discedamus a Deo: Manus autem Dei tanta efficacitate ducit et dirigit electos ad vitam aeternam, ut inde firmissimum stet ejus decretum; et simul tanta suavitate et libertate, ut inde liberrimum in bono fiat illorum arbitrium. Haec simul constare posse, fatetur Valentia, In 1. qu. 23. disp. 1. puncto 4. ubi ostendit, antiquissimos et doctissimos Scholasticos in hac opinione fuisse constitutos. Ambrosius etiam Catharinus affirmat, concessa tali justificatione, a qua non valeant excidere qui praedestinati sunt, non auferri liberrimum arbitrium, sed potius firmius et validius fieri per certitudinem luminis, et per adjectum robur fortitudinis. Unde posse non perseverare in fide, posse deficere a sanctitate, uno verbo, posse peccare et perire, non est libertas, aut pars libertatis, sed liberi arbitrii morbus vel imbecillitas. Cum igitur data voluntate contraria, eademque fortissima et perseverantissima, efficitur ut in actum non possit exire haec imbecillitas, liberum arbitrium non perimitur, sed liberum in bono stabilitur. Tanto enim magis libera est voluntas, quanto magis peccato servire non potest, ut bene Augustinus De praed. Sanct. lib. 1. cap. 15. Nihili igitur est Jesuitae argumentum; Decretum Dei antecedens facit ut electi non possint excidere a salute, ergo tollit eorum liberum arbitrium.
english: So it is God's hand, not ours, that we do not depart from God. That hand leads the elect to eternal life with such efficacy that his decree stands most firm — and with such sweetness and liberty that their choice in the good becomes most free. Valencia grants both can stand together (In 1. q.23 disp.1 p.4), and notes the oldest, most learned Scholastics held it. Ambrosius Catharinus too: grant a justification from which the predestinated cannot fall, and most free choice is not removed but made firmer and stronger by certainty of light and added fortitude. Ability not to persevere in faith, to fall from holiness — in a word, to sin and perish — is not liberty or part of liberty, but free choice's disease or weakness. When a contrary, strongest, most persevering will is given so that weakness cannot go into act, free choice is not destroyed but established free in the good. The freer the will, the less it can serve sin (Augustine, De praed. Sanct. 1.15). So the Jesuit's argument is worthless: The antecedent decree makes the elect unable to fall from salvation, therefore it takes away their free choice.

source_text: Rat. 13. Aliud argumentum huic affine est, quod etiam ab antiquis Pelagianis vibrari solebat in Augustinum; nimirum, Hanc doctrinam de electione absoluta singularum personarum ante praevisionem meritorum, hortationem omnem et correptionem evacuare, orationes inutiles facere, omnem industriam exstinguere, desperationem denique hominibus inferre. Haec apud Augustinum videre licet, De bono perseverantiae lib. 2. cap. 16. et 17. et 23. et per totum fere librum De correptione et gratia. Ex epistolis etiam Hilarii et Prosperi, quae extant inter Augustini Opera, Tom. 7. patet fuisse haec omnia invidiose objecta Augustino a Pelagianis. Quinetiam apud ipsum Faustum Regiensem haec omnia occurrunt, lib. 1. sect. 9. et 10. et passim per illud plenum veneni et pestilentiae scriptum. Summa omnium est; Ex hac sententia nostra, salutem ingerendam esse electis sive nihil agentibus, sive male agentibus, denegandam esse non-electis quantumvis laborantibus et pie viventibus.
english: Rat. 13. Another argument akin to this the ancient Pelagians also used to brandish against Augustine: namely, that this doctrine of absolute election of singular persons before foresight of merits empties every hortation and correction, makes prayers useless, extinguishes all industry, and finally brings despair on men. See Augustine, De bono perseverantiae 2.16, 17, 23, and nearly the whole of De correptione et gratia. From Hilary's and Prosper's letters among Augustine's Works (Tom. 7) it is plain the Pelagians objected all this invidiously. The same runs through Faustus of Riez, book 1 sect. 9 and 10, and that writing full of poison and pestilence. Sum of it: on our sentence, salvation is thrust on the elect whether idle or wicked, and denied to the non-elect however hard they labor and live piously.

source_text: Sol. Haec omnia dissolvuntur ab Augustino in locis modo citatis; Respondeo tamen, doctrinam electionis in piis omnibus excitare, et incendere industriam bene vivendi. Quod si impii et profani inde occasionem torporis aut desperationis accipiant, id fieri illorum vitio et innata perversitate, non ipsius doctrinae.
english: Sol. Augustine dissolves all this in the places just cited. Still I answer: the doctrine of election excites and kindles industry of living well in all the pious. If the impious and profane take from it occasion of torpor or despair, that is their vice and innate perversity — not the doctrine's.

source_text: Atque similem prorsus occasionem desumi posse ex doctrina praescientiae Divinae (quam tamen nemo nisi atheus, aut valde imperitus rejicit) demonstravit Augustinus, De bono perseverantiae lib. 2. cap. 15.
english: And Augustine showed (De bono perseverantiae 2.15) that a wholly similar occasion can be taken from the doctrine of divine foresight — which no one but an atheist, or one greatly unskilled, rejects.

source_text: Sed propius ad rem, Dico, hac doctrina gratuitae electionis stabiliri hortationes et correptiones, incendi hominum voluntates ad pie vivendum; quia sic arcanam Dei de eligendis certis hominibus voluntatem praedicamus, ut simul revelatam ejus voluntatem non taceamus, quae hosce electos non nisi per media a Deo ordinata ad finem illis destinatum perducendos decrevit. Hortationes autem, correptiones, orationes, et id genus alia, ab omnibus habentur inter illa media, quae promovendae electorum saluti Divina sapientia ordinavit.
english: Nearer the point: I say this doctrine of gratuitous election stabilizes hortations and corrections and kindles men's wills to live piously — because we preach God's secret will to elect certain persons without silencing his revealed will, which decrees those elect are led to their destined end only through means God ordained. Hortations, corrections, prayers, and the like are among those means Divine wisdom ordained to promote the elect's salvation.

source_text: Neque ulli mortalium volenti credere et pie vivere desperationem injicimus, sed certissimam fiduciam talibus praebemus, eos pertinere ad numerum electorum et salvandorum. Nam sic praedicamus gratuitam electionem, ut simul doceamus neminem posse vel fructum vel solatium inde percipere absque fide et sanctitate: quemlibet autem fideliter et sancte viventem posse ac debere seipsum in electis numerare. Haec igitur doctrina electionis tollit homini omnem gloriandi et superbiendi de suis operibus occasionem, sed non tollit ipsum studium bene operandi; quin excitat potius, dum docet, neminem aut certitudinem ullam habere de sua electione extra studium sanctitatis, aut unquam ad finem electionis, id est, vitam aeternam, pervenire posse nisi per viam sanctitatis.
english: Nor do we cast despair on any mortal willing to believe and live piously: we give such people most sure confidence they belong among the elect and those to be saved. We preach gratuitous election while teaching that no one gets fruit or comfort from it without faith and holiness — and that anyone living faithfully and holily can and ought to count himself among the elect. So the doctrine takes away every occasion of boasting and pride in one's works, but not the study of doing well; it rather kindles that study, teaching that no one has any certainty of election outside pursuit of holiness, or can ever reach election's end — eternal life — except by the way of holiness.

source_text: Rat. 14. Ultimo in loco argumentantur a conformitate quae est inter ipsum decretum electionis Divinae et temporalem exsecutionem ejusdem, hanc in modum; Eodem ordine quo res in tempore mandantur exsecutioni, Deus ab aeternitate decrevit ut mandarentur. Pertinet enim ad immutabilitatem voluntatis Divinae, ut non aliter agat in tempore, quam ab omni aeternitate se acturum esse decrevit. Quandoquidem igitur in temporali exsecutione salutis electorum, neminem perducit ad gloriam nisi intuitu bonorum operum et perseverantiae finalis, non potuit ab aeterno aliter ad gloriam illos eligere nisi ex eodem intuitu. Nam si ante jacta mundi fundamenta illos ad gloriam elegit gratuito, et non ex operibus praevisis, et cum ad exsecutionem ventum fuerit, non vult illis dare gloriam nisi ex operibus, mutavit voluntatem suam, quod est Divina sapientia indignissimum. Omnes Papistae qui electionem ex operibus praevisis fieri contendunt, huic argumento valde confidunt, et quasi Achilleum esse jactitant.
english: Rat. 14. Last they argue from the conformity between God's election decree and its temporal execution: in the same order in which things are executed in time, God from eternity decreed they should be executed. Divine immutability requires he not act otherwise in time than he from eternity decreed he would. So since in temporal execution he leads none of the elect to glory except in view of good works and final perseverance, he could not from eternity elect them to glory except under that same view. If before the world's foundations he elected them to glory freely, not from foreseen works, yet at execution will not give glory except from works, he has changed his will — most unworthy of divine wisdom. All Papists who hold election from foreseen works trust this argument heavily and boast it is their Achilles.

source_text: Sol. Ut hoc argumentum recte solvatur, distinguendum est inter ipsam actionem Dei eligentis ad vitam aeternam, et ipsam rem ad quam eligit, hoc est, ipsam vitam aeternam. Potest enim habere vim causae dispositivae quoad productionem rei, quod nullam habuit vim causae motivae quoad intentionem eligentis. Non imus inficias, bona opera, sive vitam sanctam et piam, isto modo operari ad consecutionem vitae aeternae, atque Deum ab aeterno intuitum fuisse hanc electorum sanctam vitam, tanquam praecedaneam ad illorum introitum in regnum caeleste.
english: Sol. To solve this rightly, distinguish God's act of electing to eternal life from the thing elected — eternal life itself. What can be a dispositive cause of producing the thing need not have been a motive cause of the elector's intention. We do not deny that good works, or a holy and pious life, work that way toward attaining eternal life, and that God from eternity looked on the elect's holy life as preceding their entrance into the heavenly kingdom.

source_text: Sed in hoc labuntur adversarii, quod arbitrantur ea quae sunt antecedentia ad vitam aeternam, ad quam homines eliguntur, concipi etiam necessario oportere ut antecedentia ad actum sive intentionem eligentis, id est, Dei decretum, a quo eliguntur. Nam actus ille internus et aeternus voluntatis Divinae, quo eligit, et gloria, sive caeleste gaudium, ad quod eligit, sunt valde diversa. Unde possumus aliquid recte affirmare de objecto, quod non possumus nisi falso affirmare de actu sive intentione Dei qua illud objectum singulari personae destinatur. Verbi causa; Vera est haec assertio de objecto: Vocatio Pauli, justificatio, et pia vita sive operatio videntur a Deo ut praecedanea ad ejus glorificationem: sed falsa est eadem si ad actum Dei accommodetur, hoc modo, Vocatio Pauli, et justificatio, et pia vita sive operatio videntur a Deo ut praecedanea ad intentionem Divinam de Paulo glorificando.
english: Here the adversaries slip: they think what precedes eternal life (to which men are elected) must also be conceived as preceding the elector's act or intention — God's decree by which they are elected. But that internal eternal act of the divine will by which he elects, and the glory or heavenly joy to which he elects, are greatly different. So we can rightly affirm of the object what we can only falsely affirm of God's act or intention destinating that object to a particular person. Example — true of the object: Paul's calling, justification, and pious life are seen by God as preceding his glorification. False if fitted to God's act: those same are seen by God as preceding the divine intention to glorify Paul.

source_text: Damus ergo, Deum eodem ordine quo in tempore mandat res exsecutioni, decrevisse ab aeterno et praevidisse quod mandarentur: sed negamus, eo ordine quo mandat exsecutioni, aut decrevit mandare, etiam intendisse. Nam cum in actibus voluntatis et mentis Divinae per se nulla sit prioritas aut posterioritas ordinis, secundum nostrum modum intelligendi, et rerum ipsarum habitudinem, non idem, sed plane oppositus ordo concipiendus est in exsecutione atque intentione Divina. Decretum exsecutionis orditur semper ab eo quod est remotius ab ipso fine, et sic gradatim progreditur ad effectionem finis: hoc sensu; Deus decrevit vocare Paulum prius quam justificare, justificare et bonis operibus ornare prius quam glorificare. Cum enim decretum exsecutionis, vel voluntas exsecutiva respiciat externam et actualem rei effectionem, illud prius ad hanc voluntatem referatur necesse est quod prius concurrit ad rem efficiendam. Jam vero e contra, Intentio voluntatis orditur semper ab ipso fine, et a fine sic ad media progreditur, ut semper prius id velit quod est fini propinquius.
english: So we grant God decreed from eternity and foresaw that things would be executed in the same order he executes them in time — but we deny he also intended in that execution-order. In the acts of the divine will and mind there is of themselves no priority of order; on our way of understanding and the things' relation, execution and intention take plainly opposite orders. The decree of execution always starts from what is farther from the end and steps toward effecting it: God decreed to call Paul before justifying him, to justify and adorn with good works before glorifying. Executive will regards the external actual effecting, so what concurs earlier to producing the thing is referred earlier to that will. Intention, conversely, always starts from the end itself and moves to means so that it always wills first what is nearer the end.

source_text: Quia haec spinosiora sunt, ea exemplo apposito illustrabimus. Intendo servum meum in Galliam mittere: prius hoc volo quam de navi comparanda aliquid decerno: nunquam enim apud animum meum statuissem aut cogitassem naviculam illi praeparare, nisi prius decretum fuisset illum in Galliam transmittere. Jam cum ad exsecutionem ventum fuerit, volo prius nave comparere quam illum transmittere: Intelligo enim hanc transfretationem absque navi fieri nullo modo posse. Hic si quis objiciat me voluntatem mutasse, quia ab initio prius intendebam de transmissione quam de navi, nunc prius volo illum in navim imponere quam transmittere, quis non riserit hujusmodi argutias? Cum in una voluntate prius et posterius considerentur secundum internum ordinem volitionis, in altera secundum externum ordinem effectionis.
english: These points are thorny, so an example: I intend to send my servant into Gaul — I will that before I decree anything about getting a ship; I would never have thought to prepare him a little boat unless sending him to Gaul had already been decided. At execution I will to have the ship ready before sending him across, since the crossing cannot happen without a ship. If someone objects that I changed my will — because at first I intended the crossing before the ship, and now I will to put him aboard before sending him across — who would not laugh at such subtleties? In one will earlier and later follow the internal order of willing; in the other, the external order of effecting.

source_text: Accommodemus haec instituto nostro: Deus intendit Petrum in Caelum transmittere: prius hoc vult quam media efficacia et infallibilia illi decernit: nunquam enim statuisset talia media illi suppeditare, nisi prius efficaciter decrevisset caelestem gloriam illi donare. Verum jam ad exsecutionem descendatur, Deus vult ut prius gratiae particeps fiat, ex gratia bene operetur, in bonis operibus ad finem usque perseveret, quam ad portum caelestis gloriae appellat. Hic si Jesuiticus aliquis disputator insurgat et vociferetur, Deum mutasse voluntatem suam, quia ab initio prius intendebat Petro gloriam quam gratiam aut perseverantiam in bonis operibus, nunc vult e contra ut prius gratia imbuatur, et in bonis operibus perseveranter ambulet, quam ad gloriam perveniat, ridebo hominis ineptias, et dicam diversam hanc considerationem, quoad intentionem et productionem ejusdem rei, non ponere in Deo diversam aut mutabilem voluntatem, sed ejusdem voluntatis ad eandem rem sub diversis considerationibus diversam habitudinem. Haec fere ea sunt quae a Papistis disputantur pro electione ex praevisis operibus.
english: Fit this to our case: God intends to send Peter into Heaven — he wills that before he decrees efficacious, infallible means for him; he would never have resolved to supply such means unless he had first efficaciously decreed to give him heavenly glory. At execution God wills that Peter first share in grace, work well from grace, and persevere in good works to the end, before he makes harbor at heavenly glory. If some Jesuit disputant rises and shouts that God changed his will — because at first he intended glory for Peter before grace or perseverance, and now wills the reverse, grace and persevering good works before glory — I will laugh at the man's folly, and say this diverse consideration of intention and production of the same thing does not posit a diverse or changeable will in God, but a diverse habitude of the same will toward the same thing under diverse considerations. That is nearly all the Papists dispute for election from foreseen works.

source_text: Cap. IV. Arminianorum sententia exponitur, atque argumenta refelluntur. Omissis atque rejectis Pontificiorum argumentis, cum iis deinceps agendum est, qui interpolarunt hanc controversiam, mutatis quibusdam vocabulis, et loquendi formulis, ipsa tamen errorum fundamenta retinuerunt. In his principem locum obtinet Jacobus Arminius, vir doctus et acri ingenio, sed qui parum tribuebat antiquae Ecclesiae judicio, nihil Reformatae. Is igitur, ne crassus nimis videretur in constituenda sua defensione, noluit tueri ullum hominem praedestinari ex praevisis operibus aut meritis (ut loquuntur quidam) sed ex fide praevisa; noluit etiam quod illi de operibus audacter afferebant, de hac fide asserere, illam esse causam praedestinationis nostrae ad gloriam: sed vocabulis emollitis, docet esse tantum conditionem, aut quiddam decenter antecedaneum.
english: Cap. IV. The Arminians' position is set out and their arguments refuted. Pontiff arguments omitted and rejected, we next deal with those who interpolated this controversy — changing some words and phrases while keeping the same error foundations. Chief among them is Jacobus Arminius: learned, sharp-minded, yet little regard for the ancient Church's judgment and none for the Reformed. Lest his defense look too crude, he would not hold anyone predestinated from foreseen works or merits (as some say) but from foreseen faith; nor would he boldly call that faith the cause of our predestination to glory as they did of works — with softened words he calls it only a condition, or something decently antecedent.

source_text: Verum si res ipsa spectetur, eodem redit utraque sententia, statuitque ex humano aliquo actu antecedente dependere, quod quivis a Deo praedestinetur ad vitam aeternam, aut non praedestinetur. Neque mihi videntur antiqui Patres, aut Scholastici in hac controversia Causae, imo Meriti vocabulo aliam notionem subjecisse quam hanc, ut scilicet innuant quemvis bonum actum, virtute gratiae Divinae ab homine praestitum, cujus intuitu Deus dat ex decreto sive ordinatione sua quodvis beneficium. Si igitur Deus intuitu fidei nostrae praedestinat, intuitu infidelitatis non praedestinat, negare non debuit Arminius fidem a se poni rationem vel causam motivam praedestinationis nostrae, imo meritoriam, ex phrasi et sensu antiquorum. Sed haec obiter.
english: But if you look at the thing itself, both positions come to the same: it makes anyone's predestination (or non-predestination) to eternal life depend on some antecedent human act. The ancient Fathers and Scholastics in this controversy seem to me to mean by Cause — nay Merit — nothing else than any good act a man performs by divine grace, in view of which God by his decree or ordination grants any benefit. So if God predestinates in view of our faith and does not in view of unbelief, Arminius should not have denied that he posits faith as a reason or motive cause of our predestination — even a meritorious one, in the ancients' phrase and sense. But that by the way.

source_text: Praedestinatione ergo hunc in modum ex praevisione fidei constituta, duplex Praedestinationis decretum ab Arminio, ejusque sectatoribus stabilitur. Prius generale est, quo Deus decrevit omnes credentes in gratiam recipere propter Christum, eosdemque in fide perseverantes aeterna vita donare. Posterius singulare est, et ad singulares personas terminatur: Quo Deus statuit hunc et illum nominatim, puta Petrum, Paulum, Johannem, quos ab aeterno praevidit credituros, et in fide permansuros, aeterna gloria donare.
english: With predestination thus set from foresight of faith, Arminius and his followers establish a double decree. The first is general: God decreed to receive all believers into grace for Christ's sake, and to gift those persevering in faith with eternal life. The second is singular and terminates on particular persons: God established to gift with eternal glory this one and that by name — Peter, Paul, John — whom from eternity he foresaw would believe and remain in faith.

source_text: Est autem observatu dignum, prius illud generale decretum, quod neminem singulariter ad salutem designat, urgeri tamen maxime ab Arminio, et obtrudi pro illa praedestinatione, quam sacra Scriptura nobis commendavit. Sic in Responsione sua ad articulos, artic. 4. Hoc decretum (loquitur de isto generali et indeterminato) dico esse fundamentum Christianismi, salutis, et certitudinis de salute; deque illo agi ad Rom. 8, 10, 11. et primo capite ad Ephesios. Idem plane docet in Epistola ad Hippolytum, in qua illam praedestinationem, qua Deus dicitur decrevisse singulares quasdam personas salvare et fide donare, quasi rem parvi momenti, et in sacris Scripturis minime fundatam, transilit. Remonstrantes autem in Collatione Hagiensi, plane immemores particularis cujuscunque decreti, eo dirigunt argumenta sua, ut probent hoc unicum decretum, quo Deus indiscriminatim statuit, velle se quoslibet in fide perseverantes servare, iram vero super omnibus incredulis effundere, esse totum et integrum decretum Praedestinationis, pag. 62.
english: Note well: that prior general decree, which names no one singularly to salvation, is what Arminius most urges and thrusts forward as the predestination Scripture recommends. So in his Response to the articles, art. 4: This decree (the general, indeterminate one) I say is the foundation of Christianity, salvation, and certainty of salvation; and Rom. 8, 10, 11 and Ephesians 1 treat of it. The same in his Letter to Hippolytus, where he skips the predestination by which God decreed to save certain singular persons and gift them faith — as a small matter, scarcely founded in Scripture. The Remonstrants at the Hague Conference, forgetting any particular decree, aim to prove this sole decree — God indiscriminately wills to save any who persevere in faith and pour wrath on all unbelievers — is the whole and entire decree of Predestination (p. 62).

source_text: Nos autem e contra statuimus, neque illud generale Dei decretum in hanc formulam conceptum, Ego volo omnes in fide perseverantes servare, Neque illud singulare praescientia interveniente nixum, Ego Petrum, Paulum, Johannem, quos praevideo perseveranter credituros, aeterna vita donabo, esse eam praedestinationem de qua Apostolus in Epistola ad Romanos, ac sacrae Scripturae loquuntur. Pro posteriore hoc decreto (quod sciam) non solent pugnare adversarii, verbo asseruisse contenti: Pro priore acriter dimicant. Nos illorum argumentis primo in loco occurremus; dein sententiam nostram confirmabimus, ac contrariam eadem opera impugnabimus. Quia autem in Colloquio Hagiensi ea quae sparsim apud alios exstant argumenta, quasi in unum fasciculum comportantur, nos illorum Collocutorum objectiunculis respondebimus.
english: We hold the contrary: neither that general decree framed I will to save all who persevere in faith, nor that singular one resting on intervening foresight — I will gift eternal life to Peter, Paul, John, whom I foresee will perseveringly believe — is the predestination of which the Apostle speaks in Romans, and sacred Scripture. For the latter decree (so far as I know) adversaries rarely fight, content to assert it in a word; for the former they contend sharply. We will first meet their arguments, then confirm our position and impugn the contrary. And because at the Hague Colloquy arguments scattered elsewhere are gathered as into one fascicle, we will answer those Colloquists' little objections.

source_text: Arg. 1. Voluntas Dei de salute et exitio hominum in Evangelio patefacta, est totum integrum decretum praedestinationis: Perseverantes in fide velle servare, iram vero super incredulis et impoenitentibus velle relinquere, est voluntas Dei de salute et exitio hominum in Evangelio patefacta: Ergo perseverantes in fide velle servare, iram vero super incredulis relinquere, est totum et integrum decretum praedestinationis. Majorem dicunt esse per se manifestam, nec probatione indigere; Minorem in hisce Scripturae locis expresse fundatam Joh. iii. 36, Qui credit in Filium, habet vitam aeternam; qui vero Filio non obtemperat, non videbit vitam, sed ira Dei manet super ipsum. Et Joh. vi. 40, Haec est voluntas ejus qui misit me, ut quisquis videt Filium, et credit in eum, habeat vitam aeternam.
english: Arg. 1. God's will concerning men's salvation and ruin, revealed in the Gospel, is the whole entire decree of predestination. To will to save those persevering in faith, and to leave wrath on the unbelieving and impenitent, is that gospel-revealed will. Therefore to will to save perseverers in faith and leave wrath on unbelievers is the whole and entire decree of predestination. They say the major is self-evident and needs no proof; the minor is expressly founded in John 3:36 — Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever does not obey the Son will not see life, but God's wrath remains on him — and John 6:40 — This is the will of him who sent me, that whoever sees the Son and believes in him may have eternal life.

source_text: Sol. Priusquam ad argumenti solutionem veniamus, quia in ipso vocabulo praedestinationis subinde nobis illudunt adversarii, de eo aliquid dicemus. Est igitur primo notandum, posse quidem sensu largo quodlibet Dei decretum de re qualibet vocari decretum praedestinationis. Ratio aperta est; quia omnia Dei decreta sunt ab aeterno in mente Divina concepta, et secundum destinatum propositum voluntatis Divinae. Verum cum usus loquendi in sacra Theologia hoc vocabulum praedestinationis ad specialem quandam significationem arctaverit, non est ingenui Theologi sub generali notione vocabuli ludum facere auditoribus.
english: Sol. Before solving the argument: adversaries keep playing with the word predestination, so a word on that. First: in a broad sense any decree of God about anything can be called a decree of predestination — all God's decrees are conceived from eternity in the divine mind according to the destined purpose of the divine will. But sacred theology has narrowed that word to a special sense; it is not candid theology to play games with hearers under the general notion.

source_text: Secundo et illud perpendendum, In praesenti nostra controversia Theologos nunquam per decretum praedestinationis intellexisse quodlibet placitum Divinae voluntatis de salute et exitio hominum, sub qualibet forma conceptum et in verbo revelatum. Nam si eo hoc vocabulum torquere libeat, ipsissimum decretum praedestinationis continebitur illis verbis Matth. xxv. 34. &c. Dicet Rex iis qui sunt ad dextram, Venite benedicti Patris mei, possidete regnum paratum vobis a jactis mundi fundamentis. Esurivi enim et dedistis mihi quo vescerer, &c. Dicet iis qui ad sinistram erunt, Abite maledicti in ignem aeternum, qui paratus est diabolo et angelis ejus. Esurivi enim, et non dedistis mihi quo vescerer, &c. Exprimetur etiam praedestinationis decretum et in illis ad Rom. ii. 6. Deus reddet unicuique secundum opera ipsius: iis quidem qui perstant, boni operis gloriam et honorem et immortalitatem: iis vero qui sunt contentiosi, et qui veritati non obtemperant, sed obtemperant injustitiae, reddetur excandescentia et ira, &c. In hisce enim et similibus locis, patefit nobis voluntas Dei de salute et exitio hominum, et tamen in hujusmodi decretis ponere illam altam et inscrutabilem praedestinationem quam Paulus cantopere celebrat et admiratur, est a sensu et sententia Scripturarum, atque omnium sanorum Theologorum alienissimum.
english: Second: in our controversy theologians have never meant by the predestination decree any revealed pleasure of the divine will about men's salvation and ruin, under any form. Twist the word that way and Matt. 25:34ff. itself becomes the decree — Come, blessed of my Father… Depart, cursed… — and so does Rom. 2:6, God will render to each according to his works. Those places do open God's will about salvation and ruin; but to lodge in them that high, inscrutable predestination Paul so celebrates is most alien to Scripture and to all sound theologians.

source_text: Tertio cognoscere oportet, praedestinationis decretum proprie sumptum denotare, non legem universalem ostendentem omnibus ex aequo, quo modo, vel quibus mediis, salus obtineatur, aut mors incurratur: Qualia sunt illa, Quisquis crediderit, quisquis in pietate perseveraverit, salvus erit; et contra, Quisquis non crediderit, quisquis opera pietatis non exercuerit, damnabitur. Sed praedestinatio designat practicum Dei decretum, quo ab aeterno statuit singulares quasdam personas singularibus bonis, hoc est, gratia efficaci et vita aeterna, infallibiliter donare. Sic Paulus praedestinationem accipit Rom. viii; quando illam ad quasdam certas personas restringit, et cum glorificatione inseparabili nexu conjungit: sic Schola Theologorum, quae illam definivit Praeparationem gratiae in praesenti, et gloriae in futuro. Decreta ergo illa in quibus exponitur tantum generatim qualibus hominibus vita aeterna donabitur, qualibus mors aeterna infligetur, interim autem nihil statuitur de danda gratia et gloria ullis singularibus personis; talia, inquam, decreta vim naturamque praedestinationis non exprimunt.
english: Third: predestination properly taken does not mean a universal law showing all alike how salvation is obtained or death incurred — Whoever believes and perseveres in piety will be saved; whoever does not believe or practice piety will be damned. It designates a practical decree by which from eternity God established to gift certain singular persons infallibly with singular goods: efficacious grace and eternal life. So Paul takes it in Rom. 8, restricting it to definite persons and joining it inseparably with glorification; so the School, which defined it Preparation of grace in the present and of glory in the future. Decrees that only say generally what sort of men get eternal life or death, while settling nothing about grace and glory for any singular persons, do not express predestination's force and nature.

source_text: Hisce praemissis accedo ad rationem propositam, ac dico Majorem, cujus illi veritatem manifestam esse clamant, aut manifeste falsam esse, aut particularem, atque tum ex omnibus particularibus inepta erit conclusio. Si Major universalis sit, hoc modo, Quaelibet Dei voluntas de salute et exitio hominum in Evangelio patefacta, est totum et integrum decretum praedestinationis, manifeste falsa est. Deus enim revelavit voluntatem suam quoad qualitates quibus praediti debent esse omnes qui futuri sunt aeternae vitae participes; revelavit voluntatem suam quoad actus, qui exerceri debent ab omnibus, qui ingredi volunt vitam aeternam; hisce tamen quasi statutis humano generi revelatis, non continetur formale decretum praedestinationis Divinae; sed in illa arcana intentione sive voluntate efficaciter et infallibiliter donandi electis quibusdam illas qualitates, eos actus, qui ducunt ad vitam aeternam, ipsamque vitam aeternam.
english: With that premised I turn to their reason. The Major they call self-evident is either manifestly false, or particular — and then from particulars the conclusion is inept. If universal — Any gospel-revealed will of God about men's salvation and ruin is the whole entire decree of predestination — it is manifestly false. God has revealed his will about the qualities all who will share eternal life must have, and about the acts all who will enter that life must exercise; yet those revealed statutes do not contain the formal decree of divine predestination. That lies in the secret intention or will to gift certain elect efficaciously and infallibly those qualities and acts that lead to eternal life, and eternal life itself.

source_text: Tota siquidem Dei voluntas de salute hominum non continetur tali decreto, Qui crediderit habebit vitam aeternam. Nam in sacris Scripturis Deus insuper patefecit, se quibusdam, quorum ex mero beneplacito vult prae aliis misereri, velle donare vocationem secundum propositum; ex tali vocatione poenitentiam, fidem, sanctificationem, et demum glorificationem, atque haec omnia infallibiliter. Haec voluntas Dei est vera et proprie voluntas praedestinans, estque in Evangelio patefacta quoad rem, quamvis individua quoad nomen non inibi exprimantur. Haec de Majore.
english: For God's whole will about men's salvation is not contained in Whoever believes will have eternal life. Scripture further opens that to certain ones — of whom from mere good pleasure he wills to have mercy before others — he wills to gift vocation according to purpose; from that vocation repentance, faith, sanctification, and finally glorification, all infallibly. That is the true, properly predestinating will, opened in the Gospel as to the thing, though individuals are not there named. So much for the Major.

source_text: De Minore, quae fundatur in expressis quibusdam Scripturae locis, sufficiat hoc unum dixisse, Verissimum esse quod assumitur, Deum patefecisse in Evangelio hanc suam voluntatem servandi illos omnes qui in fide perseverabunt, et damnandi incredulos; sed infirmissimum esse quod inde inferre volunt, In hoc decreto voluntatis Divinae positam esse praedestinationem hominum, imo totum et integrum decretum praedestinationis nostrae. Verum cum ad nostra argumenta ventum fuerit, hoc insomnia Arminianum dispellemus.
english: On the Minor, founded in certain express Scripture places, one thing suffices: what they assume is most true — God has opened in the Gospel his will to save all who will persevere in faith and to damn unbelievers. What they infer from it is weakest: that in this decree of the divine will men's predestination is placed — nay the whole and entire decree of our predestination. When we come to our own arguments, we will dispel this Arminian dream.

source_text: Arg. 2. Secundo argumentantur ex verbis Apostoli, Hebr. xi. 6. Sine fide impossibile est placere Deo. Unde tale argumentum exstruunt; Sine quo impossibile est placere Deo, sine eo impossibile est a Deo quenquam eligi ad salutem: Sine fide impossibile est placere Deo: Ergo. Majorem certam esse pronunciant, quandoquidem eligere ad salutem, summa est dilectio quam homini Deus praestare potest, sive maxima ipsius in homine dilectio.
english: Arg. 2. Second they argue from Heb. 11:6 — Without faith it is impossible to please God — and build this: Without that without which one cannot please God, no one can be elected by God to salvation; without faith one cannot please God; therefore. They call the Major certain, since electing to salvation is the highest love God can show a man — his greatest love toward a man.

source_text: Sol. Ad ipsa verba Apostoli primo respondemus, Ea pessime, et in sensum ab instituto Apostolico prorsus alienum, torqueri. Nam fides hoc in loco non praevisam fidem hominis nondum existentis, sed actualem, atque jam vires suas exercentem demonstrat. Hoc perspicuum est ex illo altero verbo εὐηρέστησεν, Placere, quod Apostolus ex Septuaginta Interpretum versione mutuatus est. Sic enim illi Genes. v. 24. εὐηρέστησεν Ἐνὼχ τῷ Θεῷ. At in Hebraeo habetur, continue ambulavit cum Deo: id est, Non est imitatus ejus saeculi nequitiam, sed corde sincero jugiter Deo servivit, Deumque caste coluit. Nihil igitur aliud dicere voluit Apostolus, quam neminem posse absque fide vitam piam Deoque placentem ducere; quod exemplo Enochi voluit confirmare. Miro igitur ingenio sunt Remonstrantes, qui potuerunt electionem suam ex fidei praevisione pendulam hinc exsculpere.
english: Sol. First to the Apostle's words: they are twisted badly into a sense wholly alien to his purpose. Faith here is not the foreseen faith of a man not yet existing, but actual faith already at work. That is clear from εὐηρέστησεν, to please — which Paul takes from the LXX at Gen. 5:24, Enoch pleased God; the Hebrew is he walked continually with God — he did not imitate his age's wickedness but served God sincerely and worshiped him purely. So the Apostle means only that no one can lead a pious life pleasing to God without faith, confirmed by Enoch's example. Wondrous ingenuity in the Remonstrants, who carved from this their election hanging on foresight of faith.

source_text: Sed ipsum syllogismum ventilemus. Major propositio, Sine quo impossibile est placere Deo, sine eo impossibile est eligi quenquam ad salutem, tota farcta est aequivocationibus. Vocabula illa, sine quo, intelligi possunt dupliciter: sine quo praeviso et praeconsiderato ut antecedanea conditione nemo potest eligi ad salutem a Deo; vel, sine quo tanquam medio praeparato et destinato impossibile est eligi quenquam ad salutem. Priore sensu causam attingit, sed manifeste falsa est: Posteriore ne attingit quidem, et tamen non est absolutae veritatis. Nam quidem eatenus Deo placent, ut ad vitam aeternam eligantur, in quibus Deus non praevidet fidem omnino, nedum antecedaneam. Exemplo sint electi illi infantes qui moriuntur, priusquam per aetatem credere, aut in fide perseverare possint. Quod enim nunquam futurum est, a Deo non praevidetur: cum objectum praescientiae sit quiddam infallibiliter futurum.
english: Now the syllogism. The Major — Without that without which one cannot please God, no one can be elected to salvation — is stuffed with equivocations. Without which can mean: without which, foreseen as an antecedent condition, no one can be elected; or without which as a prepared, destined means no one can be elected. The first sense touches the cause but is manifestly false; the second does not even touch it, and still is not absolute truth. Some please God unto election to eternal life in whom God foresees no faith at all, still less antecedent faith — for example elect infants who die before they can believe or persevere. What will never be is not foreseen; foresight's object is something infallibly future.

source_text: Dein, verba illa, placere Deo, non uno modo accipi possunt. Sensu Paulino nihil aliud indicant, quam facere opera Deo placentia, vel (ut ex originali textu notavimus) ambulare cum Deo. Jam attendite quam absonum sit, neminem potuisse unquam a Deo eligi, nisi prius ea omnia habeat sine quibus opera nostra Deo placere non possunt. Profecto absque fide actuali, addo etiam, et charitate, nemo potest hoc modo placere Deo, (aut quod Enochus fecit) cum Deo ambulare. Si ulla vis inesset huic argumento, electio omnis esset temporalis, et justificationem ac sanctificationem sequeretur.
english: Further, to please God is not one sense only. Paulinely it means doing works pleasing to God, or (from the original) walking with God. Mark how absurd it is that no one could ever be elected unless he first has all that our works need to please God. Without actual faith — and charity too — no one can please God that way, or walk with God as Enoch did. If this argument had force, all election would be temporal and would follow justification and sanctification.

source_text: Porro recte dicimus quosdam placere Deo prae aliis, ut destinatos ad fidem et vitam aeternam; quosdam etiam placere Deo ut Dei filios actu jam adoptatos, sanctificatos, et ad jus vitae aeternae acceptatos. Priore sensu (quem nos respicere debemus in hac controversia) non modo possibile est ut quis ante habitam vel praevisam suam fidem placeat Deo, sed plane impossibile est ut aliter placeat. Optime Concilium Arausicanum, canone 25. Displicentes amati sumus, ut fieret in nobis unde placeremus. Si enim nullum beneficium a Deo accipere possemus, nisi prius ei placeremus, placere autem non possemus, nisi prius fidem habeamus: aut ipsum fidei beneficium a nobis, non a Deo habemus, aut dabitur processus in infinitum. Scire igitur oportet, rationem primæ complacentiae, sive amoris Divini erga lapsam creaturam, non in hominis bona aliqua qualitate antecedanea esse quaerendam, sed ex ipso fonte Divini amoris esse arcessendam. Nam amor est primum donum, in quo caetera omnia donantur: et amor Dei hoc habet singulare, quod non invenit sed facit suum objectum sibi amabile. Deut. vii. 7, 8. Te elegit Dominus Deus tuus, ut sis ei populus peculiaris, quia dilexit vos Dominus, non quia cunctas gentes numero vinceretis.
english: Further: some please God before others as destined to faith and eternal life; some please as sons already adopted, sanctified, and accepted to the right of eternal life. In the prior sense (ours in this controversy) it is not only possible that one please God before faith had or foreseen — it is plainly impossible to please otherwise. Best Orange canon 25: Displeasing we were loved, that there might be made in us whence we might please. If we could receive no gift from God unless we first pleased him, and could not please without faith first, then either faith's gift is from us not God, or you get an infinite regress. So the reason of first complacency — divine love toward the fallen creature — is not some antecedent good quality in man, but must be fetched from the fountain of divine love. Love is the first gift in which all others are given; and God's love has this singular: it does not find but makes its object lovable to itself (Deut. 7:7–8).

source_text: Denique, quod ad confirmationem Majoris afferebatur, Eligere ad salutem esse effectum summae dilectionis, ac proinde neminem posse eligi a Deo, nisi qui per fidem saltem praevisam sit ei gratus et acceptus, hoc, inquam, facile refellitur et enervatur. Nam electio est effectus amoris, sed non illius amoris amicitiae de quo intelligenda sunt illa verba, Enoch placuit Deo; sed illius amoris, quem Schola appellat amorem sive benevolentiae. Effecta prioris amoris tendunt in solos fideles et pios, sed effecta posterioris in impios et incredulos, ut illis inspiret fidem et sanctitatem, imo in nondum natos, ut illis destinet vitam aeternam. Esse quendam Dei amorem qui exseritur erga impios ante fidem et conversionem ne diffiteri quidem possunt Remonstrantes; et tamen fatendo, hujus argumenti nervos elidunt. Videte quae de Antecedente et consequente amore scribunt, Colloq. Hag. pag. 183, Edit. Bertii.
english: Finally, their Major's confirmation — electing to salvation is an effect of highest love, so no one can be elected unless through faith at least foreseen he is pleasing and acceptable — is easily refuted. Election is an effect of love, but not of that friendship-love of Enoch pleased God; rather of the love the School calls benevolence. Effects of friendship-love tend only to the faithful and pious; effects of benevolence tend to the impious and unbelieving, to inspire faith and holiness in them — even to the not-yet-born, to destine them eternal life. The Remonstrants cannot even deny a love of God put forth toward the impious before faith and conversion; and by confessing it they cut the nerves of this argument.
