Vasquez the Jesuit, pressed by this absolute gratuitous predestination of certain persons to faith and perseverance, answers: yes, predestination to grace does not hang on foresighted merits — but election to glory does, and that is the standing view of Scripture and Augustine. In vain he tries to split what Scripture and Augustine join most closely. Scripture knows no election to efficacious grace except what is tied to the will to give glory — which will, in our way of considering, is prior to the will to give efficacious grace, and its cause and rule. Hence we are predestined unto adoption as sons (Eph. 1:5) — destination of glory and the heavenly inheritance, not grace alone. So Christ to the predestined (Luke 12:32): Fear not, little flock, for it pleased your Father to give you the kingdom — the will to give the kingdom as the peculiar cause of the providence that keeps the elect and makes them persevere through dangers. The will to give glory (election to life) is why they persevere before others — not foresighted perseverance why they were elected before others.

source_text: Unica est ratio praedestinationis tum quoad Caput et membra, tum quoad membra inter se collata. Hoc est: Si praedestinatio Christi ad officium Mediatoris et Salvatoris fuerit gratuita, et non ex praevisione meritorum, tum multo magis praedestinatio nostri ad beneficium salutis gratuita esse debet. Porro, Si manifestum sit quaedam Christi membra ad vitam aeternam absque ullo respectu ad praevisae fidei aut perseverantiae conditionem fuisse praedestinata, tum idem statuendum est de reliquis omnibus. Praedestinationem enim, quoad conditiones praerequisitas aut non praerequisitas, uniformem esse, extra dubium est.
english: One ratio of predestination — Head and members, and members among themselves. If Christ's predestination to Mediator and Savior was gratuitous, not from foresight of merits, then much more must ours to the benefit of salvation be gratuitous. And if some of Christ's members were clearly predestined to eternal life with no regard to foresighted faith or perseverance, the same holds for all the rest. Predestination is uniform as to whether conditions are presupposed or not — that is beyond doubt.

source_text: Quod ad prius: Si quaeratur, Quomodo Christus in Salvatorem praedestinatus? secundum Dei gratuitum beneplacitum, an secundum praevisionem operum? audite eundem Augustinum: Est etiam praeclarissimum lumen praedestinationis et gratiae ipse Salvator, ipse Mediator Dei et hominum, homo Christus Jesus: qui ut hoc esset, quibus tandem suis, vel operum vel fidei, praecedentibus meritis naturae humanae quae in illo est comparavit? De Praed. Sanct. cap. 15.
english: First limb: how was Christ predestined Savior — by God's gratuitous good pleasure, or by foresight of works? Hear Augustine (On the Predestination of the Saints 15): the brightest light of predestination and grace is the Savior himself, the Mediator, the man Christ Jesus — and by what prior merits of his own, of works or of faith, did the human nature in him earn to be that?

source_text: Jam quod ad posterius, nempe conformitatem praedestinationis inter ipsa membra: clarum est multa membra Christi in vitam aeternam fuisse praedestinata absque antecedaneo intuitu fidei aut perseverantiae in eadem. Nam cum fides perseverans non consideretur nisi in illis qui utuntur ratione et libero arbitrio, quotquot in infantia morientes salvantur, absque hujus intuitu ad salutem fuisse destinatos est necesse. At multi ea aetate moriuntur, de quorum salute Ecclesia nunquam dubitavit. Multi ergo et electi et servati fuerunt, in quibus haec praevisio fidei et perseverantiae locum habere non potuit. Hoc argumento ab infantibus electis petito Augustinus passim occludit ora Pelagianorum, qui ex praevisis meritis praedestinationem ad vitam statuerunt: De praed. et grat. cap. 7; De bono persever. cap. 8 et 12; De peccat. mer. et remiss. lib. 1. cap. 21; Contr. 2 Epist. Pelag. lib. 2. cap. 7.
english: Second limb — conformity among the members: many of Christ's members were predestined to eternal life with no prior regard to faith or perseverance. Persevering faith is only considered in those who use reason and free choice; so all who die in infancy and are saved must have been destined to salvation without that regard. Many die at that age whose salvation the Church never doubted. Many, then, were both elect and saved in whom foresight of faith and perseverance could have no place. By elect infants Augustine everywhere stops the Pelagians' mouths — those who grounded predestination to life in foresighted merits (On Predestination and Grace 7; On the Gift of Perseverance 8, 12; On Merits and Remission 1.21; Against Two Letters of the Pelagians 2.7).

source_text: Cui suffragatur Prosper in lib. De libero arbitrio: In infantibus nec praecedens eligitur nec secutura devotio. De his loquor qui mox ut nati sunt renascuntur, et rapti ab hac vita aeternae beatitudini deputantur. Grevinchovius in Disputatione de Electione ex fide praevisa, pag. 143, hoc argumento irretitus, eo tandem delabitur, ut in dubium vocet utrum sit ulla infantium electio necne. Sed quorum est vita aeterna, illorum proculdubio est electio ad vitam aeternam, cum numerus glorificatorum numerum praedestinatorum sive electorum non excedat. Nam quos praedestinavit glorificavit, et non alios, ut recte Augustinus illum locum Apostoli exposuit. Sic sanus Prosper: Non alii venient in consortium haereditatis Christi, quam qui ante constitutionem mundi electi sunt, et praedestinati atque praesciti secundum propositum ejus, qui omnia operatur secundum consilium voluntatis suae. Si ergo quidam infantes haereditate caelesti donantur, iidem etiam praedestinantur sive eliguntur.
english: Prosper agrees (On Free Choice): in infants neither prior nor later devotion is chosen — he means those reborn as soon as born, and snatched from this life into eternal beatitude. Grevinchovius (Disputation on Election from foresighted faith, p. 143), caught by this, finally doubts whether there is any infant election at all. But whoever has eternal life surely has election to eternal life — the glorified do not outnumber the predestined. Whom he predestined, them he glorified, and no others (so Augustine on the Apostle). Sound Prosper: none enter Christ's inheritance but those elected before the world's foundation, predestined and foreknown according to his purpose. If some infants receive the heavenly inheritance, those same are predestined or elect.

source_text: Sed Grevinchovius fortasse id voluit, omnes infantes salvari promiscue, ac proinde nullam esse electionem infantium. Sed huic uni malesano disputatori oppono catholicae Ecclesiae judicium, quae semper sensit omnes infantes nasci filios irae, renasci autem non omnes, sed illos solos quos Deus indebita gratia dignatur. Summa est: Christus non est praedestinatus ex aliqua praevisione meritorum; neque infantes Christianorum: Ergo nec reliqui Christiani, quorum omnium electio est uniusmodi et ejusdem rationis cum electione sui Capitis, et inter se.
english: Or Grevinchovius meant all infants are saved alike, so there is no infant election. Against that one unsound disputant stands the catholic Church's judgment: all infants are born children of wrath; not all are reborn — only those God dignifies with unowed grace. Sum: Christ is not predestined from foresight of merits; nor Christian infants. Therefore neither are the remaining Christians — whose election is of one kind and the same ratio with their Head's, and among themselves.

source_text: In comparativa electione et rejectione hominum est abyssus quaedam inscrutabilis, et arcanum nulla humana curiositate pulsandum. Nam si ad rationis humanae calculos revocaretur, injustitiae speciem prae se ferret, quod ex duobus prorsus aequalibus unus gratioso beneplacito Dei ad vitam destinatur, alter relinquitur.
english: In comparative election and rejection of men there is an inscrutable abyss — a secret no human curiosity may pry into. Brought back to the sums of human reason, it would look like injustice: of two wholly equal, one is destined to life by God's gracious good pleasure, the other left.

source_text: Ostentum est hoc ab Apostolo, Rom. ix. ubi gratuita Jacobi electione et Esavi praeteritione declarata, statim amolitur illam objectionem, quam humana ratio suggerit, nimirum, Posito tali beneplacito, secundum quod nondum natis fratribus, priusquam nihil fecissent boni vel mali, unus diligatur, alter odio habeatur, injustitiam quandam esse apud Deum, vers. 14. Quam objectionem non solvendo solvit, dum ad inscrutabilem altitudinem sapientiae ac judicii Divini referendam docet, Rom. xi. vers. 33. 34.
english: Paul shows it in Rom. 9: after stating Jacob's gratuitous election and Esau's being passed by, he at once thrusts off the objection human reason prompts — that if by such good pleasure one unborn brother is loved and the other hated before either did good or evil, there is injustice with God (v. 14). He solves it by not solving it: he sends it up to the inscrutable height of divine wisdom and judgment (Rom. 11:33-34).

source_text: Omnes Orthodoxi in hoc praedestinationis et praeteritionis negotio tale arcanum agnoverunt, et Praedestinationem ex praevisis actibus humanis eo argumento rejiciunt, quod tale arcanum excludat. Nam si Petrus praedestinatus fuerit quia praevidebatur a Deo ut crediturus, et in fide perseveraturus, Judas praeteritus fuerit quia praevidebatur ut in sua infidelitate moriturus, ratio praedestinandi et non praedestinandi jam in propatulo erit, nec quicquam arcani in se continebit.
english: All the Orthodox in this business of predestination and passing by have owned that secret — and reject predestination from foresighted human acts just because that empties the secret. If Peter was predestined because God foresaw he would believe and persevere, and Judas passed by because foresaw he would die in unbelief, the reason for predestining and not predestining is already out in the open, with nothing secret left.

source_text: At longe aliter sanctus Augustinus Contr. 2. Epistol. Pelag. lib. 4. cap. 6: Quare istos oves facit, et istos non facit, apud quem non est acceptio personarum, ipsa est quaestio quae pertinet ad illam altitudinem, etc. Et Prosper, De vocat. gent. lib. 1. cap. 23: Frustra profunditatem inscrutabilis gratiae per liberum arbitrium conantur aperire, qui causam electionis in eorum constituunt meritis qui eliguntur. Et cap. ultimo: Profunditas illius quaestionis, quam secundum admirationem Apostoli impervestigabilem confitemur, per liberi arbitrii velle et nolle non solvitur.
english: Far otherwise Augustine (Against Two Letters of the Pelagians 4.6): why he makes these sheep and not those — with whom there is no respect of persons — that very question belongs to that height. And Prosper (On the Calling of the Gentiles 1.23): in vain they try to open the depth of inscrutable grace by free choice, who plant election's cause in the merits of the elect. And in the last chapter: that question's depth, which with the Apostle's wonder we confess unsearchable, is not solved by free choice's willing and refusing.

source_text: Quod itaque a Catholicis olim contra Semipelagianos recte dictum fuit, idem nos in Arminianos electionem ex praevisione fidei et finalis perseverantiae statuentes torquemus: Haec si ita sint, comprehensa sunt a vobis inscrutabilia judicia Dei, etc. Nos autem incomprehensibilia credentes et demonstrantes judicia Dei, ex una massa perditionis alios salvari dicimus bonitate et gratia Dei, alios justo et occulto judicio derelinqui, Petr. Diac. De Incarn. cap. 7. Est ergo rejicienda illorum omnium sententia, qui tam facili compendio rationem reddunt electorum et rejectorum, quam neque orthodoxi Patres, nec ipse Apostolus in tertium caelum raptus reddere potuit.
english: What Catholics once rightly said against the Semi-Pelagians, we turn on Arminians who ground election in foresight of faith and final perseverance: if so, you have comprehended God's inscrutable judgments. We, believing and showing those judgments incomprehensible, say that from one mass of perdition some are saved by God's goodness and grace, others left by just and hidden judgment (Peter the Deacon, On the Incarnation 7). Reject, then, all who give so easy a short-cut reason of elect and rejected — a reason neither the orthodox Fathers nor the Apostle himself, caught up to the third heaven, could give.

source_text: Illa doctrina non recte explicat praedestinationem sive electionem, quae fructum, nullam efficaciam electionis agnoscit quoad electos in via salutis dirigendos, conservandos, atque ad ipsam metam eandem perducendos. Nam sacrae Scripturae specialem quandam operationem et providentiam Dei denotant a decreto electionis manantem, quae electos ab omnibus iis malis liberat, quae illorum salutem alioquin impedirent.
english: That doctrine does not rightly explain predestination or election: it grants the fruit, but no efficacy of election toward directing, keeping, and bringing the elect through to the goal on the way of salvation. Holy Scripture marks a special operation and providence of God flowing from the election decree — freeing the elect from all those evils that would otherwise block their salvation.

source_text: Horsum spectant illa Christi Servatoris dicta, Matt. xxiv: Ita ut in errorem inducantur, si fieri posset, etiam electi. Propter electos breviabuntur dies illi. Tale est ergo decretum electionis, ut ratione illius Deus in se suscipiat omnes obices removere, quae salutem electorum impedirent, et iis ea media procurare, quae salutem eorundem infallibiliter producent.
english: So Christ's words in Matt. 24: to lead astray, if possible, even the elect — and for the elect's sake those days will be shortened. The election decree is of that kind: by it God takes on himself to remove every obstacle that would block the elect's salvation, and to procure means that will infallibly produce it.

source_text: Huc etiam tendit illud Apostoli, Rom. viii. 28: Omnia in bonum eorum cooperantur, qui praedestinati sunt, et secundum propositum vocati. Speciali nimirum Dei providentia ita res omnes dirigente, ut quae maxime infesta videantur illorum saluti, eandem nihilo minus promoveant.
english: So also Paul, Rom. 8:28: all things work together for good for those who are predestined and called according to purpose — God's special providence so steering all things that what looks most hostile to their salvation still advances it.

source_text: Jam e contra pensitemus hanc, quam fingunt Arminiani, electionem, ex antecedanea fidei perseverantis praevisione. Talis electio tollit omnem vim operatricem electionis, quoad electos in via salutis conservandos aut promovendos. Nam qui ad vitam non eliguntur, nisi ex intuitu praecedentis perseverantiae ad extremum usque halitum praestitae, illis electio nihil contulit ad hunc cursum in fide et sanctitate consummandum. Omnes siquidem difficultates superasse intelliguntur, atque ad ipsum limen caeli appulisse, priusquam a Deo ad vitam sive regnum caeleste praedestinentur. Omnes autem salvandos perrexisse in via fidei et sanctitatis, recta ad regnum caelorum tetendisse, et tantum non intra portas penetrasse, priusquam a Deo ad vitam praedestinati fuerint, aut virtute praedestinationis suae ullam specialem gratiam a Deo acceperint, horrendum plane est, et Christianis auribus intolerandum, quae libenter admittunt illud Apostoli: Quos praedestinavit, hos et vocavit; quos vocavit, hos et justificavit; quos justificavit, hos et glorificavit, Rom. viii. 30.
english: Weigh by contrast the Arminian invention — election from prior foresight of persevering faith. That sort of election strips election of all operative force for keeping or advancing the elect on the way of salvation. If they are elected to life only by regard to perseverance already kept to the last breath, election gave them nothing toward finishing the course in faith and holiness. They are taken to have overcome every difficulty and reached heaven's very threshold before God predestines them to life. That all the saved pressed on in faith and holiness, aimed straight at the kingdom, and all but entered the gates before they were predestined — or received any special grace by virtue of predestination — is plainly horrendous, intolerable to Christian ears that gladly hear Paul: whom he predestined, he also called; whom he called, he also justified; whom he justified, he also glorified (Rom. 8:30).

source_text: Si nullum aliud argumentum suppeteret nobis, hoc unicum abunde infringere et evertere posset illam praedestinationem Arminianam, quod homines ponat tum demum ad vitam aeternam praedestinari, cum ad ipsam, superatis omnibus difficultatibus et periculis, pervenerint: quae rectius Postdestinatio quam Praedestinatio dicatur.
english: Even if we had no other argument, this alone would amply shatter that Arminian predestination: it has men predestined to eternal life only once they have already arrived, every difficulty and danger overcome. That is more rightly called Postdestination than Predestination.

source_text: Verum decretum electionis est segregativum singularium personarum, quos Deus aliis praeteritis ex speciali misericordia ad salutem obtinendam infallibiliter destinavit. Ipsum vocabulum eligendi hoc arguit, sub cujus formali significatione indicatur acceptio unius, altero rejecto. At in illo Arminianae electionis decreto, Quicunque crediderit, vitam aeternam obtinebit; Quicunque incredulus manserit, peribit, nulla est singularium personarum segregatio ab aliis, nulla aliarum praeteritio aut rejectio, cum Deus tali decreto cuilibet homini ex aequo salutem polliceatur, cuilibet ex aequo perditionem interminetur.
english: The true election decree segregates singular persons — those God, others passed by, has from special mercy infallibly destined to obtain salvation. The very word elect proves it: under its formal sense one is accepted, the other rejected. But in that Arminian decree — Whoever believes shall obtain eternal life; whoever remains unbelieving shall perish — there is no segregation of singular persons, no passing by or rejection of others, since by it God promises salvation equally to anyone and threatens perdition equally to anyone.

source_text: Huic argumento respondent Remonstrantes in Colloquio Hagiensi, pag. 53: Segregationem credentium esse segregationem singularium personarum; agnoscunt enim credentes esse singulares personas, pag. 51. Verum si id volumus, electionem sese extendere erga personas quasdam singulares, tanquam singulares, citra ullas qualitates in ipsis consideratas, et nominatim absque consideratione fidei, tum se pernegare electionem hoc modo singulares personas respicere. Sed haec facile refelluntur. Agnoscimus credentes esse singulares personas; nam omnis actio est singularium: sed hoc decreto, Quisquis crediderit, salvus erit, segregari a Deo singulares aliquas personas ad fidem vel vitam, aliis praeteritis, id demum pernegamus.
english: The Remonstrants answer at the Hague Colloquy (p. 53): segregation of believers is segregation of singular persons — for believers are singular persons (p. 51). If we mean election reaches certain singulars as singulars, apart from any qualities in them, and especially without regard to faith, they flatly deny election regards singulars that way. Easily answered. We grant believers are singular persons — every act is of singulars. What we deny is that by Whoever believes shall be saved God segregates some singulars unto faith or life, others passed by.

source_text: Primo, quia staret hoc decretum firmum et immobile, etiamsi nemo crederet, etiamsi omnes perirent; et e contra, etiamsi omnes crederent, et omnes servarentur. Tali ergo decreto, per modum legis aut Edicti, declaratur quibus officiis praestitis liceat cuilibet vitam aeternam adire, quibus neglectis non liceat: at interim, per modum decreti practici et segregativi, nemo segregatur aut prae aliis eligitur, nemo praeteritur aut relinquitur. Si enim Judas crediderit et perseveraverit, virtute hujus decreti servabitur: Si Petrus non crediderit et perseveraverit, virtute ejusdem damnabitur. Nihil hic decernitur Petro, quod non sub eadem conditione decernitur Judae; nihil negatur Judae, quod non sub eadem conditione negatur Petro. Pari lege et conditione, huic decreto inhaereamus, omnes destinantur ad salutem, omnes excluduntur a salute. Nulla igitur in hoc decreto singularium personarum segregatio, aut aliis praeteritis electio.
english: First: that decree would stand firm even if no one believed and all perished — or if all believed and all were saved. As law or edict it declares by what duties done anyone may come to eternal life, and by what neglected may not. But as a practical segregating decree, no one is set apart or chosen before others, no one passed by. If Judas believes and perseveres, by it he is saved; if Peter does not, by the same he is damned. Nothing is decreed for Peter not under the same condition for Judas; nothing denied Judas not under the same for Peter. Cling to that decree on equal law, and all are destined to salvation and all excluded from it. So there is no segregation of singulars, no election with others passed by.

source_text: Secundo, agnoscimus juxta tenorem praedicti decreti Petrum ad vitam aeternam separandum, postquam in fide perseveraverit: sed haec separatio consequitur ex consequente et contingente actu ipsius Petri, non oritur ex segregativo decreto ipsius Dei. Suo enim actu fuit segregatus ad salutem postquam praevisus est credidisse et perseverasse, sed praedicto decreto non fuit singulariter segregatus, sive ad fidem sive ad salutem. Simili hoc illustretur. Si Rex tale decretum sanciat, Quisquis muros oppugnatae urbis ascenderit, eques fiet; quisquis terga verterit, capite plectetur, singulares personae sunt qui muros scandunt, singulares personae qui fugiunt: neque tamen tali decreto dicitur Rex elegisse singulares quasdam personas ad equestrem dignitatem, alias autem praeteriisse; sed contulisse in singulares personas; destinasse autem illam dignitatem ex aequo omnibus, sive obtinendam, si bene se gesserint, sive amittendam, si secus. Talis per omnia est illa electio Arminiana; ac proinde non habet inclusam veram et realem separationem singularium personarum.
english: Second: we grant that by that decree's tenor Peter is to be set apart to eternal life once he has persevered in faith — but that separation follows from Peter's own consequent contingent act, not from a segregating decree of God. By his act he was set apart to salvation after he was foreseen to have believed and persevered; by the decree itself he was not singularly segregated unto faith or salvation. Like case: if a king enacts Whoever scales the besieged city's walls shall be knighted; whoever turns his back shall die — those who climb and those who flee are singular persons; yet the king is not said to have elected certain singulars to knighthood and passed others by, but to have conferred it on singulars and destined that dignity equally to all — to be won if they behave well, lost if not. Arminian election is of that kind throughout, and so includes no true real separation of singular persons.

source_text: Tertio, ad id quod responsum est negando, electionem sese extendere ad singulares personas qua singulares, regerimus, Nos haud affirmare hoc decretum respicere singulares qua singulares, sed qua singulariter Deo ex mera gratuita benevolentia dilectos. Vide Thomas, part. 1. qu. 23. art. 4: Praedestinatio aliquorum in salutem aeternam praesupponit, quod Deus illorum velit salutem. Ad quod pertinet electio et dilectio: Dilectio, in quantum vult iis hoc bonum salutis aeternae; Electio, in quantum hoc bonum aliquibus prae aliis vult. Et haec dilectio praesupponitur electioni.
english: Third: to their denial that election reaches singulars as singulars, we reply we do not claim the decree regards singulars merely as singulars, but as singularly loved by God from mere gratuitous goodwill. So Aquinas (ST 1.23.4): predestination of some to eternal salvation presupposes that God wills their salvation. That involves dilection and election — dilection insofar as he wills them the good of eternal salvation; election insofar as he wills that good to some before others. And dilection is presupposed to election.

source_text: Denique, quod dicunt electionem non tendere in singulares personas citra considerationem fidei in illis praevisae, fatemur electionem nunquam fieri absque omni consideratione bonarum qualitatum, fidei scilicet et sanctitatis: considerantur enim tanquam virtute electionis omnibus electis praeparatae et donandae. Sed non considerantur ut praesuppositae electionis decreto, tanquam causae, conditiones, aut occasiones ipsius electionis, sicut ostendunt Arminiani. Nam praedestinatio sive electio respicit quidem id quod est ex parte nostra, hoc est, fidem et obedientiam nostram, non sicut id quod inclinat voluntatem Dei ad volendum, sed sicut id ad cujus productionem Divina voluntas gratiam ordinavit. Bona enim qualitas aut operatio quaecunque in hominibus considerata non est ratio praedestinationis sed Terminus, ut bene Thomas, Comment. in Rom. 8. Consideretur ergo fides in electione, sed ut effectus, non ut ratio vel conditio electionis.
english: Finally, they say election does not reach singulars apart from foresighted faith in them. We grant election never happens without regard to good qualities — faith and holiness — but as prepared and to be given to all the elect by virtue of election. They are not presupposed to the election decree as causes, conditions, or occasions of election itself, as Arminians claim. Predestination does regard what is on our side — our faith and obedience — not as what bends God's will to will, but as that for whose production the divine will ordained grace. Any good quality or work considered in men is not the reason of predestination but its Terminus (so Aquinas on Rom. 8). Let faith be considered in election, then — as effect, not as reason or condition of election.

source_text: Ultimum argumentum nostrum hujusmodi erit: Non debemus introducere talem electionem, quae puram Dei gratiam evertit, et discrimen electorum et rejectorum ad bonum usum liberi arbitrii reducit: Sed electio ex fide praevisa, et non-electio ex infidelitate praevisa hoc facit.
english: Last argument: we must not bring in an election that overturns pure grace and reduces the split between elect and rejected to the good use of free choice. But election from foresighted faith — and non-election from foresighted unbelief — does exactly that.

source_text: Ad Majorem quod attinet, tam clara est, ut pudeat ipsos adversarios aperte asserere hanc specialem electionis gratiam aliunde, quam ex mero et solo Dei beneplacito dependere. At sapienter hoc expendit Augustinus, non posse talem gratuitam gratiam stabiliri, nisi stabiliatur simul absoluta haec praedestinatio, et minime ex praeviis arbitrii humani operationibus suspensa, De bono persever. cap. 2. Praedestinatio, inquit, praedicenda est, ut possit vera Dei gratia, hoc est, quae non secundum merita nostra detur, insuperabili munitione defendi. Praedestinationem autem intelligit, non Arminianam ex praevisione fidei et perseverantiae humanae ortam, sed Paulinam, quae fidem et perseverantiam electis praeparat ab aeterno, donatque tempore opportuno. Sine hac igitur praedestinatione, quam toto illo libro propugnat Augustinus, judicavit veram Dei gratiam non posse defendi.
english: The major is so clear adversaries are ashamed to say outright that this special election-grace hangs on anything but God's mere sole good pleasure. Augustine wisely weighs it (On the Gift of Perseverance 2): such free grace cannot stand unless absolute predestination stands with it — not hung on prior acts of human choice. Predestination must be preached, he says, so true grace (not given according to our merits) can be defended by impregnable walls. He means not Arminian predestination from foresight of human faith and perseverance, but Pauline — which prepares faith and perseverance for the elect from eternity and gives them in due time. Without that predestination, which Augustine defends through the whole book, he judged true grace cannot be defended.

source_text: Quinetiam ipsi Scholastici saniores, qui plus aequo tribuere solent humano arbitrio, tamen non audent electorum et praeteritorum discrimen ad bonum et malum usum liberi arbitrii in gratia amplexanda vel repellenda revocare. Unde Thomas, Qu. disp. de praed. art. 2: Hoc ipsum velle accipere gratiam est ex praedestinatione Divina. Et Durandus, pag. 250: Omne bonum quod fit ab aliquo, vel quod juvat eum ad consecutionem finis supernaturalis, sive per causam, sive per occasionem, cadit sub effectu praedestinationis.
english: Even the sounder scholastics, who usually credit free choice more than is due, dare not reduce the split between elect and passed-by to good or bad use of free choice in embracing or rejecting grace. So Aquinas (Disputed Questions on Predestination, art. 2): this very willing to receive grace is from divine predestination. And Durandus (p. 250): every good done by someone, or that helps him reach the supernatural end — whether as cause or occasion — falls under predestination's effect.

source_text: Jam ad Minorem accedamus. Dicimus ergo hanc electionem et praeteritionem, quam ex fide et infidelitate praevisa fieri defendunt, gratiam Dei ex merito humanae voluntatis suspendere. Primo igitur: Gratia Dei propriissime sumpta est favor ille, vel aeterna Dei benevolentia secundum quam vult huic singulari personae vitam aeternam conferre. At hic amor sive favor Dei, quod est primum donum in quo caetera omnia donantur, ex sententia Remonstrantium datur et negatur prout homines prius bene aut male usi fuerint libero suo arbitrio, in admittenda aut repellenda illa sufficienti gratia quam omnibus oblatam asseverant. Hoc perinde est, ac si dicerent, Deus hominem ad vitam aeternam amare incepit, quia hominis liberum arbitrium ad gratiam se applicavit.
english: Now the minor. This election and passing by from foresighted faith and unbelief, we say, hangs God's grace on the merit of the human will. First: grace of God most properly is that favor — eternal benevolence — by which he wills to confer eternal life on this singular person. But that love or favor, the first gift in which all others are given, the Remonstrants have given or denied as men first used free choice well or ill in admitting or rejecting the sufficient grace they say is offered to all. That is as much as to say: God began to love a man unto eternal life because the man's free choice applied itself to grace.

source_text: Secundo, Gratia Dei dicuntur illa dona supernaturalia, quibus Spiritus sanctus imbuit, refingit et vivificat animas nostras, qualia sunt fides, charitas, reliquaque quibus omnes regenerati donantur. Haec etiam gratia juxta opinionem Arminii datur aut non datur pro diversis meritis humanarum voluntatum. Nam si electio ex fide praevisa consequatur, quaero unde haec fides in Petro potius quam in Juda fuerit praevisa. Non possunt obtendere specialem gratiam in praedestinatione Petro praeparatam causam fuisse quod is crediderit; quia hanc praedestinationem explodunt, et fidem praedestinatione priorem statuunt. Recurrant itaque necesse est ad specialem actum liberi arbitrii, in Petro specialiter sese accommodantis ad illa media, quae Deus ad fidem generandam non minus Judae quam Petro suppeditavit. At hoc quid aliud est, quam agnoscere gratiam monitricem, aut motricem humanae voluntatis ex mera Dei misericordia omnibus promiscue offerri, sed gratiam voluntatis vivificatricem pro diversis singulorum meritis in illa priore gratia accipienda aut repellenda conferri.
english: Second: grace of God also means those supernatural gifts by which the Holy Spirit imbues, reshapes, and vivifies our souls — faith, charity, and the rest given to all the regenerate. On Arminius's view that grace too is given or withheld by the diverse merits of human wills. If election follows foresighted faith, why was that faith foresighted in Peter rather than Judas? They cannot claim special grace prepared for Peter in predestination caused him to believe — they explode that predestination and set faith prior to it. So they must fall back on a special free-choice act in Peter, specially fitting itself to means God supplied no less to Judas than to Peter for generating faith. What is that but to grant that admonishing or moving grace is offered from mere mercy to all alike, while vivifying grace of the will is conferred by each one's diverse merits in accepting or rejecting that prior grace?

source_text: Scio Arminii discipulos hoc negare: sed velint nolint, stabilita hac praedestinatione hominum ex praevisione fidei, non possunt aliam gratiam admittere, quam eam quam tandem admisit ipse Pelagius; non possunt illam agnoscere, quam ubique ut fateatur, urget Augustinus. Sed qualem gratiam admisit Pelagius? Operatur Deus in nobis velle quod bonum est, velle quod sanctum est, dum nos terrenis cupiditatibus deditos futurae gloriae magnitudine et praemiorum pollicitatione succendit, dum revelatione sapientiae in desiderium Dei stupentem suscitat voluntatem, dum nobis suadet omne quod bonum est. Haec profecto sunt ea media quibus administratis Arminius fingit Deum speculari quinam credituri sunt, quinam non credituri, et sic eos ad vitam eligere, quos praevidet recte iis usuros, eos praeterire quos praevidet iisdem abusuros. Sed quid ad hoc Augustinus? Nos, inquit, eam gratiam nolumus. Istam fateatur Pelagius, qua futurae gloriae magnitudo non solum promittitur, verum etiam creditur et speratur; nec solum revelatur sapientia, verum etiam et amatur; nec suadetur solum omne quod bonum est, verum et persuadetur. Hanc autem gratiam quae fidem, spem et charitatem infundit, quae facit ut faciamus, ea est quam non ex merito dari contendebant Catholici, hoc est, non ex praeeunte bono usu liberi arbitrii, sed ex mera misericordia Dei. Sic in Concilio Diospolitano praecipitur Pelagio, ut fateatur gratiam Dei non dari secundum merita nostra: atque haec ratio subjungitur, Ut vera sit gratia, id est, gratis data per ejus misericordiam qui dixit, MISEREBOR CUIUS MISERTUS FUERO.
english: Arminius's disciples deny it — but will they or nill they, once predestination from foresight of faith is fixed, they can admit no grace but what Pelagius at last admitted; they cannot own what Augustine everywhere presses him to confess. What grace did Pelagius grant? God works in us to will the good and the holy while he kindles us by future glory and promised rewards, raises the stunned will by wisdom's revelation into desire of God, and advises us of every good. Those are the very means by whose administration Arminius has God watching who will believe and who will not — electing those he foresees will use them well, passing by those he foresees will abuse them. Augustine: We do not want that grace. Let Pelagius confess the grace by which future glory is not only promised but believed and hoped; wisdom not only revealed but loved; every good not only advised but persuaded. That grace which pours in faith, hope, and charity, and makes us do — Catholics held it is not given from merit, not from prior good use of free choice, but from God's mere mercy. So at Diospolis Pelagius is ordered to confess grace is not given according to our merits — reason: that it may be true grace, freely given through the mercy of him who said, I WILL HAVE MERCY ON WHOM I WILL HAVE MERCY.

source_text: Ut verbo absolvam: Quandoquidem haec opinio de electione singularium personarum ad vitam ex praevisa fide eorundem involvit haec duo maxime gratiae inimica, nempe, Primum Dei amorem quo ad vitam destinat singulares personas oriri ex bono usu liberi arbitrii per gratiam praeventi, et ipsam fidem non certis personis ex speciali dono infundi, sed ex speciali bono actu liberi arbitrii in certis personis concipi, ab omnibus orthodoxis explodenda est; et e contra statuendum, bonum usum gratiae a Deo praescitum non fuisse causam quae Deum movebat ut hos prae aliis eligeret, sed fuisse potius speciale beneficium electionis.
english: In a word: this view — electing singular persons to life from their foresighted faith — involves two things most hostile to grace: that God's first love destining them to life arises from the good use of grace-prevented free choice; and that faith itself is not infused into certain persons by a special gift, but conceived in them by a special good act of free choice. All the orthodox must explode it. On the contrary: the good use of grace God foreknew was not the cause that moved him to elect these before others — it was rather a special benefit of election.

source_text: De Reprobatione quaedam prolegomena una cum sententia Arminiana. Hisce praelibatis, alteram susceptae disputationis partem mox aggrediar, quae est de praeteritione, non-electione sive Reprobatione illarum personarum quas Deus eximia illa et speciali misericordia, quae ad vitam infallibiliter perducit, non est dignatus. Atque hic, et uspiam, obtinere debet illud Paulinum, Rom. xii. 3. μὴ ὑπερφρονεῖν παρ' ὃ δεῖ φρονεῖν. Nam otiosae curiositati tantum deerits discere, quantum libuerit inquirere, ut prudenter Tertullianus, De anima, in fine. In hac ergo materia tractanda duo scopuli sunt omni cautione fugiendi.
english: Cap. VII — some prolegomena on Reprobation, with the Arminian view. Preliminaries tasted, I turn next to the other half of the dispute: passing by, non-election, or Reprobation of those God has not dignified with that excellent special mercy that infallibly leads to life. Here and everywhere Paul's word must hold (Rom. 12:3): not to think beyond what one ought. Idle curiosity will always find as much to learn as it cares to ask (so Tertullian wisely, On the Soul, at the end). In treating this matter, two rocks must be fled with all caution.

source_text: Unus, quo impingitur in Bonitatem Divinam; in quam illi peccare videntur, qui docent Deum absoluta primaria voluntate, omnem peccati considerationem antecedente, quosdam creasse ut perderet: atque ex hac perdendi voluntate putant dimanare quicquid circa non-electos a Deo agitur. Nos cum Prospero potius dicendum arbitramur, Aliam esse nascendi, aliam pereundi causam: Ut nascantur homines, Conditoris esse beneficium; ut pereant, praevaricatoris esse meritum. Creantur quidem a Deo, quos praevidit aeternae vitae participes nunquam fore; creantur, quos decrevit suo libero arbitrio, idque speciali gratia minime fulto, uti; creantur denique, quos decrevit propter peccata justissime damnationi subjicere. Perditio interim haec sive damnatio non finis creationis, sed merces transgressionis aestimanda est — ut semper stet illud Dei apud Hoseam, Perditio tua ex te, Hos. xiii. 9.
english: First rock: striking divine Goodness — those who teach God by absolute primary will, before any regard to sin, created some in order to destroy them, and that from that destroying will flows whatever God does about the non-elect. With Prosper we rather say: one cause of being born, another of perishing — birth is the Creator's benefit; perishing is the transgressor's desert. God does create those he foresaw would never share eternal life; those he decreed to use free choice with no special grace undergirding it; those he decreed most justly to subject to damnation for sins. Yet that perdition or damnation is not creation's end but transgression's wage — so Hosea may always stand: Your destruction is from you (Hos. 13:9).

source_text: Porro, altum illud et arcanum non-electionis sive reprobationis decretum non est ita omnibus Dei actionibus importune ingerendum, quasi cum non-electis Deus nihil ageret, nisi ex hoc non-electionis decreto. Utcunque enim Deus quorundam noluerit eousque misereri, ut decernet eos ad vitam aeternam infallibiliter perducere, atque voluerit cosdem interveniente illorum peccato exitio destinare, tamen dum agunt in terris, atque praesertim intra Ecclesiae septa, in conferendis tum beneficiis corporalibus tum spiritualibus, atque ad salutem ex rei natura tendentibus, multa cum illis agit ex amore communi sive φιλανθρωπίᾳ, qua universum genus humanum prosequitur, multa ex foedere, quo secundum suam ordinationem omnibus Ecclesiae visibilis membris supernaturalia quaedam beneficia largitur. In eventu haec omnia Dei dona fiunt reprobis noxia et perniciosa: non tamen dicendum aut sentiendum est, Deum propter decretum reprobationis intendere abusum donorum suorum, et hostili animo ea suppeditare non-electis, ut eos hisce abutentes puniat ac perdat. Pauli potius sententia amplectanda est, qui ostendit Deum cum non-electis multa agere ex illa redundanti benignitate quae ad omnes homines se diffundit, quamvis non pari gradu aut mensura. Huc spectant illa, Rom. ii. 4. 5: An divitias bonitatis ejus et patientiae contemnis, ignorans te benignitate Dei ad resipiscentiam deduci? Sed pro duritia tua, et corde quod resipiscere nescit, thesaurizas tibi iram, etc.
english: Further: that deep secret decree of non-election or reprobation must not be awkwardly stuffed into every act of God, as if with the non-elect he did nothing except from that decree. Though he would not pity some so far as to decree their infallible leading to eternal life, and willed to destine them to ruin with their sin intervening, yet while they live on earth — especially within the Church's pale — in giving bodily and spiritual benefits that by nature tend to salvation, he does much with them from common love or φιλανθρωπία toward the whole human race, and much from the covenant by which he lavishes certain supernatural benefits on all members of the visible Church. In the event those gifts become noxious to the reprobate — yet one must not say God by the reprobation decree intends abuse of his gifts, and hostilely supplies them to the non-elect so that abusing them they may be punished and destroyed. Rather take Paul's word: God does much with the non-elect from that overflowing kindness that spreads to all, though not in equal measure (Rom. 2:4-5 — or do you despise the riches of his goodness and patience, not knowing God's kindness leads you to repentance? But by your hardness you treasure up wrath).

source_text: Jam vero ex adverso nonnulli sunt qui praedictum scopulum satis solicite vitant, sed interim in alium haud minus perniciosum incurrunt. Hi in decreto Reprobationis explicando bonitatem Dei ita defendunt, ut in opposito Electionis decreto specialem et ex gratuito beneplacito dimanantem misericordiam plane obruant. Quali illud Paulinum, Rom. ix. 18. Miserebor cui voluero, ac si sonaret, Miserebor ejus quem justum esse cognovero, cujus promptam fidem videro, quem praeceptis meis obedire perspexero, uti haec verba exposuit, vel potius corrupit Faustus Semipelagianus, De libero arbitrio lib. 1. cap. 3. Quod itaque de Iove suo cecinit poeta, Rex Jupiter omnibus idem, id illi de vero Deo affirmant, Illum scilicet ex aequo omnibus vitam aeternam velle, administratis autem mediis ad eam rem sufficientibus, quosdam ad gloriam eligere, dum praevidet eos hisce mediis recte usuros; alios praeterire, quia praevidet iisdem male usuros. Unde nulla in eligendo specialis Dei misericordia ostenditur, nec in reprobando Divinae voluntatis libertas ostenditur; nec denique in comparata illa consideratione, cur hic electus, iste praeteritus, ulla altitudo invenitur; sed eorum discrimen electorum et non-electorum ad libertatem humanarum voluntatum revocatur. Recte hoc fatetur Spalatensis, eos qui praedestinationem et reprobationem ex praescientia tenent debere efficaciam gratiae ponere in voluntate hominis, et media ad salutem humanam necessaria tanquam a Deo praeparata omnibus admittere, non tamen ut praedestinata ulli; De Republ. Eccl. lib. 7. cap. 11. num. 198.
english: Opposite rock: some carefully dodge the first, then hit another no less deadly. Explaining the reprobation decree, they so defend God's goodness that in the opposite election decree they crush special mercy flowing from gratuitous good pleasure. As if Rom. 9:18 — I will have mercy on whom I will — meant I will have mercy on him I know just, whose ready faith I see, whom I see obey my precepts (so Faustus the Semi-Pelagian exposits, or rather corrupts, On Free Choice 1.3). What the poet sang of Jupiter — King Jupiter the same to all — they affirm of the true God: he wills eternal life equally to all; with sufficient means administered, he elects to glory those he foresees will use them well, and passes by those he foresees will abuse them. So electing shows no special mercy, reprobating no liberty of divine will, and in why this one is elect and that passed by no height remains — the split is recalled to human wills' liberty. Spalato rightly grants that holders of predestination and reprobation from foresight must put grace's efficacy in man's will, and admit means to salvation as prepared by God for all, yet not as predestined to any (Ecclesiastical Republic 7.11.198).

source_text: Nos autem, sicuti ipsum electionis beneficium ex gratuito Dei beneplacito, non ex praeeunte aliquo hominis bono actu pendere docuimus, ita negationem ejusdem beneficii, quam non-electionem, praeteritionem, sive reprobationem negativam appellare solemus, ex eadem liberrima Dei voluntate arcessimus, facientis de suo quod vult. Qui in multis pessime, in hoc non male philosophatur Episcopius, in Thesibus suis Disput. 22. de Justific. thes. 3: Aliud longe est, inquit, non velle punire; aliud, summo bono aliquem afficere velle. Nos a pari etiam dicimus: Aliud longe est velle aliquem punire, aliud non velle aliquem summo bono afficere.
english: But as we taught that election's benefit hangs on God's gratuitous good pleasure, not on some prior good act of man, so the negation of that benefit — which we call non-election, passing by, or negative reprobation — we fetch from the same freest will of God, doing with his own what he wills. Episcopius, often worst in philosophy, here not badly (Theses, Disp. 22 on Justification, th. 3): it is one thing not to will to punish; another to will to affect someone with the highest good. By parity we say: it is one thing to will to punish someone; another not to will to affect someone with the highest good.

source_text: Prior illa voluntas puniendi in Deo considerari non potest aut debet, nisi cum respectu antecedaneo ad peccatum personae puniendae, tanquam causam demeritoriam; sed haec voluntas praetereundi, vel noluntas, ut ita loquar, praedestinandi, considerari potest absque respectu antecedaneo ad peccatum personae non-electae. Ratio autem hujus discriminis inde petenda est, quod punitio sit actus vindicativae justitiae, ac proinde culpam vindicta dignam praesupponit: Non-electio autem sive reprobatio negativa non poena sit, sed gratuiti beneficii negatio, quod Deus nemini tenetur exhibere; ac proinde ex natura rei culpam antecedaneam haud praerequirat.
english: The will to punish in God cannot be considered without prior regard to the sin of the one to be punished, as demeritorious cause. But the will to pass by — or nolition, so to speak, of predestinating — can be considered without prior regard to the non-elect person's sin. Why the difference? Punishment is an act of vindicative justice, and so presupposes a fault worthy of vengeance. Non-election or negative reprobation is not a punishment, but denial of a gratuitous benefit God owes no one — and so by its nature hardly requires an antecedent fault.

source_text: Atque hic notandum est, Reprobationis vocabulum apud Theologos trifariam sumi, ut recte a doctissimo Junio est observatum. Primo sumitur pro praeteritione et damnatione conjunctim: Et hoc sensu reprobi appellantur, non ex eo solummodo quod Deus decreverit gratiam efficacem illis negare, atque sic permittere ut a fine beatitudinis deficiant, sed quod insuper eos ad aeternas poenas destinaverit.
english: Note here: among theologians the word reprobation is taken three ways, as the learned Junius rightly observed. First: for passing by and damnation jointly. In that sense people are called reprobate not only because God decreed to deny them efficacious grace and so permit them to fall short of beatitude's end, but also because he destined them to eternal punishments.

source_text: Qui sub unico vocabulo reprobandi ambos hosce actus Divinae voluntatis praetereundi et damnandi conjunctim includunt, vix poterunt aliquid certi de reprobatione affirmare. Nam quod est antecedaneum ad actum praedamnandi, non erit semper antecedaneum ad actum praetereundi: quod habet rationem causae motivae ad praedamnationem, non habebit illico naturam causae motivae aut demeriti causantis ad praeteritionem.
english: Those who under one word of reprobating join both divine acts — passing by and damning — can hardly affirm anything certain about reprobation. What precedes the act of predamning is not always what precedes the act of passing by: what moves as cause toward predamnation does not at once have the nature of a moving cause or demerit causing toward praeterition.

source_text: Secundo sumitur vocabulum reprobationis a nonnullis pro solo damnationis decreto: atque hoc sensu reprobari nihil aliud est quam aeternis cruciatibus destinari. Qui huic vocabulo nihil aliud inesse volunt quam destinationem ad poenas aeternas, in eo recte agunt, quod peccatum talis destinationis causam ponant; sed in eo labuntur, quod nihil altius in decreto electionis et rejectionis agnoscunt. Tertio igitur reprobationis vocabulum, qua est electioni contradictorie oppositum, sumitur pro sola praeteritione sive non-electione, atque innuit aeternam ordinationem in mente Divina negandi certis personis gratiam efficacem, et ad gloriam de facto perducentem. Potest autem talis reprobatio intelligi absque antecedaneo intuitu ad peccata rejectorum, tanquam causas motivas praedictae praeteritionis. Nam praesupposita tali praeteritione, tum demum praevidentur homines in peccato morituri et propter peccatum cruciandi. Deus igitur ab aeterno voluit hosce praeteritos, non-electos sive reprobatos addicere aeternis cruciatibus, non tamen quia praeteriti, sed quia mali et damnatione digni. Neque voluit eos punire in primo instanti rationis, in quo noluit glorificare, sed in illo altero, in quo illos consideravit ut peccatores a peccatis suis nunquam liberandos.
english: Second sense: some take reprobation for the damnation decree alone — to be reprobated is nothing but to be destined to eternal torments. Those who put only that in the word are right to set sin as cause of such destination; they slip in acknowledging nothing higher in the decree of election and rejection. Third sense: reprobation as contradictorily opposite to election is taken for praeterition or non-election alone — an eternal ordination in the divine mind to deny certain persons efficacious grace that in fact leads to glory. That reprobation can be understood without prior regard to the rejected's sins as moving causes of the passing by. Once such praeterition is presupposed, then at last men are foresighted as about to die in sin and be tormented for sin. From eternity God willed to addict these passed-by non-elect to eternal torments — not because passed by, but because evil and worthy of damnation. He did not will to punish them in the first instant of reason in which he refused to glorify, but in that other in which he considered them sinners never to be freed from their sins.

source_text: Sententiae nostrae haec summa est: Praescientiam demeritorum non esse causam praeteritionis, non-electionis sive reprobationis stricte et proprie sumptae; sed sicuti ex mero Dei beneplacito dependet, quod certae quaedam personae per specialem providentiam, quam Praedestinationem appellamus, infallibiliter ordinentur ad gratiam et gloriam, ita ex mera Dei libertate dependet, quod aliae quaedam personae non ita ordinentur, sed a gratia hac efficaci destituantur, et a gloria deficere permittantur. Si quis ergo a nobis quaerat, cur Deus facillime et justissime potuerit tam Paulum quam Judam duritiae suae nativae relinquere, et aeternae miseriae addicere, qui etiam facillime potuit utrumque emollire, et ad aeternam gloriam perducere — si, inquam, quaeratur cur Judae non praeparaverit gratiam efficacem qua emolliretur et servaretur, Paulo praeparaverit; cur Judam non ordinaverit infallibiliter ad gloriam, Paulum ordinaverit — non confugimus ad praevisam fidem aut merita Pauli, neque ad praevisam Judae infidelitatem aut demerita, sed dicimus Deum misereri cujus vult emolliendo, et cujus vult minime misereri permissive indurando: Neque hujus tam diversae providentiae circa hasce personas aliam causam assignamus praeter Voluntatem Dei, quae est prima rectitudo. Atque sic habetis sententiam nostram.
english: Our sum: foresight of demerits is not the cause of praeterition, non-election, or reprobation strictly taken. As it hangs on mere good pleasure that certain persons by that special providence we call Predestination are infallibly ordained to grace and glory, so it hangs on mere divine liberty that others are not so ordained, but left without this efficacious grace and permitted to fall short of glory. If anyone asks why God could most easily and justly leave both Paul and Judas to native hardness and eternal misery — and could as easily soften both and lead them to eternal glory — why he prepared efficacious softening grace for Paul and not Judas, ordained Paul infallibly to glory and not Judas: we do not flee to Paul's foresighted faith or merits, nor Judas's foresighted unbelief or demerits. We say God has mercy on whom he will by softening, and on whom he will he has least mercy by permissive hardening. For providence so diverse about these persons we assign no cause but the Will of God, which is the first rectitude. So you have our opinion.

source_text: Qui nobis adversantur e contra statuunt, Causam non-electionis sive reprobationis esse ea peccata in quibus reprobati praevidentur morituri. Atque haec est sententia quorundam Jesuitarum. Alii praevisam infidelitatem cum perseverantia finali in eadem dicunt esse causam reprobationis, ita ut nemo nisi in ipso mortis articulo consideretur a Deo ut reprobatus vel non-electus, idque propter hanc contumacem infidelitatem contra Deum evocantem. Atque haec sententia est Arminii et eorum quos Remonstrantes vocare solent.
english: Those against us hold the contrary: the cause of non-election or reprobation is the sins in which the reprobate are foresighted as about to die — so certain Jesuits. Others say foresighted unbelief with final perseverance in it is the cause, so that no one is considered by God reprobate or non-elect except in the very article of death, and that for contumacious unbelief against God calling. That is Arminius's view, and of those usually called Remonstrants.

source_text: Jam quibus argumentis hanc suam sententiam fulciant, qui hanc reprobationem sive praeteritionem a praevisis demeritis, vel infidelitate et perseverantia finali in eadem, arcessunt, audiamus. Neque opus est ut accurate distinguantur argumenta Jesuitarum et Arminianorum: nam iisdem plane fundamentis nituntur. Ut igitur inter legendum se nobis obtulerunt, ea mixtim proponemus. Hisce autem refutatis, ad sententiae nostrae confirmationem erit accedendum.
english: Now let us hear by what arguments they prop this view — those who fetch reprobation or praeterition from foresighted demerits, or from unbelief and final perseverance in it. No need to split Jesuit and Arminian arguments carefully: they rest on plainly the same foundations. As they met us in reading, we will set them out mixed. Once refuted, we will turn to confirming our own opinion.

source_text: Cap. VIII. Argumenta adversariorum proponuntur et solvuntur. Accedamus jam ad argumenta adversariorum, qui contendunt peccata ea cum quibus reprobi praevidentur vita decessuri, fuisse causam meritoriam et motivam reprobationis Divinae.
english: Chapter VIII — the adversaries' arguments proposed and solved. We turn now to their arguments: they contend that the sins with which the reprobate are foresighted as about to leave life were the meritorious and moving cause of divine reprobation.

source_text: Sed priusquam horum rationes in medium afferantur, id praestruendum est: Non quaeri de reprobatione, quatenus denotat apud nonnullos Theologos voluntatem damnandi sive cruciandi reprobatos: Nam extra controversiam esse debet, hanc voluntatem Dei semper respicere peccatum ut meritoriam causam decretae punitionis. Sed quaeritur de reprobatione, quatenus denotat absolutum illud et aeternum Dei decretum, quo negavit ab aeterno Caino et Judae efficacem gratiam, quam illis praeparare et dare potuisset, si ita illi complacitum fuisset.
english: Before their reasons are brought forward, this must be prefaced: we are not asking about reprobation as some theologians mean the will to damn or torment the reprobate — that will of God always regards sin as meritorious cause of decreed punishment, beyond dispute. We ask about reprobation as that absolute eternal decree by which from eternity God denied Cain and Judas efficacious grace he could have prepared and given them, had it so pleased him.

source_text: Quibus Deus in aeterno suo decreto talem gratiam eandemque ordinationem ad gloriam denegavit, eos non elegit sed praeteriit et, uti loquuntur Theologi, reprobavit. Illud etiam adjungendum est: Nos haud negare in omnibus hominibus, in quos cadit actus Divinae reprobationis, inveniri demeritum concomitans, vel subjecto adhaerescens: sed negamus praeteritionem illam sive non-electionem, quam reprobationem negativam vocamus, ex intuitu hujus demeriti profluxisse. Deus enim demeritum originale tam in electis quam reprobis intuetur, et tamen non pro discrimine causae, sed pro suo beneplacito vult eligere Jacobum, et non vult eligere, sed reprobare Esavum.
english: Those to whom God in his eternal decree denied such grace and the same ordination to glory, he did not elect but passed by — and, as theologians speak, reprobated. Add this: we do not deny that in all on whom divine reprobation falls there is found concomitant demerit adhering to the subject. What we deny is that that praeterition or non-election we call negative reprobation flowed from regard to that demerit. God sees original demerit in elect and reprobate alike — yet not by discrimination of cause, but by his good pleasure, he wills to elect Jacob, and wills not to elect but to reprobate Esau.

source_text: Quod autem attinet ad actualia demerita ex perseverantia finali in peccatis sive infidelitate orta, certum est et haec etiam praevideri ut futura in omnibus reprobis, sed ut futura concomitanter vel consequenter, non causaliter aut antecedenter ad actum praeteritionis Divinae. Non enim praeviderentur a Deo Cain aut Judas in improbitate sua et infidelitate morituri, nisi praesupposita antecedente Dei voluntate de non concedenda illis speciali gratia, qua emollirentur et ad fidem ac paenitentiam converterentur: quae negatio non-electionis sive reprobationis manifesta probatio est. Quis enim tam impie desipiat, ut dicat Deum malas hominum voluntates, quas voluerit quando voluerit, ubi voluerit, in bonum non posse convertere? ut recte Augustinus, Enchirid. cap. 98. Sed argumenta audiamus.
english: As for actual demerits from final perseverance in sins or unbelief: yes, these too are foresighted as future in all the reprobate — but as future concomitantly or consequently, not causally or antecedently to the divine act of praeterition. God would not foresee Cain or Judas dying in their wickedness and unbelief unless his prior will not to grant them special grace — by which they would be softened and turned to faith and penitence — were presupposed. That denial is plain proof of non-election or reprobation. Who would so impiously dote as to say God cannot turn evil human wills to good when, where, and as he wills? So Augustine rightly (Enchiridion 98). But let us hear the arguments.

source_text: Reprobationem igitur fluere ex praevisis hominum demeritis, primo probare conantur nonnulli ex illis Scripturae locis, in quibus Deus dicitur nequaquam velle ut homines pereant: Quod minime verum esset, si Deus sola sua voluntate, et non propter peccata, tantam hominum multitudinem reprobaret. Huc afferunt illud Ezek. xviii. 23, Nunquid voluntatis meae est mors impii? et Hos. xiii. 9. Perditio tua ex te. Item illud Apostoli, 1 Tim. ii. 4. Deus vult omnes salvos fieri. Et illud Servatoris, Matth. xi. 28. Venite ad me omnes; ejusque generis loca alia quamplurima, quae sigillatim repetere aut discutere non est necesse.
english: First they try to prove reprobation flows from foresighted human demerits from those Scripture places where God is said not to will that men perish — which would hardly be true, they say, if God by his will alone, and not for sins, reprobated so great a multitude. They cite Ezek. 18:23 (Is the death of the wicked of my will?), Hos. 13:9 (Your destruction is from you), 1 Tim. 2:4 (God wills all to be saved), Matt. 11:28 (Come to me, all), and many like places — no need to repeat or discuss them one by one.

source_text: Si id volunt adversarii, Deum seposita praevisione et consideratione antecedente demeritorum humanorum, velle ex aequo salutem universis hominibus, hoc nos negamus ex locis allegatis effici posse. Efficitur quidem, Deum voluntate simplicis complacentiae velle ut omnes credant, ut omnes resipiscant, ut nemo pereat, ut nemo damnetur; sed non efficitur, Deum voluntate praedestinante velle ex aequo, ante praevisionem demeritorum, in omnibus operari ut credant, ut resipiscant; operari ne pereant, ne damnentur: neque efficitur, Deum voluntate reprobante haud decrevisse negare quibusdam gratiam efficacem, et infallibilem ordinationem ad gloriam. Possunt enim haec duo simul consistere: Deus vult ut omnes credant, et nemo pereat, scilicet voluntate simplicis complacentiae; et, Deus vult permittere ut quidam in infidelitate sua voluntaria persistent, et ab aeterna salute deficiant. In eo igitur errant adversarii, quod sumunt haec duo, non-eligere sive reprobare, et velle perdere vel mortem aeternam inferre, pro aequipollentibus: cum non-electio vel praeteritio competere possit in creaturam integram, quod in angelis manifestum est; at voluntas perdendi vel morte aeterna afficiendi non potest cadere nisi in creaturam vitiatam: cum non-electio sit mera negatio gratuiti beneficii, Mors sive perditio sit stipendium commissi peccati. Est quidem verissimum, omnes non-electos infallibiliter ruituros in mortem aeternam: est etiam perspicuum, omnes non-electos ab aeterno positiva Dei voluntate huic morti adjudicatos: sed haec ad mortem deputatio non concipienda est ut in eodem signo rationis peracta, quo non-electio statuitur, sed in alio posteriore, quo non-electi perseverantia finalis in statu peccati praevidetur. Ex eo igitur quod Deus neminem vult perire absque antecedanea consideratione demeritorum, non sequitur, Deum neminem velle praeterire aut non-eligere absque antecedanea consideratione eorundem.
english: If adversaries mean that God, foresight of human demerits set aside, wills salvation equally to all, we deny the cited places prove that. They do prove that by the will of simple complacence God wills that all believe and repent, that none perish or be damned. They do not prove that by predestinating will he wills equally, before foresight of demerits, to work in all so they believe and repent, and not perish or be damned — nor that by reprobating will he has not decreed to deny some efficacious grace and infallible ordination to glory. Those two can stand together: God wills that all believe and none perish (simple complacence); and God wills to permit some to persist in voluntary unbelief and fall short of eternal salvation. Adversaries err in taking not-to-elect (or to reprobate) as equipollent with willing to destroy or inflict eternal death. Non-election or praeterition can fall on an intact creature — plain in the angels — but the will to destroy or afflict with eternal death can fall only on a vitiated creature: non-election is mere denial of a gratuitous benefit; death or perdition is sin's wage. True: all the non-elect will infallibly rush into eternal death, and from eternity God's positive will adjudges them to it — but that deputing to death is not conceived in the same sign of reason as non-election, but in a later one where final perseverance in sin is foresighted. That God wills none to perish without prior regard to demerits does not entail that he wills none to pass by or not-elect without that same prior regard.

source_text: Vasques Jesuita, qui nostrae defensioni non admodum favet, tamen hac in re nobis suffragatur: Ea gratia, inquit ille, peculiari et efficaci, quae est propria praedestinatorum, Deus absque dubio omnes reprobos ex seipso antecedente voluntate exclusit, nulla prorsus ex ipsis arrepta occasione. Negatio enim hujus gratiae nostram libertatem omnino praecedit. Hoc nobis perinde est ac si dixisset, Deum ex seipso, antecedente voluntate, nulla ex ipsorum demeritis arrepta occasione, omnes reprobos praeteriisse sive reprobasse.
english: Vasquez the Jesuit — no great friend of our defense — still sides with us here. By that peculiar efficacious grace proper to the predestined, he says, God without doubt excluded all the reprobate from himself by antecedent will, seizing no occasion at all from them. Denial of that grace wholly precedes our liberty. For us that is as good as saying: God from himself, by antecedent will, with no occasion taken from their demerits, passed by or reprobated all the reprobate.

source_text: Secundo, conantur demonstrare praevisa demerita esse causam reprobationis (quod mirum alicui videri potest) ex ipsa disputatione Apostoli Rom. ix. Ubi nobis videtur contrariam sententiam stabilire. Primo ex eo quod Apostolus vocat hanc reprobationem odium; Esau odio habui: Deus autem neminem odit nisi peccati causa.
english: Second, they try to prove foresighted demerits are the cause of reprobation — oddly enough — from Paul's own debate in Romans 9, where we take him to establish the opposite. First: the Apostle calls this reprobation hatred — Esau I hated — and God hates no one except for sin.

source_text: Respondeo primo, illos directe impingere in mentem et clara verba Apostoli hac sua argutatione. Nam Paulus id agit hoc in loco, ut doceat electionem et rejectionem personarum singularium non pendere ex diversis aut contrariis actibus hominum, sed ex diverso Dei beneplacito volentis hujus misereri, illius non misereri. Atque hanc ob causam non modo removet bonas eorum actiones, sed etiam malas; Cum nondum nati fuissent, aut aliquid boni aut mali egissent. Quod autem ad eos attinet qui obtendunt Deum non spectasse quidem opera quae fecerunt, sed quae praevidit eos facturos, atque inde dilexisse Jacobum, et odisse Esavum, cum sint ipso Apostolo perspicaciores, qui hanc responsionem excogitare non potuit, ego eos non refellam, sed suo insomnia frui permittam. Id tantum monebo, Augustinum patienter audiant, qui hoc inepto effugio irritatus in haec verba prorupit: Profecto desipitis, qui dicente veritate, NON EX OPERIBUS, SED EX VOCANTE DICTUM EST, vos dicitis, ex futuris operibus quae Deus illum facturum esse praesciebat, Jacob fuisse dilectum, etc. Contr. 2. Epist. Pelag. lib. 2, cap. 7.
english: First reply: their argument strikes straight against Paul's mind and plain words. In this place he teaches that election and rejection of particular persons do not hang on diverse or contrary human acts, but on God's diverse good pleasure — willing to have mercy on one, not on another. For that cause he removes not only their good acts but their evil ones: when they were not yet born, nor had done anything good or evil. As for those who claim God regarded not works done but works he foresaw they would do — and so loved Jacob and hated Esau — since they are sharper than the Apostle himself, who could not invent that answer, I will not refute them; let them enjoy their dream. Only this: hear Augustine patiently. Irritated by that inept escape he broke out: You truly dote who, when truth says NOT OF WORKS BUT OF HIM THAT CALLS, say Jacob was loved from future works God foresaw he would do (Against two Letters of the Pelagians 2.7).

source_text: Porro et illud notandum est, nos libenter agnoscere, in subjecto reprobato residere illam contagionem et indignitatem quae possit Deum reprobantem non modo ab omni crudelitate et injustitia, sed vel a levissima ejus suspicione, liberare. Nam cuicunque negatur haec specialis misericordia, certum est, non habuisse illum jus ad hoc, quod gratia talis ei praeparetur aut conferatur. Rationabiliter autem negatur quod nulla ratione debetur, ut recte Thomas. Huc accedit, quod non modo nullum jus habet ad tale beneficium, sed est suo insito vitio quasi proxime dispositus ad vindictam Dei excipiendam. Hoc Augustinus optime explicavit, Contra 2. Epist. Pelag. lib. 2, cap. 7. Status enim totius generis humani Deo eligenti et praetereunti repraesentatus, est status peccati, status mortis et meritae damnationis. Verum cum hic status communis sit omnium, tamque Jacobum involvat quam Esavum, potest afferri ut ratio congrua cur Deus utrumque juste possit relinquere, sed non potest commode obtendi ut causa motiva cur Esavum rejecerit, electo Jacobo, qui in eadem fuit conditione. Atque hinc Dionysius Carthusianus intolerabile esse affirmat, ut praescientia demeritorum dicatur ratio reprobationis.
english: Note also: we gladly grant that in the reprobate subject there resides that contagion and unworthiness which can free the reprobating God not only from cruelty and injustice, but even from the lightest suspicion of them. Whoever is denied this special mercy had no right that such grace be prepared or conferred. What is owed by no reason is reasonably denied — so Thomas. Add that he not only has no right to such a benefit, but by inborn vice is as it were proximately disposed to receive God's vengeance (Augustine, Against two Letters of the Pelagians 2.7). The state of the whole human race as presented to God electing and passing by is a state of sin, death, and merited damnation. But since that state is common to all and wraps Jacob as much as Esau, it can stand as a congruent reason why God may justly leave both — not as the moving cause why he rejected Esau while electing Jacob, who stood in the same condition. Hence Dionysius the Carthusian calls it intolerable that foresight of demerits be named the reason of reprobation.

source_text: Postremo (quod directe nervos hujus argumenti elidit) dico Deum posse dici odisse Esavum duplici respectu: Vel odisse ad vindictam et poenam aeternae mortis illi infligendam: atque sic non odit Esavum nisi qua peccatorem, et propter ipsum peccatum, ut hujus odii causam motivam et demeritoriam: Vel odisse Esavum ad specialis alicujus et indebiti beneficii negationem, hoc est minus dilexisse: et sic potest odisse Esavum, tantum quia non vult eum diligere. Hoc sensu posteriore dicitur Deus ab Apostolo dilexisse Jacobum et odisse Esavum, quia pro liberrimo voluntatis suae proposito voluit Jacobum emollire per specialem gratiam; noluit autem hoc tanto beneficio afficere Esavum. Si hic quaeratur quare elegit Jacobum ad hanc specialem gratiam, et non Esavum, respondetur, Quia Deus sic voluit. Si cur quaeratur quare sic voluerit, stulta est quaestio, quia Divinae voluntatis in bonis suis gratuitis praeparandis et distribuendis quaeritur causa, cujus nulla est praeter suam causam. Jam vero quod odii vocabulum usurpatur pro sola negatione specialis amoris in speciali beneficio conferendo, non diffitentur ipsi Jesuitae. Vasques ad haec ipsa verba Apostoli respiciens, Odisse, inquit, idem est quod minus dilexisse. Habet enim se ad modum odientis, qui aliquod donum quod uni dat, alteri non concedit. Sic tale odisse non requirit peccatum ut causam hujus odii. Hoc sensu Jacob dicitur odio habuisse Leam, Gen. xxix. 31.
english: Lastly — and this breaks the nerve of the argument — God may be said to have hated Esau in two respects. First, hated unto vengeance and the punishment of eternal death: so he hates Esau only as a sinner, and for sin itself as moving and demeritorious cause. Second, hated unto denial of some special unowed benefit — that is, loved less: so he can hate Esau only because he does not will to love him. In that latter sense the Apostle says God loved Jacob and hated Esau: by the freest purpose of his will he chose to soften Jacob by special grace, and refused Esau that great benefit. Why choose Jacob for that grace and not Esau? Because God so willed. Why so will? A foolish question — you seek a cause of the divine will in preparing and distributing gratuitous goods beyond the will itself. That hatred here means mere denial of special love in conferring a special benefit, even the Jesuits grant. Vasquez on these very words: to hate is the same as to have loved less. He acts like one who hates who gives a gift to one and withholds it from another. Such hatred needs no sin as its cause. So Jacob is said to have hated Leah (Gen. 29:31).

source_text: Apostolus vocat reprobationem: Miserebitur cujus vult, et quem vult indurat. Haec autem voluntas indurandi peccata reprobi, in quibus is induratur, praesupponit: Ergo peccata reproborum, cum quibus e vita hac decedunt, sunt causa motiva seu meritoria reprobationis eorundem.
english: Third: the Apostle styles reprobation thus — He has mercy on whom he will, and whom he will he hardens. But the will to harden presupposes the reprobate's sins in which he is hardened. Therefore the sins with which the reprobate leave this life are the moving or meritorious cause of their reprobation.

source_text: Respondemus, hanc voluntatem indurandi, ab Apostolo eo in loco commemoratam, designare peculiarem actum Divinae voluntatis, secundum quem negat quibusdam personis singularem illam gratiam, qua corda illorum emollirentur. Deus enim, ut vere Augustinus, non obdurat impertundo malitiam, sed non impertundo misericordiam: sicut sol occidens radiosque suos retrahens dicatur aerem obtenebrare, non per influxum aliquem quo obtenebratio gignatur, sed per negationem ejus influxus, quo posito tenebrae tollerentur. Cum itaque haec obduratio fiat permittendo, et negando specialem misericordiam, manifestum est, non posse aliquem a Deo considerari et praevideri ut finaliter in peccatis suis obduratum et morientem, nisi praecedente decreto hujus permissivae obdurationis, vel hac negatione specialis misericordiae, qua novit Deus hanc in peccatis permansionem finalem impediendam fore, si concederetur. Quod igitur in argumento assumptum fuit, voluntatem hanc indurandi, quae reprobatio est, peccata reprobi praesupponere ut causam hujus reprobationis vel indurationis, non modo falsum est, sed a ratione et sensu communi alienum. Causa enim praecedit effectum suum: at haec finalis permansio reproborum in peccatis suis sequitur decretum illud non-miserendi sive indurandi. Nam si Deus miseretur, homo non induratur; ad hanc enim specialem misericordiam pertinet efficere ut emolliatur. Unde Augustinus: Si vellet Deus ipsorum misereri, posset ita vocare (quemadmodum illis aptum esset) ut et moverentur, et intelligerent, et sequerentur. Paulo post, Nullius Deus frustra miseretur. Tandem adjungit, Obdurationem Dei nihil aliud esse quam nolle misereri; scilicet appositione hujus gratiae infallibiliter et efficaciter hominem emollientis et convertentis. Cum igitur nulla finalis pertinacia cujusquam in peccatis contractis vel commissis supponi possit quam non praecedat voluntas Dei de non-emolliendo, praevisa reproborum perseverantia in peccatis suis non potest esse causa negatae hujus misericordiae aut emollitionis. Est illud quidem verum, in cursu vitae suae quotidiano, reprobos, extinguendo illud lumen quod Deus in illorum cordibus accendit, et repellendo motiones Divinas, atque turpiter parendo foedis libidinibus, mereri illam consequentem excaecationem, desertionem, et in reprobum sensum traditionem; Sed hisce omnibus praesupponitur permissio illa Divina, sive negatio gratiae specialis, quae induratio permissiva vocari potest, et a reprobatione dimanat, absque qua praeeunte, et ex liberrima Dei voluntate dependente, reprobi in praedictam finalem contumaciam non incidissent, sed specialis et indebitae misericordiae beneficio ab illa rebellione et duritia fuissent liberati.
english: We answer: the will to harden Paul names there designates a peculiar act of the divine will by which he denies certain persons that singular grace by which their hearts would be softened. God, as Augustine truly says, does not harden by imparting malice, but by not imparting mercy — as the setting sun, drawing back its rays, is said to darken the air not by an influx that begets darkness, but by denying the influx whose presence would remove the dark. Since this hardening is done by permitting and denying special mercy, no one can be considered and foresighted by God as finally hardened in sin and dying unless the decree of that permissive hardening — or that denial of special mercy — precedes, by which God knows final remaining in sin would be blocked if the mercy were granted. So the argument's assumption — that this hardening will (which is reprobation) presupposes the reprobate's sins as cause of that reprobation or hardening — is not only false but alien to reason and common sense. Cause precedes effect: yet the reprobate's final remaining in sin follows the decree of not-having-mercy or of hardening. If God has mercy, man is not hardened; that special mercy's work is to soften. So Augustine: If God willed to have mercy on them, he could so call (as apt for them) that they would be moved, understand, and follow. A little later: God has mercy on no one in vain. At length: God's hardening is nothing but not willing to have mercy — namely by withholding the grace that infallibly and efficaciously softens and converts. Since no final obstinacy in contracted or committed sins can be supposed unless God's will not to soften precedes it, foresighted perseverance of the reprobate in their sins cannot be the cause of that denied mercy or softening. True: in daily life the reprobate, by quenching the light God kindles in their hearts, repelling divine motions, and basely obeying foul lusts, merit consequent blinding, desertion, and handing over to a reprobate mind. But under all that stands the divine permission — or denial of special grace — which may be called permissive hardening and flows from reprobation. Without that going before, and depending on God's freest will, the reprobate would not have fallen into that final contumacy, but by special unowed mercy would have been freed from that rebellion and hardness.

source_text: Apostolus dicit Deum, cum reprobat, velle ostendere iram et vindictam, etc. Rom. ix. 22. At voluntas inferendi vindictam praesupponit hominem considerari a Deo ut peccatis obstrictum: Ergo peccata reproborum, quibus obstricti moriuntur, sunt causa reprobationis.
english: Fourth: the Apostle says that when God reprobates he wills to show wrath and vengeance (Rom. 9:22). But the will to inflict vengeance presupposes that God regards a man as bound by sins. Therefore the sins by which the reprobate die bound are the cause of reprobation.
