source_text: Si de negativa illa reprobatione sermo habeatur qua Deus firmiter decrevit singularis alicujus personae, puta Caini aut Judae, non eatenus misereri, ut velit illum efficaciter e statu peccati et miseriae eruere, ac simul decrevit permittere ejusdem in peccatis suis finalem indurationem; nego hoc fieri a Deo ob eum finem ut vindicandi sive damnandi propositum expleat. Non male hac de re philosophatur Cajetanus in Commentariis suis ad 1am Aquinatis, qu. 23. art. 5, ubi dicit, Deum non permittere peccata ut puniat, sed permittere et punire propter relucentiam justitiae suae. Quinetiam ipse Apostolus loco citato indicavit nobis, Deum specialem hanc misericordiam aliquibus negare, atque inde permittere ut indurentur (qua in re consistit negativa reprobatio) non intentione primaria damnandi hosce sic praeteritos, sed Manifestandi divitias misericordiae suae erga ipsos electos, Rom. ix. 23. Nam tum demum intelligunt electi se fuisse pura et mera Dei misericordia salvatos, cum constet denegatam fuisse aliis illam vocationem secundum propositum quae ipsis ex gratuito Dei beneplacito fuit concessa; cum constet illos nihilo fuisse meliores hisce praeteritis quoad conditionem naturae corruptae, in qua specialis misericordia eos deprehendit; denique cum constet eos futuros fuisse non minus induratos ipsis reprobis, nisi ex mero Dei favore hac speciali gratia fuissent emolliti.
english: If we speak of that negative reprobation by which God firmly decreed of some particular person — say Cain or Judas — not so far to have mercy as to will to draw him efficaciously out of sin and misery, and at the same time decreed to permit his final hardening in sin: I deny God does this to fulfill a purpose of vengeance or damnation. Cajetan puts it well on Aquinas I, q. 23 a. 5: God does not permit sins in order to punish, but permits and punishes for the shining forth of his justice. Paul himself in the cited place shows that God denies this special mercy to some and so permits them to be hardened — wherein negative reprobation consists — not with primary intent to damn those thus passed by, but to manifest the riches of his mercy toward the elect (Rom. 9:23). Only then do the elect see they were saved by pure mere mercy: when it is plain that the calling according to purpose granted them by gratuitous good pleasure was denied to others; that they were no better than those passed by as to corrupt nature, in which special mercy found them; and that they would have been no less hardened than the reprobate unless mere divine favor had softened them by that special grace.

source_text: Est igitur verum, Deum velle ostendere iram et vindictam in omnes reprobatos: sed haec voluntas vindictae inferendae cum reprobatione illa negativa sive non-electione, de qua disputamus, non est immediate conjuncta, sed exoritur ex praeviso interventu finalis perseverantiae in peccato: qui status omnium reproborum infallibiliter futurus praevidetur a Deo ut eventus consequens negativam reprobationem, non ut causa antecedens. Est igitur parum firma argumentatio, Deus reprobans homines, vult eosdem etiam punire, Ergo reprobationis negativae causa est peccatum praevisum.
english: True: God wills to show wrath and vengeance on all the reprobate. But that will to inflict vengeance is not immediately joined to the negative reprobation or non-election we are disputing. It arises from foresighted intervention of final perseverance in sin — a state of all the reprobate foresighted by God as infallibly future as an event consequent on negative reprobation, not as an antecedent cause. So the argument is weak: God in reprobating also wills to punish them; therefore foresighted sin is the cause of negative reprobation.

source_text: Ex eodem Apostolo conantur demonstrare, permansionem in infidelitate esse reprobationis causam; quoniam reprobationem Judaeorum rejicit in infidelitatem eorundem tanquam causam: Rom. ix. 31, 32. Israel, inquit, sectando legem justitiae, in legem justitiae non pervenit. Quare? Quia non ex fide. Ubi indicatur solutio quaestionis de causa reprobationis Judaeorum. Quod ipsum confirmatur ex illis verbis, Rom. xi. 19, 20. Dices, Fracti sunt rami, ut ego inserar. Bene: propter incredulitatem fracti sunt: Tu autem fide stas, etc. Summa argumenti haec est: Judaei reprobati fuerunt propter perseverantiam finalem in infidelitate sua: Ergo perseverantia haec in infidelitate est causa reprobationis Divinae.
english: Fifth: from the same Apostle they try to prove remaining in unbelief is the cause of reprobation, since he casts the Jews' reprobation back on their unbelief as cause (Rom. 9:31-32): Israel, pursuing the law of righteousness, did not arrive at it — Why? Because not of faith. Confirmed by Rom. 11:19-20: The branches were broken off that I might be grafted in — Well: because of unbelief they were broken off; but you stand by faith. Sum: the Jews were reprobated for final perseverance in unbelief; therefore that perseverance is the cause of divine reprobation.

source_text: Ad primum testimonium ex nono ad Romanos petitum respondeo, Non reddi rationem cur reprobati fuerint Judaei, sed cur justitiam veram coram Deo minime sunt assecuti, utcunque videantur fuisse justitiae acerrimi sectatores. Id autem inde evenisse dicit Apostolus, quod justitiam quaerebant in operibus suis, et exacta legis observatione, spreta justificatione per fidem; cum ex operibus legis justificari sit homini per peccatum infirmato et corrupto plane impossibile, et necesse sit omni peccatori ad fidem confugere, ut coram Deo justificetur. Hanc interpretationem non modo Theologi nostri, sed etiam ex Pontificiis Gulielmus Estius Professor Duacenus expresse sequitur in Commentariis suis ad hunc ipsum locum, ubi inter alia et haec verba posuit, Scito non hic reddi rationem cur reprobati fuerint Judaei, sed cur non justitiam assecuti. Prius igitur hoc testimonium a proposito plane alienum.
english: To the first witness from Romans 9: Paul is not giving the reason why the Jews were reprobated, but why they failed to attain true righteousness before God — however keen they seemed as pursuers of righteousness. That happened, he says, because they sought righteousness in their works and exact law-keeping, despising justification by faith; justification from works of the law is plainly impossible for a man weakened and corrupted by sin, and every sinner must flee to faith to be justified before God. Not only our theologians follow this reading, but among the Romanists William Estius of Douai expressly does so on this very place: Know that here no reason is given why the Jews were reprobated, but why they did not attain righteousness. So this first testimony is plainly off the point.

source_text: Neque posterius, quod in confirmationem argumenti adducitur, quicquam facit ad rem. Apostolus enim non de singularibus personis electis sed de toto corpore Judaeorum et Gentium indefinite et indiscriminatim considerato loquitur. Neque de electione et reprobatione aeterna affirmat, aliquem singularem hominem propter incredulitatem exscindi et quasi expungi e numero electorum, et denuo fide recuperata quasi postliminio inseri: sed modo Judaeos in genere sua infidelitate desiisse esse populum Dei foederatum, et Gentes amplexando fidem evangelicam in illorum locum successisse. Atque ut Gentibus adimat omnem superbiendi occasionem, ait Judaeos, si in Christum credant et in sua infidelitate persistere desinant, inserendos, hoc est, in foederatum Dei populum admittendos; Gentes autem, quae nunc gaudent nomine Ecclesiae et populi Dei, si resiliant a fide Christi, fore etiam defringendas, et a corpore Ecclesiae exscindendas. Haec interminatio in multis Gentibus effectum sortita est, quae a fide Christi ad superstitionem Mahumeticam desciscentes, a corpore Ecclesiae, hoc est, foederati Dei populi, revulsae conspiciuntur. Sed quid interim haec omnia conducunt ad probandam singularium personarum reprobationem aeternam, ex consideratione futurae illorum incredulitatis, tanquam causae motivae, profluxisse? Profecto nihil: Quia non de singularium personarum aeterna electione et reprobatione, sed de visibili Gentium insitione et defractione disserit Apostolus: quia haec insitio et defractio, cujus mentionem facit, non denotat aeternam electionem aut reprobationem singularium personarum, sed temporalem admissionem aut rejectionem alicujus gentis a statu populi foederati, quorum alterum fit mediante fide, alterum mediante infidelitate: quia ab omni sana Theologia abhorret, statuere, aliquos reprobatos fieri posse electos, aut aliquos electos reprobatos; et tamen Apostolus expresse docet hosce insitos, de quibus loquitur, posse fieri defractos, et hosce defractos posse rursus fieri insitos.
english: Nor does the confirming text from Romans 11 help. Paul is not speaking of particular elect persons but of the whole body of Jews and Gentiles taken indefinitely. He is not teaching that some singular man is cut off for unbelief and struck from the number of the elect, then grafted back by recovered faith as by postliminium. He says only that the Jews in general, by unbelief, ceased to be God's covenant people, and that the Gentiles, embracing the gospel faith, succeeded into their place. To strip the Gentiles of every occasion for pride, he adds: if the Jews believe in Christ and stop persisting in unbelief, they are to be grafted in — admitted to the covenant people; and if the Gentiles who now rejoice as Church and people of God spring back from Christ's faith, they too will be broken off and cut from the Church's body. That threat has taken effect in many Gentiles who defected from Christ's faith to Mahometan superstition and stand torn from the covenant body. How does any of this prove that eternal reprobation of particular persons flowed from regard to their future unbelief as moving cause? It proves nothing. Paul discusses visible grafting and breaking of peoples, not eternal election and reprobation of individuals. That grafting and breaking denotes temporal admission or rejection of a nation from covenant status — one by faith, the other by unbelief. Sound theology abhors making reprobates into elect or elect into reprobates; yet Paul expressly teaches that those grafted of whom he speaks can be broken off, and those broken off grafted again.

source_text: Hisce omnibus accedat, quod cum gens aliqua, puta Judaeorum, ob infidelitatem defracta sit a corpore Ecclesiae, nemo tamen ex electis defringatur: nam, eodem Apostolo autore, reliquiae secundum electionem gratiae salvae factae sunt, Rom. xi. 5, 7. Denique, quod quidam non defringantur, aliis ex eadem gente resilientibus et pereuntibus, id evenit non quia hi electi fuerunt ex praevisa fide sua, sed quia fides data fuit hisce electis ex aeterno Dei beneplacito, et reservatio secundum electionem facta est, Rom. xi. 5. Sic etiam quod quidam defringantur, mediante sua infidelitate, et pereant, id non arguit Deum eos ab aeterno reprobasse propter praevisam infidelitatem; sed quod hi reprobati duritiae suae derelicti infidelitatem, quae cordis obdurati genuinam prolem pepererunt, et per eam a corpore Ecclesiae defracti suo merito perierunt.
english: Add this: when a nation — say the Jews — is broken off from the Church's body for unbelief, still none of the elect is broken off. By the same Apostle, a remnant according to the election of grace is saved (Rom. 11:5, 7). That some are not broken off while others of the same nation spring back and perish happens not because these were elected from foresighted faith, but because faith was given to these elect from God's eternal good pleasure, and a reservation according to election was made (Rom. 11:5). So too, that some are broken off by their unbelief and perish does not prove God from eternity reprobated them for foresighted unbelief. It proves that these reprobate, left to their hardness, brought forth unbelief — the genuine child of an hardened heart — and through it, broken from the Church's body, perished by their own desert.

source_text: Reprobi monentur, ut in sua reprobatione semper justitiam Divinam agnoscant, qua propter ipsorum peccata merito reprobati fuerunt: Ergo reprobantur ex praevisione demeritorum suorum, in quibus praevidentur hanc suam vitam finitori. Horsum afferuntur multa testimonia ex Patribus, atque nominatim ex ipso Augustino: Quale est illud, De bono persever. cap. 6. Voluntate sua quisque deserit Deum, ut merito deseratur a Deo. Item et illud, De gratia et libero arbitr. cap. 21. Cum legitis in sacris literis obdurari corda hominum, nolite dubitare praecessisse mala merita eorum, ut juste ista paterentur. Et rursus, Ibid. cap. 23. Quando auditis dicentem Dominum, Cujus vult miseretur et quem vult indurat, in eo quem permittit indurari mala ejus merita credite, in eo vero cujus miseretur, Gratiam Dei reddentis bona pro malis indubitanter agnoscite. Denique apertissime hoc asseritur Epistola 105, Quaerimus meritum obdurationis, et invenimus. Merito namque peccati universa massa damnata est, Quibus Deus misericordiam non impertitur, ut non impertatur merentur. Consimilia multa passim occurrunt apud Augustinum et alios Patres, ex quibus concludunt adversarii, Praevisa demerita, cum finali perduratione in iisdem, fuisse causam motivam reprobationis Divinae.
english: Sixth: the reprobate are warned always to acknowledge in their reprobation the divine justice by which, for their own sins, they were deservedly reprobated. Therefore, say adversaries, they are reprobated from foresight of the demerits in which they are foresighted as finishing this life. Many Father-testimonies are brought, especially Augustine: On the Good of Perseverance 6 — By his own will each deserts God, that he may deservedly be deserted by God. On Grace and Free Will 21 — When you read in Scripture that men's hearts are hardened, do not doubt their evil deserts went before, that they might justly suffer it. Again, chapter 23 — When you hear the Lord say He has mercy on whom he will and whom he will he hardens, in him whom God permits to be hardened believe his evil deserts; in him on whom God has mercy, acknowledge without doubt the grace that returns goods for evils. Most openly in Epistle 105: We seek the merit of hardening, and we find it. By desert of sin the universal mass is damned; those to whom God does not impart mercy merit that it not be imparted. From many such passages in Augustine and other Fathers, adversaries conclude that foresighted demerits with final lasting in them were the moving cause of divine reprobation.

source_text: Ut haec omnia diluantur, primo in memoriam revocandum est, nos agere de reprobatione illa, quam Theologi vocant negativam; quam Scotus permissivam appellat, in Sentent. lib. 1, dist. 41, quaest. 1; non de illa quam positivam sive punitivam licet appellare. Prior ita considerata dicit solummodo Dei propositum aeternum de non-concedendo singularibus quibusdam personis gratuitum quoddam, indebitum, et speciale beneficium, quo concesso emollirentur, converterentur, et ad vitam aeternam infallibiliter perducerentur. Posterior dicit aeternum Dei propositum de quibusdam personis morte aeterna puniendis ob peccata illa quae perpetrabunt, et a quibus minime liberandi praevidentur. Si ad hoc posterius decretum respiciant adversarii, ultro largimur, hoc aeternum praedamnationis decretum non tendere in quenquam, nisi ea ratione quod peccati reatu constringatur. Nam licet Deus velit servare miseros absque ullis eorum meritis, quia bonus est, non tamen vult damnare aut punire innocentes absque ullis demeritis, quia justus est.
english: To clear all this, recall first: we are treating the reprobation theologians call negative — which Scotus calls permissive (Sentences 1, dist. 41, q. 1) — not the positive or punitive kind. Negative reprobation, so taken, means only God's eternal purpose not to grant certain particular persons some gratuitous, unowed, special benefit by which, if granted, they would be softened, converted, and infallibly led to eternal life. Positive reprobation means God's eternal purpose to punish certain persons with eternal death for the sins they will commit, and from which they are foresighted as not to be freed. If adversaries mean that latter decree, we freely grant: the eternal decree of predamnation tends to no one except as bound by sin's guilt. God wills to save the miserable without their merits, because he is good; he does not will to damn or punish innocents without demerits, because he is just.

source_text: Secundo, quando Augustinus affirmat, in reprobatione nos debere agnoscere justum Dei judicium, non id ad praevisa actualia peccata singulorum, sed ad commune debitum originale est referendum. Non igitur juvat eos qui hanc reprobationem a praevisione finalis perseverantiae in actualibus peccatis deducunt. Porro, originalis peccati considerationem in hac reprobatione negativa ita concedimus, ut fuerit adjunctum adhaerens subjecto reprobato, non autem ut fuerit causa movens voluntatem Divinam ad hunc actum reprobandi. Agnoscendum itaque est, hunc actum reprobationis negativae, qua gratia specialis neganda decernitur personae solo peccato originali contaminatae, non sine justitia, multo minus contra justitiam, exerceri. Nam (quod ante annotavimus) satis juste negatur quod ex justitia non debetur; sed interim tenendum, non ex retribuente et vindicante justitia, sed ex libertate Divinae voluntatis, cujus vult miserentis, et quem vult praetereuntis, dependere, quod in communi hoc reatu originalis peccati quidam decernantur efficaciter liberandi, quidam per negationem gratiae specialis in illo statu relinquendi.
english: Second: when Augustine says that in reprobation we ought to acknowledge God's just judgment, that refers not to foresighted actual sins of individuals, but to the common original debt. So it does not help those who derive this reprobation from foresight of final perseverance in actual sins. We do grant original sin a place in negative reprobation — as an adjunct adhering to the reprobate subject, not as a moving cause of the divine will to that act of reprobating. Negative reprobation, whereby special grace is decreed denied to a person stained by original sin alone, is exercised not without justice, still less against it. What justice does not owe is justly denied; yet the discrimination — some efficaciously freed from this common original guilt, some left in that state by denial of special grace — depends not on retributing and vindicating justice, but on the liberty of the divine will, which has mercy on whom it will and passes by whom it will.

source_text: Tertio, si contendunt adversarii, hanc reprobationem negativam ex praescientia finalis pertinaciae in actualibus peccatis esse oriundam, respondemus, hoc non modo a veritate sed ab omni verisimilitudine abhorrere. Nam ipsum decretum permittendi finalem hanc obdurationem, in quo sita est reprobatio, absolutam ejusdem obdurationis praescientiam antecedit. Unde Petrus Lombardus, lib. 1, dist. 40, ait, Reprobationem esse praescientiam malitiae in quibusdam et non miserendi. Haec autem praescientia fundatur in decreto negante specialem illam gratiam et de facto cujuscunque cordis quantumvis duri emollientem. Frustra igitur statuitur praescientiam finalem in peccatis permansionem esse reprobationis causam, cum huic finali permansioni praeintelligatur permissio illa, orta ex praevio reprobationis decreto. Haec universe de ipso argumento. Jam sigillatim ad singula testimonia apposita respondebo.
english: Third: if adversaries claim negative reprobation springs from foresight of final obstinacy in actual sins, that abhors not only truth but all likelihood. The very decree permitting that final hardening — wherein reprobation sits — precedes absolute foresight of the hardening. So Peter Lombard (Sentences 1, dist. 40): Reprobation is foresight of malice in certain ones and of not having mercy. That foresight is founded in the decree denying the special grace that in fact softens any heart, however hard. It is vain, then, to make foresight of final remaining in sins the cause of reprobation, when that remaining presupposes the permission sprung from the prior reprobation decree. So much for the argument in general. Now the testimonies one by one.

source_text: Ad primum: Quando Augustinus dicit, Homines prius deserere Deum, atque inde mereri ut deserantur a Deo, non spectat negationem hujus gratiae, quam efficacem et specialem vocamus, atque in hujus negatione hanc reprobationem sive praeteritionem proprie constitutam asserimus; sed gratiae communioris et excitantis subtractionem; quam fatemur propter demerita tolli hominibus, ita tamen ut sine praevia illa prioris gratiae specialis praeparatione, in hoc contumaciae demeritum incidissent.
english: To the first: when Augustine says men first desert God and thence merit to be deserted by God, he is not speaking of the denial of that efficacious special grace in whose denial we locate reprobation or praeterition proper. He means subtraction of a more common, exciting grace — which we grant is taken from men for demerits — yet so that without the prior preparation of that special grace they would already have fallen into this demerit of contumacy.

source_text: Ad secundum et tertium: Quando Augustinus jubet nos credere ejus mala merita non abesse, aut praecessisse, quem Deus indurari permittit, non loquitur de illa aeterna voluntate non-miserendi, non-emolliendi, quae ipsam reprobationem continet, sed de ea obduratione in qua peccator a Deo juste derelictus quasi lapideam quandam duritiem contrahit; quam esse praecedentium peccatorum mercedem haud negamus. Sed hic perpendere oportet, utcunque haec obduratio, quae aucta et provecta consideratur, ut mala dispositio hominis indurati, ex demerito praecedentium peccatorum oriatur, tamen illa prima induratio permissiva, quae consideratur ut sola negatio emollitionis ex parte Dei, non potest oriri ex eodem praeviso demerito. Nam voluntatem non-miserendi, non-emolliendi, in Deo consideratam nasci ex praevisione obdurationis in homine consideratam, aeque absurdum esset ac si quis dixerit diluculum illud solis absentem apud Cimmerios oriri ex praeeunte diuturna obtenebratione aeris.
english: To the second and third: when Augustine bids us believe evil deserts are not absent — or went before — in him whom God permits to be hardened, he is not speaking of that eternal will not to have mercy, not to soften, which contains reprobation itself. He means the hardening in which the sinner, justly forsaken by God, contracts a kind of stony hardness — and we do not deny that is the wage of preceding sins. Weigh this: however much that hardening, taken as increased and advanced as the evil disposition of the hardened man, arises from demerit of preceding sins, the first permissive hardening — mere negation of softening on God's part — cannot arise from that same foresighted demerit. To say God's will not to have mercy, not to soften, is born from foresight of human hardening would be as absurd as saying the sun's daylight, absent among the Cimmerians, arises from the air's long prior darkening.

source_text: Ad ultimum testimonium, in quo Augustinus docet facile posse nos invenire in nobis meritum obdurationis, sed meritum misericordiae Divinae non posse invenire, respondeo, loqui illum non de praevisione actualium peccatorum ad finem vitae in hoc vel illo perdurantium, sed de originali peccato, quod est quasi commune demeritum in omnibus Adae filiis, et potest allegari tanquam sufficiens causa, cur Divina misericordia cuivis possit absque omni crudelitatis specie denegari, sed non potest allegari tanquam causa, cur Deus noluerit huic vel illi singulari homini efficax remedium praeparare et adhibere, quo haec ingenita durities edomari posset. Valet igitur originalis peccati consideratio, ut inde inquiras damnationis, sed non eo valet ut inde petatur causa negativae reprobationis. Denique dicuntur omnes reprobi, praesertim qui ad usum liberi arbitrii perveniunt, mereri istam obdurationem, primo, sensu negativo, quia non merentur emollitionem, quia non merentur specialem illam misericordiam; deinde, sensu affirmativo, quia quotidianis suis peccatis merentur illam ulteriorem obdurationem et traditionem εἰς ἀδόκιμον νοῦν, de quo Apostolus Rom. i. 28. Sed interim decretum illud reprobationis, secundum quod permittuntur ita indurescere, dependet ex Dei liberrima voluntate, et non ex praevisa illorum finali duritie; quae utique praevisa esse non potuit, nisi hoc permittendi decreto praesupposito.
english: To the last testimony — Augustine teaching that we easily find in ourselves the merit of hardening, but cannot find the merit of divine mercy — I answer: he is not speaking of foresight of actual sins lasting to life's end in this or that person, but of original sin, the common demerit of all Adam's children. That can stand as sufficient cause why divine mercy may be denied anyone without any show of cruelty; it cannot stand as cause why God refused to prepare and apply to this or that particular man an efficacious remedy by which that inborn hardness could be tamed. Original sin avails for inquiring into damnation; it does not avail as the cause of negative reprobation. Finally all the reprobate — especially those who reach the use of free will — are said to merit that hardening: negatively, because they do not merit softening or that special mercy; affirmatively, because by daily sins they merit further hardening and handing over to a reprobate mind (Rom. 1:28). Yet the reprobation decree by which they are permitted so to harden depends on God's freest will, not on their foresighted final hardness — which could not be foresighted unless that permitting decree were presupposed.

source_text: Peccata reprobi sunt causa omnium effectorum reprobationis ipsius: Ergo etiam reprobationis Divinae, ut respicit illos effectus. Quod enim attinet ad primum effectum, scilicet indurationem seu subtractionem peculiaris gratiae, patet illam ex peccatorum antecedentium demeritis oriri: Rom. i.; 2 Thess. ii.; Exod. ix. Quod attinet ad ultimum effectum, nempe aeternam damnationem, patet ejus causam esse demerita humana ex ipsa forma sententiae latae in judicio finali.
english: Argument: the sins of the reprobate are the cause of all the effects of reprobation itself; therefore also of divine reprobation as it regards those effects. As to the first effect — hardening or subtraction of peculiar grace — it plainly arises from demerits of antecedent sins (Rom. 1; 2 Thess. 2; Exod. 9). As to the last — eternal damnation — human demerits are plainly its cause from the very form of the sentence passed at the final judgment.

source_text: Non negamus peccata impiorum esse causam damnationis eorundem: et si adversarii, qui contendunt causam motivam reprobationis esse peccata quibus reprobi praevidentur vitam finituri, per reprobationem intelligant nihil aliud quam damnationem sive propositum damnandi, eatenus illis adstipulamur. Verum de reprobatione negativa disputamus, quae non est ipsa damnatio, nec causa damnationis, sed quoddam antecedens. Nemo enim damnatur quia reprobatus, sed quia reus: neque mors aeterna stipendium est reprobationis, sed transgressionis. Missa igitur damnatione, quae satis improprie dicitur effectus hujus reprobationis, de reliquis videamus.
english: We do not deny that the ungodly's sins cause their damnation. If adversaries, who make the sins with which the reprobate are foresighted as finishing life the moving cause of reprobation, mean by reprobation nothing but damnation or the purpose to damn, so far we agree. But we are disputing negative reprobation — which is not damnation itself, nor damnation's cause, but a certain antecedent. No one is damned because reprobated, but because guilty; eternal death is the wage of transgression, not of reprobation. Set damnation aside, then — it is only improperly called an effect of this reprobation — and let us look at the rest.

source_text: Primo, quod arguitur, Peccata reprobi sunt causa omnium effectorum reprobationis: Ergo etiam et ipsius rei, scilicet reprobationis Divinae, ut respicit illos effectus, haec prorsus consequentia lubrica est et infirma, si ea omnia mala vocentur effecta quae eam consequuntur. Nam illud potest esse causa rei permissae quod non sit causa permissionis relatae ad rem permissam. Verbi gratia, video duos ebrios homines temere hac illuc errantes; praevideo utrumque in foveam lapsurum, et fame ibi periturum, nisi inde illis prospiciatur. Decerno apud animum alterum eorum monere, retrahere, et ab hoc periculo efficaciter liberare; alterum non monere, non retrahere; aut saltem non ita monere et retrahere ut de facto liberetur. Decidit jam iste posterior in foveam, ibi diu jacet, maceratur, et tandem fame exstinguitur.
english: First: the argument — sins of the reprobate cause all reprobation's effects; therefore also divine reprobation itself as regards those effects — is a slippery, weak consequence if every evil that follows is called an effect. What causes the permitted thing need not cause the permission of that thing. Example: I see two drunken men wandering rashly about; I foresee both will fall into a pit and starve there unless helped. I resolve to warn one, draw him back, and free him from the peril; the other I will not warn or draw back — or at least not so as actually to free him. That latter falls into the pit, lies long, wastes, and at last starves.

source_text: Jam si quaeratur causa mali permissi in omnibus et singulis hisce effectis, scilicet in ipsa praecipitatione, in diuturna illa maceratione, in denique ipsa postrema exstinctione, recte omnium causam veredixerim fuisse praedictae personae ebrietatem, caecitatem ac temeritatem. At si quaeratur causa permissionis meae sive decreti mei permittentis de eodem homine non efficaciter liberando, hic ad liberam voluntatis meae potentiam, non ad illius inscitiam aut temeritatem, est deveniendum. Sic Deus intuetur omnes homines orbitate caecos et in peccati via errantes: quibusdam praeparat efficacem gratiam, qua quasi crapulam discutiant, ad se redeant, et serventur; statuit etiam e contra, alios hac tam potente peculiari et efficaci gratia non juvare. Hi posteriores ruunt in foedas concupiscentias, peccatum addunt peccato, in peccatis obdurantur, obduratique moriuntur, et damnantur. Si quaeratur causa rebellionis, obdurationis, perditionis quoad tales, vere respondere possumus, corruptam illorum naturam et peccata voluntaria horum omnium malorum fuisse causam et originem: At si quaeratur causa decreti permittentis quoad haec omnia, ad voluntatis Divinae liberrimum placitum, non ad ipsa peccata permissa, est deveniendum. Vacillat ergo illa consequentia, Peccata reprobi sunt causa omnium effectorum reprobationis: Ergo etiam sunt causa reprobationis ipsius, sive decreti reprobantis.
english: Ask the cause of the permitted evil in each of those effects — the fall, the long wasting, the final extinction — and I rightly name that person's drunkenness, blindness, and rashness. Ask the cause of my permission, or of my decree not to free him efficaciously, and you must come to the free power of my will, not to his ignorance or rashness. So God regards all men blind and wandering in sin's way: for some he prepares efficacious grace by which they shake off the stupor, return to themselves, and are saved; for others he decrees not to help with that powerful peculiar efficacious grace. Those latter rush into foul lusts, add sin to sin, harden in sin, die hardened, and are damned. Ask the cause of their rebellion, hardening, perdition: corrupt nature and voluntary sins are truly cause and origin of all those evils. Ask the cause of the permitting decree as to all that: you must come to the freest pleasure of the divine will, not to the permitted sins themselves. So the consequence wavers: sins of the reprobate cause all reprobation's effects; therefore they also cause reprobation itself — the reprobating decree.

source_text: Secundo, videntur adversarii statuere in hoc argumento illam duritiem sive obdurationem, quae est mala dispositio aut perversa actio reprobati, esse effectum reprobationis Divinae. At hoc falsissimum est. Nam licet sit eventus consequens, non est tamen proprie dictum effectum reprobationis. Quamvis enim, ut bene notavit Cajetanus, quicquid ordinat praedestinatum ad vitam aeternam sit effectum praedestinationis, tamen in reprobatione est aliquid quod ordinat ad mortem (nimirum quicquid habet culpae aut peccati rationem, quale est praedicta obduratio et durities) quod est extra totum reprobationis effectum, In Aqu. 1. qu. 23. art. 5. Non enim (in quo nonnulli Theologi periculose errant) media et causae damnationis ita connexa sunt cum decreto reprobationis, sicuti media et causae salutis connectuntur cum decreto praedestinationis. Atque ratio discriminis in promptu est: Nam media et causae salutis sunt bona quaedam spiritualia; bonum autem subjacet providentiae Dei, ut intentum, causatum et ordinatum ab ea: sed media et causae quae ducunt ad damnationem sunt mala spiritualia; Malum autem hujusmodi subjacet Divinae providentiae, non ut intentum et causatum, sed ut praevisum, permissum, ordinatum. Sic Dionysius Carthusianus in 1. dist. 40. Quando ergo illa durities aut obduratio, quae est hominis vitium vel peccatum, supponitur effectus reprobationis, quod est merum consequens, effectus titulo improprie saltem, et non alio, insignitur.
english: Second: adversaries seem to make that hardness or hardening — the reprobate's evil disposition or perverse act — an effect of divine reprobation. Most false. It may be a consequent event; it is not properly an effect of reprobation. As Cajetan well noted (on Aquinas I, q. 23 a. 5): whatever ordains the predestined to eternal life is an effect of predestination; yet in reprobation there is something that ordains to death — whatever has the character of fault or sin, such as that hardening and hardness — and that lies outside the whole effect of reprobation. Some theologians perilously err here: the means and causes of damnation are not tied to the reprobation decree as the means and causes of salvation are tied to the predestination decree. The difference is plain. Salvation's means are spiritual goods, and good falls under God's providence as intended, caused, and ordained by it. Damnation's means are spiritual evils; such evil falls under divine providence not as intended and caused, but as foresighted, permitted, ordained (so Dionysius the Carthusian on Sentences 1, dist. 40). When that hardness — man's vice or sin — is called an effect of reprobation, a mere consequent is labeled effect only improperly.

source_text: Denique illa induratio, quam respicit Apostolus, Rom. i. 28, Quo spectant illa verba, Tradidit illos in reprobum sensum; item et illa quam 2 Thess. ii. 10, 11, 12, Apostolus hisce verbis depingit, Quia non receperunt amorem veritatis, propterea iis mittet Deus efficaciam deceptionis, ut credant mendacio, etc., non denotant negationem primae gratiae efficacis, qua posita talis obduratio nunquam evenisset, sed subductionem gratiae alicujus concessae, ex abusu ejusdem, quam subductionem fieri ex hominum demeritis non diffitemur: atque obdurationem inde consequentem et peccatum et peccati praecedentis mercedem agnoscimus. Quod autem de Pharaone dicitur Exod. ix. Obduravit Jehovah cor Pharaonis, id aut de prima negatione gratiae specialis, et permissiva obduratione intelligi debet, et tum haec voluntas obdurandi, id est, non-emolliendi, quae consideratur ut negatio gratuita actionis ex parte Dei, non potuit ex praevisis Pharaonis demeritis oriri, quia talem praevisionem antecedit. Hic igitur ad illud Apostoli confugiendum est, Miserebitur cujus vult, et quem vult indurat. Vel possunt illa verba ad ulteriorem obdurationem referri, qua Pharao voluntaria pervicacia cor suum obfirmavit, Deo exterius et interius praebente illas occasiones, quibus certo praescivit Pharaonem magis obdurandum, etiamsi ex natura sua valere debuissent ad illum emolliendum. Deus igitur obdurat hominem impium propter sua demerita, quando ejus impietate provocatus sumit occasionem subducendi gratiam concessam, et quaedam agendi, ex quibus novit talem hominem fore deteriorem. Ac Deus etiam indurare dicitur absque hoc intuitu ad finalia demerita, ideo tantum quia vult, quando homini in communi massa considerato non praeparavit, non dedit illam specialem misericordiam, quam alteri in eadem misera conditione concessit. Atque haec est illa induratio quae arguit reprobationem, quaeque ex praevisione finalis perseverantiae in peccatis haud dependet. Ex aequivoco igitur non procedit argumentatio.
english: Finally: the hardening Paul regards in Rom. 1:28 — He gave them over to a reprobate mind — and that which 2 Thess. 2:10-12 depicts — Because they received not the love of the truth, God shall send them strong delusion that they believe a lie — do not denote denial of the first efficacious grace, without which such hardening would never have come. They denote subtraction of some granted grace after its abuse — which subtraction we grant arises from men's demerits — and the hardening that follows we acknowledge as both sin and the wage of preceding sin. What is said of Pharaoh (Exod. 9: Jehovah hardened Pharaoh's heart) must either be taken of the first denial of special grace and permissive hardening — and then that will to harden, i.e. not to soften, as mere gratuitous negation of an act on God's part, could not arise from Pharaoh's foresighted demerits, because it precedes such foresight. Here refuge is Rom. 9: He has mercy on whom he will, and whom he will he hardens. Or those words may refer to a further hardening by which Pharaoh, of voluntary obstinacy, stiffened his own heart, God outwardly and inwardly furnishing occasions by which he certainly foresaw Pharaoh would be more hardened — even if by nature those occasions ought to have softened him. So God hardens an ungodly man for his demerits when, provoked by impiety, he takes occasion to withdraw granted grace and to act in ways he knows will make such a man worse. God is also said to harden without that regard to final demerits — only because he wills — when to a man considered in the common mass he has not prepared or given that special mercy he granted another in the same miserable condition. That is the hardening which argues reprobation, and it does not depend on foresight of final perseverance in sins. So the argument proceeds from an equivocation.

source_text: Sic argutantur quidam: Si Deus non propter peccata hominum, sed sua sponte et ex seipso, homines reprobaret, tum pauciores essent reprobati quam praedestinati. Nam Deus longe propensior est ex se ad miserendum et benefaciendum hominibus, quam ad deserendos, perdendos, et damnandos, juxta illud Psalmi, Psal. cxlv. 9. Suavis Dominus universis, et miserationes ejus super omnia opera ejus. Hanc rationem Gregorius de Valentia (ex quo pleraque superiora argumenta desumpsimus) suo judicio optimam esse pronunciat, eamque se a Joanne Fekio mutuatam fuisse profitetur.
english: Some argue thus: if God reprobated men not for their sins, but of his own accord and from himself, then there would be fewer reprobate than predestined. For God is far more inclined from himself to mercy and beneficence than to deserting, destroying, and damning — according to Psalm 145:9: The Lord is sweet to all, and his compassions are over all his works. Gregory of Valencia (from whom we have taken most of the earlier arguments) judges this the best reason, and says he borrowed it from John Fekius.

source_text: Hanc eandem rationem a Gregorio propositam in quaestione Praedestinationis antea dissolvimus. Nam in illa controversia conatus est probare, praedestinationem esse ex praescientia operum, quia pauci electi sunt respectu rejectorum. Jam etiam contendit, reprobationem pendere ex praevisione finalium demeritorum, quia multi sunt reprobati in comparatione ad eos paucos qui eliguntur. Respondeo igitur, consequentiam neutrobi valere. Ad reprobationem quod spectat, cum sit (ut ante dictum est) non punitio, sed gratuiti et indebiti beneficii negatio, nihil cogit nos fateri Deum, ex mero suo beneplacito agentem, non posse tale beneficium paucioribus concedere, et pluribus denegare. Videmus in angelis hoc beneficium electionis fuisse multis negatum, idque absque respectu ad praevisa demerita: an fuerit pluribus denegatum quam indultum, haud ausim definire. Si tamen in ipsa re aliquid esset incongruum, aut Deo indignum, non modo pluribus, sed nec paucioribus, imo nec uni posset hoc beneficium electionis denegare absque consideratione praevisi peccati. Hac igitur sola instantia vis argumenti eliditur.
english: We already dissolved this same reason of Gregory's in the predestination question. There he tried to prove predestination is from foresight of works because few are elect relative to the rejected. Now he contends reprobation hangs on foresight of final demerits because many are reprobate compared with the few elect. I answer: the consequence holds in neither place. As for reprobation — since it is not punishment but denial of a gratuitous unowed benefit — nothing forces us to say God, acting from mere good pleasure, cannot grant that benefit to fewer and deny it to more. We see in the angels that this benefit of election was denied to many, and without regard to foresighted demerits; whether denied to more than granted, I scarce dare say. Yet if anything in the thing itself were incongruous or unworthy of God, he could not deny election's benefit even to one without regard to foresighted sin — let alone to many. That single instance breaks the argument's force.

source_text: Sed ab angelis ad homines descendamus. Dico igitur in hominibus hujus rei aequitatem multo facilius perspici posse quam in angelis. Nam cum universa massa humani generis in statum meritae damnationis defluxerit primi parentis nostri inobedientia, si Deus nullo ulteriore ad peccata actualia respectu praeterire et rejicere velit quamvis multos in praeparatione et donatione gratiae specialis, praeterit et rejicit eos, in quibus nihil invenit propter quod ad tam eximium beneficium participandum eligantur, et in quibus multa invenit propter quae tali beneficio indignissimi censeantur. Nihil aliud hic dicendum restat praeter illud Augustini, Qui liberatur, gratiam diligat; qui non liberatur, debitum agnoscat, De bono persever. cap. 8. Et illud Apostoli, Rom. ix. 20. O homo, tu quis es qui respondeas Deo? Num dicet figmentum, etc.
english: Descend from angels to men. In men the equity of this is far easier to see. Since the whole mass of humankind has flowed down into merited damnation by our first parent's disobedience, if God with no further regard to actual sins wills to pass by and reject however many in preparing and giving special grace, he passes by and rejects those in whom he finds nothing for which they should be elect to so excellent a benefit, and in whom he finds much for which they are most unworthy of it. Nothing else need be said but Augustine (On the Good of Perseverance 8): Let him who is freed love grace; let him who is not freed acknowledge the debt — and Paul (Rom. 9:20): O man, who are you to answer God? Shall the thing formed say...?

source_text: Sed Deus propensior est ex se ad miserendum et benefaciendum hominibus, quam ad eos deserendos et perdendos. Concedimus. At qui est propensissimus ad miserendum et benefaciendum, non solet eximia et peculiaria beneficia aut omnibus aut pluribus impertiri. Sufficit ad hanc propensionem Dei in misericordiam ostendendam, quod omnium misereatur quoad multa misericordiae suae effecta, quamvis quoad hoc speciale effectum, gratiam specialem praeparandi et ad vitam aeternam infallibiliter ordinandi, nec omnium nec plurium misereatur. Dein praeterire vel reprobare non est idem quod deserere et perdere. Deseruntur quidem et perduntur tandem omnes reprobati sive non-electi: sed quod praeteriti fuerint aut non-electi ad gratiam specialem, ex mera Dei voluntate prodit; quod autem postmodum deserti et perditi, ex interveniente illorum demerito originem sumpsit. Hactenus iis argumentis satisfecimus quibus utitur Gregorius de Valentia, in 1. Aquinat. qu. 23. de Reprobatione.
english: But God is more inclined from himself to mercy and beneficence than to deserting and destroying men. We grant it. Yet the most merciful is not wont to impart excellent peculiar benefits to all or even to most. It is enough to show that propensity that he has mercy on all as to many effects of his mercy — even if, as to this special effect of preparing special grace and infallibly ordaining to eternal life, he has mercy neither on all nor on most. Further: to pass by or reprobate is not the same as to desert and destroy. Yes, all the reprobate or non-elect are at length deserted and destroyed — but that they were passed by or non-elect as to special grace proceeds from God's mere will; that afterward they were deserted and destroyed took its origin from their intervening demerit. So far we have answered the arguments Gregory of Valencia uses on Aquinas I, q. 23, on Reprobation.

source_text: Ex antiquis Scholasticis Thomas de Argentina fatetur se communem opinionem Theologorum deserere, ac conatur contra eos hanc conclusionem probare, Causam reprobationis quoad adultos esse malum usum liberi arbitrii, usque ad finem vitae in ipsis duraturum, ab aeterno a Deo praescitum. Quae opinio verbis, non sensu, differt a Jesuitica et Arminiana. Audiamus igitur Argentinae rationes.
english: Among the older Scholastics, Thomas of Argentina admits he deserts the common opinion of the theologians, and tries against them to prove this: that the cause of reprobation as to adults is the evil use of free will lasting in them to life's end, foresighted by God from eternity. That opinion differs in words, not in sense, from the Jesuit and Arminian. Let us hear Argentina's reasons.

source_text: Ad poenam aeternam, inquit, nullus ordinatur a justo Judice sine praecognitione causae. Sed omnis reprobatus est ad poenam a Deo justo Judice deputatus: Ergo non nisi ex praeviso malo usu liberi arbitrii ad finem usque duraturo. Quod idem est ac si dixisset cum Jesuitis et Arminianis, non nisi ex praevisa infidelitate et inobedientia.
english: To eternal punishment, he says, no one is ordained by a just Judge without precognition of the cause. But every reprobate is deputed to punishment by God the just Judge. Therefore only from foresighted evil use of free will lasting to the end — which is the same as saying with Jesuits and Arminians: only from foresighted unbelief and disobedience.

source_text: Respondeo, nos per reprobationem intelligere illam Divinae providentiae partem secundum quam Deus vult quibusdam negare specialem gratiam, ac permittere ut deficiant a fine beatitudinis; sicut per praedestinationem intelligimus illam alteram partem Divinae providentiae secundum quam voluit quibusdam praeparare ac donare hanc gratiam specialem, eosdemque ad gloriam ac beatitudinem infallibiliter perducere. Hoc posito, negamus reprobationem hanc esse deputationem vel adjudicationem ad poenam. Est quidem beneficii indebiti ex sola Dei voluntate libera denegatio: sed non est supplicii indebiti ex sola Dei voluntate imperiosa inflictio. Sequitur quidem in omnibus reprobis ordinatio ad poenam, et poenae impositio; atque haec utraque recte dicuntur respicere personae sic ordinatae et puniendae finalem permansionem in peccato: sed in ipso formali actu reprobationis ordinatio personae reprobatae ad mortem aeternam nondum continetur. Fallere igitur nos conantur hujusmodi argumentationibus, dum quae eidem subjecto competunt, ex iisdem causis falso nasci praesumunt; quasi necesse esset, quia omnis reprobatus est etiam ad poenam ordinatus, ideo hanc reprobationem atque hanc ad poenam ordinationem ex iisdem causis dependere. Nos autem defendimus, utcunque iidem homines, qui sunt reprobati, semper etiam sint ad poenam deputati, tamen hanc reprobationem ex sola libertate voluntatis Divinae manasse, ordinationem autem ad poenam ex praeviso eorundem peccato originem traxisse.
english: I answer: by reprobation we mean that part of divine providence by which God wills to deny certain ones special grace and permit them to fall short of beatitude's end — as by predestination we mean that other part by which he willed to prepare and give certain ones that special grace and lead them infallibly to glory and beatitude. On that footing, we deny that this reprobation is a deputation or adjudication to punishment. It is free denial of an unowed benefit from God's will alone; it is not imperious infliction of an unowed penalty from God's will alone. Yes, in all the reprobate there follows ordination to punishment and imposition of punishment — and both rightly regard that person's final remaining in sin. But in the formal act of reprobation itself, ordination of the reprobate person to eternal death is not yet contained. Such arguments try to deceive us by presuming that what belongs to the same subject must spring from the same causes — as if, because every reprobate is also ordained to punishment, reprobation and that ordination to punishment must depend on the same causes. We hold: however much the same men who are reprobated are always also deputed to punishment, this reprobation flowed from the sole liberty of the divine will, while ordination to punishment drew its origin from their foresighted sin.

source_text: Deus est quasi Sol quidam radios gratiae spiritualis ubique diffundens: Ergo quantum in se est, gratiam spiritualem omnibus impertit, nisi diffusis gratiae suae radiis obicem ponant. Quod igitur quosdam gratiae expertes relinquit et reprobat, id inde evenit, quod praevidit hosce ut obicem ponentes gratiae suae. Reprobatio igitur est ex praeviso hoc malo usu liberi arbitrii.
english: Tenth: God is as it were a Sun everywhere diffusing rays of spiritual grace. Therefore, as much as in him lies, he imparts spiritual grace to all, unless they put an obstacle to those diffused rays. That he leaves some void of grace and reprobates them happens because he foresaw them putting an obstacle to his grace. So reprobation is from that foresighted evil use of free will.

source_text: In multis deficit haec comparatio. Primo, licet Deus haud incommode dicatur Sol spiritualis, tamen non diffundit radios suos naturali necessitate, sed dispensatione voluntaria. Ergo quantum in se non ad omnes aequaliter et uniformiter eos diffundit. Secundo, ut largiamur Deum quosdam communes gratiae radios ad omnes et singulos diffundere (quae de re nunc non litigabimus), tamen specialem hunc et eximium radium specialis misericordiae, quantum in se est, omnibus et singulis promiscue eum praebere, nunquam concedemus.
english: The comparison fails in many ways. First: though God is not badly called a spiritual Sun, he does not diffuse his rays by natural necessity but by voluntary dispensation. So as much as in him lies, he does not diffuse them to all equally and uniformly. Second: even if we grant that God diffuses certain common rays of grace to each and all (we will not litigate that now), we will never concede that, as much as in him lies, he promiscuously offers this special excellent ray of special mercy to each and all.

source_text: Tertio, ubi Deus praesumitur nemini velle denegare hanc specialem misericordiam, quae electionis propria est, atque idcirco neminem reprobare, nisi qui praevisus fuerit ut gratiae Divinae obicem injiciens perverso usu liberi sui arbitrii, non animadvertit Argentina, hanc exceptionem de obice opponendo ad omnes et singulos pertinere in statu peccati consideratos. Nam prudenter observatum est ab Aquinate: Id quod dici solet, IN POTESTATE LIBERI ARBITRII ESSE NE IMPEDIMENTUM GRATIAE PRAESTET, de iis vere dicitur in quibus naturalis potentia integra fuerit: Quod per inordinationem praecedentem declinaverit ad malum, jam non erit omnino in sua potestate ut velit impedimentum praestare. Contr. Gent. lib. 3. cap. 160. Cum igitur omnes mortales ex se parati sint ad obices ponendos, et de facto ponant quamplurimos, si Deus ex tali praevisione reprobaret, omnes quotquot sumus, ne uno quidem excepto, reprobasset. Praedestinationis ergo et reprobationis specimen in hoc elucet, quod cum obices ponantur ab omnibus, Deus, ex abundantia misericordiae suae, quosdam impedimentis suis, tamen efficacibus et miris modis tandem emollire, et ad fidem et resipiscentiam convertere decrevit; alios autem eodem in modo gratiae suae obluctantes non emollire decrevit, sed in duritia sua et pervicacia obduratos relinquere. Denique quod ex praemissis infertur, nempe Deum ab aeterno praevidisse quosdam ut finaliter bene usuros libero arbitrio, alios ut finaliter male usuros eodem, atque ita decreto hanc praevisionem subsequente hos elegisse, illos reprobasse, id nullo modo potest consistere. Bonus enim et sanus usus liberi arbitrii in finem usque perseverans non nisi ex gratia electionis dimanavit; ergo electionem antecedentem praesupponit: E contra, malus usus liberi arbitrii, perdurans ad extremum usque halitum, non praevidetur nisi praesupposita in Deo voluntate negandi illam specialem gratiam, cui nullum cor, quantumvis durum, resistit: At haec voluntas Dei est voluntas reprobandi: Praevisio igitur cordis finaliter obdurati est quiddam reprobatione posterius, atque idcirco ratio sive causa reprobationis inde peti non potest.
english: Third: where God is presumed to will to deny no one that special mercy proper to election, and so to reprobate no one except who is foresighted as casting an obstacle to divine grace by perverse use of free will, Argentina misses that this exception about opposing an obstacle applies to each and all considered in the state of sin. Aquinas observed prudently (Contra Gentiles 3.160): the saying IT IS IN THE POWER OF FREE WILL NOT TO PRESENT AN IMPEDIMENT TO GRACE is truly said of those whose natural power is intact; he who by prior inordination has declined to evil is no longer altogether in his power so to will as to present an impediment. Since all mortals are of themselves ready to put obstacles, and in fact put very many, if God reprobated from such foresight he would have reprobated every one of us, not one excepted. So the pattern of predestination and reprobation shines here: though all put obstacles, God from abundance of mercy decreed finally to soften some — by efficacious and wondrous ways — out of their impediments and convert them to faith and repentance; others struggling the same way against his grace he decreed not to soften, but to leave hardened in their hardness and obstinacy. Finally the inference — that God from eternity foresaw some as finally using free will well, others ill, and by a decree following that foresight elected these and reprobated those — cannot stand. Good sound use of free will persevering to the end flowed only from election's grace, so it presupposes antecedent election. Conversely, evil use lasting to the last breath is not foresighted unless God's will to deny that special grace — which no heart, however hard, resists — is presupposed. That will of God is the will to reprobate. So foresight of a finally hardened heart is something later than reprobation; the reason or cause of reprobation cannot be sought from it.

source_text: Si Deus aliquos eligeret ab aeterno, aliquos reprobaret, absque causa se tenente ex parte hominum, tunc esset acceptor personarum. Videtur enim esse acceptor personarum, qui, duobus existentibus aequalibus, uni dat quod alteri denegat. Haec autem προσωπολημψία a Deo removetur, Actor. x. 34.
english: Argument: if from eternity God elected some and reprobated others without a cause holding on the human side, then he would be an acceptor of persons. For he seems an acceptor of persons who, when two are equal, gives to one what he denies the other. But that respect of persons is removed from God (Acts 10:34).

source_text: Hanc fuisse veterem Pelagianorum objectionem passim apud Augustinum legimus. Epist. 105. Quod autem personarum acceptorem Deum se credere existimant, si credant quod sine ullis praecedentibus meritis cujus vult miseretur, et quos dignatur vocat, et quem vult religiosum facit, parum attendunt quod debita reddatur poena damnato, indebita gratia liberato, ut nec ille se indignum queratur, nec dignum se iste glorietur, atque ibi potius acceptionem nullam fieri personarum, ubi una eademque massa damnationis et offensionis involvit, ut liberatus de non liberatis discat, quod etiam sibi supplicium conveniret, nisi gratia subveniret. Eandem objectionem repellit Epist. 106. et contra 2. Epist. Pelag. lib. 2. cap. 7. Huc igitur redit Augustini responsio, ut doceat non pertinere ad προσωπολημψία ubi quis de suo facit quod vult. Nam quamvis electo detur misericordia, reprobato tamen haud negatur justitia: Honoratur electus dono gratuito, non tamen fraudatur reprobatus beneficio sibi debito.
english: This was the old Pelagian objection — we read it everywhere in Augustine. Epistle 105: those who think they make God an acceptor of persons if they believe that without preceding merits he has mercy on whom he will, calls whom he deigns, and makes religious whom he will, little notice that due punishment is rendered to the damned and unowed grace to the freed — so neither complains as unworthy, nor the other glories as worthy. Rather there is no respect of persons where one and the same mass of damnation and offense wraps all, that the freed may learn from the not-freed that punishment would have suited him too unless grace had helped. The same objection he repels in Epistle 106 and Against two Letters of the Pelagians 2.7. Augustine's answer comes to this: it is not respect of persons where one does of his own what he wills. Mercy is given the elect; justice is not denied the reprobate. The elect is honored with a gratuitous gift; the reprobate is not cheated of any benefit owed him.

source_text: Scholastici respondent magis succinte, Non esse injustum aut vitiosum dare inaequalia aequalibus, ubi aliquid datur ex mera liberalitate, sed ubi ex debito redditur. Sic Durandus lib. 1. dist. 41. qu. 2. resp. ad 1. In eandem sententiam Thomas, Non est iniquitas apud Deum, si inaequalia aequalibus praeparet. Hoc enim esset contra justitiae rationem, si praedestinationis effectus ex debito redderetur, et non daretur. Ex his enim quae ex gratia dantur, potest aliquis pro libito suo dare cui vult plus vel minus, dummodo nulli subtrahat debitum, Part. 1. quaest. 23. art. 5. resp. ad 3. Denique Gerson in Regulis Moralibus idem affirmat, Non est acceptio personarum nisi ubi debitum est et paritas utrobique, quia in gratis faciendis unum capere, alium dimittere, non est acceptio personarum. Ex hisce igitur perspicuum est, consequentiam Majoris in praedicto argumento fuisse plane nullam: quia in praedestinatione Deus non dat praedestinato debitam sed indebitam gratiam; atque similiter in reprobatione non denegat reprobato debitae sed indebitae gratiae beneficium.
english: The Scholastics answer more briefly: it is not unjust or vicious to give unequals to equals where the gift is from mere liberality — only where something is rendered from debt. So Durandus (Sentences 1, dist. 41, q. 2 ad 1). Thomas to the same effect: There is no iniquity with God if he prepare unequals for equals. It would be against justice if the effect of predestination were rendered as debt and not given. Of things given from grace, one may at pleasure give more or less to whom he will, provided he subtracts from none what is owed (ST I, q. 23 a. 5 ad 3). Gerson in the Moral Rules: there is no respect of persons except where debt and parity stand on both sides; in free gifts, to take one and dismiss another is not respect of persons. So the major's consequence in the argument is plainly null: in predestination God gives the predestined not owed but unowed grace; in reprobation he denies the reprobate not an owed benefit but an unowed one.

source_text: Quod autem attinet ad illa Petri verba, Actor. x. 34, In veritate comperi quia non est personarum acceptor Deus, sed in omni gente qui timet eum et operatur justitiam, acceptus est ei, Spectant Dei favorem ex pacto et promisso jam quasi debitum, non aeternum illum et gratuitum favorem nullo pacto, nullo promissione obstrictum aut obligatum. Deus enim promittendo favorem suum timentibus se, ac sancte pieque viventibus, esset jam προσωπολημψία, si hominem pauperem aut ignobilem caste se colentem aspernaretur, divitem autem ac nobilem amplexaretur; aut si Judaeum religiosum favore suo prosequeretur, Gentilem vero juste, sobrie ac pie viventem negligeret. Hanc personarum acceptionem a Deo procul habendam docet Apostolus. At Deus nullo promisso aut pacto tenetur ad praedestinandum, vel non praedestinandum.
english: As for Peter's words (Acts 10:34) — Of a truth I perceive that God is not an acceptor of persons, but in every nation he who fears him and works righteousness is accepted with him — they regard God's favor from covenant and promise, already as it were owed, not that eternal gratuitous favor bound by no covenant or promise. For by promising favor to those who fear him and live holily and piously, God would already be an acceptor of persons if he spurned a poor or lowly man worshipping him chastely and embraced a rich noble, or if he favored a religious Jew and neglected a Gentile living justly, soberly, and piously. That respect of persons the Apostle teaches is far from God. But God is held by no promise or covenant to predestinate or not predestinate.

source_text: Porro, in eligendo aut praetereundo non respicit aliquam externam circumstantiam gentis, nobilitatis, aut quid consimile, sed agit ex mero beneplacito voluntatis suae. Denique, ii quos praeterit non possunt obtendere se Deum timuisse et juste vixisse, sed coguntur e contra agnoscere se fuisse irae filios, et minimo Dei beneficio indignissimos. Hic igitur locus Scripturae non probat, aut praedestinationem et reprobationem procedere ex causa aliqua se tenente ex parte hominum, aut Deum personarum acceptorem esse arguendum.
english: Further: in electing or passing by he regards no external circumstance of nation, nobility, or the like, but acts from the mere good pleasure of his will. Finally, those he passes by cannot pretend they feared God and lived justly; they are compelled instead to acknowledge they were children of wrath, most unworthy of the least divine benefit. So this Scripture place proves neither that predestination and reprobation proceed from some cause holding on the human side, nor that God is to be charged as an acceptor of persons.

source_text: Deus est dives in misericordia: Sed si aliquos reprobaret ex mera sua voluntate, et non propter praevisum peccatum, in tali actu nihil misericordiae appareret: Ergo reprobat ex praevisione demeritorum, sive ex praeviso malo usu liberi arbitrii ad finem usque duraturo.
english: Argument: God is rich in mercy. But if he reprobated some from his mere will and not for foresighted sin, nothing of mercy would appear in that act. Therefore he reprobates from foresight of demerits — or from foresighted evil use of free will lasting to the end.

source_text: Primo, id semper tenendum est, Quando negamus reprobationem ex praescientia humanorum demeritorum originem habuisse, nos loqui de reprobatione quatenus significat denegatam praeparationem efficacis gratiae certis personis, non quatenus denotat praeparationem aeternae poenae iisdem personis. Nam cum Aquinate libenter concedimus: Utcunque praescientia meritorum non potest esse aliqua ratio praedestinationis, quia ipsa merita praescita cadunt sub praedestinatione, tamen praescientia peccatorum potest esse aliqua ratio reprobationis, ex parte poenae quae praeparatur reprobis, in quantum Deus proponit se puniturum malos propter peccata quae a seipsis habent, non a Deo. Haec Thomas Comment. in Rom. ix. lect. 2, prope finem.
english: First, always hold this: when we deny that reprobation took origin from foresight of human demerits, we mean reprobation as denied preparation of efficacious grace for certain persons — not as preparation of eternal punishment for those same persons. With Aquinas we gladly grant: foresight of merits cannot be any reason of predestination, because foresighted merits themselves fall under predestination; yet foresight of sins can be some reason of reprobation on the side of the punishment prepared for the reprobate, insofar as God proposes to punish the wicked for sins they have from themselves, not from God (Thomas, Commentary on Romans 9, lect. 2, near the end).

source_text: Secundo, et illud notandum est, Eos omnes qui a Deo reprobantur, spectari ab eodem Deo ut peccati originalis reatu constrictos et damnationi obnoxios: quamvis hoc non sit simpliciter necessarium ad vindicandum Deum ab injustitia aut crudelitate, quod attinet ad reprobationem negativam, ut patet in angelis. Verum cum inter homines ita se res habeat, ut illi omnes qui reprobentur sint in se damnabiles et odio digni; Deus, quamvis dives sit in misericordia, potest aequissime pro suae voluntatis libertate ex illis quosdam eligere, quosdam reprobare, quos universos originale peccatum reddidit odio dignos et (si ita loqui liceat) reprobabiles.
english: Second, note also: all whom God reprobates are regarded by him as bound by original guilt and liable to damnation — though that is not simply necessary to clear God of injustice or cruelty as to negative reprobation, as is plain in the angels. But among men it stands thus: all who are reprobated are in themselves damnable and worthy of hatred. God, though rich in mercy, can most equitably by liberty of will elect some from among them and reprobate others — all of whom original sin has made worthy of hatred and (if one may so speak) reprobable.

source_text: Denique, quando objicitur, Si Deus reprobaret aliter quam ex praevisione finalium et actualium demeritorum, in tali actu nihil misericordiae appareret, Videtur haec objectio niti recepta quadam inter Scholasticos regula, nempe, In omnibus Dei operibus misericordiam et justitiam concurrere. Sed hujus regulae mens est, Non omnem actionem Dei esse formaliter actionem justitiae vel misericordiae, sed esse effectum Divinae providentiae ordinatum ad ostensionem vel justitiae, vel misericordiae, vel utriusque. Atque sic reprobatio haec, quam ex mera Dei voluntate factam supponimus, ordinatur ad ostensionem justitiae in damnatis, et ad ostensionem majoris misericordiae erga praedestinatos. Porro, apparet misericordia quaedam erga ipsos reprobatos, licet non illa specialis et eximia quae per gratiam efficacem infallibiliter ordinat ad gloriam. Nam reprobis conceduntur saepenumero multa gratiae ac misericordiae Divinae beneficia, quae illis non subducuntur, nisi propter abusum eorundem, et voluntariam in Deum rebellionem. Denique in ipsa damnatione horum reproborum apparet misericordia Dei, non quidem totaliter relaxans, sed aliqualiter allevians, dum punit eos citra condignum, ut bene Thomas, Part. 1. quaest. 21. artic. 4.
english: Finally: when it is objected that if God reprobated otherwise than from foresight of final and actual demerits, nothing of mercy would appear — that objection seems to rest on a Scholastic rule: in all God's works mercy and justice concur. The sense of the rule is not that every divine action is formally an act of justice or of mercy, but that it is an effect of providence ordained to show justice, or mercy, or both. So this reprobation, which we take as from God's mere will, is ordained to show justice in the damned and greater mercy toward the predestined. Further, some mercy appears even toward the reprobate themselves — not that special excellent mercy which by efficacious grace infallibly ordains to glory, but the many benefits of grace and mercy often granted them, not withdrawn except for abuse and voluntary rebellion against God. Even in their damnation God's mercy appears — not totally relaxing, but somewhat alleviating — while he punishes them short of what is condign (Thomas, ST I, q. 21 a. 4).

source_text: Nullus justus judex per se intendit justitiam punitivam, sed tantum ex suppositione punibilis culpae: Sed in reprobando Deus intendit justitiam suam punitivam et vindicativam exercere: Ergo reprobat ex praescientia mali et demeritorii usus liberi arbitrii.
english: They press further: a just judge never aims at punitive justice for its own sake — only once punishable fault is supposed. Yet God, they say, in the act of reprobating means to exercise punitive and vindicative justice. Hence reprobation must spring from foresight of free will's evil, demeritorious use.

source_text: Reprobatio negativa, quae nihil aliud dicit quam aeternum Dei propositum de non-dando quibusdam singularem gratiam qua corda illorum emollirentur, cujusque beneficio ipsi ad vitam aeternam infallibiliter dirigerentur, non procedit ex justitia punitiva, neque ex voluntate damnandi, sed ex illa Divinae providentiae ratione, qua Deus judicavit sapientiae suae convenire, ut permitteret quosdam suo vitio a fine beatitudinis deficere. Posita autem hac Dei voluntate, praevidet Deus futura reproborum peccata, et finalem eorundem permansionem in peccatis; atque simul intelligit gloriae suae manifestationem ex punitione peccatorum orituram. Intendit itaque Deus justitiam punitivam exercere circa reprobates, propter peccata in quibus praevidentur vitam finitori; sed haec intentio et praevisio secuta est reprobationis praedictae actum, sicuti et ipse finalis status peccatoris in peccatis suis. Dicere quidem possumus, et vere, semper fuisse in Deo voluntatem puniendi peccata, si fierent: sed absolutam et expressam voluntatem puniendi, ac terminatam ad hanc aut illam singularem personam, non possumus in Deo ponere, nisi praesupposita Dei permissione ut fierent, utque haec persona punitioni destinata sub reatu eorundem finaliter permaneret. Haec autem permissio, quae reprobationis negativae actum continet, prior est absoluta praescientia mali usus liberi arbitrii ad finem vitae usque perdurantis in hac aut illa persona singulari, ac proinde non potest ex illa tanquam ex causa dependere. Perperam ergo reprobandi ac vindicandi sive damnandi decreta ex iisdem causis deducuntur.
english: Negative reprobation — nothing but God's eternal purpose not to give certain ones that singular grace by which their hearts would be softened and by which they would be infallibly directed to eternal life — does not proceed from punitive justice, nor from a will to damn, but from that reason of providence by which God judged it agreeable to his wisdom to permit some, by their own vice, to fall short of beatitude's end. That will posited, God foresights the reprobate's future sins and final remaining in them, and understands that the manifestation of his glory will arise from punishing those sins. So he intends to exercise punitive justice about the reprobate for the sins in which they are foresighted as finishing life — but that intention and foresight followed the act of the foresaid reprobation, as did the sinner's final state in his sins. We may truly say there was always in God a will to punish sins if they should come to be; but an absolute express will to punish, terminated on this or that particular person, we cannot place in God unless his permission that they come to be is presupposed, and that this person destined to punishment finally remain under their guilt. That permission — which contains the act of negative reprobation — is prior to absolute foresight of evil use of free will lasting to life's end in this or that person, and so cannot depend on that foresight as cause. Wrongly, then, are the decrees of reprobating and of avenging or damning drawn from the same causes.

source_text: Hactenus Jesuitarum ac Scholasticorum argumenta ventilavimus. Urgentur et alia nonnulla a Corvino, in Defensione sententiae Arminianae adversus Tilenum: in quibus si quid occurrat novi, diluetur. Eo autem magis nobis laborandum est, ut reprobationis actum negativum, quem praeteritionem sive non-electionem vocare possumus, ad solam Divinae voluntatis libertatem revocemus, quia omnes qui hanc reprobationem ex praevisione actuum malorum deducunt, electionem etiam ex praevisione actuum bonorum suspendunt.
english: So far we have aired the Jesuits' and Scholastics' arguments. Corvinus also presses others in his Defense of the Arminian sentence against Tilenus — and if anything new appears there, it will be cleared. We must labor all the more to recall the negative act of reprobation — which we may call praeterition or non-election — to the sole liberty of the divine will. For all who derive this reprobation from foresight of evil acts also hang election on foresight of good acts.

source_text: Huc etiam accedit quod Augustinus (quo nemo doctius aut sanctius hanc causam tractavit) tam negat praevisa mala opera Esavi fuisse causam quod a Deo reprobaretur, quam praevisa bona opera Jacobi negat causam fuisse quod is a Deo eligeretur. Videte Enchir. ad Laurent. cap. 98, Ad Simpl. lib. 1. quaest. 2, et Epist. 105, ubi illorum sententiam qui inquiunt Deum nondum natorum vel hunc odisse vel illum dilexisse, quia eorum futura opera praevidebat, ex aequo rejicit. Et Epist. 106 aperte docet, Deum diligendo eos discernere, quos merita nulla discernunt. Sicut igitur praevisionem bonorum meritorum non admittit causam fuisse electionis, ita nec praevisionem malorum concedit fuisse rationem reprobationis. Nam ubi ex una parte considerantur boni actus, puta credendi, obediendi, perseverandi, ex altera mali actus hisce oppositi, illos ut meritis discretos considerari perspicuum est. Sed ad Corvini sententiam veniamus.
english: Add Augustine — no one treated this cause more learnedly or holily: he denies as much that Esau's foresighted evil works were the cause of his reprobation as that Jacob's foresighted good works were the cause of his election. See Enchiridion to Laurentius 98, To Simplicianus 1.2, and Epistle 105, where he equally rejects those who say God hated or loved the not-yet-born because he foresaw their future works. Epistle 106 openly teaches that God by loving discerns those whom no merits discern. As he will not admit foresight of good merits as election's cause, so he will not grant foresight of evils as reprobation's reason. For where good acts — believing, obeying, persevering — stand on one side and opposite evil acts on the other, those are clearly regarded as discerned by merits. But let us come to Corvinus's sentence.

source_text: Is igitur cum Arminio statuit, Deum singulares personas semper reprobare ex personali earundem propria gratiae oblatae rejectione; ita ut nec in decreto reprobationis quenquam rejecerit aut praeterierit nisi consideratum ut actu infidelem et impenitentem contra Deum actu vocantem, nec in Adae lapsu quenquam ex absoluta sua ordinatione reliquerit, aut propter solum originale peccatum damnare decreverit.
english: With Arminius he therefore holds this: God always reprobates particular persons from their own personal rejection of offered grace. In the reprobation decree, on that view, he has rejected or passed by no one except as actually unbelieving and impenitent against God who is actually calling. Nor in Adam's fall has he left anyone by absolute ordination alone, or decreed to damn for original sin only.

source_text: In hac sententia, si de adultis solis sermo sit, concedemus Arminio et Corvino, personalem ac propriam quandam indignitatem, ex voluntaria rebellione ortam, fuisse in illis omnibus ab aeterno praevisam, quos Deus ab aeterno reprobavit: sed negabimus, ex praevisa hac actuali et finali eorundem rebellione decretum reprobationis, tanquam ex causa antecedanea et motiva, emanasse. Quin potius affirmamus, in voluntate Divina prius concipi a nobis oportere decretum illud indurationis permissivae sive reprobationis, de qua Apostolus sic loquitur, Miserebitur cujus vult, et quem vult indurat, quam in mente Divina concipere possimus praevisionem istam ad quamlibet singularem personam relatam, qua ab aeterno Deus intuetur eandem personam ut gratiae suae reluctantem, et ad finem usque vitae suae eandem gratiam contumaciter aspernantem et rejicientem.
english: If the talk is of adults only, we grant Arminius and Corvinus this much: a certain personal proper unworthiness, sprung from voluntary rebellion, was foresighted from eternity in all whom God from eternity reprobated. What we deny is that from that foresighted actual and final rebellion the reprobation decree flowed as from an antecedent moving cause. Rather we affirm: in the divine will we must first conceive that decree of permissive hardening or reprobation of which Paul speaks — He has mercy on whom he will, and whom he will he hardens — before we can conceive in the divine mind that foresight of any particular person as from eternity struggling against his grace and, to life's end, contumaciously spurning and rejecting it.

source_text: Porro, quando in constituenda sua sententia dicunt, Deum in decreto reprobationis considerare homines ut actu infideles et impenitentes contra Deum actu vocantem, coguntur vocabulis uti contra receptam sacrarum Scripturarum et omnium fere Theologorum consuetudinem. Si enim norman loquendi a Scripturis et sanis Theologis accipere velimus, infidelitas denotat rejectionem Evangelii, et vocabula gratiae ac vocationis Evangelii patefactionem praesupponunt. At Arminio et Corvino ob infidelitatem praevisam reprobantur, quibus Evangelium nunquam fuit annuntiatum; gratiam ac vocationem rejecisse dicuntur, quibus gratia Christi nunquam fuit oblata. Denique, quod de originali peccato docent, illud haud facere ullum hominem aeternae mortis reum, nec propter illud solum quenquam damnari, hoc profecto tam alienum est a catholicae Ecclesiae doctrina, quam est cum Arminiana Theologia necessario conjunctum et connexum.
english: Further: when they say that in the reprobation decree God considers men as actually unbelieving and impenitent against God actually calling, they are forced to use words against the received custom of Scripture and of almost all theologians. If we take our speaking-norm from Scripture and sound theologians, unbelief denotes rejection of the Gospel, and the words grace and vocation presuppose the Gospel's manifestation. Yet on Arminius's and Corvinus's view, people are reprobated for foresighted unbelief to whom the Gospel was never announced, and said to have rejected grace and vocation to whom Christ's grace was never offered. Finally, their teaching that original sin makes no man guilty of eternal death, and that no one is damned for that alone, is as alien to the catholic Church's doctrine as it is necessarily bound up with Arminian theology.

source_text: Verum ad argumenta istorum proponenda et diluenda accingamur. Cap. IX. Corvini argumenta proponuntur et diluuntur.
english: But let us now gird ourselves to propose and dissolve their arguments. Chapter IX — Corvinus's arguments proposed and dissolved.

source_text: Cap. IX. Corvini argumenta proponuntur et diluuntur. Argumentari igitur solent adversarii ab ipso damnandi decreto ad actum sive decretum reprobationis, hoc modo: Qualiter consideratos Deus damnat in tempore, taliter consideratos decrevit damnare, et reprobavit ab aeterno. Sed damnat homines consideratos ut Evangelio immorigeros, hoc est, ut finaliter impenitentes et incredulos: Ergo etiam taliter consideratos reprobavit.
english: Chapter IX — Corvinus's arguments proposed and dissolved.
