Adversaries commonly argue from the decree of damning to the act or decree of reprobation thus: In whatever manner of consideration God damns in time, in that same manner he decreed to damn and reprobated from eternity. But he damns men considered as contumacious to the Gospel — that is, as finally impenitent and unbelieving. Therefore he also reprobated them so considered.

source_text: Majorem inde liquere putant, quod quam rationem peccatum habet ad damnationem, eandem etiam habeat ad reprobationem: atque idcirco sicuti agnoscitur habere rationem causae meritoriae et moventis ipsum Deum ad damnationem hujus vel illius singularis personae, ita etiam se habere debet ad reprobationem. Hisce omnibus adjiciunt, repugnare Divinae sapientiae, ut velit reprobare peccatorem sine meritorum malorum consideratione, et tamen eundem in tempore nisi propter mala merita nolit condemnare.
english: They take the Major as clear from this: whatever relation sin has to damnation, it has the same to reprobation — so as sin is granted meritorious and moving cause moving God to damn this or that particular person, it must likewise stand toward reprobation. They add that it clashes with divine wisdom to will to reprobate a sinner without regard to evil merits, yet refuse to condemn him in time except for evil merits.

source_text: In causa praedestinationis consimili argumento utuntur tum Jesuitae tum Arminiani, cui a nobis antea satisfactum fuit. In hoc argumento caput erroris est, quod reprobatio sive decretum reprobandi idem prorsus esse praesumitur, quod decretum damnandi. Nobis autem decretum damnandi designat sententiam peremptoriam in mente Dei Judicis ab aeterno conceptam, et voluntatis placito confirmatam, qua hominem praevisum et consideratum, ut peccati in ipso exitu hujus vitae reum, statuit propter illud peccatum aeterna morte punire: decretum autem reprobandi denotat aeternum placitum Dei, non ut Judicis, sed ut liberrimi Agentis, quo apud se statuit quibusdam personis non apponere illam specialis et indebitae misericordiae gratiam, quae de facto eos emolliret, converteret et ad vitam aeternam perduceret.
english: Jesuits and Arminians use a like argument in the predestination debate — and we answered it before. The head of the error here is presuming reprobation, or the decree to reprobate, is altogether the same as the decree to damn. For us the decree to damn names a peremptory sentence conceived from eternity in the mind of God the Judge and confirmed by his will's good pleasure: to punish with eternal death, for that sin, a man foresighted and considered guilty of sin at this life's very exit. The decree to reprobate names God's eternal good pleasure not as Judge but as freest Agent: resolving not to apply to certain persons that grace of special unowed mercy which would in fact soften, convert, and lead them to eternal life.

source_text: Inter haec duo decreta latum discrimen est. Prius ex justitia vindicante procedit, ac proinde ad finalem reatum peccatoris, tanquam causam motivam supplicii destinati, respicit. Posterius ex libertate Dei de suo quod vult facientis egreditur, ac proinde, sicuti cum Deus statuit dare speciale beneficium alicui personae singulari, non inde sequitur, illum respexisse merita ejusdem personae, tanquam praedictae beneficentiae causam motivam, ita cum statuit non dare illud idem speciale beneficium alteri, non inde recte deducitur, illum ad finalia personae hujus demerita, tanquam ad causam motivam negatae hujus beneficentiae, respexisse. Majorem igitur propositionem, atque ejusdem confirmationem, invalidam esse dicimus, quia non est uniformis consideratio neque eadem habitudo peccati quoad decretum reprobandi, quae est ejusdem quoad decretum damnandi. Neque omnino repugnat, imo optime congruit, sapientiae Divinae, ut nolit quenquam condemnare nisi propter demeritum peccati tanquam causam antecedaneam et motivam supplicii destinati, et tamen velit aliquos reprobare (hoc est, in gratiae specialis praeparatione et infallibili ad vitam aeternam ordinatione praeterire) ex mera libertate suae voluntatis, et non ex antecedaneo infidelitatis aut impoenitentiae finalis motivo.
english: Between these two decrees the difference is wide. The first proceeds from vindicating justice, and so regards the sinner's final guilt as moving cause of the destined punishment. The second goes forth from God's liberty doing of his own what he wills. As when God resolves to give a special benefit to some particular person it does not follow that he regarded that person's merits as moving cause of the beneficence, so when he resolves not to give that same special benefit to another, it is not rightly deduced that he regarded that person's final demerits as moving cause of the denied beneficence. So we call the Major and its confirmation invalid: there is neither uniform consideration nor the same relation of sin to the decree of reprobating as to the decree of damning. Far from clashing with divine wisdom, it best agrees with it that God refuse to condemn anyone except for sin's demerit as antecedent moving cause of destined punishment — and yet will to reprobate some (that is, pass them by in preparing special grace and infallibly ordaining to eternal life) from mere liberty of will, not from an antecedent motive of final unbelief or impenitence.

source_text: Recte Bannes, Haec praeteritio sive reprobatio aliquarum personarum, aliis electis, est manifestativa maximae libertatis quam habet Divina voluntas circa dispensationem bonorum supernaturalium, In 1. quaest. 23. art. 5. pag. 293. Jam vero haud alienum est a sapientia Divina, sicuti et reliqua sua attributa, ita et hoc libertatis attributum in summo bono dispensando hominibus manifestare. Unde Lombardus, lib. 1. dist. 41, Reprobavit Deus quos voluit, non propter futura merita quae praevideret, veritate tamen rectissima, a nostris sensibus remota. Haec de Majore.
english: Bannes puts it well: this praeterition or reprobation of some persons, others being elect, manifests the greatest liberty the divine will has in dispensing supernatural goods (on ST I, q. 23 a. 5, p. 293). Nor is it alien to divine wisdom — as with his other attributes — to manifest this attribute of liberty in dispensing the highest good to men. So Lombard (Sentences 1, dist. 41): God reprobated whom he willed, not for future merits he foresaw — yet by a most right truth, remote from our senses. So much for the Major.

source_text: Accedamus ad Minorem; quae non est vera, si universaliter intelligatur. Nam multi damnantur, qui ut Evangelio immorigeri minime a Deo considerantur. Exemplo sint infantes Paganorum, qui filii irae nascuntur, et in Christo minime renascuntur. Exemplo etiam esse possunt inter adultos illi omnes, quibus nec Evangelium illuxit unquam, nec Christus innotuit: Quin etiam multos per solam Legem damnari, et non propter Evangelium contemptum, concedit Arminius, Exam. Praedest. Perkins. Sed non est quod ultra laboremus de Minore. Nam sive ob contemptum Evangelii, sive ob contemptum Legis homines damnentur, tamen, quod iidem reprobentur, aliunde causam habet. Denique, damus, homines reprobari non sine consideratione spretæ Legis, aut Evangelii, quia Deus non potest aliquem reprobare, nisi ut peccati reum: sed ex praeconsideratione fidei futurae in aliquibus, et in aliis praeconsideratione peccati futuri, haud consequitur. Multa enim a Deo eligente aut reprobante praevidentur ab aeterno in electis aut reprobatis futura, quae non habent rationem causae motivae ad actum reprobandi vel eligendi.
english: Now the Minor — which is not true if taken universally. Many are damned who are not at all considered by God as contumacious to the Gospel. Example: pagan infants, born children of wrath and not reborn in Christ. Among adults, all those to whom the Gospel never shone nor Christ became known. Arminius even grants that many are damned by the Law alone, not for contempt of the Gospel (Examination of Perkins's Predestination). No need to labor further on the Minor. Whether men are damned for contempt of Gospel or of Law, that the same are reprobated has its cause elsewhere. Finally we grant men are not reprobated without regard to a despised Law or Gospel, because God cannot reprobate anyone except as guilty of sin — but it does not follow from preconsideration of future faith in some and future sin in others. God electing or reprobating foresights from eternity many future things in elect and reprobate that are not moving causes of the act of electing or reprobating.

source_text: Ab Adae peccato omnibus promiscue remisso sic disputant: Deus non valet stricto jure agere cum ullo homine in communi Adae peccato jacente, ita ut sine ulla spe veniae in ista condemnatione relinquatur: At si reprobaret quospiam tantum ut jacentes in lapsu communi Adae, et non propter actualem eorum et personalem in Deum rebellionem, stricto et summo jure cum illis ageret.
english: From Adam's sin remitted to all alike they argue thus: God cannot deal by strict right with any man lying in Adam's common sin so as to leave him in that condemnation without any hope of pardon. But if he reprobated any only as lying in Adam's common fall, and not for their actual personal rebellion against God, he would be dealing with them by strict and highest right.

source_text: Majorem dupliciter confirmare conantur. Primo, exinde quod ipsi Adamo venia data sit: Iniquum enim videatur Deum ob Adami peccatum, quod pura puta illius aestimatione nostrum est, alios quoscunque a vita aeterna excludere, cum ipsum Adamum receperit in gratiam, qui illud peccatum perpetravit. Secundo, idem probare satagunt ex eo quod Christus pro omnibus redemptionem et reconciliationem apud Deum Patrem impetravit; videtur autem parum consentaneum, ut per decretum reprobationis exitio relinquantur, pro quibus Christus ita reconciliationem impetravit, ut nihil impedire possit, praeter impoenitentiam, quo minus ejusdem usu fiant participes. Ergo nemo reprobatur nisi ex consideratione finalis impoenitentiae sive rebellionis tanquam causae motivae: haec autem reprobatio.
english: They try to confirm the Major two ways. First: pardon was given to Adam himself — so it would seem unjust that God, for Adam's sin which by mere estimation is called ours, should shut any others from eternal life, when he received into grace Adam who committed that sin. Second: Christ obtained redemption and reconciliation with the Father for all — and it seems little fitting that by a reprobation decree those be left to destruction for whom Christ so obtained reconciliation that nothing but impenitence can bar them from sharing its use. Therefore no one is reprobated except from regard to final impenitence or rebellion as moving cause — and that, they say, is reprobation.

source_text: Respondeo, Majorem propositi syllogismi quoad infantes Paganorum, qui nec in foedere censentur, nec in Christo regenerantur, aperte falsam esse. Nam si condemnare aliquem ob solum peccatum originale sit stricto jure agere, pertinet est cum talibus agi stricto jure. Atque hinc Augustinus ex catholicae Ecclesiae sententia aperte pronunciat, Universum genus humanum tam justo judicio Divino in apostatica radice esse damnatum, ut etiamsi nullus inde liberaretur, nemo possit recte Dei vituperare justitiam: et qui liberantur sic oportere liberari, ut ex pluribus non liberatis, et in damnatione justissima derelictis, ostenderetur quid meruisset universa consortio: et quo etiam ipsos debitum judicium Dei duceret nisi ejus indebita misericordia subveniret, Enchirid. cap. 99. Quin etiam Vasques Jesuita, qui praedestinationem ex praevisis meritis acriter propugnat, cogitur tamen fateri: Si de reprobatione loquamur qua quis rejicitur a gratia Dei, in parvulis reprobis nullam omnino fuisse suae reprobationis causam; Si de reprobatione, qua quis a beatitudine rejicitur, sermo sit, parvulos eos quibus Divina providentia ita disponit, ut nullum remedium humanae industriae possit adhiberi, fuisse Dei decreto exclusos a regno caelorum, statim post praevisionem originalis peccati ab ipsis contracti, In 1. qu. 23. art. 3. disp. 89. cap. 6. Arminiani igitur longius progrediuntur in defensione erroris sui quam ipsi Jesuitae.
english: I answer: as to pagan infants — neither in the covenant nor regenerated in Christ — the Major of their syllogism is openly false. If to condemn for original sin alone is to deal by strict right, then with such God does deal by strict right. So Augustine from the catholic Church's sentence (Enchiridion 99): the whole human race is by so just a divine judgment damned in the apostate root that even if none were freed from it, no one could rightly blame God's justice; and those freed ought so to be freed that from the many not freed, left in most just damnation, it would be shown what the whole fellowship had merited — and whither even they would be led by God's due judgment unless his unowed mercy helped. Even Vasquez the Jesuit, who sharply defends predestination from foresighted merits, must confess: if we mean reprobation as rejection from God's grace, reprobate infants had no cause of their reprobation at all; if rejection from beatitude, those infants for whom providence so disposes that no human remedy can be applied were by God's decree shut from the kingdom of heaven right after foresight of original sin they contracted (on ST I, q. 23 a. 3, disp. 89 c. 6). So Arminians push their error farther than the Jesuits themselves.

source_text: Sed mittamus infantes, et Majorem discutiamus quatenus adultos et rationis ac liberi arbitrii compotes spectat. Quoad tales, si stricto jure agere intelligatur, qui decernit aliquem damnandum et morte aeterna afficiendum sine consideratione peccati actualis, fatemur Deum cum talibus peccatoribus stricto jure haud agere. Hosce enim neque damnavit, neque damnationi destinavit, nisi ob praevisa peccata, et finalem in iisdem impoenitentiam. Verum si per illud, stricto jure agere, Corvinus intelligat, non praeparare gratiam eam specialem, qua adhibita Deus scit atque statuit talem hominem fore liberandum, vel talem hominem praeterire et ad vitam aeternam capessendam decreto specialis providentiae, quam praedestinationem appellamus, haud ordinare, sed suae (ut ita dicam) deficientiae relinquere, tum affirmamus, Deum cum multis sic agere ex sola libertate voluntatis suae: et si hoc sit stricto jure agere (de quo mox videbimus), stricto jure agere cum omnibus reprobis.
english: Set infants aside and take the Major as it regards adults with reason and free will. If dealing by strict right means decreeing someone damned and afflicted with eternal death without regard to actual sin, we grant God does not so deal with such sinners. He neither damned them nor destined them to damnation except for foresighted sins and final impenitence in them. But if by dealing by strict right Corvinus means not preparing that special grace which, applied, God knows and decrees will free such a man — or passing him by and not ordaining him to take hold of eternal life by the special-providence decree we call predestination, but leaving him to his deficiency (so to speak) — then we affirm God so deals with many from sole liberty of will. And if that is dealing by strict right (we shall see shortly), then he deals by strict right with all the reprobate.

source_text: Porro, assumptum illud, quod hisce verbis majori propositioni annectitur, ita ut sine ulla spe veniae in ista condemnatione relinquantur, perperam decreto Dei reprobantis tribuitur. Nam ut praedestinationis, ita et reprobationis decretum arcanum est, nec quantum ad distinctionem singularium ulli mortalium sive quoad seipsum sive quoad alium a priori notum. Sicuti ergo praedestinati, ex eo solum quod praedestinati, spem veniae nondum habent; ita nec reprobati, ex eo solum quod reprobati sunt, sine ulla spe veniae relinquuntur. Nam ut Paulus praedestinatus spem veniae concipere non potuit nisi mediante conversione et fide in Christum; ita nec Judas reprobatus sine spe veniae relinquitur, nisi mediante infidelitate sua et impietate contra Christum. Denique si propter solam eventus infallibilitatem et decreti Divini immutabilitatem Arminiani contendant, quemlibet reprobatum omni spe veniae destitutum, hoc incommodo non minus urgetur ipsorum sententia quam nostra. Nam illi agnoscunt Judam, adeoque singulares omnes homines reprobatos, fuisse ab aeterno fixa et peremptoria Dei sententia reprobatos; ita ut juxta illorum opinionem tam certum, infallibile et definitum fuerit apud Deum, quod Judas veniam et vitam aeternam nunquam consequetur, quam in nostra. Si ergo posita hac reprobatione Arminiana Judas absque omni spe veniae non relinquitur, neque posita illa quam orthodoxi defendunt relinquetur.
english: Further: the clause annexed to their Major — that such are left in that condemnation without any hope of pardon — is wrongly pinned on the reprobating decree. Like predestination, the reprobation decree is secret; as to which particulars, no mortal knows it a priori of himself or of another. As the predestined do not yet have hope of pardon from being predestined alone, so the reprobate are not left without hope of pardon from being reprobated alone. Paul the predestined could not conceive hope of pardon except through conversion and faith in Christ; Judas the reprobate is not left without hope of pardon except through his unbelief and impiety against Christ. Finally if Arminians argue from mere infallibility of the event and immutability of the decree that any reprobate is stripped of all hope of pardon, that inconvenience presses their view no less than ours. They grant Judas — and so every particular reprobate — was from eternity reprobated by God's fixed peremptory sentence; so that on their view it is as certain, infallible, and defined with God that Judas will never obtain pardon and eternal life as on ours. If, then, on that Arminian reprobation Judas is not left without all hope of pardon, neither will he be on the reprobation the orthodox defend.

source_text: Jam confirmationem Majoris attendamus. Primo, dicunt repugnare bonitati Divinae, ut immunis sit Adamus qui peccatum ipsum patravit, et alii plectantur, qui mera imputatione rei sunt. Multis vitiis laborat haec confirmatio. Primo, non de plectendis hominibus, sed de reprobandis quaeritur. Aliud enim est reprobatio, aliud damnatio vel punitio, ut saepe inculcavimus. A scopo igitur quaestionis haec verba aberrant. Deinde, nimis extenuant originale peccatum, quando dicunt illud pura puta Dei aestimatione nostrum esse, nosque non aliter quam mera imputatione reos esse. Nam nostrum est, non pura puta imputatione, sed contagiosa propagatione: nec rei tantum sumus mera Dei aestimatione, sed contracta omnium animae facultatum damnabili corruptione. Porro, non repugnat aequitati aut bonitati Divinae, Adamum poenitentem liberare, atque alios in solo originali peccato morientes punire. Nam quae fecit Adamus in statu integro, fecit ut radix generis humani, et tam nobis fecit quam sibi, adeo ut non sibi solum, sed posteris omnibus stetisse et cecidisse dicatur: at quae fecit in statu lapso, sibi fecit, non posteris; nam sibi, non posteris omnibus et singulis, poenitendo gratiam et favorem Divinum dicitur recuperasse. Denique, nec illud iniquum putandum est, quod Deus Adamo uni praeparaverit ac donaverit veram ac seriam poenitentiam ex mera sua misericordia, multis autem ex Adamo prognatis neque praeparaverit neque donaverit eandem poenitentiam salutarem. Nulla enim lege magis tenetur Deus praestare omnibus posteris Adae quod ipsi indulsit, quam exhibere Judae, quicquid Paulo aut Petro ex mera misericordia exhibuit.
english: Now their confirmation of the Major. First they say it clashes with divine goodness that Adam who committed the sin be immune while others are smitten who are guilty by mere imputation. That confirmation has many faults. First: the question is not about men to be punished, but about men to be reprobated. Reprobation is one thing; damnation or punishment another — as we have often pressed. So those words wander from the question's scope. Next they too much thin original sin when they say it is ours by mere divine estimation and that we are guilty only by bare imputation. It is ours by contagious propagation, not bare imputation; we are guilty not only by God's mere estimation but by damnable corruption contracted in all the soul's faculties. Further, it does not clash with divine equity or goodness to free penitent Adam and punish others dying in original sin alone. What Adam did in the intact state he did as root of the human race — for us as for himself — so he is said to have stood and fallen not for himself alone but for all posterity. What he did in the fallen state he did for himself, not for posterity; by repenting he is said to have recovered divine grace and favor for himself, not for every posterity. Finally it is not iniquitous that God from mere mercy prepared and gave true serious penitence to Adam alone, and neither prepared nor gave the same saving penitence to many sprung from Adam. No law binds God more to give all Adam's posterity what he indulged Adam than to give Judas whatever from mere mercy he gave Paul or Peter.

source_text: Secundo contendunt neminem reprobari ut consideratum solummodo in communi Adae peccato, quia Christus omnibus reconciliationem impetravit, cujus ut fiant participes sola obstare potest impoenitentia singulorum. Ipsi solvunt nodum quem nexuerunt. Si enim ipsa Christi oblatione applicata reconciliatio sive redemtio omnibus et singulis esset obtenta, virium aliquid huic argumento inesset: sed sicut adultis non applicatur, nisi mediante fide et poenitentia actuali, ita neque infantibus nisi mediante Regeneratione supernaturali.
english: Secondly they contend that no one is reprobated merely as lying in Adam's common sin, because Christ obtained reconciliation for all — and only each person's impenitence can bar them from sharing it. They untie the knot they tied. If reconciliation or redemption were obtained for every person by Christ's offering already applied, the argument would have some force. But as it is not applied to adults except through faith and actual penitence, so neither to infants except through supernatural regeneration.

source_text: Jam quaero, Ubi Deus promisit se omnibus et singulis adultis praeparare velle et conferre illam fidem et poenitentiam, qua efficaciter et de facto reconcilientur Deo? Aut ubi foedus iniit cum infantibus universis, ut, non obstante originali peccato, teneatur eos pro reconciliatis habere, et supernaturali regeneratione in filios et haeredes vitae aeternae adoptare? Si hoc neque facit, neque facere tenetur, quosdam in solo originali peccato jacentes praeterit sive reprobat, neque in hoc agit injuste, sed libero suo jure utitur. Atque sic videtis, neque Majorem propositionem in se firmam fuisse, nec probationibus adjunctis solide confirmatam.
english: Where, then, stands any promise that God will prep and confer on every adult the faith and penitence that actually reconcile them to him? And where has he bound himself by covenant to every infant — original sin or no — to count them reconciled and by supernatural regeneration make them sons and heirs of eternal life? He does neither, and owes neither. So when he passes over or reprobates some who lie in original sin alone, he wrongs no one; he exercises free right. The Major, therefore, was neither sound in itself nor made solid by the proofs they annexed.

source_text: Ad Minorem quod attinet, nego etiam et illud, Deum reprobantem stricto vel summo jure agere cum reprobis, si eos ut in solo originali peccato jacentes reprobet. Si summo jure ageret cum reprobis, simul ac in lucem editi essent, posset illos ut aeternae mortis reos in gehennam ablegare: Si stricto jure ageret, posset omnibus gratiae suae donis destituere.
english: As for the Minor, I also deny that God, when he reprobates, deals with the reprobate by strict or highest right if he reprobates them as lying in original sin alone. If he dealt by highest right, as soon as they were born he could cast them into Gehenna as guilty of eternal death. If he dealt by strict right, he could strip them of all gifts of his grace.

source_text: At confert in eos subinde multa tum corporalia, tum spiritualia beneficia quibus reddantur meliores, et nihil quod illis debitum est subtrahit, nec illis infundit quicquam quo reddantur deteriores. Non igitur stricto jure agit cum illis. Sed adversarii ita hanc causam agunt, quasi inter haec duo, agere ex summa misericordia, et agere ex summo vel stricto jure, nihil esset medium.
english: But he often confers on them many corporal and spiritual benefits by which they may be made better; he withdraws nothing owed them, and pours into them nothing by which they are made worse. So he does not deal with them by strict right. Yet the adversaries plead as if between dealing from highest mercy and dealing from highest or strict right there were no middle.

source_text: Fatemur Deum cum solis electis agere ex summa misericordia: sed affirmamus etiam, agere cum non-electis sive reprobatis non ex summo jure, sed ex φιλανθρωπία, bonitate ac lenitate admirabili; adeo ut convincantur in conscientiis suis se reprobationis decreto non fuisse a Deo impulsos, sed aut innata contagione aut voluntaria rebellione, aut utraque in mortem meritissimam incidisse.
english: Highest mercy, we grant, is how God deals with the elect alone. Toward the non-elect or reprobate his dealing is not highest right either, but philanthropy (φιλανθρωπία), goodness, and a mildness worth wonder. Their consciences themselves convict them: the reprobation decree did not shove them; innate contagion, voluntary rebellion, or both, brought them into a death they richly deserved.

source_text: Deus vult ut salutaris gratia Evangelii omnibus hominibus promiscue offeratur: quam suam voluntatem multis Scripturae locis patefecit, Matth. xxviii. 19, Euntes ergo docete omnes gentes, etc. Et Marc. xvi. 15. Euntes in mundum universum praedicate Evangelium omni creaturae. Hinc etiam Apostolus Coloss. i. 28. Nos annunciamus Christum, corripientes omnem hominem, et docentes omnem hominem, ut exhibeamus omnem hominem perfectum in Christo. Hic affectus Dei erga omnium hominum salutem, videtur arguere neminem ab eo fuisse reprobatum, nisi post considerationem gratiae contemtae, vel (quod eodem redit) nisi ex praevisione finalis infidelitatis et impoenitentiae.
english: God wills that the saving grace of the Gospel be offered to all men alike — a will he has opened in many Scriptures: Matt. 28:19, Go therefore and teach all nations; and Mark 16:15, Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature. So also the Apostle, Col. 1:28: We announce Christ, warning every man and teaching every man, that we may present every man perfect in Christ. This regard of God for all men's salvation seems to argue that he reprobated no one except after regard to contempt of grace — or, what comes to the same, except from foresight of final unbelief and impenitence.

source_text: Ex illis mandatis Christi Docete omnes gentes, Predicate omni creaturae, recte colligitur, Discipulis illis auctoritatem Apostolicam, id est, non particulari alicui Ecclesiae aut nationi affixam, sed ad totum terrarum orbem spectantem, fuisse demandatam. Recte etiam infertur, Maceriam illam, quae Gentes ab Ecclesia Dei disterminavit, dirutam fuisse, et debuisse Evangelium, non uni nationi Judaeorum, sed Judaeis et Gentibus, Graecis et barbaris, sapientibus et insipientibus, praedicari, ut loquitur Paulus Rom. i.
english: From Christ's charges Teach all nations and Preach to every creature it rightly follows that those disciples were given apostolic authority — not pinned to one church or nation, but aimed at the whole world. It also follows that the wall which shut Gentiles from God's church was broken down, and that the Gospel was to be preached not to Jews alone but to Jews and Gentiles, Greeks and barbarians, wise and unwise — as Paul says in Rom. 1.

source_text: Denique et illud recte deducitur, Intentionem et operam ministrorum Evangelicorum eo spectare oportere, ac Pauli operam eo spectasse, ut eos omnes et singulos ad Christum adduceret, quibus Evangelium Christi annunciavit. Nam, ut pie et prudenter Augustinus, Nos nescientes quis pertineat ad praedestinatorum numerum, quis non pertineat, sic affici debemus charitatis affectu, ut omnes velimus salvos fieri, De corrupt. et grat. cap. 15.
english: Finally it also follows that Gospel ministers' aim and labor — as Paul's did — ought to be to bring to Christ every one to whom they announce Christ's Gospel. As Augustine says with piety and prudence: not knowing who belongs to the number of the predestined and who does not, we ought to be so moved by charity that we will all to be saved (De corrept. et grat. 15).

source_text: Sed, hisce omnibus admissis, negamus illud consectarium quod ex talibus testimoniis exprimere conantur adversarii, nempe, Illos non nisi ex praevisione demeritorum suorum fuisse reprobatos, quibus hunc in modum Christus jussit Evangelium praedicari. Nam reprobare est ex decreto suae voluntatis permittere aliquos a fine beatitudinis deficere, non destinando ac praeparando illis specialem illam gratiam, qua reapse ad fidem et vitam aeternam perducerentur: sicuti eligere est ad beatitudinem consequendam aliquos infallibiliter et infrustrabiliter ordinare, destinando, praeparando, ac donando illis specialem illam gratiam, qua Deus ab aeterno statuit et intellexit eos fore emolliendos, convertendos et de facto salvandos.
english: All that granted, we still deny the adversaries' corollary from these texts: that those to whom Christ ordered the Gospel preached were reprobated only from foresight of their demerits. To reprobate is, by decree of will, to permit some to fall short of beatitude's end — not destining or preparing for them that special grace which would in fact lead them to faith and eternal life. To elect is to ordain some to obtain beatitude infallibly and without frustration — destining, preparing, and giving them that special grace by which God from eternity decreed and knew they would be softened, converted, and in fact saved.

source_text: Jam vero jubemur Evangelium multis praedicare, quos Deus in hac infallibili ordinatione ad gratiam et gloriam, ex mero suo beneplacito, voluit praeterire. Mandatum igitur Evangelizandi non pugnat cum voluntate reprobandi. Addo etiam, Praeterire illos voluit, quoad praeparationem specialis hujus gratiae et de facto salutiferae, voluntate duritiam illorum finalem antecedente, et non ex praevisione finalis hujus duritiae et infidelitatis emanante. Nam (ut saepe dictum est) finalis impoenitentia et infidelitas hujus aut illius singularis personae non praevidetur aut praeconsideratur a Deo tanquam absolute et certo futura, nisi decreto reprobationis quoad eandem personam stabilito, quo Deus statuit, nolle talis personae eousque misereri ut efficaciter eam emolliat et convertat; quo etiam statuit, velle permittere ut suo vitio quamlibet gratiam oblatam repellat, et obduratus corde ad finem usque vitae suae permaneat.
english: We are commanded to preach the Gospel to many whom God, in that infallible ordination to grace and glory, from mere good pleasure willed to pass by. So the evangelizing mandate does not clash with the reprobating will. I add: he willed to pass them by as to preparing this special, actually saving grace — by a will that precedes their final hardness, not one that flows from foresight of that final hardness and unbelief. For (as often said) a particular person's final impenitence and unbelief is not foreseen by God as absolutely certain until the reprobation decree for that person stands — whereby God decreed not to pity them so far as to soften and convert them efficaciously, and also decreed to permit them by their own vice to repel any offered grace and stay hard-hearted to life's end.

source_text: Huc spectant illa Servatoris verba, Matth. xi. 25. Gloriam tibi tribuo Pater Domine caeli ac terrae, quod absconderis haec a sapientibus et intelligentibus, et ea detexeris infantibus. Etiam, Pater, quia ita placuit tibi. Et illa, Matth. xiii. 11. Vobis datum est nosse mysteria regni caelorum; illis non est datum. Denique et illud Apostoli, saepe inculcatum ac inculcandum omnibus specialis gratiae adversariis, Cujus vult miseretur, quem autem vult indurat, Rom. ix. 18. Omnia haec loca illos respiciunt quibus Dei verbum fuit praedicatum; et tamen in hisce omnibus innuatur antecedaneum Dei beneplacitum, secundum quod efficax gratia quibusdam praeparata fuit, aliis non fuit praeparata.
english: Here belong the Savior's words, Matt. 11:25: I give you glory, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and uncovered them to infants. Yes, Father, for so it pleased you. And Matt. 13:11: To you it is given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven; to them it is not given. And that saying of the Apostle, often pressed against every foe of special grace: He has mercy on whom he will, and whom he will he hardens (Rom. 9:18). All these texts concern those to whom God's word was preached — and yet in all of them God's antecedent good pleasure is hinted: efficacious grace prepared for some, not prepared for others.

source_text: Ut verbo absolvam, sicuti ex eo quod Deus vult omnes medicos pro sua virili ea agere, parare et offerre cuilibet aegroto quem curandum suscipiunt, quae ad vitam ejus producendam conducunt, non recte infertur Deum nolle permittere ut vi morbi ullus extinguatur, nisi exinde quod eundem praeviderit ut medicinae oblatae praefractum contemptorem: sic ex eo quod jubet Deus ministros Evangelicos verbum (quod est animorum medicina) omnibus praedicare, et omni ope eniti, ut omnes et singuli a morte liberentur, non sequitur, ipsum Deum decrevisse omnes a morte efficaciter liberare, aut non decrevisse permittere quosdam sua duricordia in perditionem ruere, quos nisi reprobasset, et potuisset et voluisset speciali sua misericordia emollire. Frustra igitur ex voluntate Dei mandante, quae actiones humanas debet gubernare, de voluntate Dei praedestinante aut reprobante judicatur, quae effectum aliquem producendum infallibili actione Divina, aut ea negata non producendum, determinat.
english: In a word: from God's will that every physician do his utmost — prepare and offer each patient he takes on whatever helps prolong life — you may not infer that God will let none die of disease unless he foresaw him a stubborn scorner of the offered medicine. So from God's command that Gospel ministers preach the word (the medicine of souls) to all, and strain every nerve that every one be freed from death, it does not follow that God himself decreed to free all from death efficaciously — or that he did not decree to permit some, by their hard hearts, to rush into perdition whom, had he not reprobated them, he both could and would have softened by special mercy. Vain, then, to judge the predestinating or reprobating will — which determines an effect by infallible divine action, or withholds it — from the mandating will that ought to govern human actions.

source_text: Urgent adhuc fortius; Deus ipse ex parte sua paratus est dare omnibus media sufficientia et necessaria ad credendum et convertendum, ac dabit proculdubio nisi obicem ipsi posuerint: Videntur autem haec inter se pugnare, ut Deus voluntate antecedente aliquem reprobaverit, et tamen paratus sit ei suppeditare omnia ad salutem necessaria: Neminem ergo reprobavit nisi voluntate consequente praevisam ejusdem hominis finalem impoenitentiam, infidelitatem, gratiaeque Divinae rejectionem.
english: They press harder still: God on his part is ready to give everyone the media sufficient and needful for believing and converting, and will surely give them unless people themselves put up a barrier. But that seems to clash — that God by antecedent will should have reprobated someone, and yet be ready to supply him everything needful for salvation. Therefore, they say, he reprobated no one except by consequent will after foresight of that person's final impenitence, unbelief, and rejection of divine grace.

source_text: Illud de gratia sufficiente omnibus parata et administrata postulatum valde lubricum est, et inter ipsos gratiae universalis patronos nondum pleno et firmo consensu approbatum. Vasques (quod ante annotavimus) ipsa rei evidentia convictus concedit, quibusdam infantibus sufficientia salutis media neque humana ulla providentia potuisse applicari, neque Divina providentia fuisse applicata, In T. Aquin. disp. 95. cap. 6. Possumus igitur, quoad hosce parvulos in originali peccato sic pereuntes, retorquere hanc rationem hoc modo: Quibus infantibus media sufficientia praeparata et administrata non fuerunt, illi rejecti fuerunt sine consideratione actualis infidelitatis, aut finalis impoenitentiae.
english: The claim that sufficient grace is prepared and administered to all is very slippery — and even among patrons of universal grace it lacks full firm consent. Vasquez (as we noted before), forced by the plain fact, grants that for some infants sufficient media of salvation could not be applied by any human providence and were not applied by divine providence (In T. Aquin. disp. 95.6). So for these little ones perishing in original sin we can turn their argument back: infants for whom sufficient media were never prepared or administered were rejected without regard to actual unbelief or final impenitence.

source_text: Sed quibusdam infantibus (puta ex utroque parente infideli idololatra, Christum nesciente, diabolum colente, susceptis, quos ἀκάθαρτοι ipse Apostolus indigitavit, 1 Cor. vii. 14.) sufficientia media non fuere praeparata aut administrata: In talibus ergo coguntur agnoscere rejectionem absque respectu ad praevisam et praeconsideratam personae reprobatae infidelitatem. Sed missis infantibus, qui Divina providentia ita ordinante nascuntur et moriuntur extra Ecclesiam, Idem Vasques et illud largitur, Et a praevisione peccatorum, etiam quoad adultos et rationis ac liberi arbitrii compotes, fuisse aliquam reprobationem et repulsam a Deo praefinitam, ibid. cap. 2. Reprobationem autem intelligit, rejectionem ab illa gratia speciali, qua negata homo semper indurescit et in perditionem ruit, cap. 5.
english: Take infants born of two unbelieving idolatrous parents — knowing no Christ, serving the devil — whom the Apostle himself calls unclean (1 Cor. 7:14): for them sufficient media were neither prepared nor administered. In such cases they must grant rejection with no regard to foresight of the reprobate's unbelief. Set those infants aside who, under divine providence, are born and die outside the Church: the same Vasquez also grants that even for adults with reason and free will some reprobation and repulse was fixed by God before foresight of sins (ibid. cap. 2). By reprobation he means rejection from that special grace which, denied, leaves a man always hardening and rushing into perdition (cap. 5).

source_text: Si Arminius, Corvinus, eorumque assipulatores vel hoc nobis concesserint, sequetur sufficientis gratiae suppeditationem non excludere antecedaneam reprobationem, sed efficacis gratiae praeparationem revera illam excludere, et electionem inferre. Sumatur igitur, omnibus adultis gratiam sufficientem a Deo administrari, tamen (uti videtis) vel Jesuita judice, non inde sequitur eos non fuisse ante praevisionem finalium demeritorum reprobatos.
english: If Arminius, Corvinus, and their backers grant us even that much, it follows that supplying sufficient grace does not shut out antecedent reprobation — whereas preparing efficacious grace truly does shut it out, and brings election in. So grant that God administers sufficient grace to every adult: still (as you see), even by a Jesuit's judgment, it does not follow they were not reprobated before foresight of final demerits.

source_text: In Angelis apostatis hujus rei veritas liquido apparet. Deus non modo paratus fuit dare illis media sufficientia et necessaria ad standum et perseverandum in obsequio Divino, sed dedit: ac nihilominus omnes Theologi fatentur, inter ipsos Angelos quosdam fuisse electos, quosdam non-electos sive reprobatos. Si igitur adversarii possint evincere, omnibus et singulis hominibus gratiam sufficientem dari, non tamen idcirco recte intulerint, neminem nisi ex praevisione finalis infidelitatis reprobari. Nam sicuti posita gratia sufficiente quoad designatam aliquam personam, non ponitur idcirco antecedanea ejus praedestinatio; ita nec posita eadem gratia sufficiente quoad eandem personam negatur idcirco antecedanea ejusdem reprobatio.
english: The apostate angels make this plain. God was not only ready to give them media sufficient and needful to stand and persevere in divine obedience — he gave them. Yet every theologian grants that among the angels some were elect, some non-elect or reprobate. So even if the adversaries could prove sufficient grace is given to every human being, they still could not rightly infer that no one is reprobated except from foresight of final unbelief. Just as positing sufficient grace for a given person does not posit his antecedent predestination, so positing that same sufficient grace does not deny his antecedent reprobation.

source_text: Ratio utrobique eadem est; Quia praedestinatio non dicit quamlibet ordinationem ad finem supernaturalem per media quantovis sufficientia, sed ordinationem cum exitu et eventu infallibili copulatam; neque reprobatio negat omnem ordinationem ad finem supernaturalem, sed ordinationem infrustrabilem ex inventione et speciali operatione Dei ordinantis, ipsum salutis eventum producentem. Denique, sufficientia media ad salutem omnibus dari, non tanta facilitate probatur quanta confidentia affirmatur. Non jam ingrediar hanc disputationem, quia ad solutionem argumenti propositi (uti accepistis) non est necesse. Illud solummodo annotabo, Bellarminum, qui hanc de sufficiente gratia sententiam tuetur, primo concedere nobis, quod nulla esset in Deo iniquitas si negaret aliquibus vel omnibus hanc gratiam sufficientem, De grat. et lib. arb. l. 2. cap. 4. Hinc colligimus, Deum nullo pacto aut promissione ad hoc obligatum: Quomodo igitur adversarii audent promittere omnibus et singulis gratiam sufficientem, quam Deus non promisit?
english: The reason is the same either way. Predestination is not just any ordination to a supernatural end by media however sufficient — it is ordination joined to an infallible outcome. Reprobation does not deny every ordination to a supernatural end, but the unfrustrable ordination that comes from the ordaining God's device and special operation producing the very event of salvation. Finally: that sufficient media of salvation are given to all is asserted with more confidence than it is proved with ease. I will not enter that dispute now — it is not needed to solve the argument before us. One note only: Bellarmine, who defends this sufficient-grace view, first grants that God would do no injustice if he denied that sufficient grace to some or to all (De grat. et lib. arb. 2.4). So God is bound to it by no pact or promise. How then dare the adversaries promise every person sufficient grace that God never promised?

source_text: Secundo, Bellarminus cogitur confugere ad illam distinctionem, mediate vel immediate; nec audet sustinere sufficientem gratiam omnibus parvulis immediate dari. At quam hoc obscurum est, huic parvulo, inter Indos aut Americanos nato, in parentibus suis fuisse exhibitum auxilium sufficiens, cum quale hoc fuerit, nemo potest explicare! Porro, si ad defensionem sufficientis gratiae liceat ad majores confugere, multo tutius et certius est ad primos usque parentes ascendere, de quibus nulla quaestio est, quin sufficientem gratiam in illis et posteri acceperint, quam in aliis majoribus nostris quibuscunque subsistere, de quibus incertum erit acceperintne talem sufficientem gratiam filiorum suorum nomine, an non acceperint.
english: Second: Bellarmine is driven to the mediate-or-immediate distinction, and will not dare claim sufficient grace is given immediately to every infant. How dark that is — that an infant born among Indians or Americans had sufficient help shown in his parents, when no one can say what that help was! And if defending sufficient grace means fleeing to ancestors, it is far safer to go all the way back to the first parents — where no one doubts posterity also received sufficient grace in them — than to stop at any later ancestors, of whom it remains uncertain whether they received such sufficient grace in their children's name or not.

source_text: Denique inter ipsos adultos quamplurimi sunt, fatente Bellarmino, ibid. c. 8. quibus sufficiens auxilium ad credendum non immediate conceditur, sed hoc solummodo sensu concessum intelligitur, quia possunt cognoscere per creaturas Deum esse, et possunt a Deo excitari ad credendum quod Deus sit, et quod inquirentibus se remunerator sit; et possunt tali fide excitari ad orandum Deum, et hoc modo (quamvis destituantur praedicatione Evangelii) possunt impetrare ut vel ab ipso Deo, vel ab Angelo, vel ab aliquo homine in cognitione fidei illuminentur. Quam misera sit haec defensio, quae cum quaestio instituatur de esse, respondet solummodo de posse, non dubito quin omnes intelligatis. Eam solummodo obiter perstringere volui, ut videatis quam male fundata sit haec propositio de sufficiente gratia omnibus et singulis donata, quam disputatores nostri substernunt tanquam solidissimum fundamentum causae suae. Plura non addo, quia licet concedatur, non tamen facit ad solidam causae probationem, uti ab initio ostendimus.
english: Finally, among adults themselves, Bellarmine admits (ibid. c. 8), very many are not given immediate sufficient help to believe — only in this thin sense: they can know God through the creatures, can be stirred to believe that God is and rewards seekers, can be stirred by that faith to pray, and so (even without Gospel preaching) can obtain illumination in the faith from God, an angel, or some man. Miserable defense: the question is about what is, and the answer is only about what can be — you all see that. I touch it only in passing, to show how poorly founded is the claim that sufficient grace is given to every person, which our disputers lay as their cause's firmest base. I add nothing more: even if granted, it still does not solidly prove their cause, as we showed from the start.

source_text: A vocatione Evangelica sic disputant. Si Deus decreto antecedaneo et absoluto quosdam elegisset, quosdam reprobasset, ageret simulate gratiam offerendo hominibus indiscriminatim per ministros evangelicos. Nam neque precise ad salutem electis mandari potest ut credant sub spe salutis adipiscendae; quia nemo sub conditione exspectat, quod sibi scit absolute ordinatum: neque reprobatis mandari potest ut credant; nam Deus sic exigeret ab eis ut falsum crederent, scilicet Christum pro illis fuisse passum et mortuum, illisque vitam et reconciliationem impetrasse. Ergo statuendum est, neminem reprobari nisi ex consideratione et praevisione spretae gratiae, et finalis permansionis in hac cordis obduratione et infidelitate.
english: From the Gospel call they argue thus. If God by an antecedent absolute decree had elected some and reprobated others, he would be acting with simulation when he offers grace indiscriminately through evangelical ministers. For the elect unto salvation cannot be commanded to believe under hope of obtaining salvation — no one awaits under a condition what he knows is absolutely ordained for him. Nor can the reprobate be commanded to believe — God would then require them to believe a falsehood: that Christ suffered and died for them and obtained life and reconciliation for them. Therefore, they say, no one is reprobated except from regard and foresight of despised grace and final persistence in that hardness of heart and unbelief.

source_text: Hic in memoriam revocandum est, quod subinde cogimur repetere, nos, per reprobationem, quam ex mera Dei voluntate et non ex praevisis demeritis humanis suspendimus, intelligere, non peremptorium decretum damnandi, vel morte aeterna afficiendi singularem aliquam personam, sed fixum decretum non-impertiendi specialem illam et efficacem gratiam, sive vocationem secundum propositum, absque qua Deus videt hanc singularem personam in sua duritia, impoenitentia, et infidelitate permansuram, atque decrevit illud permittere. Est quidem Deo certissimum, ex tali praeteritione hominem sic rejectum in peccatis suis moriturum: Est etiam Deo decretissimum, eundem hominem damnare propter peccata illa in quibus morietur: interim tamen haud obscurum est, negationem talis gratiae (in qua reprobationem proprie sitam esse putamus) ex mera libertate Divinae voluntatis pendere, at damnationem talis personae ex peccato ejusdem oriri.
english: Recall again what we must keep repeating: by reprobation — which we hang from God's mere will, not from foresighted human demerits — we do not mean a peremptory decree to damn or eternally afflict some particular person, but a fixed decree not to impart that special efficacious grace, or calling according to purpose, without which God sees that person will remain in hardness, impenitence, and unbelief — and has decreed to permit that. God is most certain that from such passing-over the man so rejected will die in his sins, and most decided to damn him for those sins in which he will die. Yet it is plain: denial of that grace (where we locate reprobation properly) hangs on mere liberty of divine will, while that person's damnation arises from his own sin.

source_text: Hisce praelibatis respondeo, Deum absque omni simulatione, non obstante tali decreto reprobationis, posse per evangelicos ministros remissionem peccatorum et vitam aeternam hominibus indiscriminatim proponere sub conditione hac, Si crediderint in Christum. Neque simulat Deus quando sub hac conditione promittit salutem promiscue quibusvis hominibus, quia cuivis homini conditionem implenti promissum beneficium fideliter exhibebit. Si reprobationis decretum in hanc formam conciperetur, Etiamsi Judas crediderit, non obtinebit remissionem peccatorum, aut vitam aeternam, esset manifesta illusio quoad reprobatos in praedicatione Evangelii. Sed illud decretum hoc tantum continet, Non dabo Judae specialem illam gratiam, qua mediante conditionem propositam de facto impleret. Si Deum simulationis velint coarguere, ostendere debent, Deum promisisse per ministros evangelicos se daturum hanc specialem gratiam alicui personae, quam nihilominus antecedaneo reprobationis decreto ab eadem rejecit. Hoc si fecerint, quod nunquam facere poterunt, nos (quod absit) Deum simulationis peragi ab illis reum patiemur.
english: With that premise I answer: reprobation decree notwithstanding, God can without any simulation, through evangelical ministers, set before men indiscriminately remission of sins and eternal life on this condition — If they believe in Christ. Nor does he simulate when under that condition he promises salvation to any whatsoever: to whoever fulfills the condition he will faithfully give the promised benefit. If the reprobation decree were cast as Even if Judas believes, he will not obtain remission or eternal life, Gospel preaching to the reprobate would be open illusion. But that decree holds only this: I will not give Judas that special grace by which he would in fact fulfill the proposed condition. To convict God of simulation they must show he promised through evangelical ministers to give that special grace to someone whom he nonetheless rejected from it by antecedent reprobation. If they ever do that — which they never can — we will (God forbid) let them prosecute God as guilty of simulation.

source_text: Intelligant itaque Remonstrantes, qui hoc passim urgent, aliud esse velle serio quemlibet hominem servare si credat, aliud decernere operari in quolibet homine ut credat. Potest Deus velle prius absque omni simulatione, quamvis quoad quosdam decreverit nolle posterius in illorum reprobatione. Hic tamen in transcursu illud monere haud abs re erit, cum dicimus Deum velle servare quemlibet hominem si credat, nos nihil aliud denotare per hanc conditionatam voluntatem, quam aeternam illam et inviolabilem Dei ordinationem de nexu indissolubili fidei et salutis: propter quem nexum de qualibet persona electa vel non-electa verificatur haec promissio, Si credideris, salvus eris. Interim voluntas Dei non intelligitur versari circa salutem hominis non-electi quasi suspensa aut incerta; sed hujusmodi loquendi formulis id affirmatur, si conditio fidei in objecto poneretur, esset etiam in Deo voluntas actualis talem personam servandi: quod sufficit ad excludendam illam simulationem quam Deo impingere conantur.
english: So let the Remonstrants, who press this everywhere, understand: it is one thing seriously to will to save anyone if he believes, another to decree to work in anyone so that he believes. God can will the first without any simulation, even while for some he has decreed not to will the second in their reprobation. One passing note: when we say God wills to save anyone if he believes, by that conditioned will we mean only God's eternal inviolable ordination of the indissoluble bond of faith and salvation — for which bond the promise If you believe, you will be saved holds true of any elect or non-elect person. God's will is not thereby pictured as hanging uncertain over a non-elect man's salvation; such speech only affirms that if the faith-condition were set in the object, God would also actually will to save that person — enough to shut out the simulation they try to pin on God.

source_text: Porro quod in argumento positum fuit, Precise sive absolute electis aut reprobis non posse mandari ut credant, si eo sensu accipiunt precise et absolute ad salutem electos, ut praescindant ab usu mediorum, quasi Deus decrevisset aliquos ad salutem perducere etiamsi media salutis rejiciant, aut aliquos damnare, etiamsi in Christum crediderint, pro nostro dogmate sua insomnia obtrudunt.
english: They also put it that the precisely or absolutely elect or reprobate cannot be commanded to believe. Take that in their sense of people elected to salvation so precisely that means drop out — as if God had decreed to bring some to salvation even though they reject every means of it, or to damn some even though they believe in Christ. That is not our dogma. It is their dream forced onto ours.

source_text: Nos dicimus, Petrum, Paulum, reliquosque ad vitam aeternam absolute praedestinatos, non quod ipsi antequam credant absolute sciant hoc Dei decretum, aut quod ipsi vitam aeternam consequantur fidei conditione minime praestita; sed quod a Deo absolute et gratuito eliguntur, non modo ad ipsam vitam aeternam, sed ad totam seriem mediorum quibus ad eam perducuntur. Licet itaque in exsecutione finis pendeat a conditionali usu mediorum, tamen in Deo praedestinante Petrum, Paulum, aut quamcunque personam singularem, voluntas finis non fuit conditionata, sed absolute connexa cum voluntate mediorum; ita ut uno et eodem simplicissimo actu, quo Deus voluit Petro aut Paulo gloriam, voluerit etiam et fidem, ceteraque omnia ex quorum usu conditionali gloria promittitur. Uno verbo, Deus non decrevit servare Petrum sine conditione fidei, sed tam absolute et precise fidem Petro dare decrevit, quam salutem. Atque hoc est quod vulgo dicitur, Praedestinationem esse praeparationem gratiae in praesenti, et gloriae in futuro.
english: We say Peter, Paul, and the rest are absolutely predestined to eternal life — not that they know that decree absolutely before they believe, or that they gain eternal life with the faith-condition never performed — but that God elects them absolutely and freely not only to eternal life itself but to the whole series of means by which they are brought to it. In execution the end hangs on conditional use of means; yet in God predestining Peter, Paul, or any particular person, the will of the end was not conditioned but absolutely joined to the will of the means — so that by one and the same simplest act by which God willed glory for Peter or Paul he also willed faith and all else from whose conditional use glory is promised. In a word: God did not decree to save Peter without the condition of faith, but decreed to give Peter faith as absolutely and precisely as salvation. That is the common saying: Predestination is preparation of grace now and of glory hereafter.

source_text: Jam quod attinet ad reprobatos, non obstante aeterna antecedanea reprobatione, tam potest iis mandari ut credant, quam potuit vere mandari Angelis non-electis sive reprobatis ut obediant Deo: tam potest iis offerri salus sub conditione, Si credant, quam potuit his promitti beatitudo sub conditione, Si in obsequio Dei perseverassent. Nam ut praedestinatio Petri non tollit veritatem hujus negativae conditionalis, Si non credideris, non salvaberis: ita reprobatio Judae non enervat veritatem hujus affirmativae conditionalis, Si tu credideris, tu salvaberis: sed infert solummodo, stante indissolubili illa conditionali fidei et salutis concatenatione, non dandam eam efficacem gratiam Judae, qua de facto conditionem impleat.
english: As for the reprobate: eternal antecedent reprobation notwithstanding, they can as truly be commanded to believe as the non-elect or reprobate angels could be commanded to obey God; salvation can as truly be offered them on the condition If they believe as beatitude could be promised those angels on If they had persevered in God's obedience. Peter's predestination does not cancel the truth of If you do not believe, you will not be saved; Judas's reprobation does not weaken If you believe, you will be saved. It only implies that, that indissoluble faith-salvation bond standing, Judas is not to be given the efficacious grace by which he would in fact fulfill the condition.

source_text: Denique, quod objectum fuit, ex sententia nostra a reprobatis exigi ut falsum credant, scilicet Christum morte sua illis vitam et reconciliationem impetrasse, plane negatur. Vita enim et reconciliatio per mortem Christi non impetratur singularibus hominibus applicanda sub conditione hac arcana, Si fuerint praedestinati, sed sub conditione revelata, si fuerint fideles; neque negatur applicanda ulli singulari personae cui praedicatur, nisi sub hac conditione, si fuerit infidelis, ut aperte colligitur Joan. iii. 15, 16, etc. In hoc igitur se exserit arcanum illud electionis et reprobationis decretum, quod mors Christi, quae ex ordinatione Dei cuivis homini, si crederet, ad reconciliationem et vitam obtinendam valeret, non proficit tamen nisi electis, quibus solis ex speciali misericordia datur illa gratia, qua efficaciter possint et velint, et reapse adimpleant dictam conditionem.
english: Finally, the objection that on our view the reprobate are required to believe a falsehood — that Christ by his death obtained life and reconciliation for them — is plainly denied. Life and reconciliation through Christ's death are not applied to particulars under the secret condition If they were predestined, but under the revealed condition if they are believers; nor is application denied to any hearer except under if he is an unbeliever — as John 3:15–16 openly shows. Here the secret election/reprobation decree shows itself: Christ's death, which by God's ordination would avail any man who believed for reconciliation and life, yet profits only the elect, to whom alone from special mercy is given that grace by which they can and will efficaciously, and in fact, fulfill that condition.

source_text: Qui ponunt reprobationem absolutam et non ex praevisione finalis impoenitentiae ortam, illi causam perditionis rejiciunt non in propriam ipsorum reprobatorum malitiam, sed in gratiae Divinae defectum: At hoc nimis Deo indignum, qui semper paratus est gratiam ulteriorem addere, si homo bene utatur accepta: Non igitur ex reprobatione, sed ex voluntaria hominis neglectu accidit, quod gratia careat, aut quod majorem non accipiat, nimirum quod sese vita aeterna reddiderit indignum, Act. xiii. 46. quod veritatem in injustitia detinuerit, Rom. i. 18. quod non receperit amorem veritatis, 2 Thess. ii. 10, 11.
english: Those who set absolute reprobation not sprung from foresight of final impenitence cast perdition's cause not on the reprobates' own malice but on a defect of divine grace. That, they say, is too unworthy of God, who is always ready to add further grace if a man uses well what he has received. So not from reprobation but from a man's voluntary neglect it comes that he lacks grace or does not receive more — namely that he has made himself unworthy of eternal life (Acts 13:46), held the truth in unrighteousness (Rom. 1:18), and not received the love of the truth (2 Thess. 2:10–11).

source_text: Negamus, ex reprobatione a nobis posita aut Deum ipsum constitui causam perditionis humanae, aut Divinae gratiae defectum, nisi causa vocabulum improprie et abusive usurpetur. Perditionis enim sive damnationis vera causa est illud quod damnationem juste meretur, vel ille qui damnatione digna operatur. Sic ipse peccator cum peccatis suis est sibi vera et sola causa perditionis suae. Esse enim reprobatum, vel a gratiae ac misericordiae specialis praeparatione praeteritum, nec meretur nec operatur perditionem. Illa igitur quam docemus non rejicit causam damnationis in Divinae gratiae defectum, sed revera rejicit efficacis et specialis gratiae negationem in Divinae voluntatis libertatem. Dei voluntas causa est determinans, quod quidam per gratiam efficacem et infrustrabilem non eruantur ex perditione, aliis per talem gratiam erutis; sed propria reprobatorum malitia causa est operativa et meritoria cur perdantur et damnentur.
english: We deny that the reprobation we teach makes God himself — or a defect of divine grace — the cause of human perdition, unless 'cause' is used improperly and abusively. The true cause of perdition or damnation is what justly deserves damnation, or the one who works what damnation is due. So the sinner himself with his sins is to himself the true and sole cause of his perdition. Being reprobated, or passed by from preparation of special grace and mercy, neither deserves nor works perdition. What we teach does not cast damnation's cause on a defect of divine grace; it casts the denial of efficacious special grace on the liberty of divine will. God's will is the determining cause that some are not drawn out of perdition by efficacious unfrustrable grace while others are; the reprobates' own malice is the operative meritorious cause why they perish and are damned.

source_text: Aequivocatio in hoc vocabulo causae imposuit adversariis nostris, aut saltem suppeditavit illis occasionem imponendi aliis. Nam dupliciter aliquid dici solet causa talis eventus aut effectus: Vere, directe, et proprie, per modum influentis ad producendum effectum; Abusive, indirecte, improprie, per modum non agentis ad prohibendum effectum: Sicuti sol ortu suo vere et proprie causa dicitur cur aer illuminetur; occasu improprie et abusive causa dicitur cur obtenebretur, hoc sensu solummodo, quia sua praesentia tenebras fugasset.
english: Equivocation on the word cause has trapped our adversaries — or at least given them occasion to trap others. Something is called cause of an event or effect in two ways: truly, directly, and properly, as what flows in to produce the effect; abusively, indirectly, improperly, as what does not act to block the effect. So the sun at rising is truly and properly called cause why the air is lit; at setting it is only improperly and abusively called cause why it darkens — merely because its presence would have put darkness to flight.

source_text: Ad hunc fere modum, quia gratiae specialis donatio est causa productiva salutis humanae, quidam inducuntur ut cogitent ejusdem gratiae negationem sive defectum esse causam perditionis humanae, utpote quae sua praesentia perditionem hanc impediret. At ipse Philosophus hac de re accuratius loquitur, Metaph. lib. 4. cap. 2. Quod, cum adsit, alicujus causa est, idem cum absit, aliquando dicimus esse causam contrarii. Observanda sunt illa verba Philosophi, aliquando et dicimus. Non dicit illud per absentiam esse causam contrarii, sed nos illud causari vel tanquam causam obtendere, idque aliquando. Hinc influxus gratiae specialis, Divino decreto quibusdam hominibus negatus, obtendi potest vel cogitari ab imperitis ut causa peccati et perditionis eorundem, quia concessus eosdem servasset; sed falso obtenditur, nisi probari possit, vel Deum obligatum fuisse ad talem gratiam praestandam, vel peccata ac perditionem improborum ex illorum innata corruptione, et voluntaria rebellione, tanquam veris ac positivis causis, non manasse.
english: Much the same way: because the gift of special grace is the productive cause of human salvation, some are led to think its denial or defect is the cause of human perdition — as if by its presence it would have blocked that perdition. But the Philosopher speaks more carefully (Metaph. 4.2): what, when present, is cause of something, we sometimes say, when absent, is cause of the contrary. Note his words: sometimes and we say. He does not say absence itself is cause of the contrary, but that we allege or put it forward as a cause — and only sometimes. So the influx of special grace, denied by divine decree to some, can be held up by the unskilled as cause of their sin and perdition, because if given it would have saved them. That is false unless it can be proved either that God was bound to give such grace, or that the wicked's sins and perdition did not flow from their innate corruption and voluntary rebellion as true positive causes.

source_text: Porro, quod dicitur, Deum semper paratum esse cuivis homini adjicere gratiam ulteriorem, si bene utatur accepta, atque idcirco neminem reprobasse nisi ex consideratione antecedanea gratiae contemptae, id est, finalis impoenitentiae ac infidelitatis; nullam vim habet ad defensionem nostram infringendam: Primo, quia uti electio non hypotheticam gratiae donationem ponit, sed absolutam et infallibilem, sic reprobatio haud negat hypotheticam gratiae donationem, sub conditione nimirum, si quis hoc aut illud faceret, sed negat gratiam efficacem de facto donandam. Non ergo sequitur, Si Judas hoc aut illud fecisset, obtinuisset ulteriorem gratiam, Ergo non fuit per decretum reprobationis a gratia speciali absolute rejectus.
english: Further: the claim that God is always ready to add further grace to anyone who uses well what he has received — and therefore reprobated no one except from prior regard to despised grace, that is final impenitence and unbelief — has no force to break our defense. First: as election does not posit a hypothetical gift of grace but an absolute infallible one, so reprobation does not deny a hypothetical gift (if someone should do this or that), but denies efficacious grace actually to be given. It does not follow: If Judas had done this or that, he would have obtained further grace; therefore he was not by the reprobation decree absolutely rejected from special grace.

source_text: Secundo, contemptus gratiae datae qualiscunque potest recte assignari ut causa cur eadem subducatur, vel cur uberior non administretur; atque hoc ex allatis Scripturae locis evincitur: sed non potest nisi inepte allegari ut causa vel ratio cur specialis illa misericordia, et efficax ac secundum propositum vocatio, quae contemptum gratiae semper tollit, non fuerit huic aut illi praeparata et donata. Hoc ipsum, velle arripere hanc causam ad denegandam gratiam ulteriorem, est non-electionis sive reprobationis antecedaneae manifestum argumentum. Nam quos Deus non reprobavit, eos quamvis multa obstacula ponentes, et sua multiplici negligentia et resistentia gratiae obtationem promerentes, ex indebita tamen et speciali misericordia iterum iterumque urget, nec desistit donec eos regeneraverit et gratiae suae subjugaverit.
english: Second: contempt of whatever grace is given can rightly be named as cause why that grace is withdrawn, or why richer grace is not administered — and the cited Scriptures prove that. But it can only be alleged ineptly as cause or reason why that special mercy, and efficacious calling according to purpose which always removes contempt of grace, was never prepared and given to this or that person. To seize on that as the ground for denying further grace is itself a clear mark of non-election or antecedent reprobation. Those God has not reprobated — though they set many obstacles and by manifold negligence and resistance deserve grace to be taken away — he still from undue special mercy urges again and again, and does not stop until he has regenerated them and brought them under his grace.

source_text: Tertio, Regula illa, Bene utenti gratia (hoc est, ut exponit Corvinus, pag. 157, facienti quodcunque per gratiam sibi collatam potest facere) dabitur semper gratia ulterior, absolutum decretum reprobationis non labefactat. Quaero enim, Quis mortalium unquam fecit aut facturus est quodcunque per gratiam sibi collatam potest facere? Non fecerunt Angeli; non fecerunt primi parentes; nemo denique electorum post gratiam regenerationis acceptam hoc facit; nedum ut facere id putemus ullum ex non-renatis gratia solummodo excitante instructum, quam a junce naturae vivae distinguit Corvinus.
english: Third: the rule To him who uses grace well (that is, as Corvinus expounds, p. 157, to him who does whatever he can by the grace conferred on him) further grace shall always be given does not shake the absolute decree of reprobation. Who among mortals has ever done, or will ever do, whatever he can by the grace given him? The angels did not; the first parents did not; none of the elect after receiving regenerating grace does it — still less any of the non-regenerate, armed only with exciting grace, which Corvinus distinguishes from the living spark of nature.

source_text: Multo melius hac de re philosophatur Thomas, qui docet, in libero arbitrio per inordinationem praecedentem ad malum inclinato, non esse situm ut nullum impedimentum gratiae Divinae praestet, Contra Gent. l. 3. c. 160. Deinde adjungit, cap. 161. Deum tamen interdum ex abundantia bonitatis suae eos etiam qui impedimentum gratiae praestant, avertere a malo, et convertere ad bonum. Tandem et illud addit, Hoc fieri in illis solis, in quibus vult suam misericordiam apparere, ita quod in aliis omnibus justitiae ordo manifestetur. Hujus autem discriminis, quare hos ponentes obicem convertat, alios non convertat, rationem inquirendam non esse, quia dependet ex simplici ejus voluntate. Frustra igitur Corvinus ex eo reprobationem impugnat, quod Deus paratus sit uberiorem gratiam dare illis omnibus, qui ita utuntur gratia accepta, ut faciant quodcunque per eam possunt facere, cum nemo hoc praestet, et cum hoc ipsum, non finaliter opponere obicem gratiae Divinae, ex electione dimanet, non autem praecedat electionem.
english: Thomas reasons far better here. He teaches that free will, already disordered toward evil, is not so set that it offers no impediment to divine grace (Contra Gent. 3.160). Then (cap. 161) he adds that God nonetheless sometimes, from abundance of his goodness, turns even those who impede grace away from evil and converts them to good — and that this happens only in those in whom he wills his mercy to appear, so that in all others the order of justice is shown. Why he converts these who put an obstacle and not others is not to be sought; it hangs on his simple will. So Corvinus vainly attacks reprobation from God's readiness to give richer grace to all who use received grace so as to do whatever they can by it — since no one does that, and since not finally opposing an obstacle to divine grace itself flows from election and does not precede election.

source_text: Posita reprobatione antecedanea, et non ex praevisione futurae impoenitentiae et infidelitatis, sequetur hanc impoenitentiam et infidelitatem, propter quam reprobi damnantur, fluere ex decreto reprobationis; Est autem injustum propter illud aliquem damnare, quod ex reprobatione antecedente (quae purus putus Dei actus est) sequitur. In colloquio Hagiensi hoc urgetur a Remonstrantibus, qui videntur sentire, si ponamus reprobationem aliter factam quam ex praevisa infidelitate, consectarium esse, ut ipsam infidelitatem dictae reprobationis fructum agnoscamus. Atque hinc illa argumentatio: Si infidelitas ex reprobatione ad exitium consequitur, non potest Deus salva justitia sua reprobatos propter infidelitatem ipsorum perdere, ob id quod ex reprobatione (quae quidem est ipsius Dei opus) necessario sequitur: Reprobationem igitur ponere debemus ex praevisione infidelitatis finalis oriundam.
english: If reprobation is set as antecedent and not from foresight of future impenitence and unbelief, it will follow that the impenitence and unbelief for which the reprobate are damned flow from the reprobation decree. But it is unjust to damn anyone for what follows from antecedent reprobation — a pure mere act of God. At the Hague Colloquy the Remonstrants press this: if we place reprobation otherwise than from foresighted unbelief, the corollary is that we must own unbelief itself as fruit of that reprobation. Hence their argument: if unbelief follows from reprobation unto destruction, God cannot, his justice safe, destroy the reprobate for their unbelief, because that necessarily follows from reprobation — which is God's own work. Therefore, they say, we must place reprobation as sprung from foresight of final unbelief.

source_text: Illud imprimis praemitto, Nos minime negare Deum reprobantem ab aeterno praevidisse omnes reprobatos fore impoenitentes et incredulos, sed negare hanc praevisam infidelitatem a Deo consideratam ut causam antecedaneam et motivam ipsius reprobationis. Neque tamen concedemus infidelitatem hanc pullulare ex decreto reprobantis tanquam fructum aut effectum reprobationis: sed pullulat ut malus fructus ex malo et perverso corde reprobati. Quando igitur objiciunt, Si ex reprobatione sequitur infidelitas, homines injuste damnantur propter hanc infidelitatem, ex Divino reprobationis decreto sequentem: si sequelam ordinis vel temporis intelligant, negamus consequentiam; si sequelam causalitatis, negamus infidelitatem ex reprobatione tanquam effectum ex causa consequi.
english: First I premise: we do not deny that God, reprobating from eternity, foresaw that all the reprobate would be impenitent and unbelieving. We deny that that foresighted unbelief was taken by God as antecedent moving cause of reprobation itself. Nor do we grant that this unbelief sprouts from the reprobating decree as fruit or effect of reprobation: it sprouts as bad fruit from the reprobate's bad perverse heart. When they object — If unbelief follows from reprobation, men are unjustly damned for that unbelief following from the divine reprobation decree — if they mean sequel of order or time, we deny the consequence; if sequel of causality, we deny that unbelief follows from reprobation as effect from cause.

source_text: Nam quamvis Deus eligat quosdam ut fideles essent, et per gratiam electionis eos fideles efficiat, tamen non dicendus est reprobasse homines ut infideles essent, aut reprobando eosdem infideles reddidisse. Communis enim sententia est Theologorum, quam Magister Sententiarum posuit lib. 1. dist. 40. lit. D. hisce verbis, Non enim sicut praeparavit sanctos ad justitiam percipiendam, sic praeparavit iniquos ad justitiam amittendam; quia pravitatis praeparator nunquam fuit. Et adhuc planius, dist. 41. lit. E, Quaeritur utrum sicut dicitur elegisse quosdam ut boni fierent et fideles, ita etiam concedi debeat reprobasse quosdam ut mali essent et infideles, et obdurare ut peccent; quod nullatenus concedi oportet. Non enim reprobatio ita est causa mali sicut praedestinatio est causa boni; neque obduratio ita facit hominem malum quemadmodum misericordia facit bonum.
english: Though God elects some that they may be faithful, and by electing grace makes them faithful, he is not to be said to have reprobated men that they might be unbelievers, or by reprobating to have made them so. That is the common sentence of theologians, which the Master of the Sentences sets (lib. 1 dist. 40 lit. D): For not as he prepared the saints to receive righteousness did he prepare the wicked to lose it — he was never a preparer of wickedness. And still plainer (dist. 41 lit. E): it is asked whether, as he is said to have elected some that they might become good and faithful, we ought also grant he reprobated some that they might be evil and unbelieving, and hardens that they may sin — which must in no wise be granted. Reprobation is not cause of evil as predestination is cause of good; nor does hardening make a man evil as mercy makes him good.

source_text: Sed qui fit quod omnes reprobati semper evadunt infideles et impoenitentes, si infidelitas haec et impoenitentia non sint fructus aut effecta antecedentis reprobationis? Respondeo ex Augustino, Ad Simpl. l. 1. qu. 2. Non quod a Deo reprobante irrogetur aliquid quo sit homo deterior, sed tantum quod quo sit melior non erogetur. Non est ergo consequens, ut Deus quibus poenitentiam non dederit, resipiscentiam abstulerit; et quos non levaverit, alliserit, etc. ut optime Prosper, Ad Object. Vinc. Resp. 15. Et in eandem sententiam alibi respondet, Ad cap. Gallor. resp. 14. Infidelitatem non credentium Evangelio nequaquam ex Dei praedestinatione generari; sed omnes non-praedestinatos perire infidelitate voluntaria, non coacta, Sentent. super 14.
english: But how is it that all the reprobate always turn out unbelieving and impenitent, if that unbelief and impenitence are not fruits or effects of antecedent reprobation? I answer with Augustine (Ad Simpl. 1.2): not that God by reprobating inflicts anything by which a man is made worse, but only that what would make him better is not bestowed. So it does not follow that those to whom God has not given penitence he has robbed of repentance, or that those he has not lifted he has dashed down — as Prosper well says (Ad Object. Vinc. Resp. 15). And elsewhere to the same effect (Ad cap. Gallor. resp. 14): the unbelief of those who do not believe the Gospel is in no way generated from God's predestination; all the non-predestined perish by voluntary, not forced, unbelief (Sentent. super 14).

source_text: Nam omnibus filiis Adae rebellio, impoenitentia, infidelitas domi nascuntur, ut minime opus sit a reprobatione Divina hujusmodi effecta arcessere: haec enim omnia, etiam inter multa gratiae Divinae remedia et auxilia, erumpunt tamen ex corde vitiato, nisi specialis misericordiae beneficio ex electionis decreto manante sanetur, et in bono statuminetur. In argumento igitur proposito caput erroris illud est, quod sumatur, Deum reprobantem eodem prorsus modo procurare media quae ducunt postea reprobatos ad mortem aeternam, quo procurat media quae ducunt electos ad vitam aeternam: atque hinc, quia perspicuum est, Deum praedestinantem propria et speciali quadam operatione efficere in praedestinatis fidem, sanctitatem, perseverantiam reliquaque omnia, quibus tanquam mediis ad vitam pervenitur; putant etiam consequens esse, ut si Deus antecedenter aliquos reprobaverit, in iisdem efficiat infidelitatem, impoenitentiam, ceteraque omnia quibus tanquam mediis postmodum in mortem ruitur. Sed longe aliter se res habet.
