english: For in all Adam's children rebellion, impenitence, and unbelief are born in-house — so there is little need to fetch such effects from divine reprobation. All these, even amid many remedies and helps of divine grace, still break out from a vitiated heart unless healed and set firm in good by the benefit of special mercy flowing from the election decree. The head of error in their argument is this assumption: that God, when he reprobates, procures in the very same way the media that later lead the reprobate to eternal death as he procures the media that lead the elect to eternal life. And since it is plain that God predestinating by a proper special operation works in the predestined faith, holiness, perseverance, and all else by which as means life is reached, they think it follows that if God has antecedently reprobated some, in them he works unbelief, impenitence, and all else by which as means they later rush to death. But the matter stands far otherwise.

source_text: Nam reprobare est Negando gratiam specialem permittere aliquos a fine beatitudinis deficere, non infundendo malitiam spiritualem in abyssum miseriae per vim eos impellere. Huc etiam accedit, quod media quibus praedestinati ducuntur ad vitam, sunt bona quaedam supernaturalia, ac proinde non aliunde quam a Fonte boni petenda: ad Deum igitur praedestinantem pertinet providere de mediis efficacibus, quorum interventu praedestinati salventur: At media quibus reprobati in mortem ruunt, sunt mala spiritualia, sunt actiones deficientes et depravatae: ergo non a summo Bono, neque a Deo efficiente, sed ab infito nostro malo, et a causa deficiente petantur. Ineptum igitur et impium est propter antecedaneum reprobationis decretum putare, id Deo incumbere, ut producat in reprobatis infidelitatem, impoenitentiam, et id genus alia, quorum interventu damnentur. Denique, et illud sciendum est, Infidelitatem, impoenitentiam, et quicquid peccati rationem subit, dici posse media quibus ipse reprobatus sibi mortem procurat: Sed respectu Reprobantis non sunt media a Deo effecta et adhibita ad damnationem reprobati, sed potius materia quam ex se parit reprobatus, Deo praevidente et circa eandem materiam justitiam suam vindicativam exercente.
english: To reprobate is, by denying special grace, to permit some to fall short of beatitude's end — not by pouring spiritual malice in to drive them by force into the abyss of misery. Add this: the media by which the predestined are led to life are supernatural goods, and so to be sought only from the Fountain of good — it belongs to God predestinating to provide efficacious media by whose intervention the predestined are saved. But the media by which the reprobate rush to death are spiritual evils — deficient, depraved acts — and so are sought not from the highest Good, nor from God as efficient, but from our implanted evil and a deficient cause. It is therefore inept and impious, because of an antecedent reprobation decree, to think God must produce in the reprobate unbelief, impenitence, and the like by which they are damned. Finally: unbelief, impenitence, and whatever counts as sin can be called media by which the reprobate himself procures his own death. But respecting the Reprobating One they are not media God effects and applies unto the reprobate's damnation — rather matter the reprobate brings forth from himself, God foreseeing and about that matter exercising his vindicative justice.

source_text: Sicut igitur furtum aut homicidium non praecedit suspendium furis aut homicidae tanquam medium a judice in eum finem procuratum et adhibitum, sed tantum ut quiddam praesuppositum, sic peccata reprobatorum praecedunt eorum damnationem. Potest igitur Deus justissime damnare omnes infideles et impoenitentes, quia licet infidelitas sequatur reprobationem, tamen est extra totum reprobationis effectum, et nascitur ex corde reprobati; non eam operante, efficiente, aut proliciente Deo, sed praevidente, permittente, et per gratiam specialis misericordiae non impediente, quia non tenetur eum in modum impedire. Vide Cajetanum, in 1. quaest. 23. art. 5.
english: Just as theft or homicide does not precede the hanging of thief or murderer as a means the judge procured and applied for that end — only as something presupposed — so the reprobates' sins precede their damnation. God can therefore most justly damn all unbelievers and impenitents: though unbelief follows reprobation, it lies outside the whole effect of reprobation and is born from the reprobate's heart. God does not work, effect, or draw it forth; he foresees, permits, and by special-mercy grace does not impede it — for he is not bound so to impede it. See Cajetan on ST 1 q.23 a.5.

source_text: Qui statuunt Deum mera sua voluntate, et non ex praevisione actualium peccatorum et finalis perseverantiae in iisdem, quosdam reprobasse, illi statuunt Deum longe rigidius agere cum hominibus quibusdam, quam cum ipsis diabolis: Cum enim diaboli excludantur a vita ob peccata quae propria sua malitia commiserunt, homines quidam reprobati ponuntur, non propter propria peccata quae in personis suis commiserunt, sed tantum considerati uti alieno peccato Adami ex imputatione Divina rei.
english: Those who hold that God by mere will — not from foresight of actual sins and final perseverance in them — has reprobated some, thereby hold that God deals far more rigidly with certain men than with the very devils. For the devils are shut out of life for sins they committed by their own malice; yet some reprobated men are set not for sins done in their own persons, but only as guilty by divine imputation of Adam's alien sin.

source_text: Borrius quidam hoc argumento probare conatus est, ob peccatum originale neminem condemnari, atque idcirco omnes omnium gentilium infantes morientes ante commissionem actualium peccatorum salvos esse: ut videre licet apud Arminium, in Respons. ad art. 13. et 14. In hac autem sententia fuisse constitutum ipsum Arminium, et Arminianos eandem nunc defendere clarum est. Corvinus, qui fuit Arminio ab intimis consiliis, sic scribit, pag. 391. Equidem Arminius statuit, neminem propter solum peccatum originis damnari. Atque Remonstrantes citati ad Synodum Dordracenam, in scripto publice et communi omnium eorum consensu exhibito, aperte dixerunt: Nullos infantes, utpote qui novae inobedientiae et rebellionis capaces non sunt, poena aeterna puniri.
english: A certain Borrius tried by this argument to prove that no one is condemned for original sin, and so that all Gentile infants dying before actual sins are saved — as may be seen in Arminius, Respons. to arts. 13–14. That Arminius himself held this, and that Arminians still defend it, is clear. Corvinus, of Arminius's inner counsel, writes (p. 391): Indeed Arminius holds that no one is damned for original sin alone. And the Remonstrants cited to the Synod of Dort, in a writing shown publicly by common consent of them all, said openly: No infants — inasmuch as they are not capable of new disobedience and rebellion — are punished with eternal pain.

source_text: Respondeo primo, Posse nos ex concessis Arminianorum non dissimile argumentum texere, quod tamen nullius momenti esse ipsi proculdubio affirmabunt. Nam illud notandum est: Quamvis constanter negent ob innatum peccatum originale damnari quenquam, tamen e contrario coguntur illorum capita, agnoscunt mortis reatum etiam in parvulos omnes esse derivatum ex imputatione actualis ejus peccati quod ab Adamo admissum fuit. Hoc itaque solummodo concesso sic licet nobis argumentari: Qui statuunt Deum omnes homines, tam infantes quam adultos, aeternae mortis reos in strictum jus conferre, ex eo solum quod imputatur illis peccatum quod non actuale in propria uniuscujusque persona commissum, sed ab Adamo perpetratum, illi faciunt Deum rigidius agentem cum hominibus quam cum diabolis: Nam nemo diabolorum reus censetur nisi ob peccatum in propria persona, et ex propria malitia commissum; at homines, ex sententia Arminii, rei mortis aeternae constituuntur, tantum considerati uti alieni peccati Adami ex imputatione Divina rei. Quicquid responsi nobis dederint, idem nos et illis regeremus.
english: First I answer: from Arminian concessions we can weave a like argument, which they themselves will doubtless call of no moment. Note this: though they constantly deny anyone is damned for innate original sin, they are forced the other way — they grant that guilt of death has been derived even to all infants from imputation of that actual sin Adam committed. Grant only that, and we may argue: those who hold God puts all men, infants and adults, under strict right as guilty of eternal death merely because a sin not done in each one's own person but by Adam is imputed to them, make God deal more rigidly with men than with demons. No demon is counted guilty except for sin done in his own person from his own malice; yet on Arminius's view men are made guilty of eternal death only as guilty by divine imputation of Adam's alien sin. Whatever reply they give us, we will turn the same back on them.

source_text: Verum quia, ut vulgo dici solet, contra agere non est solvere, respondemus secundo: Quando quaeritur utrum major justitiae rigor exerceatur in reprobatione hominum an Daemonum, ineptam prorsus esse comparationem, si constet rigidam justitiam neutris reprobandis exerceri. Cum igitur reprobatio sit indebiti beneficii negatio (puta infallibilis ordinationis ad vitam aeternam per specialis gratiae praeparationem et donationem) profecto nec hominum nec angelorum reprobatio fuit actus rigidae justitiae, imo ne justitiae quidem proprie et formaliter dictae; quamvis non fuerit contra justitiam, sicut nec ullus actus Divinus, et eo sensu justissima appelletur. Inepte igitur in reprobatione rigidae justitiae gradus ponderant, cum mera reprobatio, sive hominum sive daemonum, non sit actus poenam decernentis, in quo rigor possit considerari, sed actus beneficium negantis, in quo sola Dei libertas debet attendi.
english: But as the saying goes, to counter-argue is not to solve — so second: when the question is whether greater rigor of justice is used in reprobating men or demons, the comparison is wholly inept if rigid justice is exercised in reprobating neither. Reprobation is denial of an undue benefit — namely of infallible ordination to eternal life through preparation and gift of special grace. So neither men's nor angels' reprobation was an act of rigid justice — not even of justice properly and formally so called — though it was not against justice (as no divine act is), and in that sense may be called most just. Inept, then, to weigh degrees of rigid justice in reprobation: mere reprobation, of men or demons, is not an act decreeing punishment (where rigor could be considered) but an act denying a benefit, where only God's liberty is to be regarded.

source_text: Tertio, ipsum fundamentum cui innititur tota haec argumentatio putridum est: Nam videtur pro concesso sumere, Diabolos fuisse ex praevisione actualium suorum peccatorum reprobatos. At nos e contra dicimus, Angelos beatos ante jacta mundi fundamenta fuisse electos, non ex praevisis eorundem meritis, sed ex pura gratia eligentis; et Angelos damnatos fuisse pariter ab aeterno praeteritos, non-electos, sive reprobatos, non ex praevisione futurae rebellionis et finalis in eadem obdurationis, sed ex mera voluntate sive libertate Dei hanc gratiam illis donare nolentis. Si igitur Arminiani a Diabolorum reprobatione probare volunt homines minime fuisse reprobatos, nisi ex antecedente praevisione et consideratione actualium peccatorum, debuerunt hoc prius solido argumento aliquo confirmare quoad reprobationem daemonum, quam inde de hominum reprobatione consequentias inferre.
english: Third: the very foundation this whole argument leans on is rotten. It seems to take as granted that the Devils were reprobated from foresight of their actual sins. We say the contrary: the blessed angels were elected before the world's foundations were laid — not from foresighted merits but from the electing One's pure grace; and the damned angels were likewise from eternity passed by, non-elect, or reprobated — not from foresight of future rebellion and final hardening in it, but from God's mere will or liberty not willing to give them that grace. So if Arminians from the Devils' reprobation want to prove men were reprobated only from antecedent foresight of actual sins, they ought first to confirm that by solid argument for the demons' reprobation before drawing consequences about men's.

source_text: Ultimo, perperam in hoc argumento transcursunt a reprobatione ad ipsam damnationem, et haec duo inter se commiscere et confundere conantur, quae ex diversis causis pendere supra ostendimus. Neque tamen damus illis, posita hac hypothesi (quae Catholicae Ecclesiae judicio semper fuit approbata) Damnari nonnullos propter solum originale peccatum, inde consequi Deum rigidius agere cum talibus, quam cum ipsis diabolis. Non enim dicimus judicem rigidius agere cum minore reo quovis, quam cum deterrimo proditore, quod utrumque damnet, nisi eum, qui minore peccato tenetur, pari aut majori supplicio afficiat.
english: Lastly: in this argument they wrongly slide from reprobation to damnation itself, and try to mix and confuse the two — which we have already shown hang on diverse causes. Nor do we grant that, on the hypothesis always approved by the Catholic Church's judgment — that some are damned for original sin alone — it follows God deals more rigidly with such than with the very demons. A judge is not said to deal more rigidly with a lesser offender than with the worst traitor merely because he condemns both, unless he afflicts the one held by the lesser crime with equal or greater punishment.

source_text: Jam vero, utcunque Deus damnet parvulos solo originali peccato contaminatos et constrictos, ac damnet etiam diabolos actualis et nefariae rebellionis reos, tamen in modo et gradu poenae inflictiae ingens discrimen est. Nam infantes (ut bene Augustinus, De peccat. mer. et remiss. l. 1. cap. 16.) exeunt in damnatione omnium mitissima; daemones in damnatione longe acerbissima. Nulla autem acies ingenii humani potest discernere, quot possunt esse gradus poenarum in eadem damnatione aeterna: ac proinde inconsequens est haec argumentatio, Parvuli damnantur ob peccatum originale, et Diaboli tantum damnantur ob peccatum actuale, Ergo parvuli rigidius tractantur.
english: However God damns infants stained and bound by original sin alone, and also damns demons guilty of actual wicked rebellion, there is a huge difference in the mode and degree of the punishment inflicted. Infants (as Augustine well says, De peccat. mer. et remiss. 1.16) go into the mildest of all damnation; demons into damnation far the bitterest. No edge of human wit can tell how many degrees of pains there may be in the same eternal damnation. So this argument does not follow: Infants are damned for original sin, and Devils only for actual sin; therefore infants are treated more rigidly.

source_text: Si creatio accipiatur pro illa singularium creatione qua unusquisque suum esse a Deo accipit, quae est primae creationis quasi continuatio, tum qui reprobationem ponunt haud factam ex praevisione finalis infidelitatis, faciunt illam ex diametro pugnare cum creatione. Nam creatio sua natura est communicatio boni secundum naturalem Dei bonitatem: At cum ejusmodi statuitur esse, ut hanc habeat intentionem, quod via sit per quam reprobatio jam ante facta finem suum consequatur, non est jam communicatio boni, sed medium damnationi subordinatum. Tale autem medium statuitur ab illis, qui ponunt praedestinationem et reprobationem ex mera Dei voluntate pendere, et non ex praevisione fidei et infidelitatis.
english: If creation means that making of particulars by which each receives his being from God — a kind of continuation of the first creation — then those who set reprobation as not made from foresight of final unbelief make it fight creation head-on. Creation by nature is a communication of good according to God's natural goodness. But if it is cast so as to have this intention — that it be a path by which reprobation already made reaches its end — it is no longer a communication of good, but a medium subordinated to damnation. And that is the medium set by those who hang predestination and reprobation on God's mere will, not on foresight of faith and unbelief.

source_text: Negamus consequentiam Majoris. Nam aeternum Dei decretum de non-eligendis, sive reprobandis hominibus quibusdam non magis pugnare potest cum temporali eorundem creatione, quam cum Angelorum creatione pugnavit quorundam praeteritio sive non-electio, ex mera libertate voluntatis Divinae ab aeterno constituta. Imo major videtur difficultas in causa Angelorum quam hominum; Homines enim ab aeterno electi aut praeteriti repraesentabantur menti Divinae ut in massa corrupta vitiati, et reprobabiles; at Angelos integros Deus intuitus est in eadem perfectione, in qua eos postea condidit: Si igitur aeterna reprobatio quorundam Angelorum ex beneplacito Divino, et non ex peccati praevisione, orta minime pugnavit cum creatione eorundem, non potest recte concipi pugna ulla inter reprobationem et creationem hominum, qui Deo reprobanti objiciuntur, ut peccato Adae contaminati et occisi.
english: We deny the Major's consequence. God's eternal decree concerning certain men not to be elected, or to be reprobated, can no more fight their temporal creation than the passing-by or non-election of some angels — set from eternity by mere liberty of divine will — fought angelic creation. Indeed the difficulty seems greater with angels than with men. Men from eternity elect or passed by were shown to the divine mind as vitiated in a corrupt mass and reprobable; but God looked on the angels intact in the same perfection in which he later made them. So if eternal reprobation of certain angels sprung from divine good pleasure, not from foresight of sin, and in no way fought their creation, no fight can rightly be conceived between reprobation and creation of men, who are set before God reprobating as contaminated and slain by Adam's sin.

source_text: De Angelis habemus ipsos Jesuitas nobis assipulantes. Suares, Opuscul. De concursu Dei, lib. 2. cap. 5. In Angelis nulla erat massa perditionis aut naturae infectae, et tamen quosdam elegit Deus, alios non elegit, quosdam destinavit in honorem, alios vero reliquit ut fierent vasa contumeliae. De hominibus etiam eodem modo statuendum dicit idem Suares: Si sermo sit de non-electione, quam nonnulli reprobationem negativam vocant, sic verum est, Causam illius esse solam Dei voluntatem, nulla expectata causa ex parte hominis. Quin etiam Vasques, qui minus nobis favet in hac controversia, tamen ingenue nobis largitur, Daemones ante omne peccatum praevisum fuisse reprobatos et permissos cadere in peccatum: quam reprobationem ille vocat reprobationem a gratia, decretum non miserendi, etc., In 1. Aquinat. disp. 45. cap. 3. et 5.
english: On the angels we have the Jesuits themselves with us. Suarez (Opusc. De concursu Dei 2.5): In the angels there was no mass of perdition or infected nature, and yet God elected some, did not elect others, destined some to honor, and left others to become vessels of contumely. Of men, the same Suarez says, it is to be held the same way: if the talk is of non-election, which some call negative reprobation, it is true that its cause is God's will alone, with no cause awaited from man's side. Even Vasquez, who favors us less in this controversy, frankly grants that the demons were reprobated and permitted to fall before any foresighted sin — which reprobation he calls reprobation from grace, a decree of not pitying, etc. (In 1. Aquin. disp. 45.3 and 5).

source_text: Potuerunt Jesuitae intelligere, quomodo creatio singulorum angelorum facta in tempore non pugnaverit cum reprobatione quorundam, sola Dei voluntate ab aeterno constituta: potuerunt idem de hominibus concipere: Intendat aciem ingenii sui Corvinus, et idem facile intelligat. Sed putat se confirmare posse consequentiam hac argumentatione: Creatio sua natura est communicatio boni: At praecesserit talis reprobatio qualem nos ponimus, erit via quaedam per quam reprobatio jam ante facta finem suum consequatur, erit medium hominis non-electi damnationi subordinatum. Ac proinde non erit communicatio boni; cum bonum aestimari debeat ex mente dantis, et fine propter quem datur. Sed haec parum solide disputantur. Nam primo creatio singularium hominum tam electionem quam reprobationem eorundem consequitur. Sicuti ergo creatio Petri improprie diceretur medium subordinatum ejus electioni, ita et creatio Judae improprie et falso dicitur medium subordinatum aut reprobationi aut damnationi ejusdem. Si qui sunt qui audeant sustinere creationem hominum esse medium damnationi eorundem subordinatum, ego ab illis dissentio, et amplector sententiam Augustini et Prosperi, qui hoc passim adversantur.
english: The Jesuits could see how the creation of particular angels in time did not fight the reprobation of some, set from eternity by God's will alone — and they could conceive the same of men. Let Corvinus bend his wit's edge, and he will easily see it. But he thinks he can shore up the consequence thus: Creation by nature is a communication of good; yet if such reprobation as we place preceded, it will be a path by which reprobation already made reaches its end — a medium of the non-elect man subordinated to damnation — and so will not be a communication of good, since good is to be judged from the giver's mind and the end for which it is given. That is weakly argued. First: creation of particular men follows both their election and their reprobation. As Peter's creation would improperly be called a medium subordinated to his election, so Judas's creation is improperly and falsely called a medium subordinated to his reprobation or damnation. If any dare hold that men's creation is a medium subordinated to their damnation, I dissent and embrace Augustine and Prosper, who everywhere oppose that.

source_text: Deum recte dici agere propter intentum aliquem finem, cum rebus talem dat naturam ut sint propter talem finem: Deus autem creando Judam non dedit illi naturam ad damnationem ordinatam: Falso igitur statuitur creatio Judae reprobati habere hanc intentionem, ut medium sit quod ad damnationem provehatur. Aliud enim est creare hominem reprobatum et ob demerita sua damnandum, aliud creare ut damnetur; sicut aliud est alere, vestire, solari latronem damnandum, aliud haec facere ut damnetur.
english: God is rightly said to act for some intended end when he gives things a nature ordered to that end. But in creating Judas God did not give him a nature ordained to damnation. So it is false to hold that the creation of Judas the reprobate has this intention — that it be a medium advanced toward damnation. It is one thing to create a man reprobate and to be damned for his demerits; another to create him that he may be damned — as it is one thing to feed, clothe, and comfort a thief sentenced to die, another to do those things that he may die.

source_text: Creat ergo Deus in tempore, quos ab aeterno minime praedestinavit ad beatitudinem, quos praevidit sua culpa ad interitum ruituros voluntarium, quos decrevit permittere ut inciderent in hanc miseriam sempiternam: sed interim creatio hominum (quae ordine decernendi haec omnia praecessit) habuit proprium suum finem, Dei gloriam in diffusione ac communicatione boni, non damnationem eorundem, quae habenda est eventus consequens creationem reprobatorum, non scopus intentus a Deo creante.
english: So God creates in time those he from eternity did not predestine to beatitude — whom he foresaw would by their own fault rush to voluntary ruin, whom he decreed to permit to fall into this everlasting misery. Yet men's creation (which in the order of decreeing preceded all that) had its own proper end: God's glory in the diffusion and communication of good — not their damnation, which is to be held an event following the creation of the reprobate, not a scope intended by God as creator.

source_text: Denique, si quae loca Scripturae in hunc sensum sonare videantur, quasi Deus creasset aliquos in contumeliam et perditionem, sunt, meo quidem judicio, interpretanda permissive. Creat enim indies, quos secundum decretum non-electionis seu reprobationis permittit fieri vasa contumeliae, non apponendo illam specialem gratiam quae faceret eos vasa honoris.
english: And last: wherever Scripture seems to speak as though God had fashioned some for disgrace and ruin, I judge those places to be taken permissively. Day by day he brings into being those whom, under the decree of non-election or of reprobation, he suffers to turn into vessels of contumely — withholding the special grace that would have made them vessels of honor.

source_text: Si ponamus electionem et reprobationem ex mera libertate Divinae voluntatis pendentem, et non ex discriminatis actibus ipsorum electorum et reprobatorum (puta horum poenitentia, illorum impoenitentia, horum fide perseverante, illorum finali infidelitate): tum Evangelii praedicatio quoad reprobatos ex proxima et precisa Dei intentione erit ministerium condemnationis, et non proponetur ipsis ex prima Dei intentione ad salutem ipsorum operandam, sed ut medium exsequendo decreto reprobationis damnationi subordinatum. At hoc directe cum ministerio Evangelii pugnat, utpote quod ex prima Dei intentione est ministerium vitae.
english: If we set election and reprobation as hanging on mere liberty of divine will — not on the differing acts of elect and reprobate themselves (these' penitence, those' impenitence; these' persevering faith, those' final unbelief) — then Gospel preaching toward the reprobate, from God's nearest precise intention, will be a ministry of condemnation, and will not be set before them from God's first intention to work their salvation, but as a medium subordinated to damnation in executing the reprobation decree. That fights the Gospel ministry head-on, since from God's first intention it is a ministry of life.

source_text: Consequentiam Majoris invalidam esse respondemus; atque in hoc falli adversarios affirmamus, quod posito absolutae reprobationis decreto quasi consequens assumunt, ex hoc decreto manare quicquid postea circa hosce non-electos sive reprobatos peragitur. At e contra recte observavit Vasques, Nec in praedestinato nec in reprobato omnem effectum providentiae Dei esse praedestinationis aut reprobationis, sed aliquem esse effectum communis providentiae, In 1. quaest. 23. artic. 4. cap. 4. disp. 93.
english: We answer that the Major's consequence is invalid. The adversaries err in this: having posited absolute reprobation, they take it as following that whatever is later done about these non-elect or reprobate flows from that decree. Vasquez rightly notes the contrary: neither in the predestined nor in the reprobate is every effect of God's providence an effect of predestination or reprobation — some is an effect of common providence (In 1 q.23 a.4 c.4 disp. 93).

source_text: Concedimus quidem, Deum scire Evangelii praedicationem, aliaque omnia sua beneficia hisce reprobatis fore noxia; concedimus insuper, nullius reprobati voluntatem tam feram tamque intratabilem esse, quin possit Deus illam ad fidem et poenitentiam (hoc est, ad obediendi effectum) emollire; concedimus denique, Deum decrevisse apud se hisce reprobatis non apponere illam gratiam specialem et efficacem, qua emollirentur: Sed hisce omnibus positis negamus, aut Evangelii praedicationem, aut illam parcitoris et communioris gratiae donationem ex primaria et proxima intentione damnandi proponi, aut tanquam media damnationi subordinata judicari oportere. Non enim debemus ex praevisione, aut permissione Dei, aut ex eventu subsequente inferre primariam Dei intentionem, et mediorum subordinationem ad talem eventum producendum spectasse.
english: We grant God knows Gospel preaching and his other benefits will be harmful to these reprobates. We grant further that no reprobate's will is so wild and intractable that God cannot soften it to faith and penitence — that is, to the effect of obeying. We grant finally that God has decreed with himself not to apply to these reprobates that special efficacious grace by which they would be softened. All that granted, we still deny that Gospel preaching, or that gift of scantier commoner grace, is proposed from a primary nearest intention of damning, or ought to be judged media subordinated to damnation. From foresight, or God's permission, or a following event, we may not infer that God's primary intention, and the subordination of media, aimed at producing that event.

source_text: Verbi causa; Deus praevidit quosdam Angelos eximiis donis instructos velle iisdem abuti ad superbiendum et rebellandum; decrevit hoc permittere, et propter hanc rebellionem eosdem aeternis suppliciis cruciare: nemo tamen dixerit ea dona ex primaria et propria Dei intentione fuisse ad illorum ruinam et damnationem subordinata, sed potius ad illorum obedientiam et beatitudinem.
english: Take the angels: God foresaw that some, endowed with excellent gifts, would abuse those gifts in pride and rebellion; he decreed to permit that, and for that rebellion to torment them with everlasting punishments. Yet no one would say those gifts were, by God's primary and proper intention, subordinated to their ruin and damnation — rather to their obedience and beatitude.

source_text: Nam (quod antea monuimus) intentio Dei per media semper aestimatur ex mediorum natura, et non ex eventu malo, quem Deus praevidet fore, et non vult impedire. Eodem igitur modo de Evangelica praedicatione, aliisque gratiae Divinae muneribus, quae reprobatis conceduntur, sentiendum est.
english: For — as we warned before — God's intention through means is always judged from the nature of those means, not from the evil event he foresaw and would not hinder. Judge Gospel preaching and the other gifts of divine grace granted to the reprobate the same way.

source_text: Ipsi Remonstrantes intelligunt, quando ex re ipsorum est, praedicationem Evangelii non manare ex absoluto aliquo decreto salvandi aut damnandi omnes et singulos quibus praedicatur, sed ex communiori quadam ratione providentiae, quam illi vocant sapientem, misericordem, et justam Christi gubernationem, Collat. Hagiens. pag. 95. Patiantur igitur et nos illorum sententiae subscribere, hoc addito, Evangelicam praedicationem ex decreto praedestinationis manare quoad illos, in quibus Deus decrevit ex speciali sua misericordia per illud organon poenitentiam, fidem, et salutem infallibiliter operari; Evangelicam autem praedicationem ex communiori quadam providentiae ratione manare quoad illos, in quibus Deus decrevit permittere ut illorum vitio effectum sortiatur plane contrarium; ita tamen ut quoad hosce posteriores ex decreto reprobationis fluere, aut tanquam medium damnationi eorundem primaria Dei intentione subordinatum esse, nullo modo concedamus.
english: The Remonstrants themselves, when it suits them, take Gospel preaching not to flow from some absolute decree to save or damn every hearer, but from a more common providence — what they call Christ's wise, merciful, and just government (Collat. Hagiens. p. 95). Let them then let us subscribe that view, with this added: preaching flows from the predestination decree for those in whom God decreed of special mercy to work penitence, faith, and salvation infallibly through that instrument; and it flows from a more common providence for those in whom he decreed to permit that by their fault it should take a plainly contrary effect — yet we never grant that for these latter it flows from the reprobation decree, or is subordinated as a medium to their damnation by God's primary intention.

source_text: Ipsae enim Scripturae de Evangelica praedicatione longe aliter statuunt; fieri nimirum quibusdam odorem mortis ad mortem, 2 Cor. ii. 15, 16. sed non ex primaria Dei intentione, verum ex voluntaria illorum rebellione, Hebr. ii. 3. Quomodo nos effugiemus, si tantam neglexerimus salutem? Actor. xiii. 38. Annunciatur vobis remissio peccatorum per Christum, etc. et 46. Postquam repellitis illam, et indignos vos decernitis vita aeterna. Et Coloss. i. 28. Annunciamus Christum, admonentes quosvis, et quosvis erudientes, ut quosvis sistamus perfectos in Christo Jesu.
english: Scripture itself settles Gospel preaching far differently: to some it becomes an odor of death unto death (2 Cor. ii. 15–16) — not from God's primary intention, but from their voluntary rebellion (Heb. ii. 3: How shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation?). Acts xiii. 38: Remission of sins through Christ is announced to you — and 46: After you put it from you and judge yourselves unworthy of everlasting life. Col. i. 28: We announce Christ, admonishing and teaching every one, that we may present every one perfect in Christ Jesus.

source_text: Evangelium igitur non administratur ab ipso Deo ulli homini ex proxima et precisa intentione illum damnandi; sed, interveniente ejus neglectu et contemptu, exoritur in contemnente meritum damnationis, quod Deus praevidebat fore, et nolebat impedire in omnibus reprobatis.
english: So God does not administer the Gospel to anyone from a nearest precise intention of damning him. When neglect and contempt intervene, desert of damnation arises in the despiser — which God foresaw and was unwilling to hinder in all the reprobate.

source_text: Denique, ut vitium negatae consequentiae magis appareat, hoc unum addemus; Deum dici a nobis aliquid intendere dupliciter; uno modo, quando ex providentia disponit apta media ad finis alicujus productionem. Hoc sensu dicimus voluisse atque intendisse Deum ut Adamus in obedientia mandati Divini staret ac perseveraret, quia scilicet concessit illi apta media ad standum et perseverandum. Alio modo et specialiore, quando ex decreto praedestinationis talia media suppeditat, quibus novit et decrevit ipsum finem fore obtinendum. Hoc sensu dicimus Deum intendisse et voluisse fidem, perseverantiam et salutem omnium electorum. Jam vero tertius ille modus, quem fingere conantur Arminiani, ut Deus scilicet dicatur primaria intentione illud malum velle per Evangelicam praedicationem, aut per beneficium quodcunque hominibus concessum, quod ex tali beneficio, mediante reprobatorum malitia, quam Deus non vult impedire, exorietur; hic, inquam, modus est plane inauditus et explodendus.
english: Finally, to show more clearly the flaw in the denied consequence, add this: we say God 'intends' something in two ways. First, when by providence he disposes apt means toward producing some end — in that sense we say he willed and intended that Adam stand and persevere in obedience to the divine command, because he granted him apt means for standing and persevering. Second, more specially, when by the predestination decree he supplies means by which he knew and decreed the end itself would be obtained — in that sense we say he intended and willed the faith, perseverance, and salvation of all the elect. The third mode the Arminians invent — that God by primary intention wills that evil through Gospel preaching or any benefit granted to men, which will arise from that benefit through the reprobates' malice that God will not hinder — that mode is plainly unheard-of and to be exploded.

source_text: Media igitur salutis quae offeruntur reprobatis non sunt effectus praedestinationis; quia sic finem consequerentur: neque fluunt a decreto reprobationis, tanquam media ad procurandam reprobatorum damnationem a Deo subordinata; quia non pertinet ad Deum providere de mediis reprobatos ad mortem aeternam ducentibus, quae ex ipsis abunde pullulant, si Deus gratiam specialem non opponat; sed manant ab illa φιλανθρωπίᾳ et generaliore providentia, quae media ad aliquem finem ita disponit, ut interim permittat causam secundam a consecutione finis suo vitio excidere. Hoc discrimen inter Praedestinationem et Providentiam bene explicavit Thomas, Quaest. Disp. De praed. art. 1. Eamque agnoscit ipse Vasques, In 1. quaest. 22. disp. 87. cap. 4. in ipso fine capitis.
english: So the means of salvation offered to the reprobate are not effects of predestination — else they would reach the end. Nor do they flow from the reprobation decree as media God subordinated to procuring their damnation — for it is not God's part to furnish means that lead reprobates to everlasting death; those sprout abundantly from themselves if he does not oppose special grace. They flow instead from that philanthropy and more general providence which so disposes means toward an end that it meanwhile permits the second cause, by its own fault, to fall short of attaining it. Thomas well explains this distinction between Predestination and Providence (Quaest. Disp. De praed. art. 1); Vasquez acknowledges the same (In 1 q.22 disp. 87 c.4, at the chapter's end).

source_text: Qui ponunt praedestinationem et reprobationem ex liberrima Dei voluntate absolute pendentem, et non ex praevisa fide et infidelitate praedestinatorum et reprobatorum, illi faciunt Baptismum circa multos infantes administratum, ex prima Dei intentione statui inutilem, et nihil obsignare, idque citra culpam infantium quibus administratur. Nam si ponamus multos infantes fidelium praecise reprobatos, nihil ipsis per Baptismum obsignari certissimum est.
english: Those who set predestination and reprobation as hanging absolutely on God's freest will — not on foreseen faith and unbelief of the predestined and reprobate — make baptism administered to many infants useless by God's first intention, and sealing nothing, and that without fault in the infants who receive it. For if we set many infants of the faithful as precisely reprobated, it is most certain that baptism seals nothing for them.

source_text: Praedestinatio et reprobatio illa absoluta, quam nos a liberrima Dei voluntate dependere asserimus, nil aliud designat quam aeternum illud Dei decretum, quo statuit pro mero suo beneplacito, et ex summa misericordia, quosdam per specialis gratiae media ad gloriam infallibiliter perducere, aliisque pro mera libertate voluntatis suae hanc summam misericordiam specialis gratiae praeparatricem denegare, qua negatione praesupposita, Deus videt eosdem reatu peccati finaliter constringendos, et propter eundem reatum decernit puniendos.
english: The absolute predestination and reprobation we affirm depends on God's freest will. It means nothing other than his eternal decree. By that decree, of mere good pleasure and supreme mercy, he established to lead some infallibly to glory through the means of special grace. To others, of mere liberty of will, he denies that supreme mercy which prepares special grace. That denial presupposed, God sees them finally bound by sin's guilt, and decrees them punished for that guilt.

source_text: Hoc praemisso, quaero cur ex nostra sententia Baptismus circa multos infantes administratus inutilis statuatur, et nihil obsignare, potius quam ex sententia adversariorum. An quia Deo decretum est ab omni aeternitate damnare reprobatos? At hoc ipsi non audent negare. An quia Reprobari ex decreto Dei et Baptizari ex mandato Dei sibi adversentur? At ipsi etiam agnoscunt omnes in Ecclesia natos ex mandato Dei baptizandos, et multos horum nihilominus aeterno Dei decreto fuisse reprobatos antequam nascerentur. An denique quia illi damnationem infixam docent aeternae, certae et infallibili notitiae Dei, qua veluti ante oculos cernebat hominem peccati reatu constrictum? At nos etiam idem profitemur.
english: That premised, I ask why baptism of many infants is called useless and sealing nothing on our view rather than on theirs. Because God from all eternity decreed to damn the reprobate? They dare not deny that. Because reprobation by decree and baptism by command clash? They too grant that all born in the Church must be baptized by God's command, and that many of them were nonetheless reprobated by his eternal decree before they were born. Or because they teach damnation fixed in God's eternal, certain, infallible knowledge, whereby as before his eyes he saw a man bound by sin's guilt? We profess the same.

source_text: Illud igitur unum reliquum est, ut quia nos dicimus specialem gratiam, et de facto ad gloriam perducentem quibusdam ex mero Dei beneplacito praeparari et donari, aliis nec praeparari nec donari, idcirco judicemur statuere Baptismum quoad hosce posteriores prorsus inutilem. Nos negamus hanc consequentiam.
english: So only this remains: because we say special grace that in fact leads to glory is prepared and given to some of God's mere good pleasure, and to others neither prepared nor given, we are judged to make baptism altogether useless for these latter. We deny that consequence.

source_text: Et dicere possumus non minus quam ipsi Arminiani, Baptismum obsignare cuivis infanti originalis peccati remissionem, quo solo tenetur aetas infantilis; obsignare etiam actualium peccatorum remissionem in Christi sanguine paratam resipiscentibus et credentibus, cum ad aetatem adultam pervenerint, et in actualia inciderint; obsignare etiam regenerationem et innovationem ex incorruptibili semine verbi Spiritusque efficiendam in omnibus credentibus, postquam ad aetatem verbi Divini capacem vixerint.
english: And we can say no less than the Arminians themselves. Baptism seals to every infant the remission of original sin, by which alone infant age is held. It also seals remission of actual sins prepared in Christ's blood for those who repent and believe when they come to adulthood and fall into actual sins. It seals, further, regeneration and renewal wrought from the incorruptible seed of word and Spirit in all believers, once they live to an age capable of the divine word.

source_text: De remissione peccati originalis habemus Augustinum ubique adstipulantem: De pecc. mer. et remiss. lib. 1. cap. 28. et lib. 2. cap. 4. Prosper etiam ad Cap. Gall. Resp. 2. eandem sententiam amplexatur. Denique, in Concilio Valentino, cap. 5. hoc firmissime tenendum proponitur. Porro, de remissione peccatorum actualium, sub conditione novi foederis impetranda, idem statuendum est: Hoc enim firmissime omni baptizato obsignatur, non solum quoad ipsum momentum quando Baptismum suscipit, sed quoad reliquum cursum vitae suae. Nam quicunque baptizatus est in nomen Jesu Christi, ille si post Baptismum peccaverit, in sanguine ejusdem Christi paratam habet per fidem peccatorum suorum expiationem; 1 Joann. i. 9.
english: On remission of original sin Augustine agrees everywhere (De pecc. mer. et remiss. 1.28 and 2.4). Prosper also, ad Cap. Gall. Resp. 2, embraces the same view. Finally the Council of Valence, cap. 5, proposes this as to be held most firmly. Likewise for remission of actual sins under the new covenant's condition: that is sealed most firmly to every baptized person — not only at the moment of receiving baptism, but for the rest of life's course. Whoever is baptized into the name of Jesus Christ, if he sins after baptism, has in that same Christ's blood, through faith, expiation of his sins prepared (1 John i. 9).

source_text: Denique, de renovatione sive regeneratione actuali adultorum, quae fit cum quis virtute verbi Divini Spiritusque convertitur, et credendo justificatur, sic scribit Augustinus, In baptizatis infantibus praecedit regenerationis sacramentum, et si Christianam pietatem tenuerint, sequitur etiam in corde conversio, cujus mysterium praecessit in corpore, lib. 4. Contra Donatist. cap. 24. Nos itaque de omnibus infantibus baptizatis cum Fulgentio asserimus, Sacramentum fidei, quod est sanctum baptisma, quamdiu rationis aetas infantium capax esse non potest, sufficit eis ad salutem, De fid. ad Petrum Diac. cap. 30. Neque Aquinatis hac de re dictum adspernamur; Qui, inquit, non habent infantes unde possint se convertere ad causam justificantem, ipse causa justificans, scilicet passio Christi, applicatur eis per sacramentum baptismi, Quaest. disp. de Justific. art. 3.
english: Finally, on adults' actual renewal or regeneration — when by the power of divine word and Spirit one is converted and by believing justified — Augustine writes: In baptized infants the sacrament of regeneration precedes, and if they hold Christian piety, conversion of heart also follows, whose mystery preceded in the body (lib. 4 Contra Donatist. cap. 24). So of all baptized infants we assert with Fulgentius: The sacrament of faith, which is holy baptism, while infants' age cannot be capable of reason, suffices them for salvation (De fid. ad Petrum Diac. cap. 30). Nor do we scorn Aquinas on this: Infants who have nothing whereby they can turn themselves to the justifying cause have that cause itself — Christ's passion — applied to them through the sacrament of baptism (Quaest. disp. de Justific. art. 3).

source_text: Isti non recte explicant doctrinam reprobationis, qui talem statuunt reprobationem, quae impediat quo minus publicae preces Deo offerri possint cum debita fide et fiducia quod omnibus verbum Dei audientibus sint profutura. Nam quis animum inducere potest ut pro eorum salute oret, quos Deus aeterna et antecedente voluntate damnare voluit? Apostolus hoc argumento nos acuit ad precandum pro omnibus, quia Deus vult omnes salvos fieri.
english: They do not rightly explain reprobation who set such a reprobation as would block public prayers from being offered to God with due faith and confidence that the Word will profit all who hear it. Who can bring himself to pray for the salvation of those God by an eternal antecedent will has willed to damn? The Apostle sharpens us to pray for all with this argument: God wills all to be saved.

source_text: Ad preces rite concipiendas pro aliis hominibus non requiritur, ut certitudine fidei nobis persuasum sit, preces nostras illis ad salutem profuturas. Nam fidei nostrae nihil aut falsum aut contingens subesse potest; at plane contingens et incertum est, utrum illi aliquid emolumenti ex precibus nostris sint percepturi. Sufficit quod Deus praeceperit nos omnes homines charitate complecti, et pro aliis, etiam pro inimicis, orare.
english: To form prayers rightly for other people, we need not be persuaded by certainty of faith that our prayers will profit them unto salvation. Nothing false or contingent can underlie our faith; yet whether they will gain any profit from our prayers is plainly contingent and uncertain. It is enough that God has commanded us to embrace all men in charity, and to pray for others — even for enemies.

source_text: Vulgo hoc notum est in Schola Theologorum, qui dicere solent, quatuor conditiones requiri ut oratio alicujus habeat certitudinem impetrandi, quarum una est, ut pro se quis oret. Nam licet sit pia, perseverans, et de pertinentibus ad salutem, tamen si pro alio fiat non semper impetrat oratio. Major itaque propositio, uti videtis, labascit, quae falso supponit preces recte fieri non posse pro aliis, nisi adsit certa fides, quod sint iisdem profuturae. Nec potest nostra de reprobatione doctrina inde refutari, quod ea posita sequatur publicas preces non posse Deo offerri cum fide quod prodessent omnibus verbum Dei audientibus.
english: This is common knowledge in the School of Theologians. They say four conditions are required for a prayer to have certainty of obtaining; one is that one pray for oneself. For though the prayer be pious, persevering, and about things that belong to salvation, yet if it is made for another it does not always obtain. So the Major totters: it falsely assumes prayers cannot rightly be made for others unless certain faith is present that they will profit them. Nor is our doctrine of reprobation refuted by saying that, once posited, public prayers cannot be offered to God with faith that they would profit all who hear the Word.

source_text: Sed pergamus ad Minorem, in qua dicunt reprobationem a nobis positam impedire quo minus preces cum debita fiducia Deo offerantur. Nos hoc negamus, et dicimus ad debitam fiduciam sufficere, quod certi sumus hoc officium orandi pro aliis Deo placere, et nos pro illis impetraturos, quatenus Deo visum fuerit, ac Divinae gloriae fuerit consentaneum. Haec fiducia stare potest aeque cum nostra doctrina, ac cum Arminiana. Nam illi non audent negare decretum reprobationis esse aeternum et irrevocabile, quamvis asserant illud niti aeterna humanae infidelitatis praevisione. Certum itaque est, Judam ab aeterno reprobatum nullis aliorum precibus posse ad salutem perduci, vel posita illa reprobatione quam tuetur Arminius.
english: But let us take the Minor: they say the reprobation we posit blocks prayers from being offered to God with due confidence. We deny that. Due confidence needs only this: we are certain the duty of praying for others pleases God, and that we shall obtain for them insofar as God sees fit and as agrees with divine glory. That confidence stands as well with our doctrine as with the Arminian. For they dare not deny that the reprobation decree is eternal and irrevocable, though they say it rests on eternal foresight of human unbelief. So it is certain: Judas reprobated from eternity can by no others' prayers be led to salvation — even on the reprobation Arminius maintains.

source_text: Sed hic recurrunt ad limitationes illas conditionales; quibus ipsi suum argumentum planissime enervarunt. Nam quando dicunt se non requirere fiduciam absolutam sed conditionalem, nempe ut credamus preces nostras aliis quibuscunque profuturas, si crediderint, si sua pertinacia sibi ipsis non obstent, uno verbo, nisi ipsi sese Divina gratia praestent indignos, hoc et nos totidem verbis affirmare possumus. Non obstante enim decreto reprobationis, certo credimus preces Ecclesiae profuturas omnibus et singulis verbum Dei audientibus, si credant, si sua pertinacia sibi non obsint, et gratia Divina indignos sese reddant.
english: But here they fall back on those conditional limitations — by which they themselves most plainly enervate their argument. When they say they require not absolute but conditional confidence — namely that we believe our prayers will profit any others if they believe, if their own pertinacity does not hinder them, in a word unless they make themselves unworthy of divine grace — we can affirm the same in so many words. For notwithstanding the reprobation decree, we certainly believe the Church's prayers will profit all and each who hear God's word, if they believe, if their own pertinacity does not hinder them, and they do not make themselves unworthy of divine grace.

source_text: At hoc nos addimus, quod illi obstinato silentio cupiunt occultare, Deum, qui vult omnes Evangelium audientes servare si credant, si sua pertinacia sibi minime obsint, non velle tamen omnium eousque misereri ut emolliantur, et credant, et sua pertinacia sibi non obsint, sed electorum tantum; velle autem permittere ut alii suo vitio indurentur, et in sua voluntaria pertinacia permaneant. Quia vero nobis incognitum est cujus vult misereri, et quem vult suae duritiae relinquere, nostrum est pro omnibus orare, ut convertantur, et neminem singulariter pro reprobato habere.
english: But we add what they by obstinate silence wish to hide. God wills to save all who hear the Gospel if they believe and their own pertinacity does not hinder them. Yet he does not will to have mercy on all so far that they are softened, believe, and cease to hinder themselves — but on the elect only. He wills to permit that others by their own fault be hardened and remain in voluntary pertinacity. Because it is unknown to us of whom he wills to have mercy, and whom he wills to leave to their own hardness, it is ours to pray for all that they be converted, and to treat no one in particular as reprobate.

source_text: Sed adhuc urgent; Quis potest in animum inducere ut pro ejus salute oret, quem Deus praecise nolit servari, cum Apostolus hoc argumento nos acuat ad precandum pro omnibus, quia Deus vult omnes salvos fieri? Respondeo primo, Deus non solet hoc arcanum electionis et reprobationis hominibus patefacere; actiones igitur nostrae ad regulam incognitam nec debent, nec possunt conformari. Secundo, in decreto reprobationis absolutae sive praecisae, ut illi loquuntur, Deus non sic statuit apud se, Ego damnabo Judam, sive non credat sive credat, sed, Ego non ita miserebor Judae, ut emolliatur, ut credat, ut denique de facto convertatur et servetur — sicuti in decreto praedestinationis absolutae Deus non dicit, Ego salvabo Petrum, sive credat sive non, sed Ego ita miserebor Petri, ut credat, ut poeniteat, ut servetur. Si igitur per praecisam et absolutam praedestinationem et reprobationem putant nos intelligere nescio quam praecisionem mediorum a fine, chimaeram suam, non sententiam nostram oppugnant.
english: But they still urge: Who can bring himself to pray for the salvation of one whom God precisely wills not to save, when the Apostle sharpens us to pray for all because God wills all to be saved? I answer first: God does not usually lay open to men this secret of election and reprobation; so our actions neither ought nor can be conformed to an unknown rule. Second: in the decree of absolute or precise reprobation, as they speak, God has not settled with himself, I will damn Judas whether he believe or not — but, I will not so have mercy on Judas that he be softened, believe, and in fact be converted and saved. Just so in absolute predestination God does not say, I will save Peter whether he believe or not — but, I will so have mercy on Peter that he believe, repent, and be saved. If by precise absolute predestination and reprobation they think we mean some cutting of means from the end, they fight their own chimera, not our view.

source_text: Porro, quod putant reprobationis decreto a nobis posito adversari illud Apostolicum, Deus vult omnes salvos fieri, multum falluntur opinione sua. Nam (ut minime ingrediar prolixam aliquam explicationem verborum, de quibus in initio hujus disputationis multa disseruimus) illud Apostoli, Deus vult omnes salvos fieri, non negat aut evertit illam quam ponimus multorum reprobationem. Sicuti enim electio minime sita est in hac affirmatione, Volo hunc salvum fieri, sed, Volo hunc salvum facere; ita non-electio sive reprobatio non sita est in hac negatione, Nolo hunc salvum fieri, sed, Nolo hunc salvum facere. Admittamus igitur Arminii expositionem, Deum velle omnes salvos fieri, nimirum, ita ut velit eosdem servare sub hac conditione, Si crediderint et perseveraverint; dico hanc voluntatem conditionalem servandi stare posse cum decreto absoluto reprobandi; quia non denotat actum voluntatis Divinae ad personam aliquam singularem servandam terminatum, sed decretum voluntatis Divinae de universali et perpetuo nexu duarum rerum, fidei scilicet et salutis. Unde recte colligamus, si fides perseverans in quacunque singulari persona reperiretur, esset quoque in Deo voluntas eandem personam servandi; sed non recte inferamus, in decreto efficacem gratiam praeparante, et ad vitam infallibiliter ordinante, neminem fuisse a Deo antecedenter praeteritum. Ut verbo expediamus nos ab hac objectione; Sicut nulla pugna est inter haec duo, Deus praedestinavit Paulum ad vitam aeternam, et, Deus damnaret Paulum si non crederet, si non perseveraret, ita nec inter haec duo, Deus non praedestinavit, vel Deus praeteriit et rejecit Judam, et Deus salvaret Judam si crederet et perseveraret. Nam sub conditione velle servare, nec arguit electionem, nec negat reprobationem.
english: Further: they think the Apostolic saying 'God wills all to be saved' fights the reprobation decree we posit. They are much deceived. Without entering the long word-debate we already treated at this disputation's start — that saying does not deny or overturn the reprobation of many we place. Election does not sit in 'I will this one to be saved,' but in 'I will to make this one saved.' So non-election or reprobation does not sit in 'I will not this one to be saved,' but in 'I will not to make this one saved.' Admit Arminius's exposition: God wills all to be saved — namely, wills to save them under this condition, if they believe and persevere. That conditional will to save can stand with an absolute decree to reprobate. It does not denote a divine-will act terminated on saving some singular person, but a decree of the universal perpetual nexus of two things: faith and salvation. So we may rightly gather: if persevering faith were found in any singular person, God would also will to save that person. We may not rightly infer that in the decree preparing efficacious grace and infallibly ordaining to life, no one was antecedently passed over by God. In a word: as there is no fight between 'God predestined Paul to everlasting life' and 'God would damn Paul if he did not believe and persevere,' so neither between 'God did not predestine — or passed over and rejected — Judas' and 'God would save Judas if he believed and persevered.' To will to save under a condition neither proves election nor denies reprobation.

source_text: Nostra doctrina, inquit Corvinus, de reprobatione quorundam ex mera libertate Divinae voluntatis, et non ex praevisione finalium demeritorum in ipsis reprobatis, Dei ministros in suo ministerio segnes reddit; utpote ex qua sequatur, ipsorum diligentiam non posse prodesse nisi iis quos Deus absolute vult servare, et qui perire non possunt; et negligentiam rursus ipsorum non posse nocere nisi iis, quos Deus absolute vult perdere, quique non possunt servari: Necesse autem est, hoc dogmate admisso, inertes et torpidos reddi verbi ministros.
english: Our doctrine, says Corvinus, of reprobating some from mere liberty of divine will — not from foresight of final demerits in the reprobate themselves — makes God's ministers sluggish in their work. From it, he says, it follows that their diligence can profit only those God absolutely wills to save, who cannot perish; and that their negligence can harm only those God absolutely wills to destroy, who cannot be saved. Admit that dogma, and ministers of the word must turn idle and torpid.

source_text: Respondeo, etsi inde ministri nonnulli segnes redderentur, non tamen efficitur doctrinam in se falsam aut malam esse. Ex Pauli doctrina nonnulli captabant occasionem licentiae, dicentes, Faciamus mala ut veniant bona. Ex doctrina praescientiae Divinae, fuit quidam Monachus (referente Augustino) qui corripientibus fratribus cum quaedam non facienda faceret, et facienda non faceret, identidem respondebat, Qualiscunque nunc sim, talis olim ero qualem me Deus futurum esse praescivit. Ille Monachus et verum dicebat, et hoc vero non proficiebat in bonum, sed in malum. Propter hujusmodi igitur objectiunculas ea quae de praedestinatione ac reprobatione vera dicuntur, nec neganda sunt, nec tacenda.
english: I answer: even if some ministers grew sluggish from it, that does not make the doctrine itself false or evil. From Paul's teaching some took occasion for license, saying, Let us do evil that good may come. From the doctrine of divine foresight, Augustine tells of a monk who, when the brethren corrected him for doing what he should not and leaving undone what he should, answered again and again: Whatever I am now, I shall one day be what God foresaw I would be. That monk spoke truth — and used that truth not for good but for evil. For such little objections, then, what is truly said of predestination and reprobation is neither to be denied nor kept silent.

source_text: Porro sententia Arminii de reprobatione tam segnes reddit ministros quam nostra. Nam utcunque ille ponat praedestinationem ex praevisa fide, et reprobationem ex praevisione infidelitatis, tamen hanc praevisionem Divinam aeternam fatetur, eademque interveniente, aeternum, fixum, et immobile decretum, sive electionis sive reprobationis, quoad singulos homines ante jacta mundi fundamenta constitutum agnoscit. Minister igitur sperare non potest se aliquem ab aeterno sic reprobatum posse sua diligentia ad vitam aeternam perducere, nisi simul credat posse se efficere ut Divina praescientia fallatur, atque aeternum Dei decretum revocetur. Sive ergo reprobatio ponatur ex mera Divinae voluntatis libertate, omnes causas extrinsecas antegrediente, sive ex praescientia infidelitatis considerationem subsequente, perinde est: Nam nemo erit ex auditoribus, quin sit in hanc vel illam partem ab aeterno praedestinatus, ex qua in contrariam partem nunquam transferetur.
english: Further: Arminius's view of reprobation makes ministers as sluggish as ours. However he sets predestination from foreseen faith and reprobation from foresight of unbelief, he still confesses that divine foresight eternal — and with it intervening, he acknowledges an eternal, fixed, immovable decree of election or reprobation for each person, set before the world's foundations were laid. So a minister cannot hope by diligence to lead to everlasting life someone thus reprobated from eternity, unless he also believes he can make divine foresight err and revoke God's eternal decree. Whether reprobation is set from mere liberty of divine will before all extrinsic causes, or from foresight of unbelief after consideration, it is the same: no hearer but is from eternity predestined to this side or that, from which he will never be transferred to the other.

source_text: Sed hoc non debet impedire aut retardare operam ministrorum, quia, ut pie et prudenter Augustinus, De corrept. et grat. cap. 15. et 16. nescientes quis pertineat ad praedestinatorum numerum, quis non pertineat, sic affici debent charitatis affectu, ut omnes velint salvos fieri. Proinde quantum ad nos pertinet, qui praedestinatos a non praedestinatis discernere non valemus, omnibus ne pereant, vel ne alios perdant, adhibenda est correptio.
english: But that ought not to hinder or slow ministers' labor. As Augustine says piously and wisely (De corrept. et grat. cap. 15–16): not knowing who belongs to the number of the predestined and who does not, they ought to be so moved by charity that they will all to be saved. So far as concerns us, who cannot tell the predestined from the non-predestined, rebuke is to be applied to all, lest they perish or destroy others.

source_text: Verum adhuc aliquanto propius ad rem accedamus: Fac diligentiam ministrorum non posse prodesse nisi iis, quos Deus absolute vult servare, et qui perire non possunt, tamen nihil licet segnitiei neque socordiae. Primo, quia hoc ipsum prodesse suo ministerio iis, quos Deus eximie amavit, quosque ante jacta mundi fundamenta absolute servare decrevit, est valde honorificum et desiderabile. Quis enim, cui ulla inest pietatis guttula, si certo sciret aliquem infantem esse a Deo praedestinatum, non eo enixius laboraret ut in salute ejusdem promovenda Dei συνεργοὶ habeatur? 1 Cor. iii. 9. Sic Paulus animatus fuit, qui omnia propter electos sustinenda dicit, 2 Tim. ii. 10. Porro, vel illud potest ministris torporem excutere, quod licet Deus haud patietur ullum ex electis perire, tamen ipsi negligendo officium suum damnabilem reatum incurrant, juxta illud Apostoli, Vae mihi si non evangelizavero, 1 Cor. ix. 16.
english: But come nearer still. Grant that ministers' diligence can profit only those God absolutely wills to save, who cannot perish — still neither sluggishness nor sloth is allowed. First: to profit by one's ministry those God has loved exceedingly, and whom before the world's foundations he decreed absolutely to save, is greatly honorable and desirable. Who, with any drop of piety, if he knew for certain some infant was predestined by God, would not labor the more earnestly to be counted God's fellow-worker in promoting that one's salvation (1 Cor. iii. 9)? So Paul was animated, who says all things are to be endured for the elect's sake (2 Tim. ii. 10). Further: even this can shake torpor from ministers — though God will not suffer any of the elect to perish, yet by neglecting their office they themselves incur damnable guilt, per the Apostle: Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel (1 Cor. ix. 16).

source_text: Denique, quamvis nemo tam impius, aut rei Theologicae imperitus sit, qui cogitet ministrorum socordia quemlibet ex praedestinatis fieri posse non praedestinatum, aut excidere posse gloria praedestinatis praeparata, tamen nemo tam imprudens est, qui non intelligat ministrorum socordiam posse variis modis cuivis praedestinato obesse. Nam licet ipsum aeternum decretum Dei praedestinantis neque procuretur, neque juvetur, neque impediatur ullis actibus humanis, tamen effecta praedestinationis, vel beneficia in praedestinatione hominibus praeparata, possunt et debent ministrorum diligentia promoveri. Unde Thomas, Part. 1. quaest. 23. artic. 8. Praedestinatio non tollit causas secundas, sed sic providet effectui ut etiam ordo causarum secundarum subjaceat providentiae. Ministri igitur scire debent suam diligentiam esse a Deo subordinatam saluti electorum promovendae.
english: Finally: no one is so impious, or so unskilled in theology, as to think ministers' sloth can make any of the predestined non-predestined, or make them fall from the glory prepared for them. Yet no one is so foolish as not to see that ministers' sloth can harm any predestined person in many ways. For though the eternal decree of God predestinating is neither procured, helped, nor hindered by any human acts, the effects of predestination — or the benefits prepared for men in it — can and ought to be advanced by ministers' diligence. So Thomas (Part. 1 q.23 a.8): Predestination does not take away second causes, but so provides for the effect that even the order of second causes lies under providence. Ministers therefore ought to know their diligence is subordinated by God to promoting the elect's salvation.

source_text: Neque quicquam juvat adversarios vocabulum illud, absolute sive praecise, quod toties inculcant. Deus enim dicitur absolute praedestinasse, et absolute velle servare praedestinatos, non quod sine ullis mediis adhibendis, aut ullis conditionibus ex parte hominum implendis, eosdem velit servare, sed quod pro summa sui misericordia tam de mediis quam de fine prospicit. De utrisque autem ita prospexit, ut quamvis ordo praedestinationis certus sit, et, posito quod talis persona praedestinetur, sit impossibile quod pereat et damnetur, tamen effectus praedestinationis producantur secundum conditionem subjecti, et secundum naturam causarum proximarum quas ad tales effectus Divina providentia ordinavit (ut inquit Aquinas, ibid. art. 6.), hoc est, libere et contingenter. Hinc Paulus, Rom. viii. 38, qui respectu electionis et ordinationis Divinae intellexit se non potuisse a salute excidere, tamen nihilo segnior evasit in salute sua promovenda, sed contundit corpus suum, et in servitutem redigit, ne quo modo cum aliis praedicavit ipse reprobus fieret, 1 Cor. ix. 27. Firmitas igitur electionis Divinae non facit ut supervacaneum sit officium diligentiae humanae, sive respectu sui ipsius sive aliorum.
english: That word absolute or precise, which they hammer so often, does the adversaries no good. When God is said absolutely to have predestined, and absolutely to will the predestined's salvation, the point is not that he saves them with no means used and no conditions on men's part fulfilled. It is that of supreme mercy he looks ahead to means and end alike. He has so looked to both that the order of predestination stays certain — and once such a person is predestined, perishing and damnation are impossible — while still the effects of predestination come forth by the subject's condition and by the nature of the near causes providence set for those effects (Aquinas, ibid. art. 6): freely, contingently. So Paul, who with an eye to divine election and ordination knew he could not fall from salvation (Rom. viii. 38), did not grow idle in pressing his own: he bruises his body and brings it under, lest after preaching to others he himself somehow prove a reprobate (1 Cor. ix. 27). Divine election's firmness, then, leaves human diligence no spare office — for oneself or for others.

source_text: Hactenus de electis. Jam quod de reprobatis objiciunt, negligentiam ministrorum non posse, ex sententia nostra, nocere nisi iis quos Deus absolute vult perdere, quique non possunt servari, id primo falsum est: Nam potest etiam nocere, et saepe nocet, electis, dum patitur eos suis peccatis ad tempus indormire, et hac sua securitate iram Dei ac varia flagella contra se provocare. Dein, nemo est reprobatorum quem Deus absolute vult perdere, hoc est (ut adversarii videntur intelligere) sive poeniteant sive non poeniteant, sive credant sive non credant, sive peccatis immoriantur sive non. Sunt multi quorum Deus non sic miseretur ut praeparaverit illis gratiam specialem et efficacem atque operaturam ut credant, ut poeniteant, ut indurare sua corda desinant. Sed quia ministris ignotum est, quorum Deus vult misereri, et quos vult indurare, debent cum omni lenitate erudire eos qui contrario animo sunt affecti, si quando det illis Deus poenitentiam, etc. 2 Tim. ii. 25. Adhaec, si verum esset, negligentiam ministrorum non posse nocere nisi iis, quos Deus absolute vult perdere, tamen hoc non eximit negligentes ministros vel a culpa vel a poena capitali; sicuti custos carceris a culpa non eximeretur, si latronem gladio transfoderet, aut media extingueret, quem judex apud animum suum absolute decrevisset damnare, et morte afficere. Denique, quod obtendunt, rebus praecise sic vel aliter a Deo semel decretis, curam et solicitudinem earundem rerum frustra postmodum ab hominibus suscipi, est planissime ignava illa ratio, sive ἀργολογία, cui si assentiamur, nihil est omnino quod agamus invita, ut inquit Cicero De fato. Absoluta enim sive praecisa Dei decreta non praescindunt media a fine destinato, sed et media et finem ad infallibilis cujusdam providentiae ordinem reducunt. Neque haec infallibilitas rei decretae tollit naturalem possibilitatem ad eventum contrarium, sed ipsum eventum contrarium: neque etiam innuit aut effectum sine causis secundis producendum, aut propriam operationem secundarum causarum infringendam. Aeternum et arcanum igitur praedestinationis et reprobationis decretum nemini praebet causam socordiae, quamvis impii et socordes possint hoc suae ignaviae falso praetexere.
english: Thus far of the elect. Now their objection about the reprobate — that on our view ministers' negligence can harm only those God absolutely wills to destroy, who cannot be saved — is first false. It can also harm, and often does harm, the elect, while it lets them sleep for a time in their sins, and by that security provoke God's wrath and various scourges against themselves. Next: there is no reprobate whom God absolutely wills to destroy — that is (as the adversaries seem to take it) whether they repent or not, believe or not, die in their sins or not. There are many of whom God does not so have mercy as to have prepared for them special efficacious grace that will also work belief, repentance, and an end to hardening their hearts. But because ministers do not know of whom God wills to have mercy, and whom he wills to harden, they ought with all gentleness to instruct those of a contrary mind, if at any time God give them repentance (2 Tim. ii. 25). Moreover, even if it were true that ministers' negligence can harm only those God absolutely wills to destroy, that does not exempt negligent ministers from guilt or capital punishment — as a jailer would not be exempt from guilt if he ran a thief through with a sword, or extinguished the means, whom the judge in his mind had absolutely decreed to damn and put to death. Finally: what they pretend — that once God has precisely decreed things thus or otherwise, care and solicitude for those same things is afterward taken up by men in vain — is most plainly that idle argument, or lazy reasoning; if we assent to it, there is nothing at all we do unwillingly (Cicero, De fato). For absolute or precise decrees of God do not cut means from the destined end, but bring both means and end under the order of a certain infallible providence. That infallibility of the thing decreed does not take away natural possibility of a contrary event — only the contrary event itself. Nor does it imply that the effect is produced without second causes, or that second causes' proper operation is broken. So the eternal secret decree of predestination and reprobation gives no one a cause of sloth — though the impious and the slothful may falsely pretext it for their idleness.

source_text: Hoc posito conantur ostendere sententiam nostram hoc fundamentum religionis duplici modo evertere. Primo, quia statuit Deum sine ullius obedientiae intuitu aliquos praecise ad salutem elegisse: unde sequitur, Deum illos homines magis amasse quam justitiam suam: Quo posito, tollitur obedientiae praestandae necessitas omnisque de religione solicitudo.
english: That assumed, they try to show our view overturns religion's foundation in two ways. First: it sets God as having precisely elected some to salvation without any gaze upon obedience — from which it follows that God loved those men more than his own justice. That granted, the necessity of rendering obedience is taken away, and all care about religion.

source_text: Secundo, quia (ut illi aiunt) statuit Deus aliquos homines ad damnationem praedestinasse sine intuitu inobedientiae: unde rursus sequitur, Deum creaturam suam odisse citra nullam ex amore erga justitiam necessitatem: Quo posito, tollitur spes in Deum. Qui enim certe sibi persuadet se a salute citra peccati intuitum esse reprobatum, credet nihil sibi posse prodesse, quomodocunque studeat peccatum vitare.
english: Second: as they say, it sets God as having predestined some men to damnation without any gaze on disobedience — from which again it follows that God hates his creature with no necessity arising from love of justice. That granted, hope in God is taken away. For whoever is sure he has been reprobated from salvation apart from any gaze on sin will believe nothing can profit him, however hard he strives to avoid sin.

source_text: Utrumque hoc incommodum ex nostra sententia sequi contendunt, quia docemus, Deum quosdam peccatores ita amasse, ut praecise eos voluerit servare, antequam amori suo erga justitiam satisfecerit in Christo, aut eos ut in Christum credentes sit intuitus; atque e contra, Deum quosdam peccatores velle damnare citra considerationem impoenitentiae, licet justitiae suae in Christo Deus satisfecerit.
english: They contend that both inconveniences follow from our view. Why? Because we teach that God so loved certain sinners that he precisely willed to save them before he satisfied his love of justice in Christ, or before he looked on them as believing in Christ. And on the other side, we teach that God wills to damn certain sinners apart from considering impenitence — even though he has satisfied his justice in Christ.

source_text: Grave profecto hoc crimen est quod nobis objicitur. Nam si sententia nostra convellat religionis Christianae fundamenta, est ipsa quidem ab imis fundamentis revellenda. Expendamus igitur quam vera sit haec criminatio. Atque inprimis non intendimus ullam litem adversariis de duplici illo amore in quo religionis fundamentum collocant; sed negamus sententiam nostram huic amori repugnare.
english: Truly this charge against us is grave. If our view uproots Christianity's foundations, it must itself be torn up from the roots. So let us weigh how true the accusation is. First: we pick no quarrel with the adversaries over that twofold love in which they set religion's foundation — but we deny that our view fights that love.

source_text: Instant, nos statuere Deum sine ullius obedientiae intuitu aliquos praecise ad salutem elegisse: Quam opinionem duobus incommodis urgeri arbitrantur. Unum est, quod ponat Deum taliter praedestinatos magis amare quam justitiam suam, quia vult eos servare, antequam amori suo erga justitiam satisfecerit in Christo, aut eos ut in Christo credentes praeviderit. Alterum est, quod tollat omnem necessitatem fidei et obedientiae, omnemque religionis solicitudinem, quia dicimus taliter praedestinatos amari a Deo ad salutem ante et citra praevisionem fidei et obedientiae in iisdem.
english: They press that we set God as having precisely elected some to salvation without any gaze on obedience. That opinion, they think, is pressed by two inconveniences. One: it makes God love those so predestined more than his own justice, because he wills to save them before he has satisfied his love of justice in Christ, or foresaw them as believing in Christ. The other: it takes away all need of faith and obedience, and all care for religion, because we say those so predestined are loved by God unto salvation before and apart from foresight of faith and obedience in them.

source_text: Respondeo: Non in eo situm est discrimen sententiae nostrae ab Arminiana, quod ille electos non posse salvari statuat absque praestita fidei et obedientiae conditione, nos autem opinemur eos servari posse etiamsi maneant infideles et Deo rebelles: sed quod ille hanc fidei et obedientiae conditionem facit antecedaneum electionis motivum, et hunc actum credendi suspendit a libero arbitrio per gratiam Dei excitato et quasi ad aequilibrium quoddam reducto, sed seipsum ante electionem determinante, et inde electionem Divinam procurante.
english: I answer: Our view does not differ from the Arminian in this — that he holds the elect cannot be saved without faith and obedience rendered, while we think they can be saved even if they stay unbelieving and rebellious to God. The difference is this: he makes that condition of faith and obedience an antecedent motive of election, and hangs the act of believing on free choice excited by God's grace and as it were brought to a certain balance, yet determining itself before election and thereby procuring divine election.

source_text: Nos e contra, quamvis fidei et obedientiae conditionem (si de adultis loquamur) ad vitam aeternam consequendam, ex Dei fixo decreto plane necessariam judicemus, tamen agnoscimus hanc fidem et obedientiam non praevisam fuisse in hac aut illa singulari persona, tanquam ex libero ejus arbitrio per gratiam communem excitato enascentem, et electionis beneficium post se trahentem; sed tanquam speciale donum fuisse huic et illi singulari personae in decreto praedestinationis ab aeterno praeparatum, et ex humana voluntate speciali quadam operatione ab eodem decreto dependente producendam, et inde ab aeterno praevisam in omnibus electis, non tanquam motivum quo ipsi consequantur suam electionem, sed tanquam medium quo praecedente consequentur regnum caelorum ad quod fuerunt electi.
english: We take the other side. For adults we judge faith and obedience plainly necessary to everlasting life by God's fixed decree. Yet we deny that this faith and obedience was foreseen in this or that person as something springing from free choice stirred by common grace, and then dragging election's benefit after it. We hold instead that it was a special gift, prepared from eternity for each elect person in the predestination decree. It is to be produced from the human will by a special operation that depends on that decree. From eternity, then, it was foreseen in all the elect — not as the motive by which they win their election, but as the preceding medium by which they reach the kingdom of heaven to which they were elect.

source_text: Hoc praemisso, sententia nostra praedictis duobus incommodis haud implicatur.
