Non priore; Quia Deus non arguitur magis amasse Petrum aut Paulum quam suam justitiam, si illos ab aeterno elegit et designavit ad infallibilem participationem Christi, fidei, et salutis, antequam praevidit liberum illorum arbitrium per oblationem gratiae sufficientis ad Christum amplexandum, fidem concipiendam, salutisque viam capiessendam, efficaciter et perseveranter inclinatum. Imo hoc arguit summum amorem justitiae in Deo, quod Petrum et Paulum, quos ad salutem ex mera misericordia eximie dilexit, noluerit tamen ad hanc salutem illis destinatam perducere nisi talibus mediis adhibitis quibus justitiae suae prius satisfaceret.
english: That premised, our view is not caught in those two inconveniences. Not the first: God is not charged with loving Peter or Paul more than his own justice if from eternity he elected and designated them to infallible share in Christ, faith, and salvation before he foresaw their free choice efficaciously and perseveringly inclined — through the offer of sufficient grace — to embrace Christ, conceive faith, and take the way of salvation. Nay, this argues supreme love of justice in God: that Peter and Paul, whom of mere mercy he loved exceedingly unto salvation, he yet would not lead to that destined salvation unless such means were used by which his justice would first be satisfied.

source_text: Ut in pauca contraham responsionem nostram, dico, Amorem justitiae requirere ut nemo in Christo ad salutem ametur, nisi qui fide ipsum apprehenderit; sed hoc sensu, ut minime ametur ad actualem et fructuosam participationem salutis priusquam in fide perseveraverit, amari tamen possit ad aeternam salutis in mente et voluntate Divina preparationem priusquam consideretur ut credens et in hac fide perseverans. Nam ipsa praeparatio fidei et perseverantiae sunt amoris Divini argumenta: praeparantur autem prius quam infallibiliter praevidentur in Petro infallibiliter futurae. Atque praeparantur haec dona salutifera singularibus personis infallibiliter conferenda, non nisi ex amore ad salutem illorum spectante. Neque in hac praeparatione Deus violare putandus est leges justitiae suae, sed explicare opes specialis misericordiae suae.
english: To put our answer in few words: love of justice requires that no one be loved in Christ unto salvation unless he has apprehended him by faith. Take that in this sense: he is not loved unto actual fruitful share of salvation before he has persevered in faith — yet he can be loved unto the eternal preparation of salvation in God's mind and will before he is considered as believing and persevering in that faith. For the very preparation of faith and perseverance are marks of divine love: they are prepared before they are infallibly foreseen in Peter as infallibly about to be. And these saving gifts are prepared to be infallibly conferred on singular persons only from a love that looks to their salvation. In that preparation God is not to be thought to violate the laws of his justice, but to unfold the riches of his special mercy.

source_text: Sed alter scrupulus hic eximendus est. Urget Arminius, nos ponere Deum non modo amare quosdam ad salutem ante praevisam fidem et obedientiam eorundem, sed antequam Christus sit ordinatus ut sua obedientia peccata expiaret; quia docemus Christum ideo fuisse datum in Mediatorem, quia Deus decreverat servare electos: quod perinde est ac si dicamus, Deum magis amasse homines peccatores, quam suam justitiam.
english: But another scruple must be cleared here. Arminius urges that we set God as loving some unto salvation not only before their foreseen faith and obedience, but before Christ was ordained to expiate sins by his obedience — because we teach that Christ was given as Mediator because God had decreed to save the elect. That, he says, is as if we said God loved sinful men more than his own justice.

source_text: Haec argutatio vocat nos ad speculationem valde difficilem, et dogmaticae Theologiae fundandae minime accommodatam. Nicitur enim consideratione Prioritatis et Posterioritatis in illis duobus voluntatis Divinae decretis, de dando Mediatore, et de electis servandis, quae utraque ab aeterno fuerunt concepta et constituta. Ad me quod attinet, scio ordinem exsecutionis, secundum quem Deus voluit beneficia ad homines pervenire, nullo negotio posse delineari: at quo ordine Deus ea consignata tenuit ab aeterno in mente ac voluntate sua, is solus enarrare praesumat qui se Deo ab arcanis et aeternis consiliis fuisse etiam affirmare audeat.
english: This argument calls us into a very hard speculation, poorly fitted to founding dogmatic theology. It hangs on priority and posteriority between those two decrees of divine will — giving a Mediator, and saving the elect — both conceived and established from eternity. As for me: I know the order of execution, by which God willed benefits to reach men, can be sketched with no trouble. But in what order he held them sealed from eternity in his mind and will — let only him presume to tell who dares claim he has been with God from the secret eternal counsels.

source_text: Fatemur igitur Deum ab aeterno constituisse ut omnibus salvandis Christus primo in loco proponeretur, dein per fidem apprehenderetur, hinc ut eorundem justificatio sequeretur, tum sanctificatio, et demum glorificatio: Sed si quis minime contentus hoc ordine exsecutionis, velit etiam nobis describere seriem decretorum Divinorum, ordine conceptionis in mente ac voluntate Dei quasi distinctam, atque urgeat cum Arminio, Divinam justitiam impugnari, nisi hoc consideretur ut illo prius, is mihi videtur nimium ingenio suo fidere.
english: So we confess that from eternity God established this for all who are to be saved: Christ first proposed, then apprehended by faith, then their justification, then sanctification, and at last glorification. But if anyone, not content with that order of execution, also wants to map for us a distinct series of divine decrees in the order of conception in God's mind and will, and with Arminius urges that divine justice is attacked unless one decree is set prior to the other — he seems to me to trust his own wit too much.

source_text: Quod igitur objectum fuit, labefactari Divinam justitiam, si ponamus Deum prius elegisse quosdam ad vitam, quam ordinaverit Christum ad expianda peccata, hic scrupulus dissolvi potest. Primo, si quis cum subtili Doctore respondeat, Utcunque Christus Christique merita erga homines ordinata fuerunt post praedestinationem, tamen cum in exsecutione meritum Christi sit causa cujuscunque effectus a praedestinatione manantis, nihil fit contra justitiam Dei in salute electorum. Nam ex mera misericordia intendere salutem alicujus peccatoris, atque ex hac intentione providere illi talia media, ut hoc minime fiat priusquam justitiae fuerit satisfactum, non est peccatorem magis amare quam justitiam, sed velle exercere gratuitam misericordiam erga peccatorem, potius quam debitam justitiam.
english: So the objection that divine justice is shaken if we set God as electing some to life before ordaining Christ to expiate sins — that scruple can be loosed. First, with the subtle Doctor: however Christ and his merits toward men were ordered after predestination, yet in execution Christ's merit is the cause of every effect flowing from predestination — so nothing is done against God's justice in the elect's salvation. Of mere mercy to intend a sinner's salvation, and from that intention to provide him such means that it is never done before justice is satisfied, is not to love the sinner more than justice — it is to will to exercise free mercy toward the sinner rather than due justice.

source_text: Secundo nodus iste discindi potest, si quis cum Biele defendat, Prioritates illas in Divinis hisce decretis non esse ponendas, sicut nec pluralitates actuum ordinatorum; ac proinde si quis considerare velit talem ordinem horum decretorum ut ponat Christi incarnationem electione priorem, vel e contra, hanc considerationem esse falsam speculationem. Sic Biel, in 3. dist. 2. qu. dub. 3.
english: Second, this knot can be cut with Biel: those priorities are not to be set among these divine decrees — nor pluralities of ordered acts. So if anyone wants to consider an order of these decrees that sets Christ's incarnation before election, or the reverse, that consideration is false speculation (Biel, in 3. dist. 2. qu. dub. 3).

source_text: Denique, si ad sustentandam intellectus nostri imbecillitatem haec Dei decreta distinguamus secundum prius et posterius, per respectus ad objecta, quae varia et distincta sunt, arbitror nos commodissime concipere in Deo 1. voluntatem generalem redimendi humanum genus sub conditione fidei, per incarnandum Salvatorem nostrum et Mediatorem Jesum Christum; uti exprimitur Joann. iii. 16, Sic Deus dilexit mundum, etc. 2. voluntatem specialem, secundum quam Christus a Patre ordinatus Mediator constituitur Caput omnium praedestinatorum, in quo et per quem, quicquid ad gratiam et gloriam infallibiliter consequendam necessarium est, iisdem praeparandum et donandum decernitur. Hoc posito, evanescit praedicta objectio, quia Christus concipitur ut ordinatus Mediator et datus in Caput Ecclesiae, hoc est, omnium electorum, priusquam illi considerentur ut ordinati ad efficacem participationem sive gratiae sive gloriae.
english: Finally: if to prop up our weak intellect we distinguish these decrees of God as prior and posterior by respect to varied distinct objects, I judge we most conveniently conceive in God (1) a general will to redeem the human race under the condition of faith, through our Savior to be incarnate and Mediator Jesus Christ — as John iii. 16 expresses: So God loved the world, etc.; (2) a special will, whereby Christ ordained by the Father as Mediator is made Head of all the predestined, in whom and through whom whatever is needed for infallibly obtaining grace and glory is decreed to be prepared and given them. That posited, the objection vanishes: Christ is conceived as ordained Mediator and given as Head of the Church — that is, of all the elect — before they are considered as ordained to efficacious share of grace or glory.

source_text: Ad alteram partem objectionis jam accedo, nempe quod sententia nostra omnem obedientiae necessitatem et religionis curam extinguat, quia statuit Deum praecise aliquos ad salutem ordinasse sine fidei praecedentis, aut obedientiae nostrae intuitu: Hinc enim qui est electus concludet, non opus esse ut de praestanda obedientia multum sit solicitus. Nihil dici aut cogitari potest perversius. Nam sententia nostra negat quidem necessitatem fidei aut obedientiae praevisae in nobis tanquam motivi ad actum electionis ex parte Dei considerati; sed requirit fidem et obedientiam a nobis tanquam conditionem, ad fructum electionis, id est vitam aeternam, ex parte nostra consequendum. Qui enim docent Deum ita praedestinasse quosdam ad vitam, ut non nisi per fidem et sanctitatem eo perducantur, non negant fidei necessitatem, sed agnoscunt specialem Dei in hac fide quibusdam praeparanda et donanda misericordiam.
english: I now take the other part of the objection: that our view extinguishes all need of obedience and care for religion, because it sets God as having precisely ordained some to salvation without any gaze on preceding faith or our obedience — so the elect will conclude he need not be much solicitous about rendering obedience. Nothing more perverse can be said or thought. Our view does deny that faith or obedience foreseen in us is necessary as a motive of the election-act considered on God's part. But it requires faith and obedience from us as a condition for obtaining on our part the fruit of election — that is, everlasting life. Those who teach that God so predestined some to life that they are led there only through faith and holiness do not deny faith's necessity — they acknowledge God's special mercy in preparing and giving that faith to certain ones.

source_text: Porro, cum electionis decretum sit hominibus a priori plane incognitum, et non nisi ex effectis et Spiritus testimonio ipsis electis revelatum, non modo falsum, sed a ratione et sensu communi alienum est, quod colligunt Arminiani, posse hosce electos concludere apud se nil opus esse ut soliciti sint de praestanda obedientia. Nam ipsi electi ne tenuissimam quidem suae electionis cognitionem habere possunt, priusquam sentiant in se hoc studium obediendi Deo, et vitam suam religiose transigendi: neque Spiritus Dei dignabitur hoc testimonium homini in caeno libidinum turpissimarum volutanti exhibere. Quomodo igitur concludet ex apprehensione electionis suae nil sibi opus esse sanctitate vitae, qui aliter colligere non potest se esse electum, quam ex effectis Spiritus sancti et sanctificantis?
english: Further: the election decree is plainly unknown to men a priori, and is revealed to the elect themselves only from effects and the Spirit's testimony. So what the Arminians gather — that these elect can conclude they need not be solicitous about rendering obedience — is not only false, but alien to reason and common sense. The elect themselves cannot have even the slenderest knowledge of their election before they feel in themselves this study of obeying God and living religiously. Nor will God's Spirit deign to give that testimony to a man wallowing in the mire of foulest lusts. How then will he conclude from apprehending his election that he needs no holiness of life — when he can gather he is elect no other way than from the effects of the Holy and sanctifying Spirit?

source_text: Denique reclamat Arminio omnium sanctorum praxis, quos certum est eo studiosiores fuisse pietatis et verae obedientiae, quo certiores fuerunt suae electionis et vitae aeternae. Exemplo esse possunt sancti Patriarchae, Abrahamus, Isaacus, Jacobus, Beatissima mulierum Mater Domini nostri Jesu Christi, Petrus, Paulus, reliquique Apostoli: Imo omnis qui habet hanc spem in seipso, sanctificat se, sicut ille sanctus est, 1 Joann. iii. 3. Profani igitur homines, qui stulte praesumere solent, et otiose garrire de sua praedestinatione, inde redduntur de Deo colendo minus soliciti: sed piorum pectora, qui vivide sentiunt hoc beneficium ad se pertinere, inde incenduntur incredibili amore Dei et ardentissimo studio pietatis. Sic Bernardus, Epist. 107. Justus quis est nisi qui amanti se Deo vicem rependit amoris? Quod non fit, nisi revelante Spiritu per fidem, homini aeternum Dei propositum super sua salute futura.
english: Finally the praxis of all the saints cries out against Arminius. It is certain they were the more studious of piety and true obedience, the more certain they were of their election and everlasting life. Example: the holy Patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, Jacob; the most Blessed of women, the Mother of our Lord Jesus Christ; Peter, Paul, and the other Apostles. Nay, everyone who has this hope in himself sanctifies himself, as he is holy (1 John iii. 3). So profane men, who foolishly presume and idly chatter of their predestination, grow less careful about worshipping God. But pious hearts, who vividly feel this benefit belongs to them, are kindled with incredible love of God and most ardent study of piety. So Bernard (Epist. 107): Who is just but he who repays love to God who loves him? That is not done unless the Spirit reveals through faith to a man God's eternal purpose concerning his future salvation.

source_text: Hactenus de praedestinatione dictum est: Jam ad eam partem objectionis quae reprobationem spectat veniamus; Cui respondemus breviter, Neminem ex nostra sententia ad damnationem deputatum esse nisi ex intuitu praecedentis peccati, originalis nempe, actualis, aut utriusque. Neminem enim Deus odit ad damnationem absque consideratione peccati; Nec magis odit homines quam peccatum, quos nunquam ita odisset nisi propter peccatum.
english: Thus far of predestination. Now to that part of the objection which looks to reprobation. We answer briefly: on our view no one is appointed to damnation except from a gaze on preceding sin — original, actual, or both. For God hates no one unto damnation without considering sin. Nor does he hate men more than sin — he would never have hated them so except because of sin.

source_text: Nemo denique mortalium est quem nostra sententia de reprobatione ad desperationem potest adigere, si studeat vitare peccatum et Deo obedire; quia hoc ipsum studium est nostro judicio certissimum electionis argumentum. Nec debent desperare, qui nondum sentiunt tale studium, sed iis mediis uti, quae sunt illis a Deo concessa, haud dubitantes quin Deus sic agentibus suam misericordiam sit exhibiturus.
english: Finally: our doctrine of reprobation can drive no mortal to despair if he studies to avoid sin and obey God — for that very study is in our judgment the surest mark of election. Nor should those despair who do not yet feel such a study. They should use the means God has granted them, not doubting that God will show his mercy to those who so act.

source_text: CAP. X. Nostra de Reprobatione sententia exponitur et confirmatur. Hactenus Adversariorum sententiam et argumenta expendimus. Jam quae sit nostra de reprobatione sententia, quibusque firmamentis nitatur, videamus.
english: CHAPTER X. Our sentence on Reprobation is set forth and confirmed. Thus far we have weighed the adversaries' view and arguments. Now let us see what our view of reprobation is, and on what stays it rests.

source_text: Atque hic, ut vitemus malevolorum calumnias, subinde cogimur repetere, Ecclesiam nostram non minus rejicere portentosas illorum opiniones, qui sic reprobationis decretum nobis depingunt, ut Deum infidelitatis et impoenitentiae humanae causam statuant, ipsamque adeo perditionem et damnationem hominum in Dei absolutam et antecedentem voluntatem revocent, quam Arminianorum ex Pelagii faecibus haustos errores, qui sic praedestinationis et reprobationis decreta nobis proponunt, ut interim unumquemque, post decretum de administranda communiter gratia sufficiente, constituant in gratuitis et aeternis bonis fabrum fortunae suae; Deo scilicet praestolante et intuente quid homines sint facturi, et prout praeviderit eos credituros, aut non credituros, eligente eos vel non eligente, hoc est, reprobante.
english: And here, to avoid malevolent calumnies, we must keep repeating: our Church rejects no less those portentous opinions that so paint the reprobation decree as to make God the cause of human unbelief and impenitence, and even refer men's very perdition and damnation to God's absolute antecedent will — than the Arminian errors drawn from Pelagius's dregs, which so set the decrees of predestination and reprobation that after the decree to administer common sufficient grace, each man is made smith of his own fortune in free and everlasting goods. God waits and watches what men will do, and as he foresaw them about to believe or not, elects them or does not elect — that is, reprobates.

source_text: Hanc praedestinationem et reprobationem, in qua humana voluntas ducit Divinam, nec Deo dignam putamus, nec sacris literis consentaneam. E contra igitur, sicuti monstravimus, Praedestinationem non esse singularium personarum ex praevisa illarum fide et perseverantia electionem ad vitam aeternam, sed praeparationem gratiae efficacis certis quibusdam personis ex mera Dei misericordia, et praeparationem gloriae sempiternae iisdem ex eadem misericordia.
english: We judge that scheme — predestination and reprobation in which human will leads the divine — neither worthy of God nor agreeable to Scripture. On the contrary side, as we have shown, Predestination is something else. It is not election of singular persons to everlasting life from their foreseen faith and perseverance. It is God's mere-mercy preparation of efficacious grace for certain persons, and of everlasting glory for them from that same mercy.

source_text: Ita dicimus, Non-electionem, praeteritionem sive reprobationem negativam haud esse singularium personarum ex praevisa finali earundem infidelitate et impoenitentia praedamnationem, (quamvis tale decretum agnoscamus) sed ex mera Dei voluntate denegationem ejus specialis misericordiae, quae infidelitatem et impoenitentiam tollit emolliendo, et ad vitam aeternam perducit in fide et sanctitate stabiliendo et conservando. Vel brevius ex Bradwardino nostro, qui profundi Doctoris cognomentum sibi meruit, Praedestinatio est aeterna praeparatio a voluntate Divina gratiae finalis in via, et beatitudinis aeternae in patria, creaturis quibusdam rationalibus, lib. 1. cap. 45. pag. 421. Et reprobatio est aeterna Dei nolitio conferendi talia in quibusdam personis, Ibid. pag. 426. Cum Apostolo defendimus hanc electionem non esse volentis, neque currentis, sed miserentis Dei, Rom. ix. 16. et hanc non-electionem, reprobationem sive nolitionem aeternam non esse ortam ex praevisa infidelitate, aut impoenitentia hominum, sed ex mera ejus libertate, qui cujus vult miseretur, et quem vult indurat, Rom. ix. 18. Quod, interprete Augustino, perinde est ac si dixisset Apostolus, cujus vult miseretur, et cujus non vult non miseretur, De praedest. et grat. cap. 6.
english: So we put it this way. Non-election — preterition, negative reprobation — is not pre-damnation of singular persons from foreseen final unbelief and impenitence. (We do acknowledge a decree of that kind.) What it is, from God's mere will, is denial of that special mercy which softens away unbelief and impenitence, and which leads to everlasting life by fixing and keeping a person in faith and holiness. Bradwardine, our profound Doctor, says it shorter: Predestination is the eternal preparation by divine will of final grace in the way, and of eternal beatitude in the fatherland, for certain rational creatures (lib. 1. cap. 45. pag. 421). Reprobation is God's eternal nilling to confer such things in certain persons (Ibid. pag. 426). With the Apostle we hold that this election is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy (Rom. ix. 16). And this non-election — this reprobation or eternal nilling — did not spring from men's foreseen unbelief or impenitence. It sprang from his mere liberty: who has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens (Rom. ix. 18). Augustine's reading is as if the Apostle had said: on whom he wills he has mercy, and on whom he wills not he has not mercy (De praedest. et grat. cap. 6).

source_text: De hoc igitur reprobationis decreto disputaturi, id unum agemus, ut ostendatur, Aeternam illam distinctionem electorum et non-electorum in mente et voluntate Divina non habuisse originem, occasionem, aut motivum qualecunque ex antecedanea praevisione bonorum actuum in personis electis, puta poenitentiae, fidei et perseverantiae in Petro et Paulo, et ex antecedanea praevisione oppositorum in non-electis, scilicet impoenitentiae, infidelitatis et contumaciae finalis in Caino, Juda, reliquisque; sed meram Dei voluntatem primo divisisse inter filios ad participationem gratiae et gloriae infallibiliter ordinatos, et inter rejecticios sive quoad talem ordinem praeteritos.
english: So in disputing this reprobation decree we shall do one thing: show that the eternal distinction of elect and non-elect in God's mind and will had no origin, occasion, or motive of any kind from antecedent foresight of good acts in the elect — penitence, faith, and perseverance in Peter and Paul — or from antecedent foresight of the opposites in the non-elect — impenitence, unbelief, and final contumacy in Cain, Judas, and the rest. Rather, God's mere will first divided between sons infallibly ordained to share grace and glory, and those rejected or passed over as to that order.

source_text: Huc redit summa hujus controversiae: Si in aeterno decreto electionis et reprobationis personae quaedam fuerunt a Deo praeconsideratae tanquam aliis digniores, meliores et sanctiores, atque inde ad vitam infallibiliter praedestinatae, atque e contra aliae quaedam praeconsideratae ut hisce indigniores, nequiores et improbiores, atque inde a praedestinatione ad vitam exclusae, vincit Arminius, nos causa cadimus: Si autem, ex adverso, quotquot ad vitam fuerunt ante jacta mundi fundamenta praedestinati, fuerunt a Deo considerati ut peccatores aeterno exitio digni, per specialem misericordiam Dei, et singularem quandam et secundum propositum vocationem, fide, resipiscentia, perseverantia, ipsaque salute infallibiliter donandi, non autem praevisi ante electionem suam tanquam prae aliis recto liberi arbitrii usu ex oblata gratia ad concipiendam fidem in eaque perseverandum sese determinantes.
english: The sum of this controversy comes to this. If in the eternal decree of election and reprobation God preconceived certain persons as worthier, better, and holier than others, and thence infallibly predestined them to life — and preconceived others as unworthier, worse, and more wicked, and thence shut them out from predestination to life — Arminius wins, we lose the cause. But if, on the contrary side, all who were predestined to life before the world's foundations were laid were considered by God as sinners worthy of everlasting ruin, to be infallibly gifted — by God's special mercy and a singular calling according to purpose — with faith, repentance, perseverance, and salvation itself, and were not foreseen before their election as determining themselves ahead of others by a right use of free choice from offered grace to conceive faith and persevere in it.

source_text: Et e contra, si qui non-electi, praeteriti sive reprobati dicuntur, fuerunt etiam a Deo considerati ut peccatores morte digni, etsi in se nihilo deteriores, sed liberrima Dei voluntate minime dignati eadem speciali misericordia et efficaci vocatione quae electis praeparata fidem, resipiscentiam et salutem eorum operata est, tum succumbits Arminius, nos causam obtinemus.
english: And on the other side take the non-elect — those called passed over or reprobate. They too were considered by God as sinners worthy of death. In themselves they were no worse. Yet by God's freest will they were not dignified with that same special mercy and efficacious calling which, prepared for the elect, wrought their faith, repentance, and salvation. Then Arminius sinks, and we obtain the cause.

source_text: Quod attinet ad praedestinationem, multis rationibus ostensum est, illam ex liberrimo Dei beneplacito, et non ex antecedanea consideratione humanorum actuum dependere. Restat igitur ut de non-electione sive reprobatione idem ostendatur: Nihil autem aliud hic nobis agendum erit, quam ut rationes eas quasi sub signa, et in ordinem revocemus, quae in confirmatione causae nostrae et in responsionibus ad argumenta adversariorum non nisi dispersae, et palantes conspici potuerunt.
english: As for predestination: many reasons have already shown that it depends on God's freest good pleasure, not on antecedent consideration of human acts. It remains to show the same of non-election or reprobation. Here we need only recall those reasons into order — as under standards — which in confirming our cause and answering the adversaries could be seen only dispersed and straggling.

source_text: Primo, argumentari possumus ab illis sive definitionibus sive descriptionibus reprobationis, quae subinde occurrunt apud adversarios nostros: Nam ex hisce ipsis perspicue concludi potest, Praescientiam absolutam finalis impoenitentiae et infidelitatis, quoad hanc aut illam personam singularem, praesupponere decretum reprobandi, ac proinde hoc decretum ex illa praevisione non manare.
english: First: we can argue from the definitions or descriptions of reprobation that keep turning up among our adversaries. From those themselves it is plain: absolute forescience of final impenitence and unbelief, as to this or that singular person, presupposes the decree to reprobate — and so that decree does not flow from that foresight.

source_text: Gregorius Valentia reprobationem ita nobis depingit, In Aquin. qu. 23. de reprobatione, punct. 1. Reprobatio est actus Divini intellectus, quo firmiter statuit Deus reprobatorum peccata permittere, non dando iis singularem gratiam qua ab iis liberarentur, et propter illa eos a regno caelesti excludere, ac in aeternum punire.
english: Gregory of Valencia paints the picture this way (In Aquin. qu. 23. on reprobation, punct. 1). Reprobation, he says, is an act of the divine intellect. By it God firmly establishes that he will permit the reprobates' sins — not giving them the singular grace by which they would be freed from those sins — and for those sins will shut them out of the heavenly kingdom and punish them forever.

source_text: At firmissimum hoc Divini intellectus ac voluntatis statutum de permittendis peccatis quarundam personarum, et de non-apponenda gratia qua ab iis liberarentur, praevisae earundem impoenitentiae, infidelitati et contumaciae praesupponi debet, utpote quae non praeviderentur ut absolute futurae si non permitterentur. Hoc igitur obtinimus, Quod utcunque voluntas puniendi hanc singularem personam, puta Judam aut Cainum, subsequatur peccati praevisionem, tamen voluntas permittendi infidelitatem et impoenitentiam ejusdem, ac voluntas negandi specialem gratiam, qua ad fidem et poenitentiam efficaciter flecteretur, praecedit hanc praescientiam absolutam malitiae finaliter in eadem duraturae. At hoc nobis satis est, qui illum reprobatum intelligimus, cui Deus ab aeterno denegare voluit illam gratiam qua liberaretur, et quem permittere voluit suo vitio indurescere in peccatis suis; sicut e contra illum praedestinatum dicimus, cui Deus ab aeterno praeparare voluit illam singularem gratiam qua liberaretur, quemque permittere noluit in peccatis suis finaliter indurescere.
english: But that most firm statute of divine intellect and will — to permit certain persons' sins, and not to apply the grace by which they would be freed — must be presupposed to their foreseen impenitence, unbelief, and contumacy. Those would not be foreseen as absolutely about to be if they were not permitted. So we obtain this: however the will to punish this singular person — Judas or Cain — follows foresight of sin, the will to permit his unbelief and impenitence, and the will to deny the special grace by which he would be efficaciously bent to faith and penitence, precede that absolute forescience of malice finally to endure in him. That is enough for us. We take as reprobate the one to whom God from eternity willed to deny that freeing grace, and whom he willed to permit by his own fault to harden in his sins. On the contrary we call predestined the one for whom God from eternity willed to prepare that singular freeing grace, and whom he would not permit to harden finally in his sins.

source_text: Nam Qui potest, ut loquitur Augustinus, De bono persever. cap. 8. aversas et adversas quorumvis convertere voluntates, et hoc ab aeterno statuit in quibusdam facere, in quibusdam non facere, ille non secundum praescitam differentiam humanarum voluntatum, sed secundum merum beneplacitum suae voluntatis, eligit et praeterit, miseretur et non miseretur. Jam Vasques audiatur: Si reprobatio usurpetur pro actu quo quis rejicitur a Deo, aut loquimur de actu quo quis rejicitur a gratia Dei, aut quo rejicitur a regno caelorum. Si de priore sermo sit, asserendum est nullam causam ex parte ejus dari qui rejicitur, praeter peccatum primi parentis, In 1. disp. 89. c. 5. p. 701. Quamvis igitur nemo e caelo excludatur et in gehennam ablegetur ex sententia Dei judicantis, nisi propter peccata propria: tamen, vel hoc Jesuita ultro confitente, omnes reprobati rejiciuntur a gratia praedestinatorum ex libertate Dei, de suo quod vult facientis.
english: For he who can — as Augustine says (De bono persever. cap. 8) — convert anyone's averse and adverse wills, and from eternity established to do this in some and not in others, elects and passes over, has mercy and has not mercy, not by a foreknown difference of human wills, but by the mere good pleasure of his will. Hear Vasquez: If reprobation is used for the act whereby someone is rejected by God, we speak either of rejection from God's grace, or of rejection from the kingdom of heaven. If of the former, it must be asserted that no cause is given on the rejected one's part beyond the first parent's sin (In 1. disp. 89. c. 5. p. 701). So although no one is shut out of heaven and sent to gehenna by God's judging sentence except for his own sins — yet, even this Jesuit freely confessing, all the reprobate are rejected from the predestined's grace by God's liberty, doing of his own what he wills.

source_text: Idque non ex praevisa eorundem infidelitate aut impoenitentia finali, sed quatenus considerantur in communi Adae peccato jacentes. Quinetiam ipse Arminius in Collatione cum Junio, non infidelitatem aut impoenitentiam finalem, sed peccatum illud in quo omnes communiter concepti sunt, contendit praesupponendum esse electioni et praeteritioni: neque illud audet ponere causam cur Deus aliquos praetereat, sed solummodo cur aliquos praeterire possit, Pag. 96.
english: And that rejection is not from their foreseen unbelief or final impenitence, but inasmuch as they are considered lying in Adam's common sin. Nay, Arminius himself, in the Collation with Junius, contends that what must be presupposed to election and preterition is not final unbelief or impenitence, but that sin in which all are commonly conceived. Nor does he dare make that the cause why God passes some over — only why he can pass some over (Pag. 96).

source_text: Jam vero in Examine Praedestinationis Perkinsianae, pag. 57. etc. ex mente Augustini, forte et Scripturae sensu (sic enim ipse loquitur) agnoscit quibusdam hominibus ex decreto providentiae administrari gratiam tantummodo sufficientem, ac cum certa Dei praescientia quod sit rejicienda a libero hominis arbitrio; ex decreto autem praedestinationis administrari aliis non modo sufficientem gratiam, sed efficacem, cum certa Dei praescientia fore ut beneficio hujus gratiae reipsa velint, credant et convertantur illi quibus accommodatur et adhibetur. Paulo post: Deus hanc gratiam efficacem quibusdam non dare statuit, idque decreto reprobationis.
english: But now in his Examination of Perkins's Predestination (pag. 57 etc.), from Augustine's mind — and perhaps Scripture's sense, as he himself says — he acknowledges this: to some men, from the providence decree, only sufficient grace is administered, with God's certain forescience that free choice will reject it; to others, from the predestination decree, not only sufficient grace but efficacious, with God's certain forescience that by that grace's benefit those to whom it is fitted and applied will in fact will, believe, and be converted. A little later: God established not to give this efficacious grace to certain ones — and that by the reprobation decree.

source_text: Videtis quid ipsi adversarii fateantur: ex quibus concludamus, esse in praeparanda et non praeparanda gratia efficaci arcanum quoddam et inscrutabile beneplacitum Dei, quod non sequitur praescientiam fidei et gratiae acceptatae in electis, ac praescientiam infidelitatis et gratiae finaliter rejectae in reprobatis, sed utriusque praescientiam antecedit. Ridiculus enim fuerit qui diceret, ex decreto providentiae praeparari aliquibus gratiam solummodo sufficientem, cum praescientia certa quod rejicietur, atque iisdem ex decreto reprobationis negari gratiam efficacem, quae a nullo duro corde respuitur, ac postea doceret hoc fieri quia Deus praevidebat hosce gratiam suam rejecturos et in sua infidelitate et pertinacia morituros. Qui igitur prius non audent negare, non debuerunt posterius tam confidenter affirmare.
english: You see what the adversaries themselves confess. From that let us conclude: in preparing and not preparing efficacious grace there is a secret, inscrutable good pleasure of God. It does not follow forescience of faith and accepted grace in the elect, or forescience of unbelief and grace finally rejected in the reprobate — it precedes both. For it would be ridiculous to say that from the providence decree only sufficient grace is prepared for some, with certain forescience it will be rejected, and that from the reprobation decree efficacious grace — which no hard heart refuses — is denied them, and then to teach that this happens because God foresaw they would reject his grace and die in unbelief and pertinacity. Those who dare not deny the first ought not so confidently to have affirmed the second.

source_text: Si decretum reprobationis penderet ex praevisa finali impoenitentia et infidelitate reprobatorum, tum nemo reprobaretur nisi consideratus a Deo ut moribundus, imo ut mortuus. Ratio perspicua est; Quia dum hic vivitur, neque finalis cujusquam perseverantia in fide, neque finalis pertinacia in infidelitate adimpletur. Quicquid enim ante finem fuerit, gradus est quo ad fastigium ascenditur, non terminus quo jam culminis summa teneatur.
english: Suppose the reprobation decree hung on the reprobates' foreseen final impenitence and unbelief. Then no one would be reprobated except as God considered him dying — nay, dead. Why is that plain? Because while life is lived here, neither anyone's final perseverance in faith, nor final pertinacity in unbelief, is fulfilled. Whatever comes before the end is only a step by which one climbs toward the summit, not the term by which the height's top is already held.

source_text: At electionem et reprobationem prius spectare homines qua mortuos, vel saltem qua in extremis positos, inauditum est, et sacris Scripturis ac rationi plane contrarium. Scripturae electionem et rejectionem Jacobi et Esavi nobis depingunt, non considerandam post decursum hujus vitae spatium ab utroque; sed cum nondum nascerentur, et nihil adhuc boni aut mali fecissent, Rom. ix. 11, 12, 13. Quorum vero unus eligitur absque consideratione ullius boni, ab eo antecedenter praestiti, alter rejicitur absque consideratione peccati alicujus actualis antecedenter ab eo perpetrati, illorum neutrum ex hac praevisione Arminiana anteelectum fuisse aut rejectum, liquido constat.
english: But that election and reprobation should first look on men as dead, or at least as at their last extremity, is unheard-of — and plainly contrary to Scripture and reason. Scripture depicts Jacob and Esau's election and rejection not as considered after both had run this life's course, but when they were not yet born and had done nothing yet of good or evil (Rom. ix. 11–13). Of those of whom one is elected without considering any good he antecedently rendered, and the other rejected without considering any actual sin he antecedently committed, it is plain neither was ante-elected or rejected from this Arminian foresight.

source_text: Scio nonnullos minime concedere praedicta Apostoli verba ad aeternam praedestinationem et reprobationem Jacobi et Esavi esse referenda, sed solummodo ad illud propositum quo constituit Deus pro beneplacito suo honorare Jacobum, et subjicere illi Esavum, saltem in posteris utriusque. Sit ita: Tamen ex consensu Theologorum, et ex toto discursu Apostoli illud liquet, hoc exemplum fuisse introductum a Paulo saltem ad repraesentandum aeternae praedestinationis et reprobationis mysterium, atque demonstrandum argumento a figura ad rem figuratam, neque electionem hominum ad aeternam salutem, neque reprobationem esse ex contrariis operum meritis, sed Deum ex solo voluntatis suae arbitrio alios eligere ad salutem, alios autem reprobare.
english: I know some will not grant that those Apostolic words refer to Jacob and Esau's eternal predestination and reprobation — only to that purpose by which God of his good pleasure established to honor Jacob and subject Esau to him, at least in both their posterities. Be it so. Still, from theologians' consent and from the Apostle's whole discourse, this is clear: Paul introduced that example at least to represent the mystery of eternal predestination and reprobation, and to prove by argument from figure to thing figured that neither election of men to everlasting salvation, nor reprobation, is from contrary merits of works — but that God, of the sole choice of his will, elects some to salvation and reprobates others.

source_text: Sed adhuc apertius confirmamus Minorem, nempe, Reprobationem non cadere in homines postquam ad extremum halitum in peccatis suis perseverasse considerantur; Quia multa consequentia reprobationis pertinent ad reprobatos in hujus vitae cursu constitutos; qualia sunt negatio gratiae efficacis sive vocationis secundum propositum, permissio improborum ut impune pergant hic in peccatis suis, traditio eorundem in reprobum sensum. Haec et alia hujusmodi.
english: But we confirm the Minor still more openly: reprobation does not fall on men only after they are considered to have persevered in their sins to the last breath. Many consequences of reprobation belong to the reprobate while they are set in this life's course — denial of efficacious grace or of calling according to purpose; permission of the wicked to go on here in their sins unpunished; delivering them over to a reprobate mind. These and the like.

source_text: Haec et alia hujusmodi sunt acta reprobandi posteriora, et tamen finali reprobatorum duritia et infidelitate priora: Ergo ex praevisa finali infidelitate hujus aut illius non consequitur reprobatio ejusdem, sed hanc praevisionem potius antecedit: Quod ex illis Christi verbis facile colligitur, Vos non creditis: non enim estis ex ovibus meis, Joann. x. 26.
english: These and the like are acts of reprobating that come later in the life's course, and yet are prior to the reprobates' final hardness and unbelief. So from this or that one's foreseen final unbelief, his reprobation does not follow — rather it precedes that foresight. Christ's words make it easy: "You do not believe, because you are not of my sheep" (John x. 26).

source_text: Non esse ovem hisce in verbis consideratur ut antecedaneum ad non credere: At quid aliud est Non esse ovem quam non esse praedestinatum, vel esse a gratia praedestinatorum rejectum, ut explicat Augustinus, Tract. 48. in Evang. Joan. hisce verbis, Quomodo ergo istis dixit, NON ESTIS EX OVIBUS MEIS? Quia videbat eos ad sempiternum interitum praedestinatos, non ad vitam aeternam sui sanguinis pretio comparatos.
english: In these words, not being a sheep is treated as antecedent to not believing. And what else is not being a sheep than not being predestined — or being rejected from the predestined's grace? So Augustine explains (Tract. 48. on John's Gospel): How then did he say to them, "YOU ARE NOT OF MY SHEEP"? Because he saw them predestined to everlasting ruin, not purchased for eternal life by the price of his blood.

source_text: Si Deus neminem praeteriret aut reprobaret nisi ex praevisione gratiae suae sufficientis finaliter spretæ et contemptae, sive (quod eodem redit) ex praevisione finalis impoenitentiae et infidelitatis, tum situm esset in potestate uniuscujusque, ut pro arbitrio suo reprobetur vel non reprobetur, atque electus vel non-electus esset. Imo omne discrimen electorum et reprobatorum non ex diversis placitis Divinae voluntatis, sed ex diversis actibus humanarum voluntatum primo exoriretur.
english: Suppose God passed over or reprobated no one except from foresight of his sufficient grace finally despised and contemned — or, what comes to the same thing, from foresight of final impenitence and unbelief. Then it would lie in each person's power, at his own choice, whether he be reprobated or not, elect or non-elect. Nay more: the whole difference between elect and reprobate would first spring not from diverse placita of the divine will, but from diverse acts of human wills.

source_text: Id inde evincitur, quia in cujus potestate est antecedens necessarium, in ejusdem etiam est consequens, quod ex eodem antecedente infallibiliter dependet: Si igitur credere, et gratiam oblatam amplecti sit antecedens necessarium ad electionem, et non credere, seu gratiam oblatam finaliter respuere sit antecedens ad reprobationem, et utrumque horum ex libero actu humanae voluntatis sufficienti gratia excitatae dependeat, quid apertius quam esse in potestate singulorum ut reprobentur vel non reprobentur, cum inter haec tanquam contradictoria medium assignari nullo modo possit?
english: That is proved thus: whoever has power over the necessary antecedent also has power over the consequent that depends infallibly on it. So if believing and embracing offered grace is the necessary antecedent to election, and not believing — or finally refusing offered grace — is the antecedent to reprobation, and both hang on a free act of the human will excited by sufficient grace, what is plainer than that it lies in each one's power to be reprobated or not? Between those as contradictories no middle can be assigned.

source_text: Qui apertius hanc causam agunt, agnoscunt vim consequentiae, sed minime absurdum arbitrantur, complecti (ut illi loquuntur) electionem et reprobationem ex humani arbitrii actibus dependere. Sic philosophatur Lessius Jesuita. Sed quia Apostolus tam reprobationem quam electionem clare et perspicue retulit ad antecedentem Dei voluntatem, miserentis et non miserentis pro suo beneplacito, alii coguntur aliter respondere.
english: Those who plead this cause more openly grant the force of the consequence, yet find no absurdity in holding — as they speak — that election and reprobation depend on acts of human choice. So the Jesuit Lessius philosophizes. But because the Apostle clearly and plainly referred both reprobation and election to God's antecedent will — having mercy and not having mercy according to his good pleasure — others are forced to answer otherwise.

source_text: Vasques igitur, In 1. quaest. 23. disp. 95. cap. 9. in vocabulo reprobationis latebram quaerit, atque respondet, Esse in potestate cujusque reprobari aut non reprobari, si sermo sit de reprobatione quae incipit a destinatione ad poenam. Sed nos (uti saepe praemonuimus) per reprobationem non intelligimus destinationem singularis alicujus personae ad poenam, vel praedamnationem ejusdem, sed negatam praeparationem talis gratiae, quae stantem creaturam efficaciter sustentasset, et ad gloriam perduxisset, ut cernitur in causa Angelorum non-electorum; vel quae lapsam creaturam efficaciter erexisset, et ad vitam aeternam perduxisset, ut in causa hominum non-electorum sive reprobatorum cernitur. Atque hac in re habemus confitentem (qui in aliis nobis adversatur) ipsum Jesuitam, cujus verba apponam: Quum Praedestinari sit gratiam illam, quam Deus novit in nobis effectum habituram, nobis praeparari; et non-praedestinari sit gratiam illam nobis non praeparari, et neutrum horum sit in nostra potestate, efficitur ut praedestinari aut non praedestinari non sit in nostra potestate. Quare hac de causa diximus, non esse in nostra potestate reprobari, si reprobatio pro gratiae negatione sumatur. Haec ille. Ibid. pag. 709.
english: So Vasquez (In 1. quaest. 23. disp. 95. cap. 9) seeks a refuge in the word reprobation, and answers that it is in each one's power to be reprobated or not — if the talk is of reprobation that begins from destination to punishment. But we (as we have often warned) do not mean by reprobation the destination of some singular person to punishment, or his pre-damnation. We mean the denied preparation of such grace as would have efficaciously sustained a standing creature and led it to glory — as in the non-elect angels — or would have efficaciously raised a fallen creature and led it to everlasting life — as in non-elect or reprobate men. And on this point we have the Jesuit himself confessing (though elsewhere he opposes us). His words: Since to be Predestined is that grace which God knew would have effect in us be prepared for us, and not to be predestined is that that grace not be prepared for us, and neither is in our power, it follows that to be predestined or not is not in our power. For that reason we have said it is not in our power to be reprobated, if reprobation is taken for negation of grace (Ibid. pag. 709).

source_text: Non est ergo veritati consentanea illorum opinio, qui electionis et reprobationis libertatem, sub praetextu praevisae fidei et infidelitatis, Deo plane eripiunt; et quod homines in electos et reprobatos dispeccati, id discriminis quoad personas singulares ex antecedaneis et discriminatis hominum actibus contingenter evenisse docent. Nos, si ulla in re, tum praecipue in hac electione et praeteritione, cum Apostolo dicimus, Deum facere omnia ex consilio voluntatis suae, Ephes. i. 11.
english: So their opinion is not agreeable to truth — those who, under pretext of foreseen faith and unbelief, plainly snatch from God the liberty of election and reprobation, and teach that the discrimination which has sorted men into elect and reprobate, as to singular persons, has contingently come about from men's antecedent and differing acts. We — if in anything, then especially in this election and preterition — say with the Apostle that God does all things by the counsel of his will (Eph. i. 11).

source_text: Dari et non dari Christo est per praedestinationem et praeteritionem ordinari aut non ordinari in vitam aeternam: At haec datorum et non datorum distinctio antecedit nostrum credere et non credere, perseverare aut non perseverare.
english: To be given to Christ, and not to be given to him, is — by predestination and preterition — to be ordained, or not ordained, unto everlasting life. That distinction between those given and those not given comes before our believing and not believing, before our persevering or failing to persevere.

source_text: Electio sive praedestinatio, et praeteritio sive reprobatio non pendent ex praevisione antecedanea fidei et perseverantiae in quibusdam, ac infidelitatis et pertinaciae in aliis, sed talem praevisionem antecedunt.
english: So election — that is, predestination — and preterition — that is, reprobation — do not hang on antecedent foresight of faith and perseverance in some, and of unbelief and pertinacity in others. They precede that foresight.

source_text: Majoris veritas ex hisce Scripturarum testimoniis patet; Joann. x. 28, 29. Nemo rapit oves meas de manu mea. Pater meus, qui eas dedit mihi, major omnibus est: neque quisquam potest eas rapere e manu Patris mei. Quaero quis sensus horum verborum, Pater Christo dedit oves certas, quas nulla vis potest rapere, nisi, Deus Pater eligendo dedit Christo singulares quasdam personas, quas decrevit contra omnes carnis, mundi, et diaboli impetus insidiasque defendere, atque tandem ad fruitionem aeternae vitae infallibiliter perducere?
english: The Major's truth is plain from these Scripture witnesses (John x. 28–29): No one snatches my sheep out of my hand. My Father, who gave them to me, is greater than all; and no one can snatch them out of my Father's hand. What sense have the words The Father gave Christ certain sheep that no force can snatch — unless this: God the Father, by electing, gave Christ certain singular persons, whom he decreed to defend against all assaults and snares of flesh, world, and devil, and at last to lead infallibly to the fruition of everlasting life?

source_text: E contra, quid est non dari Christo a Patre, nisi tali gratioso decreto ad vitam aeternam in Christo et per Christum infallibiliter obtinendam minime ordinari? Quo etiam spectant illa verba, Joann. xvii. 9. Non pro mundo rogo, sed pro iis quos dedisti mihi, quia tui sunt. Sunt igitur quidam non-dati Christo, non numerati in peculio Dei Patris, hoc est, non-electi antequam jacerentur mundi fundamenta, non-praedestinati in adoptionem filiorum pro benevolo affectu voluntatis Divinae, Eph. i. 4, 5, etc.
english: On the contrary: what is it not to be given to Christ by the Father, except this — not to be ordained by that gracious decree to obtain everlasting life infallibly in Christ and through Christ? Those words look the same way (John xvii. 9): I ask not for the world, but for those whom you have given me, because they are yours. So there are some not-given to Christ, not numbered in God the Father's peculiar flock — that is, non-elect before the world's foundations were laid, not predestined to the adoption of sons according to the benevolent affection of the divine will (Eph. i. 4–5, etc.).

source_text: Augustino haec praedictorum verborum semper placuit sententia: Hi Christo intelliguntur dari, qui ordinati sunt in vitam aeternam. Ipsi sunt illi praedestinati, et secundum propositum vocati, quorum nullus perit, De corr. et grat. cap. 9. Et in Evang. Joann. Tractat. 106. Quos Deus Filius de mundo elegit cum Patre, idem ipse homo Filius de mundo accepit a Patre. Non enim Pater illos Filio dedisset, nisi elegisset. Videtis igitur per datos Christo, ex mente Augustini, nil aliud intelligi, quam electos sive praedestinatos: Et e contra, per non-datos intelligi reprobatos, hoc est, praeteritos et minime praedestinatos, apud eundem Augustinum aeque in confesso est.
english: Augustine always liked this reading of those words: These are understood as given to Christ who are ordained to everlasting life. They are the predestined, and called according to purpose, of whom none perishes (De corr. et grat. cap. 9). And in Tract. 106 on John's Gospel: Those whom God the Son elected from the world with the Father, the same as man the Son received from the world from the Father. For the Father would not have given them to the Son unless he had elected them. So you see: by those given to Christ, on Augustine's mind, nothing else is meant than the elect or predestined. And on the contrary, by the not-given the reprobate are meant — that is, the passed over and not predestined — which Augustine equally confesses.

source_text: Hinc Tract. 107. in Evang. Joann. ad haec verba, Non pro mundo rogo, sed pro his quos dedisti mihi, sic scribit; Mundum vult intelligi, qui vivunt secundum concupiscentiam mundi, et non sunt in ea sorte gratiae ut ab illo eligantur ex mundo. Et Tract. 111: Non ei dati sunt, quibus vitam non dabit aeternam. At quinam tandem illi sunt, quibus Christus non dabit vitam aeternam, nisi illi, et illi soli, quos appellamus praeteritos, non-electos sive reprobatos? nam omnibus electis dabit eam.
english: Hence on Tract. 107 on John's Gospel, at the words I ask not for the world, but for these whom you have given me, he writes: By world he means those who live by the world's lust, and are not in that lot of grace to be chosen by him out of the world. And Tract. 111: They have not been given to him to whom he will not give everlasting life. But who finally are those to whom Christ will not give everlasting life, except those — and those alone — whom we call the passed over, non-elect or reprobate? For to all the elect he will give it.

source_text: Veniamus nunc ad Minorem, et ostendamus hanc distinctionem datorum et non-datorum Christo antecedere fidem et perseverantiam humanam, antecedere etiam praevisionem absolutam infidelitatis et pertinaciae humanae. Quod fidem et perseverantiam antecedat ex illis verbis colligitur, Quicquid mihi dat Pater, ad me veniet: et eum qui venit ad me non ejiciam foras, Joann. vi. 37. Manifestum est ex hisce verbis, venire ad Christum et permanere in Christo, quod est credere in Christum et in fide perseverare, ex hac datione Patris, tanquam ex antecedente causa dependere.
english: Now to the Minor: let us show that this distinction of those given and not-given to Christ precedes human faith and perseverance, and also precedes absolute foresight of human unbelief and pertinacity. That it precedes faith and perseverance is gathered from these words: Whatever the Father gives me will come to me; and him who comes to me I will not cast out (John vi. 37). From those words it is plain: coming to Christ and remaining in Christ — that is, believing in Christ and persevering in faith — depends on this giving of the Father as on an antecedent cause.

source_text: Idem patet Joann. xvii. 6. Ubi Christus dicit se manifestasse nomen Patris sui hominibus, quos dedit illi de mundo. Et vers. 15. Rogat specialim pro hisce, ut serventur a malo illo, et ad gloriam aeternam perducantur vers. 24. Huc etiam faciunt illa verba Matth. xiii. 11. Vobis datum est nosse mysteria regni caelorum, illis non est datum. In quibus locis ipse ordo est diligenter observandus. Primo, certae quaedam personae dantur Christo vivificandae et salvandae ex speciali beneplacito Dei Patris. Tum Christus speciali operatione Spiritus sui aperit horum corda, ut salutiferam Dei cognitionem ac fidem concipiant. Tandem illuminatos et conversos ita gubernat et sustentat, ut nullis diaboli tentationibus ad interitum seducantur. Non ergo speculatur Deus quinam sunt libero suo arbitrio per gratiam excitato credituri et perseveraturi, et ex hac praevisione aliis praeteritis eos eligit, sed eligit quosdam ex mero suo beneplacito, donatque Christo, quibus Christus inspirat fidem ut accedant ad Deum, et indit perseverantiam ne recedant ab eo.
english: The same is plain in John xvii. 6, where Christ says he has manifested his Father's name to the men the Father gave him from the world. And verse 15: he asks specially for these, that they be kept from that evil one, and led to everlasting glory (verse 24). Matthew xiii. 11 serves the same point: To you it is given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven; to them it is not given. In these places the order itself must be carefully watched. First, certain persons are given to Christ to be quickened and saved from God the Father's special good pleasure. Then Christ, by a special operation of his Spirit, opens their hearts so they conceive saving knowledge of God and faith. At last he so governs and sustains the illuminated and converted that no devil's temptations seduce them to ruin. God does not look to see who by free choice excited by grace will believe and persevere, and from that foresight elect them while passing others over. He elects some from his mere good pleasure, and gives them to Christ; Christ inspires faith in them that they may come to God, and implants perseverance that they may not withdraw from him.

source_text: Audiamus eundem quem antea audivimus Augustinum; Sic se Filium glorificat, ut omnibus quos dedisti ei te cognitum faciat, Tract. 105. in Evang. Joann. Est igitur prius Christo donari a Patre, hoc est eligi, quam cognoscere.
english: Hear again the same Augustine: So he glorifies the Son, that to all whom you have given him he may make you known (Tract. 105. on John's Gospel). Therefore being given to Christ by the Father — that is, being elected — is prior to knowing.

source_text: Et Tract. 107. Per hoc quod eos illi Pater jam dedit, factum est ut non pertineant ad eum mundum pro quo non rogat Christus. Quasi dixisset, Per antecedaneam electionem factum est ut essent fideles, non per antecedaneam fidem ut essent electi.
english: And Tractate 107: By this—that the Father has already given them to him—it comes about that they do not belong to that world for which Christ does not pray. As if to say: antecedent election made them faithful; antecedent faith did not make them elect.

source_text: Jam et alteram partem Minoris pensitemus, nimirum, Quod non-credere, vel a fide incepta resilire sit posterius hac non-datione Divina, sive non-electione in Christo, et per consequens quod non-electio sive reprobatio ex tali praevisione tanquam ex antecedaneo motivo minime oriatur. De Infidelitate valde perspicuum est illud, quod antea citavimus testimonium, Joann. x. 26. Non creditis: non enim estis ex ovibus meis. Sic etiam de Apostasia a fide suscepta satis clarum est illud, 1 Joann. ii. 19. E nobis exierunt, sed ex nobis non fuerunt: nam si fuissent ex nobis, permansissent utique nobiscum, &c. Ostendat nobis Arminius, aut Corvinus quid sit non esse ex ovibus Christi, nisi non esse ex electis: quod si verum sit, tum non esse electum est quiddam prius consideratione nostra quam esse incredulum.
english: Now weigh the Minor’s other part: not believing, or springing back from faith once begun, comes after this divine not-giving—non-election in Christ—and so non-election or reprobation does not arise from such foresight as from an antecedent motive. On unbelief the witness already cited is plain (John x. 26): You do not believe, because you are not of my sheep. On apostasy from faith once received, 1 John ii. 19 is clear enough: They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have remained with us. Let Arminius or Corvinus show what not being of Christ’s sheep means, if not not being of the elect. If that is true, then in our order of thought not being elect comes before being an unbeliever.

source_text: Expediat etiam quid illud sit per quod apostatae etiam cum nobiscum sunt, non sunt tamen ex nobis. Nihil profecto aliud reperient in quo consistere possunt, praeterquam quod non fuerunt donati Christo a Patre, hoc est praeteriti, reprobati fuerunt, et in libro vitae, sive catalogo electionis Divinae, minime conscripti. Esse ergo reprobatum vel non-electum est ordine prius quam esse praevisum ut in apostasiam labentem et in eadem permanentem. Hoc recte observavit Augustinus, De corr. et grat. cap. 7. hisce verbis, Qui perseveraturi non sunt, non sunt a massa illa perditionis praescientia Dei et praedestinatione discreti, et ideo nec secundum propositum vocati, ac per hoc nec electi. Non dicit Augustinus, quia praevidebantur minime perseveraturi, ideo non fuisse electos: sed docet, eos non esse perseveraturos qui non fuerunt antecedenter electi et a massa perditionis discreti.
english: Explain also that by which apostates, even while with us, are still not of us. They will find nothing to rest in except this: they were not given to Christ by the Father—passed by, reprobated, and not written in the book of life, the catalogue of divine election. So being reprobate or non-elect is prior in order to being foreseen as one who will fall into apostasy and stay there. Augustine saw this rightly (De correptione et gratia 7): Those who will not persevere are not set apart by God’s foreknowledge and predestination from that mass of perdition, and so are neither called according to purpose, nor elect. He does not say they were not elect because they were foreseen as non-persevering; he teaches that those will not persevere who were not antecedently elect and set apart from the mass of perdition.

source_text: Sed ne quis inde errandi occasionem arripiat quod dictum est, non-dare Christo vel non-eligere esse prius considerandum ex parte Dei reprobantis, quam non-credere aut non-perseverare absolute praevideatur ex parte personae reprobatae; id moneo non esse ita intelligendum, quasi Deus, aut Dei decretum, causa productiva esset infidelitatis, apostasiae, aut pertinaciae humanae, (haec enim omnia nascuntur ex insita hominum corruptione) sed quia cum fides et perseverantia sint dona Dei miserentis, quae omnibus posset impertire, ipso actu reprobandi decernat apud se non efficere in aliquibus, quod in aliis effecturus est, quodque in omnibus efficere potuisset. Nam (ut vere Augustinus, De corr. et grat. cap. 24.) Deo volenti salvum facere nullum hominum resistit arbitrium. Ipsum itaque resistere, sive in infidelitate perseverare, quod praevidetur in omnibus reprobates, aperte evincit illum qui habet humanorum cordium quocunque placuerit inclinandorum omnipotentissimam potestatem, ut inquit Augustinus ibidem, non habuisse hanc efficacem hosce salvandi voluntatem: quod nil aliud est quam eos non-elegisse sive reprobasse. Quinto arguitur ab illo principatu qui Deo tribuendus est, non modo circa res futuras, sed etiam circa res non futuras. Nam (ut recte statuit Bradwardinus, lib. 3. c. 33.) Deus non solum super entia, sed etiam super non-entia tenet principatum.
english: But lest anyone twist what was said—that not giving to Christ, or not electing, is prior on God’s reprobating side to absolute foresight of not-believing or not-persevering on the reprobate’s side—I warn: this does not mean God or his decree is the productive cause of human unbelief, apostasy, or stubbornness (those spring from inbred corruption). It means that since faith and perseverance are gifts of the merciful God, which he could give to all, by the very act of reprobating he decrees not to work in some what he will work in others and could have worked in all. For as Augustine truly says (De correptione et gratia 24), no human will resists God when he wills to save. So that very resisting—or persevering in unbelief—foreseen in all the reprobate plainly proves that he who holds most omnipotent power to incline human hearts wherever he pleases did not have this efficacious will to save these; which is nothing other than not electing them, or reprobating them. Fifth, the argument is from that principate due to God not only over future things but also over non-future things. For as Bradwardine rightly holds (lib. 3, c. 33), God holds principate not only over beings but also over non-beings.

source_text: Hoc posito, cum ab aeterno certum Deo sit et definitum, quod in quibusdam hominibus nec poenitentia, nec fides, nec perseverantia unquam sit futura, quaeso quorsum reducemus harum rerum non futurarum principatum ad Divinam voluntatem? Non possumus affirmare aeternam Dei voluntatem, aut decretum aliquod Divinum, in istis hominibus efficere sive gignere infidelitatem, impoenitentiam et apostasiam: Deus enim autor non est ejus rei cujus est ultor. Neque sufficit dicere, Deum ab aeterno praevidisse, quod tales homines, administrata illis gratia sufficienti ad poenitendum, credendum et perseverandum, propria sua malitia exsisterent impoenitentes, infideles aut apostatae. Nam hoc Deo quidem tribuit rerum futurarum aut non futurarum praescientiam infallibilem, sed interim humanae voluntati adscribit de futura earundem existentia aut non-futura determinationem principalem.
english: That granted: since it is certain and defined for God from eternity that in some men neither repentance nor faith nor perseverance will ever come to be, where do we lodge the principate over these non-futures in the divine will? We cannot say God’s eternal will or some divine decree effects or begets unbelief, impenitence, and apostasy in those men—for God is not author of what he avenges. Nor is it enough to say he foresaw from eternity that such men, given sufficient grace to repent, believe, and persevere, would by their own malice prove impenitent, unbelieving, or apostate. That gives God infallible foresight of futures and non-futures, but still leaves the human will the principal determination of whether those things will exist or not.

source_text: Eo igitur tandem redeundum est, ut fateamur penes Deum esse principalem rerum futurarum et non-futurarum determinationem; quatenus in bonis actibus decrevit ad eos producendos efficacem suam operationem adhibere; quatenus in malis, quae ab hominibus improbis producuntur, decrevit eos minime impedire; denique, quatenus in bonis actibus, qui ab iisdem omitterentur, decrevit non dare gratiam efficacem qua fierent. Et sic voluntas Dei est causa predominans et praedeterminans quoad non-esse rerum minime futurarum, quoniam cum possit facere ut essent futurae si vellet, non vult tamen hoc facere quod posset. Jam vero ab aeterno non velle facere cum posset, ut Cain poeniteat, ut Judas credat, ut Hymenaeus perseveret, est antecedaneae non-electionis firma demonstratio; sicut velle efficere ut Petrus poeniteat, ut Paulus credat et perseveret, est antecedaneae electionis clara probatio. Hoc autem reprobationis decretum, quod continet determinatum actum Divinae voluntatis de non danda fide, poenitentia, perseverantia certis quibusdam personis, earundem infidelitatem, impoenitentiam et praevisam et certo futuram praecedat est necesse.
english: So we must come back to this: with God lies the principal determination of futures and non-futures—in good acts, by decreeing to apply his efficacious operation to produce them; in evils produced by the wicked, by decreeing not to hinder them; and in good acts those same would omit, by decreeing not to give the efficacious grace by which they would be done. Thus God’s will is the predominating, predetermining cause of the non-being of things that will not be: he can make them future if he wills, yet he does not will to do what he could. Not willing from eternity—though he could—that Cain repent, Judas believe, Hymenaeus persevere, firmly demonstrates antecedent non-election; willing to bring about that Peter repent, Paul believe and persevere, clearly proves antecedent election. And this reprobation decree—the determined act of the divine will not to give faith, repentance, perseverance to certain persons—must precede their unbelief and impenitence, foreseen and certainly future.

source_text: Non ergo reprobatio ponenda est ex praevisione antecedaneae infidelitatis, nec electio ex praevisione fidei; sed infidelitas reprobatorum finalis praevidetur in antecedente negatione gratiae efficacis, et fides electorum perseverans praevidetur in antecedente praeparatione gratiae efficacis: ut utrobique principatus, authoritas, superioritas et determinativa potestas sive rerum futurarum sive non-futurarum sit penes Deum tanquam supremum arbitrum. Hoc illud est quod docuit Augustinus, de praedest. sanct. cap. 6. Alii credunt, alii contradictunt. Volunt ergo isti credere; nolunt autem illi. Quis hoc ignoret? quis hoc neget? Sed cum aliis praeparetur, aliis non praeparetur voluntas a Domino, &c. Unde patet decretum de praeparandis et non praeparandis humanis voluntatibus esse praevisa sive fide sive infidelitate humana prius: Quod perinde est ac si diceremus, praedestinationem et praeteritionem singularium personarum esse absoluta praescientia fidei aut infidelitatis in eisdem priorem.
english: So reprobation is not to be set from foresight of antecedent unbelief, nor election from foresight of faith. Final unbelief in the reprobate is foreseen in the antecedent denial of efficacious grace; persevering faith in the elect is foreseen in the antecedent preparation of that grace—so that on both sides principate, authority, superiority, and determining power over futures and non-futures rest with God as supreme arbiter. That is what Augustine taught (De praedestinatione sanctorum 6): Some believe; others contradict. These will to believe; those will not. Who does not know this? Who denies it? But since the Lord prepares the will for some and not for others, and so on. So the decree to prepare or not prepare human wills is prior to foresight of human faith or unbelief—which is as much as to say that predestination and preterition of singular persons is prior to absolute foreknowledge of faith or unbelief in them.

source_text: Si, ut ponit Arminius, post decretum Dei de dando Christo Mediatore et Salvatore, et illud alterum quo decrevit quosvis sub conditione resipiscentiae, fidei et perseverantiae salvos facere, itemque et illud tertium quo decrevit media ad resipiscentiam et fidem necessaria omnibus administrare; si, inquam, positis hisce tribus decretis, singularium personarum electio et reprobatio, salus et damnatio dependeat ex praevisa hominum sive fide sive infidelitate, tum sequitur, hominum libero arbitrio relictum fuisse, ut possent finem Dominicae passionis, hoc est, acquisitionem Ecclesiae, prorsus evacuare: Ita ut, quod Christus frustra mortuus non fuerit, quod habeat Ecclesiam electorum sanguine suo efficaciter redemptam, non ex antecedaneo aliquo decreto, aut speciali gratia Dei membra quaedam Christo Capiti eligentis et per Christum vivificanda et salvanda praedestinantis, sed ex contingente operatione humanarum voluntatum evenerit. Universi enim mortales, si considerentur ut nondum electi, nec speciali illa providentia Dei, quam Praedestinationem vocamus, ad habendam fidem et perseverandum in eadem praedeterminati, possunt in sua incredulitate manere, possunt a fide suscepta resilire, possunt, uno verbo, a salute excidere, et Christum Redemptorem, absque Ecclesia redempta prorsus relinquere. Hanc consequentiam non possunt negare, qui electionem et reprobationem ex praevisione fidei et infidelitatis conantur arcessere. Ingenue itaque illam admisit Grevinchovius, Dissert. De morte Christi, pag. 14. Asserimus, inquit, potuisse omnibus impetratam esse redemptionem, et tamen nullis applicatam propter intervenientem omnium infidelitatem. Sic etiam Episcopius hoc principio Arminiano innixus, fatetur totam Ecclesiam in terris deficere posse, neque necesse esse ad hoc, ut Christus Rex et Caput maneat, illum habere semper Ecclesiam aliquam veram in terris.
english: If, as Arminius sets it, after God’s decree to give Christ as Mediator and Savior, and the second decree to save any under the condition of repentance, faith, and perseverance, and the third to administer to all the means needed for repentance and faith—if, with those three decrees in place, election and reprobation of singular persons, salvation and damnation, hang on foresight of men’s faith or unbelief—then it follows that free will was left able to empty out the end of the Lord’s passion, the acquiring of the Church. So that Christ not dying in vain, and having a church of elect efficaciously redeemed by his blood, would come not from some antecedent decree or special grace of God electing certain members to Christ the Head and predestining them to be made alive and saved through him, but from the contingent working of human wills. For all mortals, if taken as not yet elect and not predetermined by that special providence we call Predestination to have faith and persevere in it, can stay in unbelief, spring back from faith once received, in a word fall from salvation and leave Christ the Redeemer with no redeemed church at all. Those who fetch election and reprobation from foresight of faith and unbelief cannot deny this consequence. Grevinchovius admitted it candidly (Dissert. De morte Christi, p. 14): We assert that redemption could have been obtained for all, and yet applied to none because of the intervening unbelief of all. So Episcopius, resting on this Arminian principle, confesses the whole church on earth can fail, and that Christ need not always have some true church on earth in order to remain King and Head.

source_text: At quicquid isti tenent, est prorsus alienum a Theologia, et Scripturis contrarium, mortem Christi fuisse quasi aleam jactam, ita ut posita anima sua, an quisquam per mortem ejus salvus fieret, ex contingentia liberi hominum arbitrii prorsus penderet. Longe aliter Isaias, Isa. liii. 10. Si posuerit animam suam hostiam pro peccato, semen longaevum videbit. Deus igitur promittit Christo Ecclesiam, si animam posuerit hostiam pro peccato.
english: But whatever they hold is wholly alien to theology and contrary to Scripture: that Christ’s death was like a lot cast, so that—his soul once laid down—whether anyone would be saved by that death hung wholly on the contingency of human free will. Isaiah speaks far otherwise (Isa. liii. 10): If he shall lay down his soul as a sacrifice for sin, he shall see a long-lived seed. So God promises Christ a church if he lays down his soul as a sacrifice for sin.

source_text: Quod autem Deus promisit Filio, ejus impletio non ex incerta operatione humani arbitrii, sed ex firmissimo divinae voluntatis decreto, et operatione eidem decreto respondente arcessenda est.
english: What God promised the Son must be fetched not from the uncertain working of human free will, but from the firmest decree of the divine will and from an operation that answers to that decree.

source_text: Horsum facit illud Augustini, De praedest. sanctorum, cap. 10. Non de nostrae voluntatis potestate, sed de sua praedestinatione promisit. Promisit enim quod ipse facturus fuerat, non quod homines: quia etsi faciunt homines bona quae pertinent ad colendum Deum, ipse facit ut illi faciant quae praecepit, non illi faciunt ut ipse faciat quod promisit: alioquin ut Dei promissa compleantur, non in Dei sed in hominum esset potestate.
english: Here belongs Augustine (De praedestinatione sanctorum 10): He promised not from the power of our will, but from his own predestination. For he promised what he himself would do, not what men would do: though men do the goods that belong to worshipping God, he makes them do what he commanded; they do not make him do what he promised—otherwise the fulfillment of God’s promises would lie not in God’s power but in men’s.

source_text: Videtis vim argumenti; Electio et reprobatio ex praevisione actuum humanorum contingenter prodeuntium aut non-prodeuntium e voluntate humana, libero hominum arbitrio committit utrum Dei promissio implebitur necne, utrum Christus morte sua Ecclesiam aliquam sibi acquiret an secus, uno verbo, utrum Christus erit Caput sine membris, Redemptor sine redemptis, Servator sine servatis, necne, quae omnia in divina praedestinatione et operatione habent suam firmitatem et infallibilem certitudinem, non in nuda praevisione, quid homines pro libertate arbitrii sui acturi sint, aut non acturi.
english: See the force of the argument: election and reprobation from foresight of human acts that contingently proceed or fail to proceed from the human will hands over to free will whether God’s promise will be fulfilled, whether Christ by his death will gain a church for himself or not—in a word, whether Christ will be a Head without members, a Redeemer without redeemed, a Savior without saved. All that has its firmness and infallible certainty in divine predestination and operation, not in bare foresight of what men will or will not do by free will.

source_text: Posita reprobatione non nisi ex antecedente infidelitate et contemtu actuali sive neglectu gratiae Divinae, necesse est ut ponamus tanquam certum fide catholica, omnes infantes, etiam Paganorum, qui moriuntur ante usum liberi arbitrii, electos esse et salvos fore. Ratio in promptu est, Quia tales infidelitatis reatum ex contemptu Evangelii et gratiae Divinae contrahere nondum potuerunt.
english: Grant reprobation only from antecedent unbelief plus actual contempt or neglect of divine grace, and catholic faith would have to treat as certain that every infant who dies before free will—even a pagan’s—is elect and will be saved. Why? Such a child could not yet incur unbelief’s guilt from scorning the Gospel and divine grace.

source_text: At Ecclesia Christi nunquam hoc ausa est statuere: sed e contra, de statu infantium extra Ecclesiam natorum in se considerato pronunciat, Omnes nasci impuros, omnes mori aeternae mortis reos, nisi arcana nobis minime revelata Dei misericordia quibusdam extra ordinem succurrat.
english: But Christ’s church never dared to settle that. On the contrary, of infants born outside the church considered in themselves she pronounces: All are born unclean; all die debtors of eternal death, unless God’s secret mercy—not revealed to us—helps certain ones beyond the ordinary order.

source_text: Hoc argumento ab infantium quorundam electione, quorundam reprobatione, petito Augustinus passim obstruit ora Pelagianorum et Semipelagianorum, qui hoc discrimen electorum et non-electorum ad praevisos actus humanarum voluntatum sive bonos sive malos revocarunt, sicuti et Arminiani jam revocant. Infinitum esset omnia Augustini testimonia in hanc sententiam accumulare. Videte De Praed. Sanct. cap. 12, De bono persev. cap. 11. ubi diserte asserit, Deus parvulis, quibus vult, etiam non volentibus neque currentibus subvenire; quos scilicet ante constitutionem mundi elegit; quibus vero non vult non subvenire, de quibus in sua praedestinatione occulte quidem, sed juste aliud judicavit.
