english: From this argument—election of some infants, reprobation of others—Augustine everywhere stops the mouths of Pelagians and Semipelagians, who traced the divide of elect and non-elect to foreseen acts of human wills, good or evil, as the Arminians now do. It would be endless to pile up all his witnesses on this point. See De praedestinatione sanctorum 12 and De bono perseverantiae 11, where he expressly asserts: God helps the little ones he wills, even when they are not willing or running—those he chose before the foundation of the world; those he does not will, he does not help, of whom in his predestination he judged otherwise, secretly but justly.

source_text: Prosper etiam eandem sententiam ubique amplectitur: De lib. arbitr. ad Ruffin. In infantibus nec praecedens eligitur, nec futura devotio. In Epistola ad Augustinum, Parvuli, inquit, nullas adhuc habentes voluntates, nullas proprias actiones, non sine Dei judicio secernuntur, cum alii per regenerationem inter caelestis regni assumantur heredes, alii sine Baptismo inter mortis perpetuae transeant debitores. Denique ut brevi absolvam, constans fuit totius Ecclesiae catholicae sententia, (reservatis semper Deo arcanis suis) Infantes omnes nasci reos mortis aeternae, multos non regeneratos, et transire debitores mortis aeternae, ut ex Prospero accepimus. Arminii igitur sententia, quae reprobationem nullam concedit nisi ex praevisa reprobatorum infidelitate et perseverantia in eadem, fuit semper totius Ecclesiae orthodoxae calculo rejecta et condemnata.
english: Prosper everywhere holds the same (De libero arbitrio ad Ruffinum): In infants neither what precedes is chosen, nor future devotion. In his letter to Augustine: Little ones, he says, still having no wills and no acts of their own, are not parted without God’s judgment—some through regeneration taken up among heirs of the heavenly kingdom, others without baptism passing among debtors of perpetual death. In short, the whole catholic church’s constant sense (always reserving God’s secrets to him) has been: All infants are born debtors of eternal death; many pass unregenerate as debtors of eternal death—as we have it from Prosper. So Arminius’s view, which grants no reprobation except from the reprobate’s foreseen unbelief and perseverance in it, was always rejected and condemned by the whole orthodox church’s reckoning.

source_text: A natura non-electionis sive reprobationis negativae ita possumus argumentari; haec reprobatio formaliter considerata non est impositio poenae, sed negata appositio indebitae gratiae. Ac tale beneficium negare vel concedere pertinet ad absolutam Dei potestatem, juxta illud Apostoli ex Mose petitum, Miserebor cujus misertus fuero, et commiserabor quem commiseratus fuero, Rom. ix. 15.
english: From the nature of non-election—negative reprobation—we argue thus: formally considered, this reprobation is not laying on a penalty, but refusing to place grace that was never owed. To deny or grant such a benefit belongs to God’s absolute power, after the Apostle’s word from Moses (Rom. ix. 15): I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion.

source_text: Reprobationem autem sive non-electionem non esse poenam; quamvis reprobati semper in poenas incidant sempiternas, patet exemplo Angelorum reprobatorum, sive non-electorum, in quibus nihil erat quod poenam sive supplicium mereretur, et tamen Deus quosdam ex illis elegit, alios non elegit sed praeteriit, fatente Suarez, Bellarmino, Vasquez, ac consentientibus omnibus Theologis.
english: That reprobation or non-election is not itself a penalty—though the reprobate always fall into everlasting pains—is plain from the reprobate or non-elect angels: in them there was nothing that deserved penalty or torment, yet God chose some and passed others by. Suarez, Bellarmine, and Vasquez confess it, and the theologians agree.

source_text: Neque id solum dicunt, Deum absoluta et antecedente voluntate quosdam ex hisce Angelis elegisse, quosdam praeteriisse, sed addunt expresse, solam Dei voluntatem esse causam hujus non-electionis, nulla exspectata causa ex parte non-electorum: Sic Suarez Opusc. pag. 175. Dicunt, Hanc reprobationem factam ante omne peccatum praevisum in ipsis daemonibus: Sic Vasquez in 1. pag. 698, et 701. Docent denique et probant, Hanc reprobationem non pependisse ex praevisione peccati in iisdem: Sic Bellarminus, De grat. et lib. arbitr. lib. 2. cap. 17.
english: They say more: God by absolute antecedent will chose some angels and passed others by—and they add expressly that God’s will alone is the cause of that non-election, with no cause looked for on the non-elect’s side. So Suarez (Opusc. p. 175): this reprobation was made before any sin foreseen in the demons. So Vasquez (in 1, pp. 698, 701). And they teach and prove that this reprobation did not hang on foresight of sin in them—so Bellarmine (De gratia et libero arbitrio 2.17).

source_text: Quod si quis obtendat, In Angelis quidem hanc reprobationem non habuisse rationem supplicii, sed fuisse nudam negationem indebiti beneficii, atque idcirco haud requirere antecedaneam praevisionem rebellionis tanquam causam ejus motivam, in hominibus autem esse veram et proprie dictam poenam, atque eapropter ex praevisione infidelitatis et perseverantiae in eadem necessario arcessendam, id facile refellitur. Nam circa hominem lapsum et peccatis constrictum, atque tandem propter peccata puniendum, decreta divinae voluntatis diversa, et sub diversis respectibus possunt et debent considerari.
english: If someone objects that in angels this reprobation was not torment but bare denial of an unowed benefit—and so needs no antecedent foresight of rebellion as its motive—yet in men it is true punishment properly so called, and must therefore be fetched from foresight of unbelief and perseverance in it: that is easily answered. About fallen man, bound in sins and at last to be punished for them, the decrees of the divine will are diverse and must be weighed under diverse respects.

source_text: Quod Deus ab omni aeternitate decreverit Judam aeterna morte punire, id decretum respicit finalem Judae in peccatis suis obdurationem, tanquam causam ejusdem supplicii-decreti motivam et meritoriam: Sed quod Deus ab omni aeternitate decreverit non liberare Judam e statu miseriae et peccati per specialem misericordiam, sicuti decrevit liberare Paulum et Petrum; quod decreverit non emollire cor Judae, sed permittere ut obduresceret finaliter in impoenitentia et infidelitate sua—hoc decretum non potest referri ad praevisam Judae infidelitatem, tanquam causam motivam, quia nullum malum Deo praevidetur tanquam certo et absolute futurum nisi praemisso et praesupposito decreto Dei de permissione ejusdem.
english: That God from eternity decreed to punish Judas with everlasting death looks to Judas’s final hardness in his sins as that torment-decree’s motive and meritorious cause. But that from eternity he decreed not to free Judas from misery and sin by special mercy—as he decreed to free Paul and Peter—and not to soften Judas’s heart, but to permit final hardening in impenitence and unbelief: that decree cannot be referred to Judas’s foreseen unbelief as its motive, because no evil is foreseen to God as certainly and absolutely future unless his decree to permit it is already premised and presupposed.

source_text: At hoc ipsum decretum quo Deus statuit apud se velle permittere, ut quis obdurescat et extremum diem claudat in sua impoenitentia et infidelitate, est ipsissimum reprobationis decretum. Frustra igitur hac in re ad praevisam infidelitatem refertur voluntas Dei non praeparantis huic aut illi singulari personae gratiam illam quae cor emollit, quae fidem, resipiscentiam, et perseverantiam gignit, cum hic necessario confugiendum sit ad illud Apostoli, Deus cujus vult miseretur, et quem vult indurat, Rom. ix. 18.
english: But the very decree by which God settles with himself to permit someone to harden and close his last day in impenitence and unbelief is reprobation’s own decree. So it is futile here to refer to foreseen unbelief God’s will not to prepare for this or that singular person the grace that softens the heart and begets faith, repentance, and perseverance—for here one must flee to the Apostle (Rom. ix. 18): God has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens.

source_text: Si post administratam sufficientem gratiam electio et reprobatio hominum oriretur ex praevisa horum fide, illorum infidelitate, tum discretio electorum et reprobatorum inciperet, non per aliquod uni praeparatum et donatum quod non est praeparatum et donatum alteri, sed per aliquem actum auxilio gratiae indifferenter administratae ab uno praestitum, ab altero non praestitum. At hoc nullo modo admittendum est, nisi gloriam electionis nostrae a pura Dei misericordia ad liberi arbitrii laudem velimus transferre.
english: If after sufficient grace is administered, men’s election and reprobation arose from foresight of these men’s faith and those men’s unbelief, then the divide of elect and reprobate would begin not by something prepared and given to one and not to the other, but by an act one performs and another does not under help from grace given indifferently. That must not be admitted unless we mean to shift the glory of our election from God’s pure mercy to the praise of free will.

source_text: De consequentia dubitari non potest, quia ex sententia adversariorum, administrata tam Judae quam Petro gratia sufficiente ad credendum et resipiscendum, bonus usus liberi arbitrii amplectentis hanc gratiam sufficientem utrique communiter oblatam posuit Petrum in numero credentium et electorum, et malus usus liberi arbitrii repellentis eandem arcuit Judam a numero credentium et electorum. Sed hoc e diametro adversatur sententiae illi Paulinae 1 Cor. iv. 7, Quis te discernit? quid habes quod non acceperis? quod si accepisti, quid gloriaris ut qui non acceperis?
english: The consequence cannot be doubted. On the adversaries’ view, with sufficient grace to believe and repent administered to Judas and Peter alike, free will’s good use embracing that common offer put Peter among believers and elect, and free will’s bad use thrusting it back shut Judas out. That stands diametrically against Paul’s word (1 Cor. iv. 7): Who makes you to differ? What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why boast as though you did not?

source_text: Si hoc in gratia gratis data (ut Schola loquitur) verum sit, tum multo magis in gratia gratum faciente, et maxime omnium in prima illa gratia electionis ad vitam, quae fons est et quasi scaturigo beneficiorum omnium ad salutem conferentium.
english: If that holds of gratia gratis data, as the School calls it, it holds much more of the grace that makes acceptable—and most of all of that first grace of election to life, the fountain and spring of every benefit that serves salvation.

source_text: Sed audiamus Augustinum Pauli vestigiis et doctrinae inhaerentem: De praedest. sanct. cap. 5. Numquid, inquit, per haec dona, quae omnibus communia sunt hominibus, discernuntur homines ab hominibus? Paulo post, Gratia quae bonos discernit a malis, non communis est et bonis et malis. Adhuc planius; Deus te discernit ab alio, cui non donavit, quod donavit tibi.
english: Hear Augustine keeping Paul’s steps and teaching (De praedestinatione sanctorum 5): Are men set apart from men by gifts common to all? A little later: The grace that sets the good apart from the evil is not common to both. Still plainer: God sets you apart from another, to whom he has not given what he gave you.

source_text: Ex quibus omnibus manifestum est, Discrimen electorum et non-electorum, credentium et non-credentium, perseverantium et non-perseverantium oriri non ex antecedaneis et discretis humanarum voluntatum circa gratiam communiter oblatam operationibus, sed ex antecedaneis et diversis Dei decretis et operationibus, in decernendo, praeparando et donando uni quod non decrevit, neque praeparavit neque donavit alteri. Intoleranda est igitur Arminii sententia, quae ad Deum refert communem quandam gratiae praeparationem et oblationem, ad singulorum autem hominum liberum arbitrium hac communi gratia excitatum refert ipsam discriminationem credentium et non-credentium, electorum et non-electorum.
english: From all this it is plain: the divide of elect and non-elect, believers and unbelievers, those who persevere and those who do not, does not arise from prior, distinct human-will operations about commonly offered grace, but from God’s prior, diverse decrees and workings—decreeing, preparing, and giving to one what he neither decreed nor prepared nor gave to the other. So Arminius’s view is intolerable: it credits God with a common preparation and offer of grace, but credits each person’s free will, stirred by that common grace, with the very discrimination of believers and unbelievers, elect and non-elect.

source_text: Quod attinet ad vitam aeternam, ille antecedenter ad praevisam suam infidelitatem praeteritus, non-electus, sive reprobatus consideratur, cui Deus ab aeterno non destinavit, praeparavit, ac cui in tempore non donavit efficacia media ad fidem et perseverantiam ingenerandam, vitamque aeternam infallibiliter obtinendam: At multis (sicut eventus ipse declarat) Deus nec destinavit, nec praeparavit, nec donavit hanc gratiam efficacem. Ergo, multi sunt praeteriti sive non-electi antecedenter ad praevisam suam infidelitatem et contumaciam finalem in eadem. De Minore nulla potest esse quaestio: Majorem igitur explicemus et confirmemus.
english: As for everlasting life: the one passed by, non-elect, or reprobate before foresight of his unbelief is the one to whom God from eternity neither destined nor prepared, and in time did not give, efficacious means to beget faith and perseverance and obtain everlasting life infallibly. But to many—as the event itself shows—God neither destined nor prepared nor gave that efficacious grace. Therefore many are passed by or non-elect before foresight of their unbelief and final stubbornness in it. The Minor is beyond dispute; so let us open and confirm the Major.

source_text: Illud imprimis sumo; Deum nosse infinitos modos quibus cor cujuscunque hominis flectere possit ad libere poenitendum, credendum, et perseverandum. Qui hoc negat, negat Dei omnipotentiam, negat Dei supra voluntates humanas absolutum dominium, contra illud Solomonis, Cor regis in manu Domini; quocunque voluerit inclinavit illud, Prov. xxi. 1. Cui subscribit Augustinus, De corrept. et gratia, cap. 14. De ipsis hominum voluntatibus facit quod vult, et quando vult, habens humanorum cordium quo vult inclinandorum omnipotentissimam potestatem.
english: First I take this: God knows infinite ways to bend any man’s heart to repent, believe, and persevere freely. Who denies it denies God’s omnipotence and his absolute lordship over human wills—against Solomon (Prov. xxi. 1): The king’s heart is in the Lord’s hand; he turns it wherever he wills. Augustine subscribes (De correptione et gratia 14): Of men’s very wills he does what he wills, when he wills, holding most omnipotent power to incline human hearts wherever he wills.

source_text: Hisce addo, Illum qui novit et potuit adhibere tam Judae quam Petro ea media, quibus ad fidem et obedientiam flecteretur, et in fide et obedientia ad extremum usque conservaretur, atque haec media Petro ab aeterno destinavit et donavit, Judae nec destinavit nec donavit, unum eorum elegisse ad salutem, alterum praeteriisse, id est, reprobasse. Hoc illud est quod Ambrosius celebri illo dicto innuabat, Deus quos dignatur vocat, et quem vult religiosum facit. Quae verba accurate expenduntur ab Augustino, De grat. Christi contra Pelag. et Caelest. lib. 1. cap. 46.
english: Add this: he who knew and could apply to Judas as to Peter the means to bend him to faith and obedience and keep him in them to the end, yet from eternity destined and gave those means to Peter and neither destined nor gave them to Judas, elected one to salvation and passed the other by—that is, reprobated him. That is what Ambrose meant in the famous saying: God calls whom he deigns, and makes religious whom he wills—words Augustine weighs carefully (De gratia Christi contra Pelagium et Caelestium 1.46).

source_text: Hisce consonat illud Basilii, in oratione quadam quae refertur a Petro Diacono, lib. De incarn. et grat. cap. 8. Dona, Domine, virtutem ac tutamentum. Malos, quos sumis, bonos facito; bonos in bonitate conservato: omnia enim potes, et non est qui contradicat tibi. Cum enim volueris, salvas, et non est qui resistat tibi. Uterque a Propheta hoc didicit, qui de voluntate divina ita nos instituit, Isa. xlvi. 10 et 11. Juravit Dominus exercituum, Si non ut putavi ita erit, et quomodo mente tractavi ita eveniet. Dominus exercituum decrevit, et quis poterit infirmare? Ex hisce omnibus infero, quod eos qui non vocantur vocatione efficaci, et qui religiosi non efficiuntur, qui non in fide et sancta obedientia conservantur; uno verbo, qui reapse non salvantur, defuisse Deo illam voluntatem et infrustrabilem eos convertendi, religiosos et fideles efficiendi, in fide conservandi, atque tandem de facto salvandi.
english: Basil agrees, in an oration Peter the Deacon reports (De incarnatione et gratia 8): Give, Lord, strength and safeguard. Make good the evil you take; keep the good in goodness—for you can do all things, and none contradicts you. When you will, you save, and none resists you. Both learned it from the Prophet on the divine will (Isa. xlvi. 10–11): The Lord of hosts has sworn: It shall be as I thought; as I planned in mind, so it shall happen. The Lord of hosts has decreed—and who can weaken it? From all this I infer: for those not called with an efficacious call, not made religious, not kept in faith and holy obedience—in a word, not actually saved—God lacked that unfrustrable will to convert them, make them religious and faithful, keep them in faith, and at last save them in fact.

source_text: sicut e contra, quoad eos qui religiosi, fideles, perseverantes efficiuntur, et ad vitam aeternam perducuntur, colligere possumus ab aeterno adfuisse Deo illam voluntatem, quae haec omnia in illis efficaciter operaretur. Haec autem voluntas salvandi, et noluntas (si ita loqui liceat) electionem aliquorum et praeteritionem aliorum manifeste evincit. Denique, sicut ineptum esset obtendere hanc specialem voluntatem de fide, perseverantia et salute Petri operanda ex praevisa ejusdem Petri fide et perseverantia profluxisse, ita non minus falsum et ineptum est asserere, hanc negatam voluntatem efficiendi fidem, poenitentiam et perseverantiam in Juda, aut quolibet reprobato, ex praevisa ejusdem infidelitate, impoenitentia et finali gratiae Divinae contemptu originem habuisse.
english: Conversely, of those made religious, faithful, persevering, and led to everlasting life, we may gather that from eternity God had that will which would efficaciously work all this in them. That will to save—and non-will, if one may so speak—plainly proves election of some and preterition of others. Finally: as it would be inept to claim that the special will to work faith, perseverance, and salvation in Peter flowed from foresight of Peter’s faith and perseverance, so it is no less false and inept to assert that the denied will to effect faith, repentance, and perseverance in Judas or any reprobate arose from foresight of his unbelief, impenitence, and final contempt of divine grace.

source_text: Nullius momenti est quod huic argumento respondetur a Corvino, Contra Tilen. pag. 148. Non sequitur, inquit, Deus huic non dat fidem aut perseverantiam aut salutem, Ergo non voluit ei dare fidem, perseverantiam aut salutem: sed hoc potius; Deus non vult dare praedicta dona nisi parvulis, laborantibus et voluntatem Patris facientibus. Ergo huic data haec dona non fuerunt, quia talis non fuit, culpa scilicet sua.
english: Corvinus’s reply (Contra Tilenum, p. 148) is of no weight. It does not follow, he says, that because God does not give this man faith, perseverance, or salvation, therefore he never willed to give them—but rather this: God wills those gifts only to the little, to those who labor and do the Father’s will. So this man did not receive them because he was not such—namely by his own fault.

source_text: Respondeo, Corvinum immemorem plane esse qua de re disputetur. Non enim quaestio est de voluntate Dei sub qualibet notione, sed de voluntate Dei praedestinantis aliquid facere aut non facere. Est autem optima et firmissima consequentia; Deus dedit fidem, perseverantiam, et vitam aeternam Petro, Ergo voluntate praedestinante ab aeterno voluit illi dare fidem, perseverantiam et vitam aeternam. Et e contra non minus firma est illa: Deus non dedit Judae fidem, perseverantiam et vitam aeternam: Ergo illum praeteriit, non praedestinavit, reprobavit, tantis bonis afficere noluit.
english: I answer: Corvinus has plainly forgotten what is under dispute. The question is not God’s will under any notion, but God’s will as predestinating to do or not do. This consequence is best and firmest: God gave Peter faith, perseverance, and everlasting life; therefore by predestinating will from eternity he willed to give him those goods. No less firm the reverse: God did not give Judas faith, perseverance, and everlasting life; therefore he passed him by, did not predestine him, reprobated him, and would not affect him with such great goods.

source_text: Quod autem subjungit Corvinus, id solum sequi, Deum non velle dare praedicta bona nisi parvulis et obedientibus, atque idcirco non fuisse data Judae, quia sua culpa talis non fuit; primo non valet; quia eadem quaestio adhuc manet de hac parvitate et obedientia, quae mota fuit de fide et salute. Quaero enim cur Deus non dederit hanc parvitatem et obedientiam Judae quam dedit Petro. Si voluisset pariter dare utrique, in utroque pariter exstitisset. Nam Deo volenti bonam humilitatis aut parvitatis qualitatem indere humanae voluntati, nullum resistit hominis arbitrium: Tali equidem voluntati non resistitur, quia velle non resistere in ipso homine operatur: Non enim ultra resistit voluntas cui velle resistere sublatum est.
english: What Corvinus adds—that it only follows God wills those goods to the little and obedient, so Judas lacked them by his own fault—fails first: the same question returns about that littleness and obedience that was asked about faith and salvation. Why did God not give Judas the littleness and obedience he gave Peter? Had he willed to give alike to both, it would have stood alike in both. When God wills to plant humility or littleness in the human will, no free will resists—such a will is not resisted, because willing not to resist is worked in the man himself; the will resists no further once willing to resist is taken away.

source_text: Dein, qui haec dona Dei suspendunt ex parvitate praeeunte, nisi fateantur hanc ipsam parvitatem esse speciale donum Dei, in Pelagianismum incidunt, et incurrunt in Canonem 6. Concilii Arausicani: Si autem fateantur, perinde est concedere Deum praeparasse et donasse hanc parvitatem, unde fides et salus dependet, uni et non alteri, atque praeparasse et donasse ipsam fidem et salutem; quod nihil aliud est, quam unum elegisse, alterum reprobasse.
english: Next: those who hang these gifts on prior littleness, unless they admit that littleness itself is God’s special gift, fall into Pelagianism and hit Orange canon 6. If they do admit it, that is the same as granting God prepared and gave that littleness—on which faith and salvation hang—to one and not the other, and prepared and gave faith and salvation themselves; which is nothing other than electing one and reprobating the other.

source_text: Denique, quod dicit Corvinus, reprobis non dari gratiam salutiferam, quia sua culpa tales non sunt, quales Deus praerequirit, hoc ipsum arguit eos fuisse antecedenter rejectos sive praeteritos: Nam Deus decrevit omnes electos tales efficere, quales ad capessendum gratiam et gloriam ipse solet praerequirere, Coloss. i. 12. Quos ergo tales non effecit, eos non elegit; et quia non datur medium inter electionem et reprobationem, eosdem reprobavit. Post tot anfractus et gyros huc itaque redeamus oportet, ut quibus gratia fidei, poenitentiae et perseverantiae data non fuerit, eos in ordinatione ad vitam aeternam praeteritos agnoscamus; sicut e contra, eos quibus haec fuerunt praeparata et donata, electos confiteamur. Atque ut quidam electi fuerunt misericorditer ad haec bona ante praevisionem eorundem ut in illis existentium, ita quidam praeteriti fuerunt, et ad talia accipienda haud praedestinati, antequam praeviderentur ut talibus bonis finaliter carentes.
english: Finally Corvinus says saving grace is not given to the reprobate because by their fault they are not what God prerequires—and that itself proves they were antecedently rejected or passed by. For God has decreed to make all the elect such as he is wont to prerequire for laying hold of grace and glory (Col. i. 12). Those he has not made such, he has not elected; and since there is no middle between election and reprobation, he has reprobated them. After so many twists we must come back here: those not given the grace of faith, repentance, and perseverance we acknowledge as passed by in the ordination to everlasting life; those for whom these were prepared and given we confess as elect. And as some were mercifully elected to these goods before foresight of them as existing in them, so some were passed by and not predestined to receive such things before they were foreseen as finally lacking them.

source_text: Ultimum nostrum argumentum jam proponemus, in quo conabimur ostendere hanc sententiam de praedestinatione quorundam, et praeteritione aliorum ex mero voluntatis Divinae beneplacito, absque omni praecedaneo respectu ad oppositos hominum actus, sive bonos sive malos, non fuisse singularem quandam Augustini aut discipulorum ejus opinionem, sed receptam et probatam ab illis Conciliis quae contra Pelagium et Semipelagianos fuerunt celebrata. Hoc idcirco faciendum putavimus, quia Arminius, Corvinus, reliquique novatores confidenter asserunt, doctrinam hanc nostram in nullo Concilio fuisse approbatam, ne quidem in iis quae contra Pelagium fuere habita. Huic tamen argumento quaedam sunt a nobis necessario praemittenda.
english: We now propose our last argument: to show that this teaching—the predestination of some and preterition of others from the mere good pleasure of the divine will, with no prior regard to opposite human acts, good or evil—was not some private opinion of Augustine or his disciples, but received and approved by the councils held against Pelagius and the Semipelagians. We do this because Arminius, Corvinus, and the other innovators boldly claim our doctrine was approved in no council—not even those against Pelagius. Yet certain premises must first be laid down.

source_text: Primo, fatemur, Concilia quae celebrata fuerunt contra Pelagium et Semipelagianos ipsius Augustini temporibus, aut saeculo ab obitu ejus proximo, qualia fuerunt Diospolitanum, Milevitanum, Carthaginense, Arausicanum, aliaque nonnulla, non expresse, directe et particulariter sanxisse doctrinam de absoluta praedestinatione, aut condemnasse opinionem contrariam de electione et reprobatione ex praevisione diversorum actuum in hominibus. Illud tamen affirmamus, in hisce Conciliis multa fuisse definita quae stare non possunt absoluta et gratuita praedestinatione eversa, aut posita illa conditionata electione et praeteritione quam Faustus, et post illum alii nonnulli, ac tandem Arminius excolendam et defendendam susceperunt. Huc accedit, Fausti libros in quibus conditionatam illam electionem operose stabilire conatur, et absolutam explodere, damnatos fuisse ab antiqua Ecclesia, ut ex Gratiano liquet, Distinct. 15. Decretum extat a Tom. Conciliorum, et sancitum fuit a Gelasio in Synodo septuaginta Episcoporum. Hormisda etiam de Fausti libro consultus respondet, Doctrinam Catholicam ex Augustino et Prospero, non item e Fausto, disci oportere.
english: First we confess: the councils against Pelagius and the Semipelagians in Augustine’s time or the age just after his death—Diospolis, Milevis, Carthage, Orange, and others—did not expressly, directly, and particularly sanction absolute predestination or condemn foresight-election and reprobation. Yet we affirm that much defined in those councils cannot stand if absolute gratuitous predestination is overturned, or if that conditioned election and preterition is set up which Faustus, then others, and at last Arminius undertook to cultivate and defend. Add that Faustus’s books, which labor to fix conditioned election and explode the absolute, were condemned by the ancient church—clear from Gratian, Distinctio 15; the decree stands in the councils’ Tomus, sanctioned by Gelasius in a synod of seventy bishops. Hormisdas, asked about Faustus’s book, answers that catholic doctrine should be learned from Augustine and Prosper, not from Faustus.

source_text: Atque inter caetera vel praecipue spectasse doctrinam hanc de conditionata praedestinatione, inde probabile est: quod Petrus Diaconus, aliique orthodoxi ex Oriente Romam missi, hoc nomine potissimum Fausti libros anathematizandos censuerunt, quod contra praedestinationis sententiam scripti essent, De incarn. et grat. cap. ultimo. Secundo dicimus, Nos et posse et debere colligere quae fuerit Orthodoxorum de praedestinatione sententia ex illis quae de Gratia contra Pelagianos et Pelagianorum reliquias statuerunt. Nam ut inquit Augustinus, De praedest. sanctor. cap. 10, inter gratiam et praedestinationem hoc tantum interest, quod praedestinatio sit gratiae praeparatio, gratia vero ipsa donatio. Si quis igitur doceat gratiam Christi salutiferam ex absoluta Dei voluntate dependere, et minime dari hominibus aut negari pro diversis illorum operationibus, is de praedestinatione et praeteritione, si sibi constare velit, idem statuat est necesse.
english: That conditioned predestination was chiefly in view is likely from this: Peter the Deacon and other eastern orthodox sent to Rome judged Faustus’s books especially to be anathematized because they were written against the sentence of predestination (De incarnatione et gratia, last chapter). Second: we can and must gather the Orthodox view of predestination from what they settled on Grace against the Pelagians and their remnants. For as Augustine says (De praedestinatione sanctorum 10), between grace and predestination this alone differs: predestination is grace’s preparation; grace itself is the gift. So anyone who teaches that Christ’s saving grace hangs on God’s absolute will, and is not given or denied according to men’s diverse operations, must—if he would be consistent—hold the same of predestination and preterition.

limits: Sampling and structural checks do not prove whole-work fidelity or completeness.
